Chilhuacle Negro is one of the most important and irreplaceable chiles in Oaxacan cuisine — the primary chile in mole negro, one of the canonical seven moles of Oaxaca and arguably the most complex mole sauce in Mexican gastronomy. The fresh chile is a medium-large (2–3 inch wide, 3–5 inch long), slightly squat, triangular to shoulder-shaped fruit with thick, dark green walls that transitions through red to a very deep reddish-black at full maturity — the darkened color indicating the presence of additional flavor compounds that develop in the fully mature and dried state. The dried chilhuacle negro is unique among Mexican dried chiles for its distinctive flavor: deeply complex, somewhat fruity, mildly earthy with a chocolate-like depth, moderately hot (2,500–5,000 Scoville units), and with a characteristic thick skin that retains more texture when rehydrated than thinner-skinned chiles. Only three types of chilhuacle exist: negro (black), rojo (red), and amarillo (yellow) — all grown in the Cañada region of the northern Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, particularly around the town of Huajuapan de León and the Mixteca Alta, where the specific combination of altitude, temperature, and local soil conditions produces chiles with flavor characteristics impossible to replicate elsewhere. A critical ingredient for cooks interested in authentic Oaxacan cuisine.

common_name: Chilhuacle Rojo Pepper (Red Chilhuacle, Oaxacan Red Chile)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes; chilhuacle rojo matures slightly earlier than negro, turning vivid bright red at full maturity; it is the key ingredient in Oaxacan mole coloradito and enchiladas coloradas — a brighter, somewhat fruitier dried chile than the negro with moderate heat.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes in fertile, well-drained soil; harvest at full red maturity for drying; dry on screens in a single layer in a warm, airy location until leathery-crisp; store dried chiles in airtight containers away from light. Chilhuacle Rojo is the red form of the chilhuacle chile, one of the three varieties grown specifically in the Cañada district of Oaxaca state in Mexico. While the chilhuacle negro (black) is the defining ingredient of mole negro, the chilhuacle rojo plays the lead role in Oaxacan mole coloradito — a complex red mole that, while less dark and mysterious than mole negro, is equally complex and represents one of the pillars of Oaxacan cooking. The dried rojo chile is a vivid brick-red to deep red color with moderately thick walls that rehydrate to a smooth, velvety texture. The flavor is distinctively fruity and somewhat tart-sweet, with moderate heat (3,000–6,000 Scoville units), and a characteristic sweetness that distinguishes it from the guajillo and other red dried chiles with which it is sometimes confused. The shoulder-shaped, somewhat flattened form (wider near the stem, tapering to the tip) is characteristic of all three chilhuacle varieties and distinguishes them from other Oaxacan chiles like the negro or costeño. In Mexican markets, chilhuacle rojo is sometimes substituted with a blend of ancho and guajillo chiles, but genuine chilhuacle rojo has a unique flavor profile that the blend does not replicate. Increasingly available from specialty seed companies as interest in authentic regional Mexican cuisine grows among American gardeners and home cooks.

common_name: Chilly Chili Pepper (Heatless Kid-Friendly Ornamental Pepper)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55°F; Chilly Chili is bred specifically to lack capsaicin, the compound responsible for pepper heat, making it safe to grow around children who may be tempted to pick and taste the colorful fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off, and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Chilly Chili won an All-America Selections award as the first heatless ornamental pepper, bred to eliminate capsaicin entirely so its abundant small, slender, upright fruit — which ripens through a colorful progression of purple, yellow, orange, and red, often several colors present on the plant at once — can be safely tasted by curious children without any burning heat. Its compact, tidy habit and long-lasting, weather-resistant fruit display make it an excellent choice for children's gardens, containers, and edging where the bright, changing fruit color provides months of interest from summer through fall. Because the fruit holds its color and shape well after ripening, plants often remain colorful and attractive right up until frost.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; germination is slow and erratic, sometimes taking up to 6 weeks — bottom heat at 80°F and light scarification improve rates. Transplant after all frost danger passes in full sun; in zones 8b–11 established plants may re-sprout perennially from the base if mulched heavily.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; the chiltepin is the only wild chile pepper native to the United States, growing in rocky canyon bottoms and shaded washes from Texas through Arizona and south into Mexico. The tiny round to oval fruits — barely the size of a pea — ripen from green to vivid red and pack an intense, clean heat (50,000–100,000 Scoville) that fades quickly unlike cultivated chiles. Birds disperse the seeds and are unaffected by capsaicin, making this a superb wildlife plant as well as a culinary one. In mild winter zones (8b+) plants are truly perennial and can reach shrub size over several seasons; in colder climates grow as an annual started indoors. Harvest fruits as they redden or allow birds to disperse naturally for a self-seeding colony.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil timed for a fall harvest; thin plants to their full spacing early so uniform heads can develop.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil timed for a fall harvest, since this fast-growing hybrid is bred for slow bolting and reliably forms dense, barrel-shaped heads even under variable weather. Thin plants to their full spacing early so uniform, well-wrapped heads can develop without stress cracking. The crisp, mildly sweet leaves are well suited to fresh salads, quick stir-fries, and kimchi, and mature heads store well in a cold, humid location for several weeks.

common_name: China Rose Radish (Rose China Winter Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since this radish is slower to mature and stores better than quick spring types.
directions: Sow seeds directly a half-inch deep and thin seedlings to a few inches apart, since crowded roots stay thin and pithy. Unlike fast-maturing spring radishes, this nineteenth-century heirloom is grown as a fall crop and left in the ground longer, forming a smooth, tapered root five to six inches long with rose-pink skin and crisp white flesh. Its flavor is notably more pungent than spring salad radishes, and its roots hold their quality in the ground or in cold storage well into winter, making it a traditional keeper variety for root cellars. Cool fall temperatures improve both texture and flavor, so avoid sowing it for a hot-weather harvest.

plant_note: Grown indoors year-round in a jar or tray; not sown in garden soil.
directions: Rose-colored radish sprouts deliver a spicy bite popular in Chinese and Japanese cooking, from raw salads to sushi. Soak seed briefly, then drain and spread in a sprouting jar or tray out of direct sun. Rinse and drain two to three times daily until the sprouts stand an inch or two tall with open leaves. Harvest in four to six days and refrigerate, using within a week for the freshest peppery flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; this short, early-maturing bush bean suits short-season gardens and can also be fall-sown in mild climates.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the danger of frost; the low, compact bushes need no support and mature quickly compared with most dry beans. China Yellow, also called the Sulphur Bean, is a New England heirloom documented before 1870, valued for its small, plump, pale sulphur-yellow seeds that cook down quickly to a soft, creamy consistency ideal for stewing and baking. Despite the name, it has no connection to China; the name simply describes its distinctive pale yellow color. Let pods dry fully on the plant, then thresh and store the beans in an airtight container.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep and 6 inches apart in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early spring; Chinese artichoke spreads readily by tuber and can be difficult to eradicate once established — plant in a contained bed.
directions: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese artichoke produces the most visually distinctive tubers in the vegetable garden — small (1–2 inch), cream-white, segmented underground stems that resemble tiny white caterpillars or coiled seashells. Known in French cuisine as 'crosnes' (from the French town where they were introduced in the late 19th century), they have a crisp, sweet, delicate flavor similar to water chestnuts, used raw in salads, lightly stir-fried, or pickled. The plant is in the mint family and spreads by tubers — contain it or plan for its spread. Harvest in fall after frost kills the tops, when the tubers are at their crisp best. The tubers discolor quickly after harvesting; use immediately. Tolerates partial shade, making it useful in a shaded food garden where few vegetables thrive.

plant_note: In zone 9 direct sow September through November for a fall and winter harvest, or February through March for a brief spring crop before heat causes bolting. Chinese broccoli tolerates light frost but bolts quickly in temperatures above 75°F; the fall planting window is the primary season for the Gulf Coast.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun during the cool season; Chinese broccoli is more heat-tolerant than heading broccoli but still performs best between 50–70°F. Harvest the central flower head and 6–8 inches of stem just as the first buds show color but before flowers open; side shoots continue to develop for weeks of successive harvest. The stems are sweet and tender when young — the entire harvested shoot including leaves and stem is eaten, typically stir-fried with oyster sauce in Cantonese cuisine. Mulch to retain moisture and keep roots cool; consistent watering prevents the stems from becoming fibrous.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant; grows in spring and fall and tolerates some heat.
directions: Also called gai lan, this Asian green offers tender flowering stems, juicy stalks, and leaves with a sweet, slightly bitter flavor. Sow seed directly half an inch deep and thin to six to ten inches apart. It is more heat tolerant than regular broccoli, so it can be sown across a longer season. Harvest the whole plant or cut the main stem to encourage tender side shoots before the flower buds fully open.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant; an aromatic thin-stalked heirloom celery for cooking.
directions: Start the tiny seeds indoors, pressing them into the surface since they need light to germinate, and keep them evenly moist. Transplant into rich, damp soil and grow through the cooler parts of the season. This variety forms slender, hollow, intensely aromatic stalks used more as a seasoning than a raw snack, so cut stalks as needed for stir-fries and soups.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 3–4 weeks before last frost as plants can handle light frost.
directions: Sow tiny seeds on the surface of moist starting mix and press lightly without covering; seeds need light to germinate and are very slow — allow 2–3 weeks. Chinese celery produces slender, hollow stems and abundant leaves with intense celery flavor far more pungent than Western stalk celery; it is used primarily as an herb and flavoring rather than eaten in large quantities raw. Transplant into moisture-retentive, fertile soil and keep evenly moist throughout the season, as drought causes bitterness and premature bolting. Harvest outer stalks continuously once plants are established; the leaves are the most intensely flavored part.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost date; transplant after soil warms to 65°F and all frost danger has passed. Chinese eggplant requires a longer growing season than peppers so do not delay starting seeds indoors.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F soil temperature 8–10 weeks before last frost, then transplant into warm, deeply tilled, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after nighttime temperatures stay above 55°F; Chinese eggplant varieties produce long, slender, lavender to deep purple fruits that are less bitter, have thinner skin, and contain fewer seeds than standard Italian-type eggplants, making them ideal for stir-frying, grilling, and steaming. Plants are highly productive in hot, humid climates and are better adapted to the Gulf South than globe types. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch heavily to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature. Support plants with stakes if fruit load causes stem breakage.

common_name: Chinese Five-Color Pepper (Multicolor Ornamental Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay above 55°F.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Chinese Five-Color is a compact ornamental hot pepper prized for producing small, upward-facing fruit in purple, cream, yellow, orange, and red all at once on the same plant, since individual peppers ripen through this color sequence at slightly different rates, creating a constantly shifting, jewel-like display against the plant's purple-tinged green foliage and purple flowers. The small, tapered fruit carries real heat in the cayenne range and is fully edible, useful in hot sauces or pickling, though most growers treat the plant primarily as a container or bedding ornamental. The compact, well-branched habit needs no staking and performs equally well in the ground or in a decorative pot on a sunny patio; harvest fruit at any color stage once past the initial pale coloring.

common_name: Chinese Flowering Kale (Yod Fah, Flowering Gai Lan)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or, better, in fall for a winter crop in mild climates, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese flowering kale is grown specifically to flower and is intentionally allowed to bolt for harvest, unlike most brassicas.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and thin seedlings to allow strong flowering stalks to develop. Known in Thai and Southeast Asian markets as yod fah ('flower tip'), Chinese flowering kale is a gai lan (Chinese broccoli) type grown specifically for its tender, slightly sweet flowering stems, harvested with the small buds still tightly closed or just beginning to open, rather than for leaves or heads as with most brassicas. Stems, leaves, and unopened flower buds are all edible with a mild, cabbage-broccoli flavor and pleasant crunch, commonly stir-fried with garlic and oyster sauce. Harvest the main flowering stalk when buds are plump but unopened, which encourages side shoots to develop for a continued harvest over several weeks; plants that are allowed to fully flower and set seed turn tough and bitter.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese mallow (dong kui zi) is a major leafy vegetable in Chinese traditional cuisine and medicine — the large, round, mallow-family leaves are eaten fresh in salads or cooked like spinach, and the clusters of round, button-like seeds (malva nuts) are used medicinally in Traditional Chinese Medicine.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; harvest young leaves frequently to promote continuous leaf production; very easy and fast-growing. Malva verticillata (Chinese mallow, cluster mallow, or dong kui) is a tall, fast-growing cool-season annual or biennial in the mallow family (Malvaceae) — widely grown as a vegetable and medicinal plant in China, Korea, and Japan, but largely unknown in Western vegetable gardens despite being exceptionally easy to grow. The plant produces large, round, slightly lobed, bright-green leaves arranged in whorls up tall stems, with tiny, pale-pink to white flowers clustered tightly in the leaf axils (verticillate = whorled) — the common name 'cluster mallow' refers to this tight clustering of flowers. The young leaves are mild, slightly mucilaginous (like okra, a mallow family relative), tender, and nutritious — eaten raw in salads when small, or cooked like spinach, added to soups, or stir-fried. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the seeds (dong kui zi — 'mallow seeds') are used as a urinary tonic and to promote milk flow in nursing mothers. The plant is exceptionally productive and self-sows readily; in mild climates it functions as a perennial, re-growing from the base. The curly-leafed form (var. crispa) is especially popular as a leaf vegetable.

plant_note: Plant corms or divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; Chinese taro is one of the most cold-hardy alocasias and one of the very few that grows well in true shade conditions.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained to moist soil in partial to full shade in zones 8–11; Chinese taro is the most cold-hardy member of Alocasia and one of the few genuinely shade-tolerant large-leaved tropical plants, making it extraordinarily valuable for filling shaded spaces in zone 8–11 gardens with bold, architectural foliage. The waxy, medium-green, upright-pointing leaves on sturdy petioles have a distinctive hooded appearance (cucullata means 'hooded' in Latin). In Buddhist traditions across Southeast Asia, this plant is kept in temple gardens as a sacred plant and is associated with good fortune. In zone 9, it grows as a reliable outdoor perennial in shade, dying back in hard freezes and re-emerging from the corm in spring. The corms are technically edible after thorough cooking (raw alocasia contains calcium oxalate crystals), but this species is primarily ornamental rather than a food crop.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy soil in full sun; Chinese toon grows very rapidly in moist, fertile conditions and can be kept as a large shrub by hard pruning (coppicing), which stimulates abundant new shoot production — the young shoots are the edible harvest. Coppice annually in late winter for a continuous supply of young, tender edible shoots.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy soil in full sun; Chinese toon is one of the most unusual food plants in world horticulture — a large, fast-growing deciduous tree whose young leaves and shoot tips are a prized traditional vegetable in Chinese cuisine ('xiang chun' in Mandarin), with a distinctive, complex, slightly onion-garlicky, savory, slightly resinous flavor unlike any other leaf vegetable. The young spring shoots — harvested when the leaves are emerging, brilliantly colored in red-bronze to burgundy — are stir-fried, used in tofu dishes, scrambled eggs, and pancakes, or eaten raw as a garnish. The harvest window is narrow (only the youngest, most tender growth is palatable; older leaves become tough and more bitter). Coppicing the tree in late winter each year keeps it shrub-sized (4–8 feet) and maximizes the production of young, tender shoots. One of the very few trees in the world cultivated specifically for its edible leaves. An extraordinary permaculture and forest garden plant for zones 6–9.

plant_note: Plant small brown corms 2 inches deep in pots of wet soil or directly in a pond or container with standing water 2–4 inches deep; transplant container-started plants outdoors after the last frost.
directions: Plant corms in large containers or pond margins filled with fertile soil kept saturated or covered with 2–4 inches of standing water; Chinese water chestnuts are aquatic sedges that produce sweet, crisp, walnut-sized brown corms in fall after the above-ground foliage dies back. Start corms in pots indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost, keep them sitting in shallow water in a warm, sunny spot, then move containers outdoors after last frost. In October or November when the hollow cylindrical foliage yellows and collapses, drain the container and harvest corms by rummaging through the mud. Fresh-harvested corms are intensely sweet and crunchy — a completely different experience from the bland canned version.

common_name: Chinese Yam (Asiatic Yam, Sweet Yam, Lesser Yam, Intoxicating Yam)
plant_note: Plant cut tuber sections or small tubers in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, sandy to loamy soil after last frost; Dioscorea esculenta produces multiple smaller tubers rather than one or two large ones — loosened, deep, fertile soil maximizes tuber development. Provide a tall climbing support. Unlike some other Dioscorea species, D. esculenta tubers may be eaten with the skin on after cooking. The tubers are sweet and have a distinctive, pleasant starchy flavor. Harvest when the vine begins to die back. Zone 9-12 outdoor production.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil with a tall climbing support — Chinese Yam produces a vigorous twining vine that requires sturdy vertical support and rewards deep soil preparation with a generous yield of multiple smaller tubers around the central plant. Dioscorea esculenta is a tuberous, climbing vine native to Southeast Asia (India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia through Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines) and widely cultivated across the Pacific Islands and tropical world in the Dioscoreaceae family. Unlike the large, single-tuber yam species (D. rotundata, D. cayennensis), D. esculenta produces clusters of multiple smaller, ovoid to elongated tubers 2–6 inches long, smooth to slightly warty, with white flesh and a naturally sweet, pleasant starchy flavor — one of the most palatable raw-flavor yam species and one that can be eaten simply baked, boiled, or roasted with a sweet, potato-like quality. The vines are typically spined at the base (small spines on the lower stems), climbing vigorously 10–15 feet per season. D. esculenta is the most widely grown yam species in the Pacific Islands and southern Asia, where it is valued both for its edible tubers and for the medicinal compounds in the leaves and skin. In zone 9-12 Gulf Coast and Florida gardens, it provides a productive, tropical root vegetable harvest from fall plantings or spring starts, with harvest occurring before the first frost in zone 9 or when the vine dies back naturally in zone 10-12.

plant_note: Plant tuber sections or bulbils in spring after last frost once soil reaches 60°F; established crowns are hardy to zone 5.
directions: Plant tuber sections or aerial bulbils (small potato-like growths that form in the leaf axils) 2–3 inches deep in deep, loose, stone-free soil; the main tuber can grow 3 feet straight down, so deep, well-prepared beds are essential. Provide a trellis or fence immediately as this vigorous twining vine can reach 15 feet in a season. Harvest main tubers in late fall after the vine dies back, being careful to dig deeply and extract the entire tuber without breaking; the secondary bulbils can also be harvested and eaten or saved for replanting. The raw tuber is one of the few yams that can be eaten uncooked and grated — called nagaimo in Japanese cuisine — where its distinctive gluey texture is prized.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to a close final spacing; also sown in early spring after last frost.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to a close final spacing, since Ching-Chiang forms a compact, vase-shaped baby Shanghai-type plant with pale-green, spoon-shaped petioles and medium-green leaves. This variety is notably tolerant of heat, rain, cold, and dampness, which makes it more forgiving than many pak choi types for both early spring and late summer sowings. Harvest whole plants at about 6 inches tall for tender stir-fry and soup greens with a mild, sweet flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 sow September–February for winter-spring harvest. Chioggia beet is best harvested at 2–3 inches diameter — the candy-stripe pattern is most vivid and the texture most tender at medium size. Large over-mature Chioggia beets lose the distinct stripe clarity as the rings merge. Thin seedlings to 3–4 inches apart; the thinnings are edible as beet greens. In zone 9 the cool season from fall through early spring is the primary growing window.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, loose, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of stones and compaction; Chioggia is an 1840s Italian heirloom beet from the town of Chioggia near Venice, producing medium-sized, round roots with distinctive alternating concentric rings of deep rose-red and white when sliced — resembling a bulls-eye or candy cane pattern that makes the cross-section one of the most visually striking of any vegetable. The candy-stripe pattern is most vivid in raw beets; cooking softens the color contrast. Chioggia has a notably milder, sweeter, less earthy flavor than standard red beet varieties — the 'dirt' or 'earthiness' commonly associated with beets is less pronounced in Chioggia, making it preferred by people who enjoy the sweetness of beets but find the strong earthy undertone of red beets off-putting. Raw Chioggia slices are excellent in salads and cheese boards where the color pattern can be appreciated, and they don't stain hands and cutting boards with the deep red juice of standard beets.

plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked; succession sow through summer.
directions: This Italian heirloom reveals concentric pink-and-white rings when sliced, and the rings show best when eaten raw or lightly cooked. Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3 inches once true leaves appear. Keep soil consistently moist to prevent woody, zoned roots and to encourage tender growth. Harvest when roots reach 1.5 to 2 inches across for the sweetest flavor. The greens are also edible and can be cooked like chard.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil, or start indoors 4–6 weeks early; chipilin grows as a perennial shrub in zones 9–11 and can reach 4–6 feet. Scarify seeds before planting to improve germination.
directions: Scarify and sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after last frost; chipilin is a traditional leafy vegetable and nitrogen-fixing shrub-legume of Central America and southern Mexico, where the young leaves, shoots, and tender pods are eaten as a cooked green vegetable with a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor. It is a dietary staple in Chiapas, Guatemala, and El Salvador, added to soups, tamales, and rice. The plant is a prolific nitrogen fixer that can improve soil fertility significantly over a few seasons. Young growth is harvested continuously — cutting the stem tips promotes bushy, tender new growth. The yellow flowers are also edible and attract pollinators. In Gulf Coast zones 9–11 it grows as a multi-year perennial subshrub.

plant_note: Start indoors early and transplant after warm-up; a sweet bell ripening chocolate brown.
directions: Start seeds indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and keep them warm for good germination. Transplant into full sun once nights stay warm, and allow the blocky fruits to ripen fully from green to glossy chocolate brown for the sweetest flavor and thickest walls. Support laden plants and harvest regularly to keep new fruit setting.

common_name: Chocolate Bhutlah Pepper (Ghost x Trinidad Scorpion Superhot Hybrid)
plant_note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; Bhutlah is among the slowest superhots to mature and needs the longest season possible.
directions: Bhutlah, sometimes sold as Chocolate Bhutlah, is a deliberate cross of bhut jolokia (ghost pepper) and Trinidad Scorpion lines, producing small, extremely gnarled dark-brown pods that rank among the most searing chiles grown by home superhot enthusiasts. Because the fruit is slow to size up and slower still to fully color from green to chocolate-brown, gardeners in short-season climates should start seed as early as feasible and consider container culture so plants can be moved to protect them from early frost. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since chinense superhots are prone to root stress that shows up as blossom drop weeks later. Handle harvested pods with gloves, as oleoresin transfer from Bhutlah is unusually persistent even after washing.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; stake or cage this indeterminate vine.
directions: A prolific indeterminate cherry tomato bearing one-inch purplish-red fruits that add sweetness to salads and pastas. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. The vigorous vines set long trusses of six to eight crack-resistant fruits, so give them a tall trellis and prune for airflow. Water evenly and harvest when the fruit turns dusky red for the fullest flavor.

common_name: Chocolate Cherry Tomato (Brownish-Red Heirloom Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; stake or cage firmly, since Chocolate Cherry is a vigorous, sprawling indeterminate producer.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, staking or caging plants firmly to support their vigorous, indeterminate vines. Chocolate Cherry is an heirloom cherry tomato bearing clusters of round, one-inch fruit in an unusual dusky brownish-red color reminiscent of the larger Cherokee Purple, carrying the same rich, complex, sweet-and-smoky flavor in a bite-sized package rather than a full beefsteak-size fruit. Its productive, long-season vines yield heavily from midsummer through frost, making it a favorite for snacking, salads, and roasting where its deep color and complex flavor stand out from ordinary red cherry tomatoes. Harvest when fruits soften slightly and the color deepens fully, as the dusky skin tone makes visual ripeness cues subtler than on standard red tomatoes.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; chocolate habanero requires warm germination temps (80–90°F) — use a heat mat for reliable sprouting; transplant outdoors only after soil is consistently warm.
directions: Start seeds on a heat mat at 85°F for reliable germination 10–21 days; transplant after last frost when nighttime temperatures stay above 60°F. Chocolate Habanero (also called Congo Black or Dark Habanero) is a Capsicum chinense variety that ripens to a deep chocolate brown color rather than the typical orange, with heat levels of 300,000–400,000 Scoville units — significantly hotter than standard orange habaneros and with a distinctive earthy, smoky-sweet flavor that many hot pepper enthusiasts consider more complex and interesting. Originally from Jamaica and Trinidad, it is prized by hot sauce makers for its unique color and flavor profile; the pods are slightly larger than standard habaneros, with thick walls and a rich, fruity aroma. Grow in full sun with warm nights for the best fruit set; perennial in zone 9–12, often producing for multiple years as a shrubby plant.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; stake or cage this indeterminate vine.
directions: An extraordinarily productive cherry tomato with elongated, deep-red fruits striped in green and brown and a rich, sweet flavor. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. Provide a tall cage or trellis for the vigorous indeterminate vines and prune suckers for airflow. Water consistently and keep picking, as the fruit keeps coming all season long.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, fertile soil after frost danger passes; give the large-fruited indeterminate vine strong support and even watering for the best-formed fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Chocolate Stripes is a dark-fruited heirloom beefsteak tomato with dusky mahogany-brown skin overlaid with darker green-brown stripes radiating from the stem, and rich, complex, slightly smoky-sweet flesh characteristic of the best dark-colored heirloom tomatoes. Fruit runs large for slicing and sandwiches, and the deep coloring makes it a striking addition to a mixed heirloom tomato platter. Stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vine well, water evenly to reduce cracking and blossom end rot, and harvest once fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure and the shoulders have darkened fully.

common_name: Choppee Okra (South Carolina Lowcountry Heirloom Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably warm; Choppee is a South Carolina Lowcountry heirloom named for the community along the Black River, prized for its early, heavy-yielding, nearly spineless pods.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep after the soil has warmed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Choppee is an heirloom okra passed down among South Carolina Lowcountry gardening families near the Choppee community in Georgetown County, valued for producing tender, nearly spineless, slightly ridged green pods with a reddish tinge at the base earlier in the season than many other Southern heirlooms. The plants are productive and well adapted to the humid, hot conditions of the coastal Southeast, and pods should be picked at 3-5 inches for the best table quality. Like most heirloom okras it is open-pollinated and easily saved from year to year, helping preserve a piece of Lowcountry foodways history.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost date in spring, or 6–8 weeks before first fall frost; best in cool weather but tolerates mild warmth better than other brassicas.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows, thinning to 6–10 inches; plants can be sown more densely and thinned progressively, using the thinnings as greens. Harvest the central flower stalk when buds are just beginning to show yellow but before flowers open, cutting 6 inches down to leave side shoots. The stems, leaves, and flower buds are all edible; successive harvesting keeps production going for several weeks. Even soil moisture and cool temperatures produce the sweetest, most tender stalks.

common_name: Christmas Lima Bean (Speckled Lima, Chestnut Lima)
plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Christmas Lima is a large-seeded pole type needing 5–6 feet of trellis support; plant along fences or provide sturdy poles.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil (above 65°F) after last frost at the base of a sturdy trellis, fence, or poles in full sun, in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Christmas Lima is a striking heirloom pole lima with large seeds dramatically streaked and mottled in red-maroon and cream — the colors fade somewhat on cooking but the flavor more than compensates, often described as chestnut-like with a rich, buttery texture superior to common limas. A long-season variety that rewards gardeners in warm climates; in zone 9–10, the extended growing season produces heavy yields late into fall. Dry the seeds for storage as beautiful speckled beans that are prized for soups, stews, and succotash. Requires cross-pollination and benefits from hand removal of diseased pods.

plant_note: Soak tubers overnight before planting 1–2 inches deep in moist to wet soil at or just after the last frost date, when soil temperature reaches at least 65°F; keep soil consistently moist to saturated throughout the growing season.
directions: Plant soaked tubers of the cultivated variety (var. sativus) 1–2 inches deep in loose, moist soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing 6–12 inches apart; this is the domesticated food crop, not the invasive weed form. Keep soil continuously moist to encourage dense networks of underground stolons tipped with nutty, sweet tubers that mature in 90–120 days. Harvest after foliage yellows in early autumn by loosening the soil deeply with a fork and sifting through to collect the small, wrinkled tubers; yield can reach several pounds per plant under ideal conditions. Dried tubers keep for months and are eaten raw as a snack, soaked and blended into the Spanish drink horchata de chufa, or ground into gluten-free flour.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chullpi quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather.
directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chullpi quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather. A traditional Andean landrace distinct from the more familiar white, red, and black quinoa sold commercially, this variety is prized in its native Peru and Bolivia for translucent, pale golden seed with a naturally sweet flavor reminiscent of corn, traditionally toasted and eaten as a snack rather than cooked as a grain like standard quinoa. It grows on tall, colorful seed-head spikes typical of quinoa and is naturally low in the bitter seed coating (saponin) found on many quinoa varieties, requiring less rinsing before cooking or toasting. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before storing or toasting.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant divisions into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland margin in early spring; established clumps can also be divided in fall to start new plantings.
directions: Plant chwinamul in cool, humus-rich soil under the broken light of deciduous trees, where the broad basal leaves stay tender longer than they do in open sun. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips repeatedly through spring; a quick blanch mellows their mild, herbal, faintly sesame-like flavor before they are tossed with sesame oil, garlic, and soy for the classic Korean namul side dish. It is one of the most widely grown wild greens in Korean home gardens precisely because it tolerates the shady, moist corners where lettuce and other sun-loving greens struggle. Left unharvested in late summer it produces small white daisy-like flowers that draw pollinators to the shade garden.

plant_note: Direct sow thinly with 0.125 inch soil coverage; thin to 8–12 inches for full-sized heads or 4–6 inches for small heads. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest, February–March for spring. Cimarron shows notably better heat tolerance than standard romaine varieties, making it suitable for late spring production in the Gulf South when other lettuces have bolted — a practical advantage for extending the spring lettuce season by 2–3 weeks.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.125 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 8–12 inches for full-sized heads. Cimarron is a heat-tolerant romaine-type (cos) lettuce with beautiful bronze-red outer leaves that fade to green-red at the interior — a coloring that is visually distinctive from standard green romaine types while maintaining the characteristic romaine form: tall, upright, with a slightly folded, elongated head and the crisp, crunchy mid-rib texture that makes romaine the preferred lettuce for Caesar salad. The red pigmentation in Cimarron is not as deep or uniform as fully red romaines, but the attractive mottled bronze-red appearance combined with the green interior gives a bicolor effect that is especially attractive when heads are cut crosswise to reveal the color contrast. Cimarron's standout characteristic is its heat tolerance — while standard romaine types bolt (send up a seed stalk and become bitter) at sustained temperatures above 75–80°F, Cimarron holds its quality better at higher temperatures, extending the productive window by 2–3 weeks in warm spring conditions. This heat tolerance makes Cimarron particularly valuable in zone 8–10 gardens where spring temperatures rise quickly and the window for lettuce production is narrow. Named for the Cimarron Territory of the historic Southwest.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Cimmaron is a full-sized red romaine that heads up well in zone 9 cool-season conditions. The tall, upright habit makes it efficient in raised beds. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through fall provide a continuous supply through winter.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Cimmaron is a large, full-headed red romaine lettuce from the American Southwest — its name evokes the Cimarron River of the Oklahoma-Kansas plains country. It produces tall, upright, well-formed romaine heads with bronze-red to mahogany-red outer leaves and a pale green-to-cream interior heart, combining the classic romaine flavor and crunch with deep red coloration. The large, mature heads at 58–68 days are suitable for Caesar salad in the traditional whole-leaf format, where the combination of romaine structure and visual color impact makes Cimmaron stands out among red romaine options. Cimmaron is slower-bolting than most red looseleaf types and holds quality in the garden longer as a planted head. The flavor is mild, crisp, and slightly sweet — traditional romaine quality with no bitterness. In zone 9 fall planting produces the most satisfying heads; spring-planted Cimmaron benefits from light shade cloth in late spring to delay bolting.

common_name: Cincinnati Market Radish (Long Red Heirloom Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; Cincinnati Market is a nineteenth-century heirloom producing long, slender, bright red roots with crisp, mild white flesh.
directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep directly in loose, well-worked soil, and thin seedlings early to a couple of inches apart so roots have room to elongate without forking. Cincinnati Market is an old market-garden heirloom prized for its long, cylindrical, bright scarlet-red roots with crisp, mild-flavored white flesh that stays tender without turning pithy or overly hot if harvested promptly at full size. It matures quickly, making it a reliable choice for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season for a steady radish supply, and its uniform, attractive shape made it a historic favorite for market bunching. Keep the soil consistently moist as roots size up, since inconsistent watering causes cracking and harsh flavor, and harvest promptly once roots reach full size, since radishes left too long in warm soil quickly turn woody and overly pungent.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; needs a long, warm season.
directions: The French heirloom Rouge Vif d'Etampes, a deeply ridged, flattened pumpkin twelve to twenty-four inches across weighing fifteen to twenty pounds. Sow seed directly one inch deep in warm soil and give the vigorous vines ample room to sprawl. Keep soil evenly moist while fruit develops and set ripening fruit on a board to prevent rot. Harvest when the rind hardens to a vivid red-orange and the stem begins to cork.

common_name: Cinderella's Carriage Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Hybrid Flat Heirloom-Type Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Cinderella's Carriage is an AAS-winning hybrid version of the classic flattened, deep-orange Cinderella-type pumpkin, bred for powdery mildew resistance and higher, more reliable yields than the older open-pollinated heirloom.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vigorous vines ample room to spread. Cinderella's Carriage is an AAS-winning hybrid take on the classic Cinderella-type pumpkin — the flattened, deeply ribbed, deep-orange-red fruit famously associated with the Rouge Vif d'Etampes heirloom — bred to add meaningful powdery mildew resistance and more consistent, higher yields than the older open-pollinated version, while keeping the same striking flattened silhouette prized for fall display. Fruit reaches 15-25 pounds with dense, good-flavored flesh usable for cooking as well as decoration. Because it is naturally more disease-resistant than the heirloom, the vines tend to stay productive and healthy later into the season in humid climates. Harvest when the rind hardens and color deepens fully, cutting the stem rather than pulling to avoid damaging the fruit, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing.

common_name: Cinnamon Girl Squash (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Butternut Hybrid)
plant_note: Sow directly outdoors once soil has warmed thoroughly, allowing semi-compact vines room to spread, and water consistently until fruit sets to support even sizing.
directions: Sow directly outdoors once soil has warmed thoroughly, allowing semi-compact vines room to spread, and water consistently until fruit sets to support even sizing. Named an All-America Selections winner in 2018, this hybrid butternut produces uniform, single-serving fruit around a pound each with deep tan skin and dense, sweet, richly colored flesh well suited to roasting whole. Bred for strong disease tolerance and heavy yields of personal-portion squash, it fits neatly into small households and market growers wanting consistent, easy-to-handle fruit. Cure harvested squash in a warm spot for a week or two to improve storage life and sweetness.

plant_note: Choose day-length-appropriate strain for your latitude.
directions: These flat, disc-shaped Italian onions are prized for roasting whole and caramelizing due to their high sugar content. Start seed indoors ten weeks before last frost and transplant seedlings when pencil-thick. Keep beds weed-free since onions compete poorly, and water steadily until tops begin to fall. Stop watering once necks soften and leaves yellow, then lift and cure in a dry airy place. Well-cured bulbs store for several months in a cool spot.

plant_note: Start true seed indoors, then transplant; unusual for a potato grown from botanical seed.
directions: A rare potato grown from true botanical seed, producing a diverse mix of round and fingerling tubers in rose-gold and red shades. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings after hardening off. Hill soil or mulch around the stems as they grow to keep developing tubers covered and prevent greening. Harvest once the tops die back and cure the small, flavorful tubers before storage.

common_name: Clara Eggplant (Italian White Oval Hybrid Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Clara is a vigorous, disease-tolerant Italian hybrid that yields heavily over a long harvest window.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Clara is an Italian hybrid eggplant grown for its striking, brilliantly white, oval fruit set off by a bright green calyx, giving it strong visual appeal at market and in the garden alike. The dense white flesh is mild and free of the bitterness that can affect some white-skinned types, holding its color well when cut and cooking down smoothly for baked and roasted preparations. Clara shows good tolerance to common eggplant diseases and sets fruit heavily and early relative to many other Italian-type hybrids, extending the productive harvest window in a single season. Harvest fruit at 6 to 7 inches long while the skin is still glossy and firm, since white eggplant dulls and toughens quickly once past its prime.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm; okra loves heat and dislikes cold soil.
directions: An improved 1980 selection of the classic Clemson okra, bearing dark green, grooved, straight, spineless pods with full-bodied flavor. Soak seed overnight and sow directly one inch deep once the soil is warm, since okra sulks in cold ground. The tall, hollyhock-related plants bear hibiscus-like blooms and thrive in summer heat. Pick pods young at two to four inches every day or two, as they toughen quickly if left on the plant.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); in zone 9 plant March–June. Okra thrives in zone 9's hot, humid summers and is one of the most productive and reliable summer vegetables for the Gulf South — plants can produce continuously for months in summer heat. Soak seeds overnight before planting to improve germination; okra seeds have a hard seed coat that benefits from scarification. Harvest pods every 2–3 days when 2–4 inches long — larger pods become fibrous and tough and should be removed to keep the plant producing. Mature plants (3–6 feet) may need support in wind-prone locations.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — okra thrives in the same hot, humid conditions that challenge most other vegetables; Clemson Spineless is the most widely grown okra variety in the United States, a 1980 All-America Selections winner and the standard against which all other okras are measured — smooth, bright green, spineless pods in the classic okra shape eliminate the spine irritation that makes harvesting traditional okra varieties uncomfortable. The spineless pods (technically very few small, soft spines compared to original okra types) can be harvested without gloves, a significant practical improvement over older varieties. Clemson Spineless produces straight, uniform 5-ribbed pods with the mild, slightly mucilaginous flavor that defines okra — the mucilage (a natural thickener) is the basis for gumbo's characteristic body-giving quality that makes real gumbo unmistakably different from any other soup. In zone 9 okra is among the most productive and reliable summer vegetables available — it is native to Africa and genuinely thrives in the same conditions (intense heat, humidity, heat soil) that defeat cool-season crops and stress many warm-season vegetables.

plant_note: Direct sow into hot soil; an AAS-winning spineless okra for heavy yields.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and sow an inch deep only after the soil is truly warm, since okra sulks in cold ground. This 1939 AAS winner grows into tall, productive plants that set spineless pods over a long season. Pick the pods young at about three inches every couple of days, as they toughen quickly and frequent harvest keeps the plants producing.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant in February–March. The white tomatoes can be difficult to judge for ripeness by color — ripe fruits develop a creamy, slightly yellowish blush and become slightly soft to the touch. Cloud Nine is indeterminate and produces most productively with cage or stake support. In zone 9 the fall planting in August produces exceptional quality fruit.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with cage or stake support; Cloud Nine is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing very large (often 1–2 pound) fruits with ivory-white to pale cream skin and nearly white flesh — one of the few tomato varieties that is genuinely white rather than pale yellow or cream-colored at full ripeness. Like other white tomatoes, Cloud Nine lacks the red lycopene pigment that colors standard tomatoes, instead producing a nearly colorless fruit with very low acid content. The flavor is exceptionally mild, honey-sweet, and rich without the sharpness of red varieties — often described as having a complex sweetness that is difficult to describe as 'tomato-like' in the traditional sense, more like eating a sweet, meaty fruit with subtle complexity. Cloud Nine is preferred for fresh eating and mild preparations where the low-acid, ultra-sweet character can be fully appreciated — it is less well-suited to cooking where the delicate pale color and mild flavor are lost.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; cluster bean does not transplant well and performs best in hot, dry summer conditions similar to the arid tropics of South Asia.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, warm soil after last frost; cluster bean (guar) is a summer-annual legume with clusters of small pods along the stems that are harvested young as a vegetable — particularly popular in Indian cooking, where the tender young pods (called gawar phalli) are stir-fried with spices. Mature seeds are the source of guar gum, a key industrial thickener used worldwide in food production, oil drilling, and manufacturing. The plant is a nitrogen-fixing cover crop adapted to hot, dry conditions and marginal soils. In South Asia it is grown over millions of acres. In the home garden it provides an unusual, prolific summer vegetable with minimal water requirements, excellent for Gulf Coast and arid Southwest climates.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; Coastal Star is a heat-tolerant romaine bred to hold full-size, heavy hearts and resist bolting longer than standard romaine types, extending the spring harvest window before summer heat sets in.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Coastal Star is a dark green romaine bred for heat tolerance and slow bolting, producing full-size, dense, heavy hearts even as temperatures climb toward the point where most romaine varieties turn bitter and send up a seed stalk. The upright heads have crisp, sweet leaves with excellent texture through to the crunchy heart. Provide afternoon shade during the hottest stretches of a Gulf Coast spring to further extend the harvest window, and keep soil consistently moist, since drought stress accelerates bolting even in heat-tolerant varieties. Harvest whole heads once hearts have filled out, or pick outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop.

plant_note: Direct sow thinly in deeply worked ground, thin seedlings to a few inches apart, and harvest after frost for the sweetest flavor.
directions: A classic English heirloom developed from the older Marrow parsnip type and long favored by British allotment gardeners for its short neck and broad shoulders that taper to a blunt, well-filled root. It shows better resistance to canker than many older parsnip lines, an important trait in the damp, heavy soils common in British gardens. Direct sow thinly in deeply worked ground, thin seedlings to a few inches apart, and harvest after frost for the sweetest flavor; it has long held a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for reliable garden performance.

subcategory: Mexican dye cactus edible nopal pad
plant_note: Root dried pad cuttings in dry, sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun in zone 9–12; Cochineal Nopal (Tuna Mansa, Nopal Cardón) is a tall, tree-like, spineless or nearly-spineless cactus from Mexico — the primary host plant historically cultivated for the cochineal insect (Dactylopius coccus) that produces the brilliant red carmine dye used in textiles, cosmetics, and food coloring — with edible, mild pads (nopales) and small red fruits.
directions: Root a dried Nopalea cochenillifera pad cutting (allow cut end to callus for 1–2 weeks before planting) in dry, coarse sandy soil in full sun; plant only 2–3 inches deep; water sparingly until established, then infrequently; the plant is highly drought-tolerant once established and susceptible to root rot in wet soils. Cochineal Nopal is the cactus at the center of one of the most remarkable stories in natural dye history — the basis of carmine (E120), the brilliant scarlet-red dye that became one of the most valuable trade commodities between the Americas and Europe after Spanish conquest, worth more than silver by weight in 16th-century Spain. The cactus is the host of the cochineal insect (Dactylopius coccus), tiny scale insects that feed on the cactus pads and produce carminic acid as a defense compound — the source of intense, colorfast red dye. Pre-Columbian Aztec and Mixtec civilizations had cultivated cochineal production for centuries before European contact; after conquest, the Spanish maintained it as a closely guarded trade secret for two centuries. Carmine remains important today in natural food coloring, cosmetics (lipstick, rouge), and textiles; it is the red in many 'natural' food colorings. The pads (nopales) are edible like other Opuntia species and can be harvested as young, tender pads for cooking; small red fruits also edible. A large, dramatic, sculptural cactus for hot, dry gardens.

common_name: Cocke's Prolific Corn (Colonial Virginia Multi-Ear Dent Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60F; Cocke's Prolific is one of the oldest documented Virginia dent corns, grown since the colonial era for its habit of setting two to four ears per stalk rather than the single large ear typical of most modern corn.
directions: Direct sow in blocks for good wind pollination and give plants extra room, since Cocke's Prolific grows tall and leafy and puts its energy into multiple smaller ears rather than one big one. This Virginia heirloom dent corn has been passed down since the 1700s and was long valued by small farmers precisely because a prolific, multi-eared plant hedges against a poor pollination year better than a single-ear hybrid does. Ears are white to pale yellow dent kernels good for cornmeal and grits once fully dried on the stalk, and the tall, leafy plants also produce useful fodder. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it by distance or timing from other corn varieties to keep the seed line true for saving.

plant_note: Sow directly once the soil has warmed after last frost, providing light support such as brush or netting for its semi-climbing habit.
directions: Sow directly once the soil has warmed after last frost, providing light support such as brush or netting for its semi-climbing habit near the cool, damp Brittany coast where it was traditionally grown. Coco de Paimpol earned its own French protected designation for a distinctive fresh-shelling bean — plump, cream-colored seeds lightly speckled with rose, picked while the pods are still green rather than left to fully dry. Harvest pods when the seeds inside have filled out but the pods remain supple, then shell immediately for the tender, buttery texture the variety is prized for. It can also be left to dry fully on the vine for storage as a soup bean, though the fresh-shell stage is when its flavor is best known.

plant_note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65F; in zone 9 plant April-May for harvest August-September. Cocodrie is an LSU AgCenter long-grain release once grown on more Gulf South acreage than any other rice variety.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Cocodrie is a semi-dwarf, long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter in 1998 and named for Louisiana's Bayou Cocodrie, quickly becoming the dominant commercial rice variety across the Gulf South rice belt because of its early maturity, high milling yield, and reliable performance under both flooded and continuously moist conditions. Home gardeners can grow it in beds kept saturated through the season rather than in true paddies, though yields are highest with standing water for at least part of the cycle. The semi-dwarf, sturdy stalks resist lodging (falling over) better than older tall varieties, which matters most in wet, windy Gulf Coast summers. Harvest when the seed heads droop and turn golden-tan, then dry and hull. As a widely proven Louisiana-bred variety, Cocodrie is an accessible entry point for gardeners curious about growing their own rice in zone 8-10 conditions.

plant_note: Plant corm divisions or small cormels 2–4 weeks after last frost in warm soil (70°F+) in a deep, humus-rich, consistently moist site; in frost-free zones 10–11, tannia can be planted at any time but does best with a long warm season.
directions: Plant corm divisions or small cormels 4–6 inches deep in deep, rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost risk has passed and the soil has warmed to 70°F; tannia requires a long hot growing season of 6–9 months to produce well-developed corms. Xanthosoma sagittifolium is a large, dramatic tropical plant grown throughout the Caribbean, West Africa, and Latin America for its starchy, edible corms (harvested at 7–10 months when leaves begin to yellow) and young leaves, which are used as a spinach substitute after thorough cooking to neutralize calcium oxalate crystals. Unlike taro (Colocasia esculenta), tannia corms are generally less mucilaginous and somewhat easier to peel; they are boiled, mashed, fried, or pureed and have a nutty, earthy flavor. In frost-prone climates, lift corms before the first frost and store in a cool, dry, frost-free location.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; squash resents root disturbance.
directions: An Italian heirloom zucchini with long, cylindrical dark-green fruit striped in lighter green, best picked around eight inches. Sow seed directly one inch deep once the soil is warm and settled. The bush-type plants are productive, so harvest fruit young and often before they grow seedy past twelve inches. Keep soil evenly moist and watch for squash bugs and vine borers common to summer squash.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; an Italian heirloom bush zucchini with striped ribbed fruit.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm soil, planting a few per hill and thinning to the strongest. This compact Italian bush type produces slender, ribbed fruits striped in light and dark green with firm, flavorful flesh. Harvest zucchini young at six to eight inches and pick often, since a single missed fruit quickly grows into a marrow and slows the plant.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; Cole's Early was bred by A.B. Cole of Iowa in 1908 specifically to ripen watermelon reliably in a short northern growing season.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bred by A.B. Cole in Iowa in 1908, this heirloom was developed specifically to bring reliable, sweet watermelon to gardeners in short-season Northern climates where later-maturing Southern varieties often failed to ripen before fall frost. It bears medium-sized, oval, dark green striped melons with crisp, sweet red flesh on vigorous, productive vines. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and browned and the underside spot has turned from white to cream-yellow, reliable signs of ripeness in a short-season melon bred for gardens with a narrow window to work with.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 10–12 weeks before first fall frost for the main crop, or transplant in early fall; in zone 7–10 collards can be grown as a year-round biennial, harvesting through winter and spring before the plants bolt in their second year.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep or transplant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun 10–12 weeks before first fall frost; collard greens are the signature leafy vegetable of the American South, producing large, broad, blue-green, somewhat waxy leaves with a mild, slightly bitter, cabbage-like flavor that mellows considerably after frost or slow cooking. More heat-tolerant than most brassicas, collards can grow year-round in zone 8–11 and are the most cold-hardy of all the non-kale brassica greens. The traditional Southern preparation is slow-braising with smoked pork, but the leaves are also excellent blanched, stir-fried, and used as a low-carbohydrate wrap. Harvest outer leaves continuously; well-maintained plants can produce for a full year or more in mild climates.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills; Collective Farm Woman (Kolkhoznitsa) is the most widely grown open-pollinated melon in Russia and Eastern Europe, developed in the Soviet era and still the standard home-garden melon across the former Soviet republics — extraordinarily flavorful despite the unglamorous name.
directions: Sow 3–4 seeds per hill after last frost in well-amended, well-drained soil; thin to 2 strongest plants per hill; direct vines along rows or up a strong trellis. Collective Farm Woman (Russian: Kolkhoznitsa) is a Ukrainian/Russian heirloom muskmelon introduced in 1930 that became the standard garden melon across the Soviet Union and is still the most widely grown open-pollinated melon in Russia and Ukraine; the small (1–2 lb) round to oval fruits ripen to creamy-white to yellow with thin, smooth skin and extremely aromatic, sweet, creamy-white flesh that has an exceptional honey-floral fragrance when perfectly ripe. Despite its short ripening window once mature, the flavor is outstanding — rich, sweet, and intensely perfumed. One of the earliest-maturing muskmelons (75–85 days from transplant), making it excellent for short-season northern gardens and for early production in the South and Gulf Coast. Harvest when skin turns creamy-yellow and the blossom end softens slightly.

common_name: Colorado Star Artichoke (Cold-Tolerant Purple AAS Winner)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; Colorado Star sets buds reliably in its first year with only modest cold exposure, making it one of the easier annual artichokes to bring to harvest in a single season without precise vernalization timing.
directions: Start seed indoors and set transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes; Colorado Star is a compact, early-maturing F1 hybrid bred for reliable first-year flowering across a wide range of climates, including regions with cooler or shorter growing seasons than traditional artichoke territory. Buds are medium-sized with an attractive purple-tinged blush over green, tender at a smaller size than many varieties, and produced in good quantity on a plant more compact than older perennial types, making it a reasonable choice for smaller gardens. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its ease of first-year production from seed. Water regularly and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat, and harvest buds promptly while tightly closed for the best texture and flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring and July–August for fall. Colossus is named for its exceptionally large seeds and long pods — it is one of the largest-seeded blackeye-type cowpeas available, making shelling more efficient than small-seeded varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; Colossus is a vigorous, bush-type Southern pea selected for exceptionally large seeds and long, productive pods — the big, cream-colored seeds with the characteristic black eye shell out more quickly than the smaller-seeded varieties, making it a practical choice for preserving and cooking in large quantities. Like all cowpeas, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers when most other legumes fail. The high yield per plant and large seed size make Colossus a commercial and home-garden standard in the Gulf Coast South, particularly for fresh-shell operations. Harvest when pods are fully plump and light green, before the hull begins to dry and yellow.

subcategory: wild edible shoots / native climbing vine
plant_note: Plant root divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge, prairie margin, or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures; common carrionflower ranges farther into the central prairie states than the more Atlantic-coastal Smilax herbacea.
directions: Plant root divisions in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures. Common carrionflower is a thornless, herbaceous Smilax found from the Appalachians west across the prairie states and into the Rockies foothills, dying back to its tuberous rootstock each winter and resprouting reliably each spring, much like its more eastern relative Smilax herbacea. Young emerging shoots and tendril tips are harvested and cooked much like asparagus before the vine toughens, while the small, globe-shaped clusters of greenish flowers give off a mild carrion scent in late spring to draw in fly pollinators, followed by dark blue-black berries relished by birds. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is best left undisturbed once established at a woodland or prairie-edge planting.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in shallow water or saturated soil at the edge of a pond, stream, or rain garden; cattail is highly invasive in open water — plant only in contained garden ponds or where spread can be managed.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions or seeds in saturated soil or up to 12 inches of standing water in full sun; common cattail is one of the most comprehensively edible native plants in North America, with nearly every part edible at different seasons: the tender white shoots in spring are eaten like asparagus, the immature green female flower spikes can be boiled and eaten like corn on the cob in late spring, the golden pollen is collected in early summer and used as a flour supplement, and the starchy rhizomes can be processed into flour year-round. The familiar brown hotdog-shaped seed heads are iconic in wetland and rain gardens. Spreads aggressively by rhizome — grow in contained pond pockets or regularly remove rhizomes from the margins to prevent dominance.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring for leaf harvest or in early summer for forcing chicory; witloof types are sown in late spring, roots lifted in fall and forced in darkness to produce the tight, pale 'Belgian endive' chicons used as winter salad.
directions: Sow direct in spring for leaf chicory or late spring for forcing types; for witloof (Belgian endive) production, sow in May–June, lift roots in fall, and force in a dark, warm (55–65°F) location in moist sand to produce the tender, pale, bullet-shaped chicons used as winter salad. Cichorium intybus is a remarkably versatile species encompassing leaf chicories (radicchio, puntarelle), forcing chicories (witloof/Belgian endive), and the roasted-root coffee substitute; all types are naturally bitter, a quality that can be reduced by blanching or frost exposure. The wild roadside plant with brilliant blue flowers is also the same species and is strikingly beautiful in naturalized plantings; the flowers are edible and the roasted root is a caffeine-free coffee substitute. Perennial in the garden but usually grown as an annual for leaf and root crops.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds around the last frost date in full sun in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil — common mallow is a tough, adaptable plant that germinates quickly across a wide range of soil types and is largely indifferent to soil quality. Sow seeds about a quarter-inch deep and thin seedlings to 12–18 inches apart once they reach 2 inches tall. Harvest young leaves and immature fruits continuously throughout the season to promote new growth and extend the edible harvest.
directions: Sow seeds directly in spring around the last frost date, pressing them a quarter-inch into the soil in a sunny location with average, well-drained ground — this adaptable plant thrives in poor soils with minimal fertility and water. Thin seedlings to 12–18 inches apart and begin harvesting the mild, slightly mucilaginous young leaves once plants reach 6 inches tall, using them raw in salads or cooked as a spinach substitute. The round, segmented fruits known as 'cheeses' are also edible and have a mild, slightly starchy flavor when harvested young and green. Plants will self-sow readily and may persist as short-lived perennials in warmer zones, so deadhead spent flowers if you wish to limit volunteer seedlings.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm; in zone 9 this is February–March or July–August. Purslane is an edible succulent that thrives in poor, dry soil where little else grows, making it a valuable summer green. It self-seeds prolifically once established.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the surface of poor to moderately fertile, well-drained soil — do not bury them, as they require light to germinate. Purslane is one of the most nutritious leafy greens available, with the highest plant-based omega-3 fatty acid (alpha-linolenic acid) content of any vegetable, plus high levels of vitamins C and E, beta-carotene, and glutathione. Harvest the succulent stem tips and young leaves when plants are 3–4 inches tall; the plants regrow vigorously after cutting. The mild, slightly lemony flavor works raw in salads (a staple in Turkish cacik and Middle Eastern fattoush), cooked in stews, or pickled. Remove plants before they set seed if you don't want them naturalizing throughout the garden.

plant_note: Self-sows freely in garden beds, disturbed ground, and compost areas; if deliberately cultivating, direct sow in early spring or fall in average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Harvest young leaves before the plant bolts for mildest flavor.
directions: Common sow-thistle appears spontaneously in garden beds, compost areas, and disturbed ground across virtually all of North America — a Eurasian annual naturalized worldwide. The leaves are edible at all stages but mildest and most pleasant when harvested young (before the plant bolts), tasting somewhat like a milder, less bitter version of dandelion greens. Young rosette leaves are excellent in salads, stir-fries, or as a cooked pot herb — used in this way throughout the Mediterranean, China, and Africa as a common food plant. Despite the name and resemblance, it is in the Asteraceae family and not related to true thistles. The milky sap is harmless. Hares and rabbits eat the leaves avidly (hence 'hare's lettuce'). Recognized as a valuable foraging green in many food traditions. The daisy-like yellow flowers attract small native bees. Best harvested regularly as it appears in the garden, rather than deliberately cultivated in good beds where it would compete with food crops.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and give young seedlings a period of cool temperatures once they have several true leaves to encourage first-year bud formation. Transplant outdoors after frost danger has passed into full sun and fertile, well-drained soil.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and give young seedlings a period of cool temperatures once they have several true leaves to encourage first-year bud formation. Transplant outdoors after frost danger has passed into full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest buds while the scales are still tightly closed. Concerto is a compact F1 hybrid bred to reliably flower and produce full-sized rounded green buds in its very first season, making globe artichoke growing practical in shorter-season gardens that could not otherwise ripen a traditional perennial variety in time. Where winters are mild it can also be left in the ground to behave as a genuine short-lived perennial, cropping again in subsequent years.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed, spacing plants for their semi-bush habit, and maintain even moisture as small acorn-shaped fruit begin to form.
directions: Direct sow after frost danger has passed, spacing plants for their semi-bush habit, and maintain even moisture as small acorn-shaped fruit begin to form and ripen to deep orange. Recognized as an All-America Selections winner in 2017, this hybrid was bred for markedly sweeter, less fibrous flesh than typical acorn squash along with strong resistance to powdery mildew that keeps foliage productive later into the season. Its semi-compact vines produce a heavy, uniform set of small fruit ideal for roasting or stuffing whole. Harvest once rinds are fully colored and hardened, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry space.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost, since Capsicum chinense types are slow to germinate and mature; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay above 60°F.
directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the season, since Capsicum chinense types germinate slowly and need a long, hot growing season to fully ripen; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Congo Pepper is a traditional Trinidad and Tobago chile closely related to the island's famous Trinidad Scorpion and Moruga Scorpion lines, producing wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through yellow, orange, and finally deep red, carrying extreme superhot heat well beyond a habanero. Beneath the heat is a distinctly fruity, almost tropical flavor that makes it prized in Trinidadian pepper sauces and hot sauce blends despite its intensity. Handle ripe fruit with gloves, since the capsaicin level is high enough to cause skin irritation, and harvest as pods fully color for the best flavor and heat development.

common_name: Congo Trinidad Pepper (Wrinkled Orange-Red Very Hot Habanero-Type)
plant_note: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Congo Trinidad is a traditional Trinidadian habanero-type pepper with wrinkled orange-red pods and intense heat.
directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Congo Trinidad bears wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through orange to red, carrying intense heat well into superhot territory along with the characteristic fruity habanero aroma, a traditional variety long grown in home gardens across Trinidad. It is prized for hot sauce and pepper sauce making, where its heat and fruity depth of flavor come through strongly. The vigorous plants are productive in warm climates over a long season; handle ripe pods with gloves.
