plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-prepared, well-drained soil; Congo is a classic Southern 'picnic' watermelon producing enormous oblong fruits (35–50+ lbs) with dark green skin and excellent deep red flesh — one of the largest-fruited traditional Southern watermelon varieties and a staple of Gulf Coast summer gardens and roadside stands.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Congo requires plenty of space (hills or rows 6–8 feet apart) for its vigorous, spreading vines and very large fruits. Congo is a classic Southern summer watermelon of the 'picnic' or 'family' type, producing very large, elongated-oblong fruits (35–50+ lbs) with dark green skin patterned with lighter green stripes and solid deep red flesh with excellent sweetness and rich melon flavor; Congo-type watermelons were an important part of Gulf Coast and Deep South truck farming and summer culture in the first half of the 20th century, when enormous watermelons were hauled to market and sold by the slice from wagons and stands. The very large size makes Congo impractical for modern small households (a single fruit can feed 30 people) but it remains grown by enthusiasts of traditional Southern garden culture and heirloom melon growers. Best suited to long-season Southern gardens (zones 7–11) where 85–95 day maturity can be fully achieved.

common_name: Connecticut Field Pumpkin (New England Field Pumpkin, Classic Carving Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills (3–4 seeds per hill, thinned to 2 plants) after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; Connecticut Field requires a long growing season (100–120 days) and ample space for the sprawling vines (8–12 feet). For fall pumpkin harvest, count back 110–120 days from desired harvest date in October. In zone 9, plant in late May for a September–October harvest, or plant in February–March for a summer harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost in full sun; provide ample space for vigorous vines and fertilize generously with balanced fertilizer or compost. Connecticut Field Pumpkin is the traditional American carving and field pumpkin — an open-pollinated heirloom that has been the archetypal 'pumpkin' in American agriculture and home gardens for well over a century, serving as the standard from which Halloween carving pumpkins, field decoration pumpkins, and processing pumpkins have all descended. The deeply ribbed, round to slightly flattened fruits typically weigh 15–25 pounds, develop a deep, saturated orange color at maturity, and have thick, firm walls that support carving without collapsing — the defining characteristics for jack-o-lantern use. Connecticut Field has a very long cultivation history in New England and the mid-Atlantic states where it was grown both for decorative autumn use and as a livestock feed crop; the tough, fibrous flesh is not considered prime for pie (Long Island Cheese, Small Sugar, and Winter Luxury pie pumpkins have been favored for baking), but it is edible and was historically used for pumpkin butter and pie. One of the most iconic American vegetables with strong cultural associations to autumn, harvest season, and Americana — a variety that connects any garden to a centuries-long tradition of pumpkin growing in the Eastern United States.

common_name: Connover's Colossal Asparagus (Classic Victorian Heirloom Asparagus)
plant_note: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring into a trench 6-8 inches deep with a ridge of loosened, compost-enriched soil, spreading the roots over the ridge before backfilling. Let all spears grow into fern the first year and delay harvest until the third spring to build strong root reserves.
directions: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring into a trench 6-8 inches deep with a ridge of loosened, compost-enriched soil, spreading the roots over the ridge before backfilling. Let all spears grow into fern the first year and delay harvest until the third spring to build strong root reserves. Connover's Colossal is a nineteenth-century English heirloom, one of the oldest named asparagus varieties still commercially available, originally selected for its unusually thick, early spears at a time when most asparagus was thin and slow to establish. It is an open-pollinated, non-hybrid variety, so it comes true enough from seed for home seed-saving, and it remains popular with heirloom vegetable growers for its historic pedigree and dependable, tender spears.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; a compact determinate ideal for pots and grow bags.
directions: A compact determinate hybrid bred for containers, producing red beefsteak-style tomatoes of six to eight ounces in about seventy days. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant into large pots or grow bags after nights warm. Its tidy habit needs only light support and suits small spaces and balconies. Keep container soil evenly moist and feed regularly, since potted tomatoes are heavy feeders.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; an early, heat-tolerant bush snap bean.
directions: Sow seeds about an inch deep directly in the garden after the last frost, as beans dislike root disturbance. This early, adaptable variety sets heavy crops of crisp, flavorful pods and tolerates both cooler and warmer conditions than many bush beans. Harvest the tender pods young and pick frequently to keep the plants productive over several weeks.

common_name: Contender Bush Bean (Popular Early Snap Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in warm soil; Contender is a widely grown early bush snap bean prized for producing a full crop in a short window, making it ideal for succession planting through the season.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Contender is a longtime favorite early bush snap bean, valued for reaching harvest size faster than most other bush beans and tolerating somewhat cooler soil at planting than many varieties, giving Gulf South gardeners an early start on the bean season. Its round, meaty, stringless pods have good flavor and hold quality well for a short window before toughening, making regular harvest important. Because the whole crop tends to mature at once, Contender is an excellent choice for succession sowing every two to three weeks to maintain a steady bean harvest through summer, and for canning or freezing a full batch at one time.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and late August–September for fall. Contender is slightly more heat-tolerant than other bush snap beans — a meaningful advantage in zone 9 where spring heat arrives early. Succession sow every 2 weeks for continuous harvest.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Contender is a classic open-pollinated bush snap bean introduced by Asgrow Seed Company in 1949 and one of the most reliable and widely grown snap beans in the southeastern US. It is valued particularly for its heat tolerance — Contender sets pods at higher temperatures than most bush beans and continues producing when Blue Lake and other popular varieties quit in early summer heat. The straight, round, 6–7 inch pods are tender, stringless, and have excellent classic green bean flavor with no fibrous texture. Contender produces a heavy concentrated crop that is ideal for large-scale fresh picking, canning, and freezing. It was the standard commercial and home canning bean for decades in the South and still recommended by extension services across the region. In zone 9, Contender's heat tolerance makes it the go-to bush snap bean for the spring garden; successive plantings starting in late February through April can yield beans from April through early June before summer heat becomes too intense for fruit set.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions (corms or pups) after soil has warmed to 65°F or above; in zones 9–11 plants may be set out year-round in frost-free periods.
directions: Plant corms or rooted pups in deep, rich, well-drained soil amended heavily with compost; cooking plantains require consistent moisture, warmth, and fertility to produce heavy fruit bunches. Unlike dessert bananas, plantains are starchy and low in sugar when unripe, requiring cooking at all stages — green plantains are fried (tostones), boiled, or baked; yellow-ripe plantains are sweet-fried (maduros). Each pseudostem produces one bunch of 100–200 fruits over 12–18 months, then dies back — remove it at the base and allow suckers to replace it. Mulch heavily in zones 8–9 where tops may freeze back to the rhizome; established rhizomes often survive to 20°F. Fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer high in potassium.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant; also grows well as a fall crop.
directions: A Danish heirloom from 1909 that became the standard for round, early cabbages, forming tight six-to-eight-inch heads of three to four pounds. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before the last frost and transplant twelve to eighteen inches apart. Its uniform, quick-maturing heads sit compactly on short stems, saving garden space. Keep evenly watered and harvest when heads feel solid to avoid splitting.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost risk passes; Copia is a vigorous indeterminate vine that benefits from sturdy staking or caging and consistent moisture to keep the large bicolor fruit from cracking.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, fertile soil in full sun. Copia is a striking modern heirloom, named for the American food and wine culture center in Napa where it was introduced, prized for its large, meaty fruit that ripens to a warm golden-yellow background overlaid with red marbling and streaks radiating from the blossom end. The flesh is sweet with balanced acidity and holds its shape well for slicing, making the fruit as good on a cheese board as in a sandwich. Provide sturdy staking or caging for the tall indeterminate vine, water evenly to reduce cracking, and pick fruit once fully colored for the best sweetness.

common_name: Copra Onion (F1 Hybrid Long-Storage Brown Onion)
plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; Copra is a long-day to intermediate-day onion best suited for zone 5–7 where summer day lengths exceed 14 hours for proper bulbing. It can be grown in zone 8–9 with early spring planting (February–March transplants) where days lengthen adequately before heat arrives. In zone 9, fall-planted varieties like 1015Y are more reliably adapted. Copra excels at long-term storage: cured bulbs keep 6–9 months in proper cool, dry, dark conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; set transplants 3–5 inches apart in rows 12 inches apart. Cure harvested bulbs with tops intact in warm, airy conditions for 2–3 weeks before storage. Copra is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid onion that has earned a reputation as one of the best long-keeping onions available — consistently ranking among the top storage onions in variety trials for its combination of high solids content (which concentrates flavor and extends keeping time), thin, tight-fitting brown outer scales, and small, tight-necked tops that dry down cleanly. The 'copra' connection (the dried coconut meat used in oil production) suggests the dried, concentrated character of the bulbs — high in solids, relatively low in water — which gives Copra good pungency but exceptional storage quality (6–9 months in proper conditions versus the 1–3 months of most sweet onions). Copra produces medium-sized (2.5–3 inch), globe-shaped, uniformly brown-skinned bulbs of consistently good quality. The pungency makes Copra most appropriate for cooking (caramelized onions, soups, braises) rather than raw eating, but the storage capability means gardeners can harvest a crop in late summer and have homegrown onions through the following spring.

plant_note: Sow in late summer for a fall and winter crop, or very early spring for a quick harvest before heat sets in; this French heirloom is named for its distinctive shell-shaped leaves.
directions: Direct sow shallowly into cool, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist through germination, which is slow and improved by a period of cold stratification if sowing in late summer heat. Coquille de Louviers is a traditional French heirloom named for its cupped, shell-like leaves, which form dense, slightly domed rosettes distinct from flatter mâche types. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, surviving hard freezes under light mulch or row cover to provide fresh greens deep into winter. Harvest whole rosettes at the base and use raw in salads for its mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor.

common_name: Corbaci Pepper (Turkish Long Sweet Frying Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Corbaci is a Turkish heirloom sweet frying pepper producing long, slender fruits (8–12 inches) that taper to a point. The name 'Corbaci' derives from a Turkish rank (commander) and reflects the regional importance of this pepper type in Turkish cuisine. Fruits are harvested green (lime green) for fresh eating and frying, or left to ripen fully to red; both stages are sweet with no heat. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production and again August–September for fall harvest. Corbaci is extremely productive and performs well in warm Gulf Coast conditions, where its heat tolerance gives it an advantage over thicker-walled sweet bell types that suffer in high summer temperatures.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun and harvest green at 8–10 inches or allow to ripen red. Corbaci Pepper is a long-standing Turkish heirloom sweet frying pepper that has gained significant popularity among American specialty growers and seed-savers for its combination of outstanding productivity, heat tolerance, and distinctive flavor profile. Unlike standard bell peppers, which develop thick walls that can flag in extreme heat, Corbaci's thin-walled, elongated fruits tolerate zone 9 summer temperatures without developing bitter off-flavors or collapsing at the blossom end — a common issue with large-fruited sweet peppers in the Deep South. The fruits ripen from lime green through yellow to vivid red; all stages are usable, but the fully red fruit develops a richer, slightly sweeter flavor with a soft, tender texture ideal for roasting, grilling, or raw eating. Corbaci is particularly well-suited to frying in olive oil (a classic Turkish preparation called 'körbacı biber tava'), where the thin walls soften quickly and the skin blisters attractively without the need for extended cooking time. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved true-to-type each season. The plants are vigorous and upright with good leaf cover that provides some protection to the pendant fruits in intense afternoon sun. Corbaci performs best with consistent moisture but tolerates brief drought better than bell types due to its smaller fruit size and lower water demand per fruit.

common_name: Corbarino Tomato (Small Campanian Plum-Cherry Preserving Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Corbarino is a small plum-cherry tomato from Corbara in Campania, Italy, traditionally used for sauce and preserving.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Corbarino bears small, oval, bright red fruit in loose clusters, a traditional variety of the Corbara area near Naples valued for concentrated, sweet-tart flavor and thick flesh that holds up well to preserving whole in jars or drying, a regional specialty product in its home area. Its compact fruit size and productive habit make it a good choice for a home preserving garden. Harvest clusters as fruit fully colors for the best flavor.

common_name: Cordner Sweet Potato (Louisiana Heirloom Baking Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm, in loose, well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; Cordner is a Louisiana heirloom sweet potato with purple-blushed skin and moist orange flesh, long grown by home gardeners in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun, and hill soil up over the row as vines run to keep developing roots covered. Cordner is a Louisiana dooryard heirloom with pinkish-purple-blushed skin and moist, deep-orange flesh that bakes up sweet and soft, grown by Gulf South home gardeners for generations before modern commercial varieties took over most production. The vigorous, sprawling vines tolerate the heat and humidity of a Louisiana summer with ease and provide good ground cover that shades out weeds once established. Dig roots once vines begin to yellow in fall and before frost threatens, and cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to firm the skin and sweeten the flesh before storing in a cool, dry place.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Corinto is a parthenocarpic (self-pollinating) seedless mini slicer cucumber producing small (5–6 inch), thin-skinned, seedless to nearly seedless fruits without the need for pollinating bees — ideal for high tunnel production, greenhouses, and gardens with limited pollinator activity; fruits remain sweet and non-bitter even when slightly oversized.
directions: Sow directly 1 inch deep and provide a trellis for vertical growing; Corinto is parthenocarpic and sets fruit without pollination, making it more reliable in cool springs or greenhouses where bees are absent; harvest frequently (every 2–3 days) at 5–6 inches for the sweetest quality. Corinto is an F1 parthenocarpic (self-pollinating) cucumber from Seminis/Monsanto Seeds specifically bred for high tunnel and greenhouse production but equally excellent in open garden conditions — the key 'parthenocarpic' characteristic means the plant sets fruit without requiring pollinating bees, an advantage in enclosed structures, in cool early spring conditions when bees are inactive, or in suburban gardens with limited pollinator activity. The fruits are small to medium (5–6 inches), cylindrical, dark green, and nearly seedless with very thin, tender skin that doesn't require peeling — the 'mini seedless cucumber' style increasingly available in grocery stores. The thin skin and near-absence of seeds gives Corinto a different texture from seeded slicing cucumbers — more uniformly crisp and mild throughout without the slightly bitter jelly surrounding seeds. The flavor is mild, sweet, and clean; Corinto stays mild and non-bitter even when slightly over-mature (unlike seeded types which become more bitter as they yellow). Excellent for fresh eating, salads, and pickling whole.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer for fall harvest or in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost; corn salad germinates best in cool soil and will self-sow to provide spring and fall crops with no replanting effort once established.
directions: Direct sow thinly in late summer or early spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, barely covering seeds with fine soil; corn salad (mâche) produces rosettes of tender, spoon-shaped, dark-green leaves with a mild, slightly nutty flavor that is sweeter and less assertive than arugula or watercress. It grows through frost and even light snow — the foliage sweetens with cold — making it one of the most valuable winter salad crops in zones 5–9. In the Gulf South sow in fall for winter and early spring harvest; it will struggle in summer heat. Self-sows freely and can naturalize as a seasonal gap-filler in kitchen gardens. Cut individual outer leaves or harvest whole rosettes as needed.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall; a very cold-hardy salad green also called lamb's lettuce.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in cool soil in late summer or fall, since this green germinates poorly in heat. The small, spoon-shaped leaves form tight rosettes that shrug off hard frosts and can be harvested through winter under a light cover. Cut whole rosettes at the base for their mild, nutty flavor, and let the very cold-hardy plants stand in the garden as a living winter salad supply.

common_name: Corne de Bélier Snow Pea (Ram's Horn Pea)
scientific_name: Pisum sativum var. saccharatum 'Corne de Bélier'
plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil as early as it can be worked and provide a trellis; pick pods while still young and flat for the best flavor and texture, since this snow pea toughens quickly once peas begin to swell.
directions: Corne de Bélier, French for ram's horn, is a classic French heirloom snow pea named for its long, curved, flattened pods. The vigorous climbing vines produce attractive bicolor flowers followed by an abundant set of stringless, tender pods best harvested while young and flat for stir-fries, salads, and quick sautés. It is a long-standing favorite in French market gardens and heirloom seed collections both for its culinary use and for its ornamental flowers. Provide a trellis and pick frequently to keep pods tender and encourage continued production.

common_name: Corne de Cerf Chicory (Stag Horn Chicory)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer for fall and winter cutting; this historic French chicory is named for its deeply antler-like, jagged leaf lobes.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained garden soil in full sun and thin young plants to give room for the sprawling rosette to develop. Corne de Cerf is an old French cutting chicory documented in nineteenth-century seed catalogs, prized for its long, narrow leaves cut into sharp, irregular lobes reminiscent of deer antlers, giving the variety its name. The leaves are eaten young as a pleasantly bitter salad green or cooked briefly like other chicories to mellow the flavor. It is closely related to the Catalogna and asparagus chicory group and, like them, can be allowed to bolt in late winter for tender, blanched inner shoots.

common_name: Cornell Bush Delicata Squash (Compact Non-Vining Delicata)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into warm, fertile soil in full sun; the compact bush habit fits in far less space than standard vining delicata types, making it a good choice for smaller gardens.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing hills to allow the compact bush to fill in without crowding. Cornell Bush Delicata was bred at Cornell University to bring the sweet, nutty, edible-skinned delicata squash into a compact, non-vining bush habit that takes up a fraction of the space of standard vining delicata varieties, making winter squash growing practical in small gardens and raised beds. The oblong, cream-colored fruit striped with green matures with the same rich, sweet, dense orange flesh delicata is prized for, excellent roasted with the thin skin left on. Harvest once the rind has hardened and stripes have deepened in color, and cure fruit in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to improve keeping quality.

common_name: Cornito Giallo Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Yellow Mini Frying Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Cornito Giallo is a compact, container-friendly mini Italian frying pepper bred for heavy yields of small, sweet, thin-walled yellow fruit on a smaller plant than standard Corno di Toro types.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container on a sunny patio. Cornito Giallo is an AAS-winning miniature Italian frying pepper, a scaled-down version of the classic Corno di Toro type, producing an abundance of small, slender, sweet yellow fruits on a compact plant well suited to container culture. Fruits can be picked young and green-yellow for a milder flavor or left to fully color for peak sweetness; the thin walls cook down quickly when sautéed whole. The heavy, continuous fruit set on a relatively small plant makes it one of the more productive choices for patio and small-space pepper growing. Harvest regularly to keep new flowers and fruit coming.

common_name: Cornito Rosso Pepper (Sweet Red Mini Snack Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed.
directions: Transplant into full sun after the soil has warmed, staking lightly if the compact plant becomes heavy with fruit. Cornito Rosso is the red-ripening companion to the yellow Cornito Giallo, an elongated, tapered mini pepper bred for sweet, thin-walled flesh that is equally good eaten fresh as a snack or quickly pan-fried whole. Fruits ripen to a glossy deep red about a week later than the yellow type and hold well on the plant for a long harvest window.

common_name: Corno di Toro Pepper (Bull's Horn Italian Frying Pepper, Sweet and Thin-Walled for Roasting)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Corno di Toro (Italian for 'Bull's Horn') refers to the distinctive elongated, curved form of the ripe pepper, which resembles a bovine horn. Both red and yellow ripening strains are grown in Italy and available in North America. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production; the variety produces vigorously through the Gulf Coast summer and into fall. The thin walls and long curved form make Corno di Toro the ideal roasting pepper: the thin flesh chars and caramelizes quickly under high heat, and the long shape provides a good ratio of skin to flesh. Harvest green for mild flavor or allow to ripen to full red or yellow for maximum sweetness. In Italian cuisine, Corno di Toro is one of the most important culinary peppers — used grilled, fried in olive oil, stuffed, and in antipasto — distinct from bell peppers in texture, sweetness, and cooking properties.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or fully ripe. Corno di Toro (Bull's Horn Pepper) is one of Italy's most beloved culinary peppers — a sweet, thin-walled frying and roasting pepper grown throughout southern and central Italy and named for the long, tapering, curved shape of the ripe fruit that resembles a bull's horn. The typical fruit is 6–10 inches long, 1.5–2 inches wide at the shoulder, tapering to a point, with a slight irregular curve along the length — distinctly different in shape from both the blocky bell pepper and the narrow frying types like Jimmy Nardello. Red-ripening ('Corno di Toro Rosso') and yellow-ripening ('Corno di Toro Giallo') strains are both traditional in Italy and both produce sweet, mild fruit with no heat. The thin walls are the key culinary property: Corno di Toro lacks the thick, watery flesh of bell peppers and has instead a thinner, more concentrated flesh layer that caramelizes deeply and quickly under high cooking heat — roasted in a hot oven or over open flame, the peppers char and soften to a silky, intensely sweet texture that is quite different from the same cooking treatment applied to thick-walled bell peppers. In Italian antipasto tradition, roasted Corno di Toro peppers are dressed with olive oil, garlic, and capers, or sautéed in olive oil until very soft and served as a condiment with grilled meat. The variety has been grown by Italian-American gardeners in the United States for generations and has become more widely available through specialty seed companies.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil has thoroughly warmed and all frost danger has passed; this compact, semi-bush type is well suited to gardens with a history of root-knot nematode or Fusarium wilt problems.
directions: Coronet was developed through a Southern land-grant university breeding program as a compact, semi-bush cream-type southern pea selected for resistance to root-knot nematodes and Fusarium wilt, two soil-borne problems that plague many older cowpea varieties in the Deep South. It holds its pods well above the foliage, making hand-picking easier than with sprawling types. Like other cowpeas, it thrives in hot, humid summer weather that stresses most other vegetable crops and fixes nitrogen in the soil through root nodules, benefiting whatever is planted after it. Harvest pods at the green-shell stage for fresh cream peas or allow them to dry fully on the vine for storage.

plant_note: Sow in fall for winter production in mild climates, or 4-5 weeks before the last spring frost elsewhere; good bolt tolerance allows a later spring sowing than most types.
directions: Direct sow shallowly into cool, moist soil and thin seedlings as they develop, harvesting the upright, easy-to-clean leaves individually or as whole plants. This hybrid forms a distinctly vertical rosette of smooth, dark green leaves that stay cleaner and easier to bunch than sprawling types, while its strong resistance to bolting extends the practical harvest window. Extension programs in warm-winter regions have recommended it for both fall and late-winter plantings where standard spinach would bolt too quickly.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for cool-season production, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Corvair carries resistance to numerous downy mildew races and is slow to bolt, making it a strong choice for the Gulf South's mild winter spinach window.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2-4 inch spacing and use thinnings in salads. Corvair is a smooth-leaf hybrid spinach bred with resistance to numerous races of downy mildew, the fungal disease that most commonly cuts a spinach planting short in humid or damp conditions, and it holds an upright habit that keeps leaves cleaner and easier to harvest than sprawling types. Its slow-bolting habit extends the productive window into warmer weather better than many older varieties, useful for stretching a Gulf Coast spring or fall spinach crop. Harvest by cutting outer leaves for continued production or cutting the whole plant at the base once it has filled out.

plant_note: Direct sow only; carrots do not transplant well. Keep soil surface moist until germination.
directions: A striking carrot with bright purple skin and orange interior, reviving a color grown for over a thousand years. Sow seed directly a quarter inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the surface moist through the slow germination. Thin seedlings to two to three inches so the roots can size up evenly. Harvest when roots reach full size and enjoy the sweet flavor and extra antioxidants in the purple skin.

common_name: Cosmonaut Volkoff Tomato (Russian Red Beefsteak Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Cosmonaut Volkoff is a Russian heirloom tomato said to be named for a Soviet cosmonaut, valued for productive, flavorful red fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Cosmonaut Volkoff bears medium-to-large, deep red, round beefsteak-type fruit with rich, well-balanced flavor on vigorous, productive indeterminate vines, a Russian heirloom that has become a steady favorite among tomato collectors for combining classic flavor with reliable yields. It performs well across a range of climates and continues fruiting over a long summer season. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Cossack Pineapple is a well-known named variety of ground cherry with especially large fruits (for a ground cherry) and an intense pineapple-vanilla flavor, reportedly brought from Russia to the US and long maintained in the Seed Savers Exchange network as one of the finest ground cherry selections.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cossack Pineapple is a well-regarded heirloom ground cherry variety that produces larger fruits than most ground cherry types — up to 3/4 inch — with an intense, complex flavor combining pineapple, vanilla, and a citrus-caramel sweetness that makes it one of the most acclaimed varieties in Seed Savers Exchange evaluations. Like other ground cherries, the fruits are enclosed in papery husks (calyces) that dry and tan as the fruit ripens, and the fruit drops naturally when ripe; collect from the ground and remove the papery husk before eating. Delicious fresh, in pies (ground cherry pie has been popular in the Midwest and Appalachia for generations), in preserves, and dried. Self-sows readily and can naturalize in the garden if left to drop seed.

plant_note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: This Italian heirloom zucchini bears ribbed, mottled fruit with a firm texture and rich, nutty flavor. Harvest young at 4 to 8 inches for the best tenderness, or let fruit reach up to 18 inches for cooking. Pick often to keep the compact plants producing all season. The abundant male blossoms are also excellent stuffed or fried. Water evenly and give plants room for good airflow to reduce powdery mildew.

plant_note: Ribbed Italian heirloom prized for flavor over sheer yield.
directions: This ribbed Italian heirloom zucchini has firm, richly flavored flesh and produces attractive star-shaped slices. Direct sow in warm, fertile soil and give the large, somewhat sprawling plants plenty of room. It yields fewer fruit than hybrids but each has superior nutty flavor and holds up well when grilled. Its abundant male blossoms are excellent for stuffing and frying. Harvest fruit young at 6 to 8 inches for the best texture and to keep production going.

common_name: Costeño Amarillo Pepper (Yellow Coastal Oaxacan Chile)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes; costeño amarillo matures relatively quickly to a golden-yellow to orange color and is the primary chile of the coastal Oaxacan (Isthmus of Tehuantepec) cuisine — it produces the bright yellow color and citrusy flavor characteristic of Oaxacan amarillo mole and the yellow version of memelas and other Isthmus preparations.
directions: Start indoors and transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after frost; harvest at full golden-yellow to orange maturity for drying or fresh use; costeño amarillo is one of the hotter Oaxacan chiles (5,000–15,000 Scoville units) and can be used fresh at the yellow stage or dried to a papery, wrinkled yellow-orange state; the dried chile keeps well for 1–2 years. Costeño Amarillo is a distinctive Mexican landrace chile native to the southern coast of Oaxaca state — particularly the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and the Pacific coastal plain of the Costa Chica region — where it grows in the hot, humid tropical climate and is the defining chile of coastal (costeño) Oaxacan cuisine as distinct from the highland Sierra Norte tradition that uses chilhuacle negro and rojo. The name means simply 'coastal yellow chile' — named for its place of origin and its golden-yellow to orange color when ripe. The fresh and dried chile is distinctive: thin-skinned, elongated (3–4 inches), tapering to a point, and at full maturity a vivid golden-yellow to orange-yellow color that produces the characteristic bright golden color in authentic mole amarillo and the yellow-orange sauces of Tehuantepec cooking. The flavor is moderately hot (5,000–15,000 Scoville units), with a fruity-citrusy quality and a pleasant tartness distinct from the earthier highland varieties. Costeño amarillo is the chile for authentic yellow mole — the sauce for which Oaxacan 'Zapotec-style' tamales are famous — and cannot be genuinely replicated with any other dried chile variety. A critical piece of the Oaxacan chile puzzle for gardeners interested in authentic regional Mexican cooking.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out after the last frost.
directions: A classic Italian heirloom, this indeterminate variety produces deeply ribbed, rich-red fruit of 6 to 8 ounces with an intense, old-world flavor balancing sweetness and acidity. The thick, meaty walls make it ideal for sauces and paste. Provide sturdy staking or a tall cage since vines grow long and heavy. Prune suckers for larger fruit and better airflow. Feed and water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; this classic Italian heirloom is better adapted to warm climates than many northern types, making it an excellent choice for zone 8–10 spring plantings.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant deeply after all frost risk has passed; Costoluto Genovese is a centuries-old Italian heirloom widely grown around Genoa and throughout the Mediterranean, recognizable by its distinctive deeply ribbed, lobed, oblate-flattened fruits with rugged, almost corrugated red skin and intensely flavored, somewhat acidic, meaty flesh that makes it arguably the finest sauce and paste tomato in the heirloom world. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive; fruits weigh 6–10 ounces and are best used cooked, as the complex, tart flavor concentrates beautifully in sauces and soups. Stake or cage firmly and harvest when fully red and slightly soft; in warm climates this variety often produces two flushes — early spring and again in fall.

plant_note: Direct sow with fresh seed once soil is workable in spring, in deep, loose, stone-free soil for straight roots.
directions: Countess is a modern F1 hybrid parsnip bred for strong resistance to canker, the fungal disease that causes unsightly brown-black shoulder rot in many older open-pollinated varieties. It produces long, smooth, uniform roots with a sweet, refined flavor and a notably high percentage of usable roots even in less-than-ideal soil. Because it is an F1 hybrid, seed should be purchased fresh each season rather than saved, and parsnip seed in general loses viability quickly regardless of source. Choose Countess over heirloom types like Hollow Crown where canker has historically been a problem in the garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks after last frost; Country Gentleman is an 1890 white sweet corn heirloom with the distinctive 'shoepeg' kernel arrangement — narrow, crowded, irregular-rowed white kernels packed so densely they have no defined row pattern — producing exceptionally sweet, tender, richly flavored corn considered by many heirloom growers to be the finest-flavored of all old sweet corn varieties.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; isolate from other corn by 250–400 feet or by planting to mature 14 days apart to prevent cross-pollination. Country Gentleman sweet corn dates to 1890 and is a distinctive old SU (standard sugary) type characterized by its 'shoepeg' kernel arrangement — the narrow, elongated, irregular-spaced white kernels are packed so closely they fill the space between rows and lack the defined row pattern of normal corn, a characteristic shared with Stowell's Evergreen and a handful of other white heirloom corns. This unique kernel arrangement has been prized by cooks for generations because the irregular corn can be packed more densely into cans and jars; Country Gentleman shoepeg corn canned at home was a Southern kitchen staple for much of the 20th century. The flavor is rich, complex, and exceptionally sweet for an old-type corn. The variety is a late-season type (88–95 days) suited to long-season gardens; the tall plants (6–8 feet) are vigorous and productive.

common_name: County Fair Cucumber (Bacterial Wilt-Resistant Pickling Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; County Fair was bred at the University of Wisconsin and is one of the few cucumber varieties with genetic resistance to bacterial wilt, a cucumber beetle-vectored disease that can kill an entire planting within days once beetle populations build up in a Gulf South summer.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed; County Fair is a compact, gynoecious pickling cucumber notable among cucumber varieties for carrying real genetic resistance to bacterial wilt, a serious disease spread by cucumber beetle feeding that quickly wilts and kills susceptible vines with no cure once infected. It also shows tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus, powdery mildew, angular leaf spot, and anthracnose, giving it an unusually broad disease package for a pickling type. Fruit is blocky and uniformly sized, ideal for dill or bread-and-butter pickles when picked at 3-5 inches. Because cucumber beetles and the wilt they spread are a persistent problem in warm, humid Gulf Coast gardens, County Fair is a strong choice where bacterial wilt has wiped out other cucumber plantings in the past.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; cousa is the traditional squash of Lebanese, Syrian, and Egyptian cooking — fat, pale green, and slightly sweet, it is the classic squash for stuffing (mahshi kousa) and is exceptionally heat-tolerant for zone 9–11 production.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost; cousa squash is a compact bush type that produces prolifically even in hot weather, making it well-suited to the Gulf Coast and zone 8–11 summer conditions where European zucchini often fails under humidity and heat stress. Cousa is a traditional Middle Eastern summer squash with fat, club-shaped to slightly bulging, light-green to pale-grey-green fruits harvested at 4–6 inches for the classic Levantine stuffed squash dish (mahshi kousa), where the flesh is hollowed out, filled with seasoned rice and meat, and braised in tomato broth; the compact interior, firm flesh, and mild, sweet flavor make it superior to standard zucchini for stuffing as it holds its shape better. Also excellent sliced and sautéed or grilled.

common_name: Covington Sweet Potato (NCSU-Developed Leading Eastern US Commercial Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified slips after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, sandy loam to loamy, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Covington produces the most uniform, symmetrical tubers of commonly available sweet potato varieties — the consistent shape reduces culling and improves yields relative to older varieties.
directions: Plant certified sweet potato slips after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Covington was developed by North Carolina State University and released in 2005 — and has rapidly become the dominant commercial sweet potato variety across the Eastern United States, particularly in North Carolina (the leading sweet potato production state) and throughout the Gulf South. The combination of outstanding tuber uniformity (straight, symmetrical, consistent-sized roots), excellent deep-orange flesh color, good sweetness, exceptional storage quality, and broad adaptability drove Covington's rapid adoption over the previously dominant Beauregard. The copper-orange skin over vivid orange flesh produces the familiar market sweet potato appearance, but the distinctive Covington quality is the remarkable uniformity — roots are notably more consistent in size and shape than Beauregard or older varieties, reducing culled roots and improving marketable yield. The eating quality is excellent: moist, sweet, flavorful orange flesh with good texture after baking, boiling, or roasting. Covington is resistant to Fusarium wilt and several other sweet potato pathogens important in southeastern production. Cure harvested tubers for 5–7 days at 85–90°F with high humidity to convert starches to sugars and develop maximum sweetness.

common_name: Cow Horn Okra (Long-Podded Southern Heirloom Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm and above 70°F; Cow Horn is a tall heirloom producing very long, curved pods that must be harvested at 4–6 inches for eating tenderness — pods left on the plant quickly become fibrous and woody beyond this point. Harvest daily or every other day during peak production.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 70°F, soaking seeds overnight to improve germination; harvest pods at 4–6 inches length before they become fibrous. Cow Horn is a distinctive heirloom okra producing very long, slender, slightly curved pods that visually resemble a cow's horn when mature — one of the more unusual and visually interesting okra types in the Southern heritage seed tradition, with pods that can reach 10–14 inches at full maturity but should be harvested young for eating quality. The curved, ribbed, light-green pods are tender and excellent when harvested young, with the mild okra flavor and characteristic mucilaginous texture that thickens gumbo and gives fried okra its character. Cow Horn plants are tall and vigorous (5–7 feet), producing abundantly through the Southern summer heat season; the large plant size requires adequate spacing and is well-suited to garden rows where height is not a constraint. The variety has been passed down through Southern seed-saving traditions, particularly in the Deep South where heirloom okra varieties have been maintained for generations. The extended pod length also makes Cow Horn excellent for pickled whole okra, where the elongated pods are visually striking in the jar.

common_name: Cow Parsley (Wild Chervil, Queen Anne's Lace Look-alike)
plant_note: CRITICAL WARNING — cow parsley closely resembles poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) and other toxic umbellifers; never harvest or eat any plant in this family unless you are 100% certain of identification; consult multiple expert references before consuming.
directions: Sow seed in fall for natural stratification in moist, fertile soil at woodland edges, shaded borders, or hedgerow margins in partial shade; cow parsley is a widespread European biennial or short-lived perennial with frothy white umbel flowers that naturalize readily in hedgerows and woodland margins. Young stems and leaves have a pleasant, mild parsley-carrot flavor and have been eaten in Britain and Europe as a spring potherb, in salads, and cooked as a vegetable. Despite its culinary history, extreme caution is warranted: cow parsley closely resembles the deadly poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) and water hemlock (Cicuta species); even experienced foragers have been poisoned by misidentification. Learn positive identification from multiple authoritative sources before ever considering consumption.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; cow parsnip is monocarpic (blooms once then dies) but self-seeds freely to maintain a colony. Seeds must be fresh — viability drops sharply after several months. CAUTION: The sap causes severe phototoxic burns (photodermatitis) when skin exposure is followed by sunlight. Always wear gloves when handling plants.
directions: Grow in moist to average, humus-rich soil in partial shade or at woodland edges and stream margins; cow parsnip is the largest native North American member of the carrot family, with enormous palmate leaves and flat-topped white flower umbels up to 12 inches across that serve as insect landing pads for hundreds of pollinator species. The young peeled shoots and leaf stems have been eaten by Indigenous peoples across North America — cooked, the flavor resembles a mild celery-like vegetable. IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: The sap of cow parsnip contains furanocoumarins that cause severe photodermatitis — blisters and burns when sap-exposed skin is hit by sunlight. Always wear gloves and long sleeves when harvesting or handling, and wash hands thoroughly afterward. Do not confuse with the invasive and more toxic giant hogweed (H. mantegazzianum), which is larger with a purple-blotched stem.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches at least 70°F; Cowhorn Okra is an old Southern heirloom named for its unusually long (8–12 inch), slightly curved, pale green pods — much longer than the standard 3–4 inch pods of modern varieties like Clemson Spineless — and is prized by traditional Southern gardeners who prefer large pods for okra pickles and who enjoy the long harvesting window before pods become fibrous.
directions: Soak seeds 8–12 hours in warm water before planting to improve germination; direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun, well-drained soil, 12–18 inches apart; harvest pods at 6–8 inches for tender eating quality — Cowhorn pods remain tender longer than standard varieties at larger sizes. Cowhorn Okra is a traditional Southern heirloom variety whose long, pale green, slightly curved pods inspired the name — resembling the curved horn of a cow — and it has been grown throughout the Gulf South and Deep South for generations as the preferred okra of gardeners who want large pods for pickling and traditional okra dishes. The plants are vigorous and tall (4–6 feet), producing prolifically through the summer heat of zone 9 and the Gulf South, and the pods remain tender at longer lengths (6–8 inches) compared to modern commercial varieties that become fibrous past 3–4 inches. This extended tenderness window makes Cowhorn particularly valued for whole-pod pickling, where large uniform pods are cut to fit mason jars, and for large-format gumbo preparations where longer pod segments are preferred. Cowhorn is a classic open-pollinated heirloom that can be saved seed from year to year; the plants also reseed readily in warm climates if any pods are left to mature. An important ecological note: okra in general is adapted to the same climate as cotton (to which it is related in the Malvaceae family) and handles the heat, humidity, and occasional drought of Gulf Coast summers better than almost any other food crop.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 this is typically February–March for spring and again July–August for a fall crop. Cowpeas actually germinate fastest and produce best at soil temperatures above 70°F — they thrive in summer heat that kills most other legumes.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep into any well-drained soil, including poor sandy or clay soils — cowpeas fix nitrogen and improve soil fertility without added fertilizer. They are exceptionally heat and drought tolerant once established, making them the premier summer legume for the Gulf Coast and similar hot, humid climates. Harvest green-shell peas when pods are plump but skins are still soft, or leave pods to dry on the vine for dry beans. Bush types need no support; vining or half-runner types benefit from a simple trellis. Inoculate seeds with cowpea rhizobia if growing in new ground for maximum nitrogen fixation.

plant_note: Sow directly in early spring; can be harvested leaf by leaf or cut whole, often regrowing a second flush in cool conditions.
directions: Sow directly in early spring; a Polish heirloom loose-leaf lettuce, named for Kraków, with deeply notched, savoyed red-bronze leaves and a fast cut-and-come-again habit. It matures quickly from an early spring sowing and can be harvested leaf by leaf or cut whole, often regrowing a second flush in cool conditions. Central European seed keepers have maintained it for generations as a colorful, reliable early salad green.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost when soil is reliably above 60°F; avoid planting in wet, cold soil which causes seed rot.
directions: Sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; cranberry beans can be grown as a bush or pole type depending on variety. Harvest at the fresh shell stage when pods are colorfully streaked with red and cream and beans inside are plump but not yet dry — this is the classic fresh borlotti stage prized in Italian cooking. For dried beans, leave pods on the plant until they are papery and rattle when shaken, then pull entire plants and cure under cover before threshing. Regular watering during pod fill prevents shriveled beans.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4–6 weeks earlier for an earlier harvest; in frost-free zones sow any time of year.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after soil warms to 70°F; the deep burgundy-red, deeply lobed foliage is ornamental throughout the season, making this one of the most attractive edible plants for a zone 9–11 garden. The young leaves have a tart, cranberry-sorrel flavor excellent in salads, wraps, and as a garnish; the fuchsia flowers are also edible and make a vivid cranberry-colored tea. In zone 9–11 it grows as a perennial but blooms only in short days, producing flowers in late fall; in cooler zones treat as a warm-season annual for leaf harvest. Cut back by half in late summer to promote fresh tender growth.

common_name: Crane Melon (California Heirloom Sonoma County Specialty Melon)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Crane melon was developed for California's cool coastal conditions (Sonoma County summers are cool compared to inland valleys) and is worth trying in zone 9 with selective timing. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–August harvest. Crane melons have an unusual asymmetric, lopsided shape as they develop — this is normal and characteristic. Reduce irrigation 2 weeks before expected maturity to concentrate sugars.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; reduce irrigation as fruits near maturity. Harvest when the skin turns from green to cream-white to pale gold and a sweet, complex aroma is detectable at the stem end. Crane melon is a California heirloom developed by Oliver Crane in Santa Rosa, Sonoma County, California in the 1920s–1930s — a melon variety born from the crossing of several melon types over multiple generations that became a regional specialty deeply associated with its place of origin, to the point that authentic Crane melons are considered a Slow Food Ark of Taste variety. The fruits are large (5–10 lbs or more), irregularly shaped — often lopsided, elongated, or vaguely oblong with uneven shoulders — with cream-white to pale tan, slightly netted or smooth skin that looks nothing like the standard cantaloupe. The appearance is rustic and non-commercial, which partly explains why the Crane melon never became a commercial crop despite extraordinary flavor. The white to pale cream-colored flesh is extremely sweet and aromatic, with a complex vanilla-floral character that many tasters describe as the best-flavored melon they have ever tasted — a flavor profile unlike any other commonly available melon type. Crane melons are a California heirloom of significant regional importance and represent the type of locally-adapted, place-specific vegetable variety that defines the Slow Food movement's preservation work.

plant_note: Sow directly into loose, deep soil once the ground can be worked, and allow a long season for full-size roots since it bulks up more slowly than modern hybrid beets.
directions: Considered one of the oldest documented beet varieties still in cultivation, tracing back to at least the 1600s in France, where its name (French for toad) refers to the rough, dark gray-brown bark-like skin that develops as the root matures. Sow directly into loose, deep soil once the ground can be worked, and expect a slower bulking rate than modern hybrid beets, so allow a long season for full-size roots. The deep garnet flesh stays firm and sweet, making Crapaudine one of the best-keeping beets for winter root cellar storage. Light frost before harvest improves its already rich, earthy sweetness.

plant_note: Sow directly in the cool season; notably slow to bolt, suited to late-spring and early-summer sowings.
directions: Sow directly in the cool season; this heirloom Batavia lettuce from southern France, its name loosely translating to crunchy one of the Midi, produces elongated, savoyed, crisp heads bred to withstand the hot, dry summers of Provence. It is notably slow to bolt, making it well suited to late-spring and early-summer sowings when many other lettuces would turn bitter. Heirloom seed houses reintroduced it to American gardeners as a heat-season alternative to iceberg.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring and July–August for fall. Cream crowder peas are among the most heat-tolerant of all pea types and are the traditional crowder style of the Gulf Coast South.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun, without pre-soaking or inoculation unless growing in new ground. Cream crowder peas take their name from the cream-colored seeds that pack (crowd) tightly into the pods, producing a high yield per pod. The large, plump seeds are preferred for fresh shelling over black-eye or purple hull types in much of Louisiana and Mississippi, where cream peas have been a kitchen garden tradition for generations. The mild, starchy flavor cooks smoothly into soups and side dishes; combine with hog jowl and rice for the classic Louisiana New Year's Day luck dish. Plants are drought-tolerant once established and thrive in the summer heat that ends most other legumes.

plant_note: Start indoors and set out after frost danger passes.
directions: This determinate variety bears cylindrical, cream to pale-yellow fruit best picked at about 3 inches when they resemble small sausages. The smooth, buttery, mild flavor is excellent eaten fresh or simmered into pale sauces. The compact bush habit suits containers and small beds and needs little staking. Because it sets fruit over a concentrated window, it is well suited to canning batches. Keep watering steady to avoid cracking.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors 3 weeks early in short-season areas.
directions: This heirloom watermelon produces round, 6 to 11 pound fruit about 10 inches across with sweet, creamy pale-white flesh under a thin, delicate rind. Its relatively short season makes it a good choice for northern gardens, especially with a black plastic mulch to warm the soil. Handle the fragile rind gently at harvest. Water deeply but reduce moisture as fruit ripens to concentrate sweetness. Give vines ample space to sprawl.

common_name: Cream of the Crop Acorn Squash (White Bush Acorn Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed, once soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil once frost risk has passed, spacing plants for their compact bush habit which suits smaller garden beds. Cream of the Crop was named an All-America Selections winner in 1990 for its productive bush vines and creamy white-skinned acorn-type fruit with golden, nutty-flavored flesh. Its space-saving growth habit made it notable among winter squash of its time, since most acorn squash varieties before it required significantly more sprawling room.

plant_note: Direct-sow after the last frost in a partially shaded spot with consistent moisture, such as a woodland edge or the base of a fence in dappled light. This native vine self-seeds freely and may naturalize in suitable gardens.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in moist, well-amended soil in a partly shaded location after the last frost date. This delicate, tendriling vine climbs readily through neighboring shrubs, fences, or trellises and requires little care beyond consistent moisture. Harvest the tiny, striped-green fruits while they are still firm and cucumber-green — they are mild and crisp eaten fresh or pickled; never eat fruits that have turned black, as ripe fruits have a strong laxative effect. The plant often self-seeds generously, so allow a few mature fruits to drop if you want it to return next season.

plant_note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant out around the last frost.
directions: This award-winning eschalion produces oblong, 4 to 5 inch bulbs with coppery-pink skin and rosy-purple inner rings, combining the fruity sweetness of shallots with the easy peeling of onions. Start seed indoors early since it needs a long season to size up. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Keep beds weed-free and evenly watered until tops begin to fall, then cure bulbs in a dry, airy spot. Stored properly they keep for months.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost when soil has reached 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for summer harvest, or August for fall. Crenshaw is a large melon requiring 90–110 days and very hot conditions for full ripening — best in zone 9 gardens with a long, warm summer. Requires 6–8 feet between plants.
directions: Plant in hills of 3–4 seeds in full sun, well-drained, fertile soil; Crenshaw (also spelled Cranshaw) is an old American hybrid between Casaba and Persian melon types, producing very large (8–10 pound), distinctively shaped fruits — pointed at the stem end, rounded at the blossom end, with smooth, pale green-yellow skin that turns golden-yellow at maturity. The flesh is thick, deep salmon-orange, nearly seed-free in the center, very juicy, extremely sweet and fragrant with a complex flavor combining the rich sweetness of cantaloupe with the floral aromatics of a Persian melon — widely considered among the finest-flavored melons available. Crenshaw requires intense heat to develop its characteristic sweetness, making zone 9's long summer ideal. Harvest when the blossom end yields to gentle thumb pressure and the skin turns golden and waxy; a fully ripe Crenshaw has a heavenly, heady fragrance. They do not keep long after picking — eat within a few days. For years they were a fixture at high-end produce markets and disappearing from supply chains has made them a garden treasure.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in October–November in zone 9; Creole garlic requires less vernalization (cold) than northern hardneck varieties and is specifically adapted to the mild winters of the Gulf South. It is the RECOMMENDED garlic type for zone 9 — hardneck varieties (Rocambole, Porcelain) fail to bulb properly in mild winters without pre-chilling.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Creole garlic (Allium sativum subsp. sativum) is a group of softneck garlic varieties historically cultivated in the hot, humid regions of southern Spain and the Americas, and the only garlic group that performs consistently well in zone 9 Gulf Coast conditions. While northern hardneck varieties (Rocambole, Purple Stripe, Porcelain) require 6–8 weeks of cold below 40°F for proper bulb formation, Creole types bulb reliably in zone 9 mild winters without pre-chilling. Named varieties include 'Ajo Rojo,' 'Burgundy,' 'Creole Red,' and 'Pescadero Red.' The bulbs are medium to large with 8–12 purple-streaked cloves per head; flavor is complex, rich, and moderately hot with a lingering sweet aftertaste distinctly different from commercial Chinese garlic. Creole garlic also stores significantly longer than most hardneck types — up to 9–12 months in a cool, dry location. For zone 9 gardeners who struggle to grow garlic successfully, switching to Creole types is transformative. Harvest when lower leaves die and 4–5 green leaves remain; cure for 3–4 weeks in a shaded, airy location.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes for a summer harvest.
directions: This heat-tolerant Creole-type garlic has bright pinkish-red wrappers and yields the largest bulbs in mild-winter regions, with a distinctive shallot-like flavor. Plant single cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart, in fall in loose, fertile, well-drained soil. Mulch after planting, keep evenly watered in spring, and stop watering as the lower leaves brown. Harvest when several lower leaves have died back, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing.

common_name: Creole Rose Garlic (Warm-Climate Softneck Garlic for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves (pointed end up, blunt end down) 1–2 inches deep and 6 inches apart in fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Creole garlic does NOT require the long cold vernalization needed by northern hardneck varieties — a key distinction making it one of the only garlic types that reliably forms full-size bulbs in zone 8-10.
directions: Plant individual cloves 1–2 inches deep, pointed end up, 4–6 inches apart in fall (October–November in zone 9) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Creole Rose is a Creole-type garlic — one of the most important garlic types for Gulf South gardeners because it forms full, large bulbs without the cold-vernalization requirement that makes most northern hardneck garlic types unreliable in zone 8-10. While Rocambole, Purple Stripe, and Porcelain hardneck garlics require many weeks of cold temperatures below 40°F to form proper bulbs, Creole garlics originated in warm-climate regions of Spain and the American South and thrive with the mild winters of zone 8-10. 'Creole Rose' produces attractive bulbs with rose-pink to rosy-purple outer wrappers and large, flavorful, ivory cloves with a rich, complex, moderately sharp garlic flavor — excellent for roasting, where the flavor becomes sweet and nutty, and for raw preparations where its full-bodied character is distinctive. Plant in fall for spring harvest: in zone 9, plant October through December for a late March–May harvest when the lower leaves begin to brown and fall over. Allow at least two weeks of drying in a warm, airy location after harvest before storage. The scape (central flower stalk) of softneck types is not produced, unlike the decorative and edible scapes of hardneck types.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. In zone 9, Creole tomato is also widely grown as a fall crop from a mid-to-late-summer sowing for harvest before the first frost.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage for support; consistent moisture prevents blossom end rot and cracking in humid conditions. Creole is an indeterminate tomato developed by the LSU AgCenter specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the lower Mississippi River valley, and it gave its name to the famous 'Creole tomatoes' grown in the rich alluvial soil of Louisiana's river parishes and sold at the long-running French Market in New Orleans. It sets fruit reliably even through the hot, muggy stretches of a Gulf South summer that cause many other tomatoes to drop blossoms, and carries useful resistance to fusarium wilt and other soilborne diseases common in southern gardens. The medium-large, deep red, globe-shaped fruits have the rich, well-balanced sweet-acid flavor that built the Creole tomato's regional reputation, celebrated every June at the New Orleans French Market Creole Tomato Festival. A dependable, disease-resistant choice for zone 4–11 gardeners who want a genuinely Deep South tomato.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or earliest spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop.
directions: This English heritage broad bean dates to at least the early 1800s and was nearly lost before a handful of seeds were rescued and redistributed by heirloom seed preservationists, making it as much a conservation story as a garden vegetable. Unlike the white blossoms of most fava beans, Crimson Flowered produces clusters of deep magenta-crimson flowers that make the plant genuinely ornamental as well as productive, followed by shorter, upright pods holding 3 to 4 beans each. Grow it exactly as any fava, sowing directly into cool, fertile soil and pinching growing tips once the lowest pods have set to discourage aphids. Shell the beans young and tender for the best flavor, or let a portion of the crop dry fully for storage and traditional slow-cooked dishes.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: This large spring radish reaches 1 to 2 inches across with a crisp white interior and a mild flavor perfect for salads and sandwiches. It grows fast, making it a great choice for children and impatient gardeners. Sow directly in cool weather since heat causes it to bolt and turn pithy. Thin seedlings early to give roots room to swell. Keep soil evenly moist for tender, uncracked roots.

plant_note: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while dormant; in zone 7 plant January–February. Crimson Red rhubarb performs best in zones 3–7 where reliable cold winters provide the 500+ chilling hours it requires for dormancy break and vigorous growth. In zone 8 it may perform adequately for several seasons before declining. Do not harvest stalks in the first year to allow full establishment. In spring only take no more than one-third of the stalks to preserve plant vigor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with good organic matter; Crimson Red is a named rhubarb variety selected for deep red stalk color throughout the length of the stalk — many rhubarb varieties, including the popular Victoria, produce stalks that are primarily green with only a reddish blush at the base, while Crimson Red maintains the desirable deep red color from base to tip. The red color has no effect on flavor (rhubarb's characteristic tart-sour character comes from oxalic and malic acids regardless of color) but makes the stalks more visually appealing in fresh preparations and strawberry-rhubarb pies where the vivid red shows through the filling. The flavor is the same bright, intense rhubarb tartness that defines the species. Crimson Red is also grown as an ornamental vegetable — the large, dramatic dark red stalks and enormous ribbed leaves create a striking architectural effect in the garden before harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow into hot soil; a heat-tolerant heirloom with striped rind and red flesh.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in hills only after the soil is thoroughly hot, since watermelons demand warmth. Give the long vines ample room and steady water while the fruits size up, then ease off watering as they near ripeness to concentrate sugars. The 20 to 25 pound striped melons are ripe when the ground spot turns creamy yellow and the tendril nearest the fruit dries.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 4–6 seeds (thin to 2–3 plants per hill) after soil warms to 70°F and all frost danger passes; in zone 9, plant late March through late April; watermelon needs a long warm season and abundant water through fruit development — irrigation is essential in dry periods.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil warms; Crimson Sweet is the most widely planted home-garden slicing watermelon in American horticulture — an open-pollinated variety introduced in 1964 that set the standard for the modern round-to-oblong, striped watermelon with deep crimson flesh and excellent crisp texture. The light green fruits with dark green stripes grow to 15–25 pounds with a hard rind, making them good keepers and suited for roadside stands and home storage. The deep crimson, firm-textured flesh has excellent flavor — very sweet with the quintessential watermelon aroma. Crimson Sweet introduced the high lycopene, disease-resistant genetics that are the foundation of modern watermelon breeding programs. In zone 9, watermelon is a warm-season crop that thrives in the heat — plant after the last frost in late March or April for summer harvest in July–August. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil, abundant space, and consistent irrigation through fruit development; drought stress during fruit fill causes small fruit and hollow heart. Determine ripeness by the ground spot yellowing from white to yellow, the curling of the tendril nearest the fruit, and a hollow 'thump' sound when knocked.

common_name: Crimson Tide Watermelon (Fusarium-Resistant Crimson Sweet Type Hybrid)
plant_note: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, or transplant young seedlings; this hybrid's Fusarium wilt resistance makes it a dependable choice for fields or beds with a history of vine decline.
directions: Crimson Tide is a Crimson Sweet-type F1 hybrid bred for growers who need reliable Fusarium wilt resistance without giving up the classic bright red, crisp-fleshed eating quality that made Crimson Sweet famous. Fruits run large, around 20-25 pounds, semi-elongated in shape, with a slightly darker green stripe pattern than standard Crimson Sweet. Because seed-borne and soil-borne wilts can build up in beds planted to melons repeatedly, this hybrid is a practical option for gardeners rotating crops on limited space where full rotation isn't always possible. Manage it like any full-size vining watermelon: full sun, warm soil, steady moisture through fruit fill, and a dry-down period before harvest to maximize sweetness.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting. Crista carries a broad disease-resistance package developed for Southeastern growing conditions, reducing spray needs in humid gardens.
directions: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Crista is a determinate hybrid slicing tomato bred as part of the North Carolina State University Southeastern tomato improvement program, which targets the combination of diseases (Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt, and gray leaf spot chief among them) that most often cut short a tomato season in the humid Southeast. Fruits are medium-large, round, and firm with reliable, well-rounded flavor rather than novelty sweetness, making Crista a workhorse slicer for the kitchen rather than a specialty variety. The compact determinate plants concentrate their harvest over a few weeks, which suits gardeners who want a predictable crop for canning or sharing. Stake or cage for support and clean fruit, and keep watering consistent through fruit set to avoid blossom end rot in the Gulf South's swings between downpours and dry spells.

common_name: Crosby's Egyptian Beet (Flat-Root Heirloom Early Beet)
plant_note: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in well-amended, deeply tilled soil; thin to 4–5 inches apart after germination. Crosby's Egyptian is a somewhat flat-rooted variety that develops well even in shallow or compacted soils where globe-shaped varieties may also struggle; the flat shape is an adaptation to the heavy soils where Egyptian-type beets were historically grown. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall/winter harvest; excellent flavor after light frosts.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in well-amended, fertile soil with consistent moisture; thin to 4–5 inch spacing after germination for root development. Crosby's Egyptian is an American heirloom beet dating to before 1869, developed by Josiah Crosby of Massachusetts from the older Egyptian type and named for both its creator and the flat-topped root shape associated with Egyptian-type beets — a distinctly different root form from the round globe shape of Detroit-type beets and the cylindrical shape of Cylindra and Formanova. The flat-topped, medium-sized roots have very dark, nearly black-red skin, deep red flesh with excellent texture, and a rich, sweet, earthy flavor that beet enthusiasts often consider superior to modern round types — more complex and less sweet without being harsh. Crosby's Egyptian is one of the earlier-maturing beet varieties (55–65 days) and was particularly valued in New England gardens for its early productivity when other beets were still sizing up. The slightly flattened shape makes the beets easy to peel evenly after boiling and gives them a distinctive appearance in pickled or roasted presentations. Widely grown in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic states throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, Crosby's Egyptian represents the heirloom beet tradition at its finest and remains a deserving choice for gardeners who want historical authenticity alongside excellent eating quality.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep around the time of last frost; crosne prefers cool growing conditions and produces its best tubers in fall before heavy frost.
directions: Plant small knobbly tubers 2–3 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost; crosne has a straggly growth habit with square stems and small lavender flowers typical of the mint family. The tops die back in fall, signaling that tubers have reached full size — harvest by digging carefully, as the small spiral tubers break easily. Leave some tubers in the ground for next season’s planting stock. Tubers are eaten unpeeled; the thin ivory skin is too delicate and intricate to remove. Steam or sauté briefly — the texture is crunchy like a water chestnut with a mild, slightly nutty flavor.

common_name: Crowder Pea (Iron and Clay, Mississippi Purple)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms to at least 65°F; crowder peas are extremely heat-tolerant and thrive in the deep South when planted through summer — successive plantings every 3–4 weeks extend the harvest season through first fall frost.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in rows 18–24 inches apart in full sun in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; crowder peas get their name because the seeds are crowded so tightly in the pod that they press against each other and develop flat sides. They are a cornerstone of Southern cuisine — shelled fresh and cooked with pot likker and fatback, or dried for winter storage — and also a superb summer cover crop that fixes atmospheric nitrogen at high rates in hot weather. Bush-type plants need no support and mature quickly even in poor, sandy soils. Pick pods when they have turned fully colored (purple, tan, or buff depending on variety) and the seeds feel firm but not hard for fresh-shell use; allow pods to dry completely on the vine for dry peas.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is warm; Crown Prince requires a long warm season (95–110 days) and ample space for the vigorous sprawling vines (up to 12 feet). Harvest when the skin has hardened and turned from green to its characteristic steel-blue-grey tone; the skin does not 'slip' like butternut but the stem begins to dry. Store in a cool, dry location for outstanding long-term keeping (up to 12 months).
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills (3–4 seeds per hill, thin to 2 plants) after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; harvest when the stem begins to cork and dry and the skin is completely firm. Crown Prince is a Cucurbita maxima winter squash of Japanese origin that became a dominant market squash in the United Kingdom and Australia and has grown in popularity in the US — producing medium-large (6–12 lb) flat-lobed fruits with an unusual and striking steel-blue to silver-grey skin color that makes them one of the most distinctive vegetables in the fall garden. The skin color is unlike any other commonly grown squash and makes Crown Prince exceptional as both a culinary and ornamental squash.
