The flesh is deep orange, dense, smooth-textured, and richly sweet with a complex, almost butterscotch-like flavor profile that many tasters consider among the best of any squash; it lacks the wateriness of less concentrated types and has a low seed cavity relative to flesh volume. Crown Prince keeps exceptionally well (6–12 months in proper cool, dry storage) and the long storage window makes it valuable for extended autumn and winter cooking. In zone 9, direct sow in March–April for a July–August harvest, or in August for a November harvest if the growing season allows. An excellent choice for serious squash growers wanting a variety with both superior flavor and visual impact.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; Crystal Apple is a New Zealand heirloom cucumber that ripens to a creamy-white to ivory color and round to oval apple shape rather than the typical green cylinder, with thin, non-bitter skin, crisp texture, and mild, sweet flavor that makes it one of the most delicious and heat-tolerant cucumbers for warm-climate gardens.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in warm soil; Crystal Apple can sprawl on the ground or be trellised — vertical growing keeps fruits cleaner and makes them easier to find. Crystal Apple is a New Zealand heirloom cucumber producing distinctively rounded to oval fruits about the size and shape of a small apple, ripening from green to creamy-white to ivory-yellow; the fruits are tender-skinned with no bitterness at any stage, with exceptionally mild, refreshing, sweet flavor even when large. They are best harvested at the white-to-pale-ivory stage before turning yellow, when the interior is crisp and seeds are still small. An outstanding cucumber for warm-climate gardens: more heat-tolerant than most slicing types, with less bitterness in hot conditions; highly productive and self-trellising if grown on a support. Popular at farmers markets for the unusual appearance and superior flavor.

common_name: Crystal Lemon Cucumber (Lemon Cucumber, Crystal Apple)
plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost or direct sow after last frost; harvest when fruits are pale yellow-ivory and 2–3 inches in diameter — they become seedy and bitter if allowed to ripen further to full yellow.
directions: Direct sow or transplant to well-drained, warm, enriched soil in full sun after last frost; Crystal Lemon cucumber (sometimes called Crystal Apple) produces round to oval fruits roughly the size and color of a lemon at harvest — pale ivory to pale yellow, 2–3 inches in diameter, with a very mild, sweet, almost non-existent bitterness and a thin skin that does not need peeling. One of the most productive and heat-tolerant cucumbers available, and excellent for gardeners who find regular cucumbers too bitter or those who want a conversation-starting variety. Fruits should be harvested while still pale ivory-yellow; fully yellow fruits are over-ripe and seedy. Very popular with children for its unusual round shape.

common_name: Crystal White Wax Onion (Heirloom Pickling and Sweet Onion)
plant_note: Start seed indoors in late winter and set transplants out about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost.
directions: Sow seed thickly for baby pickling-size bulbs or space more widely for larger fresh-eating onions, transplanting into loose, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Harvest small bulbs young for pickling once they reach the desired size, or allow later sowings to size up further for fresh use, since this variety does not store well long-term. Crystal White Wax is a historic short-day southern heirloom whose small, flattened, pure-white bulbs and mild flavor made it the classic choice for cocktail onions and pickled onions, and it was among the parent stock used to develop the modern Vidalia sweet onion.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil warms to at least 60°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and maintain soil at 80°F for best germination; grow seedlings in bright light to prevent stretching. The cubanelle produces thin-walled, tapered fruits 4–6 inches long that ripen from pale yellowish-green to red; they are nearly sweet with very mild heat and excellent for frying, stuffing, and fresh eating. Harvest green fruits at 65 days or leave on the plant to ripen red for sweeter flavor. Plants are prolific producers; side-dress with a balanced fertilizer midseason to maintain yield.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; cucamelon dislikes root disturbance so use biodegradable pots.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep in warm mix indoors and pot on without disturbing the root ball when transplanting; cucamelon develops a large tuberous root that can overwinter in frost-free climates. Train the delicate vines up a trellis or netting and keep soil consistently moist for best fruit set. Harvest the grape-sized fruits when they look like tiny watermelons and feel firm — they become seedy and bitter if left too long. The flavor is a pleasant combination of cucumber and lime; pick frequently to maintain heavy production.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil temperature is at least 65°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills or rows once soil has warmed to at least 65°F. Cucumbers are high feeders; amend beds with compost and side-dress with nitrogen once vines begin running. Train vines onto a trellis to improve airflow and make harvest easier. Pick slicing types at 6–8 inches and pickling types at 2–4 inches to keep plants productive and prevent bitterness from over-ripe fruit.

common_name: Cucuzza (Italian Edible Gourd, Sicilian Snake Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and danger of frost has passed, giving the sprawling vine a sturdy arbor or fence so the long, pale-green fruit can hang straight rather than curl on the ground.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and danger of frost has passed, and give the sprawling vine a sturdy arbor or fence so the long, pale-green fruit can hang straight rather than curl on the ground. Cucuzza is a long-season Italian-American heirloom bottle gourd grown throughout Louisiana's historically Sicilian communities, where the immature fruit is peeled and cooked like a mild summer squash in soups, stews, and sautés. Left on the vine past the edible stage, the mature shell dries into a hard, lightweight gourd useful for crafts. It thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity and, like other bottle gourds, benefits from hand-pollination in the evening since its flowers open at night for moth pollinators.

common_name: Cue Ball Squash (Round Pale Green Hybrid Summer Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed; open bush habit works well in raised beds.
directions: Cue Ball is a round-fruited hybrid squash bred as a paler, milder companion to the dark-skinned Eight Ball type, producing pale green fruit mottled with white on an open, upright bush that keeps the golf-ball to billiard-ball-sized squash easy to spot. Harvest at around 3 inches in diameter for the best texture, since the round shape can hide inside the foliage and size up quickly in hot weather. Its resistance to watermelon mosaic virus and zucchini yellow mosaic virus is a real advantage in humid Gulf Coast summers where aphid-spread viruses build up on cucurbits. The compact plant works well in raised beds where a standard vining summer squash would be too sprawling.

common_name: Cumari do Pará Pepper (Brazilian Wild Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 7-9 weeks before the last frost on gentle bottom heat, then transplant once the weather is reliably warm.
directions: Start seed indoors 7-9 weeks before the last frost with gentle bottom heat, since this small-fruited chinense type is slow to establish, and transplant once nights stay warm. The bushy plants benefit from routine picking, which encourages continuous flowering and fruit set through the season. Cumari do Pará comes from the Pará region of Brazil and produces tiny, round to oval berry-like fruits on long thin stems that belie an intense, sharp heat, and it is traditionally used fresh, pickled in vinegar, or as a garnish. Its diminutive size makes it a good candidate for container growing despite the plant's habanero-relative heat level.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Cuostralee is a regular-leaf indeterminate that needs sturdy staking to hold up its one- to two-pound fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, fertile soil, staking firmly to support the heavy fruit. Cuostralee is an old French family heirloom obtained from a grower in Hellimer, France in 1992 by American tomato collectors Craig LeHoullier and Carolyn Male, who helped introduce it to North American gardeners. Its deeply ribbed, pink-red fruit can top a pound or more per tomato and is known for dense, meaty flesh and a rich, old-fashioned sweet flavor.

common_name: Cupid's Shaving Brush (Ebolo, Yoruba Tassel Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cupid's shaving brush self-sows readily in warm, humid climates and is typically grown as a cut-and-come-again warm-season green.
directions: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Cupid's shaving brush self-sows readily in warm, humid climates and is typically grown as a cut-and-come-again warm-season green. Known as ebolo in West African cooking, this fast-growing, weedy annual produces tender, slightly bitter, mineral-rich leaves used cooked in soups and stews much like a spinach substitute, along with small, tufted, magenta-pink brush-like flower heads that give the plant its whimsical common name. It tolerates the heat, humidity, and light shade of a Gulf South summer better than most temperate greens, continuing to produce through the hottest months when lettuce and spinach have long since bolted. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips regularly to keep plants productive and delay flowering, and expect volunteer seedlings the following season once it is established in a bed.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop; sow again in late summer for a fall harvest when flavor improves with light frost exposure. Successive sowings every 2-3 weeks extend the harvest window considerably.
directions: Scatter seeds thinly in rows 12 inches apart and cover lightly with 1/4 inch of fine soil; curled mustard germinates rapidly and can be thinned progressively, using the thinnings as baby salad greens while allowing remaining plants to develop full size. Young leaves are mild and work well fresh in salads or as a peppery sandwich green, while more mature leaves develop significant heat and are best wilted briefly in a hot pan or added to soups and stir-fries. The frilly, often purple-tinged foliage is among the most ornamental of the edible brassicas and lends visual appeal to the kitchen garden through the cool months. Avoid overhead watering late in the day, and pull plants promptly when they begin to bolt, as the leaves become very pungent and tough once the flower stalk elongates.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or fall in a dedicated patch; curly dock is a very vigorous perennial that naturalizes readily and can become difficult to remove once established — choose the site carefully, as the deep taproot is hard to eradicate. It thrives in disturbed ground, roadsides, and moist areas in virtually every temperate climate.
directions: Plant in a controlled bed or harvest wild populations growing in moist, disturbed soils; the young spring leaves of curly dock are one of the first edible wild greens available in early spring, with a pleasantly tart, lemony flavor from the oxalic acid content. They are excellent raw in small quantities in salads, or cooked briefly to reduce the oxalates in soups, stews, and egg dishes. Larger, older leaves are tougher and more strongly flavored — cook with one change of water to moderate the sourness. The seeds, which form on tall russet-colored stalks in summer, can be winnowed, ground into meal, and added to flatbread or porridge. The thick yellow taproot (yellow dock) has a long history of use in herbal medicine as a digestive bitter. Moderately invasive in the garden; contain by removing seed stalks before they mature.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for the main crop, or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last spring frost for spring planting. Kale is frost-hardy and actually improves in flavor after light frosts convert starches to sugars.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost, or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last spring frost; curly kale is one of the most cold-hardy and nutritious leafy vegetables available, withstanding temperatures well below freezing and actually improving dramatically in sweetness and flavor after repeated light frosts convert the leaf starches to sugars. Harvest outer leaves continuously from midsummer or fall onward, leaving the growing center intact — plants will continue producing through winter in zone 7–11 and into early spring in colder zones. Rich in vitamins K, A, and C as well as minerals; the tightly curled, dark-green to blue-green leaves are widely used raw in salads, massaged in dressings, and cooked in soups, stir-fries, and braised dishes. Excellent companion to short-day cover crops and a staple of the fall-to-spring kitchen garden.

common_name: Currant Tomato (Wild-Species Ancestor Tomato with Intensely Complex Flavor, Tiny Fruits)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Currant Tomato (Solanum pimpinellifolium) is a wild-species tomato or near-wild type — the wild ancestor of cultivated tomatoes — producing tiny (1/4 to 1/2 inch) fruits on vigorous, sprawling vines that can spread 4–6 feet or more. In zone 9, transplant March–April; S. pimpinellifolium is more heat and drought tolerant than cultivated tomatoes and continues producing through Gulf Coast summers that stress standard varieties. The vines behave somewhat like perennials in zone 9b, potentially surviving mild winters to produce again the following year. Provide a large cage or trellis — the vines are more vigorous than most garden tomatoes. The tiny fruits are produced in very large clusters and ripen red, producing a seemingly endless supply of intensely-flavored small tomatoes through the season. This species is extremely easy to grow and extremely productive in zone 9's warm conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after last frost; provide large cage or trellis. Harvest clusters when red throughout. Solanum pimpinellifolium, the currant tomato, is the wild progenitor species of modern cultivated tomatoes — one of the wild species native to western South America (Ecuador and Peru) from which Solanum lycopersicum was domesticated thousands of years ago by indigenous peoples of the Americas. The currant tomato has been preserved as a distinct variety in seed collections and home gardens and represents a connection to the pre-domestication history of the tomato: the tiny fruits (roughly the size of a pea or large currant, giving the species its common name) look nothing like modern beefsteak or even cherry tomatoes, but they represent the ancestral form before artificial selection increased fruit size dramatically over millennia. Despite or because of this wild ancestry, the flavor of currant tomatoes is frequently described as intense, complex, and distinctly more flavorful than larger cultivated varieties — a small amount of wild material containing concentrated flavor compounds produces a dramatically different eating experience from a standard cherry tomato. The flavor is balanced sweet-acid with herbal, almost earthy notes that have led food writers to describe currant tomatoes as tasting 'more like a real tomato' than most cultivated varieties. The species is also significantly more heat, drought, and disease tolerant than cultivated tomatoes — traits expected from a wild plant that survived without human irrigation or disease management. In zone 9, S. pimpinellifolium plants perform exceptionally well through the full summer growing season and can sometimes persist as short-lived perennials in the mildest locations.

plant_note: Plant small whole tubers or cut tuber pieces in spring in well-drained, loose, humus-rich, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; cush cush is the only domesticated yam native to the Americas — a South American and Caribbean vine yam producing high-quality, purple-fleshed or white-fleshed tubers with excellent flavor and a smooth, non-mucilaginous texture; it was an important food crop of Caribbean indigenous peoples before European contact.
directions: Plant small tubers in loose, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; provide trellis for the climbing vine. Dioscorea trifida (cush cush yam or mapuey) is the only major cultivated yam native to the Americas — all other important yams (D. alata, D. cayenensis, D. rotundata) originate from Asia or Africa. Native to the Caribbean, Central America, and the Amazon Basin, where it was cultivated as an important food crop by indigenous peoples before European contact, cush cush yam produces distinctive tubers — often three-lobed (hence 'trifida' and the name 'cush cush') — with high-quality flesh ranging from white to cream to purple-violet, depending on variety. The flesh is notably smooth and non-mucilaginous (unlike many Asian yams), with a mildly sweet, earthy, chestnut-like flavor. Cush cush yam is considered one of the finest-flavored yams in terms of culinary quality: the texture cooks to a smooth, dry, mealy consistency similar to the best potatoes. Purple-fleshed varieties have high anthocyanin content and a spectacular color. The vine is ornamental — the deeply three-lobed, arrowhead-shaped leaves are distinctive and attractive. One of the most overlooked Native American food crops, now rare even in its home region.

plant_note: Long-season winter squash; some resistance to vine borers.
directions: This heirloom winter squash bears large crook-necked fruit with sweet flesh traditional in Southern pies. Direct sow several seeds per hill in warm soil, thinning to the two strongest plants. Give the vigorous vines ample room to ramble, as they can run 12 feet or more. Cushaws show useful resistance to squash vine borers compared with pumpkin types. Harvest when the rind hardens and the vine dies back, then cure in a warm spot to sweeten and improve storage.

plant_note: Plant seeds directly outdoors once soil has warmed after the last frost, giving vines plenty of room to ramble, and water deeply but infrequently to encourage strong root development.
directions: Plant seeds directly outdoors once soil has warmed after the last frost, giving vines plenty of room to ramble, and water deeply but infrequently to encourage strong root development. A colonial-era American heirloom closely related to Green Striped Cushaw, this variety bears crookneck-shaped fruit with smooth cream-white rind and pale flesh that is drier and less sweet, making it especially favored for savory cooking and livestock feed. Its resistance to squash vine borer and adaptability to hot, humid conditions kept it popular across the South long before modern butternut types became dominant. Store cured fruit in a cool, dry space where it will keep for several months.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cutleaf ground cherry self-sows prolifically and often naturalizes in warm gardens. In zone 9, it may grow as a self-sowing perennial annual, emerging from seed each spring.
directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; cutleaf ground cherry is a tropical annual widely distributed throughout warm regions of the Americas, distinguished from other ground cherries by its more deeply lobed, angular leaves that give the plant a distinctive, fernlike texture among the lantern-papery husked physalis clan. The small yellow berries with papery, lantern-shaped husks ripen inside the husk from green to yellow and have a sweet, tropical flavor suitable for eating raw, making jam, or drying. Widely used as a traditional food plant in Mexico and Central America, where it grows as a weed of agricultural fields and gardens. Very drought-tolerant once established and naturalistic in garden settings where it self-sows to maintain a permanent colony. Distinguished from the toxic black nightshade (Solanum) relatives by the distinctive papery husk enclosing each fruit.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for winter-spring harvest. Cylindra requires loose, deep soil to develop its characteristically long (4–6 inch) cylindrical root — in compacted or rocky soil it will branch and distort. Thin to 4 inches between plants. The cylindrical shape means most of the root develops underground without the shoulder protrusion common in round beets. In zone 9 the cool season from October through March produces the best root quality.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of compaction and stones; Cylindra (also known as Formanova) is a Danish heirloom beet producing an unusual elongated, cylindrical root shape — 4–6 inches long and 1.5–2 inches across — completely different from the familiar round beet shape. The cylindrical form was developed specifically for sliced beet production: when cut crosswise, Cylindra produces perfectly uniform, consistently sized circular slices from the entire length of the root, making it the preferred variety for home canning, pickled beet slices, and any preparation requiring uniform beet rounds. A round beet produces irregularly sized slices (small at the shoulders, large in the middle, small at the base), while every slice from Cylindra is the same diameter. The dark red flesh and rich, classic beet flavor are typical of traditional red beet varieties. Cylindra is also highly productive per square foot of garden space because the elongated root utilizes vertical growing space rather than lateral.

plant_note: Long roots grow partly above soil; hill lightly to keep them covered.
directions: This Danish heirloom produces long cylindrical roots that yield uniform slices, ideal for pickling and canning. Sow seed half an inch deep in loose, stone-free soil so the elongated roots can develop straight. Thin to 3 inches and keep the beds evenly moist to prevent zoning and cracking. As roots push upward, draw a little soil over exposed shoulders to prevent greening. Harvest when roots reach about 6 inches long and 2 inches thick.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, and set up climbing supports before the vigorous vines take off.
directions: Czar is a British heritage runner bean distinguished by pure white flowers rather than the scarlet blooms of most runner beans, and by its dual use as both a fresh snap bean and a dry shelling bean. Young pods are broad, fleshy, and stringless when picked at 8 to 10 inches, while pods left to mature yield plump, pure-white seeds prized for drying and cooking like butter beans. Give plants a tall, sturdy trellis or bean poles and consistent moisture, since runner beans are shallow-rooted and stop setting pods readily in dry or very hot conditions. This heirloom performs especially well in cooler summer climates where heat can otherwise cause runner beans to drop blossoms.

scientific_name: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis 'Da Cheong Chae'
plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop; this Korean-style hybrid holds well before bolting in warm weather compared with older pak choi types.
directions: A vigorous Korean-style F1 hybrid pak choi with dark green, upright leaves and thick, crunchy pale-green petioles, distinct from the flatter, whiter-stemmed Chinese pak choi types most familiar to American gardeners. Keep soil consistently moist for tender, non-fibrous stems, and harvest whole heads or individual outer leaves as needed. Its upright, semi-savoyed leaf habit and good bolt tolerance make it well suited to Korean-style kimchi and soups as well as general stir-frying, and it can be succession sown through spring and again in fall for a steady supply.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); Dade was bred at a Florida research station for reliable production and better tolerance of the wilt and virus pressure common in hot, humid gardens.
directions: Soak seed overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F. Dade was developed at a University of Florida research station and selected for improved tolerance of the fusarium wilt and virus pressure that build up in hot, humid gardens over a long growing season, making it a dependable choice for the Gulf South's extended okra harvest. Plants stay a bit more compact than rangy heirloom types, setting smooth, tapered, medium-green pods that stay tender well past the usual 3-inch mark. Harvest every one to two days once pods start forming to keep plants productive, and remove any pods that slip past picking size, since leaving them on the plant slows new flowering.

common_name: Dade Pole Bean (University of Florida Heat-Tolerant Snap Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost and again in late summer; Dade tolerates the heat and brief flooding that stall many other snap beans in Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Dade was introduced by the University of Florida in 1962 as a vigorous, leafy pole bean bred for the state's heat, humidity, and disease pressure. Pods are straight, flattened, and about 7 inches long, staying stringless and tender well past the point most snap beans turn tough, giving a wider harvest window before quality drops. The variety carries resistance to rust and several mosaic viruses and tolerates brief waterlogging better than most snap beans, a useful trait during Gulf Coast summer downpours. Set a sturdy 6-foot pole or trellis at planting, since Dade is a true climbing type that will keep producing later into the season than bush varieties.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/2 inch deep, 2–3 inches apart, and thin to 6 inches as they grow; daikon bolts quickly in long days and summer heat, making fall planting (8–10 weeks before first frost) far more successful than spring planting in most climates.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/2 inch deep and thin to 6 inches apart in deep, loose, stone-free, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; daikon is a large, long-rooted Japanese radish that develops roots 12–18 inches long and 2–4 inches wide with mild, crisp, slightly peppery white flesh that is essential in Japanese, Korean, and Southeast Asian cuisines for pickling (takuan), salads (daikon salad), braising (oden), and grated as a fresh condiment (oroshi daikon) for tempura and sashimi. Fall planting (8–10 weeks before first frost) avoids the premature bolting that ruins spring-planted crops. In cover-cropping applications, 'tillage radish' varieties (deep-rooting daikon types) are grown as cover crops to break up compacted soil and capture nitrogen; the large roots freeze and decompose over winter, creating channels for water infiltration. Harvest when roots reach full size but before they become pithy.

common_name: Dakota Black Popcorn (Deep Purple-Black Heirloom Popcorn with White Pop)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; Dakota Black is a standard-height (5–6 foot) popcorn that can be grown anywhere standard corn grows. In zone 9, plant March–May; popcorn requires a longer season than sweet corn (95–110 days) and must be fully dried on the plant or after harvest before popping — harvest in October–November when husks are completely dry and kernels hard. Isolate from sweet corn and other corn types by 400 feet or 2-week planting-date offset to prevent cross-pollination that ruins both crops. Popcorn must be fully dry before popping — test a handful; if it pops well, the rest is ready.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks for pollination; let ears dry completely on the stalk, then harvest and cure an additional 3–4 weeks indoors before popping. Dakota Black is an heirloom popcorn variety with some of the most visually striking dried ears available in home-grown popcorn — the kernels are very deep purple-black, almost jet black, creating ears that are dramatically different from the pale yellow, red, or multicolored ears of other popcorn types. The deep coloration comes from a very high concentration of anthocyanins in the kernel pericarp — the same class of pigments found in black rice, black beans, and blueberries, associated with antioxidant properties. Like all colored popcorn types, Dakota Black pops white (the dark pigment is in the outer pericarp layer, not the starchy endosperm that expands during popping), producing attractive, white, tender-crisp popcorn with good flavor. Dakota Black has a place in the Native American Great Plains agricultural tradition where black, dark purple, and multicolored corns were cultivated alongside white and yellow types — the variety's association with Dakota peoples and plains agriculture gives it cultural significance beyond its ornamental appeal. The dried ears are as valuable for ornamental use (fall decoration, wreaths, dried corn displays) as for eating, making Dakota Black one of the most versatile specialty corns for home gardeners.

common_name: Danish Ballhead Cabbage (Large Late-Season Storage Cabbage for Sauerkraut)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Danish Ballhead is a long-season cabbage (100–115 days) best suited for fall production in zone 9 — start indoors in June–July and transplant late August for November–January harvest. Provide consistent moisture and fertility throughout the long growing season. Danish Ballhead produces very large heads (5–8 lbs) that hold well in the garden after reaching maturity without cracking, making it flexible for harvest timing in cool fall conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil. Danish Ballhead is a classic large-headed fall/storage cabbage from the Scandinavian and Northern European tradition — one of the primary heirloom cabbages for sauerkraut production, coleslaw for large quantities, and long-term cold storage. The very large (5–8 lb), perfectly round, extremely dense, blue-green heads form tight, compact, hard balls — the firmness that gives Ballhead its name means the heads have a very high leaf-to-air-space ratio, ideal for shredding into sauerkraut. Danish Ballhead has been the reference variety for Scandinavian sauerkraut production for generations — Scandinavian food traditions rely heavily on fermented cabbage through the winter months, and the large, dense, sweet heads of late-season cabbage like Danish Ballhead are the ideal base. The variety keeps very well after harvest — 3–4 months in proper cold storage (near 32°F with high humidity) — providing fresh cabbage through winter. Excellent for coleslaw, braised preparations, and fresh use.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring as soon as soil is workable; carrots resent transplanting.
directions: This late-19th-century heirloom offers strong color, high yield, and uniform, tapered roots that perform well even in heavy soils thanks to their vigorous tops. Sow seed thinly directly in the garden and keep the surface consistently moist until the slow seeds sprout. Thin seedlings to prevent crowding and forked roots. It interplants nicely with onions. Loosen and deeply cultivate the bed before sowing for the straightest roots.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil can be worked; sow again in mid to late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Danvers 126 is a dependable heirloom that produces tapered, deep-orange roots even in heavier or imperfect soils. Loosen the bed deeply and remove stones so roots stay uniform, then sow seed thinly about a quarter inch deep. Keep the surface consistently moist during the slow germination period, and thin seedlings to a couple inches apart once they establish. Harvest at roughly 70 to 80 days when shoulders reach three-quarters of an inch, and hold roots in cool storage for winter use.

plant_note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, providing a tall trellis; this vigorous hybrid vine can climb well beyond 10 feet.
directions: An Indian-type F1 hybrid bitter melon bred for high yield and noticeably reduced bitterness compared with older open-pollinated Indian types, making it a good entry point for gardeners new to the crop. Fruit is slender and spindle-shaped, 8-10 inches long, with dark green, densely bumpy skin and roughly half a pound in weight. Both immature fruit and tender young shoots are edible, and the fruit holds well on the vine without rapidly yellowing, giving a longer harvest window than many heirloom types. Provide a strong trellis in full sun and rich, well-drained soil for best production through the hot summer months.

common_name: Dark Star Zucchini (Near-Black Dark-Striped Hybrid Zucchini with Superior Heat Tolerance)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Dark Star is a hybrid zucchini notable for its extremely dark green to near-black fruit color, vigorous plant habit, and better-than-average heat tolerance in warm climates. In zone 9, plant March–May for spring production and again in August–September for fall production. The fruit color — very dark green with fine lighter green speckles or striping — is among the darkest of any common zucchini variety, a contrast to the medium green of standard zucchini. The very dark color is more visually striking at farmers markets and in salads. Dark Star was recognized as an AAS winner for its outstanding performance in trials across diverse growing conditions, including warm-summer locations where many zucchini varieties decline earlier in the season. Harvest at 6–8 inches for best flavor; the skin remains tender and the flesh dense at this size.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 6–8 inches when skin is uniformly very dark green. Dark Star Zucchini is an F1 hybrid summer squash variety developed for its dramatically dark fruit color, vigor, and heat performance in warm-summer conditions — qualities that make it particularly appropriate for Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens where summer zucchini production is challenging due to the combination of heat, powdery mildew pressure, and vine borer activity. Standard zucchini typically produces well in spring (March–May in zone 9) and again in fall (August–October) but struggles during the July–August peak summer period. Dark Star's improved heat tolerance extends the productive period somewhat beyond what standard green zucchini varieties manage, though no summer squash is fully tolerant of zone 9 peak summer conditions. The fruit's near-black to very dark green color (produced by high concentrations of chlorophyll and other pigments in the skin) is the variety's most immediately distinctive characteristic — a mature Dark Star fruit at 6–8 inches harvest size is substantially darker than a standard green zucchini, with a glossy, nearly black-green skin that stands out dramatically when displayed with lighter-colored vegetables. The flesh is standard zucchini quality — white, mild, with good flavor at proper harvest size — with no meaningful flavor difference from standard green varieties. The AAS recognition for Dark Star reflected consistent performance advantages in vine health, production duration, and uniformity across trial locations including warmer growing regions.

common_name: Darkibor Kale (Dark Blue-Green Curly Hybrid Kale)
plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow; kale is also an excellent fall crop, since cool weather and light frost sweeten the leaves' flavor.
directions: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Darkibor is a vigorous hybrid curly kale producing densely ruffled, dark blue-green leaves on a productive, uniform plant, valued commercially and by home gardeners alike for reliable yields and good cold tolerance that lets it stand in the garden well into winter in many climates. The tightly curled leaf texture holds up well to cooking methods like sauteing and braising, and the dark color signals a good concentration of nutrients typical of kale. Harvest outer leaves as needed, working from the bottom up, and expect improved sweetness after the plant experiences a light frost.

common_name: Darto Kale (Very Dark Blue-Black Lacinato-Type Kale)
plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow; kale is also an excellent fall crop, since cool weather and light frost sweeten the leaves' flavor.
directions: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Darto is a striking Lacinato-type (dinosaur kale) selection with unusually dark, almost blue-black, deeply savoyed leaves, even darker than standard Lacinato kale, giving it strong ornamental value in addition to its classic sweet, nutty flavor prized in Tuscan cooking. The long, narrow, crinkled leaves hold their quality well in cool weather and are excellent massaged raw into salads, sauteed, or added to soups. Harvest outer leaves as needed, allowing the central growing point to continue producing new leaves over a long season, and expect the flavor to sweeten further after light frost.

plant_note: Establish Daruma wasabi by planting healthy rhizome divisions or crowns in spring into cool, constantly moist, richly organic soil kept below about 70F, ideally alongside a shaded stream bank or in a heavily mulched bog bed fed by clean, moving water.
directions: Establish Daruma wasabi by planting healthy rhizome divisions or crowns in spring into cool, constantly moist, richly organic soil kept below about 70F, ideally alongside a shaded stream bank or in a heavily mulched bog bed fed by clean, moving water. Daruma is the cultivar most commonly grown by commercial wasabi farms in North America because of its vigorous growth and comparatively good tolerance of temperature swings, though it still demands full to partial shade and unfailing moisture to avoid rot or stunting. After 18 to 24 months the thick rhizome is ready to harvest and grate fresh, releasing the same clean, sinus-clearing heat that fades within minutes, a world apart from the horseradish-and-dye paste sold as wasabi in most restaurants. Its dense, heart-shaped leaves also make an attractive textural groundcover for a deeply shaded, moisture-rich corner of the garden.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Dasher II is a gynoecious (predominantly female) cucumber requiring a male-flowering pollenizer (included in mixed seed packets) for fruit set. Train vines to a trellis for straighter fruits and better air circulation; harvest frequently at 7–8 inches for best quality and continued production.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Dasher II is a gynoecious hybrid slicing cucumber that has been one of the most consistently recommended disease-resistant slicing cucumber varieties since its release — carrying resistance to cucumber mosaic virus, scab, angular leaf spot, powdery mildew, and anthracnose, providing protection against the most common disease failures in cucumber production across a wide range of climates. The dark green, 7–8 inch, slightly tapered fruits have a smooth, attractive appearance with small, even bumps and white spines; the flesh is crisp, mild, and refreshing with very low bitterness (very low cucurbitacin content), making Dasher II distinctly more palatable than older cucumber varieties that could be quite bitter. The gynoecious character concentrates fruit set into a more uniform harvest window than open-pollinated types. In humid Gulf South conditions where cucumber diseases (especially powdery mildew and angular leaf spot) severely limit cucumber production in summer, Dasher II's comprehensive disease resistance is particularly valuable, allowing productive summer growing that standard varieties cannot sustain. An excellent backbone slicer for any home garden or market garden where disease pressure is a concern.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost and transplant after all cold risk has passed; in zone 9 transplant March–April. Datil peppers are closely tied to St. Augustine, Florida, and perform exceptionally well in the long, hot, humid growing season of the Gulf Coast and Florida.
directions: Start seeds at 80–85°F soil temperature; germination is slow and benefits from bottom heat. Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Datil peppers are a habanero-type (Capsicum chinense) variety historically grown in and around St. Augustine, Florida, for at least 200 years — their exact origin is debated but they are deeply embedded in Minorcan and northeast Florida food culture. The small, wrinkled, yellow-orange fruits are fiercely hot (100,000–300,000 Scoville) with a distinctive fruity, citrusy sweetness that sets them apart from pure heat bombs. They are the defining ingredient in St. Augustine's datil pepper sauce tradition, used in chowders, seafood dishes, and condiments. Plants thrive in Florida's humid summers and can be treated as perennials in zone 9b–11 when protected from frost. Mulch heavily, water consistently, and side-dress with compost mid-season to sustain productivity.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Daubenton's kale rarely sets viable seed and is propagated almost exclusively by stem cuttings, which root readily. The plant is truly perennial, regrowning from established roots each season and surviving indefinitely in frost-free conditions or with winter protection.
directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Daubenton's kale is one of the oldest known perennial brassicas, grown continuously as a cutting-propagated vegetable in European kitchen gardens since at least the 18th century — named after the French naturalist and physician Louis Jean-Marie Daubenton (1716–1800). The plant never (or rarely) sets seed, remaining in a perpetual vegetative state and producing edible, tender, kale-like leaves throughout the growing season year after year. In zones 7–10, plants survive winter outdoors and return each spring with renewed vigor. Flavor is mild and pleasant, similar to curly kale but without the toughness of mature kale leaves. Harvest by cutting young side shoots and leaves regularly. An excellent plant for low-maintenance, productive food forests and permaculture gardens where a perennial harvest of leafy greens is desired. Propagate from 6-inch stem cuttings at any time.

plant_note: Start indoors for spring, or direct sow in mid-summer for a fall and winter crop.
directions: This extra-cold-hardy lacinato-type kale features striking purple midribs against blue-green, savoyed leaves that deepen in color during cool fall weather. It withstands frost better than most dinosaur kales, and flavor sweetens after a light freeze. Grow in full sun to partial shade in rich, moist soil. Harvest outer leaves as needed to keep plants producing. It overwinters well in mild regions for early spring greens.

common_name: De 18 Jours Radish (Classic French Ultra-Fast Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; De 18 Jours ('of 18 days') is a classic French heirloom radish named for its remarkably fast maturity, among the quickest radishes traditionally grown.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. De 18 Jours, French for 'of 18 days,' is a classic heirloom radish named for its exceptionally fast maturity, historically prized by French market gardeners for getting a crop to harvest faster than almost any other vegetable. Roots are small, round to oval, bright red, and crisp, with a clean, mild flavor typical of quick spring radishes when harvested promptly at the right size. Because it matures so quickly, it is well suited to intercropping between slower-growing vegetables or squeezing in an extra succession planting in a short cool window. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows, and succession sowing every two weeks keeps a steady supply coming.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for an earlier harvest; pick fruit small and often to keep vines productive.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger has passed, providing a trellis or light support to keep fruit clean and straight. De Bourbonne is a traditional French heirloom from the Burgundy region bred specifically for pickling, producing short, blocky, black-spined fruit typically harvested at two to four inches long for classic French-style cornichons and gherkins. The vigorous vines set fruit prolifically over a long season, and frequent picking is essential since the cucumbers mature quickly and turn seedy and bitter if left too long on the vine. Its small size and firm, crisp texture make it well suited to whole-fruit pickling rather than fresh slicing.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or direct sow in late summer for fall harvest; De Cicco is an Italian heirloom broccoli from the Lazio region dating to at least 1890, producing a small central head followed by an abundant, continuous harvest of tender sideshoots that can continue for weeks — the classic sprouting broccoli of Italian tradition.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant when daytime temperatures are below 75°F and after hardening off. De Cicco is one of America's oldest and most beloved heirloom broccolis, introduced to the US from the Lazio region of Italy and appearing in seed catalogs since at least 1890; unlike modern large-headed hybrids, De Cicco produces a smaller, open, bluish-green central head (4–6 inches) that is best harvested before flowers open, then rebounds with a prolific and sustained harvest of tender, slender sideshoots that are more delicate and sweet-flavored than the central head — this sideshot harvest can continue for weeks in cool weather, making De Cicco arguably more productive than single-heading types over the full season. The tender sideshoots (broccoletti) are the classic vegetable of Italian cooking braised with olive oil and garlic. An outstanding variety for Gulf Coast fall and winter production and for cool-climate spring gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring for a summer crop, or sow again in mid-to-late summer for a fall harvest, since roots develop their sweetest flavor in cool weather.
directions: Named for Croissy-sur-Seine, a historic market-gardening town near Paris, this French heirloom produces slightly curved, cylindrical white roots that were traditionally bunched and sold young for their tender, sweet flesh. It matures faster than globe-type turnips, making it well suited to close spring and late-summer sowings where a quick, mild crop is wanted before or after the main season. Its half-long, tapered shape and old-market-garden history distinguish it from the round purple-top types that dominate most American gardens.

common_name: Deadon Cabbage (Dark Red Savoy-Type Winter Cabbage)
plant_note: Start indoors in mid to late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Deadon's deep red-purple color intensifies with cold exposure, much like January King, and the heads store and hold in the garden exceptionally well through winter.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into well-amended, firm soil in full sun, giving plants room for a dense, round head. Deadon is a modern British-bred winter cabbage prized for producing solid, deep red-purple heads with excellent flavor and remarkably long field-holding ability, standing in good condition through hard frosts and well into winter without splitting or losing quality. Its rich color, cold hardiness, and dense, slow-to-bolt heads make it a favorite for extending the fresh cabbage harvest deep into the cold season, and the color deepens further after frost. Firm transplants in well to prevent wind-rock, protect young plants from cabbage worms and aphids, and harvest as needed through winter, since mature heads hold in the garden far longer than most summer cabbages.

plant_note: Direct sow or start transplants in early spring; can also be sown in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9. Purple color develops best with cool temperatures and full sun.
directions: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart for straight, uniform stalks. Deep Purple is a non-bulbing bunching onion selected for shanks that flush a striking violet-purple, especially in cool weather, contrasting with its blue-green tops; the color makes it a standout in salads, garnishes, and pickles compared with standard green scallions. Flavor is typical mild-to-sharp onion, good raw or cooked, and the plant is otherwise grown exactly like any other bunching onion. Harvest at scallion size for the best color and tenderness, or let a portion mature further for thicker stalks; successive small sowings keep a continuous supply.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for a spring crop; Deer Tongue is an American heirloom lettuce dating to at least 1740, listed in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden journal, with distinctively tongue-shaped, slightly succulent leaves in a loose, non-heading rosette — one of the most heat-tolerant lettuces for spring gardens.
directions: Scatter seed on the soil surface in early spring or fall in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; thin to 9–12 inches for full rosettes or 6 inches for cut-and-come-again harvest. Deer Tongue (also known as Matchless) is one of America's oldest heirloom lettuces, documented in seed catalogs since at least 1740 and recorded in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden journals; the distinctive tongue-shaped, elongated, slightly pointed, wavy-edged leaves form loose, open rosettes with a crisp-yet-buttery texture and mild, sweet flavor. A green variety ('Green Deer Tongue') and a bronze or red variant ('Bronze Deer Tongue') exist; both are more heat-tolerant than most lettuce types, slower to bolt in warm conditions, and excellent for spring and fall production in warm climates. The elongated leaf shape is immediately distinctive and visually striking in the garden; makes beautiful salad contributions for the unusual leaf form.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Defiant PhR carries the Ph-3 resistance gene against late blight along with tolerance to early blight and septoria leaf spot, making it a strong choice for humid, disease-prone gardens like the Gulf South where fungal pressure builds quickly in summer.
directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, and cage or stake the semi-determinate plants; Defiant PhR was bred by Dr. Randy Gardner at North Carolina State University to give home and organic growers a reliably productive slicing tomato that resists late blight, the fast-moving fungal disease capable of destroying an entire planting within days in wet, humid weather. It bears a heavy crop of medium to large (6-8 oz), round, deep red fruit with solid, meaty flesh and good classic tomato flavor, ripening early enough to get well ahead of peak disease season in many climates. Because it also shows good tolerance to early blight and septoria leaf spot, it tends to hold healthy foliage later into the season than most slicing tomatoes grown in the humid Gulf South, keeping plants productive longer. Harvest as fruit ripens to full red color and keep picking regularly to encourage continued fruit set.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, in hills spaced widely to allow the sprawling vines room to run.
directions: Delica is the dark green, deeply lobed kabocha type most widely sold as fresh kabocha in North American grocery stores, prized for its dry, deep-orange flesh with a dense, chestnut-like sweetness. Vines are vigorous and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit set, tapering off as the rind hardens near harvest. Cure fruit for one to two weeks in a warm spot to concentrate sugars before moving to cool storage, where it keeps for two to three months. Choose Delica when you want the classic Japanese squash experience for tempura, soups, and roasting rather than a sweeter American-bred kabocha hybrid.

plant_note: Start indoors a few weeks before the last frost, or direct sow after danger of hard frost passes; sow again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Delicacy Purple forms a smooth, deep violet globe above the soil line while the interior flesh stays crisp white, giving a striking contrast when sliced for a vegetable tray. Its bulb stays tender and mild even as it sizes up, resisting the woodiness that affects many kohlrabi types if harvest is delayed slightly. Fast to mature and compact in the row, it works well tucked into small spaces or grown in quick succession through spring and fall. Choose Delicacy Purple for its ornamental color and reliably sweet, crunchy texture in both raw and cooked preparations.

plant_note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: This 1894 heirloom develops oblong fruits with hard cream skin striped in green and sweet, tender flesh. Sow seed an inch deep in warm soil, spacing plants generously to give the semi-vining habit room to run. Provide steady moisture through fruit set and mulch to conserve water and suppress weeds. Harvest when the skin hardens and the stripes deepen, then cure fruits in a warm spot for a week or two to improve storage and flavor.

common_name: Delicata Winter Squash (Sweet Dumpling Squash, Carnival Squash)
plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds (thinned to 2 plants per hill) after all frost danger passes and soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9, Delicata is best planted in late July to early August for fall harvest, avoiding the peak summer heat that reduces fruit set — spring planting is also possible but summer heat may interrupt fruit set.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Delicata is a compact, heirloom winter squash producing cylindrical, cream-colored to pale yellow fruits with distinctive green and orange-tan longitudinal stripes — an exceptionally attractive squash with outstanding flavor quality. The flesh is deep orange, very sweet, very dry, and intensely flavored — widely considered one of the finest-flavored winter squash cultivars, with a sweet, almost chestnut-like richness that needs little added fat or sugar when roasted or baked. The thin skin is completely edible after roasting — one of the few winter squash varieties where peeling is unnecessary. The manageable fruit size (6–9 inches long, 3–4 lbs) is practical for single-meal preparation. Delicata vines are more compact than most winter squash — the semi-bush to short-vine habit reaches 4–6 feet — making it more manageable in smaller garden spaces. In zone 9, the summer planting (late July–early August) for fall harvest generally works better than spring planting, as the hottest summer temperatures tend to prevent adequate fruit set. The fruit stores well at room temperature for 2–3 months. Squash vine borers and squash bugs are the primary pests; row covers at planting and prompt removal of egg masses help manage populations.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed and frost danger has passed; Delicious 51, a classic 1951 USDA commercial release, was a standard cantaloupe variety for decades before modern hybrids became dominant.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills of two to three plants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has thoroughly warmed. Delicious 51, released by the USDA in 1951, was a standard commercial cantaloupe variety for decades, prized for well-netted rind, thick, sweet, aromatic salmon-orange flesh, and good disease tolerance for its era, and it remains a solid, reliable open-pollinated choice for home gardeners today. The vigorous, sprawling vines need plenty of room to run and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development, tapering off as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine at full slip, with a strong, sweet aroma at the blossom end signaling peak ripeness.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deep, well-worked beds once soil has warmed.
directions: Delicious is an old Burpee introduction famous for producing some of the largest tomato fruit of any variety, including the fruit that held the Guinness World Record for heaviest tomato for nearly three decades. Stake or cage plants heavily and prune to a few main leaders so the vigorous indeterminate vines can channel energy into fewer, larger scarlet-red beefsteak fruits. Consistent deep watering and calcium availability help reduce cracking and blossom end rot on fruit that can exceed a pound. Choose this variety when garden bragging rights and classic rich tomato flavor matter more than earliness or disease-package breadth.

plant_note: Start indoors early and transplant out only after nights stay warm.
directions: This blend of mini sweet snack peppers ripens to red, yellow, and orange, all prized for crunchy, juicy texture and vibrant color. Start seed indoors early since peppers need a long warm season. Harden off carefully and transplant only after soil and nights are reliably warm. Plants are productive and well suited to containers and small beds. Pick regularly once fruit colors up to encourage continued set.

plant_note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; Della was bred at the LSU AgCenter as one of the first domestic aromatic rice varieties and remains a parent of many Louisiana popcorn rice types.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated through the growing season whether in a flooded paddy or a well-watered garden bed. Released by the LSU AgCenter in the 1970s, Della was one of the first American-bred aromatic long-grain rices, developed by crossing domestic rice lines with basmati-type genetics to produce a fragrant, popcorn-scented grain that helped establish Louisiana's aromatic rice industry and became a parent behind several later Southern aromatic varieties. The tall plants yield well in the hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season, and the cooked grain carries a distinctive nutty, toasted-popcorn aroma prized in Cajun and Creole cooking. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain turns golden-brown, then thresh and dry thoroughly before storage or milling.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed past last frost; Densuke originates from a limited cooperative harvest in Toma, Hokkaido, Japan, where its solid black rind and short cool-summer growing window made it a prized specialty melon.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after all danger of frost has passed, spacing vines 3-6 feet apart in rows with ample room to sprawl. Densuke is distinguished from typical striped watermelons by a rind that ripens to an almost uniform matte black rather than developing stripes, enclosing crisp, sweet red flesh; the fruit was originally developed and marketed by a small growers' cooperative in Toma, Hokkaido, where the cooler northern Japanese summers and volcanic soil were credited with its intense sweetness. Give plants full sun and consistent moisture through fruit set, then ease off watering as melons near maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest by checking the dulling of the ground spot and the drying of the tendril nearest the fruit stem, since the solid dark rind makes the classic thump test and stripe patterns unreliable ripeness cues.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, and make succession sowings every couple of weeks for a continuous harvest.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep directly in the garden after soil has warmed, spacing plants close together in rows since compact bushy plants need little support. This dependable bush bean produces long, straight, round pods about five to six inches long that stay tender and stringless even when picked slightly larger than average. Vigorous, heavy-yielding plants tend to hold their pods up off the ground and above the foliage, which keeps them cleaner and makes for faster picking. It has long been a standard choice for home gardeners wanting a reliable, high-quality green bean for fresh eating, freezing, or canning.

common_name: Des Vertus Savoy Cabbage (French Heirloom Drumhead Savoy)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a summer harvest, or sow in early summer for a fall crop; Des Vertus holds especially well and even overwinters in mild climates.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost for a summer harvest, or sow in early summer for transplanting out for a fall crop, since Des Vertus develops its full flavor and holds especially well after cool autumn weather sets in. Des Vertus Savoy, also known as Large Drumhead Savoy, is a French heirloom cabbage dating to the early 1800s that produces large, rounded, medium-green heads of four to six pounds with deeply crinkled, blistered savoy-type leaves. Its flavor is notably mild, sweet, and tender compared to smooth-leaved cabbage, and the crinkled leaves make it a traditional choice for stuffed cabbage preparations across French and other European cuisines. It is more cold-tolerant than many cabbages, standing well into fall and even overwintering in mild climates, and offers moderate storage life once harvested.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container-grown plants in spring in full sun in very well-drained, rocky to sandy desert soil; desert agave requires near-zero summer irrigation once established and is the most drought tolerant agave for the Sonoran Desert region.
directions: Plant offset pups or young container specimens in full sun in gravelly, sandy, extremely well-drained desert soil with no summer irrigation once established; desert agave (Agave deserti) is the agave of the Sonoran and Mojave Deserts, historically one of the most important food plants for desert-dwelling indigenous peoples of California, Arizona, and Mexico — the Cahuilla, Kumeyaay, and Coahuilla people harvested the immature flower stalks (quiote) and the heart of the plant (piña) before flowering, roasting them in earth ovens to produce a sweet, molasses-like food that sustained desert communities. Plants live 10–20 years before producing a single tall flower stalk, then dying, leaving behind pup offsets. The leaf tips are sharp and require care during placement.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring.
directions: This early Dutch heirloom shelling pea charms with pink blooms and vivid purple pods on compact, productive vines. Sow seed an inch deep as soon as the soil is workable, since peas thrive in cool spring weather. Provide a short trellis or brushy support to keep the vines tidy and the pods clean. Harvest the purple pods while plump and shell out the sweet green peas promptly, as flavor is best right after picking.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January-February for harvest before summer heat sets in. Cut seed pieces to egg size with 1-2 eyes each and let cut surfaces cure a day or two before planting.
directions: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. Desiree is a widely grown Dutch-bred potato with smooth, rosy-red skin and pale yellow, moderately waxy flesh that holds its shape well when boiled, making it a versatile choice for roasting, salads, and general cooking. It is a vigorous, heavy-yielding variety with good tolerance for a range of soil conditions and reasonably good drought tolerance compared to some other cultivars. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to prevent tubers from greening in the sun, and harvest for storage once the vines have died back naturally.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F; this vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from sturdy staking.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant deeply into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, then stake or cage the vine early. Dester is a French heirloom beefsteak prized for its smooth, rounded, deep pink-red fruit that runs unusually free of the cracking and catfacing that plague many large heirloom slicers, often reaching a pound or more with very few seeds and a thin, tender skin. The flesh is dense, low in acid, and richly sweet, making it a favorite among heirloom growers for fresh eating despite the plant's somewhat unassuming, ordinary-looking foliage. Water evenly and mulch well through fruit set, since the smooth skin is still thin enough to split under drought-then-deluge conditions; the vigorous, disease-tolerant vine keeps setting fruit steadily through a long Gulf Coast season.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall harvest.
directions: Detroit Dark Red is a classic heirloom prized for deep crimson roots, tender texture, and sweet flavor that holds up for canning and storage. Sow seed about half an inch deep in loose, well-drained soil, keeping the bed evenly moist to aid the multi-seeded clusters. Thin seedlings to three or four inches apart so roots size up well, and use the thinnings as tender greens. Pull roots at two to three inches for the best eating quality, and hold larger roots in cool, damp storage over winter.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for fall harvest.
directions: A beloved heirloom with sweet, non-bleeding orange roots and nutritious edible greens that stay mild whether raw or cooked. Direct sow seed clusters half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping moisture steady during germination. Thin seedlings to a few inches apart and remove weeds so roots can swell evenly. Harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for tender eating, and cure larger roots for cool storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; devil's claw sprawls widely and needs plenty of room, and its sticky, glandular foliage can irritate sensitive skin.
directions: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; devil's claw sprawls widely and needs plenty of room, and its sticky, glandular foliage can irritate sensitive skin. Large, sprawling, sticky-hairy leaves and showy, orchid-like, pale pink to lavender flowers give way to the plant's real claim to fame: long, curved, green seed pods that, when young and tender, are pickled or cooked like okra, and when mature dry to a woody, split, two-pronged 'claw' historically gathered by Indigenous peoples of the Southwest and used as a black fiber in basketry. Native to the central and southwestern United States, it grows easily from seed in ordinary garden soil and self-sows readily once established, sometimes appearing as a volunteer weed in disturbed garden soil in following years. Harvest pods young and tender (a few inches long) for pickling and eating, or let some mature and dry fully on the plant to collect the distinctive woody claws for craft use or seed saving.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost; sow successive plantings every 2-3 weeks for continuous harvest.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in cool, fertile soil and thin seedlings to 8-10 inches once they have several true leaves. Devil's Tongue is a small upright cos-type lettuce whose older outer leaves flush dramatically from light green to deep wine-red at the margins while new growth stays a contrasting fresh green, giving each head a striking mottled two-tone look. The heads stay relatively compact at 6-7 inches, so it works well in small beds or containers, and the crisp ribs and mild sweet flavor hold up better than many red lettuces as temperatures warm. Harvest whole heads once firm, or pick outer leaves individually for a longer cut-and-come-again harvest window.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since this chinense type needs a long, warm season to fully ripen.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat to improve germination, then transplant into well-drained, fertile soil once the weather is reliably warm. Feed lightly and keep moisture consistent, since chinense peppers are prone to blossom drop under heat stress or drought. Devil's Tongue produces distinctively wrinkled, tapering pods and is closely related to habanero types, with heat that reaches well into the habanero-to-superhot range along with a fruity flavor. It is grown in shades ranging from pale yellow to deep red depending on the strain.

common_name: Di Cicco Broccoli (Italian Sprouting Broccoli, Continuous-Harvest Broccoli)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, transplant in September–October for the main fall crop — the primary production window is October through March, with spring planting often too brief before heat ends production in May.
directions: Set out transplants in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun during cool seasons; Di Cicco is a classic Italian heirloom sprouting broccoli dating to the nineteenth century — producing smaller, blue-green central heads followed by prolific side shoots (sideshoots) that continue producing edible florets for weeks or months after the central head is harvested. Unlike compact heading broccoli (Calabrese, Marathon) that produces one large head and then is done, Di Cicco is a continuous-harvest type — the plant continues to produce side shoot clusters for 6–10 weeks after the main head is cut, giving each plant a much longer productive season. In zone 9, Di Cicco is best planted in September–October for fall production, with continued harvest through the winter months. The open, branching plant habit and the loose, smaller head size of Di Cicco give it a more old-fashioned, informal appearance compared to tight-headed modern cultivars — but the flavor and the extended harvest period make it an excellent choice for the Gulf Coast kitchen garden where a long, productive cool-season broccoli is needed. Cold-tolerant to light freezes; protect from temperatures below 26°F.

common_name: Di Sicilia Viola Cauliflower (Sicilian Purple Heritage Cauliflower)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. botrytis 'Di Sicilia Viola'
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before fall transplanting (best as a fall crop in most climates); Di Sicilia Viola is a Sicilian heirloom purple cauliflower with deep traditional roots in the vegetable gardens of Sicily, where purple cauliflower has been grown for centuries — it matures later than modern purple hybrids but has exceptional flavor and cultural significance as a true heirloom variety.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before planned fall transplanting date; set out in rich, fertile, moist soil; Di Sicilia Viola matures later than modern hybrids (85–100 days) but produces heads of exceptional flavor — considered by Italian cooks to be superior to any hybrid purple cauliflower. Di Sicilia Viola (Sicilian Violet) is a traditional heirloom purple cauliflower from Sicily, where purple and violet cauliflower varieties have been grown for centuries as an important winter vegetable in Sicilian cuisine. The Sicilian purple types are the oldest cultivated purple cauliflowers in the world and are quite distinct from modern purple hybrids like Graffiti — they mature later (85–100 days versus 70–80 for hybrids), produce looser, less uniformly round heads, and have a distinctly different flavor: richer, more complex, and sweeter than modern varieties, with a particular quality when braised or roasted that traditional Sicilian cooks consider superior to any modern hybrid. In Sicily, Di Sicilia Viola is used in pasta con i cavolfiori alla palermitana (pasta with cauliflower, olives, pine nuts, raisins, and saffron — one of the signature dishes of Palermo), roasted with olive oil and capers, and in arancini (Sicilian rice balls). The longer maturity makes it best suited as a fall crop in zones 5–9, where it matures into cool fall weather that intensifies the purple color and sweetens the flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant, or time as a fall crop to mature in cool weather.
directions: This rare Italian heirloom forms striking violet-purple curds with a tender texture and mild, subtly nutty flavor. Start seed indoors about six weeks before setting out, then transplant into rich, evenly moist soil for steady, uninterrupted growth. Feed regularly and keep water consistent, since stress can cause loose or bitter heads. Cut heads while the curds are firm and richly colored, knowing the purple may soften toward green when cooked.

common_name: Diablo Brussels Sprout (Disease-Resistant Frost-Sweetened F1 Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost for a fall-into-winter crop; Diablo carries strong overall disease resistance including tolerance to white blister and ring spot, and sprouts sweeten with frost exposure, well suited to an extended Gulf Coast winter harvest.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants; when bottom sprouts reach marble size, remove the growing tip to concentrate the plant's energy into sprout development. Diablo is a hybrid Brussels sprout bred with strong overall disease resistance, including tolerance to white blister and ring spot, two fungal diseases that can disfigure sprouts in humid, wet conditions. Its sprouts sweeten after exposure to frost, so a Gulf Coast fall planting that carries into the region's cool but mild winter can produce a long, steadily improving harvest. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach 1-1.5 inches across and are still tight and firm.

plant_note: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, since germination is slow; transplant out only once nights stay reliably above freezing.
directions: A German-bred open-pollinated celeriac long favored by market growers for producing round, relatively smooth globes with fewer fibrous rootlets than older celeriac types, which makes peeling and trimming considerably easier. Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, since germination is slow, and transplant out only once nights stay reliably above freezing. Keep the bed evenly and constantly moist through the long growing season, and periodically strip away side shoots and surface roots to concentrate growth into a dense, clean-skinned globe that stores well into winter.

common_name: Diamond Eggplant (Classic Large Globe Purple Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date; in zone 9, also transplant in late July through August for a productive fall crop harvested through November.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Diamond is a classic open-pollinated eggplant variety of Eastern European origin — an old, reliable, large-fruited cultivar producing oval to slightly pear-shaped, deep purple-black fruits with a glossy, smooth skin and white, firm, mild-flavored flesh with minimal bitterness. The fruits reach 4–6 inches long and 3–4 inches in diameter at ideal harvest size — large, substantial fruits with good wall thickness and flavor. Diamond is one of the most commonly grown open-pollinated eggplant varieties in American home gardens for its combination of large fruit size, classic flavor, outstanding productivity, and the practical advantage of being a true open-pollinated variety from which seeds can be saved true to type season after season. The compact, upright plants (24–36 inches) produce prolifically from transplanting through the first killing frost. The key to quality eggplant is harvesting before the seeds fully develop: pick when the skin is shiny and fruits yield slightly to gentle pressure — dull skin indicates over-ripeness and bitter, seedy flesh. In zone 9, eggplants are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables and produce reliably from a spring planting through early summer, with a fall crop from an August transplanting that often outlasts the tomatoes.

common_name: Diane Sweet Potato (Heavy-Yielding Louisiana Copper-Skin Type)
plant_note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost in warm, well-drained ridged soil; give Diane a full season since it is a heavier yielder than many faster-maturing cultivars.
directions: Diane was released by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station as a high-yielding sweet potato with smooth copper skin and deep orange flesh, developed to out-produce older Louisiana standards of its era. It shows useful tolerance to soil pox and resistance to white grubs, though like many older cultivars it is susceptible to root-knot nematode, so rotate beds or choose a nematode-resistant companion cultivar if that pest is a known problem in the garden. The vigorous vines and heavy root set reward rich, deeply worked soil and consistent moisture during the bulking stage in mid-to-late summer. Its dependable heavy yield made it a longtime favorite among Gulf Coast home growers before newer LSU releases like Beauregard and Evangeline became more widely available.

common_name: Dickinson Pumpkin (Kentucky Field Pumpkin, Libby's Select)
subcategory: 19th-century field pumpkin, primary source of U.S. canned pumpkin
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after the last frost, in soil that has warmed and with plenty of room for long sprawling vines.
directions: Direct sow in hills after frost danger has passed, giving vines ample room to sprawl, and let fruit fully mature on the vine until the rind hardens and dulls in color.
