Traced to early nineteenth-century Kentucky and carried to central Illinois by farmer Elijah Dickinson, this tan, oblong pumpkin is more closely related botanically to butternut squash than to typical jack-o'-lantern types. Libby's acquired rights to the strain in 1929, and the Dickinson pumpkin remains the primary variety grown for canned pumpkin in the United States today, prized for its dense, smooth-textured, deep orange flesh.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring, or midsummer for fall; Diplomat carries resistance to downy mildew and shows good tolerance of both heat and cold, giving it flexibility across the Gulf South's fall, winter, and spring broccoli windows.
directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist soil; Diplomat is a broccoli hybrid bred with resistance to downy mildew, a fungal disease that thrives in the cool, damp weather typical of a Gulf South winter broccoli crop and can otherwise blemish and stunt developing heads. It forms dense, uniform, blue-green heads on a plant that tolerates both heat during establishment and cold during head development, giving it flexibility across spring and fall plantings. After the central head is cut, side shoots continue to develop, extending the harvest for several more weeks. Cut the main head while the buds are still tight and before any yellow petals show, then keep harvesting side shoots as they reach a similar tight-bud stage.

plant_note: Sow after frost in warm soil; a trellis keeps the long-handled fruits straight.
directions: This heirloom hardshell gourd produces distinctive long-handled fruits reaching up to two feet, useful for ladles, birdhouses, and crafts. Sow seed an inch deep in warm soil and give the vigorous vines a sturdy trellis so the handles hang straight. Water steadily through the long season and let fruits fully mature on the vine. Harvest after the stems dry and cure the gourds in a dry, airy space for several weeks until the shells harden and rattle.

plant_note: Sow directly after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: This pale, tender squash is ideal for the Middle Eastern stuffed dish koosa, thanks to its firm flesh and hollow-friendly shape. The compact plants produce continuously all summer, and large leaves shade and protect developing fruit. Harvest young and often to keep production going. Sow directly into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Provide steady moisture and good airflow to limit mildew.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 70°F, or start transplants indoors 3 weeks early; provide a trellis for vertical growing to maximize air circulation and ease of harvest; in zone 9, sow March–April for spring and again August for fall.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Diva is an All-America Selections Award winner (2002) and one of the most acclaimed cucumbers introduced in the past quarter century — a parthenocarpic (self-fruitful, seedless) cucumber that produces extremely uniform, smooth-skinned, 6–8 inch fruits with thin, tender, never-bitter skin that requires no peeling and no bitterness removal. Unlike most cucumbers that require cross-pollination by insects for reliable fruit set, Diva is parthenocarpic — each flower sets fruit without pollination, ensuring consistent production regardless of pollinator activity. The fruit is reliably seedless or nearly so, with crisp, mild, sweet flesh and completely absent the bitterness that affects some cucumbers. Diva's thin skin, which requires no peeling, and its mild, sweet, never-bitter flavor make it outstanding for fresh eating, salads, and children's snacking. The vigorous, prolific vines produce heavily over a long season — harvest fruits at 6–8 inches before seeds begin to develop for the best eating quality. In zone 9, Diva performs well in the spring and fall growing windows and is among the most heat-tolerant, productive cucumbers for the Gulf South.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Divergent is a galia-cantaloupe cross bred for high resistance to Fusarium wilt races 0-2 and intermediate powdery mildew resistance, a strong disease package for humid Gulf South melon growing.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil, thinning to 2 plants per hill spaced 3-4 feet apart; Divergent is a galia-type melon crossed with cantaloupe genetics, bred for high resistance to Fusarium wilt (a soil-borne fungal disease that can persist in garden soil for years) along with intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, making it a resilient choice for gardens where melons have struggled with disease in the past. The smaller, aromatic fruit has the sweet, floral flavor typical of galia melons with the familiar netted rind of a cantaloupe, ripening earlier than many standard cantaloupe varieties. Harvest when the skin turns from green to golden-tan under the netting and the fruit slips easily from the vine with a fragrant aroma at the stem end. Because it is an organic-bred hybrid popular with market growers, it performs well under lower-input, disease-conscious growing conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; the compact bush habit needs no trellis, unlike pole-type limas.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F. Dixie Butterpea is a compact bush-type lima bean, sparing gardeners the trellising that pole lima varieties require while still delivering the classic small, mild-flavored, buttery-textured seeds Southern cooks know as butterpeas or butter beans. The bush habit concentrates its harvest into a shorter window than pole types, making it convenient for a single large batch of shelling and canning or freezing, and the plant's heat tolerance suits it well to Southern growing conditions. Harvest pods at the green shell stage once well filled for classic butterpea flavor, and succession sow every few weeks through summer for a more continuous supply if desired.

common_name: Dixie Crimson Clover (Long-Season Gulf South Winter Annual Cover Crop Clover)
plant_note: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in fall (October–November in zone 9) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; inoculate seeds with Rhizobium trifolii inoculant before planting to ensure effective nitrogen fixation in new planting areas.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Dixie is the preferred crimson clover variety for Gulf South cover crop use — selected specifically for the warmer winter conditions of the Deep South where it outperforms northern varieties by remaining vegetative longer before bolting to flower, providing a longer window of ground cover, weed suppression, and nitrogen fixation. Crimson clover is the most widely used winter annual legume cover crop in the Gulf South, seeded after the main crop harvest in October–November, establishing through the cool months, fixing atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis, then terminated by mowing, rolling, or light tillage in spring before planting warm-season vegetables. A well-established stand of crimson clover can fix 50–100 pounds of nitrogen per acre — equivalent to a significant fertilizer application — while also improving soil organic matter, preventing winter erosion, and suppressing winter weeds. The 'Dixie' variety's later bolting (compared to 'Autauga' and other early varieties) is its primary advantage in zone 9: it maintains active vegetative growth through February and into March in most years, providing several extra weeks of weed suppression and soil coverage before initiating the red, conical flower heads that signal the end of the vegetative growth period. The showy crimson flower heads that precede termination are also excellent for early-spring pollinators. Inoculate seed with legume inoculant when planting in fields with no history of crimson clover.

common_name: Dixie Golden Giant Tomato (Very Large Golden-Yellow Southern Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Dixie Golden Giant has been maintained and distributed through southern seed saving networks as a locally-adapted golden variety that performs reliably in Gulf South heat.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Dixie Golden Giant is a southern heirloom beefsteak tomato producing very large (1–2+ lb), round to slightly flattened fruits in a golden-yellow to deep-yellow color with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid, meaty flesh that is characteristic of the finest golden beefsteak types. The very large size and golden-yellow color combine to make Dixie Golden Giant one of the most visually impressive golden tomatoes — the large yellow fruits sliced on a plate have a beautiful, rich golden color and the thick, dense flesh produces substantial slices without excess seeding or gel. The flavor is typical of the best large yellow heirlooms: very sweet, very mild, fruity, and low in acid — appealing to those who find standard red tomatoes too sharp or acidic. As a southern-adapted heirloom that has been selected and maintained in Gulf South gardens, Dixie Golden Giant may show somewhat better adaptation to zone 9 conditions than northern golden beefsteak types — though all very large beefsteak tomatoes are challenging to grow through Gulf South summer heat and produce best in the spring growing season (February–June). An open-pollinated variety with saveable seed that grows true-to-type from season to season.

common_name: Dixie Queen Watermelon (Round Striped Southern Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 6-8 feet of room to sprawl.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Dixie Queen is a classic Southern heirloom watermelon dating to the early 20th century, producing round-to-oval fruit with light and dark green striping and sweet, bright red flesh with good old-fashioned watermelon flavor. It was once a popular commercial variety before being largely displaced by modern hybrids bred for tougher rinds and shipping durability, but it remains a favorite among heirloom growers for its reliable production and classic taste in the home garden. Vines are vigorous and productive over a moderate-length season, and fruits typically run in the 15-25 pound range, a manageable size for home use. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true when isolated from other watermelon varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after all frost danger has passed; Dixielee carries strong resistance to root-knot nematode and fusarium wilt, making it a dependable choice for southern gardens where those soilborne problems have limited other southern pea varieties.
directions: Direct sow in full sun into warm, well-drained soil, choosing this variety over other cream peas if root-knot nematode or fusarium wilt has been a problem in the bed. Dixielee was released by the University of Georgia specifically for its combined resistance to root-knot nematode, fusarium wilt, and southern pea mosaic virus, packaged into a productive, semi-vining plant that yields extra-large cream-colored peas with excellent fresh and canning quality. Pods are borne well above the foliage for easy picking and hold their quality over a longer harvest window than many older cream-type varieties. As with other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen in the soil, benefiting whatever crop follows. Harvest pods once they fill out and begin to yellow for fresh shelling, or leave to dry fully for storage.

common_name: Djena Lee's Golden Girl Tomato (Sweet Low-Acid Yellow Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; this productive indeterminate vine benefits from staking and consistent watering through fruit set.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Djena Lee's Golden Girl is an American heirloom yellow beefsteak tomato producing large, smooth, deep-golden fruit with sweet, mild, notably low-acid flesh that is easy on sensitive stomachs and a favorite for gardeners who find red tomatoes too sharp. It is a heavy, dependable producer for an heirloom, setting good yields of large fruit over a long season on a vigorous indeterminate vine. Stake or cage plants for support, water evenly to prevent cracking and blossom end rot, and pick fruit once the skin turns fully golden-yellow and gives slightly to gentle pressure.

common_name: Doe Hill Pepper (Doe Hill Golden Bell, Pre-1900 Virginia Heirloom Sweet Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55F; a pre-1900 family heirloom sweet pepper from Doe Hill in Highland County, Virginia.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost at warm soil temperatures, then transplant into the garden once nights stay reliably above 55F and space plants 18-24 inches apart. Doe Hill is a pre-1900 Appalachian family heirloom named for the small town in Highland County, Virginia, prized for its small, flattened, deeply lobed bells that mature quickly from green to bright orange. The thick flesh and sweet, multidimensional flavor are notably good for such a small fruit, and its early, dependable production makes it an excellent choice for short-season gardens. Plants are compact and disease tolerant; harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or wait for full orange color and maximum sweetness.

plant_note: Plant root divisions or container stock in spring into deep, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil under high open shade; seed germinates slowly after cold stratification, so divisions from an established crown are the faster route to a harvestable clump.
directions: This robust herbaceous perennial dies back to a woody crown each winter and pushes up thick new shoots in spring that are harvested young, before the huge compound leaves fully expand, in the same manner as Japanese angelica tree shoots. Peel and blanch the shoots to soften a mild, resinous bitterness, then stir-fry or season with sesame oil for a classic Korean spring vegetable known as dokwallamul. The root has a long history in Korean herbal medicine as well, though it is the tender shoots that make it worth growing in a shaded vegetable bed. Give it deep, rich soil and generous moisture and it will return reliably for many years from the same crown.

common_name: Doric Brussels Sprout (RHS AGM Early Season F1 Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; Doric is a sturdy, shorter-statured early variety well suited to exposed or windy gardens, cropping from November into February.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant firmly into rich, well-drained soil and firm the base of each plant well since Doric's strength is its short, sturdy stem rather than height; harvest sprouts from the bottom upward as they firm and tighten. Doric is a widely grown F1 hybrid Brussels sprout that carries the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, prized for its strong, compact, wind-resistant stems and heavy yields of smooth, bright, tightly rounded sprouts with good resistance to fusarium and useful tolerance of white blister and mildew. Because the plants stay shorter and stockier than many hybrids, staking needs are minimal even in exposed sites, and the whole stalk can be cut and stood in a cool spot to extend the usable harvest well past when the sprouts would otherwise be picked. Doric's long cropping window, from late autumn through midwinter, and its dependable disease tolerance make it a practical workhorse choice for a sustained home sprout harvest.

common_name: Dorset Naga Pepper (UK-Bred Superhot Capsicum chinense)
plant_note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since chinense superhots germinate slowly and need consistent warmth.
directions: Give Dorset Naga a long, warm season indoors before transplanting, since it needs more heat units than a standard habanero to fully ripen its fruit to deep red. This English-developed selection was bred from Bangladeshi naga stock and yields smoother, more elongated pods than typical wrinkled bhut jolokia types, with fruity aroma alongside intense heat. Stake plants once fruit load builds, and pick some pods slightly early if frost threatens since later flushes often fail to color up in short seasons. It is best suited to collectors in long, hot-summer regions or to greenhouse culture where a longer ripening window can be guaranteed.

common_name: Double Standard Sweet Corn (Bicolor SE Hybrid Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Double Standard is a sugary-enhanced (SE) bicolor hybrid bred for tender, evenly sweet kernels and reliable germination in cooler soil than supersweet types allow.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows rather than one long row, since corn is wind-pollinated and needs neighbors on all sides for full ears. Double Standard is a sugary-enhanced bicolor hybrid that carries the classic tender-creamy texture of older SE types rather than the crisper, sometimes tough texture of supersweet (sh2) hybrids, and it germinates dependably in soil a bit cooler than most supersweets tolerate, which suits an early planting. Ears fill out with a mix of white and yellow kernels and hold good eating quality in the garden for several days past peak without turning starchy as fast as older open-pollinated types. Succession-sow every two to three weeks through early summer for a extended harvest, and pick when silks have browned and a punctured kernel weeps milky juice.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors 3 weeks early and transplant carefully.
directions: Introduced in 1924, this prolific heirloom bears slender, dark-green fruit 4 to 6 inches long, ideal for pickling or fresh slicing. Frequent picking spurs even heavier production, living up to the name. Grow on a trellis to save space and keep fruit clean and straight. Sow into warm, rich soil and water consistently to avoid bitterness. Keep vines evenly moist during flowering and fruiting.

common_name: Doux d'Espagne Pepper (Sweet of Spain Frying Pepper)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55°F; this old French heirloom sets fruit reliably in warm weather but benefits from afternoon shade cloth during the hottest stretch of Gulf Coast summers. In zone 9, transplant in March and again in midsummer for a fall crop.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off seedlings, and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Harvest elongated fruit green for a mild, grassy flavor or let them ripen fully to red for a sweeter, richer taste well suited to roasting and frying. Doux d'Espagne ('Sweet of Spain') is a 19th-century French heirloom frying pepper producing long, tapered, blocky-shouldered fruit up to 6–8 inches that are thin-walled and entirely sweet with no heat, similar in use to Italian frying types but with a distinctively rich, old-world flavor. Plants are productive and tolerate a range of soils, making this a dependable choice for gardeners wanting a classic European sweet pepper for skillet cooking rather than fresh salad use. Fruit is best picked while walls are still tender, since older peppers can develop a slightly tougher skin.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set transplants out 2-4 weeks after last frost once nighttime temperatures stay above 50°F. Protect from late-season frost, as plants die with the first hard freeze.
directions: Start seeds indoors in individual cells 6-8 weeks before the last frost date, transplanting to the garden once soils are reliably warm and settled; downy ground cherry is a more compact, earlier-maturing species than the common tomatillo, and its small yellow fruits — each wrapped in a papery tan husk — carry a distinctive sweetness with vanilla and citrus undertones that makes them exceptional for jams, pies, salsas, and fresh eating. Fruits are ready to harvest when they fall from the plant or when the husk turns papery-tan and the fruit fills it completely. Like its relatives, this Physalis will self-sow freely in warm climates, often returning year after year from fallen fruits. Space plants generously and stake or cage them as they develop a somewhat sprawling, branching habit under productive conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply prepared soil after all frost risk passes; this is an indeterminate variety that needs staking or caging to support the heavy orange beefsteak fruits.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost, transplant into fertile, well-draining soil in full sun, and bury the stem deeply for a stronger root system. Dr. Wyche's Orange honors Dr. John Wyche, a Cherokee chief and circus impresario from Hugo, Oklahoma, who grew tomatoes fertilized with circus animal manure and shared his seeds with Seed Savers Exchange; the variety produces large, up to 2-pound, brilliant orange beefsteak fruits with very meaty, nearly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, low-acid flavor that appeals especially to those who find red tomatoes too acidic. Stake or cage plants solidly as the vines are vigorous and the fruits are heavy; consistent watering prevents cracking. Harvest when fully orange and slightly soft at the blossom end.

common_name: Dr. Wyche's Yellow Tomato (Oklahoma Heirloom Large Orange-Yellow Beefsteak Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Dr. Wyche's Yellow is an indeterminate beefsteak type requiring staking or caging. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring production; the tomato's excellent flavor quality at full orange-yellow ripeness makes timely harvest important — overripe fruits crack and lose flavor. The color at full ripeness is a warm orange-gold to orange-yellow, not pale yellow or greenish — harvest when the fruit has achieved a uniform orange-gold color and has slight give to gentle pressure.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly orange-gold and slightly soft. Dr. Wyche's Yellow is a large-fruited heirloom tomato from an extraordinary source: Dr. John Wyche, a circus man from Hugo, Oklahoma, who operated King Brothers Circus and simultaneously maintained an extensive collection of heirloom seeds that he distributed to seed savers and gardeners over many years. Dr. Wyche reportedly used manure from the circus animals (elephants, big cats, and other exotic animals) to fertilize his prodigious garden at his Hugo farm, giving his tomatoes — which he claimed grew unusually large and vigorous — the colorful story of being 'circus-fertilized.' The tomatoes that bear his name are large beefsteak-type fruits ripening to a warm orange-gold to orange-yellow, with a complex, rich flavor that many tasters describe as fruity, sweet, and low-acid with more depth than typical yellow tomatoes. The fruits are large (often 12–16 oz or more under ideal conditions) and meaty — the solid orange-yellow flesh is dense and flavorful with relatively few seed cavities for a beefsteak type. Dr. Wyche's Yellow has been distributed by Seed Savers Exchange and other heirloom seed sources and has gained a devoted following among heirloom tomato enthusiasts who value the combination of large size, distinctive warm orange-gold color, and excellent flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (August–September in zone 9) in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Dragon's intense skin color develops most vividly in full sun and cool temperatures — the purple-red pigmentation is an anthocyanin response to sunlight and cold that peaks in fall conditions.
directions: Direct sow in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Dragon is a distinctive heirloom carrot producing long, tapered roots with deep red-purple to maroon skin — an unusually vivid exterior color caused by high anthocyanin content — and orange interior flesh with a reddish core that bleeds red-orange color when cut. The flavor is excellent: sweet, slightly spicy, and more complex than standard orange carrots, with the characteristic flavor depth often associated with high-anthocyanin vegetables. Raw Dragon carrots turn a stunning deep red-orange when sliced, making them visually dramatic in fresh salads, crudité platters, and fresh presentations — the color contrast of the purple-red exterior against the orange-red interior is striking and unique. When cooked, the anthocyanin pigments partially convert to blue-gray tones (as with all purple vegetables cooked without acid), so Dragon carrots are best appreciated raw, lightly pickled in vinegar, or roasted at high heat for caramelized flavor development. The excellent flavor and extraordinary color make Dragon an outstanding choice for market gardeners and home gardeners who value both flavor and visual interest. In zone 9, sow in August through September for a fall/winter crop — the cool temperatures intensify both the purple skin color and the sweetness of the flesh.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Dragon Egg is a Croatian heirloom cucumber with egg-shaped, creamy-white to pale yellow fruits harvested before they turn orange, with a mild, sweet flavor, thin skin, and exceptional heat tolerance — one of the most productive and beautiful novelty cucumbers for warm summer gardens.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; train vines on a trellis or fence to make harvesting easier and keep fruits off the ground. Dragon Egg is a Croatian heirloom cucumber with a charming and unusual appearance — the fruits are oval to distinctly egg-shaped, smooth-skinned, and creamy-white to pale yellow when ripe, with a delicate internal structure of mild, sweet flesh and small seeds. They are harvested when fully white-to-cream colored (before they turn orange, which indicates over-maturity and seedy, bitter flesh); at the right stage the flavor is mild, refreshing, and virtually non-bitter even in hot conditions. The plants are extremely productive in warm weather and the fruits hang in clusters, making them easy to spot and harvest. Outstanding for hot summer gardens where standard cucumbers become bitter; one of the most reliably productive white-fruited novelty cucumbers.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is at least 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. Dragon Tongue is a bush bean requiring no support. The distinctive yellow and purple streaked pods should be harvested at 6–7 inches when pods are still flat — the purple markings disappear entirely when cooked, leaving a uniform golden-yellow wax bean. For use as a shelled bean, allow pods to fill and seeds to plump. In zone 9 summer heat can cause plants to drop flowers; fall plantings often produce higher quality pods.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Dragon Tongue is a Dutch heirloom wax bean producing flat, wide, golden-yellow pods dramatically streaked and splashed with deep purple markings — one of the most visually striking beans in the garden and the most eye-catching bean at farmers markets and in kitchen displays. The pods are harvested as a wax bean (snap bean without strings) in the flat stage before seeds swell, when the crisp, flat pods have a buttery, mild wax bean flavor noticeably different from standard round snap beans. The purple streaking serves no flavor function but makes the pods immediately recognizable and appealing; the color vanishes completely during cooking. Dragon Tongue also works as a shellout bean if pods are allowed to mature fully, with cream-colored seeds streaked with black-purple markings. The bush habit and early maturity (55–60 days) make Dragon Tongue productive in relatively short growing seasons, and the ornamental pods add visual interest to the vegetable garden beyond what most productive bush beans offer.

plant_note: Bush habit needs no support; sow after frost danger passes.
directions: This Dutch heirloom wax bean produces buttery yellow pods streaked with purple that fade when cooked. Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil, spacing seeds 4 inches apart in rows 18 inches apart. Harvest as a snap bean at 5-6 inches or leave to mature for a fine shell bean. Pods are stringless and tender when picked young, so gather every few days. Avoid working among wet plants to reduce spread of bacterial blight.

common_name: Dragon Tongue Mustard (Colorful Streaked Chinese Mustard Green)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall for best production in zone 9; Dragon Tongue Mustard is a cool-season green that performs best when temperatures are below 75°F. In zone 9, sow August–November for fall and winter harvest, or February–March for spring. Harvest young leaves at 30–40 days for mildest flavor, or allow plants to reach full size (45+ days) for more pungent, mature leaves. The distinctive red-purple veining on bright green leaves intensifies in cool weather.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest outer leaves from 30 days or cut the whole plant at 40–45 days. Dragon Tongue Mustard is a visually striking Asian mustard green with broad, frilly, bright green leaves overlaid with vivid red-purple veining and midribs — the colorful contrasting veination giving the leaves a dramatic appearance unlike any other mustard type and making Dragon Tongue one of the most ornamental edible greens in the winter garden. The name describes the leaf form: long, broad, and pointed like a tongue, with the red-purple coloring suggesting the fieriness appropriate to a dragon. The flavor is spicy, sharp, and pungent in the characteristic Asian mustard style — more aggressive than mild Asian greens like tatsoi or pak choi, but that pungency mellows significantly with cooking. Raw leaves are assertive and best used in small quantities as a spicy accent in salad mixes; cooked leaves (sautéed, steamed, or braised) are excellent alongside other winter vegetables and complement pork, sausage, and beans. Dragon Tongue grows rapidly in cool weather and is one of the most productive and visually interesting additions to a fall and winter garden in the Gulf South.

common_name: Dragon's Tongue Cucumber (Dragon Tongue, Dutch Yellow Cucumber)
plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost or direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; harvest while fruits are cream with purple stripes — they become fully yellow and bitter if left on the vine too long.
directions: Direct sow or transplant to well-amended, warm soil in full sun after last frost; Dragon's Tongue is a strikingly beautiful Dutch heirloom cucumber producing medium-sized (5–6 inch) cucumbers with creamy-white skin dramatically streaked and splashed with purple-violet, resulting in an ornamental appearance unlike any standard green cucumber. Harvest when fruits are creamy-white with purple markings and firm to the touch — as they continue to mature they turn yellow then bitter. The flavor when harvested at prime ripeness is mild, crisp, and slightly sweet, excellent for fresh eating and pickling. A productive and prolific vining type that does not require trellis but benefits from it.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. The slow-bolting tendency of this Italian heirloom variety makes it an excellent choice for late-spring extension in zone 9, where it holds quality 1–2 weeks longer than standard looseleaf varieties before bolting. Successive sowings extend the harvest window through the cool season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Drunken Woman Frizzy-Headed is an Italian heirloom looseleaf lettuce with one of the most whimsical names in the vegetable kingdom — a literal translation of the Italian 'Ubriaca della Testa Frizzy' — producing large, loosely-headed plants with heavily frilled, ruffled, wavy leaves in a mix of red-bronze tones on green, giving the plant an exuberant, disheveled appearance that the name aptly describes. The large, floppy, curly leaves have a mild, tender, slightly buttery flavor with the red-bronze pigmentation adding a slight edge of complexity over standard green looseleaf. The decorative appearance makes it a standout in the garden and at market, where the dramatic frilly form catches the eye among more uniform types. Drunken Woman Frizzy-Headed is notably slow to bolt and holds in the garden longer than many other looseleaf types, a quality valued in warm climates. The large leaf size makes it easy to harvest by stripping outer leaves for a continuous cut-and-come-again operation.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost risk passes; stake or cage firmly as an indeterminate variety known for good crack resistance.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed. Druzba is a Bulgarian heirloom whose name means 'friendship,' prized for combining an unusually early harvest window with the deep, balanced flavor more typical of longer-season tomatoes. The smooth, red, slightly flattened globes resist cracking better than many heirlooms and the vigorous indeterminate vines stay productive over a long season. Stake or cage securely and pinch suckers lightly to keep the sprawling growth manageable.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into rich, heavy soil kept flooded with 1-2 inches of water through the growing season in full sun; Duborskian rice is a short-season, cold-adapted paddy variety that can mature even in cool-summer northern climates.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into rich, heavy soil kept flooded with 1-2 inches of water through the growing season in full sun; Duborskian rice is a short-season, cold-adapted paddy variety that can mature even in cool-summer northern climates. Bred in Russia for a much shorter and more cold-tolerant growing season than typical rice, it is one of the few rice varieties that home gardeners in temperate, non-tropical climates can realistically bring to harvest, maturing in around 100 days compared to 150 or more for most tropical rice. Grow it in a lined kiddie pool, stock tank, or purpose-built paddy bed that can hold standing water, keeping the bed flooded through most of the growing season and draining it as the grain heads mature and dry down in late summer. Hand-harvest by cutting whole seed heads once grains have hardened and the plant has yellowed, then dry, thresh, and hull before cooking.

plant_note: Plant tubers or rooted divisions in spring directly into shallow water (2–12 inches deep) or saturated pond-margin soil in full sun to partial shade once water has warmed; duck potato spreads by rhizomes and stoloniferous tubers to form a colony over a season or two.
directions: Plant in shallow standing water or saturated soil at a pond, ditch, or rain garden margin in full sun to partial shade; requires permanently wet to submerged conditions and will not persist in soil that dries out. Sagittaria latifolia (duck potato, broadleaf arrowhead, or wapato) is a native wetland perennial named for its distinctive arrow-shaped leaves rising above the water's surface, and for the starchy, walnut-sized tubers it produces at the tips of its underwater rhizomes — a food source of major historical importance to Indigenous peoples across North America, who harvested the tubers by wading into shallow water and dislodging them with bare feet so they floated free for collection. The tubers have a mild, potato-like flavor and can be boiled, roasted, or fried much like a small potato, while the plant's white, three-petaled summer flowers and bold foliage also make it a valuable ornamental and wildlife plant, providing food for waterfowl (hence 'duck potato') and habitat for aquatic insects. An excellent dual-purpose edible and ornamental for a pond margin or rain garden in zone 4–10.

common_name: Duganski Garlic (Spicy Russian Purple Stripe Hardneck)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Duganski is a purple stripe hardneck that needs a real winter chill for good bulb formation and performs best in zone 3-7.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Duganski is a purple stripe hardneck garlic originally from Russia, valued for its notably strong, hot, spicy raw flavor that mellows into a rich, robust taste when roasted or cooked, making it a favorite among gardeners who want an assertive, full-flavored garlic. Bulbs have deep reddish-purple streaked skin over 8-10 tightly packed cloves. As a hardneck, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus the plant's energy on bulb development; scapes are tender and flavorful when harvested young. Duganski also stores somewhat better than many other purple stripe types, often holding for 6-8 months in a cool, dry location. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, then cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot before trimming.

common_name: Dunja Zucchini (Organic Multi-Virus-Resistant Green Summer Squash)
plant_note: Sow directly in warm soil about 1-2 weeks after the last spring frost, or start indoors slightly earlier for a head start in short-season regions.
directions: Sow seeds directly in warm soil 1-2 weeks after the last spring frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for short-season climates. Dunja was bred specifically for organic growers and shows strong resistance to zucchini yellow mosaic virus, watermelon mosaic virus, and papaya ringspot virus, making it dependable where aphid-transmitted viruses commonly cut a squash planting short. The medium-green, cylindrical fruit forms on an open, easy-to-harvest plant; picking regularly at 6-8 inches keeps vigorous plants producing all season.

plant_note: Start indoors early and transplant out after nights are reliably warm.
directions: This dual-purpose chile is used mirasol-style when fresh with a fruity, mild-to-medium heat around 2,500 to 5,000 Scoville units, then becomes guajillo when dried into deep-burgundy pods. Vigorous plants yield tapered fruit of 6.5 to 8 inches with good dry weight for sauces, rubs, and powders. Start seed indoors early for a long warm season. Transplant into full sun after frost danger passes. Harvest fully ripe pods and dry them in a warm, airy place.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Dusky is one of the earliest classic dark-skinned hybrid eggplants to reach harvest size.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dusky is a compact hybrid eggplant that became a home-garden standard for its combination of early maturity, good disease resistance, and heavy sets of deep purple, glossy, oval-to-teardrop fruit. Fruits reach a full 8 to 9 inches while still maturing notably faster than many older large-fruited eggplants, which lets gardeners in shorter-season regions get a reliable harvest before fall cooling slows production. The dense, disease-tolerant bush habit performs well in raised beds and large containers as well as open garden rows. Pick fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm and the flesh gives slightly to gentle pressure, since fruit left to overripen turns dull, seedy, and bitter.

plant_note: Start indoors for spring, or sow mid-summer for fall and overwintering.
directions: This hardy 1800s variety forms compact, deeply curled blue-green leaves and overwinters in all but the coldest climates. It grows best in cool weather but tolerates some heat, and flavor sweetens after frost. The nutrient-dense leaves are low in calories and rich in vitamins. Harvest outer leaves regularly to keep the plant producing. Grow in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist soil.

common_name: Dwarf Blue Scotch Kale (Blue-Green Curly Dwarf Kale)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. sabellica 'Dwarf Blue Scotch'
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer 8–12 weeks before first fall frost, or in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost; Dwarf Blue Scotch is one of the most cold-hardy and compact kale varieties available — the low-growing (12–18 inch), intensely blue-green, finely curled plants survive temperatures well below 0°F in established gardens and produce some of their finest quality after repeated frost exposure through winter.
directions: Sow directly 1/2 inch deep in cool weather and thin to 12–18 inches apart; Dwarf Blue Scotch is very compact and can be planted more closely than full-size curly kales; harvest outer leaves continuously as cut-and-come-again; the plants tolerate temperatures well below 0°F and produce through winter in zones 5–7 without protection. Dwarf Blue Scotch is an old heirloom curly kale variety that combines three notable characteristics: exceptional cold hardiness, compact plant habit, and an attractive, intensely blue-gray-green leaf color that gives it its name. The plants grow only 12–18 inches tall with tightly packed, finely curled and ruffled leaves of a distinctive blue-green color — sometimes described as 'glaucous' or 'sea blue' — that deepens and intensifies after cold exposure, making Dwarf Blue Scotch one of the most visually attractive kales in the winter garden. The flavor is traditional curly kale — somewhat peppery and earthy raw, becoming sweet and mellow after frost exposure, with the classic kale character that mellows beautifully with cooking in soups, stews, sautés, and traditional Scottish 'kail' preparations. The 'Scotch' name reflects the deep Scottish culinary tradition of kale (kail in Scots dialect), where kale was so central to the diet that the kitchen garden was historically called the 'kailyard' and kale broth (kail brose) was a daily staple. The dwarf habit makes it ideal for raised beds, intensive planting, and smaller gardens where space is limited.

plant_note: Direct sow into wet, saline mud or sand at the tidal margin in full sun; dwarf glasswort is a true halophyte adapted to regular tidal flooding with salt water and will not thrive in ordinary garden soil or fresh water alone.
directions: Direct sow into wet, saline mud or sand at the tidal margin in full sun; dwarf glasswort is a true halophyte adapted to regular tidal flooding with salt water and will not thrive in ordinary garden soil or fresh water alone. Leafless, jointed, bright green succulent stems form dense colonies along salt marsh and tidal flat margins, turning red as they mature in fall, and the crisp, salty, juicy young stem tips are harvested and eaten raw or lightly cooked as a gourmet vegetable known variously as sea bean, sea asparagus, or samphire greens. Unlike the perennial glassworts, this annual species completes its life cycle in a single season, germinating on bare tidal mud in spring and setting seed by fall, making it useful both as a foraged coastal vegetable and as a candidate crop for experimental saline agriculture research irrigated with seawater. It requires the specific conditions of a real tidal or brackish marsh edge to thrive and is not a candidate for a typical home garden setting away from the coast.

plant_note: Direct sow 1-3 weeks after the last frost once the soil is warm, spacing seed to allow the compact bushy plants room to branch.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after the last frost, soaking seed overnight to promote even germination, then thin to give plants adequate spacing for good air circulation. Harvest the ribbed, tapering pods young and often to keep the compact plants producing steadily. Dwarf Green Long Pod is a long-standing heirloom selected for its shorter, bushier habit compared to older tall okra types, making it easier to harvest while still delivering abundant, tender green pods. Its manageable size has kept it a staple in home gardens with limited space.

common_name: Dwarf Grey Sugar Pea (Snow Pea, Grey Sugar)
plant_note: One of the earliest snow peas to mature; sow very early in spring (8 weeks before last frost) for a quick cool-season harvest before summer heat arrives; compact habit needs only minimal support (24–30 in twiggy branches or short netting).
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in early spring (up to 8 weeks before last frost) in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dwarf Grey Sugar is an old heirloom snow pea, documented since at least the 1800s, distinguished by its unusually attractive purple-tinged vines and flowers against blue-grey foliage — the purplish cast coming from anthocyanins that also make the young tendrils and pods slightly reddish before the pods mature to green. Compact habit (24–30 inches) makes it ideal for small gardens and containers. An early and productive snow pea; harvest pods frequently when flat and young before seeds swell.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (zone 8-10) or in spring 2 weeks before last frost; dwarf nasturtium is a compact, bushy form that does not trail. Sow directly where it is to grow — nasturtiums resent transplanting. In zone 9, fall-spring is the prime growing season.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; dwarf nasturtium is a compact, bushy form of nasturtium that stays under 14 inches — ideal for containers, edging, and small gardens where the larger trailing species would overrun the space. All parts are edible: the peppery, watercress-flavored leaves are used in salads, the bright flowers as garnish and salad decoration, and the young seed pods pickled as a caper substitute. Unlike many edible flowers, nasturtiums are genuinely flavorful rather than merely decorative. The abundant flowers are rich in nectar and attract hummingbirds and long-tongued bumblebees. The plants prefer lean soil — rich, highly fertilized soils produce lush leaves at the expense of flowers. In zone 9a, grow as a winter annual sown in October for winter and spring display.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or late summer; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: This compact heirloom kale grows low and wide with finely curled green leaves that stay sweet and mild, and it tolerates both cold and heat. Sow seed a quarter to half an inch deep in fertile soil, thinning to give plants room to spread. Harvest outer leaves for baby greens or let plants size up for cut-and-come-again picking. Cold weather and light frost improve the flavor, making it ideal for containers, raised beds, and small-space fall gardens.

common_name: Dwarf Wild Fred Tomato (Compact Red Potato-Leaf Dwarf Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Dwarf Wild Fred is one of the original releases from the international, all-volunteer Dwarf Tomato Project, bred to combine full-size tomato flavor on compact, container-friendly plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy, stout stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Wild Fred bears clusters of medium red fruit with good, rich flavor on a compact, potato-leaf plant that stays under 4 feet, one of the early releases from the Dwarf Tomato Project, an international collaboration of home breeders working to create full-flavored heirloom-quality tomatoes on space-saving dwarf plants. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers where sprawling indeterminate tomatoes would be impractical. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine.

common_name: Eagle Pass Okra (South Texas Heirloom Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed thoroughly; Eagle Pass is a Texas borderland heirloom valued for exceptional heat and drought tolerance, well suited to South Texas and other hot, dry summer gardens.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep once soil is thoroughly warm, since this variety germinates poorly in cool soil; space plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Eagle Pass is a Texas heirloom okra originating from the border region around Eagle Pass, Texas, selected over generations for tolerance of extreme heat and limited water, making it a strong performer in South Texas and other arid warm-climate gardens where many other okra varieties struggle. Plants grow tall and produce ribbed green pods that should be harvested young, at around 3-4 inches, for best tenderness. It remains a favorite among regional seed savers for its resilience and reliable yields under harsh summer conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has warmed well past 70°F, since honeydew is slower to establish than cantaloupe.
directions: Earlidew was developed to bring honeydew melon within reach of gardeners in shorter, cooler growing seasons where standard honeydew varieties often fail to ripen before fall. It produces smooth, pale green-white rinds around sweet, light green flesh on vines noticeably more compact than typical honeydew types. Because honeydew does not slip from the vine at maturity the way cantaloupe does, watch for the blossom end to soften slightly and the rind to take on a faint yellow cast as ripeness cues. Its earlier maturity window makes it one of the more practical honeydew choices for northern vegetable gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and again July–August for a fall crop. Early Acre is one of the quickest-maturing field peas available, making it valuable for both short-season production and getting a crop into the ground before summer heat peaks.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Early Acre is a compact, early-maturing bush cowpea that completes its fresh-shell harvest in just 55–65 days, among the earliest of any southern pea type. The small, cream-colored seeds with a small eye have a mild, slightly sweet flavor preferred by many over the stronger-flavored crowder and black-eye types. This variety is well-adapted to the Gulf Coast's brief spring and fall shoulder seasons, fitting in a productive crop before summer extremes take hold or closing out the season after summer heat breaks. The drought tolerance of cowpeas generally extends to Early Acre, which needs minimal irrigation once established. Harvest pods while the hulls are firm and the seeds have fully plumped but before the hull begins to dry.

plant_note: Direct sow 6–10 weeks before last frost — one of the earliest peas available, germinating in soils as cold as 38°F; Early Alaska is the traditional extra-early pea for late winter and earliest spring planting, maturing before all other commonly grown varieties and finishing before summer heat arrives — ideal for short-season northern gardens and earliest-possible spring pea harvests in the South.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep as soon as soil can be worked in early spring; in zone 6+ this means January–February; in zone 3–5, as soon as soil thaws. Early Alaska is one of the oldest and most cold-tolerant pea varieties, germinating in soils as cold as 38–40°F and maturing in 55–60 days from seed — making it one of the fastest peas available. The smooth-seeded peas are not as sweet as wrinkled-seed types but have traditional pea flavor and historically represent the 'early pea' of American kitchen gardens. Short (24–30 inch), self-supporting plants produce cylindrical pods with 5–7 peas; smooth seeds tolerate cold, wet soil better than wrinkled types that can rot. In Gulf Coast and Southern gardens (zones 8–10), Early Alaska planted in January finishes before March heat ends the pea season.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as the soil is workable in spring; can be resown for a fall crop.
directions: One of the earliest American beet varieties on record, grown widely since the early 1800s and named for its flattened, turnip-like shape rather than any relation to actual turnips. It was the dominant garden beet in the United States for much of the 19th century before newer selections like Detroit Dark Red largely replaced it commercially. Direct sow as soon as the soil is workable in spring; the deep red roots have dense, sweet flesh good for both fresh eating and pickling, and the plant can be resown for a fall crop as well.

common_name: Early Girl Tomato (Classic Early-Season Slicing Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Early Girl is named for its ability to produce ripe tomatoes weeks earlier than standard-season varieties.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Early Girl is one of the most popular home garden tomato varieties in American history — a determinate-to-indeterminate hybrid introduced by Petoseed in 1975 that produces medium-sized (4–6 oz), globe-shaped, deep-red slicing tomatoes 50–60 days from transplant, weeks before most main-season varieties ripen. The combination of early maturity, classic tomato flavor, reliable production, and adaptability to a wide range of climates made Early Girl the best-selling tomato variety in many US markets for decades. In zone 9, Early Girl performs best in the spring window (February–June transplanting), producing the first ripe tomatoes well ahead of main-season varieties while temperatures are still moderate. The plant is a compact to medium-sized indeterminate that requires staking but is less vigorous than large-vined cherry tomatoes — a cage of 48–60 inches is usually sufficient. The classic red, round, full-flavored fruits are excellent for fresh slicing, sandwiches, and summer salads where a moderately sized, well-flavored tomato is preferred over giant beefsteak types. Good disease resistance package makes it dependable in humid Gulf South conditions.

common_name: Early Golden Summer Crookneck Squash (Colonial-Era Yellow Crookneck)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Early Golden Summer Crookneck is a colonial-era heirloom squash, first listed commercially in 1828, with warty, curved-neck golden-yellow fruit.
directions: Direct sow in hills in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the danger of frost has passed. Early Golden Summer Crookneck is one of the oldest documented American squash varieties, first offered commercially by Thorburn's seed catalog in 1828 and grown in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden, producing bright golden-yellow, warty-skinned fruit with the classic curved neck of crookneck squash. Its early, prolific bearing and compact bush habit make it a reliable, fast-producing choice for a home vegetable garden. Harvest young, four to six inches long, for the best tenderness and flavor, picking every day or two during peak production to keep the plant setting new fruit.

plant_note: Direct-sow 1/4 inch deep in spring for an early crop or in late summer for a fall crop; this fast, slow-bolting hybrid tolerates a wider sowing window than older gai lan strains.
directions: A fast, uniform hybrid Chinese broccoli bred for reliable slow-bolting performance across spring, summer, and fall plantings. Dark green, tender leaves and thick, juicy stalks top out with small clusters of edible white buds that taste milder and sweeter than standard broccoli. Cut the main stalk once it reaches pencil thickness and buds are just starting to open, then keep harvesting side shoots for several more weeks of production. Its speed and dependable bolt resistance make it a good choice for gardeners who want repeated gai lan harvests through an entire growing season rather than a single spring or fall flush.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant out after nights stay warm.
directions: This jalapeno bears bold flavor in a compact 3 inch pepper and is better adapted to cooler climates than most jalapenos, making it a good choice for short-season gardens. Enjoy pods green for a mild-to-medium kick or let them ripen red for added sweetness. Start seed indoors early and transplant into full sun after the soil warms. Pick regularly to encourage continued production. Fruit sets best with warm days and consistent moisture.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Early Jersey Wakefield'
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 2–3 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop; in zone 8–9, also sow in fall (August–September) for a mild-winter crop, since the small, quick-maturing heads beat both spring heat and hard freezes.
directions: Set transplants 12–15 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the tight spacing and quick maturity make this variety well suited to succession planting and small-space gardens. Early Jersey Wakefield is one of the oldest cabbage varieties still in cultivation, introduced to American gardens from England in the 1840s and named for Wakefield, England, where it was developed. It forms small, dense, distinctively cone-shaped (pointed) heads of 2–3 pounds that mature earlier than nearly any other cabbage, historically prized for beating both the spring heat and cabbage-worm buildup that plague later varieties. The compact plants and short row-space needs make it a classic choice for small kitchen gardens, and its speed makes it valuable for a quick spring crop ahead of summer vegetables, or a fast fall crop in mild-winter climates. A true living heirloom with over 180 years of continuous garden use, in zone 3–9.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant once the soil is consistently warm and nights are frost-free.
directions: Sow indoors under warm conditions and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once temperatures are reliably warm, since this heirloom is sensitive to cold snaps. Space plants generously and water evenly to keep the slender fruit from developing a bitter edge. Early Long Purple is a traditional Italian variety valued for producing its slim, curved, deep-purple fruit earlier than many other eggplant types, making it a useful choice for gardeners in shorter-season regions. Its thin skin and few seeds make it popular for frying and grilling whole.

common_name: Early Prolific Straightneck Squash (Classic American Yellow Summer Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; in zone 9, plant spring crops in February–March and fall crops in August–September; summer squash is susceptible to squash vine borers in zone 9 — the fall crop planted in August often misses peak vine borer pressure and may produce more reliably than the spring planting.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Early Prolific Straightneck is the classic American yellow summer squash — the standard straightneck type that has defined the yellow summer squash category in American home gardens and commercial production for decades. The smooth, straight, medium-yellow to golden-yellow squash (6–8 inches at ideal harvest) has the classic straight-neck shape (no bulge or curve at the blossom end) that distinguishes straightneck from crookneck types. The tender, mild-flavored flesh is excellent sautéed, grilled, steamed, stuffed, and in casseroles — the standard all-purpose yellow summer squash for every culinary application. An All-America Selections winner recognized for its exceptional productive performance and consistent quality. Harvest squash when small to medium (6–8 inches) for best flavor and tenderness — oversized squash develop tough skin, large hard seeds, and coarse, watery flesh. In zone 9, summer squash is best grown in spring (February–April) and fall (August–October) — the summer heat accelerates production to the point of difficulty managing harvests. The squash vine borer is the primary pest challenge in zone 9; fall planting (August) often escapes the peak infestation period. Extremely productive — a few plants provide more squash than most families can use during peak season; succession planting at 2–3 week intervals provides more manageable quantities.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil has warmed.
directions: This award-winning yellow straightneck squash yields thick, firm, fine-grained fruit in as little as 45 days. Versatile in the kitchen, it can be eaten raw, pickled, cooked, or baked into sweet breads. Harvest young, around 4 to 6 inches, for the best texture and to keep plants producing. Sow directly into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Keep evenly watered and pick frequently.

plant_note: Sow in summer and overwinter plants for late winter to spring sprouts.
directions: Unlike single-head types, this cold-hardy heirloom produces a flush of deep purple florets on many side shoots for an extended harvest. Start seed in summer and set robust transplants into rich soil so they establish before winter. Plants overwinter in mild climates and reward growers with tender sprouts in late winter and early spring. Pick shoots regularly while the buds are tight to keep new sprouts coming; a brief cook preserves the color.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant for spring, or sow midsummer for fall heads.
directions: This 19th-century heirloom produces compact, round green heads with a mild flavor and dependable cold tolerance. Start seed indoors about five to six weeks before transplanting into firm, fertile soil. Keep watering even and steady, since fluctuations can split maturing heads. Harvest once heads feel solid and firm, cutting cleanly at the base; it performs well in both spring and fall plantings.

common_name: Early Scarlet Globe Radish (Classic Fast Spring Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil is workable in spring; Early Scarlet Globe is one of the oldest and most widely grown spring radish varieties in American gardens — a very fast-maturing (22–28 days), perfectly round, bright scarlet-red radish with crisp white flesh, mild peppery flavor, and a slow tendency to become pithy after maturity, making it one of the most reliable and forgiving of the traditional spring radish varieties.
directions: Sow in thin rows 1/4 inch deep; no need to thin closely if sown sparsely; harvest when roots are 3/4 to 1 inch across; Early Scarlet Globe holds slightly better in the ground than some varieties without becoming immediately pithy — useful for succession plantings where exact harvest timing is impractical. Early Scarlet Globe is a foundational heirloom spring radish that has appeared continuously in American seed catalogs since the 19th century and remains one of the most widely recognized and consistently reliable spring radish varieties for home garden use. The name describes it precisely: the variety matures early, produces globe-shaped (round, not oval or elongated) roots, and has the classic bright scarlet skin color of traditional spring radishes. The roots are smooth and round, typically reaching 3/4 to 1 inch in diameter at the ideal harvest stage, with bright white, crisp, mildly peppery flesh that is refreshing and clean-flavored. Early Scarlet Globe is somewhat more forgiving than some spring radish varieties — it maintains quality for a few extra days in the ground after reaching harvest size before becoming pithy or hollow — a useful characteristic when garden timing is imprecise. Its very fast maturity (22–28 days) makes it one of the quickest-maturing vegetables a gardener can grow and ideal for teaching children about gardening: almost immediate gratification. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Early Scarlet Globe thrives in the short cool season windows of January–March and October–November before heat forces bolting.

common_name: Early Sunglow Sweet Corn (Ultra-Early Yellow Short-Vine Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows wide for wind pollination; Early Sunglow germinates in cooler soils than most hybrid sweet corn (as low as 55°F), allowing it to be planted 1–2 weeks before standard hybrids in spring. The short (4–4.5 foot) stalks and compact habit make Early Sunglow suitable for smaller garden spaces. In zone 9, plant February–March for a May harvest as one of the first corn varieties of the season.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Early Sunglow is the gold standard of early-maturing sweet corn for home gardeners who want corn on the table as soon as possible in the season — a yellow su (standard sugary) hybrid that ripens in just 62–68 days from planting, providing corn approximately 3–4 weeks before mid-season varieties like Silver Queen. The compact (4–4.5 foot) stalks are one of Early Sunglow's most practical attributes for home gardens: shorter plants are less susceptible to lodging in wind or storms and fit better in smaller garden plots where standard 6–7 foot corn would be too tall. Early Sunglow's germination in cooler soils (down to about 55°F) also allows planting 1–2 weeks earlier in spring before soils warm fully, extending the effective growing season at the front end. The ears are smaller than mid-season varieties (6–7 inches, 12–14 rows) but are well-filled with tender, sweet, yellow kernels with the classic su corn flavor — pleasantly sweet without the overwhelming intensity of sh2 supersweet types. For gardeners in zones 4–6 with short seasons, Early Sunglow may be the only way to reliably produce sweet corn before fall frosts; in zones 7–10, it provides the season's earliest fresh corn while later varieties are still maturing.

common_name: Early White Bush Scallop Squash (Classic White Patty Pan Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, spacing hills to give the bushy plants room to spread.
directions: This is one of the oldest American summer squash types, grown by colonial gardeners well before it was formally selected and named in the 19th century, producing the classic ivory-white, scallop-edged flying-saucer fruit. Harvest at 2-3 inches across while the rind is still soft enough to pierce with a fingernail; older fruit turns starchy and tough quickly. The compact bush habit suits small beds and containers better than vining winter squash, and steady picking every couple of days keeps the plant setting new fruit through the season. Its pale color and mild, delicate flavor make it a good choice for gardeners wanting a change from the more common yellow and green scallop types.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes 'Early White Vienna'
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Kohlrabi is one of the fastest-maturing Brassica crops — ready in 45–60 days from seed. Harvest when the swollen stem reaches 2–3 inches diameter; larger sizes can become woody and fibrous. In zone 9 fall planting produces excellent quality; plants handle light frost with no damage. The rapid maturity makes kohlrabi valuable for succession planting between other slower crops. Peel the tough outer skin before eating.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Early White Vienna is the standard open-pollinated kohlrabi variety — the pale green, globe-shaped swollen stem that has defined kohlrabi's appearance in seed catalogs and markets for more than a century. Kohlrabi is among the most distinctive of all vegetables because the edible part is neither a root nor a leaf but a dramatically swollen, above-ground stem that balloons into a globe shape at the base of the plant with the leaves attached at the sides — a growth habit that surprises gardeners encountering kohlrabi for the first time. The crisp, juicy white flesh beneath the thin pale-green skin has a flavor often described as a mild, sweet, slightly broccoli-stem-flavored apple — kohlrabi is excellent eaten raw like an apple, cut into sticks for snacking and dipping, shredded into slaws, or cooked in stir-fries and soups where it retains some crunch even when heated. The flavor is far milder and sweeter than most brassicas, making kohlrabi one of the most approachable and snackable vegetables directly from the garden, particularly attractive to children who enjoy the mild sweetness and the theatrical process of peeling and eating the unusual globe.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Grown since the early 1900s, this early variety delivers abundant, tasty greens up to 18 inches tall along with flavorful roots, and is ideal where multiple crops fit the season. The leaves are high in vitamins A and C, iron, and potassium. Since each seed is a cluster, thin seedlings for well-shaped roots. Sow in cool weather and keep soil evenly moist. Harvest roots young and tender or let them size up.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep in spring in well-drained soil; earth pea is easiest to establish from tubers rather than seed, which can be slow. The vine dies back in winter and re-emerges from the tubers in spring. Give stems something to climb.
directions: Plant tubers in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun, giving the climbing stems support from a trellis, fence, or neighboring plants; earth pea is a remarkable perennial legume from central Europe that forms small, chestnut-flavored starchy tubers along its root system — the edible reward in addition to the ornamental rose-pink flowers. The tubers can be eaten raw, boiled, or roasted and have a pleasant, sweet, slightly floury flavor. Historically the plant was gathered as a famine food across rural Europe and was cultivated as a minor food crop in the Netherlands and France. Like other legumes, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and gradually improves soil fertility. The vine is vigorous and twining, to about 3–6 feet, and the fragrant flowers attract bumblebees. An unusual, under-exploited edible perennial for food forest and permaculture plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for fall.
directions: This colorful mix produces red, white, rose-pink, purple, and bicolor spring radishes for a rainbow at harvest, making it a fun crop for kids. As a spring type it grows best in the cool periods of spring and fall and turns pithy in summer heat. Sow directly and thin seedlings early for well-formed roots. Keep soil evenly moist for crisp, mild radishes. Eat fresh in salads or as a crunchy snack.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall/winter/spring crops. Easter Egg radishes mature in 25–35 days and should be harvested promptly before roots become pithy in warm weather. Succession sow every 10 days for continuous harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and 1 inch apart, thinning to 2–3 inches after germination; Easter Egg is a blend of radish varieties producing a cheerful mix of purple, red, white, and pink round radishes (all similar in size to a chicken egg) in the same row — the variety gets its name from the surprise of digging mixed-color 'eggs' from the soil. Individual plants in the blend mature at slightly different rates over 2–3 weeks, naturally extending the harvest window. The crisp, mild, slightly spicy roots are excellent raw in salads, on veggie platters, or sliced and eaten with butter and salt in the classic French crudités style. This mixed-color planting is particularly popular in children's gardens for its surprise-reveal at harvest. In zone 9, fall and winter plantings (October–January) produce the crispest, mildest roots — spring radishes bolt quickly as temperatures rise. Harvest promptly when roots reach egg size; leaving them too long makes them hollow and pithy. One of the fastest and most satisfying crops for impatient gardeners.

plant_note: Detach a pad and allow the cut end to callous for 3–5 days, then set in dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; Eastern prickly pear establishes quickly and requires essentially no irrigation or care once established.
directions: Plant callused pad sections in very well-drained, dry, sandy to rocky soil in full sun — eastern prickly pear is the most cold-hardy prickly pear cactus in North America, native from New England to the Gulf Coast and surviving zone 4 winters without damage. The flattened pads (2–4 inches across) grow close to the ground in a spreading mat; large, showy yellow flowers with numerous prominent orange stamens appear in May–June and are followed by barrel-shaped, red to purple-red edible fruits (tunas) that persist through winter. Both the young pads (nopales) and the fruits are traditional foods: young pads are peeled of their glochids and eaten as a vegetable; fruits are juiced, made into jelly, candy, and syrup. The glochids (tiny barbed hair-spines) on the fruits require careful handling — burn or scrub them off before consuming. An outstanding, zero-care native groundcover for dry, rocky, sandy, full-sun spots where lawn and conventional plants would fail.

common_name: Ebenezer Onion (Old Dutch Yellow Storage Heirloom)
plant_note: Can also be grown from sets planted as soon as the soil is workable in spring; Ebenezer is an old long-day storage onion best suited to northern gardens with long summer daylength.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free through bulb development. Ebenezer is a classic Dutch-derived heirloom onion, long grown in American gardens both from seed and from sets, producing firm, globe-to-slightly-flattened yellow-brown bulbs with pungent flesh and outstanding storage life compared to sweeter modern hybrids. It is one of the parent lines behind several later commercial yellow storage onions and remains popular with gardeners who want an old-fashioned, strong-flavored keeper for cooking rather than fresh eating. Stop watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall, then pull, cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for a few weeks, and store in a cool, dry place where it will keep considerably longer than sweet onion types.

plant_note: Direct-sow shallowly after the soil has warmed, in moist, fertile soil in partial shade; ebolo germinates and grows quickly in warm weather, self-sows readily, and can also be started from stem cuttings rooted in water.
directions: Sow or transplant into moist, fertile soil in partial shade; ebolo is a fast-growing, soft-stemmed leafy green widely eaten across West and Central Africa and parts of Southeast Asia, where the tender young leaves and shoot tips have a distinctive bitter-savory, slightly peppery flavor often compared to a cross between spinach and arugula. It performs best with some relief from the hottest afternoon sun, which keeps leaves tender and delays the small, brush-like reddish-orange flowers that signal the plant is turning bitter and going to seed. Pinch shoot tips regularly for continuous harvest and to keep plants bushy and productive; in frost-free areas it behaves as a short-lived perennial and self-sows freely, while gardeners farther north grow it as a warm-season annual.

plant_note: Sow 1–3 weeks after last frost when soil has reached at least 60°F; cold, wet soil causes seed rot.
directions: Sow seeds 1 to 1.5 in deep in rows 18–24 in apart; inoculate with soybean-specific rhizobium for best nitrogen fixation. Edamame is self-supporting but benefits from well-drained, fertile soil with only modest added nitrogen. Harvest when pods are bright green, plump, and the seeds fill the pod but the shell has not yet begun to yellow. To harvest, pull the entire plant and strip pods at once; blanch immediately for best flavor and color.

plant_note: Plant cormels or divisions after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Eddo taro is root-hardy in zone 9 and may overwinter in the ground with mulch protection, resuming growth in spring from the persistent corm. Plants grown in zone 9 can be left in the ground for multiple seasons, harvesting corms and cormels as needed without replanting.
directions: Plant cormels in moist, organically rich soil in partial shade to full sun with consistent moisture; Eddo (eddoe, eddo taro) is the small-corm type of Colocasia esculenta widely grown in the Caribbean, West Africa, and Southeast Asia for its edible corms and cormels — small, round to ovoid corms 1–2 inches across with hairy brown skin and white-to-purple-tinged starchy flesh. Unlike the large dasheen-type taro that produces a single massive central corm, eddo produces numerous small cormels clustered around a small central corm, making harvest easy — simply pull the plant and break apart the cormel cluster. The flesh is starchy and mild, with a slightly mucilaginous, creamier texture than dasheen, and is used in soups, stews, boiled as a side dish, and fried into chips throughout the African and Caribbean diaspora. The oxalic acid in raw taro requires thorough cooking; always boil or roast before eating. Eddo tolerates partial shade and moist soils and thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast.

common_name: Eden's Gem Melon (Rocky Ford Green-Flesh Muskmelon)
plant_note: Direct sow once soil has warmed and all danger of frost has passed, in hills spaced to give vines room to spread.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger has passed, spacing hills to let the compact vines spread, and water evenly while fruit is sizing. Developed at Rocky Ford, Colorado and introduced in 1905 as a descendant of the older Green Nutmeg melon, Eden's Gem produces softball-sized, heavily netted fruit with green flesh and a distinctive spicy-sweet flavor. Its early maturity made it a popular shipping melon in the early twentieth century, and it remains prized by heirloom growers for its complex flavor in a compact package.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; edible amaranth (tampala) is an Asian and tropical leafy vegetable amaranth grown for its exceptionally nutritious, mild-flavored leaves — it is the primary amaranth vegetable of South and Southeast Asian cuisine, used in stir-fries, curries, and soups in China, India, the Philippines, and throughout tropical Asia.
