directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; harvest outer leaves from 30 days; pull entire plant at 50–60 days before flowering. Amaranthus tricolor (edible amaranth or tampala) is a South and Southeast Asian edible leafy vegetable that is one of the most important leaf vegetables in tropical Asian cooking — the primary amaranth grown for its edible leaves (as distinct from grain amaranths like A. cruentus). The plant produces large, oval, slightly crinkled leaves in spectacular color combinations ranging from solid green or red-tinged green to dramatic tricolor varieties with patches and blotches of red, gold, and green or entirely deep crimson to magenta — the basis for the ornamental varieties sold as 'Joseph's Coat' in Western gardens. The leaves are nutritionally outstanding: very high in protein (15–20% on a dry-weight basis), iron, calcium, and vitamins A and C — one of the most nutrient-dense leafy vegetables. In Chinese cooking (where it is called 'xian cai'), the leaves are stir-fried with garlic; in Indian cooking (used as 'chaulai' in Hindi), the leaves are sauteed with spices; throughout Southeast Asia, it is used in soups and curries as a heat-tolerant spinach substitute. The heat tolerance of tampala — thriving in temperatures that cause spinach and other cool-season greens to bolt — makes it especially valuable in Gulf Coast and tropical summer gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Amaranthus dubius is one of the primary leafy vegetables of tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean and is exceptionally heat-tolerant — it thrives in Gulf Coast summer conditions when most cool-season greens have bolted and failed.
directions: Scatter seed thinly on the soil surface and press in gently — amaranth seeds need light to germinate and should not be buried more than 1/8 inch deep; thin to 6–12 inches when plants are 3 inches tall. Amaranthus dubius is the primary edible-leaf amaranth of the Caribbean and tropical Africa, where it is known as callaloo, bhaji, or Chinese spinach and harvested as a highly nutritious leafy green with more than twice the iron, calcium, and protein of spinach per serving; it is one of the few leafy vegetables that produces abundantly through Gulf Coast and tropical zone summers when temperatures exceed 95°F and humidity is high. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips from the time plants are 6 inches tall; regular cutting encourages bushy growth and delays flowering. The entire young plant can be cooked like spinach in soups, stews, and sautés.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep in spring after last frost in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile soil; Edible Canna grows vigorously in Gulf Coast humid conditions and requires regular irrigation for best rhizome production. Harvest rhizomes in fall when the plant begins to die back, leaving some in the ground to regenerate next season. Unlike ornamental Canna hybrids bred for flowers, Edible Canna is grown primarily for its large, starchy rhizomes used as food. Direct sow scarified seeds after filing the hard seed coat.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately wet soil; Edible Canna produces its largest, most nutritious rhizomes in rich, consistently moist conditions with full sun, but tolerates partial shade in hot zone 9 summers. Canna indica (the species form, as opposed to modern ornamental Canna hybrids) is an edible perennial from tropical and subtropical America that has been cultivated as a food crop in the Andes, Central America, and the Caribbean for over 4,500 years — rhizomes found at archaeological sites in coastal Peru date to 2500 BCE. The starchy rhizomes — large, horizontal, thick, and up to 2 feet long in well-grown plants — are processed like arrowroot: washed, peeled, grated, pressed to extract starch, dried, and used as a thickener and flour substitute called 'Queensland Arrowroot' (in Australia) or 'Tous-les-Mois' (in the French Caribbean). The fresh rhizomes can also be cooked and eaten like potatoes or dried and ground into a fine, easily digestible starch valuable for people with wheat sensitivities. The plant produces small orange-red flowers (much less showy than ornamental Canna hybrids) and bold, paddle-shaped tropical leaves. In zone 9, it overwinters in the ground and regrows rapidly each spring.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; edible hibiscus grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and begins producing harvestable leaves within 6–8 weeks — one of the most productive leafy vegetables per square foot in tropical gardens.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; edible hibiscus grows rapidly and may be harvested as a cut-and-come-again leafy green from 6 weeks. Abelmoschus manihot (edible hibiscus, aibika, or sunset muskmallow) is a large, fast-growing, tropical Asian shrub that produces an edible leaf crop as important as spinach across much of Melanesia, Papua New Guinea, and the Pacific Islands — the large, lobed, maple-leaf-like leaves (4–8 inches wide) are harvested young and cooked as a spinach substitute in stews, stir-fries, and soups; the young leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous (okra-like) texture and are highly nutritious, rich in protein, calcium, and vitamins A and C. The plant also produces very large, 4-to-6-inch, sulfur-yellow hibiscus flowers with a dark-purple eye that are strikingly ornamental; the flowers are also edible (used in salads and desserts). In zone 9, edible hibiscus grows as a fast annual or short-lived perennial, easily reaching 6–8 feet in a single season. The plants are closely related to okra (A. esculentus) and share its preference for heat, humidity, and well-drained, fertile soil; they cross readily with ornamental hibiscus but not with roselle (H. sabdariffa).

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil has warmed; loves heat.
directions: This heat-loving green offers nutritious, colorful foliage with a hearty spinach flavor that is sweet and slightly tangy. It thrives when spring greens bolt in warm weather and is drought tolerant once established. Use it fresh in salads or steamed, stir-fried, or added to soups. Sow directly into warm soil in full sun. Harvest young leaves regularly to keep plants tender and productive.

plant_note: Direct sow in sandy, well-drained soil in hills after last frost; Edisto 47 was specifically developed at the Edisto Research and Education Center in Blackville, South Carolina, for the hot, humid Southeast and has outstanding resistance to powdery mildew and other diseases that devastate most cantaloupe varieties in the Deep South.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun, well-drained sandy soil, 1–2 weeks after last frost; Edisto 47 is a Clemson University (South Carolina) heirloom cantaloupe developed in 1953 specifically for the humid, disease-pressure conditions of the Deep South where most cantaloupe varieties fail to powdery mildew, downy mildew, and Alternaria blight. It produces medium-sized (3–5 lb), oval, heavily netted fruits with thick, salmon-orange flesh of very good, rich cantaloupe flavor. The 'Edisto' name honors the Edisto Research and Education Center in Blackville, SC, and '47' the year development began. For over 50 years it was the cantaloupe of choice for Deep South gardeners because no other variety could reliably produce through summer humidity — even as newer hybrids have been developed, Edisto 47 remains a benchmark for disease resistance and regional adaptation.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 2–3 weeks after frost danger has passed when soil is warm.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and maintain soil temperature above 80°F for the best germination rates. Eggplant demands the warmest possible spot in the garden; cold soil stunts growth significantly, so do not rush transplanting. Mulch heavily to hold soil warmth and moisture, and fertilize with a phosphorus-rich blend to promote flowering. Harvest fruits while the skin is still glossy, as dull skin signals over-maturity and bitterness.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of warm, fertile, well-drained soil once soil has warmed past 70°F and frost danger has passed; egusi is grown for its oil- and protein-rich seed rather than sweet flesh, so let fruit fully mature and dry on the vine before harvest.
directions: Sow in hills of warm, well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing vines to sprawl across at least 6 feet of row; egusi is a distinct culinary melon from dessert watermelon, grown throughout West Africa for its flat, oil-rich seeds that are dried, ground, and used to thicken egusi soup and stews. The round, pale green fruit has bland, unpalatably bitter to fibrous flesh that is discarded — do not harvest young for eating like watermelon. Leave fruit on the vine well past the point a watermelon would be picked, until the rind dulls and the vine begins to dry back, then split fruits open and ferment or wash the pulp away to recover the flat white seeds for drying. Rotate away from other cucurbits each year to limit vine borer and powdery mildew buildup.

plant_note: Plant topset bulbils in early fall so they establish before winter; spring planting is also possible but fall-planted bulbils produce larger plants more quickly.
directions: Plant the small topset bulbils 1–2 inches deep in fall or early spring, pressing firmly into well-drained soil; established clumps need dividing every 2–3 years to maintain vigor. Egyptian walking onions produce clusters of small bulbils at the top of the flower stalk; as these become heavy the stalk bends and the bulbils root where they land, effectively 'walking' across the garden. Harvest underground bulbs in early summer after the foliage begins to die back, or harvest green tops continuously throughout the growing season like scallions. The topset bulbils can be harvested for pickling or used as transplants.

plant_note: Plant aerial bulblets 1–2 inches deep in fall or spring in any well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Egyptian walking onion is essentially indestructible and multiplies vigorously with no special care — an excellent permanent addition to the perennial food garden.
directions: Plant aerial bulblets 1–2 inches deep in fall in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Egyptian walking onion is a perennial onion cross that 'walks' itself across the garden by producing clusters of small bulblets at the top of its flowering stalks — when the bulblets become heavy enough, the stalk bends to the ground and the bulblets root where they touch soil, establishing a new cluster a foot away. The entire plant is edible year-round: the underground bulbs are used like small onions, the hollow green tops are used like green onions or chives, and the aerial bulblets are pickled or used as pearl onions. Varieties with particularly fine bulblet clusters and flavor include 'Zebrune' and 'Catawissa'. Essentially zero-maintenance once established — just harvest and leave the rest to multiply. An outstanding permanent edible for the low-maintenance food garden.

common_name: Egyptian Wheat (Tall Forage Sorghum Biomass and Screening Cover Crop)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed above 65°F; Egyptian Wheat is an exceptionally tall, sturdy forage sorghum type grown for biomass, screening, and wildlife habitat rather than as a food grain.
directions: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, and thin or drill to a moderate stand since plants grow extremely tall and can shade neighboring rows. Egyptian Wheat is a tall, robust forage sorghum, despite the common name it is not a true wheat, prized for reaching 8 to 12 feet with thick, sturdy stalks and broad leaves that produce heavy summer biomass, build organic matter, and outcompete summer weeds. Its height and density make it a popular seasonal screen, windbreak, or living privacy hedge in addition to its cover-crop role, and the seed heads that follow provide valuable food for doves, quail, and songbirds through fall and winter. Mow, roll, or cut and drop the stalks at the end of the season to return biomass to the soil, or leave standing for winter wildlife cover; it is killed outright by the first hard freeze.

common_name: Eight Ball Squash (Round Dark Green Zucchini, Compact Summer Squash for Stuffing)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Eight Ball is a round zucchini type producing perfectly round, dark green fruits on a compact, upright bush plant. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August–September for fall production. The round form is Eight Ball's defining characteristic — rather than the elongated cylinder of standard zucchini, Eight Ball fruits are globose (round), producing a shape ideal for hollowing and stuffing. Harvest at 3–4 inches diameter (roughly golf ball to baseball size) for best flavor and tenderness; the skin toughens and the flesh becomes starchy if allowed to grow to tennis ball or softball size. Eight Ball's compact plant (18–24 inches tall) makes it excellent for raised beds and containers. The round shape also means the squash sits stably when stuffed and baked, without rolling — a practical advantage over elongated zucchini in stuffed preparations.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 18–24 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches diameter when skin is dark green and glossy. Eight Ball is a compact, round-fruited zucchini variety that produces unusually shaped globose fruits — perfectly spherical when harvested at optimal size — on upright, compact bush plants significantly smaller than standard elongated zucchini types. The name 'Eight Ball' references the eight-ball billiards ball — a solid black sphere — which the dark green, round squash resembles at small harvest size. The round form is the primary distinctive quality: while standard zucchini is selected for elongated cylindrical shape that makes it easy to slice into uniform rounds, Eight Ball's round form creates a naturally shaped container ideal for hollowing and stuffing. For stuffed squash preparations, Eight Ball provides several practical advantages: the round form creates a stable base for baking without additional support, the natural cavity when the top is removed is more generous relative to fruit size than elongated squash, and individual fruits at optimal 3–4 inch harvest size provide a single-serving portion that is visually appealing when presented whole. The flavor is typical mild zucchini with slightly denser flesh than elongated types at comparable harvest sizes — the round form concentrates more flesh relative to surface area than a cylinder of comparable diameter. Eight Ball was developed and released by Park Seed, with the AAS award confirming performance across diverse North American trial conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, enriched soil; Eight Ball is an AAS winner round zucchini producing billiard-ball-shaped, dark green, glossy fruits ideal for stuffing whole — an outstanding novelty-and-culinary squash for the summer garden that produces prolifically on compact bush plants.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained, enriched soil; Eight Ball is a compact bush type that needs 2–3 feet of space but no support. Eight Ball is an All-America Selections award-winning round zucchini producing compact, perfectly spherical, dark green fruits 2–4 inches in diameter — essentially billiard ball-shaped summer squash with the same mild, tender, slightly sweet flavor as regular zucchini but in a form perfect for stuffing whole. Hollow them out (a melon baller works perfectly), fill with cheese, rice, meat, and herbs, and bake for a complete stuffed vegetable presentation; they hold their round shape beautifully when baked. Harvest at 2–3 inches for perfect stuffing size; larger fruits become seedy and tougher. Highly productive on compact, bushy plants; good for small-space and container gardens.

common_name: Eight-Row Flint Corn (New England Flint, Rhode Island Flint)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in blocks; Eight-Row Flint is the original New England corn of the Narragansett, Wampanoag, and other Indigenous peoples of the Northeast — the corn that the Pilgrims learned to grow and which sustained early colonial New England, and the genetic ancestor of nearly all modern flour and sweet corn varieties.
directions: Sow in blocks of 4+ rows after last frost; Eight-Row Flint is earlier-maturing than most heritage corns and well-suited to shorter northern seasons. Eight-Row Flint (also called New England Flint, Rhode Island Flint, and Narragansett Flint) is the traditional corn of the Algonquian peoples of the northeastern United States — the corn that sustained the Wampanoag, Narragansett, Mohegan, and neighboring peoples for centuries before European contact, and the corn that taught early colonists of Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay how to survive in New England. It bears exactly eight rows of hard, flinty, small kernels in orange-red, white, or multi-colored patterns on slender 7–9 inch ears; the flint kernel type (hard, glass-like outer layer rather than dented) grinds into a fine, sweet, dense cornmeal. This is the corn of traditional New England johnnycakes, the grain type tested by Narragansett Flint Corn restoration projects. A critical piece of American agricultural heritage.

plant_note: Sow 2–6 weeks before the first fall frost to allow establishment before winter; einkorn overwinters as a low rosette and resumes growth in early spring.
directions: Sow seed 1 in deep in fall at 80–100 lb per acre (about 2–3 oz per 100 sq ft); einkorn is an ancient hulled wheat that outperforms modern wheats on poor, low-fertility soils and has exceptional drought tolerance. It overwinters, then bolts in spring to reach harvest in early summer, about 2 weeks earlier than modern winter wheat. Harvest when the grain is in the hard dough stage — the straw turns yellow but the heads have not yet shattered — by cutting and binding into sheaves left to dry for a week before threshing. Einkorn retains a tough hull after threshing that requires dehulling before milling; the flour is notably nutty and golden from higher carotenoid content.

common_name: Elephant Foot Yam (Whitespot Giant Arum, Suran)
plant_note: Plant corm divisions or small offsets in spring after soil warms to 65°F or above in well-drained, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; elephant foot yam produces the second-largest underground corm of any cultivated plant (second only to giant taro) and is an important food crop throughout South and Southeast Asia.
directions: Plant corm sections in well-drained, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade in spring after soil warms; lift corms before first frost in zone 9. Amorphophallus paeoniifolius (elephant foot yam or suran) is a tropical Asian aroid producing a single, enormous, deeply divided, umbrella-like leaf (resembling a tropical fern frond writ large) on a mottled green-and-grey petiole, and a massive underground corm that can reach 20–30 lbs in a single season. The corm is an important starchy food crop throughout South and Southeast Asia — particularly in India and Sri Lanka, where it is cooked as a curry vegetable, fried in oil, and made into a popular Bengal-region dish. The flesh is white, somewhat mucilaginous (like taro), with a mild, slightly bitter flavor that is neutralized by cooking with acidic ingredients like tamarind. Like all amorphophallus species, the occasional flower is an extraordinary, though briefly malodorous structure — a large, purple-maroon spathe and spadix with the characteristic carrion-flower smell that attracts pollinators. The plant is entirely ornamental in terms of foliage, with a single dramatic leaf reaching 4–6 feet across. Must be cooked thoroughly before eating — raw corms contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Plant cloves in fall 2–4 weeks before hard ground freeze to allow root establishment before winter dormancy.
directions: Plant individual cloves 2–4 inches deep pointed end up in well-drained, fertile soil in fall, with the flat base downward. Elephant garlic is technically a leek relative (Allium ampeloprasum) rather than a true garlic; its flavor is much milder and sweeter than hardneck garlic, lacking the pungent bite, and the huge cloves are easy to peel. Remove flower scapes (curling stems) in early summer to redirect energy into bulb development, just as with true garlic. Harvest when the lower third of the leaves has browned, dig carefully, and cure in a warm, ventilated location for 3–4 weeks before storing or braiding.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes.
directions: More closely related to leeks than true garlic, elephant garlic produces very large bulbs of 1 to 6 mild, tan cloves that are superb roasted. Plant individual cloves in fall, pointed end up, in fertile, well-drained soil and mulch for winter protection. Remove the edible scapes in early summer to direct energy into the bulbs. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy place. Space plants generously since they grow tall and wide.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil is warm.
directions: This zucchini was bred with a more compact, open habit so fruit is easier to spot and harvest before it grows oversized. Plants produce reliably all summer, yielding versatile dark-green squash for countless dishes. Harvest young at 6 to 8 inches and pick often to keep production high. Sow directly into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Water consistently and allow airflow to reduce mildew.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Emerald Gem arose as a chance seedling in a Michigan garden, was purchased and introduced by W. Atlee Burpee in 1886, and quickly became one of the most popular American muskmelons of the late 19th century for its rich, spicy-sweet flavor.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after last frost, thinning to the strongest two or three plants per hill. Emerald Gem produces small, globe-shaped, deeply ribbed fruits with smooth, dark emerald-green skin that conceals thick, richly flavored, pale orange flesh often described as having a distinctive spicy sweetness beyond typical cantaloupe. Discovered as a chance seedling in the Michigan garden of William G. Voorhees, it was purchased and introduced commercially by W. Atlee Burpee in 1886 and quickly became a benchmark variety praised for combining fine flavor with dependable, uniform type. Because the fruit is compact and matures relatively quickly for a melon, it suits shorter-season gardens; keep soil evenly moist through fruit set and harvest at full slip, when the stem releases cleanly from the vine.

common_name: Emerald Giant Sweet Pepper (Very Large Thick-Walled Green Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Emerald Giant is a commercial-type pepper that responds well to consistent fertility — apply a balanced fertilizer at transplanting and a calcium-containing fertilizer mid-season to prevent blossom-end rot.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; Emerald Giant is one of the standard large-fruited bell pepper varieties for American home and commercial gardens — producing very large (4–5 inch long, 3–4 inch wide), blocky, 4-lobed, thick-walled green bell peppers with the classic sweet bell pepper flavor and firm, crunchy flesh that defines the standard bell pepper for American cooking. The name reflects both the large fruit size ('Giant') and the deep green color at the typical fresh-market harvest stage — the brilliant, deep-green, shiny-skinned fruits are the archetypal green bell pepper form. Left to ripen fully, Emerald Giant turns red, producing a sweeter, more complex flavor than the green stage. The thick walls (3/8–1/2 inch) provide more usable pepper flesh per fruit than thin-walled types, better heat retention in cooking preparations, and superior durability at harvest. In zone 9, bell peppers produce best in the spring season (March–June) and a brief fall window (September–October) — the extended summer heat reduces fruit set and causes sunscald on exposed fruits. The large, heavy fruits on 'Emerald Giant' require staking or caging to prevent branch breakage when the plant is heavily loaded.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil is warm; soaking seed overnight speeds germination.
directions: This heirloom okra is prized for smooth, rich green pods that stay tender even when they grow larger than usual, over a long harvest window. Sow seed about an inch deep in warm soil, soaking overnight first to hasten sprouting. Give plants full sun and steady moisture, and they will grow tall and productive through the heat of summer. Pick pods every day or two while young to keep the plants setting; frequent harvest greatly increases total yield.

common_name: Emerite Filet Bean (French Haricot Vert Pole Bean for Thin Tender Pods)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to 60°F; Emerite is a French pole-type filet bean (haricot vert) producing slender round pods (under 0.25 inch diameter) at pencil-thin harvest stage of 4–6 inches. The pole habit (to 5–6 feet) requires trellis support but produces far more heavily and over a much longer period than bush filet types. Harvest daily or every other day at pencil-thin stage for the finest texture; pods become starchy and coarse within 2–3 days of reaching optimal harvest size. Emerite is one of the most productive filet pole beans available, making it a practical choice for gardeners who want restaurant-quality haricots verts without the heavy labor input of bush varieties that must be replanted every 2–3 weeks.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart; provide trellis or pole support to 6 feet and harvest every 1–2 days when pods reach 4–5 inches and are no thicker than a pencil. Emerite Filet Bean is a French-bred pole-type haricot vert that delivers the classic thin-podded, tender filet bean quality of French cuisine on a vigorous climbing plant that produces heavily over months rather than the 2–3-week harvest window of bush filet types. The haricot vert category — defined by pod diameter under 6mm and harvest at pencil-thin stage before any internal seed development is visible — requires frequent harvesting to maintain pod quality; pods left on the plant for even an extra day begin to develop seeds and shift from the tender, fine-textured filet bean to a coarser snap bean. This harvesting discipline rewards with pods of extraordinary tenderness: lightly steamed for 3–4 minutes, Emerite haricots verts have a delicate, slightly squeaky texture and refined mild flavor that is categorically different from mature-harvested snap beans. Pole-type filet beans like Emerite provide a practical advantage over bush types for home production: a single planting in spring can continue producing through fall in zone 9 (with a brief mid-summer slowdown during peak heat), whereas bush filet varieties exhaust themselves within 2–3 weeks and require successive plantings every 3 weeks to maintain a continuous harvest. The climbing habit also improves air circulation around pods in the humid Gulf Coast environment, reducing the fungal disease pressure that can limit bush bean production in midsummer heat and humidity. Blanch harvested pods in salted boiling water for 2–3 minutes, shock in ice water to set the bright green color, then serve simply with butter, lemon, and salt to showcase the delicate flavor.

plant_note: Sow direct in late summer 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for a fall/early winter harvest; endive tolerates light frost and improves in flavor after frost exposure — in Gulf Coast zones 8–10 it is an excellent fall through spring crop.
directions: Sow direct in late summer (8–10 weeks before first fall frost) or in early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in the Gulf South (zones 8–10), sow from September through January for a fall through spring season. Cichorium endivia encompasses two main types: curly endive (frisée) with very finely cut, curly, frilly leaves and a pronounced bitter flavor, and escarole (broad-leaved endive) with flat, broader, less curly leaves and a milder flavor; both can be blanched by tying outer leaves over the heart for 1–2 weeks to reduce bitterness and produce the pale, creamy heart used in bistro salads. Endive is an outstanding fall and winter salad plant in the Gulf South, tolerating light frost and performing through the cool season. The bitter compounds are reduced by cold temperatures.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Enterprise is a hybrid zucchini bred for resistance to a broad package of common cucurbit mosaic viruses, an important advantage in aphid-prone Gulf South gardens where virus pressure often shortens the summer squash season.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Enterprise is a hybrid zucchini bred for resistance to a broad spectrum of the mosaic viruses that commonly spread through squash plantings via aphids, keeping foliage healthier and fruit better colored later into a humid Gulf South summer than more virus-susceptible varieties. The compact, open bush habit produces uniform, dark green cylindrical fruit that is easy to spot and harvest as the plant fills in. Pick fruit at 6-8 inches for the best texture and flavor, checking plants daily during peak production since summer squash quickly grows oversized and tough if missed for even a couple of days.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil has reached at least 60°F; Envy is one of the earliest-maturing edamame cultivars available and tolerates cooler soil at planting better than many other edamame varieties, allowing an earlier sowing date in spring.
directions: Sow seed 1 to 1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart in full sun; inoculate with soybean-specific rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Envy is a widely grown edamame cultivar valued for its notably early maturity — among the fastest edamame varieties to reach harvest — and for better cold-soil tolerance at planting than many other edamame types, making it a good choice for gardeners wanting the earliest possible edamame crop or a second planting for fall harvest. Plants are compact and productive, with pods clustering densely on relatively short, sturdy bushes. Harvest when pods are bright green, plump, and fully filled but before the shell begins to yellow — sample a pod for tenderness and flavor to judge exact timing. For the classic preparation, boil or steam whole pods briefly in well-salted water, then squeeze the beans directly from the pod to eat; pods themselves are fibrous and not eaten.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Epic carries resistance to tobacco mosaic virus and is specifically recommended for Florida and Texas growing conditions, making it a solid choice for Gulf Coast eggplant growers.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Epic is a vigorous, high-yielding hybrid eggplant carrying resistance to tobacco mosaic virus and is specifically recommended by Southern extension programs for Florida and Texas growing conditions. It produces large, classic glossy black-purple, oval fruit on a sturdy, well-branched plant that holds up well to summer heat. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure — dull skin and hard flesh signal overripe fruit with more seeds and a bitter edge. Keep picking regularly through the season to encourage continued flowering and fruit set, and provide consistent moisture, since eggplant grown under drought stress tends to develop tougher skin and more bitterness.

plant_note: In mild-winter regions sow in early fall for a winter-into-spring harvest; elsewhere direct sow around the last frost date.
directions: Broadcast or row sow seed clusters thickly and shallowly, since this type is grown for its abundant tender leaves rather than for large stalks. This unusual Italian chard lacks the thick, wide ribs of standard Swiss chard, instead producing slender stems and smooth, spinach-like leaves that regrow quickly after cutting. Favored by cooks for its mild flavor and quick-cooking texture, it tolerates both cool weather and mild heat better than many leafy greens, making it useful for extended cutting through a Gulf Coast winter.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in shaded, humid nursery beds or plant established liners after the last frost against a stake or trellis; seed is rarely used since it loses viability within days of falling.
directions: Establish rooted cuttings in deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil at the base of a tree, pole, or trellis, since this dioecious woody liana climbs by twining and will scramble many feet into a support if left unchecked. Eru is a slow-growing rainforest understory vine from Central and West Africa whose thick, glossy, leathery leaves are shredded fine and cooked into the beloved eru and okazi soups of Cameroon, Nigeria, and the Congo Basin, usually simmered with palm oil, meat or fish, and other greens. Because wild populations have been heavily overharvested, cultivating a few vines on a shaded fence or living trellis provides a sustainable home supply once the plant is established, after which stems can be selectively cut back for repeated leaf harvest for many years. Keep roots shaded and evenly moist and mulch heavily, as the plant resents drought and full, hot sun.

common_name: Escamillo Pepper (AAS-Winning Golden Italian Frying Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Escamillo is an early-maturing Corno di Toro-type Italian frying pepper that colors up to gold well before most sweet peppers finish ripening.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Escamillo is an AAS-winning Italian frying-type sweet pepper producing long, tapered, elegantly curved fruits that ripen unusually early from green to a rich golden yellow, giving a full harvest of fully ripe, sweetest-stage peppers well before many other sweet pepper varieties finish coloring. Fruits are thin-walled and sweet, excellent sautéed or grilled as well as eaten fresh, and the plant is productive and reasonably compact for a frying-pepper type. Stake plants loosely if fruit load bends the branches, and harvest continuously once fruits reach full gold color to keep new peppers setting.

plant_note: Sow in midsummer so the broad-leaved head matures in cool fall weather, 12–14 weeks before first frost.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in well-amended soil; escarole forms broad, flat rosettes with broad wavy leaves that are less bitter than curly endive. Blanch by gathering outer leaves and tying them over the center for 10–14 days before harvest to produce a creamy, tender heart. Harvest the full rosette by cutting at the soil line when heads are 12–14 in across. Escarole holds well in the garden through light frosts, which improve its mellow, slightly bitter flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; sow every 2 weeks for a continuous supply, and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed thinly in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist to slow bolting; Esmee is a fast, cold-tolerant arugula with deeply lobed, rounded oakleaf-shaped foliage that is fluffier and more ruffled than standard salad arugula, giving noticeably more visual loft in a mixed salad bowl. Its flavor leans nutty and mild rather than sharply peppery, making it approachable for gardeners and eaters who find standard rocket too pungent. Harvest baby leaves as early as three weeks for salad mixes, or let plants grow on for a fuller-size cutting at about six weeks. Like all arugula it bolts quickly in heat, so it performs best as an early spring or fall crop.

plant_note: Plant offsets in spring in full sun in very well-drained, rocky soil; Agave angustifolia (espadín) accounts for roughly 90% of commercial mezcal production in Oaxaca and is the most widely cultivated agave for spirits production, requiring 7–15 years of growth before harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in rocky, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil with minimal irrigation once established; espadín agave (Agave angustifolia) is the workhorse of the mezcal industry in Oaxaca, Mexico — accounting for approximately 90% of mezcal production globally — and is the most planted agave for spirits production due to its vigorous growth, prolific offsetting, and the distinctive smoky, earthy mezcal flavor its roasted piña produces. The plant produces numerous offsets ('hijuelos') around the base that are used to propagate new plants; after 7–15 years the plant flowers and dies. The young flower stalks are edible when roasted and a significant food source in Oaxacan villages. An attractive, medium-sized agave for warm, dry gardens and a living connection to the ancient mezcal tradition of Mexico.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Espelette is the Basque Country's PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) chile pepper, grown in the Espelette region of southwest France since Basque explorers brought capsicums from the Americas in the 16th century and now the defining spice of Basque cuisine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed. Piment d'Espelette is the unique chile pepper of the Espelette commune and neighboring villages in the Pays Basque region of southwest France and northern Spain, where it holds PDO (Appellation d'Origine Protégée) status — meaning the authentic product can only come from that specific area. The elongated, 3–5 inch, initially green peppers ripen to brilliant red and are traditionally strung in long chains and dried in the mountain air; the resulting dried, ground powder has a distinctive mild-to-medium heat (1,500–4,000 SHU), sweet pepper aroma, and earthy-fruity flavor that is unlike any other pepper spice. Used to season virtually all savory foods in Basque cooking in place of black pepper — on eggs, fish, piperade, axoa (veal stew), chicken basquaise, and fromage de brebis (Basque sheep cheese). Grow in any warm garden; the fresh peppers have excellent flavor even without the Basque drying climate.

plant_note: Start indoors early alongside a favorite scion variety; graft the two together once stems are pencil-thick, heal in a humid shaded chamber, then transplant after frost into full sun.
directions: This vigorous interspecific hybrid rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite tomato scion variety rather than eaten itself, valued for a somewhat more moderate, better-balanced vigor than the extremely aggressive Maxifort rootstock, making it a popular choice where growers want the disease resistance and yield benefits of grafting without excessive vegetative growth crowding out fruit production. It carries strong resistance to fusarium and verticillium wilts, corky root rot, and nematodes, and its more restrained root vigor compared to Maxifort suits closer plant spacing or shorter growing seasons where overly rampant rootstock growth would be a liability. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, graft when stems are pencil-thick, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy support.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; unlike most brassica greens, Ethiopian Kale tolerates heat far better and can be sown again in early summer in the Gulf South without bolting as fast as regular kale or collards.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows 12-18 inches apart, thinning to 6-12 inches for full-sized plants or leaving dense for cut-and-come-again baby greens. Ethiopian Kale, known as gomen in its native highlands, is a vigorous leafy brassica long grown as a staple green across Ethiopia and Eritrea, valued for its notable resistance to flea beetles and other brassica pests as well as its unusual heat tolerance, which lets it keep producing tender leaves through early summer heat that would send most kales and collards straight to bolting. Leaves are broad, slightly savoyed, and blue-green, with a flavor milder than collards but more assertive than standard kale, excellent braised, sauteed, or added to stews. Harvest outer leaves starting around 30 days for baby greens or let the plant mature and harvest the whole head; regular picking of outer leaves encourages continued production from the center. Because it shares pests and diseases with other brassicas, rotate away from beds that recently grew cabbage-family crops.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Ethiopian moringa (M. stenopetala) is the 'other moringa' — a species native to southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya that produces the same edible large leaves, pods, and seeds as common moringa (M. oleifera) but with larger, softer, milder-flavored leaves eaten as a staple vegetable across the Konso region of Ethiopia, where it has been cultivated as a major food crop for centuries longer than M. oleifera.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; coppice every few months to maintain leaf production. Moringa stenopetala (Ethiopian moringa or cabbage tree) is the second commercially important moringa species after M. oleifera — native to the semi-arid highland areas of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, particularly the Konso region of the Omo Valley, where it has been cultivated and consumed as a major vegetable crop for an estimated 2,000+ years, far longer than M. oleifera in most of Africa. The tree is sometimes called 'cabbage tree' because the large, oval, blue-green leaves (much larger than M. oleifera's tiny leaflets) are eaten cooked in large quantities like cabbage — chopped and boiled or sautéed as a staple vegetable, often cooked with sorghum paste (injera dough), and also added to bean stews. The flavor is milder and less bitter than M. oleifera leaves. Like its more famous relative, M. stenopetala has exceptional nutritional density — high in protein, iron, calcium, vitamins A and C. The seeds produce a high-quality oil (ben oil) used for cooking. M. stenopetala is more adapted to cooler, higher-elevation tropical conditions than M. oleifera, and may perform better in humid tropical highland climates. Both can be grown in zone 10–12 lowland tropical gardens.

common_name: Eva Purple Ball Tomato (German Black Forest Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Eva Purple Ball is noted for holding up well in hot, humid conditions and shows useful foliar disease tolerance in the garden.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, staking the indeterminate vines as they grow. Eva Purple Ball traces to Germany's Black Forest region in the late 1800s and was carried to New Jersey by the Bratka family, producing smooth, round, rosy-pink fruit of five to seven ounces with a sweet, well-balanced flavor. Gardeners in hot, humid regions especially value it for staying productive and relatively blemish-free when many other heirlooms struggle with disease pressure.

common_name: Evangeline Sweet Potato (LSU Crack-Resistant Orange Gulf Coast Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant slips in warm soil after last frost when soil reaches 65F; Evangeline was bred at the LSU AgCenter as an earlier-maturing, crack-resistant alternative to Beauregard and performs especially well in Louisiana's heavy, sometimes wet clay soils where standard varieties are prone to splitting.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun after last frost; Evangeline is an LSU AgCenter release named for the Cajun heroine of Longfellow's poem and bred to match Beauregard's rich orange flesh and copper skin while ripening slightly earlier and resisting the growth cracking that Beauregard develops in wet Louisiana clay. Vines are moderately compact, and roots are uniform, smooth-skinned, and store well. Flavor is sweet and moist, excellent baked, mashed, or roasted. Because it matures a week or two earlier than Beauregard, Evangeline is a good choice for gardeners wanting an earlier harvest window or extra insurance against fall frost. Cure roots at 80-85F and high humidity for about a week after digging to heal skins and concentrate sugars, then store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated spot.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January and transplant February–March. Everglades tomato naturalizes readily in warm coastal climates and can reseed prolifically — once established, it may grow as a perennial in frost-free zone 10 or self-seed reliably in zone 9.
directions: Transplant into any well-drained soil in full sun; the Everglades tomato is the wild currant tomato (Solanum pimpinellifolium) as it naturalized and adapted to South Florida's extreme subtropical heat, humidity, and occasional drought over generations. It is the most heat-tolerant of all cultivated tomatoes — it reliably sets fruit at temperatures above 95°F and through humidity levels that shut down every commercial variety. The tiny (marble-sized, 1/2 inch) red fruits grow in long clusters of 20–40 and have an intensely rich, sweet-acidic tomato flavor disproportionate to their size — considered by many to have the purest tomato taste of any variety. The vines sprawl and climb enthusiastically (6–8 feet) and are extremely drought-tolerant once established. In South Florida, Everglades tomatoes produce year-round and naturalize along roadsides and garden fences. In zone 9a, they perform as a long-season annual. Seeds are collected easily and the plant passes selected characteristics to offspring, making it an important parent in breeding heat-tolerant tomatoes. Highly recommended for hot, humid, low-maintenance gardens.

common_name: Evergreen Hardy White Bunching Onion (Cold-Hardy Perennial Scallion)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop; this bunching onion does not form a bulb and is exceptionally cold-hardy, often overwintering in the ground to provide scallions the following spring even in fairly cold climates.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike bulbing onions, this classic bunching onion (Welsh onion type) never forms a true bulb, instead producing clusters of straight, white-shanked scallions with mild, tender green tops. Its exceptional cold hardiness lets it overwinter in the ground in many climates, providing an extra-early harvest the following spring, and it can be cut back repeatedly through the growing season for a continuous supply. Because it multiplies by division at the base, an established clump can be divided every year or two to keep plantings vigorous and productive.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after last frost; Evertender's spineless pods make repeat picking easier through a long harvest season.
directions: Evertender is a spineless hybrid okra bred for pods that stay tender and stringless days longer than most varieties, reducing the pressure to pick every single day to avoid tough, fibrous pods. The smooth, spineless pods and foliage also make harvest far more comfortable, since typical okra plants are covered in fine irritating spines. Direct sow after the soil has warmed, since okra germinates poorly in cool, wet ground, and pick pods at 3-4 inches for the most tender eating. Its extended tenderness window makes Evertender a practical choice for gardeners who can only harvest okra every few days rather than daily.

plant_note: Seedless triploid; start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm, and plant alongside a seeded pollenizer watermelon for fruit set. Exclamation carries intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, and was bred to reduce hollow heart, a common quality defect in large seedless melons grown in Southern heat.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Exclamation is a full-season seedless watermelon hybrid bred with intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, along with reduced tendency toward hollow heart, a cracking defect that can hollow out the center of large seedless melons grown under Southern heat stress. Because triploid seedless varieties need a seeded pollenizer nearby for fruit set, plant a compatible pollenizer variety in the same bed. It produces large, blocky, crimson-fleshed fruit with excellent sweetness and firm texture. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed thinly and shallowly, about 1/4 inch deep, in fertile soil; also excellent for fall sowing six weeks before first frost.
directions: Direct-sow seed thinly and shallowly, about 1/4 inch deep, in fertile soil, since this miniature pak choi matures in as little as 30 days and can be grown at very tight spacing for dense baby-green production. Its curled, glossy dark-green leaves sit atop short, thick white petioles, giving each plant a compact, rounded form even smaller than standard baby bok choy. Because it thrives across a wide range of temperatures, it can be succession-sown nearly year-round in mild climates for continuous harvests of whole tender plants used raw, steamed, or stir-fried.

common_name: Eye of the Goat Bean (Ojo de Cabra)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil; Eye of the Goat (Ojo de Cabra) is a traditional Mexican and Southwestern heirloom bean with striking beige seeds marked by a tan-ringed dark eye — one of the most beautiful and flavor-rich heirloom beans in the Southwestern tradition.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in warm, well-drained to dry soil; Eye of the Goat is adapted to dry conditions and does well with minimal supplemental irrigation in zones 7–11 once established. Eye of the Goat (Ojo de Cabra) is a traditional Mexican heirloom dry bean with large, oval, cream-to-beige seeds marked with a distinct tan 'eye' or ring surrounding a dark hilum — resembling, as the name suggests, the eye of a goat. This bean has been grown in Mexico and the American Southwest for generations and is particularly heat- and drought-tolerant, making it valuable in hot, dry climates. When cooked, the seeds have a rich, earthy, slightly sweet flavor with a creamy texture that holds its shape well; excellent in soups, stews, and as refried beans in traditional Mexican cooking. An outstanding heirloom for Gulf Coast and Southwest gardeners who need a reliable dry bean in hot, occasionally dry summers.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and in late summer; succession sow for a steady supply.
directions: This uniform, short-headed leaf lettuce has little core, so a single cut above the base releases evenly sized leaves for easy salad prep. It is slow to bolt for a long harvest and offers resistance to downy mildew and lettuce aphid. Grow in full sun to partial shade in cool weather, providing afternoon shade in heat. Keep soil consistently moist for tender, sweet leaves. Succession sow every couple of weeks for a continuous supply.

common_name: Facing Heaven Pepper (Chao Tian Jiao, Upward-Pointing Chinese Chile)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Facing Heaven can be grown as a perennial, producing prolifically for multiple seasons from the same plant when protected from hard frost. Harvest fruits at the red stage for fresh use or drying; dried Facing Heaven peppers are essential in many Sichuan and Hunan dishes.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; Facing Heaven pepper (朝天椒, Cháo Tiān Jiāo, meaning 'facing heaven pepper') is one of the foundational chili pepper varieties of Chinese cuisine — a small to medium-sized (1.5–2.5 inch), bright red, upward-pointing hot pepper produced in prolific clusters where each plant can carry 50–100 fruits simultaneously, the upward orientation giving the variety its evocative name as the fruits point skyward like tiny flaming torches. The peppers are hot (30,000–70,000 Scoville units), with a clean, direct heat and a characteristic bright, slightly fruity flavor that is distinct from Mexican or Caribbean chiles — a flavor that has made this pepper type essential in the cooking of Sichuan, Hunan, Yunnan, and Guizhou provinces, where it appears in red oil (hóng yóu), chili pastes, dried whole peppers for stir-fries, and fermented condiments like dòubànjiàng. The dried bright red fruits maintain excellent color and retain their heat well; they are often dry-roasted in oil with Sichuan peppercorns as the starting point for the characteristic ma-la (numbing-hot) flavor profile of Sichuan cooking. Very productive in the Gulf South's warm climate, producing abundantly from midsummer through fall.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed; Faerie was bred by Known-You Seed Company and named a 2012 All-America Selections winner for its creamy yellow, thin-striped rind, sweet pink-red flesh, and unusually compact vines that suit smaller gardens.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks earlier for a head start in cooler climates; vines are notably more restrained than most watermelons, spreading to roughly 10-11 feet rather than sprawling widely. Faerie was bred by Taiwan's Known-You Seed Company and named a 2012 All-America Selections winner for its distinctive creamy yellow rind marked with thin light stripes, enclosing crisp, high-sugar pink-red flesh, and for producing a heavy set of personal-size, 4-6 lb oval fruit on a comparatively space-efficient plant. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and fruit set, then ease back as melons near maturity. Harvest by watching the ground spot shift from white to creamy yellow and the nearby tendril dry and brown, since the pale rind makes color-based ripeness cues less obvious than on dark-skinned watermelons.

common_name: Fairy Tale Eggplant (AAS 2005 Miniature Lavender-White Striped Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Fairy Tale is an F1 hybrid from Sakata Seed that won All-America Selections in 2005 and has become one of the most popular eggplant varieties for home gardens and farmers markets. In zone 9, transplant March–April for spring and summer production; eggplants thrive in Gulf Coast heat and can produce from May through October or beyond with proper care. The compact plant size (18–24 inches) makes Fairy Tale excellent for containers and small spaces. Harvest when fruits are 3–4 inches long and still have their distinctive lavender-white striping — do not let fruits mature to full purple, which indicates overripeness and seed development.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost when nights are consistently above 55°F. Harvest fruits at 3–4 inches before they fully mature. Fairy Tale is a Sakata Seed F1 hybrid eggplant that earned All-America Selections recognition in 2005 for its exceptional productivity, compact plant habit, and near-elimination of the bitterness and seedy texture that can make standard large eggplants unpalatable to some cooks. The fruits are distinctively beautiful: elongated-oval, 3–4 inches long, with an eye-catching pattern of alternating lavender-purple and creamy white vertical stripes — a color combination different from any other commonly grown eggplant type. The white striping on mature fruits is genetically stable and does not fade with cooking, making Fairy Tale attractive in stir-fries, roasted vegetable mixes, and fresh preparations where the color contrast remains visible. The key culinary advantage of Fairy Tale over standard large eggplant varieties (Black Beauty, Diamond) is the dramatically lower seed count and virtually absent bitterness: Fairy Tale fruits have fewer, smaller seeds than large types, and the flesh requires no salting or pressing to remove bitterness before cooking. A single established plant can produce 30–50 fruits over a long season in zone 9's warm climate — significantly more than a comparable large-fruited variety — making Fairy Tale an exceptionally productive choice for gardeners who want consistent eggplant supply through summer.

plant_note: Sow after frost in warm soil; allow ample room for sprawling vines.
directions: Also called Musquee de Provence, this heirloom produces deeply lobed pumpkins that ripen from green to warm chestnut-brown with rich, flavorful flesh favored by cooks. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and give the long vines plenty of room to sprawl. Water consistently and side-dress with compost as fruits swell. Let pumpkins ripen fully to their bronze color, then cure in a warm spot to deepen flavor and extend storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; young leaves can be picked as a cut-and-come-again crop within a month of sowing.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed directly into warm, well-drained soil once temperatures are reliably warm, then thin seedlings as young leaves are harvested. False sesame is a fast-growing annual widely gathered and cultivated across West and Southern Africa's savanna zones as a leafy relish vegetable; its tender, mucilaginous leaves are cooked much like okra to thicken soups and stews and are valued as a nutritious, drought-tolerant green in the dry season. The plant produces small tubular pink to lilac flowers similar to true sesame and its close relative, followed by seed capsules that yield an edible oil in some traditions, though leaf harvest is the primary use. Repeated cutting of the growing tips encourages bushy regrowth and extends the harvest window through the warm season.

common_name: Falstaff Brussels Sprout (Deep Red-Purple Anthocyanin-Rich F1 Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 14–18 weeks before first fall frost; Falstaff is a striking purple-red Brussels sprout F1 hybrid whose intense color comes from very high anthocyanin concentrations — the same antioxidant pigments in red cabbage and blueberries — that intensify with cold exposure; it is the classic 'purple Brussels sprout' for gardeners who want visual drama alongside the vegetable's traditional nutty, sweet flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors 14–18 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil; Falstaff needs consistently cool fall temperatures to develop its deepest purple color — color intensifies dramatically after frost; harvest when sprouts are 1–1.5 inches across. Falstaff is the premier purple Brussels sprout for home gardeners and is named for the colorful, exuberant Shakespearean character Sir John Falstaff — the name suggests something robust, larger-than-life, and visually dramatic, which the deep red-purple sprouts certainly are. The intense color comes from very high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments distributed throughout the outer leaves and (to a lesser degree) the interior of each sprout; the color deepens dramatically with cold temperatures, making late-season fall-harvested Falstaff significantly more deeply purple than sprouts harvested in early fall before hard frost. The purple color fades to an unappetizing grayish-green if overcooked in water, but holds better with roasting, steaming, or quick stir-frying — and the raw purple sprouts are spectacularly visual in slaws and salads where the color impact is undiminished. The flavor is equivalent to standard green Brussels sprout varieties: nutty, slightly bitter, sweet — some gardeners find the flavor of purple types slightly milder than green types, possibly because the anthocyanin pigmentation is linked to somewhat lower glucosinolate levels.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting for an early spring crop; Farao is one of the earliest-maturing fresh-market cabbage hybrids available, bred for resistance to tip burn and to hold in the field without splitting, letting Gulf Coast gardeners bring in a cabbage crop before summer heat arrives.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Farao is one of the earliest-maturing fresh-market cabbage hybrids available, forming compact, round, 2-3 lb heads that size up quickly, an advantage for Gulf Coast gardeners racing to finish a spring cabbage crop before summer heat sets in. It is bred for resistance to tip burn, a physiological disorder that browns and damages inner leaves under fluctuating moisture and heat, and holds well in the field for a week or more past maturity without splitting. The mild, tender heads work well fresh in slaw or lightly cooked. Because of its early maturity, Farao is also a good choice for a second, fall planting timed to mature before the first hard freeze.

plant_note: Seedless triploid; start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm, and plant alongside a seeded pollenizer watermelon for fruit set. Fascination carries intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, and holds and ships well, an advantage for gardeners who store melons rather than eating them immediately.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Fascination is a seedless triploid watermelon hybrid bred with intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, two diseases that can build up quickly in warm, humid Gulf Coast soil. Because triploid seedless varieties produce little viable pollen of their own, plant a seeded pollenizer variety nearby to ensure good fruit set. It produces large, crisp, sweet red-fleshed fruit with excellent post-harvest holding quality, staying in good eating condition longer after picking than many other seedless types. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.

plant_note: Start on a heat mat 8–10 weeks before last frost; Fatalii originates from central and southern Africa, where it has been grown for generations as a culinary pepper; it ripens to bright yellow (sometimes orange or red) with a distinctive citrus-like fruity aroma combined with extreme heat of 125,000–400,000 Scoville units.
directions: Germinate seeds at 85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Fatalii is a Capsicum chinense variety originating in central Africa — most likely from the Central African Republic or surrounding region — that has been grown by chileheads and pepper enthusiasts for decades as an outstanding 'extreme fruity heat' pepper; at 125,000–400,000 SHU it surpasses most habaneros in heat while delivering a distinctive, intensely citrusy, almost lemon-lime fruity aroma that makes it popular in hot sauces and fruity salsas where both extreme heat and complex flavor are desired. The fruits are elongated, pointed, and wrinkled at maturity, ripening to a brilliant golden yellow. Highly productive in warm climates; the plants are vigorous and tall for a Capsicum chinense, often reaching 3–3.5 feet.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before the last spring frost; in mild-winter areas, sow in autumn for a spring harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 2 in deep in cool, moist soil; they germinate well even near freezing and are damaged by summer heat. Pinch out the top few inches of growth once the first pods begin to set to discourage black bean aphids, which congregate on tender new shoots. Harvest young pods when about 3 in long for eating whole, or let them fill out for shelling; seeds toughen quickly once they lighten in color. Support tall varieties with stakes and twine as plants approach flowering.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and stake the tall indeterminate vines well at transplant.
directions: Federle, also called Federle's Italian Paste, is an heirloom preserved through Seed Savers Exchange that produces unusually long, slender paste fruit up to seven inches, distinct from the more common blocky Roma shape. Indeterminate vines are highly productive and keep setting fruit steadily through the season, so gardeners canning or making salsa get an extended harvest window rather than one heavy flush. The dense, nearly seedless flesh cooks down quickly with little waste, and the deep red color holds well in finished sauce. Grow this variety when you want an open-pollinated, seed-saveable paste tomato with a distinctive elongated shape for home preserving.

common_name: Ferris Wheel Tomato (1894 Salzer's Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; a tall, regular-leaf indeterminate vine that needs sturdy staking to carry its large flattened fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared soil once all frost risk has passed. Ferris Wheel is an 1894 commercial release from the John A. Salzer Seed Company of Wisconsin that nearly vanished before being rediscovered and reintroduced by heirloom tomato researchers in the 1990s. It produces large, slightly flattened pink beefsteak fruit with colorful shoulders that blush attractively as they ripen, and the flesh is juicy, mild, and slightly sweet. Provide sturdy staking for the tall, regular-leaf indeterminate vines, which can exceed six feet over a 90-day season.

plant_note: Set small bulbs or bulbil offsets 2 inches deep in humus-rich soil under deciduous trees in early autumn; colonies spread quickly by bulbil, so site where spreading is welcome.
directions: Set small bulbs or bulbil offsets 2 inches deep in humus-rich soil under deciduous trees in early autumn, where they will naturalize alongside bluebells and other spring ephemerals. Because flower heads produce clusters of tiny bulbils instead of true seed, colonies spread quickly and can become assertive groundcover in favorable shaded sites, so site it where spreading is welcome. The mild, garlicky strap-shaped leaves emerge in late winter and are harvested young for salads or as a ramp substitute before the plant goes dormant in summer. Give it consistent moisture through spring growth and let beds go dry once foliage yellows.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost once soil temperature exceeds 55°F; plant in blocks of at least 4 rows for good wind pollination; thin to 12-inch spacing; in the Gulf South, a second crop can be planted in late June for fall harvest.
directions: Field corn (dent corn) is the primary grain corn of American agriculture and the most versatile of all corn types for the home garden and homestead — used as dried grain, cornmeal, animal feed, and the raw material for bourbon whiskey, the kernel's characteristic 'dent' or indentation forms as the starchy center dries and shrinks. For home gardeners, dent corn varieties like 'Hopi Blue', 'Reid's Yellow Dent', or 'Bloody Butcher' are grown to full dry-grain maturity (husks dry and papery, kernels hard), then shelled and ground in a stone mill for the most flavorful, nutritious cornmeal and polenta. In the Gulf South, excellent heat-tolerant open-pollinated varieties can be grown spring and fall, with adequate irrigation during tasseling and pollination being critical for good ear fill; dent corn has been a cornerstone of Gulf Coast homestead gardens since colonial times. Harvest when kernels are completely dry and hard — typically 90–120 days from planting — then shell and store in cool, dry conditions for grinding throughout the year.

plant_note: Direct sow 1-3 weeks after the last frost once the soil has warmed, since okra seedlings resent cold, wet soil and transplant poorly.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, soaking seed overnight to speed germination, then thin seedlings to allow room for these towering plants to spread. Harvest curved pods every day or two while young and tender, since they toughen quickly once mature. Fife Creek Cowhorn is a Southern heirloom known for its exceptionally tall growth, often reaching well over six feet, and its long, curved, rib-free pods reminiscent of a cow's horn. Gardeners who grow it out for seed appreciate its reliable productivity in hot, humid summers.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost or direct sow after soil warms to 70°F in full sun; figleaf gourd requires a long, warm season and performs best in zones 8–11 where the growing season is long enough for fruits to mature. It is a vigorous vine reaching 15–20 feet and requires a strong trellis or fence. Fruits keep for years at room temperature without refrigeration — a unique characteristic shared with no other cucurbit.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis; figleaf gourd is one of the most unusual cucurbits in cultivation — an Andean species producing large, distinctive fruits with white-striped, dark-green skin resembling a watermelon but with the elongated form of a large pumpkin, reaching 10–15 pounds. The most remarkable characteristic of this species is the extraordinary keeping quality of its mature fruits: when harvested fully mature, figleaf gourds can keep at room temperature for five or more years without refrigeration, decomposition, or significant quality loss — a storage capability unique among cucurbits and practical in the Andean communities of origin where refrigeration was unavailable. The white, fibrous flesh is used in traditional South American cooking — shredded in sweets, soups, and as a pasta filling — and has an interesting, neutral flavor. The seeds are edible roasted. The vine is large and requires substantial support. More cold-tolerant than many tropical cucurbits and thrives across zones 8–11 where seasons are long. A fascinating and genuinely different crop for the vegetable garden, particularly in Gulf Coast climates.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after the last frost, spacing generously since mature heads and outer leaves grow quite large.
directions: Filderkraut is a traditional German conical cabbage from the Filder plain near Stuttgart, prized for tall, dense, pointed heads that can weigh several pounds each. The tapered shape and tightly wrapped leaves pack unusually well for shredding, making this heirloom the historic variety of choice for large-batch sauerkraut production. It tends to tolerate warm spells better than round-headed cabbages while still standing up to fall frost, giving it a wide harvest window. Grow Filderkraut where a heavy-yielding, storage-friendly cabbage with genuine heirloom pedigree is wanted for preserving.

common_name: Filius Blue Ornamental Pepper (Color-Changing Compact Chile)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into containers or beds once frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings into pots or beds once nights are warm, since this compact annuum is often grown as a patio or container ornamental. Keep it evenly watered and in full sun for the heaviest, most colorful fruit display. Filius Blue is bred for its dense, upright habit and small purple-flushed leaves, with round fruits that ripen through purple and cream shades before finishing bright red, making the plant look multicolored all at once. The pods carry real heat and are edible, though the plant is grown mainly for its ornamental fruit color.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is warm; finger millet thrives in hot, humid conditions and tolerates mildly acidic or infertile soils.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in prepared rows or broadcast on a firm seedbed, thinning to 6–9 in when plants are 4 in tall; finger millet produces distinctive finger-like seed head rays that are diagnostic and easy to recognize at harvest. The seed turns dark reddish-brown when ripe and the heads curve inward; harvest before birds strip them by cutting the heads at early dough stage and finishing the dry-down on a tarp in the sun. Rub heads between palms to release the very small seeds, which need no hulling; grind into flour (ragi flour) or soak and ferment for traditional beverages. The crop is notably high in calcium and iron compared to other small grains.

common_name: First Lady Tomato (Disease-Resistant Hybrid Slicing Tomato, Classic Backyard Producer)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; First Lady is an indeterminate slicing tomato with a broad disease resistance package: resistance to Verticillium wilt (V), two races of Fusarium wilt (F, F2), nematodes (N), tobacco mosaic virus (T), and Alternaria (A). In zone 9, transplant March–April. The comprehensive disease resistance makes First Lady particularly practical for zone 9's warm, humid conditions where soilborne pathogens (Verticillium, Fusarium) and nematodes significantly limit yields in susceptible varieties. First Lady was developed specifically for home garden production and has remained one of the most widely sold tomato transplants at garden centers throughout the southeastern United States for decades. Fruits are medium (8–10 oz), round, smooth-shouldered, uniformly red, and produced abundantly through the season. The flavor is balanced — typical of the reliable but moderate flavor of disease-resistant F1 hybrids rather than the complex intensity of heirloom types.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly red and gives to slight pressure. First Lady Tomato is an F1 hybrid indeterminate slicing tomato developed by Seminis Vegetable Seeds (now Bayer Vegetable Seeds) with a comprehensive disease resistance package that has made it one of the most reliably productive backyard tomato varieties in the humid southeastern United States. The 'VFFNTAs' resistance package (Verticillium wilt, two races of Fusarium wilt, Nematodes, Tobacco Mosaic Virus, Alternaria) addresses virtually every major soil-borne and airborne pathogen that limits tomato production in the Gulf South — in humid zone 9 conditions where tomato plants commonly succumb to one or more of these diseases before the season ends, First Lady's resistance allows plants to remain productive through the summer. The variety's profile — medium-sized (8–10 oz) red tomatoes on vigorous indeterminate plants with the comprehensive disease package — represents a classic template for southeastern home garden tomato production that prioritizes plant health and extended production over extreme fruit size or complex flavor. First Lady was marketed and sold through retail garden center channels for decades and became one of the most recognized tomato variety names in southeastern garden retail, appearing consistently on transplant packs in spring garden center displays across the Gulf South. For zone 9 gardeners dealing with nematode pressure (very common in sandy Gulf Coast soils) or Fusarium wilt (endemic in soils with tomato production history), First Lady's 'N' and 'F' resistances provide practical protection that keeps plants alive and producing when susceptible varieties decline.

common_name: First Prize Pumpkin (F1 Giant Pumpkin Hybrid)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in deeply enriched soil; a hybrid giant-pumpkin selection bred for competitive weigh-off growers wanting reliably massive fruit without decades of seed-line selection.
directions: Start indoors 2-3 weeks before last frost or direct sow into hills of heavily composted soil, allowing at least 15-20 feet of space per plant since a single vine can spread over several hundred square feet. First Prize is a hybrid giant pumpkin bred for competitive growers, capable of producing fruit up to 300 pounds under intensive management, though most home-garden fruit lands well under that with less aggressive pruning and feeding. For maximum size, growers typically remove all but one or two developing fruits per vine and pinch side shoots to direct the plant's energy into the remaining pumpkins. Heavy, consistent watering and monthly feeding through the growing season are essential; harvest before hard frost once the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry.

common_name: Fish Pepper (African American Heirloom Striped Hot Pepper with Variegated Foliage)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; the spectacular variegated foliage and striped fruit coloring of Fish Pepper make it equally valuable as an ornamental in herb and pepper gardens.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Fish Pepper is an African American heirloom pepper with a unique history — the variety was maintained in the Black community of Baltimore and the Chesapeake Bay region through the 19th and early 20th centuries, where the unripe green-striped fruits were used to season fish and shellfish dishes without the red coloring that would be visible in pale-sauced seafood preparations. Rediscovered by artist and food historian William Woys Weaver through Seed Savers Exchange, Fish Pepper is now recognized as one of the most historically significant African American food heritage vegetables. The ornamental impact is extraordinary: the plant produces dramatically variegated, cream-and-dark-green streaked foliage unlike any other pepper variety, and the immature fruits are striped in cream and pale green, ripening through orange-and-cream striped stages to solid deep red at full maturity. The range of stripe patterns and color stages at different ripeness levels creates a constantly changing visual display. The heat level is medium-hot (comparable to cayenne, 30,000–50,000 SHU) — appropriate for seasoning fish sauces, seafood dishes, and hot sauces.
