The ornamental quality of both foliage and fruit at all stages makes Fish Pepper an outstanding choice for kitchen garden beds and container growing on patios.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost; tolerates heat for a long harvest.
directions: This colorful chard mix produces stems and veins in shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and white on tender, nutritious leaves. Enjoy baby greens in as little as 20 days or let leaves mature for cooking. It is as ornamental as it is edible and looks at home in vegetable beds, flower borders, and containers. Sow directly and thin seedlings, since each seed is a cluster. Harvest outer leaves regularly and it will keep producing into fall.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; flageolet is a French semi-dry bean harvested at the shell bean stage (before pods are fully dry) when the seeds are pale green — the beans retain this delicate green color when cooked, making them the classic French accompaniment to roast leg of lamb and the basis of cassoulet in some regional traditions.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; flageolet is harvested at the shell bean stage — when pods are plump and seeds are well-developed but still pale green, before the pods begin to yellow and dry. Flageolet (from the Latin 'flagellum' referring to the flute or pipe shape) is a uniquely French bean variety that occupies the role of the 'shell bean' par excellence in French cuisine — it is neither a fresh snap bean nor a fully dried bean, but is harvested at the intermediate shell-bean stage when the kidney-shaped, pale green to white seeds have developed fully in size and shape but retain their characteristic pale green color and fresh, delicate flavor. The distinctive color persists through cooking when properly prepared (not overcooked), making the finished beans a beautiful pale sage green on the plate — dramatically different from the drab gray-white of common dried beans. Flageolet is most famously the traditional accompaniment to gigot d'agneau (roast leg of lamb) in classic French cuisine, where the delicate flavor of the beans perfectly complements the rich lamb; it is also an important ingredient in traditional cassoulet and flageolets au gratin. Seeds can also be allowed to dry fully for storage and reconstituted, though the characteristic green color is then lost.

plant_note: Best sown from mid-spring through early summer for a fall harvest; a true maincrop storage carrot that keeps exceptionally well.
directions: Named for the Flakkee polder region of Zeeland in the Netherlands, this sturdy Dutch heirloom produces broad-shouldered, blunt-tapered roots up to 8-9 inches long with strong tops that hold up well for bunching. It is a true maincrop storage carrot, best sown from mid-spring through early summer for a fall harvest that keeps exceptionally well in a root cellar or clamp. Flakkee's productivity and keeping ability made it foundational breeding stock behind many of today's Imperator and Autumn King-type carrots.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in mid- to late summer for a fall crop; Flame Star is an orange-curded cauliflower that holds its color and forms well-domed heads under warmer conditions than most cauliflower tolerates.
directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or midsummer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Flame Star produces smooth, well-domed heads in a vivid, natural, sunny orange, colored throughout the curd (not just the surface) by a higher-than-normal beta-carotene content, so the color holds through cooking rather than fading like some orange cauliflower selections. It is notably more heat tolerant during head formation than white cauliflower varieties, making it a more forgiving choice for a Gulf South spring crop that runs into early-summer warmth before harvest. Blanching is unnecessary since sun exposure does not bleach or damage the orange curd the way it can discolor white types. Harvest heads while curds are still tight and firm, before the individual florets begin to separate and loosen.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once soil has warmed, after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: Transplant into full sun once the soil has warmed, growing it as either a landscape edging plant or a container specimen. Flaming Flare is an All-America Selections winner grown as much for its upright, torch-like clusters of small fruit that shift from purple to yellow to orange to red as it matures as for its edible use, giving a single compact plant several color stages at once. The fruit carries mild-to-moderate heat and can be harvested for cooking at any color stage, making the plant genuinely dual-purpose in the garden.

common_name: Flamingo Chinese Toon (Pink Spring Shoot Toona)
plant_note: Plant a young grafted or rooted-cutting specimen of 'Flamingo' in spring into fertile, well-drained soil, siting it where dappled or partial shade protects the brilliant rose-pink new growth from being bleached out by intense midday sun.
directions: Plant a young grafted or rooted-cutting specimen of 'Flamingo' in spring into fertile, well-drained soil, siting it where dappled or partial shade protects the brilliant rose-pink new growth from being bleached out by intense midday sun. Keep the root zone evenly moist while the tree establishes, and prune hard each late winter to keep the plant at a manageable shrubby size that resprouts with an even heavier flush of the prized pink shoots. The blush-colored young leaves and shoot tips share the same onion-garlic, slightly resinous flavor as the green-leaved species and are harvested the same way, stir-fried or folded into egg dishes while still tender. Because the pink coloring is most vivid in filtered light, 'Flamingo' doubles as a striking foliage accent for a partly shaded edible garden bed.

common_name: Flash Collards (Fast-Maturing Tender Smooth-Leaf Collard Hybrid)
plant_note: Direct sow 10–12 weeks before the first frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Flash is the fastest-maturing collard option, useful for late-season planting when the window for establishing standard 75–80 day varieties has closed.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Flash is a fast-maturing collard hybrid reaching harvest in only 55–65 days from sowing — significantly faster than traditional open-pollinated collard varieties (70–90 days), making Flash particularly valuable for late-season zone 9 plantings where the window for establishing slow-maturing varieties has closed. The smooth, dark-green leaves are more tender and less coarse than the thick leaves of older collard varieties — the faster maturity corresponds with a younger, more tender leaf stage at harvest, making Flash better suited to raw preparations and quick sautés where tenderness is important. Flash has the same excellent cold-hardiness as other collards — exposure to light frost sweetens the leaves by converting starches to sugars, improving flavor quality through the Gulf South winter. As a hybrid variety, Flash cannot be saved for seed but produces reliable, vigorous, uniform plants each season from purchased seed. The faster maturity also allows two consecutive collard plantings within a Gulf South fall season — a first planting in mid-August for October–November harvest and a second planting in late September for December–January harvest. Excellent disease tolerance reduces the need for preventive fungicide applications in the humid Gulf South fall garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November or January–February. Flashy Trout Back is cold-hardy and slow to bolt, making it suitable for the full cool season in zone 9. The red spotting pattern is more pronounced in cool weather and may fade in warm spring conditions. Harvest outer leaves continuously or pull entire heads at 55–65 days.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Flashy Trout Back (Forellen or Forellenschluss variant) is an Austrian heirloom romaine-type lettuce producing upright, semi-cos heads with large, spoon-shaped, bright green leaves heavily spotted with wine-red to maroon splashes and streaks — the pattern resembles the speckled back of a brown trout, giving the lettuce its evocative name. The combination of romaine structure (crisp, upright leaves with a prominent midrib) with the unique spotted coloring makes Flashy Trout Back one of the most visually distinctive lettuces for mixed plantings and specialty salad mixes. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — typical romaine quality without bitterness. The Austrian origin indicates good cold hardiness and a slow-to-bolt character that extends the harvest window in zone 9's warm springs. The dramatic spotted pattern on each leaf makes every head unique and immediately recognizable in market displays; it is one of the most frequently photographed heirloom lettuce varieties.

plant_note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant near the last frost.
directions: This Italian heirloom, grown since the late 1800s, forms wine-colored, flattened globes about 1 inch tall and 2 to 3 inches across with a sweet flavor perfect for roasting and grilled kebabs. Start seed indoors early since onions need a long season. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Keep beds weeded and evenly watered until tops flop over, then cure bulbs in a dry, airy place. Choose day-length appropriate types for your latitude for best bulbing.

plant_note: Sow in early spring up to the last frost date; flax needs cool conditions to germinate and does not tolerate summer heat.
directions: Broadcast seed at 25–30 lb per acre (about 1 oz per 40 sq ft) and rake to 1/4 in depth on a firm, weed-free seedbed; flax produces delicate sky-blue flowers that last only a morning and then forms round seed capsules (bolls) that rattle when dry. Harvest entire plants when half the bolls have turned brown and the stems are yellowing, cutting at the base and bundling into sheaves; finish drying upside-down for 10–14 days over a tarp. Thresh by beating sheaves inside a barrel, then winnow and screen; the small, oval, brown or golden seeds store for 1–2 years and are rich in omega-3 fatty acids. Grind seeds just before use for maximum nutrition, as whole seeds pass largely undigested.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost once soil exceeds 55°F; plant in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; flint corn reaches dry-grain maturity faster than dent corn and can often be grown in climates with shorter growing seasons.
directions: Flint corn is among the oldest cultivated corn types — the 'Indian corn' of the Americas, developed by indigenous peoples across North and South America over thousands of years in varieties of brilliant, diverse colors ranging from deep purple and blue-black to red, orange, yellow, cream, and multi-colored — and is both the most ornamental and among the most nutritious of all corn types for human consumption. The hard, glassy (flint-like) kernels have no dent when dry because they are mostly dense, hard starch rather than the soft floury starch of dent corn; this dense endosperm produces superior polenta and grits with more complex flavor than modern hybrid dent corn. Classic open-pollinated varieties like 'Glass Gem', 'Bloody Butcher', and 'Hopi Blue' are primarily flint types celebrated both for their ornamental dried-ear beauty and their exceptional culinary quality when ground into stone-milled cornmeal. Grow to full dry-grain maturity by allowing husks to dry completely on the stalk before harvest; cured ears can be used as autumn decorations, then shelled for grinding or replanting.

common_name: Flor de Mayo Bean (Mexican May Flower Bean, Flor de Mayo Brillante)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Flor de Mayo is one of the most important dry bean varieties in Mexican cuisine — known for its distinctive speckled appearance (magenta, pink, and cream-colored fresh seeds), quick cooking, and mild, sweet flavor that makes it the preferred bean in many regions of central Mexico for everyday frijoles, refried beans, and rice-and-bean dishes.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Flor de Mayo is well-adapted to semi-dry, warm conditions and performs particularly well in the hot, dry growing season of zone 7–10 areas with low humidity; harvest when pods are fully dry and papery. Flor de Mayo (Spanish for 'May Flower') is one of the oldest and most culturally significant dry bean varieties in Mexico, where it has been grown for centuries as a primary food staple — ranking among the most commercially important beans in the Mexican market alongside Bayo, Peruano/Canario, and Azufrado varieties. The fresh seeds are distinctively beautiful: oval, slightly plump, and marked with magenta, rose-pink, and cream-white in a speckled and streaked pattern reminiscent of the flowers it was named for; the pattern and color intensify at the fresh-shell stage and fade to a more subdued cream-and-tan speckled pattern when fully dried. When cooked, the beans become uniformly pale tan-brown, but the texture and flavor are the key appeal: Flor de Mayo cooks to a mild, slightly sweet, creamy texture with thin skins that are almost imperceptible — making them one of the quickest-cooking dry beans and one of the smoothest for refried beans where texture matters. In Mexican home cooking, Flor de Mayo is the bean that many home cooks from Jalisco, Nayarit, and Michoacán states grew up eating; it is available in Mexican markets under this name and under regional names including 'Flor de Mayo Brillante' and 'Crema'.

common_name: Floradade Tomato (Heat-Adapted Open-Pollinated Gulf South Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Floradade is an open-pollinated variety — seeds can be saved from the best fruits to maintain a self-sufficient seed supply across seasons.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Floradade is a University of Florida open-pollinated tomato variety developed specifically for Florida and Gulf South production — one of the older heat-tolerant open-pollinated varieties that has served as a reliable standard for Gulf South home garden production since its introduction. As an open-pollinated variety with good heat tolerance, Floradade produces medium-large (6–8 oz), round, firm, deep-red fruits with excellent fresh-eating and processing quality on a determinate plant that requires minimal staking. The disease resistance package includes Fusarium wilt race 1 — the most common race affecting Gulf South gardens. The primary practical advantage of Floradade over hybrid varieties is the ability to save seeds: since Floradade is open-pollinated, seeds saved from the best fruits grow true to type, allowing Gulf South gardeners to maintain a self-sufficient seed supply without annual seed purchases. This seed-saving advantage is significant for Gulf South gardeners who find locally-adapted, open-pollinated varieties often outperform northern hybrids in their specific climate. In zone 9, Floradade performs well in both spring and fall planting windows. The combination of local adaptation, open-pollination, heat tolerance, and reliable production has kept Floradade in production and recommendation by Gulf South cooperative extensions for decades.

plant_note: Best sown for a fall crop to avoid bolting in summer heat.
directions: Also known as finocchio, this cool-season crop forms a rounded bulb of swollen leaf stems topped with feathery, dill-like foliage. Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil, and thin so bulbs have room to swell. Keep water steady and consider mounding soil around the base to blanch and sweeten the bulbs. Harvest before summer heat triggers bolting; both the bulb and the anise-scented fronds are useful in the kitchen.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring 4 weeks before last frost or in late summer for a fall crop; fennel bolts readily in hot weather and should be timed to mature in cool weather. Transplanting is not recommended as fennel dislikes root disturbance.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in spring 4 weeks before last frost or in late summer for fall harvest, thinning to 6–12 inches apart; Florence fennel (finocchio) forms a crisp, anise-flavored bulb at the base of overlapping leaf sheaths and should be harvested when the bulb reaches 3–4 inches in diameter before it bolts in heat. Hill soil up around the bulb base 2–3 weeks before harvest to blanch it to a sweeter, more tender white. Succession-sow every 3 weeks for an extended harvest. Keep fennel away from tomatoes, peppers, and most garden vegetables as it produces allelochemicals that inhibit their growth — plant it at the garden edge or in its own dedicated bed.

common_name: Floriani Red Flint Corn (Italian Polenta Corn, Mais Rosso della Val di Fiemme)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows after last frost when soil has warmed; Floriani Red Flint is a long-season Italian heirloom (100–120 days) requiring a full summer to mature — in short-season climates (zones 3–5) start a week or two early under plastic mulch; this is the finest polenta corn available, producing deeply colored red-orange kernels that grind into a rich, nutty, complex polenta unequaled by commercial varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks; allow ears to dry fully on the stalks until the husks are completely papery before harvest; dry further at low heat (under 100°F) to bring moisture content below 12% before milling; stone-grind for the finest polenta texture; the distinctive deep red-orange color of the meal is unique among American corns. Floriani Red Flint is widely considered one of the finest polenta corns in the world — an Italian heirloom from the Fiemme Valley (Val di Fiemme) of Trentino, in the northeastern Italian Alps, where this particular strain of red flint corn has been grown by mountain farmers for centuries and is deeply embedded in the local food culture. The name 'Floriani' commemorates the Floriani family who maintained and preserved this specific strain. The corn produces large, deeply pigmented red-orange to brick-red flint kernels with a very hard, glassy endosperm characteristic of flint corn — the same endosperm structure that gives flint corns their superior milling quality and longer shelf life compared to dent corns. When stone-ground, the flour from Floriani Red Flint is a rich deep gold-orange color with a complex, nutty, slightly sweet fragrance quite unlike the pale, bland commercial cornmeal most American cooks know. Cooked polenta from this corn has a dense, complex flavor with depth that fully justifies the artisan price of stone-ground Italian polenta. Chefs at farm-to-table restaurants have sought out this variety specifically for its polenta quality. American growers in zones with a full summer can produce the authentic Italian-quality polenta grain that was formerly available only through import.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Florida 47 can be grown as a spring crop (transplant February–March for May harvest) or fall crop (transplant August for October–November harvest). Florida 47 is a determinate type well-adapted to the Florida and Gulf Coast growing windows.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Florida 47 is a University of Florida-developed determinate hybrid tomato bred specifically for commercial and home production in the hot, humid Florida and Gulf Coast environment — part of a long series of Florida-bred tomatoes (including Florida 91, Floradade, and Solar Set) developed by UF's tomato breeding program to address the unique challenges of Southern tomato production. The large (8–12 oz), globe to slightly flattened, firm, bright red fruits have the thick walls, uniform shape, and long shelf life that commercial producers require, but perform equally well for home gardens; the flavor is balanced and pleasant without the blandness of many commercial types. Excellent disease resistance including Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, gray leaf spot, and tobacco mosaic virus — the full-package resistance crucial for reliable performance in disease-prone Southern soils. Florida 47 is widely planted commercially in the Immokalee, Florida production region during the fall and spring seasons and performs similarly well for home gardeners across zone 8b–11.

common_name: Florida 91 Tomato (Disease-Resistant Heat-Adapted Gulf South Hybrid Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Florida 91 carries one of the most comprehensive disease resistance packages of any Gulf South tomato — V, F1, F2, N, A, L — minimizing pesticide inputs in the disease-intensive Gulf South environment.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Florida 91 is a University of Florida hybrid tomato developed specifically for Gulf South production, representing one of the most disease-resistant commercially available tomato varieties — carrying resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, Alternaria stem canker, and leaf mold (V, F1, F2, N, A, L), providing broad-spectrum protection against the primary soilborne and foliar diseases that devastate less protected varieties in the humid Gulf South climate. The large (6–8 oz), round, deep-red, firm-fleshed fruits have excellent fresh-eating and processing quality with good shelf life compared to softer varieties. Florida 91 is determinate (bush-type), maturing its crop in a compressed 4–6 week window and requiring minimal staking — a practical advantage for gardeners who prefer a defined harvest period over the continuous production of indeterminate types. In zone 9, Florida 91 is outstanding for both spring (February–June) and fall (August–November) planting windows. The comprehensive disease resistance package makes Florida 91 particularly valuable for gardeners who have experienced soilborne disease problems in their garden soil — the resistance package allows production in locations where unprotected varieties fail repeatedly. A primary recommendation from University of Florida and Louisiana State University extension services for Gulf South home garden tomato production.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9, sow September through February for fall and winter production — the primary growing season runs October through April, with spring plants bolting in May when temperatures rise.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season; Florida Broadleaf is the classic Southern mustard green — the most widely grown mustard green cultivar in the Gulf South for generations, with large, flat, broad, smooth, dark-green leaves with a pungent, spicy mustard flavor that is a cornerstone of traditional Southern cooking. Unlike curled mustard varieties (Southern Giant Curled, Green Wave) that have ruffled, frilly leaves, Florida Broadleaf has smooth, flat leaves that are easier to wash and which have a slightly more robust, bold flavor. Florida Broadleaf is grown in zone 9 gardens from September through April — the cool-season growing window when mustard greens develop the best flavor and avoid the extreme bitterness and quick bolting that heat causes. Young leaves are mild enough for salads; mature leaves are best cooked, typically braised with smoked meat (ham hock, smoked turkey) and seasoned vinegar in the traditional Southern style. Frost improves mustard green flavor — the conversion of starches to sugars after cold nights produces a richer, more complex, slightly sweeter flavor. Harvest outer leaves continuously or cut the entire plant at 4–6 inches above the crown for a cut-and-come-again harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant April–June. Florida Cranberry roselle is a short-day flowering plant — it begins setting calyces as days shorten in September–October regardless of when it was planted, so earlier planting results in a larger, more productive plant at calyx-setting time. The large calyces ripen October–November in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Florida Cranberry is a named roselle cultivar selected specifically for very large, fleshy, deeply colored calyces — the thick, star-shaped, burgundy-red sepals that encircle each seed pod after the flower drops and are the edible product of roselle cultivation. The deep cranberry-red calyces have an intensely tart, cranberry-like flavor with hibiscus floral notes, used to make a vivid crimson tea (agua de Jamaica), jam, syrup, sauce, and desserts. The exceptional calyx size and deep color of Florida Cranberry make it the standard named cultivar for calyx production in the Gulf South. In zone 9 the short-day flowering response means calyces set abundantly in October–November when temperatures are cooling — a natural alignment with the Thanksgiving and holiday season when cranberry-flavored products are in demand. Harvest calyces before the seed pod matures for best flavor; the calyces are easily separated from the seed capsule by hand.

common_name: Florida Giant Watermelon (Southern Heirloom Picnic Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for June–August harvest. Florida Giant requires a long warm season (85–100 days) and ample space for the vigorous, sprawling vines — allow 6–10 feet diameter per plant. Very heat-tolerant and well-adapted to Gulf Coast summer conditions.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F, planting 4–5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2 plants; harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and the ground spot has turned from white to cream-yellow. Florida Giant is a classic large-fruited Southern heirloom watermelon producing enormous fruits (30–60 pounds or more) with light green to dark green striped skin and deep red, sweet flesh — the quintessential 'picnic' or 'table' watermelon of the Gulf South where the long, hot summer provides adequate heat units for the 85–100 day maturation period. The very large fruits are challenging to transport single-handed but are impressive in the garden and at the table, providing abundant fresh fruit for summer gatherings. Florida Giant performs excellently under Gulf Coast hot humid summer conditions, showing reasonable tolerance of the fungal diseases (Fusarium wilt, anthracnose) common in humid climates, and is well-adapted to the sandy, fertile, moderately acid soils of Florida and the Gulf Coast region. The traditional size and flavor make it a regional staple and a nostalgic choice for gardeners who remember the giant watermelons of summer cookouts.

common_name: Florida High Bush Eggplant (Heat-Tolerant Southern Heirloom Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost at 80–85°F for germination; transplant into full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Florida High Bush grows into a tall, vigorous plant and benefits from staking once fruit load is heavy.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun once the soil and nights are warm; Florida High Bush is an old Southern heirloom eggplant bred for reliable production through the intense heat and humidity of a Deep South summer, when many standard eggplant varieties stall or drop blossoms. Plants grow tall and vigorous — notably taller than most eggplant cultivars, as the name suggests — and bear a heavy, extended crop of glossy, deep purple-black, oval to pear-shaped fruit with classic mild, creamy flesh. Because the bushes get large and top-heavy once loaded with fruit, stake or cage plants at transplanting to prevent wind and fruit-weight damage. Harvest fruit at about two-thirds of full size, while the skin is still glossy and taut — dull skin signals over-mature, seedier flesh. Regular harvesting encourages continued flowering and keeps plants productive from early summer through the first fall frost in zone 8–9.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start December–January and transplant February–March. Florida Market is specifically developed for Gulf Coast and Florida conditions, with superior heat tolerance and disease resistance compared to northern eggplant varieties. In zone 9 it will produce through the hot summer months when other eggplants pause; a second planting in July–August extends production into fall. Provide full sun and consistently warm soil for best production.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture and warm soil temperatures; Florida Market is an open-pollinated eggplant variety developed specifically for production in hot, humid, disease-prone Gulf Coast and Florida conditions — it shows markedly better performance in zone 8b–11 than northern varieties selected for cool, short-season growing conditions. The large, oval to cylindrical fruits are 6–8 inches long with smooth, glossy deep purple skin and dense, firm white flesh with relatively few seeds — the classic eggplant form ideal for slicing, grilling, roasting, baba ghanoush, moussaka, and Parmesan preparations. The superior heat tolerance allows Florida Market to continue flowering and setting fruit through Gulf Coast summers when temperatures regularly exceed 95°F — a period when many northern varieties drop their flowers. Consistent irrigation is more critical than for most vegetables, as uneven moisture causes fruit development problems and bitter flesh.

common_name: Florida Speckled Lima Bean (Heat-Tolerant Southern Pole Lima)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; this Southern heirloom pole lima tolerates the heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer better than many Northern-bred lima varieties.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, providing a trellis or pole for the climbing vine. Florida Speckled is a Southern heirloom pole lima bean grown for its handsome maroon-and-white speckled seeds and, more importantly, for genuine heat tolerance that lets it set pods reliably through the hot, humid conditions of a Deep South summer that cause many lima varieties to drop blossoms and stop producing. The vigorous vine climbs readily and produces well over an extended season once established. Harvest pods at the green shell stage for the classic buttery lima flavor, or allow pods to dry fully on the vine for a dry bean harvest that stores well through winter.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost; plant in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; isolate flour corn from dent and flint types by at least 300 feet or by timing to prevent cross-pollination if maintaining pure seed.
directions: Flour corn is the ancient soft-starch corn type developed by indigenous peoples of the Americas for grinding into fine cornmeal and masa — its kernels, composed almost entirely of soft, starchy endosperm without the hard, glassy outer layer of flint corn, grind into an exceptionally fine, silky flour with a mild, sweet flavor superior for baking cornbread, making hominy, and preparing traditional tortillas and tamales. Classic open-pollinated varieties like 'Hopi Blue' (a flour-type despite sometimes being called flint), 'Bloody Butcher', and 'Aztec Red' flour corns were grown for centuries by Pueblo peoples of the American Southwest, where soft corn was the staple grain; in the Gulf South, flour corns adapted to humid climates perform well as spring and fall crops. The soft kernels are more susceptible to corn earworm and storage fungi than hard flint or dent types — harvest promptly when husks dry, dry completely before storage, and store in sealed containers with desiccant in a cool, dry location. The beautifully colored ears of traditional flour corn varieties make outstanding autumn decorations before grinding.

subcategory: West African tropical leafy oilseed vegetable vine
plant_note: Direct sow seeds after last frost in full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, deep loamy soil in zone 9–12; Fluted Gourd (Ugu, Fluted Pumpkin) is one of the most important and widely grown leafy vegetables of southern Nigeria and West Africa — a fast-growing tropical vine bearing very large, ribbed gourds and large, soft leaves that are harvested continuously as the primary leafy vegetable in Egusi soup, Ofe Owerri, and other classic Nigerian soups; the large seeds are pressed for fluted pumpkin seed oil or eaten cooked.
directions: Sow Telfairia occidentalis seeds directly in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; provide a strong trellis or fence for the vigorous vine; harvest young, tender leaves and shoot tips continuously from 4–6 weeks after planting for use as a cooked green vegetable; harvest mature gourds for seed when the skin turns yellow-green. Fluted Gourd (known as 'ugu' in Igbo) is arguably the single most important leafy vegetable in southern Nigeria — a vine plant that is grown in virtually every family plot and kitchen garden throughout Igboland and beyond. The large, prominently ribbed leaves (resembling pumpkin leaves but more tender and palatable) are harvested in volume and sliced into fine strips before being added to soups and stews at the end of cooking to preserve their vivid green color. The leaves are especially important in Egusi soup (with ground melon seeds), Ofe Onugbu, and Ofe Owerri. The enormous, ribbed, green-striped gourds can weigh 10–30 kg and contain large, flat, oval seeds rich in oil and protein; the seeds are dried, shelled, and eaten as a protein source or pressed for cooking oil (fluted pumpkin seed oil). Unlike most gourds, Telfairia occidentalis has separate male and female plants; female plants bear the gourds while male plants are grown primarily for continuous leaf harvest. In zone 9–12 it grows as a perennial vine.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil temperature is reliably above 65 degrees F; seeds germinate quickly in warm soil. Provide a strong trellis as the vine grows 30-50 feet in a season and fruits can weigh 5-20 lbs.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a very sturdy trellis; fluted pumpkin (ugu) is one of the most important leafy vegetables in West and Central Africa, particularly Nigeria, where the tender shoots and leaves are harvested continuously for soups, stews, and cooked greens rich in iron, zinc, and protein. The flesh of the huge ribbed fruits is also eaten, and the seeds are pressed for cooking oil. In the US it is grown as a perennial vine in zones 10-12 and as an annual in frost-free areas where the season is long enough. Harvest leaves and shoot tips regularly when vines are actively growing; the fresh leaves wilt quickly and are best used the same day they are harvested.

plant_note: Broadcast fonio seed thinly onto a well-prepared, fine seedbed after last frost; the seeds are tiny (smaller than sesame) and need only shallow soil contact and moisture to germinate. Fonio tolerates very poor, dry, acidic, sandy soils where other grains fail — do not over-fertilize as excessive nitrogen produces excessive vegetative growth at the expense of grain.
directions: Broadcast seed densely onto a fine, firm seedbed after last frost in full sun; fonio (acha) is one of Africa's oldest cultivated grains, grown for at least 5,000 years across the Sahel and West Africa in the semi-arid regions of Senegal, Guinea, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Nigeria, where it is the first grain to be harvested each season and a critical food security crop. The grain is tiny — resembling a grain of sand — but nutritionally remarkable: gluten-free, high in essential amino acids methionine and cystine that are deficient in most other grains, and with a pleasant, slightly nutty, delicate flavor that is different from any familiar grain. Cooked fonio is fluffy and lighter than couscous. It is increasingly available in US natural food stores and is experiencing a culinary renaissance promoted by West African chefs. As a crop, it thrives in hot, dry, marginal conditions and completes its cycle in just 70–90 days, making it exceptionally productive per day of growing season in difficult conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September for fall production. Lima beans require warm soil and warm nights to develop properly — cool temperatures cause poor pod set and seed development. Fordhook 242 is a bush type that requires no support; harvest pods when seeds are plump and green but before the pods yellow. Shelling fresh lima beans immediately after harvest produces the sweetest, most tender flavor — the sugars begin converting to starch within hours of harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — lima beans fix atmospheric nitrogen and improve soil quality for subsequent crops; Fordhook 242 is the standard large-seeded bush lima bean — an All-America Selections award-winning variety from the Burpee Fordhook line that has defined the Fordhook (large, flat, meaty-seeded) type of lima bean in American horticulture for nearly a century. The large, flat, creamy-green seeds are the classic 'butter bean' of Southern cooking — much larger and meatier than baby lima beans, with a rich, starchy, almost buttery flavor and firm-yet-creamy texture that makes them one of the most satisfying of all shelling beans. Lima beans are often unfairly associated with canned or frozen product quality that gives no sense of their fresh garden character — freshly shelled and immediately cooked Fordhook lima beans have a completely different, far superior flavor to processed versions, with genuine sweetness and a rich, filling character. The large seeds also dry well for winter use, expanding culinary possibilities beyond the fresh-shelled season.

common_name: Fordhook Fancy Mustard (Curled Heirloom Mustard Green)
plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before the last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; harvest outer leaves young for the mildest flavor.
directions: Direct sow shallowly and thin seedlings to stand several inches apart, harvesting outer leaves regularly to keep the plant productive. This old American selection, once distributed under the Fordhook name, forms dense rosettes of tightly curled, ruffled bright green leaves with a peppery mustard bite that mellows when cooked. Its frilly texture makes it a distinctive addition to mixed braising greens, and it tends to hold in the garden a bit longer than plain-leaf mustards before bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–March for fall through spring harvest. Fordhook Giant is a large, vigorous variety that reaches impressive size in cool conditions — individual leaves can exceed 2 feet long in optimal growing. Harvest outer leaves continuously from the bottom of the plant, leaving the central growing tip intact to keep plants producing; plants can produce for many months with this cut-and-come-again approach. In zone 9 plants are productive from fall through early spring and may bolt in warming spring weather.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Fordhook Giant is the classic white-stalked Swiss chard — one of the oldest and most productive chard varieties in American seed catalogs, developed by the Burpee seed company and named for Burpee's Fordhook Farm in Pennsylvania where it was trialed and selected. The very large, heavily blistered, dark green leaves with thick, pure white, celery-like stalks represent the classic Swiss chard appearance and deliver maximum productivity per square foot — the substantial white stalks are among the meatiest and most impressive of any chard variety, making Fordhook Giant the preferred choice in preparations where stalks are eaten separately from the leaves. The thick stalks can be prepared raw like celery, steamed and buttered like asparagus, or braised for their mild, slightly sweet, beet-adjacent flavor; the large leaves cook down like spinach with a mild, earthy, slightly mineral character. Individual plants in good conditions can produce leaves exceeding 2 feet long, making the garden presence of Fordhook Giant among the most dramatically large of any leafy vegetable. The partial shade tolerance makes it one of the best vegetables for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun exposure.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; tolerates summer heat for continuous harvest into fall.
directions: This classic heirloom chard produces broad, glossy green leaves with thick white stems and a mild, tender flavor for fresh or cooked dishes. Sow the seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to give each plant room to bush out. Harvest outer leaves regularly for cut-and-come-again production while the center keeps growing. Unusually heat and cold tolerant, it yields continuously from late spring well into fall with steady moisture.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost for a long harvest into fall.
directions: This old favorite features broad, crinkled leaves and wide white stems packed with vitamins and minerals. A vigorous grower with a long season, it provides fresh greens from early summer into fall and year-round in mild climates. White-stemmed types are generally sweeter and milder than colored varieties. Sow directly, thin seedlings since seeds are clusters, and harvest outer leaves regularly. Keep evenly watered for continuous, tender growth.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil is warm; cold, wet soil rots the seed.
directions: This All-America Selections bush lima is valued for resilience, drought tolerance, and heavy crops of large, buttery beans. Sow seed an inch to an inch and a half deep only once the soil has warmed, since limas rot in cold, wet ground. Grow in full sun with even moisture through flowering and pod fill. Pick pods when they feel plump and full for fresh shelling, or leave them to dry on the bush for storage beans.

common_name: Forellenschluss Lettuce (Flashy Trout's Back, Speckled Trout)
plant_note: Direct sow 6–8 weeks before last frost; most beautiful when harvested as a whole head; also excellent as cut-and-come-again greens at baby stage.
directions: Sow seed on the soil surface in early spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; Forellenschluss is a legendary Austrian heirloom butterhead lettuce — the name means 'trout's back' in German for its distinctive pattern of bright red-bronze speckles scattered across brilliantly green leaves, giving each leaf the dappled appearance of a brook trout. Considered one of the most beautiful and best-flavored lettuces in the world, with butter-soft, sweet, melt-in-the-mouth leaves. Also sold as 'Flashy Trout's Back' in the United States. Suitable for both spring and fall, it is less tolerant of summer heat than loose-leaf types; harvest heads when full but before bolting.

plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; succession sow through the cool season for a continuous harvest.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist for smooth, tender roots. Forono is an Italian heirloom beet distinguished by its long, cylindrical, carrot-like shape rather than the typical round beet form, an advantage in the kitchen because its uniform diameter yields evenly sized slices from end to end with almost no waste, and a single root often provides several servings. The deep red flesh is sweet, tender, and free of the pale internal rings some other beets show, and because the roots grow mostly upward out of the soil rather than swelling wide, more roots can be grown in the same row space. Harvest at 4-6 inches long for the best texture, and the tops are also good cooked as greens.

plant_note: Start indoors early; graft a scion onto it, then transplant after frost.
directions: This vigorous rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite heirloom or hybrid scion to boost its performance, offering better leaf cover to reduce sunscald, more flowers and fruit weight, and improved resistance to soil stresses and diseases. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, then graft when stems are pencil-thick. Keep grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber to heal before hardening off. Transplant after frost into full sun. Support the vigorous vines with sturdy stakes or cages.

common_name: Fortex Pole Bean (Extra-Long French Filet Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Fortex is a vigorous climbing pole bean reaching 7–9 feet — provide a sturdy trellis, pole tepee, or strong fence for support. Harvest pods frequently and while still young (10–11 inches long) before seeds begin to bulge, which keeps the plants productive and maintains pod tenderness.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; provide a sturdy trellis or support structure before planting and harvest regularly while pods are still slender and young. Fortex is considered by many gardeners and chefs to be the finest French filet (haricot vert) style pole bean available — a European heirloom that produces extraordinarily long (10–12 inch), very slender, round-podded, deep green beans with exceptional tenderness and refined flavor that places it far above standard snap beans for fresh eating and French-style preparations. Unlike flat, wide snap beans, Fortex pods are round, very slender (filet-style), and remain tender and flavorful well beyond the size at which most beans become tough — they can be harvested at any point from finger-thin to full pencil thickness and maintain excellent quality. The flavor is genuinely superior, with a rich green bean taste and very fine texture that makes Fortex the preferred bean for blanching, sautéing with garlic and butter, and all preparations where bean quality is the focus. Very productive vines climb 7–9 feet and bear continuously when picked frequently. An outstanding bean for serious vegetable gardeners and those who want restaurant-quality produce from their home garden.

common_name: Fourth of July Tomato (Ultra-Early Hybrid Slicing Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Fourth of July produces ripe tomatoes 49–55 days after transplanting — approximately 2–3 weeks earlier than mid-season varieties. In zone 9, transplant in late February or early March for a first harvest in late April to early May. The very early maturation is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the summer window closes before many standard varieties finish producing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Fourth of July is an indeterminate hybrid tomato that holds the distinction of being one of the earliest-producing standard-sized tomatoes available to home gardeners — producing its first ripe fruits approximately 49–55 days after transplanting, roughly the same time that slower varieties are just beginning to set fruit. The name references the plant's ability to provide ripe tomatoes by or before the Fourth of July holiday in northern gardens when planted on schedule. The medium-small (4–6 oz), round, bright red fruits have good sweet-tart tomato flavor for an early variety — notably better than most extremely early types, which often sacrifice flavor for speed. The indeterminate vines continue producing throughout the summer and fall after early harvests, unlike determinates that produce one concentrated crop. Fourth of July is outstanding for gardeners in any climate who want fresh home-grown tomatoes as early as possible, and particularly valuable in Gulf South gardens where early production before summer heat peak extends the harvest season significantly. A practical, reliable early variety that should be in every serious tomato garden alongside a mid-season variety.

common_name: Freckles Lettuce (Forellenschluss Romaine, Trout's Back Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather with seeds barely covered; Freckles / Flashy Trout's Back is a loose-head romaine type that performs best in cool temperatures and is an excellent fall-through-spring crop in zone 9 (September–March).
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; Freckles lettuce (Austrian name: 'Forellenschluss', meaning 'Trout's Back', also sold as 'Flashy Trout's Back') is a traditional Austrian/Central European heirloom romaine-type lettuce with one of the most distinctive and beautiful appearances in the lettuce world — pale green, slightly upright loose-romaine leaves dramatically spotted and splashed with burgundy-red markings in irregular patterns that genuinely resemble the markings of a brook trout's back. Despite its ornamental appearance, Freckles is an excellent eating lettuce with the substantial, crisp, slightly crunchy texture of romaine and mild, sweet, pleasant flavor without bitterness. The visual impact makes it outstanding for decorative vegetable gardens and for using fresh as a centerpiece lettuce. Freckles is moderately heat-tolerant for a lettuce and somewhat slow to bolt, extending the spring harvest window. An outstanding conversation-piece heirloom lettuce that combines genuine beauty with excellent eating quality.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and late summer; succession sow for a steady supply.
directions: This 1793 European heirloom romaine has bright green, crisp leaves dappled with striking red freckles and a vase-like habit. The flavor is mildly bitter with a clean finish, and it tolerates heat better than many romaines, resisting bolting. Grow in full sun to partial shade in cool, moist soil, offering afternoon shade in warm spells. Harvest whole heads or pick outer leaves as needed. Succession sow for a steady supply.

plant_note: Direct sow every couple weeks in spring and fall for a steady supply.
directions: This elegant heirloom produces elongated roots with bright crimson tops and clean white tips, offering a tender, mildly peppery bite. Direct sow seed a half inch deep and keep the bed consistently moist for quick, uniform roots. Thin promptly so each radish has room, and succession sow every week or two for continuous harvest. Pull the roots young while crisp, as radishes left too long turn pithy and sharp; they excel in cool spring and fall weather.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in well-drained, loose, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9, sow September–November for the main fall crop and January–February for a spring crop; succession sow every 2 weeks for a continuous harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in well-drained, loose, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during cool seasons; French Breakfast is a classic European heirloom radish with a history dating to the early nineteenth century — producing oblong-to-cylindrical, 3–4 inch roots with a distinctive two-tone color pattern: brilliant scarlet-red over the upper two-thirds grading to crisp white at the tip. The elongated, elegant shape is distinctly different from the standard round red radish and makes French Breakfast instantly recognizable in the garden and at market. The flavor is mild and crisp — somewhat milder than globe radishes when harvested young, with a light, clean pepper-radish flavor that becomes stronger and more pungent if roots are left in the ground too long or grown during warm weather. Traditional French usage was to eat them dipped in butter with a pinch of salt at breakfast — hence the name. In zone 9, French Breakfast radishes are a cool-season crop performing best September through April; they bolt and become pungent in the summer heat. Succession sow every 2 weeks for continuous harvest. Thin to 2–3 inches for the best root development. Harvest when roots reach 3/4–1 inch diameter for the mildest flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil has warmed; beans dislike cold, wet soil.
directions: These slender French filet beans, or haricots verts, are pencil-thin at about a quarter inch across and 4 inches long, with exceptional tenderness. Pick them young and often for the best texture and to keep the compact bush plants producing. Sow directly into warm soil after frost, since seeds rot in cold, wet ground. Water at the base to keep foliage dry and reduce disease. Steam or saute lightly to preserve their delicate flavor.

common_name: French Fingerling Potato (Pink-Skinned Fingerling with Rose-Marbled Flesh)
plant_note: Plant seed potato pieces in cool soil with 2–3 eyes per piece; French Fingerling is a mid-season fingerling type that produces elongated, finger-shaped tubers 2–4 inches long with distinctive pink skin and cream to pale yellow flesh marbled with pink veins. In zone 9, plant January–February for a March–May harvest before summer heat arrives. The compact vines (18–24 inches) produce tubers in clusters that remain relatively close to the surface and are easily harvested by digging carefully around the plant. French Fingerling is not a traditional French heirloom in the way Rattes or other older varieties are, but the name reflects the variety's French-inspired culinary aesthetic and elegant appearance. Like most fingerling varieties, French Fingerling is waxy-fleshed and holds its shape well through roasting, sautéing, and boiling.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3–4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; harvest when vines begin to die back. French Fingerling is valued primarily for its visual distinction and culinary versatility: the combination of rose-pink skin and cream-yellow flesh with distinctive pink marbling through the interior makes French Fingerling one of the most visually striking fingerling varieties when halved or sliced — the pink marbling pattern within the creamy flesh is unique and makes the roasted or halved potato distinctly attractive in presentations. The texture is waxy and firm — a characteristic of fingerling potato varieties that have lower starch content than baking types (Russet Burbank) and retain their shape well through cooking. This waxy texture makes fingerlings the preferred choice for roasting whole (they develop a crispy exterior while staying firm inside), for potato salads (they don't become mushy when dressed), and for sautéed preparations where pieces need to hold their shape. French Fingerling's flavor is described as nutty, sweet, and complex — more interesting than the relatively neutral flavor of standard Russet types, with a richness that farmers market customers and restaurant chefs find particularly valuable. The variety performs well for small-scale and home garden production, producing enough tubers per plant for household use without requiring the large-scale inputs (cool storage, extensive land) of commercial Russet production.

plant_note: Plant sets (small bulbs) in early spring 4 weeks before last frost or in fall in zone 7 and warmer for overwintering; set each bulb pointy-end up, 1 inch deep, spaced 6–9 inches apart in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil.
directions: Plant small bulbs (sets) pointy-end up, 1 inch deep and 6–9 inches apart in well-drained, fertile soil in early spring or fall; the true French gray shallot (échalote grise) is considered the premier shallot of French haute cuisine, with a distinctive grayish-purple skin, elongated teardrop shape, and more complex, less harsh flavor than common shallots. Each planted bulb divides into a cluster of 8–12 daughter bulbs by harvest time in midsummer when the tops fall over. Lift, clean, and cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for 2–3 weeks before storing. Save the smallest bulbs as next year's planting sets. Do not overwater — shallots are prone to rot in wet soils.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long, cool stretch before summer heat sets in.
directions: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long, cool stretch before summer heat sets in. This variety takes its name from the volcanic plateau around Le Puy-en-Velay in France's Auvergne region, where a legally protected growing area produces small, marbled slate-green lentils famous for holding their shape and delivering a peppery, mineral flavor after cooking. Skip heavy nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes leafy growth at the expense of pods, and let the sparse, wiry plants lean on light twiggy brush if needed. Harvest the whole plant once most pods have turned tan and papery, then dry and thresh before storing the seed.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil warms; succession sow for extended harvest.
directions: This compact haricot vert produces slender, stringless pods with fine flavor on tidy dwarf bush plants ideal for small spaces and containers. Sow seed about an inch deep directly in warm soil, as beans dislike transplanting. Keep moisture even through flowering and pod set, and avoid handling wet foliage to reduce disease. Harvest the pencil-thin pods often while young and tender to keep the plants producing over several weeks.

plant_note: Sow direct or plant divisions in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; French sorrel is lower and more sprawling than garden sorrel with smaller, more arrowhead-shaped leaves and a more refined, less harsh acid flavor.
directions: Sow direct or plant divisions in early spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; French sorrel is more drought-tolerant than garden sorrel and thrives in poor, well-drained soils — rich, moist soil produces rank growth with coarser flavor. Rumex scutatus is a low-growing, somewhat sprawling European perennial herb with small, distinctive, shield-shaped or hastate (arrowhead-shaped) leaves that have a milder, more refined, less harsh acid flavor than the common garden sorrel (R. acetosa) and are preferred by many chefs for their superior taste — it is the traditional sorrel used in fine French cuisine and is sometimes called "true French sorrel." It is an excellent perennial groundcover in the kitchen garden, spilling attractively over path edges and walls; unlike R. acetosa it tolerates dry, rocky conditions. Harvest the small leaves continuously and remove flower stalks to prevent self-seeding.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is above 60°F.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep in warm mix at 80°F and pot up once seedlings have two true leaves; transplant to the garden after last frost. Fresno peppers resemble jalapeños but are slightly thinner-walled, fruitier in flavor, and ripen from green to bright red, with heat increasing as they mature (2,500–10,000 Scoville units). Harvest green fruits at 70 days for a jalapeño substitute, or ripen fully to red for a sweeter, hotter pepper that is excellent in hot sauces and salsas. Consistent deep watering (rather than frequent shallow watering) produces the best quality fruit and reduces stress-induced heat spikes.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest. Direct sowing is also possible. Frisee blanches naturally at the center as the outer leaves close over the interior; for the maximum pale center and milder flavor, tie the outer leaves loosely with twine 2 weeks before harvest. In zone 9 fall planting gives the most reliable head development; spring planting bolts too quickly in warming conditions.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Frisee is the fine-leaved, deeply curled, frizzy form of curly endive — a classic French bistro salad ingredient produced by its pale, blanched interior heart surrounded by a halo of fine, frizzy dark-green outer leaves. The pale interior (the blanched portion) has a mild, gently bitter, nutty flavor that is the defining taste of the classic frisee salad with lardons and a warm poached egg — one of the most recognizable French bistro dishes. The dark green outer leaves are more bitter and are usually removed or used for cooking. Frisee blanches naturally when the outer leaves overlap and shade the center, but deliberate blanching (tying the outer leaves for 1–2 weeks before harvest) produces a larger, more uniform pale center. In zone 9 frisee is a fall-through-winter crop that produces its characteristic delicate, pale center in the cool, short-day conditions from November through February.

plant_note: Sow in late summer or early fall for a fall and winter harvest; frisée produces best in cool weather and can be blanched by gathering and tying outer leaves around the head for 7–10 days to whiten and sweeten the center. In zone 9, direct sow September–October for harvest November through February, when the cool weather produces the most tender, flavorful heads.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; frisée (curly endive or fine curled endive) is the distinctive French salad green with deeply cut, finely fringed, pale green to yellowish leaves that create a loose, finely textured head with a pleasantly bitter flavor — one of the defining ingredients of classic French and Belgian cuisine. Unlike its flat-leaved cousin escarole, frisée has intensely ruffled, narrow, spiky-looking leaves that form a sprawling head; the outer leaves are dark green and quite bitter, while the interior (naturally or artificially blanched by excluding light from the heart for 7–10 days) turns pale yellow and becomes substantially more tender and mild. Frisée is the traditional green in salade lyonnaise (the classic Lyon salad with poached egg, lardons, and mustard vinaigrette) and in the Belgian warm salad tradition. The moderately bitter flavor pairs beautifully with rich dressings, warm bacon vinaigrettes, and strong cheeses. In zone 9, frisée is grown as a fall-through-winter crop when cool temperatures bring out its best flavor; summer production results in extremely bitter, loose plants that quickly bolt. Extremely cold-hardy once established, tolerating frosts to about 22°F.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant August–September for harvest November–January. Full Heart Batavian self-blanches at the center more reliably than other escarole types as the outer leaves naturally close over the heart. In zone 9 the mild fall allows slow, steady head development from September transplants through November harvest.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Full Heart Batavian is the classic escarole for Italian home cooking — a broad-leaved chicory endive forming a large, dense head with a characteristic self-blanching, creamy-yellow interior heart surrounded by darker outer leaves. The center heart has the mildest, most tender flavor of any escarole or endive type; the outer leaves are more bitter and are often removed or reserved for long-cooked soups and braises. Full Heart Batavian is the standard escarole used in Italian-American cooking — the primary green in Italian wedding soup (minestra maritata), in braised escarole with white beans and garlic, and as a pizza topping. The dense, substantial head stores well for 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator after harvest, making escarole one of the most practical winter greens for home cooks. In zone 9 the fall growing season from August transplants produces excellent heads by November; the plants are cold-hardy and withstand light frosts that improve flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in deeply enriched soil; a giant white pumpkin that needs a long, warm season and heavy feeding to reach its full 60-90 pound potential.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in heavily composted soil, spacing hills at least 8-10 feet apart to accommodate the large-fruited vines. Full Moon is a giant white pumpkin producing smooth, lightly sutured fruit that commonly reaches 60-90 pounds and stands roughly 3 feet tall by 2 feet wide under good growing conditions, with a long 120-day-plus season needed to size up fully. The pale rind is retained best when fruit is left to mature fully on the vine rather than harvested early, and consistent deep watering through fruit set is important to avoid rind cracking on such large specimens. Harvest before hard frost once the rind has hardened completely, and handle carefully since the size and weight make the fruit prone to bruising and stem breakage.

common_name: Fuseau Jerusalem Artichoke (Classic French Smooth-Skinned Sunchoke)
plant_note: Plant whole or cut seed tubers, each with at least one or two eyes, about 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil once the soil can be worked in spring. Because sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground, choose a bed where the planting can be permanently contained or is not a problem to leave in place.
directions: Plant whole or cut seed tubers, each with at least one or two eyes, about 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil once the soil can be worked in spring. Because sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground, choose a bed where the planting can be permanently contained or is not a problem to leave in place. Fuseau is a long-established French heirloom named for its elongated, relatively smooth, club-shaped tubers, which are far easier to scrub and peel than the knobby, eye-covered tubers typical of unnamed Jerusalem artichoke stock. Its tall late-summer sunflower-like blooms are followed by a fall and winter tuber harvest that continues after light frosts, and the tubers themselves have the same nutty, sweet flavor common to the species, sweetening further after cold exposure.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed, training vines up a sturdy trellis.
directions: A traditional Japanese heirloom bitter melon prized for exceptional heat tolerance and vigorous, dense vining growth. The long, spindle-shaped fruit has deeply ridged, heavily warted dark-green skin and can reach 7-12 inches, ripening to orange-yellow if left unpicked. Harvest while still firm and green for the classic assertively bitter flavor used in goya champuru and other Okinawan stir-fries, or let a few fruit fully color for milder, sweeter eating. Its climbing habit and heat tolerance make it a good choice for a hot, humid summer trellis planting where other bitter melon types struggle.

plant_note: Direct sow or start transplants 3-4 weeks before setting out after soil has warmed; in zone 9 sow March-July for successive summer harvests. Unlike its relative winter melon, fuzzy gourd is picked young and immature rather than left to mature and cure.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in well-drained, fertile, moderately moist soil in full sun, and grow on a sturdy trellis to keep the fuzzy fruit clean and straight. Fuzzy gourd is a smaller, fast-maturing variety group of the same species as winter melon, but it is harvested young while the cylindrical fruit is still tender, pale green, and covered in the soft fuzz that gives it its name, rather than being left to mature into the large, waxy-coated winter melon. It is a staple vegetable in Cantonese and Southeast Asian cooking, prized for its mild flavor and tender texture in soups, stir-fries, and braises, where it readily absorbs the flavors of broth, meat, and aromatics. Harvest fruits at 6-10 inches long while the skin fuzz is still soft, since older fruit develops a tougher, less palatable rind; frequent picking encourages continued production through the hot summer months that this heat-loving vine relishes.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer for fall/winter harvest in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; swollen-stem mustard (zhacai type) requires a full cool season to develop the characteristic swollen basal stem that is the primary edible portion — it grows slowly in cool weather and will bolt without making a proper stem if planted too late.
directions: Direct sow in late summer for fall/winter harvest in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; gai choy (swollen-stem mustard, zhacai type) is the Chinese mustard grown for its enlarged, knobby, swollen basal stem that forms a distinctive corm-like structure — salted, dried, and fermented with chili and Sichuan pepper to produce 'zhacai' (榨菜), the pickled Sichuan preserved vegetable that flavors noodle soups, fried rice, and countless Chinese dishes. The peppery, pungent young leaves are also edible as cooking greens. Growing your own allows fresh stem harvest for home pickling or fresh use. Requires a long, cool growing season for the stem to swell to usable size — an autumn crop planted 10–12 weeks before frost in zones 7–9 works best. A fascinating vegetable for those interested in Asian fermentation and pickling traditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: This pungent Chinese mustard, also called Indian mustard or Swatow mustard, forms curled leaves and wide, crunchy stems favored in Chinese, Korean, and Japanese cooking and pickling. The flavor is milder when young and grows sharper with maturity and heat. Grow in cool weather in full sun to partial shade, sowing in spring and fall. Keep soil evenly moist to slow bolting and keep flavor mild. Harvest whole heads or outer leaves as needed.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for fall harvest; gai lan is one of the most heat-tolerant and productive of the Asian brassica vegetables, more bolt-resistant than most and a particularly good choice for Gulf Coast fall and spring production in zones 8–11.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; thin to 9–12 inches for best results. Gai lan (also written kai-lan or gai laan) is the Chinese broccoli or Chinese kale of Cantonese cuisine, a leafy brassica producing thick, succulent stems, broad blue-green leaves, and small clusters of white flower buds that are harvested together as the edible vegetable; unlike Italian broccoli where the heads are the prize, gai lan is prized for its juicy, thick stems with a clean, mild, slightly bitter flavor that takes well to the intense heat of a wok and oyster sauce. Harvest when the first buds are just beginning to open for peak flavor and tenderness; the plants regrow from the base for additional cuts. More heat-tolerant than most brassicas and an excellent vegetable for Gulf Coast fall and spring seasons when traditional broccoli bolts quickly. Essential in Chinese restaurant cooking — the vegetable in classic 'Chinese broccoli with oyster sauce.'

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil is warm; needs a long season.
directions: This French heirloom, nicknamed peanut pumpkin for the sugar-crystal warts on its peach-colored skin, is prized for its supremely sweet, velvety orange flesh in soups and sauces. Fruit weighs 10 to 15 pounds and needs a long warm season to mature fully. Sow into rich, well-drained soil in full sun and give vines ample room to sprawl. Water deeply and feed for best size. Harvest when the rind hardens and cure in a warm, dry place before storage.

common_name: Galia Melon (Israeli Hybrid Netted Green-Flesh Muskmelon)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Galia requires warm conditions throughout its development and performs well in the Gulf South's warm summer climate. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–August harvest. Reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the skin transitions from green to golden-yellow and a sweet, tropical fragrance is detectable at the stem end — the skin color change from green to yellow-gold is the primary harvest indicator for Galia.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin turns yellow-gold and a sweet tropical aroma is detectable at the stem end. Galia is an Israeli hybrid muskmelon type developed in the 1970s at the Newe Ya'ar Research Center by Dr. Zvi Karchi, named for his daughter — an F1 hybrid that combines the netted, aromatic skin characteristics of cantaloupe/muskmelon with the pale green, spicy-sweet flesh of honeydew, creating a novel flavor profile found in no other commonly available melon type. The round to slightly oval fruits (3–5 lb) have heavily netted, yellow-green to yellow-gold skin at maturity (the skin begins green and transitions to yellow-gold as the melon ripens — a useful visual harvest cue not present in cantaloupe types that stay tan). The flesh is pale green to cream-green, aromatic, and extremely sweet with a distinctive tropical character — floral, spicy, and complex, distinctly different from both orange-fleshed cantaloupe and the blander honeydew. Galia melons are widely grown and marketed throughout Europe, Israel, and Central America and have become increasingly available in American specialty markets, where they are often sold under the name 'Israeli melon.' The flavor is among the most complex and interesting of any melon type, making Galia a top choice for gardeners who want to explore beyond standard cantaloupe.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; this fast-maturing Siberian heirloom tolerates cooler soil and air temperatures at transplant time better than most cherry tomatoes, making it a good choice for an early spring or extended fall crop.
directions: A Siberian heirloom with soft, blue-green potato-leaf foliage that sets abundant clusters of translucent, pale-yellow, one-inch cherry tomatoes with a rich, sweet flavor. Bred for a short, cool growing season, Galina's sets fruit reliably in cooler spring and fall conditions that cause many other cherry tomatoes to drop blossoms, making it a strong choice for a Gulf South fall tomato planting timed to ripen as temperatures moderate. The prolific, early-bearing vines need only routine staking and produce continuously from first ripe fruit until frost.

plant_note: Sprout indoors year-round in a jar or tray; no garden bed required.
directions: Garbanzo bean sprouts are easy to grow indoors and rich in vitamins and protein for snacking or adding to many dishes. Rinse and soak the seeds overnight, then drain and rinse two to three times a day in a sprouting jar or tray. Keep them at room temperature out of direct sun and harvest in just a few days when short sprouts appear. Cook lightly or eat the crisp sprouts fresh. Refrigerate promptly after harvest to keep them fresh.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes in a partially shaded to full-sun spot. Garden huckleberry grows quickly in warm conditions and tolerates more shade than most fruiting vegetables — a good choice for lightly shaded food gardens in zones 3–10 (grown as annual).
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; garden huckleberry is an African cultivated nightshade that produces abundant clusters of small, round, glossy black fruits about the size of a large pea. Unlike its wild nightshade relatives, the ripe fruits are edible but ONLY when fully cooked — raw berries contain solasodine alkaloids that cause digestive upset. When properly cooked, they lose their bitterness and make good pies, jams, and preserves with an earthy, slightly tart flavor. Harvest only fully black, ripe berries. The plant is extremely productive in warm climates and tolerates partial shade, making it useful for lightly shaded food gardens. It is distinct from the true huckleberry (Gaylussacia species) and true blueberry, and should not be eaten raw under any circumstances.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep as soon as soil can be worked in spring — peas tolerate light frosts and germinate in cool soil; in zone 6–9 a fall crop planted 6–8 weeks before first frost is often the most productive.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep and 4–6 inches apart as early in spring as the ground can be worked, well before the last frost; garden peas are cool-season vegetables that thrive in cool, moist conditions (45–75°F) and deteriorate rapidly when temperatures exceed 80°F, so early planting is essential for a good harvest before summer heat arrives. Bush types (60–80 cm) need no support; climbing types need a trellis or netting. Keep the soil consistently moist from flowering through pod fill — inconsistent watering causes poor pod fill. Harvest shelling peas when pods are plump but still bright green; snap peas when pods are full and sweet; snow peas when pods are flat and before seeds swell. Peas fix their own nitrogen and improve soil for subsequent crops.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Garden Peach is a unique and charming heirloom tomato that genuinely resembles a peach — producing small, round, blush-yellow to pale cream fruits covered in a delicate fuzz of dense trichomes that gives them the texture and appearance of a ripe peach skin — one of the most visually distinctive and surprising novelty tomatoes available.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Garden Peach is an indeterminate, moderately sized variety requiring staking or caging; it is quite productive and continues bearing through the season. Garden Peach tomato is a remarkable heirloom curiosity that mimics a real peach in appearance with unusual fidelity — the small (2–3 oz), round fruits have pale cream to blush-yellow skin covered in tiny dense hairs (trichomes) that create a distinctly fuzzy, velvet-textured surface virtually identical to peach fuzz; when held in the hand, a ripe Garden Peach tomato is nearly indistinguishable from a small peach by touch alone. The flavor is sweet and mild with a hint of fruity peach character, very low acidity, and soft, juicy texture — appealing to those who find standard tomatoes too acidic.
