Gold Rush produces a well-concentrated pod set ideal for once-over harvest or a 1–2 week intensive harvest window. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August–September for fall production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest pods when 4–6 inches long and still tender. Gold Rush is a 1980 All-America Selections-winning yellow wax bush bean that earned recognition for producing exceptionally straight, slim, uniformly golden-yellow pods in a well-concentrated set ideal for both fresh market and home canning. Yellow wax beans are a distinct culinary category from green snap beans — the pale golden-yellow color (which remains after cooking), slightly creamier texture, and subtle flavor difference (milder, slightly less grassy than green beans) make wax beans a favorite in German and Eastern European cooking and preferred by many home gardeners for pickled beans and canned beans. Gold Rush produces pods of exceptional straightness and uniformity — the 5–6 inch pods are nearly pencil-straight, a quality attribute for both visual appeal at the table and ease of packing for canning. The plants are compact, upright, and productive, concentrating the pod set over a 7–10 day harvest window suitable for once-over mechanical harvest or home garden batch picking.

common_name: Gold Rush Zucchini (AAS-Winning Yellow-Skinned Summer Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; in zone 9, sow spring crops in February–March and fall crops in August–September for the best production before summer heat or fall cold limits the season.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gold Rush is an All-America Selections-winning yellow zucchini hybrid — producing the classic straight, cylindrical zucchini form (6–8 inches at optimal harvest) in brilliant golden-yellow skin rather than the standard dark-green of typical zucchini. The golden-yellow skin is visually striking and creates attractive contrast with standard green zucchini in market displays, mixed vegetable dishes, and grilled presentations — the same tender, mild, slightly sweet flesh as green zucchini in a color that makes it immediately distinguishable. Gold Rush is a compact bush-type plant reaching 18–24 inches with a moderate 3–4 foot spread — appropriate for typical garden spacing without the sprawling habit of some summer squash. The AAS recognition reflects exceptional performance across multiple growing regions and conditions. In zone 9, Gold Rush is best grown as a spring crop (February–March planting for April–May harvest) or fall crop (August planting for September–October harvest) — summer heat causes powdery mildew and reduced production. Harvest at 6–8 inches for best flavor and tenderness; oversized fruits become seedy and tough. Squash vine borers are the primary pest challenge in zone 9; monitoring and early action against eggs is essential for spring production.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant for spring, or sow midsummer for fall heads.
directions: This early heirloom produces compact, round green heads quickly, making it a good fit for small gardens and short seasons. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before transplanting into firm, fertile soil. Water evenly and consistently, as swings in moisture can crack the maturing heads. Harvest as soon as heads feel solid, since the early type is prone to splitting if left too long; it succeeds in both spring and fall.

common_name: Golden Ball Turnip (Yellow-Fleshed Sweet Heirloom Fall Turnip)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall for the best turnip production in zone 9; turnips grown in cool fall weather are sweeter and less pungent than summer-grown turnips. In zone 9, sow August–October for harvest October–January. Spring planting is possible (February–March) but quality is often reduced by warming temperatures. Golden Ball's yellow flesh is notably sweeter than standard purple-top white-fleshed types and makes it excellent roasted.
directions: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches as plants establish. Golden Ball (also known as Robertson's Golden Ball and Amber Globe) is a Victorian-era heirloom turnip with a strikingly different appearance from the standard purple-top white-fleshed types that dominate American turnip culture: the round, smooth roots are golden-yellow skinned with deep golden-yellow flesh, rather than the white flesh of standard types. The yellow flesh color indicates a different carotenoid profile and, notably, a distinct flavor: Golden Ball is considered one of the sweetest, mildest turnips available — the yellow-fleshed types tend toward greater sweetness and less sulfur-pungency than white-fleshed types when grown in the same conditions. This mild, sweet quality makes Golden Ball excellent for eating raw (rare for turnips), roasted whole (the golden color makes an attractive presentation), and in preparations where the sulfur bite of standard turnips would be unwelcome. Golden Ball has been grown in British kitchen gardens since at least the 1850s and represents the traditional European approach to turnip cultivation that emphasized flavor diversity across multiple colors and flesh types rather than the American focus on the single purple-top type.

plant_note: Sow after frost in warm soil; plant in blocks for good pollination.
directions: This historic open-pollinated heirloom brought sweet yellow corn to the home table and still delivers rich, old-fashioned flavor. Sow seed an inch to an inch and a half deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows so wind pollination fills the ears. Provide plenty of water and nitrogen through tasseling and ear fill. Harvest when the silks brown and kernels are plump and milky, and cook or preserve promptly for the best flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 week after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for spring crop and August for fall. Plant in blocks of at least 3–4 rows for adequate wind pollination of ears.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; plant in blocks rather than single rows to ensure adequate pollen distribution to every silk. Golden Bantam is perhaps the most historically important sweet corn variety in American garden history. Introduced in 1902 by W. Atlee Burpee Company from a selection by E.L. Coy of New York, it was the first widely successful yellow sweet corn at a time when white corn was considered superior — Golden Bantam changed American tastes permanently and proved that yellow sweet corn could surpass white in flavor. The short (6–7 foot), early-season plants produce 6–7 inch ears with 8 rows of deep golden-yellow kernels with a distinctive rich, full sweet corn flavor different from modern supersweeet hybrids — a milk-and-sugar intensity that is the archetype of 'real corn flavor.' Still one of the best open-pollinated sweet corns and superior to any hybrid for seed saving. Harvest at milk stage (silk brown, kernel milky when pierced) and cook or freeze immediately — sugar converts to starch within hours of picking.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for winter-spring harvest. Golden beet germinates more slowly than red types and requires consistently moist soil until seedlings emerge. Thin to 3–4 inches for best root size. The golden color is most vibrant in young to medium-sized beets (2–3 inches diameter); very large golden beets may develop an orangey-brown skin. The tops are edible — harvest baby leaves for salads or cook mature greens like chard.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of rocks and hard pan; Golden Beet produces roots with bright golden-yellow skin and deep orange-gold flesh that stands out dramatically from red beet varieties — the color results from betaxanthin pigments rather than the betacyanin (red-purple) pigments of standard beets. The most important practical difference from red beets is that Golden Beet does not bleed or stain hands, cutting boards, or other foods with the intense crimson juice of red beets — a major advantage in salads and prepared dishes where red beet juice can dominate the visual presentation. The flavor of Golden Beet is also distinctly sweeter and milder than most red beet varieties, with less of the earthy 'dirty' undertone that some people find off-putting in red beets. The combination of non-staining, mild sweetness, and attractive golden color makes Golden Beet the preferred choice for beet salads, roasted vegetable medleys, and restaurant presentations.

plant_note: Germination can be erratic; sow a bit thicker to compensate.
directions: Golden beets offer a mild, sweet flavor without the earthy note of red types and do not bleed when cut. Because germination is often spotty, presoak seed for a few hours and sow slightly denser than usual. Thin ruthlessly to 3 inches so roots can size up without crowding. Keep beds weed-free and evenly watered to avoid tough, cracked roots. Harvest young for salads or at full size for roasting.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil is workable; succession sow for continuous harvest.
directions: A golden-orange fleshed beet with sweet, mild flavor that won't stain like red types, plus tender edible greens. Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked, and thin seedlings to about 3 inches since each seed cluster produces several plants. Keep soil evenly moist for smooth, uniform globes and harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots. The strong upright stems make for attractive bunches.

common_name: Golden Bush Scallop Squash (Golden Custard Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 65°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the compact bush habit needs less room than vining squash but still benefits from generous spacing for airflow and easy harvest.
directions: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest fruit young, at 2–3 inches across, for the sweetest, most tender flesh and thinnest skin, and pick every couple of days to keep the compact bush producing all summer. Golden Bush Scallop is a classic American heirloom summer squash producing the traditional flying-saucer-shaped 'patty pan' fruit in a bright, buttery golden-yellow, with a scalloped edge and creamy, mild, slightly nutty flesh when harvested young. The compact, non-vining bush habit keeps the plant tidy and productive in a relatively small footprint compared to sprawling vine squash, making it a good choice for smaller vegetable gardens and raised beds. Like all summer squash, frequent harvest at a small size is the key to extended production — fruit left to grow large quickly turns tough and seedy and signals the plant to slow down. A cheerful, productive, old-fashioned squash for zone 3–11 gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth; transplant after nights stay reliably warm.
directions: A blocky sweet bell that starts green and ripens to a sunburst yellow blushed with orange, excellent stuffed, grilled, or stir-fried. Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, then transplant after the soil and nights have warmed. Mulch to keep roots evenly moist and side-dress once fruit sets. Peppers freeze well, so harvest generously as they color up.

common_name: Golden California Wonder Pepper (Gold-Ripening Open-Pollinated Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Golden California Wonder is the gold counterpart to the standard red-ripening California Wonder — same fruit form and size, different final color.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Golden California Wonder is the gold-maturing selection from the California Wonder bell pepper family — producing the same blocky, four-lobed, large, thick-walled bell pepper fruit as standard California Wonder but ripening to a golden-yellow color rather than red. The fruits begin green and ripen to a warm, rich golden-yellow at full maturity — a color stage with sweeter, more mellow flavor than the green stage and a different flavor profile from fully red bell peppers. Golden bell peppers are noticeably sweeter and lower in Scoville units than green bell peppers — the color change from green to gold/yellow reflects the conversion of chlorophyll to carotenoids and the simultaneous conversion of starches to sugars. As an open-pollinated variety, Golden California Wonder seeds can be saved reliably from season to season. The golden fruits create visual contrast in mixed salads, stir-fries, and grilled vegetable platters where the gold color pairs beautifully with red and orange companions. The same thick walls and blocky form as California Wonder make Golden California Wonder outstanding for stuffed peppers. In zone 9, plant in spring (February–March) for a spring crop and in August for a fall crop.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil is warm; succession sow for extended yield.
directions: This classic yellow summer squash offers buttery flavor and tender texture on compact, bush-style plants that suit home gardens. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil, spacing plants for good air movement. Keep moisture steady and harvest fruits young, while the curved necks are still small and the skin is tender. Frequent picking keeps the plants producing heavily, since mature fruits left on the plant slow new set.

scientific_name: Zea mays var. saccharata 'Golden Cross Bantam'
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least four short rows after soil has warmed well past the last frost, since corn relies on wind pollination and needs neighboring plants to fill ears properly.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in blocks rather than single long rows to ensure reliable pollination, and side-dress with nitrogen once plants reach knee height. Introduced in the 1930s as one of the first widely grown hybrid sweet corns, this variety became a benchmark standard for decades thanks to its resistance to Stewart's wilt and its dependable yields of seven-inch ears filled with tender, golden-yellow kernels. Its classic old-fashioned sweet corn flavor, rather than the ultra-sugary taste of modern supersweet hybrids, still appeals to gardeners who remember it from earlier generations of home gardens. Harvest when kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pierced.

common_name: Golden Crown Watermelon (AAS-Winning Yellow-Rind Icebox Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Golden Crown is an AAS-winning early, compact icebox watermelon whose rind ripens to solid golden-yellow instead of green, giving an easy visual ripeness cue unlike most watermelons.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms. Golden Crown is an AAS-winning early, compact icebox-type watermelon with an unusual and genuinely useful feature — the rind ripens from green to a distinctive solid golden-yellow at full maturity, giving gardeners a clear, unmistakable visual cue for ripeness instead of relying only on the ground-spot color, tendril drying, and thump-sound methods needed for green-rind watermelons. Inside, the flesh is sweet and red, with a compact plant habit and fast maturity that suit smaller gardens and shorter growing seasons well. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil and consistent irrigation through fruit development for the best size and flavor; ease off watering slightly as fruit nears full color to help concentrate sugars.

plant_note: Sow directly into warm, fertile hills once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F, well after last frost.
directions: Golden Delicious is a 1920s Oregon-bred heirloom, a cross of Delicious and Boston Marrow, grown for its top-shaped, red-orange fruit and thick, fine-grained flesh originally favored for commercial baby food production. Give the long vines plenty of room and consistent moisture through fruit development, then let fruit finish on the vine until the rind resists a thumbnail. It stores exceptionally well for a maxima squash, often holding good eating quality into winter without special curing conditions. Gardeners choose it today for its old-fashioned sweetness in pies and its reliability as a dependable keeper compared to showier modern hybrids.

common_name: Golden Detroit Beet (Non-Bleeding Yellow Heirloom Beet)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; Golden Detroit's yellow-orange roots never bleed color the way red beets do.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters about half an inch deep in loose, fertile soil in full sun, and thin seedlings to three or four inches apart once true leaves appear. Golden Detroit is a yellow-fleshed sport of the classic Detroit type, producing round, orange-skinned roots that cook down to a warm mustard-gold color instead of bleeding red, so it can be roasted, pickled, or shaved raw into salads without staining hands or other ingredients. The flavor is sweet and mild, generally considered gentler and less earthy than red beet varieties, and the tender tops are excellent cooked as greens. Harvest at two to three inches across for the best texture, and keep the soil evenly moist throughout to prevent tough, fibrous roots.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall (zones 7–11) or early spring (zones 3–7); Golden Frill is a yellow-green counterpart to Ruby Streaks mustard — both have deeply serrated, feathery leaves, but Golden Frill's chartreuse to light yellow-green color provides a dramatic visual contrast when planted alongside purple or red mustard varieties; flavor is milder than red mustard types at the same leaf age, making it versatile for fresh salads.
directions: Broadcast or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep; for baby leaf harvest sow thickly and cut at 3–4 inches; for mature plants thin to 6–8 inches; harvest outer leaves continuously or cut the whole plant 4–6 inches above the crown for cut-and-come-again; milder than red frills types at the same growth stage. Golden Frill is a deeply serrated, feathery-leaved mustard green with the same fine, lacey, frilly leaf form as Ruby Streaks but with chartreuse to bright yellow-green coloring — a deliberate complement to red frills types in mesclun mixes and specialty salad production. The deeply incised, pinnately cut leaves (resembling an extremely large, pungent parsley) are the characteristic form of the 'frills' mustard group, but Golden Frill's bright color is distinctive and valuable in ornamental kitchen garden plantings where the yellow-green foliage contrasts dramatically with red-leaved varieties, dark green kales, and purple cabbages. The flavor is mustard-sharp but somewhat milder than red-leaved mustard varieties at the same stage of maturity — mild enough to use raw in quantity in salads at the baby leaf stage, with more heat developing in mature leaves. Golden Frill is a standard component of mesclun and Asian salad mixes alongside Ruby Streaks, mizuna, and tatsoi; the combination of all four creates dramatic visual contrast (red, chartreuse, dark green, and pale green) with complementary flavors. Extremely fast-growing in cool weather — baby leaves in 21 days, full plants in 35–40 days.

common_name: Golden Frills Mustard (Frilled Gold Salad Green)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop; spring sowings are more prone to flea beetle damage than late-summer ones.
directions: Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop, since Golden Frills grows best in the cool temperatures of spring and autumn and can suffer flea beetle damage in warm weather. Golden Frills is a strikingly ornamental mustard green with finely dissected, deeply lobed, chartreuse-gold leaves that add texture and bright color to salad mixes and cut-and-come-again plantings. Its flavor is sweet and aromatic with a mustard bite that is milder than many mustard greens, and mature plants sometimes develop a crisp, edible root reflecting a mustard-turnip heritage in its lineage. Harvest young for baby leaf salads at around three weeks, or allow plants to grow to full size for a spicier, more robust cooking green.

common_name: Golden Giant Amaranth (Tall Golden-Yellow Grain and Cut-Flower Amaranth)
plant_note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Golden Giant bears tall, upright, golden-yellow seed plumes on a vigorous grain amaranth suited to both harvest and cut-flower use.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covered, in warm soil after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks early. Golden Giant produces tall, dense, upright golden-yellow flower plumes on vigorous, sturdy stems, grown both for its abundant edible grain and as a dramatic fresh or dried cut flower for fall arrangements. Heat-tolerant and low-maintenance, it thrives in full sun and average soil, producing heavy yields of small, protein-rich seed by the time the plumes fully color and dry. Harvest seed heads once they rattle and the seed sheds easily when rubbed, then thresh and winnow; cut plumes for drying just as they color for the best cut-flower use, and expect self-sowing if seed heads are left in place.

common_name: Golden Globe Turnip (Classic Sweet Yellow-Fleshed Heirloom Turnip)
plant_note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep 6–10 weeks before the first fall frost for the sweetest roots, or as early as the soil can be worked in late winter; in zone 9, an October sowing usually outperforms a spring one since the roots size up in cool, mild weather without bolting.
directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to 3–4 inches apart once seedlings have their first true leaves, using the thinnings as tender salad greens. Golden Globe is a 19th-century English heirloom valued for its smooth, golden-skinned, yellow-fleshed roots, which are noticeably sweeter and milder than white-fleshed turnips and hold good texture even when they size up past baseball size. It bulks up quickly from a compact top, making it a good choice for close spacing and succession sowing, and the mild flavor suits it equally well to roasting, mashing, or eating raw and thinly sliced. Keep soil evenly moist for fast, uninterrupted growth, since checks from drought or heat toughen the roots and sharpen their flavor.

common_name: Golden Gourmet Shallot (Dutch Yellow Shallot, Banana Shallot)
plant_note: Plant shallot sets 4–8 weeks before last frost in spring, or in fall in zones 7–10 for overwintering harvest; Golden Gourmet produces uniform, elongated oval bulbs with golden-amber to bronze outer skin and pale yellow to white flesh — a Dutch-type yellow shallot with classic mild, sweet shallot flavor and excellent productivity and storage life that make it a top-selling shallot variety in European commercial production.
directions: Plant shallot sets 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart, with the tip just at or slightly above soil level; each set multiplies into a cluster of 5–8 bulbs; maintain consistent moisture during spring growth; reduce watering when tops begin to yellow and fall over; harvest when bulb skins are dry and golden, then cure 2–3 weeks in a warm, dry location before storage. Golden Gourmet is a Dutch-type yellow shallot produced by seed companies primarily in the Netherlands, the global center of commercial shallot breeding and production; the variety represents the classic 'Dutch shallot' style — elongated-oval (sometimes banana-shaped), golden to copper-amber skinned bulbs with very pale yellow to white inner flesh, as opposed to the red-violet type represented by Ambition and Zebrune. The flavor profile is mild, sweet, and delicately onion-like with the characteristic shallot complexity — somewhat different from red-type shallots, with a cleaner, lighter character that particularly suits cream sauces, light vinaigrettes, and dishes where the golden color and mild flavor complement pale or delicate ingredients. Each planted set multiplies into a cluster of 5–8 uniform bulbs that cure to a beautiful, uniform golden-amber appearance — the classic appearance of the shallots found in upscale grocery stores and restaurant supply. Stores 8–10 months under good conditions, outlasting most red-type shallots. Can be replanted from the previous year's sets.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; an 1898 introduction and one of the most widely grown Hubbard types, with brilliant red-orange skin and an easier-to-cut size than the giant Blue Hubbard.
directions: Sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 1–2 plants once true leaves appear and keep hills evenly moist through fruit set. Golden Hubbard was introduced around 1898 as a smaller, easier-to-handle alternative to the large blue Hubbard types, producing teardrop-shaped fruits 6–10 pounds in weight with vivid orange-red, bumpy skin and dense, sweet, yellow-orange flesh with excellent dry texture ideal for baking and puréeing. Harvest after the first light frost has killed the vines and the rind resists puncture with a fingernail; cure in a 70–85°F location for 10–14 days then store at 50–60°F for up to 4 months. The relatively manageable fruit size makes it more practical for home cooks than the 15–20 pound Blue Hubbard.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Golden Jenny was selected from the historic Jenny Lind muskmelon line and produces small, round, golden-skinned fruit with sweet orange flesh on a plant well suited to compact gardens and short growing seasons.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after last frost, thinning to the strongest two or three seedlings per hill; the compact vines and small fruit size make this a good candidate for raised beds or smaller vegetable plots. Golden Jenny produces round, one to two pound fruits with smooth golden-yellow skin and juicy, aromatic, orange-gold flesh, and was developed from the classic 19th-century Jenny Lind muskmelon, retaining that heirloom's sweetness and old-fashioned melon aroma in a smaller, quicker-maturing package. Keep soil evenly moist through vine growth and fruit set, then let it dry slightly as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the vine with light pressure and the fruit releases a strong, sweet fragrance at the blossom end.

common_name: Golden Midget Sweet Corn (Extra-Dwarf Heirloom Sweet Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of short rows or in large containers; compact stature makes it practical for small gardens and pots.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of short rows or in large containers, since its compact stature makes it one of the few sweet corns genuinely practical for small gardens, raised beds, and pots. Golden Midget was bred at a New Hampshire agricultural research station in the mid-1900s specifically to give home gardeners a fast, space-saving sweet corn, reaching only two to three feet tall while still producing petite four-inch ears of golden-yellow kernels. Its short season and small footprint have kept it a favorite heirloom for northern gardeners and anyone growing corn in limited space, and it remains a genuinely useful, if lesser-known, member of the open-pollinated sweet corn family.

common_name: Golden Midget Watermelon (Compact Early Watermelon with Unique Golden-Yellow Ripeness Indicator)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Golden Midget is a compact, early-maturing watermelon (70–75 days) producing icebox-sized fruits (6–8 lbs, 6–8 inches diameter) on shorter vines (4–5 feet) than standard large watermelon varieties. In zone 9, plant April–June; the short maturity allows two plantings in the season. Golden Midget's most remarkable feature is its ripeness indicator: the skin is light green with darker green stripes when unripe, and it turns golden-yellow when fully ripe — a color change that is unmistakable and provides a clear visual cue to harvest timing without the need to thump, check tendril dried status, or use other indirect indicators. This visual ripeness indicator is unique among common watermelon varieties and is Golden Midget's primary practical advantage. The flesh is red, sweet, and of good quality for an early compact variety. The compact vine size makes Golden Midget more manageable in average-sized home gardens than standard watermelon types.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms; space 4–5 feet apart. Harvest when skin turns solid golden-yellow. Golden Midget Watermelon was developed and introduced by Elwyn Meader and Albert Yeager at the University of New Hampshire in the 1950s, specifically targeting short-season northern gardens where standard large watermelons require more summer heat than is available. The breeding goals — early maturity (70–75 days), compact vine, and small fruit — made Golden Midget one of the pioneering compact watermelon varieties for home garden production. The most distinctive characteristic is the skin color change at ripeness: unlike any other standard watermelon variety, Golden Midget's skin transitions from striped green to solid golden-yellow as the fruit reaches full maturity inside, providing the clearest possible visual harvest cue. Standard watermelon ripeness indicators (dried stem tendril, ground spot color change, sound when thumped) require interpretation and experience; Golden Midget's golden skin change is unambiguous and visible from across the garden. The fruit size (6–8 lbs, fits in a refrigerator shelf whole) suits modern households that cannot easily consume a 25-pound watermelon and want a seedless or small-fruited option. The flesh is pink to red with conventional watermelon sweetness — appropriate for fresh eating, salads, and summer use — without the extraordinary flavor intensity of the best large heirloom varieties, but reliable and consistent in flavor quality across the growing season.

plant_note: Sow directly in early spring and successively every few weeks for a steady supply of tender young leaves.
directions: Sow directly in early spring and successively every few weeks for a steady supply of tender young leaves, since older leaves and stems toughen as plants approach flowering. This golden-yellow-leaved form of mountain spinach has been grown as a spinach substitute since antiquity and tolerates heat and poor soil far better than true spinach, eventually bolting to tall, ornamental seed spikes in summer. Its bright color makes it a popular contrast alongside the more familiar red and green orach forms in mixed salad plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; in zone 9 plant March–May or August–September. Golden Purslane requires warm soil and warm weather to germinate and grow — do not attempt in cool conditions. It self-sows readily in zone 9 and may naturalize in garden beds; pull unwanted seedlings before they set seed. Harvest tender stem tips continuously to keep the plant producing new growth.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun — purslane thrives in the heat and poor soils that discourage other vegetables; Golden Purslane is a cultivated, golden-yellow-stemmed selection of the common wild purslane (Portulaca oleracea), developed for the edible vegetable trade and producing larger, more succulent stems and leaves than the weedy wild type. The thick, fleshy, yellow-green leaves and golden stems have a mild, slightly lemony, succulent flavor with a mucilaginous texture when raw and a spinach-like softness when cooked. Purslane is one of the highest plant sources of omega-3 fatty acids and contains significant amounts of vitamins A, C, and E — nutritionally rich in a plant that requires almost no inputs and grows vigorously in the heat that exhausts other summer vegetables. In zone 9 it is one of the most productive summer greens from May through October when the heat prevents all other leafy green production. The golden color distinguishes it from the wild weedy type and makes it more attractive in salads. Harvest young stem tips and leaves continuously; older stems become woody.

plant_note: Direct sow thickly in warm soil (70°F+) in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; cultivated purslane is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant summer salad greens and is an outstanding vegetable for zone 9 gardens where most salad plants bolt in summer heat.
directions: Scatter seeds on warm, bare soil and press in lightly — seeds need some light to germinate; thin to 4–6 inches or harvest as a cut-and-come-again crop. Portulaca oleracea sativa (culinary or golden purslane) is the large-leaved, succulent, upright or spreading culinary form of the common purslane weed, distinguished from the weed by larger, more succulent, often golden-yellow to golden-green leaves and a more upright, less spreading habit. It is one of the most nutritious and heat-tolerant summer vegetables — extraordinarily high in omega-3 fatty acids (the highest of any leafy vegetable), vitamin C, and beta-carotene — with a mildly tart, slightly mucilaginous, fleshy texture and pleasant sour flavor used raw in salads, stir-fried, or added to soups and stews throughout Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Mexican cuisines. In zone 9, culinary purslane can be grown from April through October, thriving in summer heat and drought when all other salad plants fail — it is the definitive summer salad green for hot, dry gardens. Common golden purslane cultivars include 'Goldberg' (large, golden-yellow leaves) and 'Gruner' (green leaves, more upright).

common_name: Golden Self-Blanching Celery (1883 Naturally-Blanching Heirloom Celery)
plant_note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since celery seed germinates slowly and can take up to three weeks; transplant into rich, moist soil in tight blocks or double rows so the crowded plants self-blanche without tying or hilling.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun, spacing plants closely in a block rather than a single row; Golden Self-Blanching Celery was introduced in the United States in the early 1880s and became one of the most widely grown home garden celeries of its era because it needs no earthing up or wrapping to pale its stalks. Grown tightly together, the inner stalks naturally shade one another and turn a soft golden-green by fall, staying crisp and largely stringless with a clean, mild celery flavor. It matures somewhat faster than many older celery types, making it a practical choice for gardeners without a long, reliably cool season to spare. Water evenly and consistently throughout the growing period, since irregular moisture is the most common cause of stringy, bitter stalks in any celery.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; squash dislikes root disturbance.
directions: A classic yellow crookneck producing bright, tender fruits best picked at 6 to 8 inches long on compact bushy plants. Direct sow two or three seeds per hill once soil warms past 70F, then thin to the strongest. Keep well watered and harvest every day or two, since regular picking keeps the plants productive all season. The bushy 2-foot habit and 2 to 4 foot spread make it manageable in smaller beds.

plant_note: Sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; a tall climber (4–5 ft) with attractive purple flowers requiring trellis support; pods change from bright yellow-green to full yellow at harvest — pick when flat and yellow-green.
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in cool, fertile soil in full sun 4–6 weeks before last frost with trellis support; Golden Sweet is a distinctive heirloom snow pea from India with vivid lemon-yellow pods against deep green foliage and attractive purple flowers — one of the most ornamental edible peas available. The flavor of the bright yellow flat pods is sweet and delicate with a slightly more tender texture than green snow peas; they make a visually striking addition to salads and stir-fries. Harvest pods when fully yellow and flat before seeds begin to swell for best quality. The yellow color provides an interesting contrast to green and purple-podded pea varieties grown together.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil as early as it can be worked; provide a tall trellis.
directions: A striking heirloom snow pea with bicolor purple blossoms and flat, lemon-yellow pods that are tender raw, steamed, or stir-fried. Direct sow several weeks before the last frost as soon as the soil is workable, and set up a tall trellis for the 6 to 8 foot vines. Keep the soil cool and moist with mulch, and harvest pods young while flat and crisp. Frequent picking extends the productive window before summer heat.

common_name: Golden Udo (Sun King, Chartreuse-Leaved Edible-Shoot Ornamental)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Golden Udo, a 2020 Perennial Plant of the Year, is a golden-leaved sport of edible udo bearing brilliant chartreuse-gold foliage best colored in part shade, while still producing edible blanched shoots.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; foliage color is most vivid in a few hours of morning sun with shade during the hottest part of the day, and the leaves turn lime-green rather than scorching in fuller shade. Golden Udo, named the 2020 Perennial Plant of the Year, is a dramatic ornamental sport of the Japanese vegetable udo, producing huge, bold, compound leaves in a luminous chartreuse-gold that light up a shaded border from spring through fall, while retaining the parent species' edible young shoots, which can be blanched and harvested in spring and prepared much like asparagus. It dies back to the ground each winter and re-emerges vigorously in spring, forming a large, architectural clump within a couple of seasons. Divide congested clumps in early spring, and provide consistent moisture, since the large leaves wilt readily in dry soil.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil warms; succession sow every few weeks.
directions: This productive yellow wax bean produces bright, stringless pods with tender texture on compact 15 to 20 inch bush plants. Sow seed about an inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans resent root disturbance. Keep moisture even during flowering and pod set, and avoid working among wet plants to limit disease. Pick pods often while young and slender for fresh eating or preserving, which keeps the plants setting new pods.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil is warm; a single plant is very productive.
directions: This heirloom, open-pollinated variety produces bright yellow, cylindrical fruits with classic zucchini flavor on compact bush plants. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and give each plant room for air circulation. Water consistently at the base and harvest fruits young, around six to eight inches, for the best texture. Pick every day or two during peak season, since fruits enlarge fast and steady harvest keeps production high.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after all frost danger has passed.
directions: A 1973 heirloom zucchini with vivid yellow fruit and creamy-white flesh, most tender when picked at 8 inches or less. Direct sow into warm soil after frost, planting in hills and thinning to the strongest seedlings. Water deeply and consistently to prevent blossom-end rot, and harvest frequently to keep the plant producing. Excellent roasted, grilled, sauteed, or baked.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to garden after frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start seeds in January–February and transplant in March–April. Ground cherries drop ripe fruits in their papery husks — harvest by collecting fallen fruits daily. In zone 9 ground cherries often self-sow and naturalize as short-lived perennials in mild winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Goldie is a named ground cherry cultivar specifically selected for larger-than-average fruit size and superior sweetness compared to standard ground cherry selections — the distinctive golden-yellow to pale orange fruits inside their papery lantern-like husks are significantly larger and sweeter than wild-type plants, with a complex tropical flavor combining vanilla, pineapple, and tomatillo notes with a sweet-tart finish unlike any other common garden fruit. Ground cherries (Physalis pruinosa) are closely related to tomatillos but used as a sweet fruit rather than a savory vegetable — excellent eaten fresh, baked into pies and cobblers, or made into jam with a natural pectin content that produces a firm set. The plant grows as a sprawling, somewhat sticky annual related to tomatoes, producing continuously from midsummer until frost. In zone 9 Goldie ground cherries produce abundantly and the plants often self-sow from fallen fruits.

common_name: Goldilocks Acorn Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Bush Acorn Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Goldilocks is a semi-bush acorn squash bred for a much more compact vine than traditional sprawling acorn types, so it fits well in smaller vegetable gardens and raised beds.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously even though the semi-bush habit takes noticeably less room than traditional sprawling acorn squash vines. Goldilocks is an AAS-winning acorn squash producing golden-orange, deeply ribbed fruit with sweet, fine-textured, deep-orange flesh, on a plant compact enough for smaller gardens while still yielding a full crop of 4-6 fruits per plant. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens and the color deepens to a solid gold-orange, typically as the vine begins to decline in late summer or fall; cure harvested squash in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to improve flavor and shelf life. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, which are common problems for all Cucurbita pepo squash in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; established clumps can be divided every few years in early spring to increase leaf-harvest plantings.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, watering during dry spells since this clumping woodland species does not tolerate drought. Gomchwi is a large-leaved perennial from the mountains of Korea, northern China, and the Russian Far East, prized in Korean cuisine as one of the most sought-after wild spring greens (sannamul); the young, mildly aromatic leaves are picked in early spring and eaten as a fresh wrap green, blanched, or preserved as pickled jangajji. Unlike its ornamental Ligularia relatives, it is grown primarily for repeated leaf harvest rather than for its tall late-summer spikes of yellow daisy-like flowers, though the flower stalks are also ornamental if left to bloom. Harvest outer leaves regularly through spring and early summer to encourage a continuous flush of tender new growth from the crown.

common_name: Gonzales Baby Cabbage (Compact Small-Head Cabbage for Small Space Gardens)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Gonzales produces compact, 3–4 lb cabbage heads on plants spaced 12–14 inches apart — significantly closer spacing than standard full-sized cabbage types (18–24 inches) — making it practical for small raised beds, intensive planting, and gardens where standard cabbage would take too much space. In zone 9, start in July–August and transplant late August–September for November–December harvest. Gonzales is an F1 hybrid with excellent uniformity — plants in a block ripen within a narrow window, allowing single-harvest timing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun, fertile soil. Harvest when heads feel firm and solid. Gonzales is a compact, early-maturing F1 hybrid green cabbage designed specifically for closer plant spacing, smaller garden plots, and the restaurant/market garden demand for mini or baby vegetable formats — a market segment that has grown substantially with the trend toward smaller household sizes and the restaurant emphasis on individual-portion vegetables. The heads average 3–4 pounds (compared to 5–8 lbs for full-sized standard green cabbage types) but form a properly tight, round, firm head with the same dense, crinkle-free outer leaves and pale, crisp interior of larger standard types — not a soft or immature head, but a fully developed compact head. Gonzales's early maturity (66–75 days from transplant vs. 80–110 days for full-sized storage types) combined with its compact size makes it particularly practical in zone 9's fall garden where planting time from mid-summer is limited. The flavor is classic mild, sweet, crisp green cabbage — excellent for coleslaw, stir-fries, braises, and fresh salads. The small size is practical for household use where a standard large cabbage requires several meals to consume before it deteriorates.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in cool spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Good King Henry is a long-lived perennial once established — allow it to remain in place for several years for maximum leaf production, as the crown grows progressively larger and more productive with each passing year.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in cool spring or fall in moist, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Good King Henry is a European perennial edible plant of the goosefoot family (Chenopodiaceae, now Amaranthaceae) that was widely cultivated as a potherb and vegetable in medieval and early modern Europe but has been largely replaced by spinach and other modern leafy vegetables — leaving it as a largely forgotten but highly useful perennial edible for the shade garden. The large, arrow-shaped, dark-green leaves are produced abundantly from an expanding perennial crown that persists for many years; in spring, the young leaves and shoot tips are eaten raw or cooked (with a mild, spinach-like flavor), and the young flowering shoots are eaten like asparagus when they first emerge, blanched and steamed. The flowers themselves are used as a condiment. The primary advantage over annual spinach is permanence — once established, Good King Henry returns year after year with progressively larger harvests from an increasingly robust perennial crown, requiring virtually no replanting. It performs acceptably in partial shade, making it one of the few perennial vegetables useful in the shade vegetable garden.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 60°F; a vigorous pole bean that needs a trellis or fence 5–6 feet tall and is harvested as a dry bean in fall after the pods have dried on the vine.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil against a tall trellis; do not soak beans before planting as it can cause the seed coat to split. Good Mother Stallard is an heirloom pole bean introduced through Seed Savers Exchange with beautiful, plum-purple and white mottled pods and seeds that develop into a creamy, meaty dry bean with a remarkably rich, complex, steak-like flavor when cooked — widely considered one of the best-flavored dry beans available to home gardeners. Allow pods to mature and dry completely on the vine before harvesting; if frost threatens, pull the entire vine and hang in a protected location to finish drying. Store shelled dry beans in a cool, airtight container for up to a year.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil is workable; succession sow every few weeks.
directions: A colorful mix of beet varieties including deep-red Detroit Dark Red and candy-striped Chioggia, offering a rainbow of roots and tasty greens. Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked and thin each seed cluster to a single plant about 3 inches apart. Keep evenly moist for smooth, tender roots and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size. The assorted colors make a beautiful bunch and a striking roasted medley.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring planting or in midsummer for fall crop; Graffiti is a vivid purple cauliflower whose dramatic color comes from anthocyanins — the same antioxidant pigments in red cabbage and blueberries — and while the color fades when cooked (unlike Cheddar's beta-carotene), the raw purple makes it spectacularly visual in crudités platters, salads, and vegetable displays.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; transplant into rich, moist, fertile soil with consistent watering; fall crops typically produce the most vivid purple color as cool temperatures intensify the anthocyanin pigmentation; harvest when heads are tight. Graffiti is a vivid purple cauliflower developed by Syngenta Seeds, with intensely purple heads caused by very high anthocyanin concentrations — the same pigments responsible for the colors of red cabbage, blueberries, blackberries, and purple sweet potatoes, and associated with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory health properties. Unlike the orange beta-carotene in Cheddar cauliflower, the purple anthocyanins in Graffiti are water-soluble and somewhat heat-sensitive: the vivid purple color turns gray-blue or fades when the vegetable is boiled or steamed, though the color remains more stable with roasting or stir-frying. For maximum visual impact, Graffiti is best used raw — in crudités platters, purple cauliflower hummus, raw salads, and grain bowls where the intense purple provides a visual anchor. The flavor is typically cauliflower — slightly nutty, mild, sweet — with no unusual taste despite the dramatic color. Cool temperatures intensify the purple color, making fall-grown Graffiti more vividly colored than spring crops. An excellent conversation piece and visual anchor for vegetable gardens.

plant_note: Needs warm nights above 60 F to set fruit reliably.
directions: This Italian type bears glossy fruit striped in purple and white that fades to solid purple as it matures. Start seed indoors eight weeks before the last frost and transplant only after nights stay reliably above 60 F. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and stake plants that become top-heavy with fruit. Harvest while the skin is still glossy for the mildest, least seedy flesh. Consistent picking encourages the plant to keep flowering and fruiting.

common_name: Grain Amaranth (Kiwicha, Inca Wheat, Prince's Feather)
plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface after last frost once soil temperature exceeds 65°F; in the Gulf Coast (zone 9) plant in spring through early summer. Amaranth is drought-tolerant once established but germinates best with consistent surface moisture for the first week.
directions: Scatter seeds thinly on firm, moist, weed-free soil and press gently without covering — seeds are tiny and need light to germinate well; thin seedlings to 12–18 inches when they reach 3 inches tall. Grain amaranth is a tall, drought-resistant warm-season annual producing enormous plume-like flower heads packed with thousands of tiny seeds that are 13–16% complete protein and rich in lysine, an amino acid deficient in most grains. The seeds pop like popcorn, cook into porridge, or grind into gluten-free flour. Young leaves are edible as a potherb. Harvest when the seed heads begin to dry but before rain can cause mold — cut the stalks and dry in a ventilated space, then thresh by rubbing between hands or rolling in a cloth sack. One plant can produce several pounds of grain in a good season.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms to at least 65°F; grain sorghum is more drought-tolerant than corn and performs better in hot, dry summers — it is an excellent warm-season grain for Southern gardens in zone 8–11 where summer heat and drought stress corn. Plant in rows 30–36 inches apart.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil in full sun in rows 30–36 inches apart; grain sorghum is one of the most drought-tolerant of all cereal grains, adapted to hot, dry conditions that would devastate corn. In the South it is called 'milo' and is traditionally grown as a feed grain for livestock, but the grain is also edible for humans — it can be popped like popcorn, ground into gluten-free flour for flatbreads and porridges, cooked as a rice-like grain, or fermented into traditional African and South American beverages. White and tan grain varieties are milder-flavored than red varieties for human consumption. The upright plants top out with a dense grain head; harvest when seeds are hard and the heads have dried on the plant. Sorghum's deep root system makes it exceptionally drought-resistant once established, and it responds well to brief dry spells that would reduce corn yields.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall and January–February for spring. Grand Duke is an All-America Selections winner that performs best in cool weather — fall crops in zone 9 from September transplants have the best flavor and texture. In zone 9 summer heat causes rapid bolting and fibrous, pithy stems; stick to the cool seasons. Harvest when stems are 2–3 inches across for best tenderness.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Grand Duke is the 1979 All-America Selections-winning kohlrabi cultivar and remains the standard cool-season kohlrabi for home gardens. The pale green, smooth-skinned swollen stem enlarges more uniformly and remains tender longer than older varieties — it can be harvested at 2–3 inches and still be mild and crisp, even as other varieties turn woody and pungent. The flavor is mild, sweet, and slightly turnip-like — excellent raw, sliced thin in salads, or stir-fried. In zone 9 kohlrabi is a fall-through-winter vegetable, transplanted in September–October for harvest from November through February. The plants are relatively frost-hardy and will survive most zone 9 winters without protection. Pull the entire plant at harvest; the leaves are also edible when young and cooked like kale.

common_name: Grand Rapids Lettuce (Historic American Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in fall; fast-growing and reasonably heat tolerant for a leaf lettuce, making it a good choice for stretching the Gulf Coast lettuce season.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to six to eight inches apart. Grand Rapids is a historic American loose-leaf lettuce introduced in the late 1800s that became the standard commercial greenhouse lettuce variety across the United States for much of the early 20th century, prized for its light green, deeply frilled, crinkled leaves and fast, dependable growth. It does not form a true head, instead producing a loose rosette that can be harvested leaf by leaf for a cut-and-come-again crop or cut whole at the base once full size is reached. Grand Rapids is more heat- and cold-tolerant than many lettuce varieties, extending the usable harvest window on either end of the cool season, though very hot weather will still eventually push it to bolt and turn bitter.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant after frost and plant at least two for pollination.
directions: A compact tomatillo about 24 inches tall that yields husked green fruit nearly all at once, ideal for canning or freezing salsa verde. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant after the weather warms. Plant at least two, since tomatillos need cross-pollination to set fruit well. Harvest when the papery husks fill out and split, and stake plants if they get top-heavy.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and provide a tall trellis or pole for the vigorous climbing vines.
directions: This family heirloom pole bean traces to seed a Russian immigrant gave to Nellie Chernoff, who grew it for decades before it was passed down and eventually shared with seed preservationists. Pick pods at about 4 to 5 inches while still tender for fresh eating; cooked pods develop a distinctive savory, umami-like richness that sets this variety apart from typical green beans. Provide sturdy 6 to 8 foot poles or a trellis, as the vines are vigorous climbers that bear over a long harvest window. Keep pods picked regularly to keep the plant productive through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or again in late summer for a fall crop; thin seedlings as they grow to give each head room to fully form.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in cool, moist soil and thin plants as they grow to give each head room to fill out. Grandpa Admire's is an Ozark family heirloom lettuce preserved and distributed by Seed Savers Exchange, forming a loose, semi-heading rosette that bridges the gap between a butterhead and a romaine in both leaf shape and texture. The pale green leaves are tender and mild-flavored with a buttery crunch, and the variety is valued for holding in the garden without turning bitter longer than many spring lettuces. As a passed-down heirloom with a documented family origin, it is a good choice for gardeners interested in preserving lesser-known regional lettuce lines.

plant_note: Transplant onion sets or starts in November through January in zone 9 in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun; Granex is a short-day onion requiring 12 hours or fewer of daylight to form bulbs — it is the correct onion type for Gulf South gardens and bulbs where days are short during the winter growing season.
directions: Transplant onion sets or starts in November through January in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Granex is the foundational sweet onion cultivar behind the famous Vidalia onion — a short-day, mild, sweet onion variety grown in the Vidalia, Georgia, area since the 1940s that became the basis for the legally protected Vidalia Onion designation. The Granex onion (and closely related Granex 33 and similar cultivars) produces round to slightly flattened, large, sweet, mild bulbs with high sugar content and low pyruvic acid — a combination that creates the characteristic sweetness and lack of pungency that makes Vidalia-type onions so prized for fresh eating. Granex is a short-day onion (bulbs when day length reaches 12 hours or less), making it the correct onion type for Gulf South gardens where the short winter days trigger bulbing in March through May. Long-day onion varieties (grown in the northern US) will not bulb in the Gulf South — short-day varieties (Granex, Texas 1015, Red Creole) are essential for zone 9 production. In zone 9, transplant November through January and harvest when the tops begin to fall over (May–June), indicating full bulb development. The mild, sweet Granex onion is outstanding for fresh salads, burgers, and raw applications where a sweet onion is desired.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes and soil has warmed above 60°F. In the Gulf Coast (zone 9), plant in late February to March for a spring crop and again in late August for a fall crop — the plants struggle in peak summer heat above 95°F.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.8) with consistent moisture; grape tomatoes are distinguished by their small, elongated, thick-walled fruits — typically 1–2 inches long and grape-shaped — with a sweeter, less acidic flavor and firmer texture than cherry tomatoes, making them excellent for eating fresh, roasting, and salads. Most varieties are indeterminate and highly productive, setting fruit prolifically in large pendant clusters throughout the growing season. The thick skin resists cracking even when watering is inconsistent, a significant advantage over round cherry types. Provide a sturdy cage or stake early, keep soil evenly moist to prevent blossom-end rot, and side-dress with balanced fertilizer when the first flowers open.

plant_note: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in early spring; grass pea tolerates frost once established and can also be sown in fall in mild-winter climates (zones 7–10) for a winter-to-spring crop; inoculate with a broad-spectrum Rhizobium inoculant if growing in a new bed.
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun, 4–6 weeks before last frost; grass pea is one of the most ancient cultivated grain legumes, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent and still grown today across South Asia, Ethiopia, and the Mediterranean as a drought-resistant crop that produces nutritious, starchy seeds used whole, split, or ground into flour. It fixes atmospheric nitrogen and performs remarkably well in thin, poor, drought-stressed soils where other legumes fail — making it a resilient choice for dry-summer gardens and marginal land. Provide light support for the scrambling stems and harvest pods when fully dry on the vine. Important safety note: prolonged consumption of large quantities of grass pea seeds as a dietary staple without adequate protein diversity can cause lathyrism, a neurological condition — consume in normal dietary variety and not as a sole food source.

common_name: Greasy Back Bean (Appalachian Heirloom Cornfield Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis, corn stalks, or other tall support; this vigorous climbing pole bean traditionally grown alongside corn needs sturdy support to reach its full length.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep at the base of a trellis or tall support in fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Greasy Back belongs to a distinctive family of Appalachian heirloom 'greasy bean' varieties named for pods that lack the fine fuzz found on most bean pods, giving them a smooth, shiny, almost oiled appearance that is unmistakable at a glance. Traditionally grown climbing up corn stalks in mountain garden plots, the vigorous vines produce tender, flavorful pods that can be picked young as snap beans, allowed to mature further for flavorful fresh shell beans, or left to dry fully for a rich, hearty dry bean prized in Appalachian cooking. Pick regularly to keep vines productive over a long season, and let the last flush of pods dry on the vine if a dry bean harvest is wanted.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+), at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis, since Greasy Bean is a vigorous climber needing 6–8 feet of support.
directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young for snap beans or let pods mature for a rich, flavorful shelly or dry bean. Greasy Bean is a distinctive category of heirloom Appalachian pole bean named for the unusual smooth, glossy, almost oil-slicked appearance of the pods, which lack the fuzzy surface texture of most common beans — a trait that has made these beans prized heirlooms passed down through generations of mountain families in Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, and West Virginia, with many distinct named strains maintained within individual families. The tender, stringless pods have excellent flavor as snap beans when young, and the plump, flavorful seeds shell out well for cooking as a traditional Appalachian soup bean. Vigorous, productive vines reward a sturdy support and reliable moisture through the growing season. A true regional heirloom treasure for gardeners interested in Appalachian foodways, zone 4–10.

common_name: Greasy Cutshort Bean (Tightly-Packed Appalachian Heirloom Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 60°F; cutshort beans get their name from seeds packed so tightly inside the pod that the pod tip appears squared off.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6-9 inches apart along a trellis or corn stalks. Greasy Cutshort combines two classic Appalachian heirloom bean traits in one variety: smooth, shiny, fuzz-free 'greasy' pods, and seeds packed so densely inside each pod that the tip is squared off rather than tapered, the 'cutshort' trait long selected for by mountain gardeners saving their own seed. The tender pods are good for snapping young, and the beans shell out well for a flavorful dry bean later in the season. Allow some pods to dry fully on the vine each year to save seed and maintain the strain.

plant_note: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained soil; Greasy Grits is a pole-type Appalachian heirloom needing a trellis, teepee, or corn stalks to climb.
directions: Sow seeds 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a sturdy trellis, pole, or teepee for the vigorous climbing vines; Greasy Grits is one of the many named strains of Appalachian greasy bean, so called for the smooth, shiny, almost oil-slick sheen on the pod surface caused by a lack of the fine fuzz found on most snap beans. Pods are stringless and tender when picked young for snapping, with a rich, savory flavor prized in traditional mountain cooking, and the plant can also be left to mature for shelling as a dry bean. Like other greasy beans it is a genuine landrace maintained by generations of Appalachian seed savers rather than a modern breeding-program release, so some variation between seed lots is normal and part of its heirloom character. Provide consistent moisture through pod set and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive over a long summer harvest window.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil; this variety tolerates heat and resists bolting.
directions: A crisp iceberg-type lettuce, this 1960s improvement over the original Great Lakes is notably heat tolerant and slow to bolt. Direct sow in cool soil and thin to about 12 inches so heads can fill out fully. Keep consistently watered to avoid bitterness and tip burn, since even moisture builds those firm, crunchy heads. Harvest when heads feel solid, and enjoy the cool crunch in salads and on sandwiches.

common_name: Great Lakes Iceberg Lettuce (AAS-Winning Original American Crisphead Lettuce)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; iceberg crisphead lettuce is challenging to grow in zone 9 because of the long time-to-maturity (82–90 days from transplant) and strict cool-temperature requirements. In zone 9, start seeds in August and transplant in October for a December–January harvest — the brief cool window in zone 9 is marginally adequate for iceberg if timing is precise. Iceberg lettuce heads only in cool temperatures: if warmth arrives before heading is complete, plants bolt to seed without forming the characteristic tight, firm head. Many zone 9 gardeners find that heat-tolerant romaine or butterhead types are more reliably productive than iceberg in zone 9 conditions.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to cool-season bed. Harvest when head is firm and compact. Great Lakes is the original American crisphead (iceberg) lettuce — developed by W.D. Blystone at the Michigan Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1941 (awarded All-America Selections in 1944), Great Lakes defined the iceberg lettuce type that became the dominant American commercial and restaurant lettuce through the mid-20th century. Before Great Lakes, commercial head lettuce was dominated by softer butterhead types; Great Lakes demonstrated that crisp, tight-heading lettuce could be grown reliably across a wider range of conditions and shipped the long distances needed for national distribution — characteristics that made it the foundation of the California iceberg lettuce industry that supplied American consumers coast-to-coast. The 'iceberg' name comes from the practice of shipping these firm-headed lettuces packed in ice during rail transport — an innovation in food distribution that made fresh lettuce available nationally for the first time. Great Lakes produces large (1.5–2 lb), very firm, round, pale-green to white-interior heads with the extreme crispness and mild flavor of the classic iceberg type. While largely replaced in commercial production by more uniform hybrid iceberg varieties, Great Lakes remains the reference open-pollinated iceberg for home garden and seed-saving use.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost when soil is warm; Great Northern is a bush-type dry bean that requires a warm growing season to dry properly. In zone 9 plant in spring for early summer harvest; the plants will decline in midsummer heat, so spring planting is preferable to early summer.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Great Northern is the most widely grown white dry bean in the United States, a medium-large, oval, white-seeded bush-type bean with mild, creamy flavor and a tender skin that cooks quickly — the standard white bean for baked beans, soups, and casseroles in American cooking. Developed in the northern Great Plains, it matures in 70–85 days and stores indefinitely as a dry bean. More delicate in flavor than navy beans and larger in size, making it the preferred choice for premium baked bean recipes and New England-style preparations where the bean is the star. Harvest by pulling entire plants when most pods are dry and golden; dry in a warm, airy location and thresh to remove seeds. Great Northern beans are nutritionally excellent, high in protein and fiber.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, chalky or loamy soil in full sun; great pignut is a perennial carrot-family plant from the chalk grasslands and limestone slopes of Mediterranean Europe — producing edible, round, chestnut-like tubers 1–2 inches across with a sweet, hazelnut-chestnut flavor eaten raw or cooked — a wild food delicacy of European hedgerows and calcareous grasslands.
directions: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, chalky or loamy soil in full sun; harvest tubers in autumn when the feathery tops die back; difficult to cultivate commercially but rewarding in wild-style gardens. Bunium bulbocastanum (great pignut, earth chestnut, or ground chestnut) is a perennial carrot-family (Apiaceae) plant native to the chalk downs, limestone grasslands, and open woodland edges of southern and central Europe — from England and France south to the Mediterranean basin and Turkey. The plant produces feathery, finely-cut, carrot-like leaves above ground and a remarkable underground structure: a round, swollen tuber (1–2 inches diameter) with a thin brown skin and white, crisp, starchy flesh. The flavor is one of the most pleasant of any wild edible root: sweet, mild, and distinctly reminiscent of a blend of chestnut and hazelnut, with a crisp, juicy texture when fresh — eaten raw, cooked in stews, or roasted. 'Earth chestnut' and 'ground chestnut' both describe the remarkable resemblance of the flavor to chestnuts. In European wild food foraging, great pignut is one of the most highly regarded finds; in cultivation, it is challenging because it dislikes transplanting and requires lean, calcareous, well-drained soils. Distinct from Bunium persicum (black cumin, kala jeera), which is valued for its seeds rather than roots.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March for a spring crop. Great White is indeterminate and requires staking or caging. The white-skinned fruits can be difficult to judge for ripeness by color change — look for a subtle cream to ivory-yellow blush and a slight softening of the fruit. In zone 9 the fall planting in August often produces the finest-flavored fruits as cooler temperatures reduce stress.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy cage or stake support; Great White is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing fruits that ripen to an unusual cream-white to pale ivory-yellow color — one of the most distinctive-appearing heirloom tomatoes in any garden collection. The color difference from standard red tomatoes stems from the absence of normal red lycopene pigments: Great White produces primarily colorless carotenoids that result in the pale white-cream skin and flesh. The flavor is extraordinarily mild, sweet, and very low in acid — often described as honey-sweet with almost no tartness, making it popular for people who find acidic tomatoes hard to digest. The thick, very meaty flesh with small seed cavities makes Great White outstanding for fresh eating and mild salsas where a lower-acid tomato flavor is preferred. The pale color also makes it a striking visual contrast element in colorful heirloom tomato salads alongside red, purple, orange, and yellow varieties.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost once nights stay warm.
directions: This rare heirloom beefsteak produces creamy pale fruits of one to two pounds with sweet, low-acid, almost tropical flavor. Start seed indoors about six weeks before transplanting, then set hardened plants deep into rich, warm soil. As an indeterminate vine, it benefits from sturdy staking or caging and consistent watering to prevent cracking. Harvest when the pale fruits take on a faint blush and yield slightly to gentle pressure.

plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked; a short trellis helps.
directions: A productive heirloom shelling pea whose sweet green peas fill pods set in pairs atop compact 28-inch plants for easy harvesting. Direct sow several weeks before the last frost as soon as the soil is workable, and give the vines a short trellis or netting. Keep the soil cool and moist and pick pods when plump but still bright green. Excellent for fresh eating and freezing.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 60°F; beans rot in cold, wet soil, so waiting for warm soil is more important than planting as early as possible. Succession-sow every 2–3 weeks for a continuous harvest.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 60°F — inoculating seeds with rhizobium bacteria before planting improves nitrogen fixation and yields in soils where beans have not grown before; beans rot in cold, wet soil so waiting for warmth is essential. Bush beans form compact plants and produce all at once (60 days) while pole beans require a trellis and produce continuously over a longer season (65–80 days). Harvest green beans when pods are firm, snap crisply, and seeds inside are just beginning to swell — overmature pods become tough and stringy. Succession-sow every 2–3 weeks for a steady supply throughout summer. Avoid working in the bean patch when plants are wet to prevent spreading bacterial diseases.

plant_note: Easy brassica microgreen; sow densely and blackout two to three days.
directions: Spread cabbage seed thickly over a moist tray and cover for the first two or three days to draw the seedlings up evenly. Uncover once the stems have lengthened and give bright light to keep them stocky and green. Maintain steady moisture and light airflow to fend off damping-off. Harvest the crisp, mildly sweet shoots at the cotyledon stage in eight to ten days.

plant_note: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, since it tolerates light frost and even improves in flavor after cool weather.
directions: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, since it tolerates light frost and even improves in flavor after cool weather, or sow in early spring for a summer crop. A French heirloom frisée-type endive named for the town of Ruffec, it is prized for its finely dissected, deeply curled dark-green leaves and notable cold hardiness compared to other curly endives. Traditionally the outer leaves are gathered and tied to blanch the heart, producing the pale, tender center prized in French bistro salads.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant while weather is still cool; also good for a fall crop.
directions: A quick-growing miniature cabbage forming 5 to 6 inch heads of 2 to 3 pounds, ready in as little as 50 days. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before setting out, then transplant while temperatures remain cool. The small heads suit container and raised-bed gardens; space them a bit tighter than full-size cabbage. Keep evenly watered and harvest promptly once heads firm up to avoid splitting.

common_name: Green Glaze Collard (Waxy Insect-Resistant Heirloom Collard)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Green Glaze's thick, waxy cuticle deters cabbage worms and other leaf-chewing pests better than most collard varieties.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Green Glaze is a Southern heirloom collard, prized among organic growers for its thick, glossy, cabbage-like leaf surface that gives noticeably better natural resistance to cabbage worms, loopers, and flea beetles than standard collard varieties, reducing the need for pest control sprays. The tall, vigorous plants produce large, tender leaves with good flavor over a long cut-and-come-again harvest season, and cold exposure sweetens the flavor further, as with other collards. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season, and although the glossy leaves offer real pest resistance, monitor young transplants closely, since seedlings are more vulnerable before the waxy cuticle fully develops.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Green Glaze's waxy, glossy leaf coating gives it unusually strong resistance to cabbage worms and other leaf-feeding pests.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Green Glaze is a Southern heirloom collard distinguished by unusually smooth, thick, glossy, jade-green leaves with a waxy cuticle that makes it noticeably more resistant to cabbage worms, cabbage loopers, and other leaf-chewing pests than standard fuzzy-leaved collard varieties, an especially useful trait for organic growers. The flavor is mild and sweet for a collard, and the smooth leaf texture that deters pests also makes the leaves pleasant for fresh use in wraps as well as traditional slow-cooked greens. Like other collards it tolerates both summer heat and considerable cold, with flavor sweetening noticeably after the first light frosts of fall. Harvest outer leaves as needed and the plant continues producing new growth from the top through a long cool-season harvest window.

plant_note: Start indoors early; chilling young plants encourages first-year budding.
