directions: This heirloom perennial grows into a bold 4 to 6 foot plant producing large green buds tipped with light purple. Start seed indoors early and give young plants a cool period, which helps them form buds in the first season. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil with steady moisture and ample space for the architectural foliage. Harvest buds while tight and firm before the scales open; in mild zones the plants return and yield for several years.

scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Green Globe Improved'
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant when 8–10 inches tall. In zone 9 plant transplants in February–March or divisions in fall. Vernalization (exposure to temperatures below 50°F for several weeks) stimulates the first-year flowering that produces edible buds — in zone 9, the mild winters naturally provide this, and the plants flower each spring from February through May. After harvest, cut plants back by half in late spring and they will resprout for a fall secondary harvest in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Green Globe Improved is the primary commercial artichoke variety grown in California's Monterey County — the heart of American artichoke production — and the selection standard against which most other artichoke varieties are measured. The large, globe-shaped, tightly-closed heads of deep green overlapping bracts contain the edible fleshy bract bases and the prize, the meaty, tender artichoke heart at the center. The 'Improved' designation indicates a more consistent, uniform selection with better vigor than the original Green Globe. In zone 9, artichoke is particularly well-adapted — the mild winters provide the natural vernalization required to initiate bud production, and the plants can persist for 5–8 years as perennial specimens if given adequate space and annual fertilization. Zone 9's long growing season supports two harvesting periods: the main spring crop (February–May) and a secondary fall crop (September–October) after the summer regrowth period.

plant_note: Start indoors very early; can be grown as an annual with proper vernalization.
directions: An improved Green Globe with more uniform plants, fewer spines, and better production, allowing artichokes even in northern gardens grown as an annual. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, and expose young plants to a few weeks of cool temperatures to trigger budding. Give each plant plenty of room and rich, well-drained soil. Expect 3 to 5 tender buds per plant; harvest while the scales are still tight.

common_name: Green Goliath Broccoli (Large-Head Side-Shooting Heirloom Broccoli)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Green Goliath produces a large central head followed by prolific side shoots that continue for weeks after the main head is harvested. In zone 9, transplant August–September for November–January harvest. For spring production, start indoors January–February and transplant when temperatures allow — spring-harvested broccoli is excellent in the Gulf South before temperatures rise.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil with good calcium availability. Harvest the central head while florets are still tight and before the head begins to open or yellow; side shoots will continue for 4–6 weeks. Green Goliath is an open-pollinated broccoli that produces large central heads — typically 8–10 inches across and 1–2 lbs — with the classic well-domed, dark green form that represents the traditional ideal of quality broccoli. The 'goliath' name refers to the head size: substantially larger central heads than many modern hybrid varieties that have been bred for smaller, more uniform heads suited to commercial harvest. After the central head is harvested, Green Goliath produces abundant and persistent side shoots — small 2–4 inch heads — that continue for 4–6 weeks, extending the productive season significantly beyond a single harvest. The side-shooting characteristic makes Green Goliath particularly valuable for home gardeners who want an extended harvest rather than a single concentrated yield. The open-pollinated status means seed can be saved from year to year, making it a popular choice for seed savers and those interested in maintaining productive self-sustaining vegetable gardens. Very good flavor at both the head and side-shoot stages.

common_name: Green Grape Tomato (Sweet Amber-Green Cherry Tomato that Ripens Green)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Green Grape is an indeterminate open-pollinated cherry tomato that retains green color at maturity, ripening to an amber-green with a slight golden blush when fully ripe. The key challenge for new growers is learning to identify ripe fruits by feel and slight color shift rather than waiting for red coloration that will never arrive. When fully ripe, Green Grape fruits yield slightly to gentle pressure and develop a translucent quality that distinguishes them from the opaque green of an immature tomato. In zone 9, transplant March–April; like all indeterminate types, Green Grape benefits from caging or staking to 5–6 feet and continues producing until heat stops fruit set in midsummer or until fall frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and cage or stake to 6 feet. Harvest when fruits yield to gentle pressure and show a slight translucent amber-green glow rather than the opaque dark green of unripe fruit. Green Grape Tomato is an open-pollinated cherry tomato variety that remains green at full maturity — a characteristic that surprises first-time growers accustomed to using color change as the primary ripeness cue. The variety was developed by Tim Peters of Peters Seed and Research in Oregon and introduced in the 1990s as part of a wave of interest in non-standard-colored tomatoes that offered novel flavors and visual interest compared to standard red types. Green Grape fruits are approximately 1 inch in diameter with a round to slightly oval shape and thin green skin that ripens to a yellow-green or amber-green with characteristic translucency at peak ripeness; experienced growers learn to identify this translucency as the reliable ripeness indicator. The flavor is notably sweet with a complex, slightly tropical undertone — a combination that many tasters find more interesting than the straightforward sweetness of yellow or red cherry types. The green color is not from chlorophyll retained past ripening but from specific chloroplast development patterns that persist through the normal ripening process; the fruit is fully ripe when the color reaches amber-green, not when it turns red. Fruits cluster in medium-sized trusses of 8–12 and tend to hold well on the vine for several days after reaching peak ripeness without cracking, which is an advantage for gardeners who can't harvest daily.

common_name: Green Ice Loose-Leaf Lettuce (Crinkled Glossy Heat-Tolerant Loose-Leaf Variety)
plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting; Green Ice is a loose-leaf type harvested as individual outer leaves (cut-and-come-again) or as whole young plants (baby leaf at 25–30 days, full plant at 45–55 days). In zone 9, sow September–November and February–March. Green Ice's glossy leaf surface is unusual among loose-leaf lettuces — the glossy texture reduces water evaporation and may contribute to the variety's better-than-average heat tolerance. The deep crinkle of the leaves gives Green Ice a distinctive appearance in the garden and in harvested mixes, and provides good texture contrast when mixed with smoother lettuces. One of the most productive loose-leaf varieties for baby leaf and cut-and-come-again harvesting.
directions: Scatter seeds 0.25 inch deep; thin to 6–9 inches for full plants or leave dense for baby leaf cut-and-come-again. Harvest outer leaves, leaving 4–5 inner leaves to continue growing. Green Ice is a loose-leaf lettuce with a distinctive appearance that sets it apart from other common loose-leaf varieties: the leaves are deeply frilled and crinkled — more so than standard looseleaf types — and have an unusual, almost waxy glossiness on the upper leaf surface that gives the fresh leaves a bright, polished look unlike any other commonly grown lettuce. The deep green color is vibrant and consistent, making Green Ice one of the most visually striking lettuces in garden displays, cut flower and produce market presentations, and harvested salad mixes. The flavor is mild, clean, and slightly sweet — typical of loose-leaf types, without the bitterness of romaine or the grassiness of some outer head leaves. Green Ice's combination of heat tolerance (better than most loose-leaf types), productivity in cut-and-come-again harvest systems, glossy visual appeal, and excellent shelf life after harvest has made it a popular variety with market gardeners and home growers seeking a reliable, attractive loose-leaf for continuous harvest through the cool seasons of zone 8–10.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil and thin to stand so the thick, tender flowering stalks can develop; also direct-sown in early spring after last frost.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil and thin to stand so the thick, tender flowering stalks can develop; Green Lance is a hybrid Chinese broccoli bred for better heat tolerance than older gai lan strains, letting it be sown over a longer window without bolting prematurely. Harvest the central stalk with its small cluster of unopened flower buds once it reaches pencil thickness, then continue cutting side shoots for several more weeks. The mildly bitter, broccoli-like stems and leaves are classically blanched and stir-fried with garlic and oyster sauce.

common_name: Green Light Cucumber (Seedless Snacking Cucumber, AAS Winner)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in warm soil; Green Light is an All-America Selections winner bred as a compact, high-yielding, seedless snacking cucumber that produces thin-skinned, burpless mini cucumbers without needing a pollinator, making it well suited to small gardens and containers.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the danger of frost has passed, or set out transplants, providing a small trellis or cage for the compact vines. Green Light was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining parthenocarpic (seedless, self-fruitful) fruit set with a compact plant habit and outstanding yield of crisp, thin-skinned, 4-5 inch mini cucumbers ideal for snacking whole or slicing. Because the plant sets fruit without pollination, it performs reliably even when bee activity is low and produces cucumbers with essentially no seed cavity or bitterness, with skin tender enough that peeling is unnecessary. The compact vines are well suited to small raised beds, large containers, and gardens with limited trellis space, and the plant's dense productivity means frequent picking — every one to two days once fruiting begins — keeps cucumbers at the ideal small size and encourages continued production through the season. Consistent watering during fruit development prevents bitterness and misshapen fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant, or grow as a fall crop in cool weather.
directions: This rare Italian heirloom forms vivid green curds with a mild, buttery flavor and reliable performance across seasons. Start seed indoors about six weeks ahead, then transplant into rich, evenly moist soil for uninterrupted growth. Consistent feeding and watering prevent stress that leads to loose or off-flavored heads. Cut heads while the green curds are still tight and firm for the best eating quality.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Green Machine is a market-grower favorite bred for heavy, sustained yields and strong disease tolerance, holding up well to the mosaic virus and powdery mildew pressure that builds quickly in Gulf South summer humidity.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Green Machine is a vigorous hybrid zucchini widely grown by market farmers for its exceptionally heavy, sustained yield and improved tolerance to common summer squash viruses, which spread fast via aphids in humid conditions and can quickly stunt and discolor fruit on less tolerant varieties. It produces uniform, dark green, cylindrical fruit on an open, upright bush habit that makes harvesting easy even as the plant fills out. Because it keeps producing healthy, well-colored fruit later into the season than many older zucchini varieties, it is a strong choice for gardeners who have struggled with virus or mildew cutting squash harvests short. Pick fruit at 6–8 inches for the best eating quality, checking plants daily during peak production since zucchini left on the plant quickly grows oversized and tough.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date; in zone 9 start in August and transplant September–October for fall broccoli harvest November–January. Green Magic is an F1 hybrid with excellent downy mildew resistance — important in zone 9's humid fall conditions. After cutting the central head, side shoots continue producing small florets for weeks. In zone 9 fall-planted broccoli produces much higher quality heads than spring plantings that must mature in warming spring weather.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Green Magic is an F1 hybrid broccoli producing well-domed, tightly beaded, medium-green central heads with excellent side-shoot production after the main head is harvested — extending the productive harvest period significantly beyond varieties that produce only a central head. The hybrid vigor produces uniformly sized plants and large, dense heads that reach harvest size in 60–70 days from transplant. Broccoli flavor is at its absolute best when grown to maturity in cool weather — the combination of cool nights (below 50°F) and cool days in fall and winter concentrates the sulfur-containing compounds responsible for broccoli's characteristic flavor while reducing the bitterness that heat stress introduces. Green Magic's F1 hybrid status provides disease resistance and uniformity that open-pollinated varieties often lack, making it one of the most reliable fall broccoli varieties for humid Gulf South conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is thoroughly warm; in zone 9 plant April–June. Green Malabar Spinach produces entirely green stems and foliage, lacking the ornamental purple-red stem color of the red form but otherwise identical in culture and culinary use. Provide a trellis, fence, or string support — the vines reach 6–10 feet in a full season. Harvest regularly by cutting stem tips 4–6 inches long to stimulate branching; regular harvesting keeps production high throughout the season. Soak seeds overnight before planting to improve germination, which can be slow and irregular.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Green Malabar Spinach is the all-green form of Basella alba, producing the same climbing vine, thick succulent leaves, and heat-tolerant growth habit as the red-stemmed form but with completely green stems, petioles, and developing berries. The green form is less ornamental than the red-stemmed type but produces the same culinary product — thick, glossy, succulent leaves with a mild, slightly mucilaginous flavor that makes an excellent heat-season substitute for true spinach (Spinacia oleracea) during zone 9's summers when cool-season spinach is impossible to grow. The green form's less distinctive appearance makes it blend more naturally into vegetable garden beds without the ornamental statement of the red-stemmed variety — a practical choice for gardeners who want the culinary benefit without the color drama. The slight mucilage in the leaves and stems — the same compound that gives okra its characteristic texture — naturally thickens soups, stews, and green smoothies and contributes a smooth, slightly viscous mouthfeel to cooked preparations. In zone 9's summer heat and humidity, Malabar spinach (both forms) is one of the most productive leafy green crops available.

common_name: Green Meat Radish (Green-Skinned, Green-Fleshed Asian Radish)
plant_note: Sow in early spring or, for the best size and flavor, as a late-summer crop timed to mature in cool fall weather, similar to daikon.
directions: Direct sow about half an inch deep in loose, well-worked soil, thinning seedlings to 4-6 inches apart; because the roots grow larger than a typical spring radish, deep, stone-free soil helps them develop a smooth, well-formed shape. Green Meat is prized in Chinese cuisine for its bright green skin and vivid green-and-white interior flesh, a striking contrast to the familiar red-skinned, white-fleshed Western radishes. It has a milder, sweeter flavor than most spring radishes and holds its crisp texture well, making it good raw in salads or lightly cooked. For the best size and flavor it is often grown as a late-summer to fall crop like daikon, though early spring sowing also works.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil has warmed past 65°F; this heirloom needs a full warm season to ripen and benefits from black plastic mulch or row cover in cooler climates to speed early growth.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in enriched, well-drained hills spaced a yard apart, keeping soil evenly moist until vines establish and then easing off water as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Green Nutmeg is a 19th-century American heirloom muskmelon named for its ribbed, netted rind, which resembles the wrinkled shell of a nutmeg seed and sets it apart from smoother-skinned melon types of the same era. The pale green flesh is notably sweet and aromatic for an old variety, ripening to a musky perfume that signals harvest readiness alongside the classic full slip from the vine. It is a good choice for gardeners wanting an old American melon type distinct from the many French and Charentais heirlooms already common in seed catalogs.

plant_note: Direct sow from 4 weeks before to the time of the last frost; succession sow every 3 weeks throughout the growing season.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in bands 3–4 in wide rather than single rows to maximize bed productivity. Thin seedlings to 1–2 in apart; the thinnings are already usable as tiny scallions. Water steadily to keep growth rapid and tender; drought causes tough, hot-tasting stems. Pull bunching types when stems reach pencil width, or cut leaves an inch above the base and allow them to regrow for a second harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring and fall; succession sow for a continuous supply.
directions: This AAS award-winning oakleaf-type lettuce produces frilly green leaves that stay sweet and tender even in warm weather. Direct sow seed shallowly and press lightly into moist soil, since lettuce needs light to germinate. Thin plants for full heads or harvest as loose-leaf, cut-and-come-again greens. More heat tolerant and slow to bolt than many lettuces, it extends the salad season with steady moisture and light afternoon shade in summer.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant for spring, or sow midsummer for fall.
directions: This traditional Italian heirloom is the familiar garden broccoli, producing large blue-green central heads followed by abundant side shoots. Start seed indoors about six weeks before transplanting into rich, firm soil. Keep water and nutrients steady, since stress can cause premature buttoning. Cut the main head while the buds are still tight, then keep harvesting the smaller side shoots for weeks of continued production.

common_name: Green Star Okra (High-Yield Compact Hybrid Okra for Commercial and Home Production)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to 70°F minimum; Green Star is a compact F1 hybrid okra variety with a shorter internode spacing (reduced distance between leaves and pod sets) than standard tall varieties, producing more pods per foot of plant height and remaining productive at 4–5 feet compared to standard varieties that can reach 8–10 feet. In zone 9, plant April through July for summer production. The compact plant habit of Green Star makes it easier to manage in home gardens and more efficient in raised-bed and small-garden situations where standard tall okra varieties would overgrow their space. Harvest pods at 3–4 inches — Green Star's pods stay tender at slightly larger sizes than some varieties due to its spineless, smooth pod texture. Regular harvesting (every 2–3 days at peak production) is essential to maintain pod quality and stimulate continued production.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches every 2–3 days. Green Star is an F1 hybrid okra variety selected for compact plant habit, high productivity per plant, and good pod quality — attributes that make it one of the more practical hybrid okra varieties for small-scale and home garden production in the Gulf South. The hybrid vigor of F1 varieties (first-generation crosses between distinct parental lines) typically produces improved uniformity, vigor, and productivity compared to open-pollinated varieties, and Green Star's compact growth habit — reaching 4–5 feet rather than the 6–10 feet of some tall heirloom types — makes it easier to harvest without a ladder and fits better in standard garden plots. The pods are dark green, slightly ridged in the standard okra style, spineless to low-spine (important for comfort in harvesting), and tender and good-flavored at the 3–4 inch harvest stage. Green Star's earliness — first harvest approximately 50–55 days from direct seeding — is competitive with the fastest-maturing okra varieties and allows harvest to begin before the peak of Gulf Coast summer heat. Okra is one of the most important and culturally significant vegetables in Gulf South cooking: a staple of gumbo (where it serves as a natural thickener via its mucilaginous properties), fried okra (a Southern culinary tradition), pickled okra, and fresh vegetable side dishes. Zone 9 is ideal for okra production — the combination of heat and humidity that limits most cool-season vegetables is precisely what okra requires to thrive.

common_name: Green Striped Cushaw (Heat-Tolerant Southern Cushaw Pumpkin, Gulf Coast Staple Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm (70°F); Green Striped Cushaw is a Cucurbita argyrosperma type — the cushaw species — which has significantly better heat and humidity tolerance than the Cucurbita maxima and C. pepo species, making it one of the most reliable winter-type squash for hot-summer zone 9 and tropical climates. In zone 9, plant April–June for summer production; the heat tolerance allows Cushaw to thrive through Gulf Coast summers that stress or kill other squash species. Fruits develop over 90–110 days and can be harvested young (summer squash stage) or left to mature fully for storage. The large vines (15+ feet) require substantial space. Cushaw's heat tolerance is legendary in Gulf South gardening circles — this is the squash that produces reliably when standard varieties have died from the summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in hills 5–6 feet apart after soil is warm; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin pattern develops full color and stem begins to dry. Green Striped Cushaw is the classic variety of Cucurbita argyrosperma — the cushaw species native to Mexico and Central America — that has been grown in the American South for centuries as one of the most heat-tolerant large squash available. The 'cushaw' name is of Native American origin and has been applied to this distinctive squash type in the South since colonial times. The Green Striped Cushaw produces large fruits (10–20 lbs) with a distinctive form: a rounded to oblong base swelling to a thick, curved neck — quite different from the globular or flattened form of most Cucurbita maxima pumpkins. The skin is cream-white with longitudinal green stripes that fade to tan-green at full maturity. The flesh is cream-yellow to pale orange, mild and sweet, with less of the rich pumpkin flavor of darker-fleshed types but with an important practical advantage: it is the squash that can be grown in zone 9's summer heat when virtually all other squash species have died. Cucurbita argyrosperma's heat and humidity tolerance is substantially greater than C. maxima, C. pepo, or C. moschata, and in the historical Gulf South kitchen, cushaw was the standard large winter-storage squash precisely because it produced reliably in the climate where other species failed. Cushaw's mild flesh is used in pies (a Southern tradition), as a cooked vegetable, and in Mexican and Central American cuisines where the species originated.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start December–January and transplant February–March. Green Thai Eggplant is exceptionally heat-tolerant and continues producing through zone 9 summer heat when other eggplant varieties slow. Multiple plantings (February and July) provide nearly year-round production in zone 9. Plants may survive mild winters in zone 9b as short-lived perennials and re-grow from the base.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with warm soil temperatures; Green Thai Eggplant produces small, round to oval, golf-ball-to-tennis-ball-sized fruits in bright green to greenish-white with striping or mottling, harvested young at marble to golf ball size for the best flavor and texture. The flesh is firmer, drier, and significantly more bitter than standard globe eggplant — the characteristic bitterness and firm texture are intentional qualities in Thai and Southeast Asian cooking, where the small green eggplants are sliced and added raw to green curry pastes or braised whole in red curry. They absorb coconut milk and spice sauces without becoming mushy, maintaining their distinctive firm bite even in extended cooking. Unlike the standard Italian or Japanese eggplants where bitterness is considered a defect, the natural bitterness of green Thai eggplant is a flavor feature that rounds and deepens the overall taste of Thai curries. In zone 9 the plants are extremely heat-tolerant and productive through the hottest months.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; the standard green heirloom tomatillo produces medium to large (1.5–2 inch) green to yellow-green fruits in papery husks and is the backbone of Mexican salsa verde, enchiladas verdes, and countless other dishes — plant at least two plants for cross-pollination.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil; stake or cage plants as they sprawl. Green tomatillo is the standard culinary tomatillo of Mexican cuisine — not a green tomato but a distinct species (Physalis ixocarpa) with a characteristic papery husk that expands around the developing fruit; fruits are harvested when the husk splits and the fruit fills it completely, at a bright green to yellow-green stage with a tangy, tart, citrus-herbal flavor that is distinctly different from any tomato flavor. The tart flavor of the fresh tomatillo is the foundation of salsa verde, a primary sauce in Mexican cooking alongside salsa roja; tomatillos are also used in mole verde, enchiladas verdes, chile verde, and canned as salsa. Highly productive and heat-tolerant; does extremely well in Gulf Coast and Southwestern gardens. Two or more plants are needed for pollination — a single plant produces little to no fruit.

subcategory: classic smooth dark green heirloom okra
plant_note: Direct sow 1-3 weeks after the last frost once the soil has warmed to at least 65F, since cold soil causes poor, uneven germination.
directions: Sow seed directly in the garden after all frost danger has passed, soaking it overnight to speed germination in warm soil. Pick pods every day or two once they begin forming, since Green Velvet quickly grows past its tender stage. This long-cultivated variety produces smooth, spineless, dark green pods on a vigorous, productive plant, and it has been a dependable garden staple for generations of Southern cooks who value its mild flavor in gumbo and frying. Its smooth pod surface also makes it easier to handle at harvest than spinier heirloom types.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall crop. Green Wave is cold-tolerant to about 15°F when established, making it one of the most cold-hardy mustards for Gulf Coast winters.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 12–18 inches; Green Wave is an AAS winner mustard green producing large, beautifully ruffled, deep green leaves with a distinctive curled and frilled edge that gives it strong ornamental value as well as excellent eating quality. Flavor is pungent and spicy like Southern Giant Curled but with finer leaf texture and more cold-hardiness. Green Wave is the recommended mustard green for raw use in salads (young leaves) and sautés where texture is prized; the intricate ruffling and curling increases leaf surface area, creating both a decorative appearance in the garden and a textural interest on the plate. In zone 9, fall-planted Green Wave produces beautifully through winter, the cold sweetening and mellowing its characteristic spicy bite — the finest mustard green eating comes after temperatures drop below 40°F. Harvest outer leaves regularly; the plant regrows vigorously. An excellent substitute for kale or collards in anyone who wants a faster-maturing, more flavorful cooking green.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant after frost and provide sturdy support for tall vines.
directions: A gourmet indeterminate tomato bearing smooth, crack-free 2 to 3 inch fruits striped golden green and forest green, with a slight amber blush when ripe. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply after the weather warms. Stake or cage the vigorous 6-foot-plus vines and prune suckers for airflow. Judge ripeness by softness and blush rather than color, since the fruit stays green when ready.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; ripeness is tricky to judge by appearance — harvest when the skin softens slightly, shows yellow-green stripes against deeper green, and gives to gentle pressure.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to deeply prepared, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Green Zebra is a modern heirloom tomato developed by Tom Wagner in 1983, producing attractive 2–3 inch fruits with distinctive lime-green skin and dark green stripes that warm to yellow-green stripes against chartreuse skin when ripe, with a bright, tangy, acidic flesh that is a refreshing counterpoint to sweeter tomatoes. Excellent sliced fresh in salads, as a garnish, or for green salsa — one of the most visually striking tomatoes available. An indeterminate vine, it tends toward compact growth relative to larger beefsteak heirlooms. Yields prolifically over a long season.

common_name: Green in the Snow Mustard (Xue Li Hong)
plant_note: Exceptionally cold-hardy; sow in late summer for a fall and winter harvest that survives frost and light snow, or in early spring for a quicker crop.
directions: This traditional Chinese mustard, known as xue li hong, meaning red amid the snow, is grown specifically for its ability to keep producing tender, deeply toothed serrated leaves through hard frosts and light snow cover. Direct sow into fertile soil in late summer for the best cold-season crop, harvesting leaves continually as a cut-and-come-again green. Leaves develop a purplish tinge and a distinctive sharp, mustardy tang in cold weather, and are traditionally salted or lightly fermented as a pickle as well as used fresh in soups and stir-fries. Its extreme hardiness makes it one of the last leafy greens standing in an unheated winter garden.

common_name: Greenleaf Desmodium (Mat-Forming Nitrogen-Fixing Tropical Forage Legume)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade; Greenleaf Desmodium is a trailing, mat-forming tropical legume grown as a warm-season nitrogen-fixing cover and forage crop, treated as an annual outside its perennial zone 9-11 range.
directions: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade, inoculating seed with an appropriate Rhizobium inoculant for best nodulation on new ground. Greenleaf Desmodium is a sprawling, mat-forming tropical legume long used across the tropics as a soil-building cover crop and high-protein grazing forage, spreading vigorously by trailing stems that root at the nodes to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover while fixing substantial atmospheric nitrogen. It is also a key component of push-pull intercropping systems, where its scent helps repel stem-boring pests from adjacent food crops while trapping and disrupting their reproduction, making it useful in integrated pest management as well as soil building. In the Gulf South it behaves as a warm-season annual, killed by the first hard frost, so plant after the soil has warmed and mow or till the residue under before fall planting to release its nitrogen back to the soil.

common_name: Gregori's Altai Tomato (Early Siberian Red Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; this early, cold-set variety can go into the ground as soon as night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F, giving a jump on the Gulf Coast spring crop before summer heat shuts down fruit set.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun once nights are reliably mild, staking the moderately vigorous indeterminate vine as it grows. Gregori's Altai is a Siberian heirloom from the Altai Mountains region prized for setting medium-large, four-inch, deep red fruit with a faint golden blush at the shoulders unusually early and even in the cool, fluctuating spring temperatures that stall most other beefsteaks. The rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor rivals much larger, later-maturing heirlooms, and the plant's tolerance for cool nights makes it an excellent first-wave spring tomato for Gulf Coast gardens that need to beat the arrival of intense summer heat. Keep watering even as fruit sizes up to avoid cracking on the thin, tender skin.

common_name: Gretel Eggplant (AAS-Winning White Mini Eggplant, Tender Bitter-Free Companion to Hansel)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Gretel is the white-fruited companion variety to Hansel (purple), both from PanAmerican Seed and both AAS winners in consecutive years. Gretel produces clusters of 3–4 inch white eggplants on the same compact (20–24 inch) upright bush plant. In zone 9, start seeds January–February for March–April transplanting. Gretel's most important characteristic beyond its striking pure-white color is the complete absence of bitterness — white eggplants generally lack the anthocyanins and related phenolic compounds responsible for bitterness in purple eggplants, and Gretel has been bred for minimal astringency and very sweet, mild flavor. The flesh is tender and creamy-white with minimal seeds at proper harvest size (3–4 inches); left to overripen, the skin yellows and seeds increase. Unlike purple eggplants that can turn bitter when cut and exposed to air, Gretel's white flesh remains stable. Harvest before any yellowing appears on the skin.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 3–4 inches while skin is pure white; yellowing indicates overripeness. Gretel Eggplant won the All-America Selections award in 2009, one year after its companion Hansel (purple mini eggplant), both from the same PanAmerican Seed breeding program and sharing the same compact plant habit, prolific cluster fruiting, early maturity, and exceptional eating quality. Gretel's white fruit color distinguishes it visually and culinarily from standard purple eggplants: the white coloration (caused by the absence of the anthocyanin and chlorogenic acid pigments present in purple eggplant skin) correlates with a fundamentally different flavor profile — white eggplants, including Gretel, are consistently sweeter, milder, and less bitter than purple varieties because they lack the phenolic compounds that contribute bitterness. This means white eggplant varieties like Gretel can be used raw in preparations where purple eggplant's bitterness would require salting to draw out (a traditional technique for reducing eggplant bitterness before cooking): Gretel's naturally sweet, mild flesh is pleasant raw in thin slices or cubed in salads. The AAS recognition of Gretel in consecutive years with Hansel highlighted the appeal of offering home gardeners a white-fruited alternative to the standard purple that combined the same outstanding productivity and compact habit with meaningfully different flavor characteristics. For zone 9 gardeners growing multiple eggplant varieties for culinary diversity, Gretel and Hansel planted together provide a visually striking paired harvest of white and purple mini eggplants from compact, easily managed plants.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil is warm; tolerates heat well.
directions: This heat-tolerant heirloom produces smooth, straight fruits with mottled silver-grey skin on compact, heavy-yielding bush plants. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and space plants for good airflow. Water at the base to keep foliage dry and harvest fruits young, around six to eight inches, for tender flesh. Pick frequently during the peak of summer, as fruits size up quickly and steady harvest sustains production.

common_name: Griselle Shallot (French Grey Shallot, True Shallot)
plant_note: Plant small bulbs four to eight weeks before the last frost in spring; Griselle, the true French grey shallot, is grown from bulb divisions rather than seed and does not store as long as red or Dutch yellow shallot types.
directions: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep and four to six inches apart in loose, well-drained soil, and each will multiply into a cluster of several new bulbs by midsummer. Griselle is regarded by French cooks as the only true shallot, a distinct species from common onion-derived shallots, forming small, teardrop-shaped bulbs under a papery grey-brown skin around pinkish flesh with fine purple veining and an intensely complex, refined flavor prized raw in vinaigrettes and salads. Reduce watering once the tops yellow and topple over, then lift the cluster and cure it in a warm, airy, shaded spot for one to two weeks. Because Griselle does not keep as long as red or Dutch yellow shallots, plan to use the harvest within a few months or replant a portion of the smaller bulbs the following season.

common_name: Groninger Blue Kale (Dutch Heirloom Feathery Kale)
plant_note: Sow in mid to late summer, 10-14 weeks before the first fall frost, for a fall and winter harvest after cold sweetens the leaves.
directions: Direct sow in mid-summer and thin to wide final spacing so plants can develop their large, sprawling frames before winter sets in. This traditional Dutch farmhouse kale, long grown around the province of Groningen, produces finely divided, feathery blue-green leaves on tall stems and was historically a winter storage vegetable harvested straight from the frozen garden. Repeated frost exposure noticeably mellows its flavor, and the plant continues producing new leaves from the top through much of the winter.

plant_note: Start indoors well before the last frost; transplant only after soil has warmed.
directions: This heirloom Physalis produces small golden fruits inside papery, lantern-like husks with a sweet pineapple-vanilla flavor. Start seeds indoors six to eight weeks before your last frost and set out sprawling plants once nights stay warm. Fruits are ripe when the husks turn tan and drop naturally to the ground, so harvest from the soil below the plant. Let them cure a few days in their husks to develop full sweetness for fresh eating or preserves.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost in warm (70–80°F) conditions; transplant after all frost danger passes. In zone 9, plant in fall for a winter crop — ground cherry performs as a cool-season vegetable in the Gulf Coast South where it fruits prolifically through winter and spring before summer heat causes decline.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; ground cherry is an often-overlooked member of the Physalis family closely related to the tomatillo, producing small, marble-sized golden-yellow fruit enclosed in papery tan husks like a miniature tomatillo. The flavor is remarkable — simultaneously sweet, tropical, and slightly vanilla-like, unlike any other common garden vegetable. The plants are bushy and sprawling, reaching 2–3 feet high, and produce prodigiously once established. Fruit drops to the ground when ripe (hence the name), where it can be left in its husk for several weeks without deteriorating. Eat fresh, bake in desserts, make preserves, or dry for extended storage. In zone 9, treat as a cool-season annual planted in fall for winter through spring production. The husk protects the fruit from pests and makes storage easy. Self-seeds prolifically in warm soils and will naturalize in suitable areas. Not to be confused with the cape gooseberry (Physalis peruviana), though they are closely related.

common_name: Ground Elder (Goutweed, Bishop's Weed, Herb Gerard)
plant_note: CAUTION — ground elder is one of the most aggressive garden weeds in North America and Europe; once established it is nearly impossible to eradicate; only plant in buried containers or completely isolated beds, and choose the variegated form 'Variegatum' which is less invasive.
directions: Plant only in buried containers with solid bottoms, or in walled raised beds with no soil contact — ground elder spreads by deeply rooted, tenacious rhizomes that regenerate from small fragments and are nearly impossible to eradicate once established in open soil. Despite this invasive tendency, it is a genuinely useful shade edible: young spring leaves have a pleasant, lightly celery-like, slightly peppery flavor and have been eaten across Europe and Asia since medieval times, used in salads, soups, and as a potherb. The variegated form 'Variegatum' with cream-edged leaves is less vigorous and a better garden choice. For foragers, it is easily identified in spring before any other look-alikes emerge.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, loamy to rocky, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; ground plum has a deep taproot that makes it drought tolerant but very difficult to transplant — sow directly in its permanent location.
directions: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — ground plum is a native sprawling legume of the southern Great Plains and central prairies, historically one of the most important native edible plants of the southern prairie, producing clusters of purple to reddish-purple pea flowers in April–May followed by the remarkable, plum-like fruit pods — green when young, reddish when ripe — that gave the plant its common name. The young, unripe pods have a mild, slightly sweet, pea-like flavor and were eaten raw by Plains peoples as a seasonal vegetable and green snack food on the prairie. The pods are edible raw when fully green and firm, but become papery when ripe. An important nitrogen-fixing prairie legume that improves soil for neighboring plants. Outstanding for prairie restoration plantings in well-drained, alkaline, or rocky soils in zone 3–9.

plant_note: Plant small tubers 2–3 inches deep in spring after last frost; provide a trellis or fence for the twining stems. Tubers from the previous year planted in spring produce the largest harvest in fall.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near a support for the twining stems; this native leguminous vine was a staple food for many Indigenous nations and early European settlers and was considered for commercial cultivation before potatoes became dominant. Harvest the small, walnut-shaped tubers strung along underground rhizomes in fall after frost kills the vines; they taste like a richer, nuttier potato and can be boiled, baked, or roasted. The fragrant reddish-purple flowers in midsummer fix atmospheric nitrogen. Tubers are small in the first year but grow larger each subsequent year — the plant becomes more productive the longer it is left undisturbed.

plant_note: Sow in midsummer (July in most climates) for a spring harvest; the plants survive winter and produce their distinctive rosette heads in early spring from the overwintered root. In zone 9, sow September–October for harvest in January–March.
directions: Sow seeds in late summer and allow plants to grow through autumn; after hard frosts, the tops die back and the plant enters semi-dormancy before the root drives up a tight, flat rosette of dark green leaves in late winter or early spring — a delicacy treasured in northern Italy as a salad green when little else is available. The name 'grumolo' means 'little cluster' in Italian, describing the compressed button-rosette form. Grumolo verde is exceptionally cold-hardy and virtually maintenance-free through winter. The bitter, nutty flavor is characteristic of chicory; young spring leaves are the most tender and least bitter. In warm-winter climates like zones 8–9, the plants may not go fully dormant but still produce acceptable rosettes in winter.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; a widely used dried Mexican chile that requires a long warm season — ideal for zone 8–11 where it can produce two harvests in warm years.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost, harden transplants thoroughly, and plant into warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil after all frost risk has passed. Guajillo is one of the most commonly used dried chiles in traditional Mexican cooking, the dried form of the Mirasol pepper, producing long (3–5 inch), tapered, shiny red fruits with smooth, thin skin that dries to a deep red-brown; heat is mild to medium (2,500–5,000 SHU). The distinctive sweet, tangy, slightly fruity flavor with mild heat makes guajillo an indispensable base for authentic red enchilada sauce, pozole rojo, and adobo marinades. Harvest fully red and dry slowly on the plant or by hanging in a warm, ventilated space; dried guajillos store for 6–12 months.

common_name: Guatemalan Blue Banana Squash (Slate-Blue Elongated Heirloom Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills once soil has warmed after last frost; give vines a lot of open ground or a sturdy trellis since fruits can run two feet or more.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep after the soil has thoroughly warmed, since this Guatemalan heirloom needs a long, hot growing season to fill out its elongated, club-shaped fruit. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so allow generous room or train them up a strong trellis to keep the two-to-three-foot fruits off wet ground. The thin, slate-blue to gray-blue rind hides deep orange, dense, sweet flesh that is excellent baked, and well-cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot. Cure harvested squash in a warm location for one to two weeks before moving to long-term storage to firm the rind and concentrate sweetness.

common_name: Guelph Millennium Asparagus (High-Yield Cold-Hardy All-Male Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant 1-year-old crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench in early spring; Guelph Millennium breaks dormancy a bit later than older varieties, which helps it dodge late spring frosts, and it establishes an unusually dense, productive root system over its first two non-harvest years.
directions: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared, well-drained trench in full sun, and resist harvesting at all during the first year to let the fern grow and build root reserves. Guelph Millennium is an all-male hybrid developed at the University of Guelph in Ontario and has become the standard replacement for the older Jersey series across much of North America, valued for exceptionally high, concentrated spear yield, uniform smooth green spears with tight tips, and a root system that establishes unusually quickly for a full-sized harvest by year three. Its later spring emergence than most varieties is an advantage in regions with unpredictable late frosts, since fewer emerging spears are lost to cold snaps. Harvest lightly in year two, moderately in year three, and the full six-to-eight-week season from year four onward, snapping or cutting spears at soil level once they reach 6–8 inches.

plant_note: Sow directly as early as the ground can be worked, using fresh seed since parsnip germination declines quickly with seed age.
directions: An old Channel Islands and northern French heirloom parsnip valued for its shorter, broad-shouldered roots, a useful trait in shallow or stony soils where long-rooted parsnip types tend to fork or stall. Sow directly as early as the ground can be worked, using fresh seed since parsnip germination declines quickly with seed age. The dense white flesh has the classic sweet, nutty parsnip character and improves further after exposure to autumn frost, making it best left in the ground and dug through fall and early winter.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Guinea millet thrives on poor, marginal soils and matures quickly, traditionally valued as a fast emergency crop during lean growing seasons.
directions: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Guinea millet thrives on poor, marginal soils and matures quickly, traditionally valued as a fast emergency crop during lean growing seasons. Grown across the West African savanna, this small-grained cereal grass produces edible seed on slender panicles in a remarkably short season, earning it the common name 'hungry rice' for its traditional role as a fast-maturing food source that could be harvested before other slower crops during periods of food scarcity. It tolerates poor, sandy soils and limited rainfall better than most cereal grains, making it valuable in marginal growing conditions where more demanding crops fail, though the small grain size means threshing and hulling by hand is labor-intensive. Hand-harvest seed heads once dry, and thresh and winnow to separate the small grains before cooking as a rice or couscous substitute.

common_name: Gulf Annual Ryegrass (Fast-Establishing Gulf Coast-Bred Italian Ryegrass)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall into well-drained soil in full sun; Gulf is a Gulf Coast-bred annual ryegrass cultivar selected for rapid germination and vigorous establishment, commonly overseeded on dormant warm-season lawns and pastures across the Deep South.
directions: Broadcast seed onto well-drained, average soil in full sun in fall, raking lightly to ensure good seed-to-soil contact. Gulf is a fast-germinating, vigorous annual ryegrass cultivar developed for the humid, mild-winter conditions of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, where it is widely used to overseed dormant bermudagrass and bahiagrass lawns and pastures for winter green cover, as well as as a general-purpose erosion-control and biomass cover crop on bare fall ground. Its fibrous, shallow root system germinates and establishes faster than most other cool-season cover crops, quickly stabilizing loose or eroding soil and suppressing winter weeds, then dies back naturally with warming spring temperatures or can be mowed and turned under to add organic matter ahead of spring planting. It tolerates close, repeated mowing better than cereal grains, making it a good choice where winter foot traffic or turf appearance matters.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Gypsy's earlier maturity (60–70 days) compared to bell peppers (70–80 days) gives zone 9 gardeners an earlier start on sweet pepper harvest.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Gypsy is an All-America Selections winner (1981) — a sweet, elongated, tapering pepper that produces medium-sized (4 inches long, 2.5 inches wide), semi-thick-walled fruits that ripen through a distinctive color progression from pale creamy-yellow, through orange, to bright red, with excellent flavor at every stage. The early maturity (60–70 days) gives Gypsy a head start on the sweet pepper season compared to larger bell types, and the disease resistance package includes tobacco mosaic virus tolerance — a significant advantage. Gypsy is a semi-sweet, elongated type rather than a classic blocky bell — closer to an Italian frying pepper shape but with thicker walls and a sweeter, less pungent flavor than traditional frying types. The elongated fruits are outstanding for fresh eating, stuffing (the tapering shape holds stuffings differently than blocks), grilling, and roasting. The color progression from pale yellow through orange to red creates an attractive multi-colored harvest display when fruits at different maturity stages are present on the plant simultaneously. Plants are productive, compact, and well-suited to both spring and fall production in zone 9. An outstanding early-maturing sweet pepper for home garden use.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is reliably above 65°F, or start indoors 3–4 weeks earlier in peat pots for a head start; Ha'Ogen thrives in the long, hot Gulf South summer but needs steady moisture through fruit set. In zone 9, plant March–April for a June–July harvest and consider a fall crop in late July for October picking.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after danger of frost has passed, thinning to the strongest 2 plants per hill once true leaves appear. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and fruit set, then taper watering in the final week to concentrate sugars, and harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine with a full, sweet aroma at the blossom end. Ha'Ogen is a kibbutz-bred Israeli heirloom named for Kibbutz HaOgen, prized for its compact 2–3 lb round fruit with lightly netted, gold-green rind that streaks orange as it ripens, enclosing pale green flesh with an intensely sweet, spicy-floral flavor reminiscent of Charentais melons. Because it slips clean from the vine at peak ripeness rather than holding firm like shipping cantaloupes, it is best suited to home gardens and farmers markets rather than long-distance transport. Vigorous, disease-tolerant vines produce heavily over a relatively short window, so successive plantings extend the harvest.

plant_note: Start indoors early with strong bottom heat; transplant only after nights are warm.
directions: An intensely hot pepper prized for its fruity aroma as much as its fire, said to be many times hotter than a jalapeno. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost with warmth around 85F for even germination. Transplant into a warm, sunny spot after nights stay above 55F, and mulch to keep roots evenly moist. Wear gloves when picking and processing the ripe orange fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost due to the long growing season; transplant 2 weeks after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and maintain soil temperature at 85–90°F to achieve reliable germination, as Capsicum chinense species are notably slow to sprout. Transplant into the warmest, most sheltered spot in the garden once conditions are fully settled. Consistent feeding with a potassium-rich fertilizer during fruiting will maximize yields. Harvest when fruits reach their characteristic orange or red color and feel firm; handle with gloves due to extreme capsaicin levels.

plant_note: Hairy bittercress is primarily harvested as a foraged weed that appears in garden beds in early spring and fall; if growing intentionally, direct sow in late summer or early fall in moist, shaded, or partly shaded soil. Harvesting small plants before they flower keeps the bed clean while providing fresh greens.
directions: Harvest young plants from shaded garden beds and pathways in late winter through early spring when they appear as small rosettes; hairy bittercress is a widespread annual or overwintering weed of gardens, nurseries, and cultivated ground throughout North America that is almost universally underappreciated as food. The small, watercress-like leaves have a pleasant, sharp, peppery flavor exactly like watercress and can be eaten raw in salads, added to sandwiches, or used as a garnish — ideally harvested before the white flowers open when flavor is best. The spring-loaded seed capsules shatter explosively when ripe, scattering seeds widely; harvesting before flowering prevents this and gives you both the greens and a cleaner garden. An excellent early-spring foraged green requiring no cultivation whatsoever.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring crop; in zone 9 the ideal window is January–February for spring and September–November for fall, when mild temperatures produce the sweetest roots. Fall crops are typically superior in taste and texture.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-prepared, loosened soil and thin to 3–4 inches apart; crowding produces forked or stunted roots. Hakurei is a Japanese F1 hybrid turnip bred to be eaten raw: the pure-white, smooth globe roots (2–3 inches in diameter at harvest) are remarkably sweet, mild, and almost fruity — nothing like the sharp, peppery flavor of conventional turnip varieties. Unlike storage turnips, Hakurei is best harvested small and young; roots toughen and lose their fresh crispness if left past 2 inches. The greens are also tender and mild and excellent raw or lightly sautéed. In zone 9, fall-sown Hakurei seeded in October is often the finest salad turnip in the cool-season garden, maturing just before the holidays. A favorite for farmers' market growers because of its eye-catching appearance and reliably sweet flavor.

common_name: Hale's Best Cantaloupe (Classic California Heirloom, Sweet Orange-Flesh Standard Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F); in zone 9, plant April–May. Melons need full sun, warm soil, and consistent moisture from transplant through fruit development. Hale's Best develops fruits 5–7 inches in diameter on trailing vines 4–6 feet long. Detect harvest maturity by smell (strong sweet melon aroma from the blossom end), the fruit slipping slightly from the vine, and the underlying skin color shifting from white-green to creamy yellow. In the Gulf South, mildew can affect melon foliage by late summer; early planting for a June harvest before peak humidity helps maintain plant health. In zone 9's hot, dry springs (before the summer humidity builds), melons are ideally suited — the combination of heat and adequate moisture produces the sugar development that distinguishes a good cantaloupe from a bland one.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills 3–4 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when slip from vine and fragrant. Hale's Best is the quintessential American heirloom cantaloupe — a variety that defined the flavor standard of what a good cantaloupe should taste like for generations of American home gardeners and market growers. The variety was developed in the early 20th century by Paul Halladay of Turlock, California, from melon seed brought from Japan, and selected specifically for shipping quality, flavor, and thick, deeply netted skin. The resulting variety — medium to large, round to slightly oval, covered in a thick network of raised tan netting over a gray-green background, with a heavily perfumed blossom end and deeply orange, very sweet flesh — became so widely grown in California's San Joaquin Valley melon production region that 'Hale's Best' essentially defined the commercial cantaloupe market in mid-20th-century America. The flesh is thick, dense, and intensely orange — higher in beta-carotene than pale-fleshed cantaloupe varieties — with genuine sweetness and the rich, complex melon aroma that distinguishes a truly good cantaloupe from a bland one. The Brix (sugar content) of properly grown, vine-ripened Hale's Best in warm conditions can reach 14–16, producing sweetness comparable to the best modern hybrid melons. Several numbered strains of Hale's Best were selected for regional performance: Hale's Best #36 and Hale's Best Jumbo are among the subvarieties that have remained in commerce through heirloom seed preservation.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors briefly to get a jump.
directions: A classic heirloom muskmelon with exceptionally sweet, thick-walled flesh and a small seed cavity, in 3 to 5 pound fruits. Direct sow two or three seeds per hill once soil warms past 70F and thin to the strongest plant. Water deeply while vines grow and fruit sizes up, then ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine and smells fragrant.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Hale's Best is a classic heirloom cantaloupe prized for exceptional sweetness, tender juicy flesh, and a small seed cavity that yields more edible fruit. Sow seeds in warm soil once frost has passed, giving vines several feet to sprawl. Water consistently while fruit develops, then ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the melon separates cleanly from the vine with a light pull.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; plant 4–5 seeds per hill 1 inch deep, thin to 2 strongest plants when 3 inches tall. In zone 9 plant March–April for summer harvest; Halona's short season (73–80 days) makes it one of the better choices for zone 9's limited spring melon window before extreme summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Halona is a 2015 All-America Selections Gold Medal winner cantaloupe — one of the most highly awarded AAS winners in recent years — developed for exceptional eating quality combined with early maturation and disease resistance. Halona produces medium-sized (4–5 pound), deeply netted, tan-skinned fruits with dense, deep orange flesh and exceptional sweetness (Brix 14–17°, very high for an open-pollinated type) with complex, honey-like flavor that compares to the finest specialty melons. The fruit set is consistent and the plants show resistance to powdery mildew — a significant disease in humid climates. Halona's early maturation (73–80 days) and compact vine habit make it suitable for small gardens and shorter growing seasons; two plants produce more than enough for a family. The small seed cavity and thick, firm flesh give excellent eating quality with no watery texture. Halona is the recommended first melon for new growers due to its reliable production, disease resistance, and superior flavor — and one of the best choices for zone 9 spring production where a short fruiting window requires a reliable early variety.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; the long growing season requires an early start and the slow germination period means pre-soaking seeds is beneficial.
directions: Soak seeds in warm water for 24 hours before sowing to improve germination; sow 1/4 inch deep in deeply loosened, stone-free soil in rows, as seeds germinate slowly and unevenly over 2–4 weeks. Thin seedlings to 6–8 inches apart once established; the flat-leaf parsley-like foliage is edible throughout the season as an herb. The ivory-white, parsnip-like root develops slowly all season and tastes like a concentrated, slightly sweet parsley-parsnip hybrid — exceptional in Central European soups and stews. Harvest in fall after light frost improves sweetness; roots left in the ground over winter in milder climates will re-sprout in spring but roots lose quality as the plant prepares to bolt.

common_name: Hannah Sweet Potato (White-Fleshed Dry-Type NCSU Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F; Hannah is a white-fleshed sweet potato that produces in approximately 90–100 days and is harvested before the first fall frost. In zone 9, set slips in late March through April for a July–September harvest; mulch beds to conserve moisture and suppress weeds through the hot summer growing period.
directions: Plant rooted slips after last frost when soil is above 65°F, setting each slip 3–4 inches deep with the crown at or just above soil level; Hannah is a white-fleshed, cream-to-tan skinned sweet potato developed by North Carolina State University that has become one of the most popular white-fleshed varieties in US production — offering a substantially different culinary experience than the familiar orange-fleshed types. The flesh is cream to pale ivory, firm, and notably dry (less moist than orange varieties), with a mild, subtly sweet flavor that reads more like a russet potato than a typical sweet potato — making Hannah uniquely versatile for preparations like roasted potato dishes, gratins, soups, and anywhere a firm, dry-textured potato is preferred. The dry, non-gummy texture means it mashes cleanly, holds together in casseroles, and is excellent when baked whole with a crisp skin. Hannah produces smooth-skinned, uniform tubers in a standard 90–100 day window and yields reliably in Southern and Gulf Coast production areas. For gardeners familiar only with orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, Hannah represents a practical bridge variety that can replace russet potatoes in the garden while still being a true sweet potato culturally and agronomically.

common_name: Hanover Salad Green (Colonial-Era Southern Heirloom Salad Green)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall as temperatures moderate, or in very early spring, and thin seedlings to stand a few inches apart for continuous cut-and-come-again harvest of the smooth, rounded, non-bolting leaves.
directions: Direct sow in fall as temperatures moderate, or in very early spring, and thin seedlings to stand a few inches apart for continuous cut-and-come-again harvest of the smooth, rounded, non-bolting leaves. Hanover Salad is a colonial-era Southern heirloom green in the same species as rutabaga, prized historically in Virginia and Gulf South gardens for its mild, cabbage-like flavor eaten raw as salad greens when young or cooked like collards once mature. It tolerates both cold snaps and the on-and-off warmth of a Gulf Coast fall and winter better than many mustards, holding quality in the garden for extended picking rather than bolting at the first warm spell.

common_name: Hansel Eggplant (AAS-Winning Slender Mini Purple Eggplant, Prolific and Early Cluster Producer)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Hansel is a compact eggplant variety producing prolific clusters of slender, 3–4 inch long deep purple eggplants on an upright, bushy plant reaching 20–24 inches. In zone 9, start seeds January–February for March–April transplanting. Hansel was an All-America Selections winner in 2008, recognized for its extraordinary productivity, early maturity (55–60 days from transplant — faster than most large eggplant varieties), compact habit suitable for container growing, and excellent eating quality: the slender fruits are tender-skinned with virtually no bitterness, very few seeds, and flesh that stays white and creamy without the sponginess or discoloration that can affect larger eggplant varieties. The cluster fruiting habit — multiple fruits set in groups at each branch node rather than singly — contributes to the spectacular production that made Hansel notable in AAS trials. Harvest at 3–4 inches for best texture; fruits become slightly seedy and tough-skinned if left much longer.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 3–4 inches when skin is glossy deep purple. Hansel Eggplant was developed by PanAmerican Seed and won the All-America Selections award in 2008, one of a pair of complementary mini eggplant varieties (Hansel purple, Gretel white) from the same breeding program that were recognized in consecutive years for their outstanding performance in AAS trials. The Hansel and Gretel naming reflects the paired nature of the complementary varieties and their petite, fairy-tale proportions compared to standard full-sized eggplants. Hansel's outstanding AAS trial performance was attributed to several factors that distinguish it from both standard large eggplant varieties and other small-fruited eggplants: the combination of extremely early production (55–60 days from transplant, compared to 70–80+ days for large varieties), prolific cluster fruiting (multiple fruits per node vs. one to two for standard types), compact plant size (20–24 inches, easily managed in containers), and excellent eating quality (tender skin with no bitterness, minimal seed content, clean white flesh) created a variety with compelling advantages in every direction. For zone 9 gardeners, Hansel's short days-to-maturity is particularly valuable: zone 9 eggplant production spans March–October, but the most productive and high-quality harvest period is before the peak summer heat (June–July); Hansel's early maturity allows significant harvest before conditions become stressful.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Haogen is a celebrated Israeli melon developed at Kibbutz Ein HaMifratz, prized for its extraordinarily sweet, aromatic flesh of exceptional quality — considered by melon enthusiasts and chefs to be among the finest-flavored melons in the world, the Israeli equivalent of the French Charentais for concentrated sweetness and intense melon aroma.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-amended, well-drained soil in full sun; Haogen is ready to harvest when the skin transitions from green to orange-yellow in patches and the fruits slip from the vine with minimal pressure — like all aromatic melons, it deteriorates rapidly after peak ripeness. Haogen (also spelled Ogen) was developed at Kibbutz Ein HaMifratz in Israel and remains the most celebrated Israeli melon variety, known throughout the melon-growing world for its extraordinary flavor; the small to medium (1–3 lb), round fruits start with pale green skin that develops orange and gold patches and creeping yellow-green net as they ripen. The flesh is salmon-orange to greenish, with an intensely sweet, highly aromatic, complex melon fragrance and flavor with notes of honey and tropical fruit that many consider the finest melon eating experience available. Short shelf life after harvest (1–2 days at room temperature, 3–5 days refrigerated) means Haogen is fundamentally a garden and local market melon rather than a commercial shipping variety — its reputation rests on the incomparable quality of fruit eaten within hours of harvest. Widely grown in Israel, Netherlands, and by American melon enthusiasts.

common_name: Hardy Tapioca (Cold Hardy Cassava, Argentine Cassava)
plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Hardy tapioca is an Argentine relative of cassava (M. esculenta) that is far more cold-tolerant than true cassava — surviving freezes to zone 8 and dying back to the ground but regrowing in spring — primarily grown in warm-temperate and subtropical gardens as an ornamental foliage plant for its deeply-cut, tropical-looking leaves.
directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; dies back to roots in freezes but regrows. Manihot grahamii (hardy tapioca or Argentine cassava) is a cold-hardy Argentinian relative of true cassava (M. esculenta) — closely resembling its famous edible cousin in leaf shape (deeply palmately lobed, tropical-looking) and stem structure but significantly more cold-tolerant, surviving hard freezes to zone 8 (approximately 15°F) by dying to the ground and regenerating from tuberous roots the following spring. In zone 8–11, it is grown primarily as an ornamental for its dramatically tropical-looking, deeply cut, dark-green leaves (8–12 inches across) — creating a convincing tropical garden effect at far lower temperatures than true cassava (zone 10+). The plant can reach 4–8 feet in a single growing season, creating rapid impact as a tropical accent. The roots are reportedly edible (similar to cassava) but much less developed than commercial cassava and require the same caution about proper preparation to remove cyanogenic glycosides. Hardy tapioca is drought-tolerant, grows rapidly on poor soil, and is extremely low-maintenance — simply cut to the ground after frost and let it regrow. A remarkably useful plant for zone 8–9 gardeners seeking a tropical aesthetic without the winter protection demands of true tropical plants.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring — parsnip requires a long, cool growing season of 100–130 days and cannot tolerate summer heat. Germination is notoriously slow (14–28 days) and erratic; sow thickly and thin to 3–4 inches after germination. Parsnip performs best in zones 3–7 where hard fall frosts convert the roots' starches to sugars — the classic technique of leaving roots in the ground through fall frosts and harvesting in late fall/winter produces the sweetest, most intensely flavored roots. Zone 9 gardeners will find parsnip very challenging due to insufficient cold for sweetness development.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, stone-free soil — parsnip requires the same deep, uncompacted growing conditions as carrots but needs even more space due to the larger root; Harris Model is the standard American parsnip variety, selected in the 1880s by the Joseph Harris Seed Company as a smooth, uniform improvement over the traditional English Hollow Crown parsnip — fewer hollow crowns, smoother skin, and better root uniformity make Harris Model the most widely grown American parsnip. The long, tapering, ivory-white roots develop a rich, complex flavor that is unmistakably its own: sweet and aromatic with earthy, celery-like, and nuttily caramelized notes when roasted — a flavor that lacks any close comparison among other vegetables. The signature technique for maximizing parsnip flavor is 'frosting' — leaving harvested or in-ground roots exposed to repeated hard frosts that convert starches to sugars, creating a dramatically sweeter root than summer-harvested parsnips. Roasted parsnips (with butter, herbs, and honey) are one of the great classic British-American root vegetable preparations, where high heat caramelizes the natural sugars and transforms the texture from firm-and-dense to tender and lightly crisp at the edges.

common_name: Harvest Moon Watermelon (AAS-Winning Seedless Icebox Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Harvest Moon is an AAS-winning seedless watermelon bred for extra sweetness and very uniform, round, icebox-size fruit. Plant alongside a seeded pollinizer variety, since seedless watermelons need pollen from a seeded type to set fruit.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms, and plant a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply the pollen seedless watermelons need to set fruit. Harvest Moon is an AAS-winning seedless watermelon bred for very uniform, round, icebox-sized fruit — a manageable size for a refrigerator, unlike the largest field watermelons — with exceptionally sweet, crisp, deep-red flesh and only small, soft, edible white seed traces rather than the hard black seeds of standard watermelon. Its consistent size and shape make it a strong choice for home gardeners who want reliable, high-quality fruit without needing to manage a huge sprawling harvest. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil and consistent irrigation through fruit development; drought stress during fruit fill reduces size and quality. Judge ripeness by the ground spot turning from white to yellow and a dull, hollow thump when the fruit is tapped.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; multiple varieties exist under the 'Hatch' name (Big Jim, Joe Parker, 6-4, Sandia) — all are New Mexico-bred long green chiles best harvested green and roasted.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil rich in phosphorus after all frost risk has passed. Hatch green chile refers to New Mexico-style long green chiles — varieties such as NuMex Big Jim, Joe Parker, and the heritage 6-4 — bred at New Mexico State University and grown in the Hatch Valley of southern New Mexico; they produce 6–10 inch, elongated, thick-walled green pods with heat levels ranging from mild to hot depending on cultivar and growing conditions. The distinctive flavor comes from the dry, high-altitude climate, but home gardeners in zones 7–11 with hot, dry summers can produce excellent results in-ground. Harvest green when pods are fully sized and char-blister them on a grill or under a broiler; the roasted flavor is unmatched for green chile sauces, stews, and salsas.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights remain above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a productive spring through fall season; New Mexico type chiles produce heavily through summer heat and can be roasted and frozen in quantity for year-round use.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the New Mexico type chile, particularly Hatch and its relatives, is the defining pepper of Southwestern cuisine, eaten green (roasted), red (dried), or ground into chile powder. This long, mildly hot pepper (1,500–3,000 SHU) averages 6–8 inches and is the standard for roasting — the thick walls blister perfectly under a broiler or over an open flame, and the roasted, peeled chiles freeze beautifully for months. Harvest green through September, or leave some to ripen red for a fully different flavor profile. The Hatch designation technically refers to chiles grown in the Hatch Valley of New Mexico, but the variety performs excellently throughout zone 9.

plant_note: Plant small whole tubers 2 in deep like seed potatoes once the soil is thoroughly warm and frost danger has passed; matures faster than most tropical root crops, in about four to five months.
directions: A close relative of Livingstone potato in the mint family, Hausa potato forms a much lower, more compact plant that produces dense clusters of small, pea- to walnut-sized tubers directly at its base rather than spread along trailing stems.
