directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Hutterite Soup Bean is a pole bean heirloom preserved by the Hutterite communities of the northern Great Plains and Canada — religious agricultural communities known for maintaining exceptional heirloom seed collections. The small, round, pale yellow seeds are outstanding soup beans with a creamy, slightly buttery, mild flavor and a texture that breaks down smoothly in long-simmered soups without becoming mushy — they were specifically selected and maintained by Hutterite cooks for soup making over many generations. The small seed size (similar to a navy bean) and mild flavor make Hutterite Soup Bean versatile in white bean soups, bean salads, and cassoulet-style dishes. The climbing pole bean vines are productive and the pods dry down cleanly for harvest. The Hutterite selection demonstrates exceptional adaptation to cool, short-season climates of the northern plains, but grows successfully in a wide range of conditions.

common_name: Hutterite Soup Bean (Yellow Hutterite Bean, Great Plains Heritage Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Hutterite is a bush dry bean with buff-yellow seeds from the Hutterite communities of the northern Great Plains — a cold-adapted heritage variety maintained for generations by Hutterite colonies in Montana, South Dakota, and Canada, renowned for its extremely creamy, thick texture when cooked into soups and stews — its primary traditional use as the 'Sunday soup bean' of Hutterite communal kitchens.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Hutterite beans tolerate short cool growing seasons (80–95 days makes them practical for zones 3–4 short summers); harvest dry pods when fully papery and rattle when shaken. Hutterite Soup Bean is an heirloom dry bean variety maintained by the Hutterite communities of the northern Great Plains — communal Anabaptist communities of German and Austrian origin who settled the Montana, South Dakota, and Alberta regions in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, bringing their traditional agricultural varieties with them from Europe. The Hutterites maintain strict communal farming traditions including seed saving, and have preserved many heritage varieties of beans, grains, and vegetables that might otherwise have been lost. Hutterite beans have buff-yellow to light cream seeds with a mild, delicate flavor and an unusually thick, creamy texture when cooked — thicker than navy beans or great northern beans, with less tendency to break down or become mushy when simmered long. This creamy texture makes them particularly well-suited for thick soups and stews in the German-Russian culinary tradition of the Hutterite communities — served weekly in communal dining halls as 'bean soup Sunday.' The variety is adapted to the short, cool growing seasons of the northern plains, making it also excellent for short-season northern gardeners who struggle with longer-season dry beans. Good flavor for use in any white-bean recipe; outstanding in soups.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil reaches 65°F; provide a sturdy trellis or fence as vines grow rapidly to 10–15 feet. In zones 9–11 hyacinth bean may overwinter as a perennial; elsewhere grow as a vigorous warm-season annual.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep at the base of a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; hyacinth bean is a fast-climbing, ornamental tropical vine producing deep purple stems, lavender to violet pea flowers in upright racemes, and shiny deep-purple seed pods that are among the most spectacular of any annual vine. Young pods and fresh seeds are edible when thoroughly cooked — raw or undercooked seeds contain toxic cyanogenic glycosides (phytohaemagglutinin) and must never be eaten without boiling; immature flat pods may be eaten like snap beans after thorough cooking. The vine reaches 10–15 feet in a single season and thrives in hot, humid summer conditions where it fixes nitrogen and provides dense ornamental coverage on structures. In tropical and subtropical climates (zone 9–11), plants may persist as perennials and develop a woody base.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Amaranthus hybridus is a parent species of cultivated grain amaranths and an important leaf vegetable in many parts of Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean. It self-sows prolifically and can become weedy.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; hybrid amaranth (also called slim amaranth, green amaranth, or quelite in Mexican Spanish) is one of the most important wild and cultivated leaf vegetables in the tropical and subtropical world — a coarse, weedy-to-cultivated annual of the amaranth family widely consumed as a cooked green leaf vegetable (called 'alefu' in Ethiopia, 'callaloo' in the Caribbean, 'rajgira' leaves in India) across Africa, South Asia, and the Caribbean. The tender young leaves and shoot tips are harvested and cooked like spinach — mild in flavor, nutritious, and fast-growing in warm weather. One of the parent species of the cultivated grain amaranths (Amaranthus cruentus and others) selected for large seed production. Self-sows prolifically and establishes easily in hot, dry, disturbed soil — one of the most adaptable and heat-tolerant leaf vegetables available. Harvest young leaves continuously through the summer; the plant bolts in heat to produce seed heads used as grain in traditional cultures.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs about 1 inch deep and 6-8 inches apart from late summer through fall; I'itoi goes summer-dormant in Gulf Coast heat and resprouts as temperatures cool, making fall the most reliable planting window.
directions: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them 6-8 inches apart to give clumps room to multiply. I'itoi is a heirloom perennial multiplier onion long cultivated by the Tohono O'odham of the Sonoran Desert borderlands, and it is unusual among onions for tolerating both intense summer heat and winter cold, which lets it persist as a perennial clump in Gulf Coast gardens rather than needing yearly replanting. A single planted bulb divides into eight or more bulbs within a season, and gardeners typically harvest by pulling scallion-like greens continuously while leaving part of the clump to keep multiplying underground. Dig and divide the clump when the foliage dies back in summer dormancy, replanting a portion immediately to keep the planting going indefinitely.

common_name: Ice Plant (Crystal Ice Plant, Common Ice Plant)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall in very well-drained, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; ice plant is native to the coastal Mediterranean and South Africa and is entirely intolerant of clay, poor drainage, or humid conditions. In zone 9a, fall and winter culture avoids the summer humidity that causes disease.
directions: Sow in fall in well-drained, sandy, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; the common ice plant is one of the most visually distinctive of all edible plants — the thick, fleshy, spatula-shaped leaves and stems are covered in large, glistening, fluid-filled papillae (water cells) that catch and reflect sunlight like tiny glass beads or ice crystals, giving the plant its enchanting name. The mildly salty, refreshing leaves are edible raw in salads, as a garnish, or as a substitute for spinach, with a texture somewhere between watercress and succulent. The plant is halophytic (salt-tolerant) and is often used to bind coastal sandy soils. It is a cool-season plant that grows through winter in zone 9–11 and dies in summer heat. The species is considered invasive in California coastal areas where it has altered soil chemistry — plant only in maintained garden areas.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil; this old variety tolerates both cold and heat.
directions: Also called Reine des Glaces, this 1883 Batavian summer-crisp lettuce is cold tolerant, heat tolerant, and slow to bolt, with frilly emerald leaves and crisp texture. Direct sow in cool soil and thin to give heads room to form. Keep evenly watered to avoid bitterness, and offer light afternoon shade during heat to extend the harvest. Cut whole heads at maturity or harvest outer leaves as needed.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop; heat causes bolting.
directions: This heirloom crisphead forms compact, tight heads about eight inches across with firm, mild, refreshingly crunchy leaves. Sow in cool weather, either early spring or late summer, since heat triggers bolting and bitterness. Thin plants to give each head room to fill out and keep the soil consistently moist. Harvest when heads feel firm and full, cutting at the base in the cool part of the day.

common_name: Ichiban Eggplant (Japanese Eggplant, Long Slender Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5) soil in full sun when night temperatures remain above 55°F; in zone 9, transplant in mid-February to early March and again in late July for a productive fall crop.
directions: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun when night temperatures stay above 55°F; Ichiban is the classic Japanese-type slender eggplant — producing long (10–12 inch), slender (1.5–2 inch diameter), cylindrical, deep purple-black fruits that are harvested young and tender with exceptionally thin, delicate skin, very few seeds, and mild, sweet, non-bitter flesh. The thin skin and low seed content of Ichiban-type eggplants produce a fundamentally different culinary result from standard oval Italian-type eggplants — the flesh is tender-soft rather than dense, the flavor is milder and sweeter, and the skin is thin enough to be eaten without peeling. This makes Ichiban particularly well-suited to quick stir-frying, grilling, and Asian cooking methods. In zone 9, Ichiban is one of the most heat-tolerant vegetables available — eggplants love the hot, humid Gulf Coast summer that defeats many vegetables, and Ichiban's slender fruit type tends to size up and set fruit more reliably in extreme heat than standard round or oval types. Harvest when the fruit skin is deep, glossy purple-black and before any softening or browning of the calyx — once the skin loses its gloss, the fruit is overripe. The plants can be maintained year-round as perennial shrubs in frost-free zone 10–11, and in zone 9 they often survive mild winters and produce prolifically in their second year.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55F. Icicle is a spineless white eggplant bred for long, slender fruit with fewer seeds than most white eggplant varieties.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick fruit young and glossy for the mildest flavor and fewest seeds. Icicle is an AAS-winning eggplant producing long, slender, pure-white fruit on spineless plants, a genuine convenience for hand-harvesting compared to the sharp spines that guard the calyx of many eggplant varieties. It carries noticeably fewer seeds than typical white eggplant, giving a creamier, less bitter texture, and its tender skin needs no peeling. The productive, well-branched plants set fruit reliably over a long summer season. Harvest regularly while fruit is still glossy and firm, since letting fruit overripen on the plant both reduces quality and slows further production; the plant responds to frequent picking with a steady stream of new fruit through the season.

plant_note: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil; softneck Silverskins tolerate slightly later fall planting than hardneck types.
directions: Idaho Silverskin is a softneck garlic strain adapted to the high desert growing conditions of southern Idaho, producing tightly wrapped, bright white bulbs with 12-18 small, densely packed cloves ideal for braiding. It stores exceptionally well, often keeping firm for 9-12 months past harvest, longer than most hardneck types. Because it lacks a hard central stalk, the flexible leaves make traditional garlic braids easy to weave for kitchen storage or gifting. Choose this variety for its outstanding shelf life and adaptability to warmer, drier growing regions where hardneck types underperform.

common_name: Iditarod Red Tomato (Large-Fruited Compact Dwarf Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Iditarod Red is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bred to produce unusually large red fruit on a compact plant, named for the Alaskan sled dog race.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Iditarod Red bears notably large, deep red beefsteak-style fruit for a dwarf tomato, often rivaling full-size indeterminate slicers in fruit weight despite growing on a compact, manageable plant bred through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Its combination of big fruit and small plant footprint makes it a standout choice for gardeners short on space who still want a substantial slicing tomato. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant two to four weeks before the last frost; its short maturity window also suits a late-summer sowing for a fall crop.
directions: Igloo is a fast, open-pollinated cauliflower that reaches harvest in under two months, notably quicker than most named cauliflower cultivars. Its compact upright leaves naturally curl inward over the curd, giving a degree of self-blanching protection from sun exposure without extra tying. The speed and reliability of Igloo make it especially well suited to succession sowing through a cool season or to squeezing in a crop where the growing window is short. Select Igloo when quick, dependable snow-white curds are the priority over large head size.

plant_note: Direct sow; carrots resent transplanting. Keep seedbed moist until emergence.
directions: This AAS-winning heirloom yields long, tapered orange roots with fine-grained texture, outstanding sweetness, and thin, easy-to-peel skin. Sow seeds directly into loose, stone-free soil so the long roots can grow straight. Keep the seedbed consistently moist during the slow germination period, then thin seedlings to prevent crowding. Harvest once roots reach full size and sweeten further after a light frost.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in very deep (14–16 inches), loose, stone-free soil; Imperator-type carrots require excellent soil preparation — any stones or compaction causes forking; raised beds filled with light, sandy loam are ideal.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in very deeply prepared, loose, stone-free soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Imperator is the long, slender carrot of the grocery store — 8–10 inches long with a tapered tip, thin skin, high sugar content, and the satisfying snap of commercial carrots eaten fresh from supermarkets. It requires deep, perfectly loose, stone-free soil to reach full size without forking; raised beds with sandy loam are ideal. The flavor of home-grown Imperators freshly harvested is dramatically better than commercial versions; the high sugar content makes them outstanding for juicing, fresh eating, and the carrot sticks in lunch boxes.

common_name: Imperial Star Artichoke (Annual Seed-Grown First-Year Flowering Artichoke)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; Imperial Star requires vernalization — expose seedlings to temperatures of 50–55°F for 10 consecutive days when plants have 6–8 leaves (typically 4–6 weeks after germination) to trigger first-year flower bud production. Without this cold treatment, plants grow vegetatively but do not produce artichoke buds in their first year. In zone 9, start seeds January–February and transplant March–April after cold treatment for spring harvest (April–June); a second planting (October transplant) can produce a fall-winter harvest. The vernalization cold treatment is the critical step that distinguishes Imperial Star from older artichoke types that require a full second year to produce.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 65–70°F; expose seedlings to 50–55°F for 10 days (vernalization) before transplanting. Harvest buds when still tight and before the scales begin to open. Imperial Star is the pioneering annual artichoke variety bred by Keith Mayberry of the University of California Cooperative Extension in Imperial County — the variety that made artichoke production as an annual possible for the first time. Traditional artichoke varieties (such as Green Globe) are perennials that produce their first commercial harvest in the second or third year after planting from divisions; they require mild winters to survive (zone 8–9), making them impractical or impossible in colder climates. Imperial Star changed this by introducing the genetic characteristic of first-year flowering when exposed to a period of cool temperatures (vernalization) — the same cold-stimulus mechanism that triggers biennial flowering in brassicas, adapted to artichoke. When properly vernalized, Imperial Star plants produce their first artichoke buds in the same season they are planted, allowing artichoke cultivation as an annual across a much wider range of zones and eliminating the 2–3 year establishment period. The artichokes produced are full-sized, rounded, traditional artichoke form — not meaningfully different in size, flavor, or eating quality from perennial types. Imperial Star remains the dominant annual artichoke variety decades after its introduction, maintained by Johnny's Selected Seeds and other specialty vegetable suppliers as the standard annual artichoke reference.

common_name: Inca Red Drop Pepper (Fruity Andean Hot Pepper with Small Elongated Red Fruits)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Capsicum baccatum species benefit from a heat mat during germination — the higher soil temperature (80°F+) significantly improves germination speed and percentage compared to ambient room temperature germination.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Inca Red Drop is a Capsicum baccatum pepper from the Andean tradition of Peru — the species group that also includes Aji Amarillo and Aji Cristal, characterized by the distinctly fruity, citrusy, tropical flavor profile that distinguishes Andean peppers from the more neutral heat of C. annuum varieties. Inca Red Drop produces small to medium (2–3 inch), elongated, pendant, bright-red fruits with a pointed tip — the 'drop' shape giving the variety its name. The heat level is medium to medium-hot (30,000–60,000 SHU) — more heat than a jalapeño but less than a habanero — with the fruity, berry-like undertones characteristic of quality C. baccatum selections. The fruit flavor combines the fruity complexity of the aji family with a clean, bright heat that builds persistently. In Peruvian and Bolivian cooking, aji baccatum varieties are used fresh, dried, and as the base for sauces and marinades where the fruity complexity is as important as the heat level. The long season to maturity (90–120 days from transplant) is well-suited to zone 9's extended warm season. The ornamental value of the small red pendant fruits on attractive plants makes Inca Red Drop equally at home in ornamental pepper displays and in dedicated vegetable gardens.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes for a summer harvest.
directions: A large, mild softneck garlic with 8 to 20 cloves per bulb and a robust, taste-test-winning flavor, well suited to braiding and long storage. Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, and mulch heavily for winter protection. Keep beds weed-free and watered through spring, then stop watering as the lower leaves brown. Harvest in summer when several lower leaves have yellowed, and cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place.

common_name: Incredible Sweet Corn (Sugar-Enhanced Yellow Hybrid Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows wide for adequate wind pollination; Incredible is an se (sugar-enhanced) type that holds quality on the plant and after harvest better than su types. In zone 9, plant March–April for a May–June harvest, or plant August–September for a fall crop. SE types can be isolated from sh2 (supersweet) varieties but can be planted adjacent to su types without significant quality reduction.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; apply balanced fertilizer at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Incredible is one of the most respected and widely grown sugar-enhanced (se) yellow sweet corn hybrids in American home and market gardens — a Seminis-developed variety that consistently rates among the top performers for flavor, tenderness, and eating quality across multiple decades of university and commercial variety trials. The se (also called EH, everlasting heritage, or sugar-enhanced) gene doubles the sugar content at harvest compared to standard su varieties, and — critically — slows the conversion of sugar to starch after picking, giving se-type corn a 2–4 day postharvest quality window compared to the 24-hour window of su types. This extended holding quality made se types like Incredible a significant practical advance for home gardeners, allowing harvest and consumption at leisure rather than immediately. The 8–9 inch ears carry 16–18 rows of golden-yellow, tender, plump kernels with excellent flavor that is noticeably sweeter and more tender than older su types. Incredible consistently places first or second in tasting panels for yellow se corn and offers good disease resistance including northern corn leaf blight tolerance. An outstanding all-around sweet corn variety that has earned its perennial top-seller status.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring (after soil warms to 60°F+) in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Indian shot is the wild species ancestor of modern ornamental cannas — the starchy rhizomes (achira in South America) have been cultivated as a food crop by Andean indigenous peoples for thousands of years, the seeds are used as natural beads (too hard to eat), and the leaves are used as food wraps.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in warm soil (60°F+) in full sun to part shade in moist, humus-rich soil; in zone 8, mulch heavily in winter or lift and store rhizomes; the large starchy rhizomes can be harvested and eaten cooked. Canna indica (Indian shot or achira) is the wild species of canna from tropical America — the ancestor of modern hybrid ornamental cannas (Canna x generalis) that now dominate garden use worldwide — and a plant with a rich, ancient food history. The starchy rhizomes of Canna indica (and the closely related C. edulis, the 'purple arrowroot' or 'Queensland arrowroot') have been cultivated as a food crop by Andean indigenous peoples for an estimated 4,500–8,000 years, making achira one of the oldest cultivated food plants in the Americas. The large, starchy rhizomes are baked, boiled, or pit-roasted like sweet potatoes; the starch is uniquely large-grained (the largest starch granules of any plant), making achira starch distinctive in culinary applications. The seeds are among the hardest seeds in the plant kingdom (requiring scarification to germinate) and are traditionally used as natural beads and jewelry. As an ornamental, C. indica produces smaller flowers than modern hybrids (typically red or orange-red) but is equally spectacular, with bold, banana-like, green to sometimes bronze-purple leaves and abundant flowering on vigorous, rapidly-spreading rhizomes.

common_name: Indigo Apple Tomato (OSU Indigo Series Blue-Anthocyanin Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Indigo Apple is an indeterminate variety that requires staking or caging. The distinctive blue-black anthocyanin pigmentation develops on sun-exposed areas of the fruit and fades on shaded portions, creating a characteristic bicolor appearance (blue-black on top, red on the shaded side). In zone 9, transplant February–March; the deep blue color develops most intensely in bright sun and cool temperatures.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun for maximum anthocyanin expression — the blue-black pigmentation only develops in sun-exposed areas and fades entirely in shade. Indigo Apple is a product of the Oregon State University tomato breeding program led by Dr. Jim Myers, who developed the 'Indigo' series of tomatoes by crossing commercial tomatoes with a wild species (Solanum cheesmaniae from the Galapagos Islands) that carries genes for anthocyanin production in fruit tissue. The anthocyanins (the same pigments in blueberries and purple cabbage) accumulate in the skin of Indigo tomatoes when exposed to sunlight, creating a striking blue-black to deep purple coloration on the sun side while the shaded side remains red — a unique bicolor effect that changes as the fruit ripens and is genuinely unlike any other common tomato. Indigo Apple produces medium-sized (3–4 oz) round fruits that hang in clusters; the flesh inside is red and has good complex tomato flavor with moderate sweetness and acidity. Beyond the visual novelty, the anthocyanin compounds are genuine antioxidants of nutritional significance — the same compounds studied for potential health benefits in blueberries. Indigo Apple, Indigo Rose, Indigo Blue Berries, and other Indigo series varieties represent a fascinating example of targeted nutritional breeding combined with ornamental appeal.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant after frost and stake the tall vines.
directions: A deep purple-black cherry tomato bred at Oregon State to be rich in anthocyanin antioxidants, borne in clusters of 6 to 8 two-ounce fruits. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once weather warms. Stake or cage the 5-foot indeterminate vines and prune for airflow. Sun exposure deepens the purple color; harvest when the shoulders darken and the undersides turn red.

plant_note: Start indoors alongside a favorite watermelon, melon, or cucumber scion, timing sowing so both are the same stem thickness at grafting; graft, heal in a humid shaded chamber, then transplant after frost into full sun.
directions: This vigorous interspecific hybrid squash rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite watermelon, melon, or cucumber scion rather than eaten itself, providing a much larger, more aggressive root system that confers strong resistance to fusarium wilt and other soil-borne diseases along with improved tolerance of cool soil, drought, and salinity compared to a plant grown on its own roots. Widely used in commercial watermelon production in Asia and increasingly adopted by market and home growers elsewhere, grafted watermelon plants on this rootstock often show extended harvest windows, larger overall plant size, and better performance in soils with a history of vine crop disease. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, timing sowing so stem diameters match at grafting time, graft using a hole-insertion or splice technique, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun on raised beds or hills.

common_name: Iochief Sweet Corn (Iowa State Heirloom Open-Pollinated Sweet Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows in fertile soil with consistent moisture during pollination.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows in fertile soil with consistent moisture during pollination for full, well-filled ears. Iochief was released by Iowa State University in the early 1950s as a productive, open-pollinated main-season yellow sweet corn, at a time when hybrid sweet corns were rapidly displacing older varieties, and it has survived among heirloom growers for its vigorous stalks, large ears, and genuinely excellent old-fashioned sweet corn flavor. It remains a solid choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed year to year, something not possible with modern hybrid sweet corns.

plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked; short vines need no support.
directions: A French petit pois variety producing peas half the usual size but packed with sweet flavor, often three dark-green pods per node. Direct sow several weeks before the last frost in cool, workable soil. The productive 28-inch vines are self-supporting but benefit from a low trellis, and the plant offers powdery mildew resistance. Harvest pods when plump and pick often for the tenderest baby peas.

common_name: Ireland Creek Annie Bean (Early Bush Dry Soup Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; this English-origin bush bean was carried to British Columbia in the 1920s and has been maintained at Ireland Creek Farm ever since.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep directly in the garden once soil has warmed after the last frost, spacing plants 4-6 inches apart in rows 18-24 inches apart. Ireland Creek Annie is a compact, heavy-yielding bush dry bean prized for its unusually early maturity and cool-tolerance, making it a reliable choice for short-season gardens. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before shelling; the buff-yellow to mustard-colored seeds cook down quickly to a rich, creamy texture well suited to soups and purees. Keep beds weeded and evenly moist through flowering and pod set, then withhold water as pods mature and dry for harvest.

common_name: Iron Clay Pea (Iron and Clay Cowpea)
scientific_name: Vigna unguiculata subsp. unguiculata 'Iron and Clay'
plant_note: Broadcast or drill after soil reaches 65°F; Iron Clay is typically seeded at 40–80 lbs per acre or 1–2 lbs per 1000 sq ft. In zone 9 the primary window is April–July; a late summer planting (July–August) provides excellent late-season biomass before frost.
directions: Broadcast at 40–80 lbs per acre (or 1 lb per 1000 sq ft) onto a loosened seedbed and rake in lightly; no inoculant is required in soil with prior cowpea history, but rhizobium inoculant greatly improves nitrogen fixation in new ground. Iron Clay is a hybrid between iron cowpea and clay cowpea types bred specifically as a summer cover crop and forage legume for the southeastern US. It is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant summer cover crops available, providing dense weed suppression, substantial nitrogen fixation (80–150 lbs N/acre under ideal conditions), erosion control, and wildlife habitat simultaneously. The vining, semi-prostrate plants knit together to form a dense ground cover; deer and other wildlife browse the foliage heavily, making it popular as a food-plot crop. Terminate before seed set by mowing or incorporation. In a garden context, till under green at peak vegetative growth for maximum nitrogen credit.

common_name: Iron Lady Tomato (Multi-Disease-Resistant Cornell F1 Hybrid Slicer for Humid Climates)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Iron Lady is indeterminate, requiring staking or caging. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring production — the heat-resistance and disease package makes Iron Lady one of the better choices for the challenging Gulf South summer, though even Iron Lady will slow in peak summer heat. The disease resistance package (Early Blight, Late Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, Fusarium and Verticillium wilts, plus tolerance to TSWV) is specifically valuable in the humid Gulf South where foliar fungal diseases devastate unprotected varieties within weeks of transplant. A fall planting (September transplant) often extends production into December.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F; transplant after hardening off. Stake or cage immediately; Iron Lady is an indeterminate vine requiring vertical support. Iron Lady is a disease-resistant F1 hybrid tomato developed through the Cornell University Vegetable Program in collaboration with the Public Seed Initiative — a breeding program committed to developing open-access (non-patented) vegetable varieties for organic and conventional farmers. Iron Lady carries one of the most comprehensive disease-resistance packages available in a slicing tomato: confirmed resistance to Early Blight (Alternaria solani), Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans — the disease responsible for the Irish Potato Famine), Septoria Leaf Spot, and Fusarium and Verticillium wilt, plus tolerance to Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus. For Gulf South gardeners in zone 8–10, where the combination of high humidity, warm nights, and heavy summer rainfall creates near-ideal conditions for fungal tomato diseases, Iron Lady's disease package addresses the primary reason tomato plants fail prematurely in the region — not heat or drought, but the rapid defoliation by Early and Late Blight that kills plants before the crop is fully harvested. The tomatoes themselves are medium-sized (4–8 oz), round, deep red, with excellent flavor quality for a disease-resistant type — a notable achievement given that breeders historically faced trade-offs between disease resistance and eating quality.

common_name: Iron Man Pumpkin (F1 Hard-Shell Personal-Size Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun; the vigorous, powdery-mildew-tolerant vine and rot-resistant fruit hold up well through a long, muggy Gulf Coast season.
directions: Direct sow in hills once the soil has warmed, allowing the full, vigorous vines plenty of room to run through the second half of the growing season. Iron Man produces round, dark orange fruit only 6-7 inches across and 3-4 pounds, sized for painting projects, porch groupings, and small-space carving rather than large jack-o'-lanterns. The unusually hard rind resists Fusarium and Phytophthora fruit rot, an advantage in the wet, humid soils common along the Gulf Coast, and cured fruit stores for months without softening. Harvest once the shell has fully hardened and cannot be dented with a thumbnail, then cure in a warm, dry spot for a week before moving pumpkins into long-term storage.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last expected frost date, then transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50°F.
directions: Start seeds indoors in peat pots 3 to 4 weeks before your last frost date, or direct sow once soil has warmed past 70°F, then thin or space plants generously to allow the sprawling vines room to run. Released by Cornell plant breeder Henry Munger in 1944 as a cross of 'Minnesota 99-36' and 'Bender's Surprise', Iroquois was the first muskmelon bred specifically for resistance to Fusarium wilt. Its thick, heavily netted rind covers deep salmon-orange flesh with a rich, musky-sweet flavor, and its disease tolerance made it a long-time favorite for northern and Midwestern home gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow or start transplants in early spring; Ishikura can also be sown in late summer for a fall and winter harvest in zone 9. Successive sowings every 3-4 weeks keep a steady supply of scallions coming.
directions: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart; hilling soil up around the base as plants grow blanches the shanks white and tender. Ishikura is a classic Japanese bunching onion, or negi, that forms a long, straight, pure-white shank without ever swelling into a bulb, staying tender and mild even as it grows tall. It is slow to bolt, tolerates both summer heat and winter cold well, and can be harvested at scallion size or left to mature into thick, leek-like stalks. Because it does not form a storage bulb, Ishikura is best used fresh, sliced into stir-fries, soups, and as a raw garnish; cut-and-come-again harvesting of the outer leaves extends the picking season from a single planting.

common_name: Isis Candy Cherry Tomato (Striped Sweet Cherry Tomato with Gold Cat-Eye Markings)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Isis Candy is an indeterminate open-pollinated cherry tomato producing 1-inch round fruits that ripen to cherry-red with distinctive gold-yellow cat's-eye markings at the blossom end and subtle pink striping on the skin. In zone 9, transplant March–April and stake or cage; indeterminate types need support throughout the season. Isis Candy is an open-pollinated variety developed by tomato breeder Carolyn Male, one of the foremost American heirloom tomato breeders and authors of the landmark book '100 Heirloom Tomatoes for the American Garden.' The variety combines outstanding flavor — consistently rated among the sweetest and most complex of cherry tomatoes — with the striking visual appearance of the bicolor pattern. The gold-yellow markings develop clearly at full ripe (some cherry varieties show ambiguous color breaks; Isis Candy's blossom end marking is a clear, distinct gold circle on red). Production is prolific throughout zone 9's warm season.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake. Harvest when fully red with gold markings showing clearly at blossom end. Isis Candy is an open-pollinated cherry tomato variety developed by Carolyn Male, a New York tomato enthusiast and breeder who spent decades collecting and evaluating heirloom tomato varieties and documented her work in the widely respected '100 Heirloom Tomatoes for the American Garden.' Among cherry tomato varieties, Isis Candy stands out for both flavor quality and visual appeal: the flavor combines genuine tomato sweetness with a candy-like fruitiness and enough natural acidity to provide complexity rather than simple sweetness — the kind of balanced flavor profile that makes cherry tomatoes irresistible eaten directly off the vine. The appearance is striking: when ripe, the 1-inch round fruits display a candy-apple red with distinctive gold 'cat's-eye' markings — a golden-yellow circle centered at the blossom end — and sometimes faint pink striping on the red skin, creating a two-tone effect visible even from a distance in the garden. This visual distinction makes Isis Candy particularly attractive for multi-variety cherry tomato plantings where color diversity adds visual interest, and for farmers market and fresh-eating contexts where the unusual patterning captures attention. The variety is open-pollinated and stable, meaning saved seed reliably reproduces the variety's characteristics — an advantage over F1 hybrid cherry types that cannot be seed-saved. For zone 9 gardeners, Isis Candy's heat tolerance and prolific production throughout the Gulf Coast's long warm season make it a consistently productive choice among open-pollinated cherry varieties.

common_name: Isis Candy Tomato (Bicolor Gold-and-Red Cherry Heirloom)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Isis Candy is a productive indeterminate vine that benefits from staking or caging and bears heavily over a long season.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vines for support. Isis Candy is a beloved heirloom cherry tomato producing round, golden-yellow fruit marbled and streaked with red, with a rich, sweet, well-balanced flavor that consistently ranks among the best-tasting cherry tomatoes in home garden trials. Plants are heavy, reliable producers over a long season, and the striking bicolor fruit makes an attractive addition to a mixed cherry tomato harvest or salad. Pick fruit as it fully colors for the best flavor, and water consistently to reduce splitting, since the thin skin is prone to cracking after heavy rain.

common_name: Islander Pepper (AAS-Winning Lavender-to-Red Ornamental-Edible Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after danger of frost has passed; Islander's compact habit makes it well suited to containers and patio plantings as well as garden beds.
directions: Islander is an All-America Selections-winning bell-type pepper bred for a striking color progression, with fruits maturing from ivory through lavender-purple before finishing orange and finally red, so the plant often carries several colors simultaneously. Start seed indoors in warm conditions and transplant after the soil has warmed, since fruit color development is strongest in full sun and consistent warmth. The compact, well-branched plants were selected as much for garden and container ornamental value as for eating quality, though the blocky fruit is genuinely sweet and crisp at any ripeness stage. Pick continually through the color stages both to enjoy the visual display and to keep the plant setting new fruit.

common_name: Italian Heirloom Tomato (Large Ribbed Sweet Pink Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Italian Heirloom was preserved and shared through the Seed Savers Exchange network from a family's own long-held Italian seed stock, producing large, distinctively ribbed and slightly flattened, deep pink-red fruit with sweet, well-balanced, richly flavored flesh reminiscent of classic Italian slicing tomatoes. The pronounced ribbing and irregular shoulders give the fruit an old-world, rustic appearance that sets it apart from the smoother modern hybrids most gardeners are used to, while the vigorous indeterminate vine produces reliably through a long season. Water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking around the ribbed shoulders, and harvest once fruit fully colors for the best flavor.

common_name: Italian Red of Florence Bunching Onion
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil is workable; harvest young as scallions or let bulbs form.
directions: An Italian heirloom torpedo-shaped red onion used young as a mild scallion or grown on for elongated red bulbs. Direct sow thickly as soon as the soil can be worked, thinning for scallions and eating the thinnings. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist for tender stalks. Pull young for fresh use, or let plants mature and cure the bulbs for short-term storage.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant after frost. Determinate fruit ripens in a concentrated window good for canning.
directions: A classic heirloom paste tomato with firm, meaty, few-seeded 3-inch oblong fruits on compact, very productive determinate vines. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply after the weather warms. Because most fruit ripens together, it is an excellent choice for canning and sauce. Provide a cage for support, water evenly to prevent blossom-end rot, and harvest when fully colored.

plant_note: Sow in spring or late summer; cool weather mellows the bitterness.
directions: Despite its name, this is an Italian chicory with vivid burgundy stems and deeply lobed green leaves, grown for flavorful bitter greens. Sow directly in cool weather, spring or late summer, when the flavor is at its most balanced. Thin seedlings and keep soil moist to encourage tender leaves. Harvest young leaves for salads or let plants mature for cooking greens with a robust chicory bite.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to ten to twelve inches apart. Ithaca was bred at Cornell University for good resistance to tipburn, a physiological disorder that causes browning at leaf edges in crisphead lettuce under heat or irregular watering stress, along with a degree of heat tolerance that lets it hold quality longer into warm weather than many older iceberg-type varieties. The dense, crisp, pale green heads deliver the familiar crunchy texture prized in classic iceberg lettuce, well suited to sandwiches and salads calling for texture over deep flavor. Keep soil consistently moist through head formation to further reduce tipburn risk, and harvest once heads feel firm and solid when gently squeezed.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings (roots most easily); plant in full sun after soil warms; ivy gourd is a dioecious vine requiring both male and female plants for fruiting — in tropical gardens it spreads aggressively; contain in large containers in zone 9 where it may freeze back but resprout from roots.
directions: Propagate from stem cuttings taken from female and male plants; plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil after soil warms above 70°F, providing a sturdy trellis or fence; ivy gourd is a perennial tropical vine widely grown across South and Southeast Asia for its tender young shoots and immature green fruits (tindora), used stir-fried, curried, or pickled with a mild flavor similar to young zucchini. The 2–3 inch fruits should be harvested green before they ripen to vivid red — fully ripe fruits are sweet but mushy and unsuitable for cooking. Caution: ivy gourd is invasive in Hawaii and parts of south Florida where it escapes cultivation and smothers native vegetation; grow in containers or managed plots where spread can be controlled. Young shoots and leaves are also edible as greens.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–June. Jack Be Little is a compact vining plant that produces many fruits — allow all fruits to develop since the small size means production of 10–20 fruits per plant is achievable. The tiny fruits cure in place on the vine; harvest when stems are dry and skin is hard. Cured properly (2 weeks in warm, dry conditions) the fruits store for 3–4 months as decorative pieces and can still be eaten after the ornamental season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Jack Be Little is an All-America Selections award-winning miniature pumpkin producing perfectly proportioned, deeply ribbed, orange fruits only 2–4 inches across and weighing 3–8 ounces — a precisely scaled-down replica of a full-size pumpkin that has become one of the most popular autumn decorating elements for tabletop arrangements, wreaths, and centerpieces since winning its AAS award in 1989. The tiny fruits are also fully edible: halved and roasted in the oven or microwave, they produce a small amount of dense, sweet, pumpkin-flavored flesh that can be eaten directly from the shell — the shell becoming the natural serving bowl. The vine produces abundantly (often 10–15 fruits per plant) from a relatively compact plant footprint, making it highly space-efficient for ornamental pumpkin production. Jack Be Little became the defining mini pumpkin that launched the specialty ornamental squash market and has remained the most recognized mini pumpkin variety.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into warm soil; compact vines suit large containers.
directions: A tiny ornamental and edible pumpkin, 3 to 4 inches across and 2 inches tall, useful for decorating or as an individual stuffed-and-baked serving. Direct sow after frost into warm soil, with the compact 3 to 5 foot vines producing 6 to 10 fruits each. Keep evenly watered through fruit set and slip straw beneath the little pumpkins. Harvest when fully orange with a hardened rind, leaving a bit of stem for display.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; count back from Halloween for timing.
directions: This classic heirloom pumpkin has smooth orange skin, dependable size, and the perfect round shape for carving jack-o'-lanterns. Sow directly into warm, rich soil after frost, allowing the sprawling vines plenty of space. Feed and water consistently as fruit sets and swells, tucking a board or straw under each pumpkin to prevent rot. Harvest when rinds harden and turn deep orange, cutting with a length of stem attached for better keeping.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Jackson Wonder is earlier and more heat-tolerant than most Lima beans, making it the best-adapted Lima for the Gulf Coast and Deep South. In zone 9 plant March–May for spring and again July–August for a fall crop.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jackson Wonder is a compact, bush-type speckled lima bean that has been the standard Lima for Southern kitchen gardens since the 1880s — it is heat-tolerant where other lima varieties fail to set pods and is the recommended lima bean variety for zone 8–9 gardens. The small-seeded beans are harvested green (fresh shelled) as baby limas at 50–60 days or left to dry on the vine for use as dried beans; the dried seeds are attractively speckled in purple and white. Inoculate seeds with lima bean rhizobia at planting for nitrogen fixation; no fertilization is needed beyond a light dose of phosphorus and potassium at planting.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil; excels in hot, dry climates.
directions: This historic dwarf bush butterbean, introduced in 1888, is prized for heat tolerance, resilience, and dependable yields in hot, dry conditions. Sow directly into warm soil after frost, since lima beans will not germinate in cold ground. The compact bush plants need no support and produce speckled, buttery-textured beans. Harvest young pods for fresh shelling or let them dry fully on the plant for storage.

common_name: Jacob's Cattle Bean (Classic Maine Spotted Dry Bean for Baked Beans and Soup)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Jacob's Cattle is a dry bean grown to full maturity and dried on the plant. In zone 9, plant March–May; pods dry on the plant in August–September when the garden has dried after summer heat. Shell and store dried beans in airtight containers. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant until papery and rattling before harvest — or cut the whole plant at the soil line and hang to finish drying indoors in humid fall weather. Jacob's Cattle is a bush bean (18–24 inch plants) requiring no support.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 4–6 inches. Allow pods to dry completely on the plant before harvesting. Shell and store in airtight containers. Jacob's Cattle Bean (also called Trout Bean or Dalmatian Bean in some regions) is a New England heirloom dry bean with one of the most visually distinctive appearances in the bean world — white beans irregularly splashed and dotted with maroon-red spots in a pattern that resembles the speckled coat of Jacob's Cattle described in the Book of Genesis, from which the variety's evocative name derives. The spotted appearance is due to anthocyanin pigmentation in the seed coat that creates the irregular, non-repeating pattern on each individual bean — a genetic expression that varies slightly bean to bean within the variety but maintains the distinctive red-on-white motif overall. Jacob's Cattle has been grown in Maine and New England since at least the mid-19th century, where it became the traditional bean for authentic New England-style baked beans: the creamy, meaty texture and moderately earthy flavor of Jacob's Cattle holds up beautifully in long, slow cooking with salt pork and molasses, developing richness without falling apart or becoming mushy. The beans are also excellent in soups, stews, and chili, where the spotted appearance adds visual interest to the finished dish. Being open-pollinated, seed can be saved indefinitely from the best plants.

common_name: Jacob's Cattle Bean (Trout Bean, Dalmatian Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after all frost danger passes; Jacob's Cattle is primarily a dry bean grown to maturity — allow pods to dry fully on the vine before harvesting. It performs best in cool, northern climates but grows as a productive spring or fall crop in zone 9 with the right timing.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Jacob's Cattle is one of New England's oldest heirloom dry beans, with a distinctive white seed marked with dark red-maroon splotches in a bold, cattle-hide-like pattern that inspired its name. The beans are extraordinarily creamy and rich-flavored when cooked, with a texture that stays firm without becoming mushy — excellent in baked beans, soups, and cassoulet-style dishes. The traditional New England baked beans were made with this variety, slow-cooked with salt pork and molasses. A true bush bean, it grows compactly and requires minimal staking. The pods should be left to dry and yellow-brown on the vine; harvest when the seeds rattle loosely inside and cure indoors in a dry, ventilated area to finish drying before storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; no staking needed, as this is a compact bush-type dry bean.
directions: A stabilized cross between the classic maroon-and-white Jacob's Cattle bean and a paint-type bean, this variety produces oblong white seeds dotted with striking golden-tan spots instead of the traditional dark red. Sturdy bush plants stay compact and self-supporting, bearing 4 to 5 inch pods with 6 to 8 seeds each that should be left on the plant until pods rattle and dry down fully for storage beans. The golden speckled beans hold their shape well through long cooking and take on other flavors readily, making them a favorite for baked beans, chili, and soups. Because it is bush-habit and matures reliably within a single season, it suits gardeners who want a distinctive heirloom dry bean without trellising.

common_name: Jade Bean (Slender Dark Green French Filet-Style Bush Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; harvest Jade pods when they are 4–5 inches long and still slender — the smaller pods are more tender and flavorful. Unlike standard snap beans, Jade should not be allowed to develop visible seeds inside before harvest, or the pods become fibrous. Regular picking every 2–3 days maximizes quality and production.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Jade is a refined bush snap bean with slender, deep jade-green pods that occupies a quality niche between standard American snap beans and the more delicate French haricot vert types. The pods are round (not flat), uniformly dark green, stringless, and noticeably more tender and flavorful than standard bean varieties when harvested young at 4–5 inches — with a mild, sweet, delicate green bean taste and a fine texture that makes them excellent for light steaming, quick sautéing with butter and herbs, and all preparations where bean flavor is the centerpiece. Unlike the very slender haricot vert types (such as Maxibel or Espada), Jade has a slightly more substantial pod that is easier to harvest and handle in quantity, while still maintaining considerably more refinement than standard snap beans like Blue Lake or Provider. A popular choice for market gardeners, farm-stand vendors, and home gardeners who want a more elegant snap bean without committing to the exacting harvest schedule of true filet-type beans. Very productive and relatively heat-tolerant for a fine-podded bean.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into warmed soil; succession sow for a long harvest.
directions: A favorite green bean prized for long, straight, stringless dark-green pods that stay tender and sweet, held high on upright plants to avoid tip rot. Direct sow after the soil warms past 65F, spacing seeds a few inches apart. This variety tolerates heat and cold better than most, so it produces reliably across the season. Pick pods young and often to keep the plants setting new beans.

common_name: Jade Cross Brussels Sprout (AAS Heat-Tolerant F1 Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost for fall harvest; Jade Cross is an All-America Selections award-winning F1 hybrid Brussels sprout notably more tolerant of warm fall temperatures than heirloom types like Long Island Improved — it sets sprouts at higher temperatures, making it the recommended variety for zones 7–9 where fall temperatures remain warmer longer and standard Brussels sprouts may fail to develop tight, round sprouts.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost at 70–75°F; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants; when bottom sprouts reach marble size, remove the growing tip ('topping') to concentrate energy; harvest sprouts from the bottom upward when 1–1.5 inches across. Jade Cross is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning F1 hybrid Brussels sprout that has been a reliable performer in American gardens since its introduction; it was specifically developed for improved performance in warmer fall conditions compared to the standard heirloom types. Standard Brussels sprouts (Long Island Improved, Catskill, etc.) require consistently cool temperatures (40–60°F) to develop tight, round, high-quality sprouts; in zones 7–9 where fall remains warm well into October, these traditional varieties often produce loose, bitter, or poorly formed sprouts. Jade Cross was selected for earlier sprout initiation at warmer temperatures, allowing it to begin developing sprouts before cool weather arrives and then perfect them as temperatures fall. The sprouts are uniform, round, tightly wrapped, and excellent in flavor — milder and sweeter than heirloom types, with the classic Brussels sprout character that intensifies after frost exposure. Jade Cross is the standard recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and Louisiana State University AgCenter for Gulf South Brussels sprout production.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant April–June for main crop, or as early as March under row cover. Jade okra is spineless and one of the most productive varieties per plant. Soak seeds 8–12 hours before planting to speed germination. In zone 9 fall plantings (August–September) often produce high-quality pods as temperatures cool.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Jade is a spineless, open-pollinated okra producing straight, medium-green, ribbed pods with a texture and appearance valued in Asian cuisine — the name reflects its appeal in Chinese and Vietnamese cooking where the mild-flavored, tender pods are stir-fried, braised, and used in soups. The medium-height plant produces generous yields of pods that hold their quality for harvest at 3–4 inches without becoming fibrous as quickly as some varieties. The spineless habit makes harvesting considerably more comfortable than thorny-spine varieties and allows the plants to be handled without protective clothing. In zone 9 Jade okra thrives in the long, hot growing season and can be planted in spring for an early summer crop and again in late summer for a fall harvest — two full production cycles are achievable in zone 9.

common_name: Jade Pagoda Chinese Cabbage (Tall Columnar Napa Cabbage)
plant_note: Direct sow in well-tilled, fertile soil or start indoors and transplant; Jade Pagoda is best grown as a fall crop in zone 9 — direct sow August through September for harvest November through January. Spring crops can bolt in warming weather; direct sow March for early spring harvest. Thin to 12–15 inches for full-sized heads. Chinese cabbage is a heavy feeder and benefits from consistent moisture and regular nitrogen applications.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in well-tilled, fertile soil; thin to 12–15 inches for full-sized heads. Jade Pagoda is a tall, columnar Chinese cabbage (napa cabbage) that differs in form from the more squat, barrel-shaped types like Michihili and standard napa types — the heads are distinctly elongated (14–18 inches tall, 8–10 inches wide), with a compact, upright, tower-like form reminiscent of a pagoda spire, which gives the variety its name. The elongated form produces a higher proportion of the central, tightly blanched, pale yellow-green interior leaves relative to total head weight — the most tender and mildly flavored portion — compared to rounder, more compact types. Jade Pagoda has excellent storage quality: the tight, dense heads keep well in refrigeration (4–6 weeks) without significant quality loss. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and delicate — the characteristic Chinese cabbage flavor that is far milder than Western cabbage types — excellent raw in salads (particularly Korean kimchi-style preparations), cooked in stir-fries and soups, and in the braised Chinese preparations where the sweet, soft, cooked texture complements soy and ginger sauces. An excellent variety for gardeners who want to grow Chinese cabbage and experiment with Korean or Asian cooking traditions.

plant_note: Start indoors early; peppers need warm soil and nights above 55F to transplant.
directions: This classic heirloom produces thick-walled, three-to-four-inch fruits with moderate heat and robust flavor for stuffing, slicing, or grilling. Start seeds indoors eight weeks before the last frost, as peppers need a long warm season. Transplant only after nights stay reliably above 55 degrees and the soil has warmed. Pick fruits green for typical jalapeno flavor, or let them ripen red for extra sweetness and heat.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in a warm starting mix and maintain soil temperature above 75°F for best germination. Transplant to the garden once nights are reliably warm and the soil is fully settled. For hotter fruit, allow stress by reducing water slightly as fruits mature. Harvest at 3–4 inches long while still firm and dark green, or leave on the plant until red for a milder, slightly sweeter heat.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun 2–4 weeks after the last frost date when soil is reliably warm; in zone 9, jalapeños often overwinter as perennials and produce a second season's harvest.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the soil has warmed thoroughly; Jalapeño is the most widely grown and most universally recognized hot pepper in American gardens and cuisine — a medium-heat (2,500–8,000 Scoville units) pepper with thick-walled, cylindrical to conical, dark-green fruits that turn red when fully mature. The glossy green jalapeños are harvested at 2.5–3.5 inches long before turning red for the classic fresh, pickled, and canned jalapeño used in Mexican, Tex-Mex, and American cooking. Red-ripe jalapeños are sweeter and somewhat hotter than green-harvested fruit. In zone 9, jalapeños thrive through the warm season and often survive mild winters as perennials, re-sprouting from the base to produce a large, established second-year plant with significantly higher fruit production than first-year plants. The compact, bushy habit requires no staking and makes jalapeños appropriate for container culture as well as garden beds. Harvest green jalapeños when the fruit is firm and full-sized; allow some fruits to turn red for a sweeter product. Excellent for fresh salsa, pickling, stuffing (chile poppers/jalapeños stuffed with cream cheese), and smoking (chipotles are dried, smoked jalapeños).

common_name: Jamaican Hot Chocolate Pepper (Chocolate-Brown Fruity Habanero-Type)
plant_note: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Jamaican Hot Chocolate is a chocolate-brown habanero-type pepper from Jamaica with fruity, smoky heat.
directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Jamaican Hot Chocolate bears wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen to a deep chocolate-brown, carrying the characteristic fruity, floral habanero aroma along with intense heat and a subtly smoky depth of flavor that distinguishes it from orange and red habanero types. It is a favorite among hot sauce makers for the complex flavor it lends alongside its heat. The vigorous plants are productive in warm climates over a long season; pick pods once fully colored for the best flavor.

common_name: Jambalaya Okra (Compact Dwarf Productive Okra for Small Gardens)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost when soil is warm (70°F+) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Jambalaya's compact size (36–42 inches vs 6–8 feet for standard okra) makes it practical for raised beds and container growing — even a 5-gallon container supports one plant.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Jambalaya is a compact, dwarf okra hybrid producing the full flavor and productivity of standard okra on a plant roughly half the height of traditional okra varieties — reaching only 3–4 feet versus the 6–8 feet of older varieties like Clemson Spineless. The compact size makes Jambalaya practical for raised beds, containers (5-gallon minimum), and gardens where standard-height okra would create shade problems or require staking. Despite the reduced height, fruit production per plant is excellent — the compact branching structure holds pods within easy reach without the ladder-or-bending situation that harvesting from full-height okra plants requires. The pods are standard green okra with the classic flavor, tender at 3–4 inches and maturing at the typical rapid okra pace (daily checking required at peak production). Jambalaya's compact habit also makes it attractive as a temporary summer ornamental — the large, lightly lobed leaves, yellow hibiscus-like flowers with red centers, and developing pods create a tropical visual effect that is ornamental as well as productive. In zone 9, Jambalaya thrives through the hottest Gulf South summer months when most other vegetables are stressed — okra is one of the few crops that genuinely performs at its best during July and August heat.

plant_note: Direct sow into loosened, stone-free soil and thin early to avoid misshapen roots; roots hold well in the ground for late-season harvest.
directions: A Victorian-era English heirloom that became a staple of British kitchen gardens and allotments soon after its introduction in the 1880s, prized for combining a deep scarlet-orange color with reliably heavy yields. The roots are medium-long with a blunt tip, sitting between short stump-rooted carrots and the longest tapering types, which makes them adaptable to a range of soil depths. Direct sow into loosened, stone-free soil and thin early to avoid misshapen roots; roots hold well in the ground for late-season harvest.

plant_note: Start indoors in late summer (26–20 weeks before first frost) for a fall and winter harvest; January King is a savoy-type heirloom with semi-crinkled leaves that develop its characteristic red-purple outer coloring only after cold exposure — the heads taste best after frost has touched them.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before the transplanting date (late summer, aiming for outdoor planting in August–September for a winter harvest) or direct sow in early summer for fall maturity. January King is a centuries-old French and British heirloom winter cabbage that produces medium-sized, semi-round, savoy-type heads with beautifully crinkled, reddish-purple-flushed outer leaves and green-white inner leaves; it is exceptionally cold-hardy, standing in the garden through temperatures well below freezing and becoming sweeter with each frost. Transplant into well-amended, deeply prepared, slightly alkaline to neutral soil and firm the seedling in well to prevent wind-rocking; collar or brassica cage against caterpillars and aphids which are the main pests. In zone 8–9, grow as an overwintering crop planted in September for harvest January through March.

plant_note: Plant root cuttings or young container trees in spring in average to rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; root suckers freely once established, which is the easiest way to start new plants and also how established colonies expand and are thinned for shoot harvest.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese angelica tree is a large, sparsely branched, spiny-stemmed understory tree grown throughout Japan and Korea for its highly prized spring shoots — known as dureup or taranome — which are snapped off while still tightly furled, blanched or lightly battered and fried as tempura, and valued for a distinctive bittersweet, slightly resinous flavor. Established plants sucker readily from the roots to form a spreading colony, and shoot harvest is timed to remove the terminal buds from two- and three-year-old suckers each spring, which also keeps the colony to a manageable size. Left unharvested it becomes a bold architectural small tree with huge, twice-compound leaves and large plumes of white flowers in late summer followed by black berries relished by birds; variegated ornamental selections are grown for foliage alone. Give it room to sucker and site it away from foot traffic, since both stems and leaf stalks carry sharp prickles.

common_name: Japanese Black Trifele Tomato (Dark Pear-Shaped Rich Heirloom Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Japanese Black Trifele was actually developed in Russia (despite the 'Japanese' name) and introduced to American seed savers through Russian seed trading networks.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Japanese Black Trifele (also called Japanese Truffle) is a Russian heirloom producing unusual pear-shaped to truffle-shaped (the 'trifele' name references the truffle mushroom shape) fruits in a striking deep mahogany-black to brownish-red color with complex, rich, wine-like flavor that has made it one of the most celebrated dark-fleshed heirloom tomatoes in American seed-saving circles. The pear shape and dark color are both distinctive — the elongated, slightly rounded-bottom pear form with its near-black exterior creates an unusual appearance that is immediately recognizable at the farmers market and in the garden. The red-brown flesh has a rich, dense, complex flavor with deep savory undertones that differ from the fruity brightness of standard red or the simple sweetness of yellow tomatoes — a flavor profile well-suited to cooking, sauces, and combinations with cheese and herbs. Despite the 'Japanese' in the name, this variety was developed and preserved in Russia. The medium-sized fruits (4–6 oz) are more practical for everyday use than giant beefsteaks while still providing exceptional flavor. The dark color comes from anthocyanin production in the skin triggered by sun exposure.

plant_note: Divide rhizome sections with a bud in early spring or fall and plant in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, rich soil in full to partial shade; Japanese butterbur spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes in moist conditions — confine with buried root barriers or allow in a dedicated wet, shaded area.
directions: Divide rhizome sections in early spring or fall and plant in consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade; Japanese butterbur (fuki) is a large, bold foliage perennial with rounded leaves that can reach 2–4 feet across on stiff petioles — producing one of the most dramatic tropical-looking foliage effects achievable with a cold-hardy plant in the shade garden. Before the leaves emerge in early spring, compact clusters of small, whitish flowers rise on stout scapes, producing the first bloom of the woodland season. The thick, edible leaf stalks (petioles) are a traditional Japanese vegetable — blanched, pickled (tsukudani), or cooked in miso soup as fuki — harvested in early spring before the leaves fully expand. The plant spreads vigorously by underground rhizomes in moist conditions and can colonize large areas rapidly; manage spread by installing buried barriers or confine to a naturally wet, shaded depression. An outstanding bold-leaf specimen for water garden margins, shaded stream banks, and large-scale woodland plantings.

plant_note: Earlier and more productive than large globe types in cool summers.
directions: Long, slender, thin-skinned fruit with tender flesh that cooks quickly and rarely needs peeling. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant into black plastic mulch to boost soil temperature in cooler regions. Feed with a balanced fertilizer and keep evenly watered to prevent bitter, seedy fruit. Cut fruit with pruners while young and glossy, typically at 6 to 8 inches long. These plants often outyield globe eggplants where summers are short or mild.

plant_note: Sow in blocks after frost; isolate from other corn to keep it true.
directions: This compact heirloom reaches about five feet tall, making it well suited to smaller gardens while producing two or three short, full ears per stalk. Sow directly into warm soil in blocks of several rows to ensure good wind pollination. Keep it isolated from sweet or dent corn so the popping quality stays true. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, then cure the tender, low-hull kernels further indoors before popping.

common_name: Japanese Long Cucumber (Kyuri, Japanese Burpless Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Japanese cucumber thrives on vertical trellising — the climbing vines produce straighter fruits and better air circulation when grown vertically, and trellising is standard practice for this cucumber in Japanese and Asian-style gardens.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a trellis for straight fruits and good air circulation. Japanese long cucumber ('Kyuri' in Japanese) is the standard cucumber of Japanese cuisine and is distinct from both the thicker-skinned American slicing cucumber and the ribbed Chinese varieties — producing slender (1–1.5 inch diameter), uniformly dark green, smooth-skinned fruits 8–12 inches long with exceptionally thin, tender skin that needs no peeling, very small seed cavity, dense crisp flesh, and mild, sweet, refreshing flavor with virtually no bitterness. The thin skin and low cucurbitacin content make it 'burpless' and highly digestible, and the crisp, dense flesh holds its texture remarkably well in sliced preparations. Japanese cucumbers are the standard for pickled cucumber preparations (as in the Japanese salted tsukemono tradition) because of their superior texture, and they are equally outstanding for fresh eating, in salads, and in Korean oi sobagi kimchi. Multiple varieties are grown in Japanese commercial and home horticulture, all sharing the smooth skin, thin wall, dense flesh, and mild flavor characteristics. Production is very heavy when vines are trellised and harvested regularly, and the plants perform well in the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf South summer.

common_name: Japanese Oxheart Tomato (Meaty Pink-Red Oxheart Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Japanese Oxheart is a large, meaty, heart-shaped heirloom tomato of Japanese origin.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Japanese Oxheart bears large, heart-shaped fruit in pink to pink-red with dense, meaty flesh and few seeds, the classic oxheart form prized for slicing and sauce alike, on productive indeterminate vines. Its rich, well-balanced flavor and substantial fruit size have kept it popular among heirloom tomato collectors. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor and texture.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into warm soil; long vines need generous space.
directions: An Australian heirloom pumpkin with striking silvery blue-grey skin, deep ribbing, and a drum shape, plus sweet, nutty, stringless orange flesh, in 6 to 12 pound fruits. Direct sow after frost into warm soil, giving the long vines plenty of room. Water deeply and feed richly while fruit sizes up, resting pumpkins on straw. Harvest when the rind hardens and coloring is complete, and cure for both decoration and cooking.

common_name: Jarrahdale Squash (Australian Heritage Blue-Grey Pumpkin with Dense Sweet Orange Flesh)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Jarrahdale is a Cucurbita maxima type that requires at least 95 days and performs well in zone 9's long growing season. Plant March–April for October harvest. The distinctive flat, deeply-ribbed, blue-grey skin of Jarrahdale does not change color significantly at harvest maturity — look instead for dried stem, firm rind, and overall size (typically 7–10 lbs when ripe). The blue-grey skin of Jarrahdale is unique and is associated with a specific group of Australian heritage pumpkins that produce the grey-blue skin color from a specific combination of pigments and wax bloom; this color group includes Queensland Blue, Crown Prince, and other varieties sharing similar heritage and the distinctive blue-grey appearance. The flesh is deep orange, dense, dry, and very sweet — particularly well suited for pumpkin soups, curries, pies, and roasting where a dry, high-starch pumpkin flesh is preferred.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost; harvest when stem dries and skin is firm grey-blue. Jarrahdale Squash (also called Jarrahdale Pumpkin in its native Australia, where 'pumpkin' is the standard term for what North Americans call both pumpkin and winter squash) is an Australian heritage variety named after the town of Jarrahdale in the Darling Ranges southeast of Perth, Western Australia, where the variety was grown and maintained by local families before being recognized and distributed more widely. The Jarrahdale pumpkin belongs to a distinctive Australian heritage pumpkin group characterized by grey-blue skin — a color produced by a combination of pigmentation and a powdery wax bloom on the skin surface — that distinguishes these varieties from the orange and tan pumpkins dominating North American markets. This blue-grey color group, which includes Queensland Blue, Crown Prince (United Kingdom), and related European heritage varieties, represents a distinct aesthetic and culinary tradition in which the blue skin and dense, dry orange flesh are valued for specific culinary properties. The flesh of Jarrahdale is particularly dry and dense for a large pumpkin — significantly less watery than most carving pumpkins and many North American pie pumpkins — which makes it exceptional for preparations where moisture content affects texture: pumpkin soup (concentrated flavor without excessive water thinning), pumpkin curry, and baked preparations where excess moisture causes sogginess.
