The flavor is genuinely sweet and complex, with a depth that makes Jarrahdale one of the most culinarily respected heritage pumpkin varieties in Australian cooking and in North American heirloom vegetable circles.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Jasper is a 2013 All-America Selections winner and one of the only cherry tomatoes resistant to both early and late blight along with Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and septoria leaf spot, a rare disease package that suits the humid, blight-prone Gulf South growing season.
directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines; Jasper was named an All-America Selections winner for being one of the very few cherry tomatoes with resistance to both early and late blight, alongside resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and septoria leaf spot, giving it an outstanding disease package for humid, disease-prone gardens. It produces heavy, extended clusters of small, deep red, exceptionally sweet cherry fruit with a crack-resistant skin that holds up on the vine. Because it keeps healthy foliage even under the fungal disease pressure that builds in a wet Gulf Coast summer, Jasper tends to remain productive well after less resistant cherry tomatoes have declined. Pick fruit as clusters ripen to full red color and harvest regularly to keep the vine setting new flowers.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; transplant into warm soil after all frost danger passes and stake or cage the vines.
directions: A French heirloom prized for its abundant clusters of smooth, round, apricot-orange fruits about 2-3 ounces each, with thin skin and a balanced, fruity-sweet flavor often compared to a ripe apricot. Start seed indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, transplant into warm, fertile soil, and stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines, which crop heavily and hold up well through Gulf South heat. Pick fruit as soon as it colors fully to keep the thin skins from splitting after summer rain, and expect steady production from early summer until frost.

plant_note: Direct sow with fresh seed once soil is workable; roots sweeten after fall frost.
directions: A canker-resistant parsnip that holds well in the ground, letting you leave roots to sweeten over a long 110-day season. Direct sow fresh seed shallowly into loose, stone-free soil, keeping the surface moist through the slow germination. Thin seedlings to a few inches apart for long, well-formed roots. Harvest after fall frosts, which convert starches to sugar for the sweetest flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65F; in zone 9 plant April-May for harvest late August-September. Jazzman is an aromatic, jasmine-type long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter as a domestic alternative to imported jasmine rice.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Jazzman is an aromatic long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter and bred to rival imported jasmine rice in fragrance and cooking quality, giving Gulf South growers a domestically adapted option for fragrant rice. The grain develops a distinctive popcorn-like aroma during cooking and a soft, slightly sticky texture similar to Thai jasmine rice, making it well suited to Southeast Asian and Cajun-Creole dishes alike. Keep the bed continuously saturated through the growing season, since consistent moisture through grain fill is especially important for developing the variety's signature aroma and flavor. Harvest when seed heads droop and turn golden-tan, then dry thoroughly before hulling and storing; aromatic rice varieties are somewhat more prone to losing fragrance in storage than standard long-grain types, so use home-hulled grain within the first several months for the best aroma.

common_name: Jenny Lind Melon (Early American Heirloom Ribbed Muskmelon)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; Jenny Lind is a small (1–2 lb), very heavily ribbed, deeply lobed heirloom muskmelon with distinctive turban-like bumps at the blossom end and unusually light green to apple-green flesh — one of the oldest American named melon varieties (dating to the 1840s), named for the famous Swedish opera singer Jenny Lind who toured America in 1851 to enormous popular acclaim.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Jenny Lind melons are small and compact compared to modern varieties, making them suitable for small gardens; harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine with gentle pressure and the blossom-end softens slightly; the green flesh is unusual for American melons and has a delicate, sweet, slightly floral flavor. Jenny Lind is one of the oldest and most historically documented named melon varieties in American horticulture — it was listed in seed catalogs by the 1840s and became extremely popular in the northeastern states (particularly New Jersey, where it was widely grown for the Philadelphia and New York markets) during the latter half of the 19th century, remaining a garden standard well into the early 20th century before modern hybrids displaced it. The variety is named in honor of Jenny Lind (1820–1887), the Swedish opera singer known as the 'Swedish Nightingale,' whose American tour managed by P.T. Barnum in 1850–1851 created an extraordinary popular sensation — everything from hairstyles to trains to songs to garden plants were named for her in that era. Jenny Lind melon is distinctive in several ways: the small (typically 1–2 pound) round fruits are deeply ribbed with prominent ridges running from stem to blossom end, and the blossom end has a characteristic raised, button-like knob in the center of a depression — a 'turban' or 'navel' that is unique among common muskmelons. The flesh is a pale sea-green to apple-green color (not the familiar salmon-orange of modern cantaloupes) that is thin relative to the total fruit size but very sweet and floral in flavor. Jenny Lind ripens about 2 weeks earlier than standard cantaloupes, making it an excellent choice for short-season gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring through early summer (Jericho tolerates warmer soil and air temperatures than most lettuces), or in fall; this variety was developed in Israel for the extreme heat of the Jordan Valley — the name references Jericho, one of the hottest inhabited cities on earth — and is the premier heat-tolerant Romaine for gardeners who want salad lettuce through warm spring and early summer when other Romaine varieties bolt rapidly.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep; Jericho tolerates warmer soil and air temperatures than most lettuces, extending the spring sowing season by 2–4 weeks beyond the window suitable for other varieties; provide afternoon shade in the hottest weather; thin to 8–12 inches; harvest full heads or use as cut-and-come-again. Jericho is an Israeli-developed Romaine (Cos) type lettuce bred specifically for the extreme heat of the Jordan Valley and the Mediterranean climate of Israel, where summer temperatures regularly exceed 100°F and conventional lettuce bolts immediately. The variety was developed to remain productive longer into warm weather than any other Romaine, and delivers this through exceptional heat tolerance — it is typically the last lettuce still producing usable heads when spring heat arrives in mid-latitude gardens, and one of the earliest candidates for late-summer planting when other varieties would bolt immediately. The large, upright heads have crisp, pale green Romaine-style leaves with excellent flavor — sweet, slightly nutty, and refreshing — and the heads are notably larger than many other heat-tolerant varieties. For Gulf Coast gardeners (zones 8b–10), Jericho is the most valuable Romaine for the challenging transition from cool-season winter lettuce into warming spring, providing 2–4 extra weeks of production compared to standard varieties. Highly recommended by Territorial Seed and Johnny's for hot-summer and transition-zone gardens.

common_name: Jericho Romaine Lettuce (Israeli Heat-Tolerant Bolt-Resistant Cos Lettuce)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Jericho is exceptional for late spring and early fall planting in zone 9 where standard romaine varieties bolt quickly in warming temperatures. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring, or September–October for fall. Jericho's heat tolerance means it continues producing for 2–4 weeks longer into spring warming than standard romaine types before bolting — a significant practical advantage in zone 9 where the spring growing window for lettuce is brief. The variety's Israeli breeding (developed near the city of Jericho in a very hot, arid climate) was specifically targeted at producing quality lettuce in conditions that challenge European and North American varieties.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting in early spring or fall; transplant to partial shade in warm seasons to extend the harvest. Harvest outer leaves or whole heads when compact and firm. Jericho Romaine is an Israeli-bred romaine (cos) lettuce developed by breeders working in the conditions of the Jordan Valley near the ancient city of Jericho — an arid, extremely hot agricultural region where the development of heat-tolerant lettuce was driven by practical necessity to extend the local growing season. The breeding produced a romaine variety with substantially better heat tolerance and bolt resistance than standard European and American romaine types, and Jericho has become one of the most recommended romaine varieties for warm-climate gardeners and for late-spring plantings in temperate zones where other romaine varieties rapidly bolt when temperatures rise. The heads are upright, tightly folded, medium-large, dark green, with the crisp, mildly bitter interior quality of classic romaine. For zone 9 gardeners, Jericho's heat-tolerance advantage translates to a 2–4 week extension of the spring romaine harvest window before heat triggers bolting — a meaningful extension in climates where the transition from cool to hot weather happens rapidly. Jericho is also appropriate for early fall planting when temperatures are still warm but declining.

common_name: Jermor Shallot (French Banana Shallot, RHS AGM)
plant_note: Plant sets four to eight weeks before the last frost in spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions; Jermor is a French-bred banana-type shallot noted for its elongated shape and refined flavor.
directions: Plant individual sets about an inch deep and six to eight inches apart, with the tip just at or slightly above the soil surface, and keep the bed weeded and evenly watered through spring growth. Jermor is a French 'banana' or échalion-type shallot bred in Brittany, producing clusters of medium to large, elegantly elongated bulbs with glossy rose-copper skin and pale pink-tinged flesh prized for its refined, mild-sweet flavor. Reduce watering once the foliage begins to yellow and fall over, then lift the bulbs and cure them in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks before trimming and storing. Well-cured bulbs keep for several months in cool, dry storage.

common_name: Jersey Devil Tomato (New Jersey Heirloom Banana Paste Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Jersey Devil is an indeterminate vine that benefits from sturdy caging or trellising. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production. The elongated banana-shaped fruits (6–8 inches, pointed at the blossom end) are meaty with very few seeds — excellent for sauce, roasting, and drying, where the low moisture and dense flesh concentrate flavor and reduce cooking time.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil after last frost. Stake or cage plants before or at transplanting. Jersey Devil is a New Jersey heirloom paste tomato with an immediately recognizable elongated, banana-shaped to horn-shaped fruit form: 5–8 inches long, tapered to a sharp point at the blossom end, with bright red skin and very dense, meaty flesh. The distinctive shape — sometimes described as resembling a long red chili pepper at a glance — makes Jersey Devil one of the most visually unusual paste tomatoes. The eating quality matches the visual appeal: the flesh is very dense and dry with minimal gel and seeds, a high solid content that makes it ideal for tomato sauce (concentrates quickly without extended cooking), sun-dried tomatoes, and oven-roasted preparations where the low moisture prevents the pan from becoming soupy. Jersey Devil is an indeterminate vine that produces heavily over a long season; the fruits ripen mid-season (78–88 days from transplant) and continue until frost. The variety is strongly connected to New Jersey, where it appears in the regional heirloom seed tradition alongside other East Coast paste types.

common_name: Jersey Giant Asparagus (Rutgers All-Male Hybrid Asparagus)
plant_note: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jersey Giant is an all-male hybrid that puts no energy into seed production, channeling more resources into thick, vigorous spear growth and higher yields than older open-pollinated varieties.
directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge over the growing season. Jersey Giant is one of the Rutgers University all-male hybrid asparagus cultivars, bred so that plants never set seed and instead direct all their energy into producing thick, vigorous, high-yielding spears over a long productive lifespan. It also carries good resistance to Fusarium crown and root rot, a serious disease problem in older asparagus plantings, making it one of the more reliable modern choices for a home asparagus bed. Do not harvest any spears the first year and only lightly the second year, allowing the fern-like foliage to grow through summer to build a strong root system for many years of future harvests.

plant_note: Set dormant one-year crowns into trenches 6-8 inches deep as soon as soil is workable in spring, then gradually backfill as spears emerge.
directions: Jersey King is one of the Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus lines bred for resistance to Fusarium crown rot and asparagus rust while eliminating the volunteer seedlings that female plants produce. It sends up thick, uniform, deep-green spears with tightly closed tips over a long spring harvest window. Because energy is not diverted into seed production, established beds tend to build vigor faster than open-pollinated types like Mary Washington. Give plants a full season to establish before taking any harvest, and top-dress with compost each fall to sustain crown health for decades.

common_name: Jersey Knight Asparagus (Rutgers All-Male Hybrid Asparagus for Southern Gardens)
plant_note: Plant 1-year-old crowns (rhizomes) in early spring 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench with a mound of loose soil under each crown; spread the roots over the mound and cover. Asparagus is a long-lived perennial that may remain productive for 15–25 years if properly established — invest in thorough soil preparation (18 inches deep, well-amended with compost) before planting. Do not harvest in the establishment years: the first year after planting, allow all spears to grow into ferns (foliage) to build root reserves; in the second year, harvest for just 2 weeks; in the third year, harvest 4–6 weeks; from year four onward, harvest the full 6–8 week season. In zone 9, asparagus is challenging — it needs cold winters for adequate dormancy and in the warmest years may not set adequate root reserves for the following season.
directions: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench; allow all fern growth in the first year. Feed annually with balanced fertilizer after harvest. Jersey Knight is an all-male F1 hybrid asparagus from the New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station at Rutgers University — part of the 'Jersey' series of asparagus hybrids (including Jersey Giant and Jersey Supreme) that revolutionized asparagus production in the United States from the 1980s onward by introducing all-male genetics, disease resistance, and dramatically improved yield over the open-pollinated varieties that had been standard for a century. The key innovation of the Jersey series is their all-male genetics: asparagus is naturally dioecious (separate male and female plants), and female plants divert significant energy into berry and seed production that could otherwise go to spear production; all-male hybrids eliminate this energy diversion and direct all plant resources to the edible spears, resulting in 2–3× the yield of traditional open-pollinated varieties under the same conditions. Jersey Knight carries improved resistance to asparagus rust and Fusarium crown rot — two diseases that significantly reduce the productive lifespan of traditional varieties in warm, humid climates. In zone 9, Jersey Knight is among the better-adapted of the Jersey hybrids due to its moderate heat tolerance and disease package; while asparagus is genuinely challenging in zone 9's warm winters, Jersey Knight has performed better in southern trials than many other varieties.

common_name: Jersey Supreme Asparagus (Early High-Yield Rutgers Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jersey Supreme is an improved Rutgers all-male hybrid selected for earlier spring emergence and higher total yield than older asparagus cultivars.
directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge. Jersey Supreme is a later-generation Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus bred for earlier spring spear emergence and higher overall yield than older selections like Jersey Giant, while retaining the same good disease resistance and long-term productivity that made the Jersey series a standard choice for home and commercial asparagus plantings. As an all-male hybrid it never sets seed, so all of the plant's energy goes into vigorous spear production over what can be a fifteen-to-twenty-year productive bed lifespan. Avoid harvesting the first year and harvest only lightly the second year to let the root system establish fully before full production begins.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant in early spring; tolerates light frost.
directions: This historic heirloom, dating to the 1840s, forms distinctive pointed heads with sweet flavor and matures early on compact plants ideal for small gardens. Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant hardened seedlings in early spring. Cabbage tolerates light frost, so it can go out before tender crops. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest the conical heads when firm to avoid splitting.

plant_note: Plant tuber sections (each with 2–3 eyes) 3–5 inches deep and 12–18 inches apart in any well-drained soil in full sun; Jerusalem artichoke spreads aggressively by underground tubers and should be contained or given a dedicated bed.
directions: Plant tuber sections 3–5 inches deep around the last frost date in any well-drained soil — Jerusalem artichoke is remarkably tolerant of poor soils, drought, and neglect, producing masses of crunchy, nutty, sweet tubers in autumn that can be harvested after frost improves their flavor by converting inulin to sugars. The plants reach 6–10 feet tall and produce small yellow sunflowers in late summer. Harvest tubers from fall through early spring by digging; leave some tubers in the ground to re-sprout and produce next year's crop. Note that inulin is not digested by most people and can cause significant gas — start with small servings and cook thoroughly to reduce this effect.

common_name: Jerusalem Artichoke Sunchoke (Native Perennial Sunflower Tuber Vegetable)
plant_note: Plant tuber pieces (2–3 inch sections with at least one eye) 4–6 inches deep in spring; sunchoke is a native North American perennial that grows vigorously in the Gulf South, reaching 6–10 feet tall by summer. In zone 9, plant February–April; harvest tubers after fall frost knocks back the tops (November–February). Jerusalem artichoke naturalizes readily from missed tubers — plant in a contained bed or where spreading is acceptable, as it is difficult to fully remove once established. Harvest as needed through the winter; tubers store poorly off the plant but keep well in the ground.
directions: Plant 2–3 inch tuber pieces 4–6 inches deep in spring; harvest tubers in late fall through winter after tops die back. Jerusalem Artichoke (Helianthus tuberosus, also called Sunchoke) is a native North American perennial plant of the sunflower family — widely distributed across eastern and central North America where it was cultivated by Indigenous peoples as a staple starchy food long before European contact. The name is misleading: it has no connection to Jerusalem (possibly a corruption of the Italian girasole, meaning sunflower) and is not an artichoke (the flavor resemblance to artichoke heart inspired the name). The edible part is the knobby, irregular underground tuber — tan to purple-skinned with white, crisp flesh that tastes sweet, nutty, and faintly artichoke-like when eaten raw, and takes on a creamier, sweeter character when roasted or cooked. The distinctive carbohydrate of sunchoke tubers is inulin (not starch), a prebiotic fiber that feeds beneficial gut bacteria — making sunchokes notable for their probiotic benefits. The plants themselves are spectacular: 6–10 feet tall by summer, topped with bright yellow sunflowers in late summer and fall. In zone 9, sunchoke thrives with minimal care in the summer heat, requiring no watering once established in reasonably good soil.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start seeds in January for March transplanting. Jet Star is an indeterminate hybrid that bears over a long season and is well-suited to staking or caging in full sun.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Jet Star is a popular indeterminate hybrid tomato introduced by Harris Seeds in the late 1960s that earned a lasting following among home gardeners for its combination of large, smooth, red, globe-shaped fruits (8–12 oz) with distinctively mild, low-acid flavor that appeals to people who find standard tomatoes too tart — the low-acid character makes Jet Star the variety of choice for those who love the fresh tomato experience without acid sensitivity. The smooth, crack-resistant fruits have few seeds and thick walls, making them excellent slicing tomatoes for sandwiches and salads; they also hold up well in cooking but are really at their finest fresh off the vine at warm room temperature. VF disease resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2) keeps plants productive through the season. Jet Star is a mid-season tomato (70–75 days from transplant) and bears continuously as an indeterminate variety — plants will need staking or caging as they can reach 5–6 feet. An excellent choice for gardeners who prefer mild, low-acid tomatoes, and a reliable producer in zone 8–10 spring and fall tomato seasons.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Jetstar is a popular hybrid slicer bred for disease resistance and a mild, low-acid flavor on a productive indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the indeterminate vine. Jetstar is a widely grown hybrid slicing tomato valued for its mild, low-acid flavor that appeals to gardeners sensitive to more acidic tomatoes, combined with good resistance to verticillium and fusarium wilts that helps it stay productive through a long growing season. It produces smooth, round, meaty red fruit with few seeds and good crack resistance. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot, and feed regularly through the season to keep the vigorous vine productive from early summer into fall.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth; transplant well after frost when nights stay warm.
directions: A container-friendly eggplant with a tidy habit and glossy oval purple fruits best picked at 3 to 4.5 inches long. Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, then transplant once nights stay reliably warm. Keep evenly watered and mulched, and harvest regularly from this prolific plant to keep new fruit setting. Pick while the skin is glossy for the firmest, best texture.

common_name: Jewel Sweet Potato (1970 NCSU Orange Standard)
plant_note: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F; Jewel was released in 1970 by North Carolina State University and was the dominant American commercial sweet potato variety from the late 1970s through the 1990s, grown primarily in North Carolina, Louisiana, and Virginia — it remains a reliable home garden standard with excellent moist orange flesh and consistent yields.
directions: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms above 65°F; Jewel tolerates less-than-ideal soil conditions better than many newer varieties. Jewel was developed and released in 1970 by North Carolina State University as part of the USDA–state cooperative sweet potato breeding program and became the dominant American commercial sweet potato throughout the 1970s–1990s; it produced the standard against which American sweet potatoes were judged for two decades before Beauregard's introduction. The medium to large, elongated, smooth, coppery-orange to red-orange-skinned roots have intensely orange, moist, sweet flesh that softens to a creamy consistency when baked — an excellent texture for traditional sweet potato preparations. Flavor is sweet and complex with good caramel development during baking. Self-reliant and productive; excellent for Gulf Coast spring planting in late March through April and fall planting in June through July.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds on the soil surface in partial shade after frost, or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; jewels of opar self-seeds prolifically in warm climates and, once introduced, typically maintains itself as a self-renewing annual or short-lived perennial groundcover in partial-shade gardens without further sowing.
directions: Direct-sow seeds on soil surface in partial shade or full sun after frost; jewels of opar (Brazilian spinach, fameflower, pink baby's breath) is a tropical perennial succulent of the purslane family (Portulacaceae) that serves a dual role as an edible leafy vegetable and an ornamental plant — the fleshy, oval, bright-green leaves are eaten raw in salads (with a mildly astringent, spinach-like flavor) or cooked as a pot herb, while the plant itself produces an ornamental display of hundreds of tiny, rosy-pink to magenta, five-petaled flowers on widely branched, airy, 12–24-inch flowering stems, creating a delicate pink-mist effect above the succulent foliage. In warm climates it grows as a drought-tolerant, shade-tolerant annual or short-lived perennial that self-seeds freely to maintain permanent colonies in partially shaded garden beds, pathways, and edges. Unlike most leafy greens, it thrives in the combination of heat, drought, and partial shade that defeats most other edibles in Gulf Coast and tropical summers. An excellent dual-purpose plant for edible/ornamental shade gardens in zone 8–12.

plant_note: Sow 2–4 weeks after last frost into warm soil; jicama needs a long frost-free season of at least 5 months and thrives in zone 9–11 Gulf Coast conditions.
directions: Sow scarified seeds 1 in deep in loose, deep, well-drained soil 2–4 weeks after the last frost once soil is thoroughly warm. Jicama is a vigorous vine requiring a sturdy trellis; pinch flower buds as they appear throughout the season — leaving flowers reduces tuber size dramatically since the plant diverts energy to seed set. Begin harvesting small tubers at about 5 months; larger tubers become more fibrous if left past 9 months. Only the roots are edible — all above-ground parts, including seeds and pods, contain rotenone and are toxic.

common_name: Jimmy Nardello Pepper (Sweet Italian Frying Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Jimmy Nardello is a Slow Food Ark of Taste heirloom — an irreplaceable variety of historical and culinary significance that merits preservation in home garden seed collections.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Jimmy Nardello is one of the most beloved heirloom sweet peppers in American home gardening — an Italian variety brought to Connecticut from Basilicata, Italy, by Giuseppa and Jimmy Nardello's family in 1887 and preserved in that family for nearly a century before being donated to the Seed Savers Exchange. The long, thin, curved, brilliant red fruits (8–10 inches, very thin walls) are among the sweetest of all peppers when fully ripe red — intensely concentrated sweet pepper flavor without any heat whatsoever. Jimmy Nardello is the premier sweet frying pepper: the thin walls mean the fruits cook in seconds in hot oil (traditional Italian fritto method) or over high heat on a grill, caramelizing immediately to a concentrated, smoky-sweet, almost jammy flavor that is entirely different from the fresh fruit character. The dried fruits are also exceptional for crushing into sweet paprika with excellent color and flavor. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved indefinitely and the variety preserved — Jimmy Nardello is recognized on the Slow Food Ark of Taste as a culturally significant food variety worth preserving. In zone 9, the plants are very productive from late spring through fall. The abundant, long, curved red fruits hanging from productive plants are visually beautiful and practically abundant.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Start these Italian heirloom frying peppers indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm at 70 to 90 degrees for reliable germination. Transplant seedlings out only after nights stay above 55 degrees, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. The long, tapered 6 to 12 inch fruits ripen from green to glossy red and are exceptionally sweet, making them ideal for frying. Provide consistent moisture and a light feeding once fruit sets to keep plants productive through the season.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 2 weeks after frost danger has passed once soil is warm.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix at 75–80°F and transplant after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil. This Italian heirloom from Basilicata bears long, thin-walled, crinkled fruits that dangle in clusters and turn from green to brilliant red at maturity. The fruits are nearly heat-free and intensely sweet, making them outstanding for frying in olive oil, roasting, or drying. Harvest when fully red for peak sweetness, or dry on a string in a warm, airy location — the thin walls dehydrate rapidly and concentrate flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination, in fertile soil in full sun, after all frost danger has passed. Allow the full season to dry down on the stalk for grinding into meal or distilling.
directions: Sow in blocks at least 4 rows wide in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; let ears fully dry on the stalk for the deepest color and best grinding or distilling quality. Jimmy Red is a South Carolina heirloom dent corn with a dramatic history — the variety nearly vanished entirely, surviving through only a handful of ears kept by a single South Carolina farming family, before being rediscovered and reintroduced in the 2010s by chef and miller Glenn Roberts of Anson Mills and distiller Scott Blackwell, who used it to help revive heirloom Southern corn whiskey and grits production. The deep garnet-red, almost purple-black kernels grind into a rich, distinctively flavored meal and grits, and the variety has become especially prized by craft distillers for producing bourbon and moonshine with a uniquely deep, earthy character credited to the corn's high oil content and pigmentation. A striking, historically significant heirloom for gardeners interested in Southern foodways and heritage grain, zone 6–10.

common_name: Jing Orange Okra (Chinese Heirloom Orange-Red Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); Jing Orange is a Chinese heirloom okra grown for its striking orange-red pods and stems, doubling as an ornamental as well as edible plant.
directions: Soak seed overnight before direct sowing an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun. Jing Orange is a Chinese heirloom okra bearing vivid orange-red pods on stems and foliage tinged with the same warm color, making it as striking in the garden as it is productive, while retaining good tenderness a bit longer than typical green okra before pods toughen. Harvest at 2-4 inches for the best texture, picking every couple of days through the growing season to keep plants producing continuously in the Gulf South's long, hot summer. The colorful pods make an attractive addition to a mixed vegetable bed or ornamental edible border in addition to their culinary use in gumbo, frying, and pickling.

plant_note: Direct-sow after last frost in moist, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Job's tears grows as a perennial in zones 9–11 and as an annual in cooler climates. It tolerates partial shade and moist to wet soils — an unusual quality among grain crops — and can be grown at water's edge. The hard, bead-like grains are surrounded by glossy white or gray pseudo-involucres that can be strung as beads.
directions: Direct-sow in moist, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Job's tears is a large, tropical grass from Southeast Asia grown both as a grain crop and as an ornamental and craft plant. The plant is unmistakable: large, corn-like leaves on tall stems produce pendulous clusters of hard, rounded, bead-like structures (involucres) containing the true grain, which ripen from green to white, gray, and sometimes blue-gray or black. These natural beads have a hole through the center and have been used for necklaces, rosaries, and ceremonial jewelry for thousands of years across Asia and the Pacific. The grain itself (adlay) is nutritious, with a mild, earthy flavor resembling barley, and is used in soups, porridges, teas, and brewing in China, Korea, Japan, and Southeast Asia. It is considered medicinal in traditional Chinese medicine. In zone 9–11, the plant can grow as a short-lived perennial. It tolerates moist soil and partial shade better than most grain crops, making it suitable for wet areas of the garden.

common_name: Joi Choi Pak Choi (Vigorous Upright Bok Choy)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during cool seasons; Joi Choi bolt resistance is notably better than standard pak choi cultivars, extending the harvest window in warm spring conditions.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during cool seasons; Joi Choi is the most widely recommended pak choi (bok choy) cultivar for American home gardens — an All-America Selections award winner producing an upright, well-formed head with crisp, white, thick, succulent stems and dark-green, smooth leaf blades in a clean, classic pak choi form. Joi Choi's excellence comes from the combination of very clean, upright growth habit (the stems don't spread outward messily like some varieties), exceptional bolt resistance for an early-maturing type (30–50 days), and excellent flavor — the stems are tender and mildly sweet, the leaves are tender with mild cabbage flavor, and the whole plant can be used in stir-fries, soups, and raw preparations. In zone 9, Joi Choi is grown September through April as a cool-season crop; in the heat of summer it bolts quickly. The bolt resistance is Joi Choi's key advantage — allowing it to be planted in late February and early March (early spring zone 9) before the heat arrives, with harvest extending a week or two longer than standard varieties. Harvest the whole head at soil level when it reaches full size (10–12 inches tall) or harvest outer leaves continuously for a prolonged cut-and-come-again harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks after last frost; Jubilee is a midseason yellow sweet corn with excellent flavor, good disease resistance, and adaptability to both Northern and Southern climates — a reliable, high-quality variety that performs well throughout zones 4–11 and is particularly well-suited to Gulf Coast gardens where it can be planted for both spring and fall corn seasons.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks; Jubilee is an SU type that benefits from block planting for good pollination and is best planted at least 400 feet from supersweet (SH2) types to prevent cross-pollination that reduces sweetness. Jubilee is a midseason (82–87 days) yellow sweet corn that has been widely grown in American gardens and markets since the 1950s and maintains a reputation for reliable production, excellent flavor, and adaptability to a wide range of climates from the Upper Midwest to the Gulf Coast; the large ears (8–9 inches) carry 14–16 rows of bright golden-yellow kernels with classic, rich sweet corn flavor — the balance of sweetness and traditional corn taste that makes fresh summer sweet corn a culinary experience distinct from the excessive sweetness of modern hybrid types. Jubilee has better disease resistance than many older varieties (including some tolerance to Stewart's wilt and common rust) and holds slightly longer in the field than older SU types. Outstanding in Gulf Coast gardens for both the spring crop (April–May planting) and fall crop (late July–August planting).

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in well-amended sandy-loam soil 1–2 weeks after last frost; Jubilee is a large, long-season Florida-bred watermelon well-adapted to the Gulf Coast, requiring ample space (8–12 feet between plants) and 3 months of warm weather for best production.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds, thinning to 2 plants per hill; Jubilee is a Florida-developed heirloom watermelon introduced in 1963 by the Florida Agricultural Experiment Station, producing oblong, striped fruits weighing 25–40 pounds with bright red, crisp, sweet flesh and gray-green skin with dark stripes — one of the classic large Southern watermelons grown at commercial scale for roadside markets. The long, oblong shape distinguishes it from round varieties; the sweet, firm, seedless-type flesh holds up well for transport and has excellent flavor. Resistant to fusarium wilt, which historically decimated Southern watermelon crops. A traditional choice for gardeners in the Gulf South who want a truly large, impressive watermelon with Southern heritage adapted to regional heat and humidity.

plant_note: Sow seed around or just after last frost at the foot of a tall, sturdy trellis, since this runner-type bean is a vigorous climber that needs a strong structure to support its weight.
directions: Sow seed around or just after last frost at the foot of a tall, sturdy trellis, since this runner-type bean is a vigorous climber that needs a strong structure to support its weight through the season. Grown for centuries in the volcanic soils around La Granja de San Ildefonso in Segovia, Spain, it produces some of the largest bean seeds in cultivation — broad, flat, and ivory-white — traditionally simmered slowly into the region's celebrated judión stew. Like other runner beans it flowers and sets pods best where summer nights stay relatively cool, dropping blossoms in prolonged heat. Leave pods on the vine until fully dry and papery before shelling the outsized beans for storage.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 transplant February–March for spring. Juliet is an indeterminate grape type that grows vigorously to 6–8 feet and sets fruit abundantly even during heat, making it excellent for zone 9 spring and fall plantings.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Juliet is a 1999 All-America Selections winner widely regarded as the standard-setter for the grape tomato category. The oval, grape-sized (1.5–2 inch) fruits grow in large trusses of 30–40 tomatoes and have a particularly rich, complex flavor — a balance of sweetness and acidity often described as more 'adult' and interesting than the purely sweet cherry types. Juliet is notable for its outstanding crack resistance (thin-skinned cherry tomatoes frequently split in rain; Juliet resists this), its prolific production, and its reliable fruit set under warm conditions. The thick-walled, meaty fruits have an unusually long shelf life and hold on the vine for weeks without cracking, making them practical for casual harvesting. Disease resistance is strong. In zone 9, Juliet is especially valuable because it continues setting fruit at temperatures that shut down many indeterminate varieties; the heavy trusses of beautiful red grape tomatoes become a summer landmark in the garden.

common_name: Jumbo Romano Pole Bean (Italian Flat-Pod Romano Snap Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Jumbo Romano requires 6-foot pole or trellis support. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer harvest and again late August–September for fall. Romano-type flat-pod beans have a longer harvest window than round-pod snap beans — the wide, flat pods remain tender and flavorful at a much larger size, so harvesting every 3–4 days rather than every 1–2 days as with round-pod types is acceptable without significant quality loss.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; install a 6-foot support structure before planting. Harvest flat pods when 5–8 inches long — the wide, flat pods stay tender longer than round-pod snap beans. Romano-type flat-pod beans are the classic Italian snap bean — the distinctive wide, flat pods (0.5 to 0.75 inch wide, versus the round cross-section of standard snap beans) with a meaty, thick-walled character that gives them a very different cooking quality from American round-pod types. Romano beans are the traditional choice for Italian green bean preparations: braised with olive oil, garlic, and tomato (fagiolini al pomodoro), slow-cooked until completely tender and silky, or simply boiled and dressed with good olive oil and salt. The thick walls mean romano beans absorb oil and flavors particularly well during cooking, and the flat shape increases surface area contact with the cooking medium. Jumbo Romano is a large-podded version of the classic Italian romano pole type — pods reach 7–9 inches at full size while remaining tender — and one of the most widely available and productive romano-type beans in North America. The flavor when cooked is richer and fuller than round-pod snap beans — a deeper, more substantial bean flavor that makes romano beans a favorite of Italian cooks and everyone who discovers them.

common_name: Jupiter Bell Pepper (Large Blocky Red-Ripening Sweet Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; in zone 9, plant in late February through March and again in August–September for a productive fall crop — peppers often produce best in the cooler temperatures of fall.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Jupiter is one of the largest and most productive open-pollinated bell pepper varieties — producing extra-large, four-lobed, thick-walled fruits that are larger and more blocky than standard California Wonder types. The fruits are harvested green for fresh use or allowed to ripen fully to a rich, sweet red (occasionally yellow to orange). Jupiter is prized for its combination of very large fruit size (often 4–5 inches long, 4 inches wide), thick walls that hold up well in cooking, and outstanding sweet flavor that improves markedly when allowed to ripen fully red. As an open-pollinated, non-hybrid variety, Jupiter seeds can be saved from the best fruits for replanting — an important advantage for seed-saving gardeners who want consistent results without purchasing new seed annually. Jupiter's disease tolerance (particularly to tobacco mosaic virus) represents an improvement over older open-pollinated varieties. In zone 9, bell peppers thrive in spring (late February through June) and even more productively in fall (August transplants through November) — the fall crop in zone 9 consistently produces the largest, most flavorful fruits as temperatures moderate from the summer peak. Zone 9 gardeners have two full productive seasons for bell peppers, providing fresh peppers for much of the year.

plant_note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; Jupiter is an LSU AgCenter medium-grain release widely grown across Louisiana rice country.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated through the growing season whether in a flooded paddy or a well-watered garden bed. Jupiter is a widely grown Louisiana medium-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter, valued by commercial growers and home gardeners alike for high, dependable yields and grain that cooks up moist, tender, and slightly clingy in the style favored for jambalaya, risotto-style dishes, and sushi rice rather than the fluffy separate grains of long-grain types. The sturdy, semi-dwarf plants stand up well to wind and rain compared to older tall varieties, making it a practical choice for a home rice patch. Harvest when seed heads droop and the grain has turned golden-brown, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling or storing.

common_name: Just Right Turnip (AAS-Winning Mild Non-Pithy Hybrid Turnip)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Just Right was the first true F1 hybrid turnip and stays mild and non-pithy even at a large size, unlike most turnips which turn woody and strong-flavored once they size up.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loose soil in full sun; Just Right was the first true F1 hybrid turnip ever introduced and remains notable for staying mild, sweet, and non-pithy even when its pure-white, flattened roots are allowed to grow to a large 5-6 inches across — most turnip varieties turn woody, hollow, or sharply pungent well before reaching that size, forcing gardeners to harvest small. This gives more flexibility in harvest timing and a bigger yield per root without sacrificing quality. The tender greens are edible as well and hold up well in the kitchen. In zone 9, grow it strictly as a fall and winter crop, since heat above the mid-70s causes turnip roots to become pithy and bitter regardless of variety; sow from late summer through early fall for a harvest running into winter.

common_name: Just Sweet Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Snacking Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Just Sweet is a compact, heavily fruiting snacking pepper bred to hold up well in containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Just Sweet is an AAS-winning snack-type sweet pepper bred for a compact, well-branched plant that produces heavy clusters of small, elongated, bell-flavored fruits that ripen quickly from green to bright red and are sweet and crunchy enough to eat straight off the plant. The small, tidy plant size makes it an excellent choice for large containers and patio growing, not just garden beds. Pick fruit continuously through the season, either green or fully ripe red, to keep the plant producing; the earlier and more often fruit is harvested, the more the plant sets. Feed lightly through the season, since heavy nitrogen encourages foliage over fruit.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil temperature reaches 65°F; count back from first fall frost to confirm enough growing days.
directions: Sow 2–3 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in deeply amended, compost-rich soil and thin to the strongest vine after the first true leaves appear. Kabocha is a Japanese winter squash of the Cucurbita maxima species; its flattened, dark-green fruits have dense, dry, sweet orange flesh superior to many other squash types. Harvest when the skin is very hard, the stem corky and dry, and a small section of rind scratched with a fingernail shows no damage. Cure at room temperature for 10–14 days before storing; properly cured kabocha keeps four to six months in a cool, dry room.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 3–4 weeks early; kabocha squash produces sprawling vines that need 6–8 feet in all directions. In zone 8‑9, plant in early spring for summer harvest or plant in late summer for a fall crop to avoid the most intense heat.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; kabocha is a Japanese-style winter squash with a dumpling-shaped, dark green (or orange in some types) skin and incredibly dense, dry, sweet bright-orange flesh that has a texture more like sweet potato or chestnut than watery summer squash. The flavor is distinctive — nutty, sweet, and complex — and kabocha is prized in Japanese, Korean, and Thai cuisines for tempura, braised dishes, soups, and desserts. It stores 3–5 months in a cool, dry location. Harvest when the skin resists fingernail puncture and the stem has dried and corked over. The flavor actually improves after 2–3 weeks of curing at room temperature as starches convert to sugars.

plant_note: Sow in successive batches from spring through summer, since it holds its tender texture and mild flavor in warm weather far longer than typical soft-head lettuces.
directions: Sow in successive batches from spring through summer, since it holds its tender texture and mild flavor in warm weather far longer than typical soft-head lettuces. Developed near Kagran outside Vienna, this Austrian heirloom butterhead is prized for exceptional heat tolerance and slow bolting, unusual traits among classic butterheads. It remains a benchmark variety for gardeners needing a butterhead that survives real summer heat.

plant_note: Indian heirloom; heat-loving and quick to ripen.
directions: A striking Indian heirloom melon striped in green, orange, and cream with sweet, pale flesh. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay warm. Train vines with room to sprawl and mulch to keep fruit clean and warm. The dramatic rind color develops as the fruit ripens, and mature melons detach easily from the stem. Cut back on water near harvest to concentrate the sugars in the flesh.

common_name: Kakai Pumpkin (Styrian Hulless-Seed Pumpkin, Oil Seed Pumpkin)
plant_note: Sow seeds directly into warm soil a week or two after the last frost, spacing hills widely to accommodate sprawling vines, and keep beds evenly moist through flowering and fruit set.
directions: Sow seeds directly into warm soil a week or two after the last frost, spacing hills widely to accommodate sprawling vines, and keep beds evenly moist through flowering and fruit set. This Austrian landrace from Styria produces medium orange pumpkins prized not for their stringy flesh but for their thin-hulled, dark-green naked seeds, which are roasted or pressed for the region's famous dark green pumpkinseed oil. Harvest when rinds harden and vines die back, then cure fruit briefly before scooping and drying seeds for eating or oil pressing. It has become a staple specialty crop among home seed-savers and oil producers in North America since the late 20th century.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring; sow again in late summer for a fall and overwintering crop.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep and thin to 12–18 in; kale tolerates crowding better than most brassicas but produces larger leaves with proper spacing. Side-dress with compost or a nitrogen fertilizer midseason to support continued leaf production. Harvest outer leaves first, leaving the growing center intact to keep the plant producing. Flavor becomes noticeably sweeter after the first hard frost, and plants often survive winter in zones 7 and warmer.

plant_note: Siberian kale; reliable brassica microgreen sown densely on trays.
directions: This Siberian kale germinates quickly, so sow it densely on a moist tray and blackout for just a couple of days. Once the stems stretch, uncover and provide bright light to build sturdy, deep-green shoots. Keep the surface evenly moist and give gentle airflow to discourage mold. Cut the tender, mild greens at the cotyledon or first-true-leaf stage after eight to ten days.

plant_note: Start indoors 14–18 weeks before the first fall frost so the tall stalks mature during cool autumn weather, the same schedule used for Brussels sprouts.
directions: Kalettes are an open-pollinated cross between Brussels sprouts and kale, first bred by Tozer Seeds in the UK and released commercially in the early 2010s; the result is a tall stalk lined with loose, frilly, purple-green rosettes instead of the tight round buttons of a standard Brussels sprout. Grow exactly as you would Brussels sprouts: stake the tall stalks against wind, keep soil evenly moist, and top the growing point once the lowest rosettes reach marble size to concentrate energy in the remaining buds. Harvest rosettes from the bottom of the stalk upward as they firm up; flavor becomes noticeably sweeter and less bitter after a hard frost. A single stalk can be harvested over several weeks as rosettes mature sequentially up its length.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or sow in midsummer for a fall crop, since Kalibos develops its deepest color and best flavor with a longer, cooler growing season.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in midsummer for transplanting out in late summer, since Kalibos develops its best color and flavor with a longer, cooler fall growing season. Kalibos is a Central/Eastern European heirloom cabbage, likely developed from the older Vysoky (Vysocke) type, distinguished by small, dense, cone-shaped heads of deep purple-red leaves that form a striking pointed rosette rather than the round or flattened heads of typical cabbage. The tender, crisp, juicy leaves are deep red to violet clear through to the core, making Kalibos as prized for its color in raw slaws and pickles as for its mild, sweet flavor. It stores for a moderate period after harvest and remains something of a novelty in North American gardens despite long popularity in Eastern Europe.

common_name: Kamo Eggplant (Kamo Nasu, Kyoto Heirloom Round Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; give plants extra room since Kamo grows larger and bushier than slender Asian eggplant types.
directions: Kamo Nasu is a traditional heirloom from the Kamo district of Kyoto, grown for its large, softball-sized round fruit with thick, dense flesh that stays creamy and never turns spongy even at full size. It is the classic eggplant used for dengaku, where thick slices are grilled or pan-fried and topped with sweet miso glaze, since the dense flesh holds together better than thinner-skinned slicing types. Give plants rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture, as the large fruit can stress the plant if it dries out between waterings. Choose Kamo when you want an eggplant suited to grilling and roasting whole slices rather than the elongated Asian types more common in home gardens.

common_name: Kandy Korn Sweet Corn (EH-Type Traditional-Flavor Yellow Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate wind pollination; Kandy Korn is an EH (Everlasting Heritage) or se-type variety and can be planted adjacent to su types without significant flavor reduction. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest. The later maturity (85–92 days) means Kandy Korn is one of the last sweet corn varieties of the season for most gardens, providing continuity after mid-season types are finished.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows; side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Kandy Korn EH is a yellow EH (Everlasting Heritage) or se-type sweet corn — a variety from the Illinois Foundation Seeds stable that occupies an important niche as a late-season yellow corn with a distinctive flavor profile that many traditional corn enthusiasts prefer to modern hybrid types. The 'EH' designation refers to 'Everlasting Heritage,' a genetic trait that increases sugar content and slows the sugar-to-starch conversion rate compared to standard su types but maintains more of the complex, traditional 'field corn' flavor notes that characterize classic American sweet corn — a richer, deeper, more complex corn flavor than the clean sweetness of modern se or sh2 types. Kandy Korn is particularly popular with older gardeners and those who grew up eating sweet corn from small farms and roadside stands, where the flavor of the corn itself (rather than just sweetness) was the primary quality attribute. The medium-large ears (7.5–8 inches, 14–16 rows) carry well-filled rows of golden-yellow, tender kernels with extended holding quality compared to standard su. At 85–92 days, Kandy Korn extends the sweet corn season to the later summer window when earlier varieties have finished.

common_name: Kanthari Chili Pepper (Kerala Bird's Eye Chili)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; productive and heat-tolerant, setting clusters of two to three fruits per node.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this compact, bushy frutescens landrace from Kerala, India, is prized in South Indian cooking for its small, marble-round, glossy red pods. Heat runs high (roughly 50,000-100,000 Scoville units) but dissipates faster than many other hot peppers, leaving a bright, citrusy flavor that's central to Kerala fish curries, chutneys, and pickles. Plants are productive and heat-tolerant, setting clusters of two to three fruits per node through a long harvest season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Karma is a blocky bell pepper hybrid bred with resistance to common mosaic viruses, which spread readily through aphid activity in warm Gulf South gardens.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Karma is a hybrid bell pepper bred with resistance to common mosaic viruses, letting it keep its foliage healthier through the aphid pressure that builds over a long, warm Gulf South growing season. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant longer. The compact, well-branched plant provides good leaf cover that helps shield developing fruit from sunscald during peak summer heat. Harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness, and keep picking to encourage continued fruit set.

common_name: Katahdin Potato (1932 USDA Classic White Storage Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; Katahdin was released in 1932 by the USDA Potato Breeding Program and named for Mount Katahdin in Maine — for much of the 20th century it was the most widely grown potato in the eastern United States, prized for good yields, excellent storage quality, and versatile white flesh suitable for all cooking purposes.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30–36 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; Katahdin is a main-season variety producing large, round to oval, smooth, buff-white-skinned, white-fleshed tubers of excellent quality. Katahdin was developed by the USDA Potato Research Laboratory in Presque Isle, Maine and officially released in 1932, named for the highest peak in Maine; for the next several decades it was the most widely grown potato in the northeastern and mid-Atlantic United States, valued for its consistent productivity, reliable storage quality, and disease resistance (including moderate resistance to late blight). The large, smooth, nearly round tubers have thin, buff to light tan skin and white flesh with a slightly waxy texture when young — excellent for boiling and potato salad — that transitions toward semi-floury when fully mature, making them good for baking and mashing as well; a genuinely all-purpose variety in the tradition of the great white American storage potatoes. Flavor is clean, mild, and characteristic of the best white potato types; stores 4–6 months under proper conditions (35–40°F, high humidity). Still grown commercially in the Northeast and available from heritage potato suppliers.

common_name: Katarina Cabbage (AAS-Winning Early Compact Mini Cabbage)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop; Katarina is a very early, small-headed cabbage bred for close spacing in containers and small beds, forming a solid head faster than most cabbage varieties.
directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Katarina is an AAS-winning cabbage bred for very early maturity and a small, tidy head about 4 inches across, forming a solid, sweet, light-green head faster than nearly any other garden cabbage — a useful trait for squeezing a crop into a short spring or fall window, or for a large container where a full-size storage cabbage would be impractical. Its small stature and rapid maturity also make it a good choice for succession planting through a cool season. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm and dense, since even fast-maturing types can split if left too long once mature. Watch for cabbage worms and aphids, common pests on all brassicas in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Katuk is a Southeast Asian tropical shrub producing exceptionally nutritious, mild-flavored leaves used as a vegetable throughout Malaysia, Vietnam, and Indonesia — the leaves contain up to 7% protein by fresh weight, high levels of vitamins A and C, and a mild, slightly sweet, pea-like flavor that makes them one of the most palatable and nutritious tropical leaf vegetables.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; harvest tender shoot tips and young leaves regularly for continuous production. Sauropus androgynus (katuk or sweet leaf) is a Southeast Asian tropical shrub — native from India through mainland Southeast Asia to Indonesia — that produces one of the most nutritious and palatable leafy vegetables in the tropical world. The shoots and young leaves (the standard harvested part) contain exceptionally high levels of protein (6–8% by fresh weight — remarkably high for a vegetable), vitamins A and C, iron, and calcium; the fresh leaves taste mild, slightly sweet, and pea-like — quite different from the stronger, bitter flavors of many tropical leafy greens. In Malaysia (where it is called 'cekur manis'), Vietnam ('rau ngot'), and Indonesia, katuk is a standard, everyday vegetable used in stir-fries, soups, and as a cooked green. It is also extensively used in Singapore and among Southeast Asian diaspora communities worldwide. CAUTION: Very large quantities of raw juice (as consumed in some weight-loss protocols in Taiwan in the 1990s) caused severe pulmonary toxicity; katuk must be cooked before eating and should not be consumed raw in large amounts or as a supplement. Properly cooked as a vegetable in normal food quantities, it is safe and highly beneficial.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Katydid is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing green-striped fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Katydid bears medium fruit striped green over an amber-green background even when fully ripe, a striking novelty color pattern with tangy, well-balanced flavor typical of green-fleshed tomato types, on a compact plant bred through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Its manageable size and eye-catching fruit suit raised beds and containers. Harvest when fruit softens slightly, since color alone won't signal ripeness in green-fleshed types.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost date; kañiwa is a close, smaller-seeded relative of quinoa from the high Andes, bred for a shorter, tougher growing season, and does best with a cool finish rather than peak summer heat.
directions: Broadcast or sow seed shallowly in firm, well-drained soil in full sun and thin seedlings to 8–12 inches apart; kañiwa is an Andean pseudograin closely related to both quinoa and the already-familiar huauzontle, distinguished by tiny, dark reddish-brown seeds borne on a shorter, bushier plant. Unlike quinoa, its seed coat carries little to no bitter saponin, so it needs little or no rinsing before cooking or roasting, and the plant tends to shatter and self-sow readily once mature. Harvest when seed heads have dried and seed threshes free easily, then dry further indoors before storing whole grain in a sealed container. Roasted kañiwa (kañiwako) has a nutty flavor and is traditionally ground into a toasted flour called cañihuaco, used as a high-protein addition to porridges and baked goods.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to early autumn for a winter and early spring harvest; plants overwinter as small rosettes in mild climates and are among the first greens ready in spring.
directions: Sow seeds thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in late summer or early autumn into fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning to 4-6 inches apart. Germination is most reliable when soil temperatures have dropped below 65°F; cool nights after late-August sowings are ideal. Harvest entire rosettes by cutting at the base once they reach a few inches across, or pick outer leaves continuously throughout winter. Keeled corn salad has a mild, slightly sweet flavor well suited to winter salads alongside mâche and other cold-hardy greens.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; an indeterminate orange beefsteak with deep-meaty flesh and very small seed cavities; plant early in warm climates to get harvest before summer heat peaks.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to a rich, well-drained site in full sun after frost danger has passed, burying the stem to the lowest leaves. Kellogg's Breakfast is an American heirloom orange beefsteak tomato that originated with William Kellogg of Michigan, introduced to the larger seed-saving community through Seed Savers Exchange, and has since become one of the most celebrated orange heirlooms for its extraordinary flavor — sweet, mild, and low-acid with a rich, fruity depth that makes it ideal fresh. Fruits weigh 1–2 pounds and have very meaty, almost seedless flesh that is deep orange throughout; they ripen relatively slowly but the wait is well worth it. Stake or cage plants firmly and thin to two or three main leaders for the largest fruits.

plant_note: Sow after last frost in warm soil; kenaf grows tall rapidly and is grown for bast fiber, animal fodder, and paper pulp.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/2–1 in deep at 25–30 lb/acre for fiber production (narrower spacing promotes taller, less branched stems); kenaf is a warm-season annual related to okra that can reach 14 feet in a single season. For fiber, harvest at early flowering before stems become too woody — cut at ground level and ret the stalks in water for 10–20 days to separate the long bast fibers from the woody core. The core material (hurds) is useful as animal bedding or biomass fuel, while the bast fibers make durable rope, sacking, and paper. Young leaves and shoots are edible and nutritious — commonly cooked as a green in West African cuisine.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January–February. Kennebec is a mid-season white potato (75–90 days) that adapts well to the Gulf Coast's winter growing window. Plant 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil and hill regularly.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil; Kennebec is an All-America Selections winner introduced by the USDA in 1948 from a cross of B127 x USDA 96-56, named for the Kennebec River in Maine. For many decades it was the most widely grown potato in the eastern United States, dominating both fresh market and potato chip production because of its outstanding adaptability, disease resistance, and excellent culinary quality. The large, oval tubers have thin, buff-white skin and firm, white flesh that performs equally well baked, fried, mashed, or roasted — a true all-purpose potato. Kennebec shows good resistance to late blight and is tolerant of common scab, making it more reliable than many varieties in the variable conditions of Gulf Coast winter gardens. It remains a benchmark variety offered by heritage seed companies for its proven performance and consistent quality. In zone 9, plant January–February and harvest May–June before summer heat arrives.

common_name: Kentucky Beefsteak Tomato (Golden-Orange Low-Acid Appalachian Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Kentucky Beefsteak is an Appalachian heirloom prized for its golden-orange, notably low-acid flesh and large beefsteak-type fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors under grow lights 6-8 weeks before the last frost date; transplant outdoors after frost danger has fully passed with a wire cage or stout stake, setting the plant deep to encourage root formation along the buried stem. Kentucky Beefsteak, an heirloom collected from the hills of eastern Kentucky, produces large, meaty, golden-orange fruit with notably low acidity and a mild, sweet flavor, distinguishing it from the more common red and pink Southern beefsteak heirlooms. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive through a long summer season in hot, humid Southern conditions. Its low-acid flavor makes it a favorite for slicing and eating fresh for gardeners sensitive to the tang of more acidic tomato varieties.

common_name: Kentucky Blue Pole Bean (AAS-Winning Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; provide a sturdy trellis, pole tepee, or wire fence at least 5–6 feet tall. Kentucky Blue vines climb to 6–7 feet and require strong support. Harvest pods frequently at 5–6 inches for maximum tenderness and continued production.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Kentucky Blue is a 1991 All-America Selections-winning pole bean that crossed two of the most beloved pole bean varieties — Kentucky Wonder and Blue Lake — to combine the best traits of both parents. Kentucky Wonder contributes vigor, heavy production, excellent traditional pole bean flavor, and the characteristic meaty pod texture; Blue Lake contributes its renowned stringless quality, mild sweetness, and the refined, crisp texture that made it the gold standard of snap bean flavor. The resulting Kentucky Blue produces long (6–8 inch), round, deep green, completely stringless pods with excellent flavor that tasters consistently rate among the best of all snap beans — more substantial than filet beans but more refined than older Kentucky Wonder strains. Very productive vines climbing 6–7 feet continue bearing throughout the summer and fall when harvested regularly. The combination of classic pole bean character, genuine stringlessness, superior flavor, and heavy production has made Kentucky Blue one of the most popular and recommended pole beans in American gardens since its introduction.

common_name: Kentucky Wonder Bean (Old Homestead Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; provide a trellis, pole, or fence 5–8 feet tall for the climbing vines; in zone 9, sow February–April for spring crop and again August–September for fall crop.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; Kentucky Wonder is the most famous and most enduring American heirloom pole bean — an heirloom variety in continuous cultivation since the 1860s that remains one of the most widely grown and best-regarded pole beans in American home gardens. The vigorous climbing vines reach 5–8 feet and require a sturdy support structure — traditional pole, trellis, or fence. Kentucky Wonder produces heavy yields of long (7–9 inch), round-to-flat, stringless-when-young green pods with exceptional flavor — a rich, full, classic green bean taste that is considerably more complex and satisfying than modern bush beans bred for commercial production. Seed can be saved true-to-type from open-pollinated Kentucky Wonder. The dry seeds (beans) can be used as shell beans or dried for winter storage, giving the plant dual utility as both green snap bean and dry bean. In zone 9, the spring season (February–May) and fall season (August–October) provide two productive growing windows. The combination of outstanding flavor, prolific production, historical significance, and heirloom status makes Kentucky Wonder the gold standard of American pole beans.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed to at least 60 degrees.
directions: Direct sow this vigorous 1800s heirloom pole bean once the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep at the base of a sturdy trellis or pole 6 to 8 feet tall. Provide support early, as the climbing vines produce heavy crops of 9 inch curved, oval pods that are stringless when young. Pick regularly to encourage continued production and enjoy fresh, or leave pods to dry for shelling beans. Beans dislike root disturbance, so sow directly rather than transplanting and keep evenly moist during flowering and pod set.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Kermit thrives in Gulf South heat and humidity, continuing to produce heavily through the hottest part of summer.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young at golf-ball to ping-pong-ball size for the crisp, mild, seed-free texture prized in Thai cooking. Kermit is a small, round Thai eggplant with pale green skin streaked and mottled with cream-white striping, borne in heavy clusters on compact, productive plants that thrive in hot, humid conditions. The firm, dense flesh has very few seeds when harvested young and holds its shape well in curries, stir-fries, and stews — traditional uses in Thai cuisine, where round green eggplants are added whole or halved directly into simmering curry. Its heat tolerance and continuous production over a long summer season make it an excellent, prolific choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens, zone 4–12.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this vigorous maincrop variety tolerates a wide range of soils better than many modern cultivars.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and hill generously, as this old Scottish cultivar produces a heavy crop of round to oval tubers with distinctive rose-pink skin and creamy white, floury flesh. Bred in Scotland in 1917, Kerr's Pink became a staple maincrop potato across Ireland and Scotland thanks to its reliable yields, good disease tolerance, and adaptability to poorer, wetter soils than many refined modern varieties tolerate. The floury texture makes excellent mash and roast potatoes but causes it to break apart in soups and stews, so reserve it for dry-cooking preparations. Grow it where a rustic, high-yielding heirloom maincrop with real cold-region pedigree is wanted over a fussier modern hybrid.

scientific_name: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'Kettle River Giant'
plant_note: Plant large cloves 3 inches deep in October-November after several nights of cold weather so roots establish before hard freeze.
directions: Kettle River Giant is a Porcelain-type hardneck garlic originating from the Kettle River valley near the Washington-British Columbia border, prized for producing some of the largest bulbs of any hardneck strain, often exceeding 3 inches across with just 4-6 oversized cloves per head. Grow it in rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture through bulb sizing, and mulch heavily over winter in colder zones since Porcelain types are somewhat less cold-hardy than Rocambole strains. The flavor is strong and full-bodied with a lingering heat, and the tall, sturdy scapes make excellent garlic scape pesto in early summer. Choose this variety when garden space is limited but you still want big, easy-to-peel cloves for the kitchen.

common_name: Keystone Resistant Giant Pepper (Pennsylvania Heirloom Stuffing Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Keystone Resistant Giant is an open-pollinated heirloom that tends to produce more large fruits when staked or caged. In zone 9, transplant March–April for a June–September harvest. The 'Resistant' in the name refers to Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) resistance — important in an era before comprehensive disease resistance packages in peppers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; transplant to full sun with consistent moisture and balanced fertility. Keystone Resistant Giant is a Pennsylvania-origin heirloom bell pepper that was one of the most important commercial bell pepper varieties in the eastern United States from the 1940s through the 1970s, valued as the largest-fruited TMV-resistant open-pollinated bell pepper available during a period when disease resistance was achieved only through strain selection rather than modern breeding techniques. The 'Keystone' name connects the variety to Pennsylvania (the Keystone State), where it was grown extensively by commercial growers, home gardeners, and the Pennsylvania Dutch communities who prize large, thick-walled peppers for stuffing with meat and rice.
