The fruits are distinctly large (4–5 inches tall, 3–4 inches wide), blocky, 3-4 lobed, dark green ripening to red, with moderately thick walls and an upright, pendant orientation on strong-stemmed plants. Keystone Resistant Giant represents the pre-F1-hybrid era of American pepper breeding and occupies an important place in American heirloom pepper history — it was the standard against which American bell peppers were measured for decades and remains a valued open-pollinated option for seed savers who want a true-breeding large stuffing pepper. The flavor at the red stage is rich, sweet, and classically bell-pepper, with none of the bitterness that characterizes some heirloom types.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, about 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, so roots establish before winter dormancy.
directions: Separate cloves shortly before planting and set them pointed end up about 2 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Mulch after planting to buffer winter temperature swings and remove mulch gradually as green shoots emerge in spring; cut off curling scapes in early summer to redirect energy into bulb growth. Killarney Red is a cold-hardy rocambole strain originating from Irish and Canadian growers, prized for its rich, full-bodied garlic flavor and easy-to-peel purple-blushed skins, though like other rocamboles it does not store as long as porcelain or silverskin types.

common_name: King Philip Corn (Historic New England Flint Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow once the soil has warmed, in blocks rather than single rows; its short season lets it succeed even in cool, short-summer regions.
directions: Direct sow once the soil has warmed, in blocks rather than single rows, and take advantage of its short season to succeed even in cool, short-summer regions of northern New England. King Philip is one of the oldest documented flint corns in cultivation, recorded in Massachusetts and Rhode Island since colonial times and traditionally said to honor the Wampanoag leader Metacomet, known to English colonists as King Philip. The eight-rowed ears bear hard, deep red-brown kernels that dry quickly on the stalk and grind into a flavorful, reddish cornmeal long used for johnnycake and other traditional New England cornbreads.

plant_note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings out around the last frost.
directions: Start King Richard leeks indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings the thickness of a pencil into the garden spaced 4 to 6 inches apart. This early variety produces extra-long white stems, so hill or trench the plants and mound soil around the stems as they grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion. Leeks tolerate cold well and can be harvested from late summer through fall. Keep the soil consistently moist and weed-free for the best-quality stems.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start August–September and transplant October–November. King Sieg is selected for mild winters and performs exceptionally well in zone 9, where it can be harvested through the winter without bolting. Transplant seedlings at pencil thickness into deep, wide holes or a trench; blanch the lower shank by earthing up soil as the plant grows. Harvest from November through March in zone 9 before spring warming initiates bolting.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun; King Sieg is a Belgian-bred leek cultivar selected for the mild winter climates of the maritime Pacific Northwest and Gulf South — specifically bred to produce long, thick, white-blanche shanks without premature bolting in mild, frost-free or light-frost winters. Standard leek cultivars selected for cold northern climates often bolt prematurely when grown in mild zone 8–10 winters because the mild temperatures signal the plant that spring has arrived; King Sieg has delayed bolting response, allowing harvest through February and March in zone 9 without quality loss. The thick, tender white shanks with a mild, sweet leek flavor are excellent in potato-leek soup, braised whole, sautéed as a vegetable side, or used in place of onions where a milder allium is needed. Earth up soil around the shanks as the plants grow to extend the white, blanched portion and reduce the proportion of green.

common_name: King of Hearts Watermelon (AAS-Winning Seedless Hybrid)
plant_note: Start seed indoors and transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; as a seedless triploid, King of Hearts needs a nearby seeded watermelon variety planted for pollen to set fruit properly.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply the pollen this seedless triploid needs to set fruit. King of Hearts is an All-America Selections winning seedless hybrid producing large, oval, striped fruit with sweet, firm, deep red flesh and only soft, edible white seed traces rather than hard black seeds, a genuine convenience for fresh eating. The vigorous vine is a reliable, heavy producer when properly pollinated, and the flavor and texture rank among the better seedless hybrids available. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries and the ground spot turns creamy yellow, since seedless watermelons give fewer reliable ripeness cues than seeded types and are easy to pick too early.

common_name: King of the Garden Lima Bean
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; King of the Garden is one of the oldest and most celebrated American pole lima beans, introduced by Burpee in 1883 and prized for its very large, flat, creamy-white seeds with exceptional buttery lima flavor — the archetype of the 'large lima' bean and ideal for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens where the long season allows full development.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost with soil above 65°F; provide poles or strong trellising 6–8 feet tall for support. King of the Garden is a classic American pole lima bean introduced by W. Atlee Burpee in 1883 and considered for much of its history the finest large-seeded lima bean available; the plants are vigorous, 6–8 foot climbers that produce long, broad, flat pods with 4–6 very large (up to 1 inch), flat, creamy-white bean seeds with an extraordinarily rich, buttery, full lima bean flavor superior to most modern bush varieties. The large seeds require a relatively long, warm season to develop fully (85–95 days from seed); in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens the long growing season makes King of the Garden ideal for both spring and fall plantings. Excellent for fresh green lima use (harvested at the flat-but-not-yet-wrinkled stage when seeds are fully developed), freezing, and drying. One of the foundational American heirloom vegetables.

common_name: King of the North Pepper (Heirloom Short-Season Sweet Bell Pepper with Zone 9 Fall Use)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; King of the North is an early-maturing sweet bell pepper (57–68 days from transplant) bred for cool, short-season climates where standard bell peppers ripen too slowly to produce before frost. In zone 9, where the problem is opposite (heat rather than cold), King of the North is best suited to fall planting (starts July, transplant August, harvest October–November) when cooling temperatures approach the 65–75°F range that bell peppers prefer for fruit set and maturation. The variety's short days-to-maturity allows it to complete ripening within the fall cool window. Harvest green or allow to fully ripen red for full sweetness. King of the North is an open-pollinated heirloom available from multiple seed sources and is notable for germinating and growing vigorously at lower temperatures than most other bell pepper varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost or in late summer for fall production. Harvest green or red. King of the North is an heirloom sweet bell pepper variety bred and popularized specifically for short-season, cool-climate gardens where standard bell pepper varieties (requiring 70–90+ days and substantial heat to develop fully) cannot be relied upon to ripen before fall frosts. The breeding goal of short-season bell peppers like King of the North is to compress the fruit development timeline while maintaining adequate size, wall thickness, and flavor — a challenging tradeoff since bell peppers that ripen quickly tend to be smaller and thinner-walled than late-maturing types. King of the North succeeds reasonably well at this balance: the fruits are large enough to be genuinely useful (3–4 inches, 3-lobed form), with walls adequate for stuffing and fresh use, and flavor that develops to full sweetness when ripened to red. The variety is open-pollinated and seed-saving is straightforward, making it a practical choice for seed-saving gardeners. In zone 9, the short days-to-maturity of King of the North are most valuable for the fall growing season rather than spring: a late-July start from seed produces plants that can be transplanted in late August and begin producing before October heat drops, allowing harvest through November in a climate where long-season varieties started at the same time might not mature before plants are compromised by cool weather. This fall-planting application in zone 9 mirrors King of the North's primary value in zone 3–5 gardens — speed of production in a constrained growing window.

plant_note: Pickling type; succession sow for a steady supply.
directions: Kirby is the classic short, bumpy, thin-skinned pickling cucumber with crisp, dense flesh. Direct sow after the soil warms, either in hills or along a low trellis for cleaner fruit. Provide abundant, even water since pickling cucumbers are especially prone to bitterness and hollow centers under drought. Pick daily at 3 to 5 inches for pickling, as the vines produce heavily over a short window. Succession sowing every two to three weeks extends the harvest into late summer.

common_name: Kleckley Sweet Watermelon (Thin-Rind Southern Heirloom, Supreme Garden Eating Quality)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm (70°F minimum); Kleckley Sweet requires ample space (vines 8–12 feet), full sun, and warm nights for maximum sugar development. In zone 9, plant April–May for a June–August harvest season. Kleckley Sweet is NOT a shipping watermelon — the extremely thin rind that makes it ideal for home eating shatters and bruises too easily for any commercial transport. This restricts Kleckley Sweet to home garden and very local market production, where the fruit can be carried by hand and consumed immediately after harvest. At full maturity in zone 9 heat, Kleckley Sweet produces fruit reaching 25–40 pounds with some individual specimens heavier, bright red flesh, and a sweetness level that has made it the benchmark by which Southern watermelon enthusiasts measure the flavor of other varieties. Detect ripeness by the dried tendril nearest the fruit, the ground spot color transition to creamy yellow, and a dull thud when thumped.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; allow 6–8 feet between hills. Harvest when tendril nearest fruit dries and ground spot turns yellow. Kleckley Sweet (also called Monte Cristo in some seed catalogs) is one of the great heirloom watermelons of the American South — a variety with an extraordinary reputation for eating quality that has been maintained by home gardeners and seed savers for well over a century, despite being completely impractical for commercial production due to its extremely thin rind. The rind of a ripe Kleckley Sweet is so thin that the fruit can crack simply from being set down too hard — a catastrophic liability for commercial shipping but an indication of the rind's extreme thinness that is part of what makes it so desirable for eating, where rind thickness is inversely proportional to flesh proportion per fruit. The flesh is brilliant red, dense and fine-grained, with very small seeds relative to the flesh volume, and of the highest natural sweetness of any standard-sized watermelon variety — the flavor is intensely, purely sweet with the clean watermelon taste that distinguishes vine-ripened, heat-grown Southern watermelons from the bland, watery specimens produced from short-season varieties in cool climates. The variety was introduced by W. Atlee Burpee around the 1890s-1900s and became one of the most popular garden watermelons in the South through the mid-20th century, maintaining a devoted following among heirloom gardeners long after commercial production shifted to thick-rinded shipping varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Klondike Striped is an early 20th century California heirloom watermelon that became the commercial standard for Western US watermelon production, producing medium-large, uniformly striped, oblong fruits with firm, excellent-quality red flesh.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Klondike Striped is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in hot, dry Western climates and Gulf Coast sandy soils. Klondike Striped was developed in early 20th century California, where it became the primary commercial watermelon for California's San Joaquin Valley and other Western growing regions; the medium-large (25–35 lbs), oblong fruits have attractive, uniform, alternating light and dark green stripes and firm, deep red to scarlet flesh with excellent, rich, sweet flavor and few seeds relative to its size. The variety became widely grown in the West and South for its reliable production, attractive appearance, and good quality; the firm flesh holds well after cutting, making it a practical variety for families and market growers. Days to maturity of 80–90 suit it well for both long-season Southern and moderately short Pacific Coast growing seasons.

common_name: Knuckle Head Pumpkin (F1 Warted Novelty Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; part of the Superfreak series of warted novelty pumpkins bred by Siegers Seed Co. for exaggerated, gnarled rind texture.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6 feet apart for the sprawling vines. Knuckle Head is a hybrid novelty pumpkin from the Superfreak series, producing 12-16 pound, slightly tall, dark-orange fruit densely covered in gnarled warts that range from dark green through light green to orange; unlike some warty types, wart color is not a reliable ripeness indicator here. The variety carries useful powdery mildew resistance, which helps keep foliage productive through the fruit-finishing stage of the season. Grown almost exclusively for its shock-value texture at pumpkin patches and fall markets rather than for eating, it should be harvested once the rind is fully hard and stored in a cool, dry spot for display.

plant_note: Sow directly into warm soil; cowpeas thrive in summer heat.
directions: This productive bush-type cowpea produces plump, succulent peas with a distinctive purple eye inside richly colored purple pods. Sow directly into warm soil, as cowpeas love summer heat and tolerate dry conditions. The compact plants need no staking and set a heavy crop of easy-to-shell pods. Pick pods when the hulls turn purple and the peas inside are full for fresh use, or leave them to dry for storage.

common_name: Knuckle Purple Hull Pea (Short-Season Compact Purple Hull Southern Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Knuckle Purple Hull is a semi-determinate type that concentrates its pod set in a shorter period than indeterminate types — useful for gardeners who want a defined harvest window rather than continuous production.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Knuckle Purple Hull is a semi-determinate purple hull southern pea that matures faster and concentrates its pod set in a shorter window than standard indeterminate purple hull types — producing the characteristic purple-hulled pods on a compact, upright plant that reaches 18–24 inches without trailing vines, making it more manageable for raised-bed and intensive garden production. The name 'Knuckle' refers to the distinctive bunching habit of pod production — the pods tend to cluster near the stem joints ('knuckles') in groups rather than being spread along extended vining stems, which concentrates the harvest and makes picking more efficient. The peas themselves are the classic purple hull type: green hulls with purple coloring at maturity, and cream-colored seeds with the mild, sweet flavor characteristic of purple hull peas. At 55–65 days, Knuckle Purple Hull is also earlier than standard purple hull types (typically 65–75 days) — allowing earlier first harvests from spring plantings and more productive use of the warm season in zone 9 where succession planting through summer is common practice. The compact, determinate-tending growth habit requires no staking and makes Knuckle Purple Hull suitable for higher-density plantings than trailing types.

common_name: Kodiak Brown Mustard (High-Glucosinolate Biofumigant Cover Crop)
plant_note: Direct sow 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Kodiak is a high-glucosinolate brown mustard bred at the University of Idaho specifically for biofumigation, suppressing soilborne pathogens and nematodes when incorporated at flowering.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and mow or flail-chop the stand right at early flowering, then incorporate the shredded residue into the top few inches of soil immediately and irrigate to seal it in — the biofumigant effect depends on releasing volatile isothiocyanate compounds from the chopped tissue quickly, before they dissipate into the air. Kodiak was bred at the University of Idaho for an unusually high concentration of glucosinolates, the sulfur compounds that break down into natural soil fumigants capable of suppressing soilborne fungal pathogens, weed seed germination, and plant-parasitic nematodes, offering a lower-input alternative to chemical soil fumigation ahead of a susceptible vegetable crop. Beyond its biofumigant role, the fast, leafy growth smothers weeds and scavenges excess soil nitrogen, and the bright yellow flowers, if allowed to open, are attractive to early-season pollinators. Avoid planting into a bed just biofumigated with mustard for several weeks to allow residues to fully break down.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is warm; kodo millet is exceptionally tolerant of poor, waterlogged, or drought-prone soils and is traditionally grown as a reliable famine-reserve crop where other grains fail.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in prepared rows or broadcast on a firm seedbed, thinning to 6-10 inches when plants are established; kodo millet is a South Asian and West African grain grass valued for exceptional hardiness, tolerating both drought and temporary waterlogging better than almost any other cultivated grain, which has made it a traditional insurance crop in unpredictable growing conditions. The clumping plant produces slender seed spikes on branching stalks that ripen over an extended period; harvest by cutting mature heads as they brown and finishing the dry-down on a tarp in the sun before threshing by flailing or rubbing to release the small, hard seeds. Freshly harvested and properly dried kodo millet is safe and nutritious, but note that grain infected by a specific fungus (Aspergillus tamarii) during wet storage can become toxic, so dry and store the harvest promptly and thoroughly, a standard precaution long practiced by traditional growers. The grain is notably high in dietary fiber and has a mild, slightly nutty flavor when cooked whole like rice.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last spring frost, or sow in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/4 in deep in cool, fertile soil and thin plants to 5–8 in to give the swollen stem room to develop. Keep soil consistently moist, as drought stress causes the bulb to become woody and strongly flavored. Harvest when the swollen stem is 2–3 in across for best tenderness; larger bulbs become fibrous. Pull the whole plant and trim the leaves before storing in the refrigerator.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, and again every few weeks through midsummer plus a late-summer fall sowing, since Kolibri matures quickly and mildest in cool weather.
directions: Direct sow seed ½ inch deep in early spring 2-4 weeks before the last frost, and again in mid- to late summer for a fall crop, since Kolibri grows fastest and mildest in cool weather. Kolibri is a widely grown F1 hybrid noted as one of the most uniform and reliably deep-purple kohlrabi varieties available, forming a smooth, round, above-ground bulb with crisp, nearly fiberless white flesh beneath the vivid purple skin. Its rapid 45- to 50-day maturity and compact, neat habit make it well suited to succession planting, small-space beds, and early-season cloche or row-cover production. Harvest bulbs at about the size of a tennis ball for the sweetest, most tender texture, since kohlrabi can turn woody if left too long in the ground.

plant_note: Sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring, or 6–8 weeks before first fall frost; succession sow every 2–3 weeks.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep, thinning to 4 inches for baby greens or 8 inches for full-sized plants. Komatsuna is one of the most versatile Asian brassicas — milder than mustard, more heat-tolerant than spinach, and remarkably cold-hardy. Begin harvesting at 30 days for tender salad leaves, or allow plants to reach full size at 8–14 inches for stir-frying and braising. Water consistently to keep leaves mild and succulent.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since chinense superhots are slow to germinate and mature.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, and transplant only once the soil is thoroughly warm, since seedlings stall in cool conditions. Stake plants as the fruit load builds and keep moisture consistent to avoid blossom drop during heat spikes. Komodo Dragon was bred in the United Kingdom by chile grower Salvatore Genovese and is known as one of the hottest peppers developed in Britain, with elongated, ridged red pods and a sharp, intense burn. It is popular among superhot collectors for its productivity in cooler UK-style greenhouse growing.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost; Konan is a compact, fast-maturing globe kohlrabi bred to stay tender and crack-free even when bulbs size up, and it grows well in containers as well as open beds.
directions: Direct sow, or start transplants and set out 2-4 weeks before last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Konan is an AAS-winning kohlrabi bred for a compact plant habit and smooth, uniform, pale-green globes that stay crisp, sweet, and free of the woodiness or cracking that plagues older kohlrabi varieties even at a larger harvest size, giving gardeners a wider window to pick. The neat, upright plant fits well in small beds, raised beds, and large containers. Harvest bulbs when they reach 2-3 inches across for the best texture; peel the tough outer skin before eating raw in slaws or cooked. As a cool-season crop it can bolt and turn woody in summer heat, so grow it as an early spring or fall crop in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant corms 4–6 inches deep in rich, moist, well-drained soil in spring once night temperatures remain above 50°F; choose a site with dappled to partial shade as the large single leaf scorches in direct afternoon sun in most climates.
directions: Plant corms in rich, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and dappled shade, mimicking the forest understory conditions of its native East Asia; each corm produces a single enormous compound leaf on a mottled stalk that can reach 6 feet tall in a single season. Corms grow slowly, increasing in size each year, and are typically harvested after 2–3 years when they can weigh 5–10 pounds; the raw corm contains calcium oxalate crystals and must be processed before eating. Traditional processing involves drying, grinding, and treating the flour with an alkaline solution to form the firm, gelatinous product used in shirataki noodles and konjac blocks. In zones 6–7 mulch the planting site heavily in autumn to protect corms through winter, or dig and store them frost-free.

common_name: Korean Cucumber (Joseon Oi, Korean Pickling Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Korean cucumber vines benefit from trellising and regular harvesting — pick fruits at 6–8 inches for best flavor and texture for pickle-making, or allow to reach full size for fresh eating.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Korean cucumber (Joseon Oi or 'Korean local cucumber') is the traditional cucumber of Korean agriculture — a light green to whitish-green cucumber with a bumpy, spiny-warted surface (similar to pickling cucumbers but larger and paler), crisp, dense, mildly flavored flesh, very thin skin, and a shape that ranges from short and stout (about 6 inches) to long and slender depending on the local strain. It is the essential ingredient in oi sobagi (cucumber kimchi) where the crisp texture and thin skin allow quick pickling and absorption of spicy, garlicky brine without becoming soft or mushy — texture properties that make Korean cucumber distinctly superior to standard American slicing or pickling cucumbers for Korean-style preparations. The pale color and slightly different flavor profile also distinguish it from Japanese kyuri types; Korean cucumber has a slightly more pronounced flavor with a mild earthiness. Very heat-tolerant and productive under summer conditions; an excellent Asian specialty cucumber for Southern gardens with access to Korean or Asian seed suppliers.

common_name: Korean Long Hot Pepper (Slender Mild-to-Medium Cooking Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; Korean Long Hot is a slender, pale green pepper widely used fresh in Korean cooking, from mild to moderately spicy depending on growing conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Korean Long Hot produces long, slender, pale to medium green pods with thin walls and mild-to-medium heat that can vary with growing conditions, a staple pepper in Korean cooking eaten fresh, dipped in ssamjang, sautéed, or stuffed. The plants are productive over a long summer harvest season, and pods can be picked green or allowed to ripen to red for a sweeter, hotter flavor. Harvest regularly to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil in zone 9 February–March. Korean melons are fast-maturing and can be succession-planted for multiple crops in zone 9 — spring, summer, and fall plantings are possible. The small fruit size and bush habit make them practical for raised beds and containers. Harvest when the skin turns fully golden-yellow and the stem begins to slip.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Korean melon (chamoe, chamgwoe) is a small, oval to round melon of East Asian origin that ripens from green-striped to a brilliant golden-yellow with white stripes running longitudinally along the skin — visually distinct from any Western melon type. The small (4–8 ounce) fruits have crisp, white flesh with a delicate floral fragrance and exceptionally sweet flavor; the thin skin is edible and the seeds and surrounding gel are also consumed in Korean tradition. Unlike large Western muskmelons, Korean melons are picked at peak ripeness and eaten immediately — they do not store well, and the flavor deteriorates quickly after harvest. Grow on trellises for cleaner fruits or allow to sprawl on mulched ground. The fast maturity (60–75 days from transplant) makes Korean melon one of the quickest-maturing melons available, allowing multiple crops per season in zone 9.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for a December–February harvest. Korean radish can also be sown in early spring in zone 9 (January–February) for a spring crop before heat causes bolting. The large roots require loose, deep, well-tilled soil for straight development; rocky or compacted soil causes forking. Fall crops have the best flavor and texture.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches apart in loose, well-tilled, deep, fertile soil in full sun; Korean radish (mu, 무) is the standard radish of Korean cuisine — a large, stout, mostly white root with a green shoulder, shorter and more rounded than Japanese daikon but crisper, denser, and somewhat spicier. The typical Korean Giant root weighs 1–3 pounds with a firm, juicy, slightly peppery crunch used extensively in kimchi (kkakdugi, cubed radish kimchi), pickled banchan side dishes, and stir-fried radish sides (musaengchae). The flavor is richer and more assertive than mild daikon while remaining far milder than small European radish types. Young tops are also edible and used in soups and kimchi. Harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter for the best texture — over-mature Korean radishes become pithy and hollow at the core.

common_name: Korean Red Garlic (Vigorous Cold-Hardy Asiatic Hardneck)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Korean Red is an Asiatic-type hardneck that needs a real winter chill to form well-divided bulbs and performs best in zone 3-7.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Korean Red is a vigorous Asiatic-type hardneck garlic prized for its early maturity, reliable productivity, and strong, spicy-hot flavor with a pleasant lingering sweetness once cooked. Bulbs are medium-sized with glossy, deep reddish-purple-streaked skin and 6-10 cloves, and the plants tend to size up and mature earlier in the season than many other hardneck types, making it a good choice for gardeners who want an early garlic harvest. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to redirect energy into the bulb; the scapes are tender and flavorful when harvested young. Harvest bulbs once the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, then cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot before trimming and storing; like most hardnecks, storage life is moderate, around 4-6 months.

plant_note: Plant container-grown saplings in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil at a woodland edge or beneath high open canopy; seed needs several months of cold stratification and is slow and unreliable to germinate, so nursery stock is the practical starting point.
directions: Site this slender understory tree where it gets filtered morning sun or dappled light all day, in loamy soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged. Once established, harvest the tightly furled terminal buds just as they begin to open each spring, snapping them off the way you would pick asparagus tips. The buds carry a clean, faintly bitter, almost nutty flavor prized across Japan for tempura and quick blanching, and many foragers rank it above other spring shoots for its delicacy. Because it thrives in the dappled light beneath larger trees, it fills a niche few other food crops can occupy in a wooded garden.

common_name: Kosovo Tomato (Balkan Heirloom Meaty Pink Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Kosovo is a Balkan heirloom valued for large, smooth, pink-red, slightly oxheart-shaped fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh and a mild, sweet flavor, and it is notably productive for a tomato of its size, setting a heavier crop than many other large-fruited heirlooms of similar fruit weight. The low acidity and thick, low-moisture flesh make it especially good for slicing and sandwiches, since the fruit holds together well without excess juice. The vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from sturdy staking to support the heavy fruit load; water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and harvest once fruit fully colors for the best flavor.

common_name: Kossak Kohlrabi (Giant Kohlrabi Variety, Tennis Ball to Softball-Sized with Tender Flesh)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring production; in zone 9, plant October–November for winter-to-spring harvest (December–March). Kossak is a late-maturing giant kohlrabi variety (80–100 days) developed specifically for the ability to grow very large bulbs without becoming woody or pithy — a problem that plagues standard small-bulb kohlrabi varieties when they overstay their welcome in the garden. While standard varieties turn fibrous and tough above 3–4 inches, Kossak can be harvested at 6–10 inches diameter (tennis ball to softball size) and remain tender and sweet. In zone 9, fall planting allows a December–March harvest window before spring heat terminates cool-season growth. Kossak tolerates light frost well, making it a good choice for zone 9 winter gardens.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in cool soil; keep consistently moist for best growth. Harvest from 3 inches up to 10 inches diameter. Kossak is an F1 hybrid kohlrabi variety developed and introduced by Bejo Seeds (Dutch seed company) specifically for the giant kohlrabi market — a category of extra-large kohlrabi varieties that can reach 6–10 inches in diameter while remaining tender and palatable, unlike standard kohlrabi varieties that become woodily fibrous above 3–4 inches. The distinction between Kossak and standard kohlrabi varieties is fundamental: standard types (Purple Vienna, White Vienna, Early White Vienna) must be harvested promptly at small size or become inedible, while Kossak was specifically selected for an extended harvest window at large sizes. This makes Kossak practical for gardeners who cannot monitor their garden daily, for home gardeners who want a few large plants rather than many small ones, and for fall gardeners who want kohlrabi that overwinters in the ground without quality loss. The bulbs are pale green (white type), extremely smooth-skinned, and can reach weights of 1–2 pounds or more while retaining the characteristic kohlrabi flavor — mild, sweet, slightly peppery, somewhere between broccoli stem and turnip — without the harsh bitterness and woodiness of overmature standard types. The flesh is very juicy and crisp, excellent raw in slaws and salads (where the sweetness is most apparent), roasted (where it caramelizes beautifully), or braised. Kossak is also more cold-hardy than many kohlrabi varieties, holding quality in the garden through light freezes, which extends its usability in zone 9 winter gardens.

common_name: Krug Yellow Dent Corn (Foundation Iowa Heirloom Dent Corn)
plant_note: Sow in blocks in rich, deeply worked soil and keep watered through tasseling and silking; rewards a full-length warm season.
directions: Sow in blocks in rich, deeply worked soil and keep watered through tasseling and silking; this is a tall, vigorous dent corn that rewards a full-length warm season. Krug was developed by Iowa farm families in the second half of the 1800s through careful ear-to-row selection and became one of the most influential open-pollinated dent corns in American corn breeding, serving as parent stock for many of the early hybrid corn lines that transformed Corn Belt agriculture in the twentieth century. Its smooth yellow dent kernels grind into hearty cornmeal, and growing it today offers a direct link to the open-pollinated corns that underlie much of modern commercial corn genetics.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Kunth's wild onion is native to the rocky, limestone-based hills, prairies, and open woodlands of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico, where it blooms in spring and early summer. The bulbs are edible — both leaves and bulbs — and have been used as a food plant by indigenous peoples of the Southwest and Mexico for centuries. The strong, garlicky-onion scent distinguishes it readily from non-edible similar plants.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Kunth's wild onion is one of the most widespread and important edible native alliums of Texas and the American Southwest — a spring-blooming, small wild onion native to the limestone hills, Rocky Mountain foothills, and Chihuahuan Desert mountains of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico, where it has been harvested and eaten by indigenous peoples for thousands of years as a wild food plant. The bulbs and leaves both have a strong onion-garlic flavor and aroma, usable in the same ways as domestic onions and garlic — raw, cooked, pickled. The spring flowers are produced in small, rounded umbels of white to pale pink to deep pink star-shaped florets on stems 8–16 inches tall, serving as pollinators for native bees and beetles. In the garden it provides both a wildflower display in spring and an edible wild-food plant for harvesting — a dual-purpose native species for the Texas-Southwest edible landscape and native plant garden. The strong garlic-onion scent immediately identifies it as edible and distinguishes it safely from the non-scented, potentially toxic Nothoscordum bivalve (crow poison) with which it sometimes grows.

plant_note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: Direct sow this compact Japanese kabocha after the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep in hills spaced 3 to 4 feet apart in full sun. Each vine produces small 3 to 4 pound fruits with sweet, fine-grained flesh reminiscent of sweet potato. Allow the squash to mature fully on the vine until the rind hardens and the stem corks, then cure in a warm spot to improve storage and flavor. Give the vines room to sprawl and provide steady moisture, especially while fruit is sizing up.

plant_note: In mild-winter regions (zone 8 and warmer), direct sow 4–8 weeks before the first fall frost for a traditional Nile Delta-style winter harvest; in colder climates sow in spring after the last frost for a summer cutting crop instead.
directions: Kurrat is the same species as leek and elephant garlic but is grown exclusively for its flat, garlicky-oniony foliage rather than a swollen shank or bulb, and it is a staple flavoring green in Egyptian and eastern Mediterranean kitchens. Broadcast or drill seed thickly into rich, well-drained soil, since plants are grown in dense clumps rather than as individually spaced bulbs. Once shoots reach 8–10 in, cut foliage back to about 2 in above the crown; the clump will resprout, allowing several successive harvests over the cool season. Established clumps can also be divided in fall to propagate new plantings vegetatively.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or again in late summer for a fall crop; Kyona regrows quickly after cut-and-come-again harvest.
directions: Sow seed thinly a quarter inch deep in rich, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to reduce crowding once established. This selected mizuna strain produces dense clumps of finely serrated, feathery dark-green leaves with slender white stalks and holds flavor well without becoming overly pungent. Harvest outer leaves continually for salads and stir-fries, or cut the whole plant an inch above the crown for regrowth. Bolts in sustained heat, so it performs best as a spring or autumn crop.

plant_note: Direct sow from early spring through midsummer for a succession of harvests into fall; Kyoto Market also overwinters well in milder climates.
directions: Kyoto Market is a vigorous, fast-growing Japanese bunching onion long associated with the traditional Kyo-yasai vegetables of the Kyoto region, prized for its long, straight white shanks and heavy, uniform yields. Sow seed directly and thin as stalks develop, harvesting young plants as slender scallions or letting them grow thicker without losing tenderness or flavor. Hilling soil around the base as the plants grow lengthens the blanched white portion for a more traditional Japanese-style leek-like scallion. Its disease resistance and tolerance of both heat and cold make Kyoto Market a reliable choice for extended-season plantings from spring through fall.

common_name: Kyoto Red Carrot (Kintoki, Japanese New Year Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow into deeply worked, loose soil in mid-to-late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Kyoto Red needs a long, cool growing season to develop its full length and deep color, so it is best sown as a fall crop in zone 9.
directions: Sow seed thinly in deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun and thin seedlings to 3–4 inches apart, since this variety needs a long, undisturbed taproot run to reach its full 10- to 12-inch length. Kyoto Red, also known as Kintoki carrot, is a traditional Japanese heirloom prized for its striking, uniformly deep red-orange color that holds even after cooking, along with a sweet, dense flesh valued in Japanese New Year dishes and simmered preparations. It grows more slowly than Western carrot types and performs best with a long, cool finish, so a late-summer sowing timed to mature through fall and winter gives the best color and flavor. Harvest once roots reach full size and store dug roots cool and slightly moist for extended keeping.

common_name: La Ratte Fingerling Potato (Classic French Gourmet Fingerling)
plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January-February for harvest before summer heat sets in. Cut seed pieces to egg size with 1-2 eyes each and let cut surfaces cure a day or two before planting.
directions: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. La Ratte is a classic French fingerling potato long prized by chefs for its exceptionally rich, nutty, almost chestnut-like flavor and dense, waxy, pale yellow flesh that holds its shape beautifully when boiled or roasted whole. The small, knobby, finger-shaped tubers mature over a somewhat longer season than standard round potatoes and yield less per plant, but the superior flavor has made it a long-standing favorite for specialty and high-end cooking. Harvest once vines begin to yellow and die back, and handle the thin-skinned tubers gently, since they bruise more easily than thicker-skinned storage potatoes.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: Sow this 18th-century Tuscan heirloom in early spring for a summer harvest or in mid to late summer for fall and winter greens, as its flavor sweetens after frost. Direct sow a half inch deep and thin seedlings to 12 to 18 inches apart. Harvest tender young leaves as salad greens in about 21 days, or let plants mature for full-size, strap-shaped dark blue-green leaves prized by cooks. Pick outer leaves first to keep plants producing over a long season, and provide steady moisture for tender growth.

plant_note: Sow in spring or late summer; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: Also known as dinosaur or Tuscan kale, this heirloom features deep blue-green, bumpy-textured leaves with rich, mild flavor. Sow directly in spring or late summer, as it is a cold-hardy crop whose flavor sweetens after a frost. Thin plants to give the tall, upright rosettes room to develop. Harvest outer leaves from the bottom up, letting the center keep producing for a long, continuous cutting season.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for the main crop; alternatively start indoors 4–6 weeks before last spring frost. Lacinato kale matures more slowly than curly kale but holds better through winter and regrows vigorously in spring.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost or start indoors in early spring; lacinato kale (also called dinosaur kale, Tuscan kale, or cavolo nero) forms tall, upright plants with long, strap-like, deeply puckered, blue-black to dark-green leaves with a more tender texture and milder, slightly sweeter flavor than curly kale. It is one of the foundational vegetables of Tuscan cuisine, essential in ribollita and minestrone. Harvest by removing outer leaves as needed, working from the bottom of the stem upward — plants will continue producing from fall through winter and into spring in mild climates. Flavor intensifies significantly after frost exposure. A more elegant, slower-maturing, and culinary-preferred alternative to curly kale for the kitchen garden.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil after last frost; Lady pea is one of the smallest of the Southern peas with very small seeds, so somewhat more of them are required per planting. It is heat tolerant and produces reliably in zone 8–10 Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in any well-drained, lean soil in full sun after last frost; Lady cream pea is a traditional Southern heirloom cowpea producing small, white, round peas with a notably sweet, mild, delicate flavor — milder and less earthy than crowder peas or black-eyed peas, and considered by many Southern pea aficionados to have the finest flavor of all the cream peas for fresh eating and freezing. The small size and mild sweetness make it the variety most often served to guests unfamiliar with Southern peas, as the flavor is more approachable and universally liked. A true bush-type plant that is drought-tolerant once established; performs reliably in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast. Excellent boiled simply with butter and salt and served as a side dish, or incorporated into succotash, hoppin' John, and traditional Southern vegetable plates.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into warm, rich soil.
directions: This heirloom is grown for its unique hulless seeds, which are soft-shelled pepitas that need no peeling for roasting or snacking. Sow directly into warm, rich soil after frost, giving the vines plenty of room to spread. Keep moisture and nutrients steady as fruit develops. Harvest the mature pumpkins, then scoop and dry the green hulless seeds for a homegrown supply of pepitas.

common_name: Lakota Squash (Native American Heirloom Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Lakota is a striking Native American heirloom winter squash with vivid deep orange skin dramatically marked with irregular dark green and black mottling — one of the most visually beautiful and historically significant native food squashes, producing teardrop-shaped fruits of 5–8 pounds with exceptionally sweet, rich, deeply colored orange flesh.
directions: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2) after soil warms; provide 4–8 feet of vine space; harvest when the skin hardens completely and can no longer be dented with a fingernail, and the stem begins to dry and cork; cure at room temperature for 10–14 days after harvest to develop optimal flavor and maximize storage life. Lakota squash is an heirloom winter squash associated with the Lakota (Sioux) people of the Great Plains, one of the native peoples of North America who cultivated squash as a primary food staple long before European contact. The variety produces one of the most visually distinctive squashes in cultivation: teardrop or pear-shaped fruits with deep orange-red skin boldly marked with irregular splotches and streaks of dark green and near-black — a coloration so striking that Lakota is as ornamental as it is edible. The flesh is the intensely orange, dry, sweet, and finely textured type characteristic of the best Cucurbita maxima varieties: rich enough to need nothing added beyond butter and salt, sweet enough to serve as dessert, and dry enough to bake or purée without becoming watery. The flavor is often compared favorably to kabocha and red kuri squash — comparable sweetness and dryness but with a distinctive terroir-like richness that differentiates it from commercial varieties. Lakota stores exceptionally well — 4–6 months under cool, dry conditions — making it a true long-keeping winter provision. Average fruits weigh 5–8 lbs with moderate vine length suitable for home gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow this vigorous heirloom squash in warm soil, planting in hills spaced well apart to accommodate 10 to 20 foot vines. Beyond its striking orange and green coloring, Lakota is a superior baking variety with fine-grained, sweet, nutty flesh. Let the pear-shaped fruits ripen fully and the rind harden before harvesting, then cure in a warm, dry spot to improve storage life. Give the sprawling vines full sun and consistent moisture while the fruit develops.

plant_note: Direct sow around the time of last frost; seeds are very small and germinate best when pressed into moist soil without covering. Plants self-sow prolifically once established.
directions: Scatter seeds on bare soil and press firmly; lamb’s quarters germinates readily and requires virtually no care once established. Harvest young leaves and stem tips continuously — they taste similar to spinach, raw or cooked, and are exceptionally high in vitamins A, C, and calcium. The mealy white coating on new leaves is a natural wax secretion. Allow a few plants to set seed each year to maintain a self-sowing colony; mature seeds can be dried and cooked like quinoa. Plants grow rapidly in rich soil and may reach 6 feet if left unchecked.

plant_note: Lambsquarters is more typically managed as a welcome weed than deliberately sown; if intentionally growing, scatter seeds on the soil surface as they need light to germinate, from early spring through early summer. Self-sows prolifically and will naturalize in any disturbed garden soil.
directions: Allow to grow voluntarily in garden beds or scatter seeds on soil surface in early spring; lambsquarters is arguably the most nutritious common garden weed available as a potherb, with leaves containing more calcium, iron, and vitamins A and C than most cultivated greens. The young growing tips and leaves have a mild, spinach-like flavor that is excellent raw in salads when small or steamed, sautéed, or added to soups and egg dishes when older. The mealy white coating on young leaves is normal and edible — it is not pesticide or mildew. The seed heads, when mature in late summer, can be eaten cooked as a grain similar to quinoa (they are closely related). Control by harvesting regularly before seed set; one plant can produce 70,000 seeds that remain viable for decades.

common_name: Lancaster Surecrop Corn (Pennsylvania Dutch Heirloom Dent Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; tolerates drier conditions and lighter soils better than many dent corns.
directions: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; this variety tolerates drier conditions and lighter soils better than many dent corns, though it still performs best with even moisture during pollination. Lancaster Surecrop was developed by Pennsylvania Dutch farmers in Lancaster County and became, over generations of selection, the source of the Lancaster heterotic group that later proved foundational in commercial hybrid corn breeding across the eastern Corn Belt. Grown today, it produces sturdy stalks and well-filled ears of yellow dent kernels well suited to cornmeal and traditional livestock feed, preserving a genetic line with an outsized influence on modern corn.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Lancelot is an early-season leek variety (70–85 days from transplant) with more slender, tender stalks than overwintering types — it is harvested in summer and early fall while still tender, rather than being held through winter; ideal for gardeners who want leeks available early in the season before winter storage types are ready.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost at 65–75°F; transplant outdoors after last frost, setting transplants 4–6 inches apart in a trench 4–6 inches deep to blanch the shafts; gradually backfill the trench as plants grow; harvest beginning at 1 inch shaft diameter for best tenderness. Lancelot is a European-bred early-season leek variety that fills an important niche in the leek production calendar: unlike the classic overwintering leek varieties (such as Bleu de Solaise or Giant Musselburgh) that require 130–150+ days from transplant and are intended to overwinter in the garden for winter and spring harvest, Lancelot matures in just 70–85 days from transplant and is harvested in late summer and early fall while stalks are still slender, tender, and at their best eating quality. The stalks are typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter at harvest — more refined in texture and milder in flavor than fully mature overwintering leeks — making Lancelot the superior choice for preparations where tenderness and delicate leek flavor are paramount: vichyssoise, leek gratin, braised leeks, and fresh leek salads where the young stalks are excellent raw. The blue-green foliage and cylindrical white shaft create an attractive plant in the garden from late spring through summer. Lancelot does not have the cold hardiness or overwintering capability of late types but excels as a summer-season leek in climates too hot for fall-planted overwintering types.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed once soil is workable in spring; mark rows clearly since parsnip emergence is slow and easy to mistake for weeds.
directions: Direct sow shallowly into loose, deeply dug soil free of rocks and clods so the long roots can develop without forking, and thin seedlings early to prevent crowding. Lancer is valued by market gardeners for its smooth white skin, uniform wedge shape, and strong resistance to canker, a common fungal problem that disfigures many older parsnip varieties. Allow roots to remain in the ground after the first fall frosts to develop their full sweetness before digging for storage or immediate use.

plant_note: Direct sow in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade as early in spring as soil can be worked, or sow in late summer for a fall and overwintering crop; land cress is a cold-hardy watercress substitute that thrives in ordinary garden soil without the running water watercress requires.
directions: Direct sow in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun as soon as soil can be worked in spring or in late summer for fall harvest; land cress (upland cress, American cress, creasy greens) is a biennial European native grown as an annual salad herb that provides a peppery, watercress-like flavor in ordinary, moist garden soil — without the stream or pond edge that true watercress (Nasturtium officinale) requires. The deeply lobed, rounded basal leaves have intense, hot, peppery bite that mellows considerably with cooking. Plants remain edible through light frosts and can often be overwintered under cold frames in zones 5–7, providing very early spring greens. Harvest outer leaves beginning at 4–6 inches in height; plants withstand multiple pickings before bolting in warm weather. Sow every 4 weeks for succession harvests through the cool season. Excellent raw in small quantities to add zip to salads, or blanched and wilted as a cooked green.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost once soil warms.
directions: This classic indeterminate variety yields abundant clusters of bright red cherry tomatoes with fresh, zesty flavor all summer. Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil warms. Stake or cage the vigorous vines and remove suckers if you want to manage the sprawl. Pick tomatoes as they ripen to keep the plants setting new fruit continuously through the season.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Late Flat Dutch'
plant_note: Start seed 12–16 weeks before the first fall frost for a fall/winter-maturing crop, or start in very early spring for a summer harvest in cooler climates; in zone 8–9, Late Flat Dutch is best grown as a fall-planted crop that matures through winter, since it tolerates hard freezes and stores in the garden far better than it handles summer heat.
directions: Set transplants 24–30 inches apart in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the large, heavy heads need ample room and rich soil to size up properly over their long season. Late Flat Dutch is a 19th-century American heirloom prized for producing enormous, flattened, blue-green heads that commonly reach 10–15 pounds and can grow considerably larger under good conditions, with dense, crisp interior leaves that make it an outstanding keeper — heads store for months in a root cellar or cool garage, and the variety was historically favored for large-batch sauerkraut and winter storage before refrigeration was common. Its long season and excellent cold hardiness make it best suited to fall planting in mild-winter climates like the Gulf South, where the heads mature slowly through the cool months and can stand in the garden through hard freezes without splitting. A workhorse heirloom for gardeners who want maximum storage cabbage from a single planting, in zone 3–9.

plant_note: Direct sow 12–16 weeks before first fall frost so roots mature in cool fall weather; in zones 3–7 sow June–July. Rutabaga requires a long, cool growing season — unlike turnips, which can be harvested young in 50–60 days, rutabagas need the full 85–95 days to develop their full size and flavor. Frost dramatically improves rutabaga flavor by converting starches to sugars — leave roots in the ground through hard frosts and harvest in late fall or winter. Thin to 6–8 inches apart. In zone 9 the late-fall/winter growing season is too short for full rutabaga development — zones 3–7 are the primary growing regions.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, stone-free soil; Laurentian is the standard North American rutabaga variety — a natural hybrid between turnip and cabbage producing large, round to slightly elongated roots with the characteristic purple shoulder above ground and yellow-tan below, with golden-yellow, dense, starchy flesh distinctly different from the white flesh of turnips. Rutabaga (called 'swede' in British English, reflecting its Swedish origin) has a richer, more complex flavor than turnip — the yellow flesh is denser, starchier, and more nutrionally robust with a sweeter, more earthy, complex flavor that becomes significantly more intense and sweet after hard frost exposure. The classic rutabaga preparations — mashed ('neeps' in Scotland, traditionally served with haggis), chunked in beef stew, roasted with butter and herbs, or pureed into soups — take full advantage of the dense, deeply flavored flesh that holds its shape better than potato while contributing its own distinctive sweetness and earthiness. Laurentian's large size (roots can reach softball size in good conditions), excellent storage quality (roots keep for months in cool storage), and consistent purple-top appearance make it the most reliable and widely grown rutabaga for home and market garden production.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, and again in late summer for fall.
directions: Sow Lavewa spinach directly in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since spinach bolts in heat and long days. This open-pollinated variety offers good heat tolerance and mildew resistance, rivaling hybrids for flavor. Thin seedlings to about 4 to 6 inches apart and keep the soil consistently moist and cool. Harvest outer leaves individually or cut whole plants, and provide light afternoon shade to extend the harvest in warm weather.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Lazy Housewife is an 1810 German heirloom pole bean that is one of the oldest and most historically significant American heirloom beans, documented in German seed catalogs since the early 1800s and named for the ease of shelling — the pods are stringless and the beans pop out with minimal effort.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis, teepee poles, or corn stalks; provide 6 feet of vertical support for the vigorous vines. Lazy Housewife is one of America's most documented heirloom pole beans, appearing in American seed catalogs since at least 1810 and recorded by seed historian William Woys Weaver as a bean brought to America by German immigrants; the name refers to the ease of preparation — the pods are stringless when harvested young as snap beans, and the mature white seeds shell out of the dried pods with minimal effort, hence 'lazy housewife.' The pods are 5–7 inches long, round, and stringless, with plump white seeds marked with a distinctive black eye at maturity. Equally excellent as a snap bean (harvest young), shell bean (harvest green pods when seeds have filled), or dry bean; the cooked flavor of the mature seeds is rich, creamy, and outstanding.

common_name: Lazy Wife Pole Bean (Stringless German Heirloom Pole Bean, 1810 American Classic)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Lazy Wife requires a pole or trellis 6–8 feet tall and produces abundantly over a long season. In zone 9, plant April–May; the variety performs adequately but prefers somewhat cooler conditions than the peak Gulf South summer. A late-July or August planting for fall production is often more productive in zone 9 than a late spring planting that encounters July-August heat. The 'lazy' in the variety's name refers not to any person but to the ease of preparation: Lazy Wife is stringless and requires no tedious stringing of the pods before cooking — a significant advantage in the era when most snap beans had tough, fibrous strings running the length of each pod. This stringless quality was unusual and highly valued when the variety was widely grown in the 19th century.
directions: Direct sow 1.5 inches deep after last frost; provide tall support (6–8 feet). Harvest at 5–7 inches as snap bean or leave to dry for shell/dry use. Lazy Wife is a German immigrant heirloom pole bean that was introduced to American seed catalogs around 1810 and became one of the most popular snap beans in the 19th century — a status maintained until modern stringless hybrid varieties provided equivalent ease of preparation with higher yield. The name 'Lazy Wife' refers to the bean's stringless character: in the 19th-century farm kitchen where snap bean preparation required long sessions of stringing pods by hand before cooking, a truly stringless bean required no stringing at all — hence the tongue-in-cheek name suggesting the homemaker could be 'lazy' about bean preparation. The implied humor of the name was accepted in its era; the bean's quality was the real selling point. Lazy Wife produces broad, flat, pale green pods (5–7 inches long, 0.75 inches wide) with a somewhat different form than round-pod types — the flat pod shape and relatively thick walls give Lazy Wife a characteristic visual distinction from most modern snap beans. The pods are truly stringless through their snap-bean stage and have rich, full flavor that heirloom enthusiasts prize. The seeds are creamy-white and excellent as a shell bean (picked young) or dry bean (left to fully mature), giving Lazy Wife three-stage versatility as a snap, shell, or dry bean from a single planting.

common_name: Leaf Amaranth (Chinese Spinach, Callaloo, Joseph's Coat)
plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface or barely covered — seeds need light to germinate; in zone 9 plant from March through September for continuous warm-season production. Leaf amaranth is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens available, thriving when spinach and lettuce have long since bolted.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface or barely 1/8 inch deep in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; leaf amaranth germinates quickly in warm conditions and grows rapidly to a productive harvest-ready size in as little as 30 days. The young leaves taste mild and spinach-like when harvested small; older leaves are cooked like spinach, steamed, sautéed, or stewed into the Caribbean callaloo and West African soups that this plant anchors. It is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens for southern gardens, producing abundantly through summer temperatures that wilt most other greens. The tricolor varieties display striking red, gold, and green foliage useful as an ornamental. Pinch the growing tip frequently to encourage bushy lateral branching and delay seed formation; once the plant flowers heavily, leaf quality declines.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; succession sow every 2 weeks through spring, then again in fall.
directions: Scatter or row-sow seed on the surface or barely cover with 1/8 in of soil, as light aids germination. Thin to 6–10 in and use thinnings as baby greens in salads to avoid waste. Harvest outer leaves continuously once plants are 4–6 in tall, or cut the entire plant an inch above the soil line for a cut-and-come-again harvest. Bolting in warm weather makes leaves bitter; provide shade cloth in late spring to extend the season.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; transplant seedlings into deep trenches after the last frost date.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors in flats and thin to 2 in; transplant pencil-thick seedlings into 6-in-deep trenches, dropping each plant into a dibber hole and filling with water rather than soil to encourage a long white shank. Gradually fill trenches and hill up soil around stems as they grow to blanch the shanks. Leeks tolerate hard frost and can be left in the ground well into winter for a late harvest. Dig as needed once shanks reach 1 in or more in diameter.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Legend is an Oregon State University tomato released in 1996 with the highest level of late blight (Phytophthora infestans) resistance available in an open-pollinated tomato variety — developed specifically for the damp, foggy conditions of the Pacific Coast where late blight is a persistent annual challenge that can devastate unprotected tomato crops.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Legend is determinate and does not require staking, though a cage prevents fruit from resting on the soil; provides excellent production without fungicide sprays in conditions where late blight is present. Legend was released in 1996 by Dr. Jim Baggett at Oregon State University, culminating many years of breeding for late blight resistance in open-pollinated tomatoes; at the time of release it had the highest documented level of late blight resistance in any open-pollinated variety, making it a breakthrough for organic and low-spray gardeners in humid, blight-prone climates. The large (10–16 oz), round to slightly flattened, smooth, uniform deep red fruits have thick walls, good meaty texture, and classic sweet-balanced tomato flavor superior to most disease-resistant commercial varieties; the determinate plant ripens a heavy concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks rather than producing continuously. Legend performs exceptionally well in the Pacific Northwest and humid Eastern climates; it is also valuable in Gulf Coast gardens planted in fall (August–September) when late blight risk from summer thunderstorm humidity is highest. One of the most important contributions to open-pollinated tomato breeding in the late 20th century.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; one of the most reliable large yellow tomatoes available, with good disease resistance and consistent fruit set even in warm, humid conditions — well-suited to zone 8–10 spring planting.
directions: Start seed indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem deeply and providing a sturdy cage or stake from the outset. Lemon Boy is one of the most widely grown large yellow tomatoes, an F1 hybrid introduced in 1984 that remains a top performer for home gardeners seeking a reliable, large, lemon-yellow salad tomato; it produces 6–8 ounce round fruits with smooth, bright canary-yellow skin and mild, sweet, very low-acid flesh that is ideal for slicing fresh, for guests who find red tomatoes too acidic, and for adding visual contrast in salads and on plates. Disease resistance to verticillium, fusarium, and nematodes makes it particularly valuable in humid southern gardens. Water consistently and stake firmly as the indeterminate vines are tall and productive.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for a spring crop and again July–August for fall. Lemon Cucumber is best harvested when pale yellow to ivory colored — fully yellow fruits are overripe and develop a slightly bitter skin. The round shape and distinctive color make it easy to spot on the vine when it's time to harvest. Plants are productive and compact enough for small trellises and can be grown in containers.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with trellis support; Lemon Cucumber is an 1894 American heirloom producing distinctive round to oval, lemon-sized fruits with pale yellow-white skin when ripe — the resemblance to a lemon is strictly visual, as the flavor is mild, sweet, and refreshing with none of the tartness of actual lemon. The thin skin, small seeds, and crisp, sweet, very low-bitterness flesh make Lemon Cucumber one of the most palatable cucumbers for fresh eating without peeling — the skin remains tender and palatable throughout the eating-ripe stage (pale yellow to ivory) unlike the tough skins of slicing cucumbers. The round shape also makes Lemon Cucumber excellent for serving as a natural bowl — hollow out the round fruit and fill with dips, salads, or other fillings. The mild, sweet flavor and easy digestibility (lower cucurbitacin bitterness than many cucumbers) makes it popular for people who find regular cucumbers hard to digest.

plant_note: Sow in warm soil; seedlings resent cold, wet conditions.
directions: This heirloom bears round, yellow, lemon-sized fruit with sweet, mild, non-bitter flesh. Sow seeds an inch deep in warm soil and grow on a trellis to keep the round fruit clean and easy to spot. Keep evenly watered to avoid bitterness and misshapen fruit during dry spells. Harvest while the skin is still pale yellow and before it turns deep gold and seedy. Frequent picking keeps the prolific vines producing until frost.

common_name: Lemon Cucumber (Crystal Apple Cucumber, Round Yellow Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Lemon cucumber (Crystal Apple) produces round to oval, tennis-ball-sized, pale-creamy-yellow fruits with exceptionally mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor — harvest when the skin is pale yellow to white; allowing it to turn deeper yellow indicates overripeness and seed development.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil reaches 65°F; thin or transplant to 18–24 inches; harvest when pale yellow. Cucumis sativus 'Crystal Apple' (Lemon cucumber) is a heritage cucumber variety — one of the best-loved heirloom types — producing distinctive round to oval, tennis-ball-sized fruits with pale cream to pale yellow skin and white flesh that is exceptionally mild, sweet, and non-bitter compared to most standard cucumbers. Despite the name, the flavor is not lemony — it tastes like a very mild, sweet, refreshing cucumber. The thin skin makes peeling unnecessary, and the mild flavor means the seeds and seed cavity are also mild and not bitter, unlike some full-sized cucumbers. Lemon cucumbers are extremely popular with home gardeners for several reasons: the unusual round shape is attractive and different from grocery store varieties; the mild, non-bitter flavor appeals to people who find standard cucumbers too strong; and the fruits are easy to spot when harvesting (by size and color rather than hunting in dense vines). The variety produces prolifically over a long season. Best harvested young — large, deep-yellow specimens tend toward bitterness and seedness. An excellent choice for fresh eating, quick pickles, and cucumber water.

plant_note: Start indoors early; this species is slow to germinate and needs a long, warm season.
directions: Start this Peruvian aji pepper indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, as baccatum peppers germinate slowly and need a long, warm growing season. Provide bottom heat and warm soil around 80 degrees for best germination, then transplant out well after frost when nights stay warm. The bright yellow, wrinkled pods rate 30,000 to 50,000 Scoville units with a distinct citrus flavor and lemony aroma. Give plants full sun, stake them if they grow tall, and harvest fruits fully colored for the best flavor.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum baccatum species takes longer to germinate and matures more slowly than C. annuum. In zone 9 start in January and transplant March–April. Lemon Drop thrives as a perennial in zone 9 and 10 — cut back hard in late winter and the plant will regrow from the roots, producing earlier and more heavily in its second year.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Lemon Drop is a Peruvian aji pepper (Capsicum baccatum) producing small, wrinkled, bright lemon-yellow fruits that ripen from pale green through various shades of yellow with a distinctive fruity, citrusy, bright heat very different from the harsher burn of jalapeños or the floral heat of habaneros. The heat level is medium-hot (15,000–30,000 Scoville units) with a pronounced fruity, lemony flavor note that makes Lemon Drop one of the most culinarily versatile hot peppers — used in salsas, ceviches, hot sauces, and Peruvian-style pepper pastes where the citrus-forward flavor complements seafood and poultry. Capsicum baccatum species peppers are widely grown in South America and increasingly popular in North American specialty gardening. In zone 9 the perennial habit is a major advantage — the plant can grow to a small shrub 4–5 feet tall over multiple seasons, producing far more fruit than annual plantings.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; aji limon is a Peruvian species (Capsicum baccatum) that germinates more slowly than C. annuum peppers and benefits from a longer indoor growing period. Needs consistently warm conditions to thrive.
directions: Start indoors in warm conditions and transplant after frost danger has passed; lemon drop pepper (aji limon) is a Peruvian Capsicum baccatum cultivar producing small, tapered, bright yellow fruits 2–3 inches long with a distinctive intensely fruity, citrusy, lemon-like flavor combined with a clean, building heat (30,000–50,000 SHU). The lemon aroma and flavor make it quite different from other yellow hot peppers and it is used extensively in Peruvian cuisine — in ceviche, aji de gallina, and fresh salsas where its fruitiness and brightness are essential. The plants are productive and quite ornamental with their pendant yellow fruits. Fresh or dried and ground, it is one of the most versatile and distinctive of the South American aji peppers.

common_name: Lemon Drop Pepper (Fruity Lemon-Yellow Peruvian Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting (C. chinense is slower to germinate and develop than C. annuum); transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Lemon Drop requires a long warm season — in zone 9, the long growing season supports full production.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Lemon Drop is a traditional Peruvian pepper (Ají Lemon in Peru) — a small (1–1.5 inch), thin-walled, conical fruit with a distinctive bright-lemon-yellow color at maturity and a unique combination of intense heat (15,000–30,000 Scoville units — comparable to a serrano but with more heat variability) and fruity, distinctly citrus-lemon flavor. The characteristic lemon flavor — a fruity, citrus-forward quality quite unlike the neutral heat of jalapeños or the fruity sweetness of habaneros — makes Lemon Drop one of the most flavorful hot peppers for cooking applications where heat AND flavor complexity are desired simultaneously. The dried and powdered fruit has an exceptional flavor that is widely used in traditional Peruvian cuisine for adding heat and bright citrus notes. As a Capsicum chinense species, Lemon Drop requires somewhat higher temperatures for germination (80–90°F) and a longer season than C. annuum peppers — start seeds 10–12 weeks before transplanting for adequate development time. The plant is productive in zone 9's long warm season, producing prolifically from late spring through frost. Fresh fruits, dried fruits, and powder form are all excellent culinary applications. The vivid yellow color and intense fruity aroma make Lemon Drop a distinctive addition to the pepper garden.

plant_note: Plant cloves 2-3 inches deep 4-6 weeks before hard freeze so roots establish before ground freezes solid.
directions: Leningrad is a Porcelain-type hardneck garlic sourced from the historic seed collections of St. Petersburg, Russia, valued by cold-climate growers for exceptional winter hardiness and vigorous growth even after harsh, deep-freeze winters. Bulbs form with 4-6 large, easy-to-peel white-wrapped cloves and a robust, sharp flavor that mellows nicely when roasted. Because Porcelain types need a strong cold vernalization period, Leningrad performs best in northern gardens with reliably cold winters and struggles in warm-winter regions. Select this cultivar for its proven reliability in USDA zones 3-5 where many other garlic strains falter.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in early spring, 2–4 weeks before the last expected frost, as young plants tolerate light frost and benefit from a long, cool growing period. Inoculating seeds with a legume-specific rhizobium inoculant before planting improves nitrogen fixation and yields.
directions: Direct-sow lentils in early spring as soon as the soil is workable, planting seeds 1 inch deep in rows 12–18 inches apart; they germinate readily in cool soil and tolerate light frost. Choose a well-drained bed in full sun and avoid high-nitrogen soil, which promotes leafy growth at the expense of pods. Plants need little water once established and are highly drought-tolerant.
