Harvest when the lower pods turn tan and begin to rattle but before the stems dry completely; pull the entire plant and hang it upside down in a dry, airy space to finish curing before threshing.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; lentils prefer cool growing conditions and deteriorate in summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds 1 in deep in rows 18 in apart in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that delay podding. The slender, branching plants benefit from brushy twigs as supports to keep pods off the ground and improve air circulation. Harvest the entire plant when the majority of lower pods have turned tan but before they shatter. Thresh by beating dried plants on a tarp and winnow lightly to clean seed before storage.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or offsets in warm, moist, rich soil in partial shade to shade once the soil is thoroughly warm; leren is strictly tropical and cannot tolerate any frost or cool soil.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in warm, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; leren is a Caribbean and northern South American relative of the ornamental Calathea houseplants, grown in dooryard gardens for the cluster of small, crisp, ivory-white tubers it forms around its base, which are boiled or steamed and eaten much like a delicate, sweet-flavored water chestnut or corn-flavored potato. The broad, upright, paddle-shaped leaves make it an attractive foliage plant for a shaded tropical bed in addition to its root crop, and clumps expand steadily by rhizome offsets that are simply divided to start new plantings or lifted for harvest. Keep soil evenly moist throughout the growing season, since dry spells check tuber development, and harvest by digging the whole clump eight to twelve months after planting once the foliage begins to decline.

plant_note: Scatter seeds thinly on prepared soil and press lightly onto the surface without covering — lettuce seeds need light to germinate; start as early as soil can be worked in spring, 2–4 weeks before last frost. Seeds germinate poorly above 80°F; refrigerate them for 1–2 days before sowing in summer.
directions: Scatter seeds on the surface of moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil and press lightly without covering — lettuce seeds need light for germination; succession-sow every 2–3 weeks from early spring through fall for a continuous harvest. Thin seedlings to 6–12 inches apart (wider spacing produces larger heads). Lettuce prefers cool temperatures (60–70°F) and bolts quickly in summer heat, becoming bitter and inedible; choose heat-tolerant varieties for summer planting and provide afternoon shade in hot climates. The four main types — crisphead, butterhead, loose-leaf, and romaine — have different maturity times and uses but similar growing requirements. Harvest leaf types by cutting outer leaves; harvest head types when the head feels firm.

plant_note: Light-sensitive seed germinates best cool; sow shallow on moist medium.
directions: Sow lettuce seed thinly pressed onto the surface of a moist tray, since it germinates best in cooler conditions and with some light. Keep only a light cover for a day or two, then bring the seedlings into bright light to prevent leggy growth. Mist gently and avoid overwatering, as tender lettuce seedlings rot easily. Harvest the mild, sweet, crunchy greens after about ten days to two weeks once the cotyledons are fully expanded.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Leutschauer Paprika is a slow-to-ripen variety — allow the full season for fruits to turn deep red; in zone 9 the long warm season suits this variety particularly well and allows full color development without rushing.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Leutschauer Paprika is a Slovak heirloom paprika pepper that produces elongated, pendant, 5–6 inch fruits with exceptionally thin walls and high sugar content — characteristics that make it one of the premier varieties for drying and grinding into fresh paprika. The bright red, fully ripe fruits are dried whole in strings (paprika ristras) or sliced and dehydrated before grinding. The flavor is sweet, slightly fruity, and aromatic — quite different from commercially ground paprika that has lost volatile compounds in processing. Plants are productive on fertile soil with consistent moisture; fruit set can stall during the hottest weeks in zone 9 but resumes in September. This is primarily a drying variety, though the fresh ripe fruits are also edible.

plant_note: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Levant cotton is the Old World species long grown across Africa and the Middle East and matures slightly faster than American upland cotton.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has thoroughly warmed; Levant cotton is one of the two Old World cultivated cotton species, historically grown across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia long before American upland cotton became the dominant commercial fiber crop, and it remains a favorite of heirloom-crop growers and fiber crafters for its distinct, shorter, coarser staple. Pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers open over summer and fade before dropping, revealing bolls that split open at maturity to expose the cottony lint, ready to hand-pick once fully open and dry. It generally matures a touch faster than upland cotton, making it a reasonable choice where the growing season runs a little shorter, and its compact, shrubby habit and smaller stature suit a raised bed or container planting as well as a row. Grow it as a curiosity, dye-garden, or spinning-fiber crop, and rotate its planting site yearly like any other cotton to limit soil-borne disease buildup.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once the soil is thoroughly warm, providing a tall, sturdy trellis for the vigorous 10- to 12-foot vines to climb.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once the soil is thoroughly warm, providing a tall, sturdy trellis for the vigorous 10- to 12-foot vines to climb. Bred to be day-length neutral, Liana is one of the earliest-maturing yardlong bean types and performs reliably in both northern and southern gardens, tolerating heat and humidity better than many snap bean varieties. Harvest the slender green pods at 12-18 inches, well before they reach their full 23-inch potential, for the most tender texture in stir-fries and braised dishes.

plant_note: Sow 2–3 weeks after last frost; lima beans demand warm soil and will rot in cold, wet ground.
directions: Sow seeds 1 to 1.5 in deep in loose, warm soil with the eye of the bean facing downward. Lima beans are sensitive to drought during flowering; irregular moisture can cause blossom drop and reduced pod set. For fresh shell use, harvest pods when they are bright green and plump but before they begin to fade or yellow. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine for dry bean storage.

common_name: Lincoln Leek (Dual-Purpose Baby and Full-Size Leek)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out once pencil-thick; Lincoln is a dual-purpose open-pollinated leek that can be pulled young as tender 'baby' finger leeks in about 50-60 days or left to size up to a full 16-20 inch stalk.
directions: Start Lincoln leeks indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Lincoln is a flexible, open-pollinated leek that rewards impatient gardeners as well as patient ones — pull it young at 50-60 days for slender, tender 'baby' or finger leeks with a mild, delicate flavor, or let it grow on to a full-sized 16-20 inch stalk for a heartier harvest later in the season. Hill or trench soil around the growing stems to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion as the plants mature. Keep the soil consistently moist and weed-free, and harvest through fall and into winter in mild climates, since leeks tolerate cold far better than onions.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before last frost; Lincoln (also sold as Homesteader, the same variety under a different name) is one of the most highly regarded American shelling peas for flavor — a mid-season bush pea with wrinkled seeds and large, well-filled pods that many home gardeners consider the finest-flavored of all commonly available shelling peas.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep, 2–4 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; direct seed as soon as soil can be worked in early spring. Lincoln (sold as Homesteader in Britain and by some American companies — both names refer to the same variety) is a mid-season American shelling pea considered by many gardeners and seed savers to produce the finest overall flavor and texture among commonly available bush peas; the compact plants produce blunt-tipped pods with 7–9 large, wrinkled (sweeter) peas each, ripening in 65–70 days from sowing. The wrinkled seed type indicates higher sugar content compared to smooth-seeded varieties; like all garden peas, Lincoln must be harvested at precise peak ripeness and eaten promptly before sugars convert to starch. An excellent variety for freezing as well as fresh eating; it remains the benchmark for shelling pea flavor among serious home gardeners.

common_name: Lipstick Pepper (AAS-Winning Sweet Pimento-Type Pepper, Compact and Prolific)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Lipstick is a compact sweet pepper producing small to medium pimento-shaped fruits (about 4 inches long, heart-shaped with a pointed tip). In zone 9, transplant March–April. Lipstick produces prolifically on compact plants (18–24 inches) suitable for containers and small gardens. Harvest green or allow to fully ripen to deep red for sweetest flavor — red-ripe Lipstick has exceptional sweetness and thick walls ideal for roasting, fresh eating, and stuffing. The compact plant habit means Lipstick can be grown in 5-gallon containers on patios, making it useful for zone 9 gardeners without significant ground space. Unlike the large, blocky bell pepper types that often struggle to set fruit in zone 9's summer heat, the pimento type peppers like Lipstick are generally more heat-tolerant and continue producing through the Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or red; red is sweeter. Lipstick Pepper is an All-America Selections (AAS) winner in the sweet pepper category, recognized for its combination of compact plant size, prolific productivity, and exceptional fruit quality in the pimento pepper class. The variety belongs to the pimento type — a group of sweet peppers distinct from bell peppers in fruit shape (heart-shaped, conical, or tapered rather than blocky), flesh thickness (very thick walls with small seed cavity), and flavor (sweeter, with less of the grassy quality of green bell peppers). Pimento peppers have a long history in American cooking: the red pimento paste used to stuff olives and fill pimento cheese sandwiches is made from this type, and the pimento's thick, sweet walls make it the preferred pepper for roasting, where the flesh caramelizes to an exceptional sweetness. Lipstick's AAS recognition was awarded specifically for its performance across diverse North American climates — including hot-summer regions where standard bell peppers underperform — making it a practical choice for gardeners in zone 9 who find that large bell peppers drop their blossoms or produce poorly during the Gulf South's summer heat peak. The fruit is medium-sized (3–4 inches long, 2.5 inches wide), heart-shaped to conical with a small pointed tip, and ripens from green to a deep, brilliant red. The skin is thinner than a bell pepper and the flesh is proportionally thicker, with a small, easily removed seed cavity. The flavor at red-ripe stage is very sweet, almost candy-like, with none of the bitterness that some tasters detect in green bell peppers.

common_name: Lipstick Sweet Pepper (Pimiento-Type Mini Sweet Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Lipstick is a compact plant (24 inches) bearing 3–4 inch pimiento-type fruits that ripen from green to deep, vivid red. Unlike most bell peppers, Lipstick ripens to red relatively quickly (70–80 days) without the extended 3-week+ green-to-red window of larger types. In zone 9, transplant March–April; plants often continue producing into fall. Lipstick does not require as much fertilizer as standard bell types — moderate fertility produces best flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost with spacing of 15–20 inches. Lipstick is a Burpee-developed pimiento-type sweet pepper that produces small to medium (3 x 3.5 inch), heart-shaped, very thick-walled fruits of the pimiento class — a pepper type characterized by a rounder, more compact form than standard bell peppers, extraordinarily thick walls relative to total size, very few seeds, and exceptional sweetness. The pimiento type has been prized by Spanish and Mediterranean cooks for centuries for its superior eating quality (pimientos are what give pimento-stuffed olives their distinctive flavor and the Spanish name 'pimiento' itself means pepper in Spanish). Lipstick delivers the classic pimiento character in a compact, prolific plant suitable for small gardens and containers: the fruits have very thick walls that hold up to heat, an extremely sweet, mild flavor with no heat, and the characteristic heart-shaped cross-section when sliced that makes them visually distinctive from bell peppers. The vivid, saturated red color at full ripeness is striking and the thick walls make Lipstick excellent for roasting, stuffing with cheese, and eating raw where the thickness provides a satisfying crunch. Ripens more completely and uniformly than many larger bell types, making it practical for gardeners who want to harvest primarily red-ripe peppers.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; an early-maturing pimento-type pepper that performs well in shorter seasons; transplant after all frost has passed and soil warms to 60°F.
directions: Start seeds at 75–85°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Lipstick is an early-maturing sweet pimento-type pepper that produces heart-shaped, 4-inch fruits with thick, candy-sweet walls, minimal seed cavity, and zero heat; they ripen from green to a brilliant lipstick red earlier than most pimentos, making it one of the better sweet pepper choices for northern gardens and short-season growers. The fruits are remarkably thick-walled and sweet when roasted, and they peel cleanly after charring, making them ideal for preserving as roasted red peppers. Compact plants are well-suited to containers.

plant_note: Heat-loving Spanish heirloom; mulch to retain warmth and moisture.
directions: A Spanish heirloom with teardrop fruit striped purple and white and a notably sweet, mild flavor. Give it a long warm season, starting seed indoors early and transplanting into the warmest bed available. Fruit skin is thin and bruises easily, so handle carefully and harvest with shears. Pick when fruit is 5 to 7 inches and still shiny, before seeds harden. Steady watering prevents blossom-end problems and keeps flesh creamy.

common_name: Listada de Gandia Eggplant (Striped Italian Heirloom Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after the last frost date; in zone 9 also transplant in August for a fall crop — eggplants often produce their most abundant crop in the cooler fall weather.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Listada de Gandia is one of the most beautiful and visually distinctive eggplant varieties — a traditional Italian heirloom from the Valencia region of Spain producing oval to oblong, medium-large fruits with a stunning two-tone pattern of cream-white base with vivid purple-lavender stripes or splashes covering much of the surface. No two fruits have exactly the same pattern, making each harvest visually unique. Beyond its striking appearance, Listada de Gandia is prized for its exceptionally mild, tender, low-bitterness flesh — the thin skin and low seed content make it one of the finest eggplants for fresh preparations, grilling, and Italian dishes where eggplant bitterness would be unwelcome. The mild, creamy flesh has a slightly sweet, delicate flavor that is quite different from the stronger flavor of large black globe eggplants. Harvest at medium size (4–6 inches long) when the skin is shiny — the stripes fade and seeds become noticeable if left too long. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved true-to-type. The ornamental quality of the fruits and foliage makes Listada de Gandia attractive even as an edible ornamental in mixed garden beds and containers. In zone 9, eggplants are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables, thriving in the Gulf South summer.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed; Little Darling is a compact hybrid bred to deliver classic dark-rind, red-fleshed watermelon flavor and high sugar content on vines that take up notably less garden space than standard icebox types.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart since vines run only about 4-5 feet, considerably shorter than traditional watermelon varieties. Little Darling produces oblong, dark-striped fruits around 5 by 8 inches and 5-7 lbs, with crisp, sweet red flesh rating around 12 on the Brix sugar scale, making it a good choice for gardeners who want full-flavored, classic watermelon character without the space demands of large-vine heirlooms. Water deeply and consistently through flowering and fruit set, then reduce watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip and by checking that the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and browned, since the compact plant can otherwise make ripeness easy to misjudge.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; carrots resent transplanting so always sow in place.
directions: Direct sow this French baby carrot in loose, stone-free soil, since carrots dislike transplanting and forked roots result from compacted ground. Sow seed shallowly and keep the surface consistently moist until germination, which can take two to three weeks. Thin seedlings to about an inch apart so the slender 3 inch roots can size up sweet and crisp. Little Finger is ideal for shallow beds and containers and is best harvested young; succession sow every few weeks for a continuous supply.

common_name: Little Finger Eggplant (Slender Baby Asian Finger Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Little Finger is a productive, compact eggplant that performs extremely well in zone 9 hot summers. In zone 9, transplant March–April for June–November production. Harvest fruits when 3–5 inches long and deep purple-black — do not allow to over-ripen, as the thin skin becomes tough and the few seeds develop rapidly. The plants produce prolifically in clusters, and frequent harvesting encourages continued production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun in well-drained, fertile soil. Harvest slender purple-black fruits at 3–5 inches. Little Finger is a slender, finger-shaped Asian eggplant — a compact variety producing clusters of elongated, narrow fruits (2–5 inches long, 0.5–1 inch in diameter) of the finger eggplant type. The finger eggplant category is distinct from the large, globe-shaped Italian types and the longer Asian slicers: finger eggplants are the smallest category, producing bite-sized to small fruits in prolific clusters on bushy plants. Little Finger's small fruits are characterized by very thin, tender skin; virtually no seeds; and mildly sweet, creamy flesh without the bitterness sometimes found in large-fruited types. The thin skin means no peeling is required — fruits can be cooked whole (roasted, grilled, or sautéed) without preparation. The compact cluster-fruiting habit makes Little Finger one of the most productive eggplants per plant for its size, making it excellent for small gardens and containers. The fruits are harvested frequently (every 2–3 days at peak production), and the small size makes them ideal for stir-fries, kebabs, and preparations where bite-sized pieces are desired.

plant_note: Direct sow; ideal for containers and shallow beds.
directions: This heirloom baby carrot produces small, vibrant orange roots packed with sweet flavor, bred originally for canning but excellent fresh or in containers. Sow seeds directly into loose soil and keep the bed evenly moist during the slow germination. Thin seedlings so the short roots can size up cleanly. Harvest while the roots are still small and tender for the sweetest, most delicate flavor.

common_name: Little Fingers Eggplant (AAS-Winning Slender Asian-Type Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed; Little Fingers, a 1985 All-America Selections winner, is a slender, finger-sized Asian-type eggplant well suited to container growing.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60°F. Little Fingers, a 1985 All-America Selections winner, produces clusters of slender, finger-sized, deep purple Asian-type eggplant fruit that mature quickly and prolifically, giving a much faster and heavier harvest than large-fruited standard eggplant types. Its compact plant size and quick maturity make it a good fit for containers, small raised beds, or gardeners wanting an early eggplant harvest. Pick fruit young while still glossy and tender, several inches long, since Asian-type eggplant quickly becomes seedy and bitter if left to overmature, and harvest often to keep clusters coming through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Little Gem is a miniature romaine-butterhead cross that produces small, compact, dense heads of exceptional quality — the 'sucrine' of French cuisine, considered by many the most flavorful lettuce for whole-head salads and prized by restaurant chefs for its combination of crunch and buttery flavor.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50–70°F. Little Gem is a miniature romaine/butterhead cross producing small (4–5 inch), compact, upright heads with firm, crunchy outer leaves and a sweet, butter-cream interior heart — essentially a mini Caesar salad head in one plant. Also known as 'Sucrine' in France (from the French for 'sugar'), it has become extremely popular in restaurant and farmers market contexts as a whole-head salad lettuce grilled or served halved with dressings. The outer leaves have romaine's crunch while the hearts are as sweet and buttery as buttercrunch — the best of both types in a small, space-efficient package. 4-6 inch spacing allows intensive planting; harvest the whole head when firm and compact. More heat-tolerant than standard butterhead and holds well in the garden without bolting quickly.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and succession sow; sow in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow this English heirloom mini-romaine directly in cool weather, barely covering the seed since lettuce needs light to germinate. The petite heads reach just 6 inches tall and 4 inches wide, forming the perfect size for a single-serving salad with tender, sweet, succulent leaves. Thin plants to 6 to 8 inches apart and keep them evenly moist to prevent bitterness and bolting. Succession sow every couple of weeks and give afternoon shade in warm weather to extend the harvest.

common_name: Little Leaf Cucumber (H-19, Beetle-Resistant Pickling Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; this Cornell-bred pickling cucumber has unusually small leaves that reduce cucumber beetle damage and improve airflow, making it a favorite for organic growers.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing plants to allow good air circulation. Little Leaf, formally H-19, was developed by Cornell University plant breeders specifically for its diminutive foliage, a trait that exposes fewer leaf surfaces to cucumber beetles and their associated bacterial wilt while still allowing plenty of sunlight to reach developing fruit and improving disease airflow around the vines. It is gynoecious, so interplanting with a small percentage of a standard pollenizer variety, or relying on nearby bees for cross-pollination from other varieties, improves fruit set. Fruits are small, blocky, and dark green, ideal for classic dill pickles, and should be harvested every one to two days at 2-4 inches for best quality.

common_name: Little Lucy Okra (Dwarf Ornamental-Edible AAS Winner)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Little Lucy is a 1998 All-America Selections-winning dwarf hybrid okra, only about 2 feet tall with burgundy pods and maroon-veined foliage, doubling as an ornamental in a small Gulf Coast bed or container.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Little Lucy is a genuine dwarf okra, growing only about 2 feet tall with attractive maroon-veined foliage and burgundy-red pods, making it as much an ornamental accent for a small bed or large container as a food crop. Despite its small stature it produces a real, usable harvest of tender pods best picked young at 2-3 inches, since the compact plant sets pods close together on short internodes. Its diminutive size means it needs no staking and takes up a fraction of the space of full-size okra varieties, a practical advantage for small Gulf Coast gardens where summer heat makes okra one of the most reliable producers. Harvest every couple of days during peak summer heat to keep pods tender and encourage continued flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before last frost; Little Marvel is a 1934 All-America Selections winner — a remarkably compact dwarf bush pea (15 inches tall) that produces an outsized crop relative to its tiny size, making it ideal for small-space gardens, raised beds, containers, and intensive succession planting.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep; Little Marvel can be planted in raised beds at 15-inch row spacing due to its dwarf habit and needs only minimal support. Little Marvel pea won an All-America Selections award in 1934 and remains one of the most productive and most compact garden shelling peas available — the dwarf 15-inch plants are among the shortest of all shelling peas while producing an outsized crop of well-filled pods with 6–8 wrinkled, sweet peas each. The compact habit makes Little Marvel excellent for small raised beds, succession planting in containers, and tight-spaced intensive gardens where full-sized pea varieties would be impractical. Does not require staking even in wind, though a small 12–18 inch support fence improves harvestability. The 60–65 day maturity is relatively early for a sweet wrinkled-seeded pea.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, and again for a fall crop.
directions: Direct sow this compact heirloom shelling pea as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, since peas thrive in cool weather. The short vines grow only 18 to 24 inches tall and do not require support, making them ideal for small gardens and containers. Plants produce an abundance of 3 to 4 inch pods filled with sweet, tender peas perfect for fresh eating. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod fill, and harvest promptly to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is warm; little millet is one of the fastest-maturing small grains and tolerates poor, dry soils and short growing seasons better than most other millets.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in prepared rows or broadcast on a firm seedbed, thinning to 4-8 inches when plants are established; little millet is an ancient South Asian grain crop, among the earliest domesticated grasses on the subcontinent, valued today for its very short growing season (as little as 60 days to maturity), drought tolerance, and ability to produce a reliable crop on poor, marginal soils where other grains fail. The compact plant produces loose, open seed panicles that ripen unevenly, so many growers harvest by cutting whole panicles as they mature rather than waiting for a single uniform harvest date. Thresh by rubbing or flailing dried panicles to release the small seeds, then winnow to remove chaff; the tiny grains are hulled before cooking (whole grain, similar to other millets) and are notably high in fiber and micronutrients compared to rice or wheat. Its short season and drought tolerance make it a useful catch crop or dry-season grain trial in Gulf South gardens.

common_name: Livingston's Beauty Tomato (1880s Foundational American Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, staking the vine as it grows. Livingston's Beauty was introduced in 1886 by Alexander W. Livingston of Reynoldsburg, Ohio, one of the most important early tomato breeders in American history, whose systematic selection work through the late 1800s helped transform the tomato from a distrusted curiosity into a smooth, reliably productive garden staple. The medium to medium-large fruit is a rosy pink-red, smooth, and globe-shaped with good, well-balanced flavor for its era — a marked improvement over the ribbed, irregular tomatoes common before Livingston's breeding program, and a variety that directly influenced the smooth, round tomato shape gardeners now take for granted. Grow it as a piece of American horticultural history as much as a garden tomato; water and feed evenly through the season for the best fruit set and flavor.

plant_note: Plant tuber pieces or rooted stem cuttings 2–3 in deep after soil has warmed well past the last frost; this tropical African crop needs a long, frost-free warm season similar to sweet potato.
directions: A minor but locally important root crop of the mint family, Livingstone potato is grown across the savanna belt of southern and central Africa for the small clusters of starchy, nutty-flavored tubers that form along its sprawling, square-stemmed, aromatic foliage. Because flowering and seed set are unreliable, it is propagated vegetatively from saved tuber pieces or leafy stem cuttings rather than from seed. Plants form a low, spreading mound and benefit from loose, well-drained soil that allows the tuber clusters to expand freely at the base of each stem. Dig tubers once the foliage yellows and dies back at the end of the growing season, handling them gently since the skins are thin and bruise easily.

common_name: Lizzano Tomato (Trailing Cherry Tomato for Hanging Baskets)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a hanging basket or rail planter after frost danger passes, letting the trailing stems cascade over the container edge.
directions: Transplant into a hanging basket or rail-mounted container after the last frost and let the trailing stems spill downward rather than staking them upright. Lizzano is an All-America Selections winner noted for combining a true cascading habit with strong early blight tolerance, an unusual pairing that keeps foliage healthier through the season than most basket-type tomatoes. It produces abundant clusters of sweet, 1-inch red cherry tomatoes continuously from mid-summer until frost.

plant_note: Sow directly; reliably slow to bolt for a romaine type, allowing extended spring and early-summer sowings.
directions: Sow directly in cool soil; this classic English cos lettuce from the early twentieth century forms tall, upright, dark-green heads that fold in on themselves to blanch a firm, sweet heart. It is reliably slow to bolt for a romaine type, allowing extended spring and early-summer sowings in cooler climates. Long a favorite of British kitchen gardeners, it is still maintained by seed-saving groups as one of the best-flavored traditional cos varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Lolla Rossa can be harvested as baby leaves (cut 2–3 inches tall) or allowed to develop to full rosettes. Successive sowings every 3 weeks provide a continuous supply. The red color is most intense in cool weather; warm temperatures reduce pigmentation.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Lolla Rossa is an Italian looseleaf lettuce producing rosettes of tightly frilled, deeply ruffled, deep burgundy-red to crimson leaves — the most intensely frilled and ruffled of all red lettuces, with a texture often compared to coral or ruffled fabric. The heavy frilling maximizes surface area and catches dressings exceptionally well, making Lolla Rossa a favorite in mixed salad bowls and mesclun mixes where its dramatic appearance creates visual impact. The flavor is mild and tender with a slight bitterness from the red pigments that is barely perceptible in young leaves and becomes slightly more pronounced in older, larger leaves. The deep red color makes Lolla Rossa one of the highest-anthocyanin lettuces, providing significant antioxidant content. It is the standard red frilly lettuce in European market and supermarket displays, where it has been in continuous commercial production since the 1970s, and is equally valuable in North American specialty salad production and home gardens.

plant_note: Sow in spring or late summer; heat causes bolting and bitterness.
directions: This Italian heirloom loose-leaf lettuce forms frilly rosettes of magenta-red and green leaves with mild flavor and striking color. Sow directly in cool weather, spring or late summer, since heat prompts bolting and bitterness. Sow in succession for a continuous supply of tender leaves. Harvest outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut whole rosettes when full, keeping soil evenly moist throughout.

common_name: Lollo Bionda Lettuce (Italian Ruffled Green Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow thinly with minimal soil coverage; grow as cut-and-come-again from 40 days or harvest whole heads at 55–65 days. Often grown alongside Lollo Rosso for visual contrast in mixed salad plantings. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall/winter production and February–March for spring. Performs best in cool weather and does not tolerate summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile, well-drained soil or barely cover with 0.125 inch of fine soil; maintain consistent moisture through germination. Lollo Bionda (Italian for 'blonde curly') is the green counterpart to Lollo Rosso — sharing the identical intensely frilled, ruffled leaf margin and open loose-leaf habit but expressing uniformly bright chartreuse-green to golden-green coloring throughout rather than the Rosso type's red pigmentation. The two varieties are frequently grown together in alternating rows or blocks, where the intense green-and-crimson contrast creates a visually striking planting that is both ornamental and practical. Mixed bags of Lollo Bionda and Lollo Rosso leaves form the foundation of the Italian insalata mista tradition. Like Lollo Rosso, Lollo Bionda has a mildly bitter, distinctly Italian loose-leaf character — more complex and interesting than flat-leafed American loose-leaf types — and the same extremely frilled, ruffled texture that gives the leaves visual and textural interest in salads. Lollo Bionda is somewhat more heat-tolerant than Lollo Rosso in some trials, extending the spring salad season by 1–2 weeks before bolting. Both Lollo types are excellent for cut-and-come-again harvesting, where the plant continues producing from the center after outer leaves are removed, providing multiple harvests from a single planting.

common_name: Lollo Rosso Lettuce (Italian Ruffled Red Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow thinly and barely cover with fine soil (lettuce needs light for germination); Lollo Rosso is best grown as a cut-and-come-again crop, harvesting outer leaves from 40 days onward or cutting the whole plant at 55–65 days when full size. In zone 9, sow September through November for fall and winter harvest, and again February through March for spring. Lollo Rosso performs best in cool weather (50–70°F) and tends to bolt quickly in summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile, well-drained soil or cover with 0.125 inch of fine soil; keep moist until germination. Lollo Rosso is the defining Italian loose-leaf lettuce — a variety whose intensely frilled, ruffled, deeply cut leaf margins and vibrant crimson-red to dark wine-red coloring at the leaf tips (fading through red-purple to green at the base) have made it the visual centerpiece of European mixed salad culture and one of the most recognizable lettuce varieties in the world. The name means 'red curly' in Italian, describing both the color and the extraordinarily frilled leaf margin that distinguishes Lollo Rosso from all other common loose-leaf types. The frilling is dramatic and consistent — the leaf margins curl so tightly that they create a lace-like appearance when the lettuce is displayed whole, making Lollo Rosso not only a component of salads but a visual garnish in its own right. The flavor is mildly bitter in the Italian leaf lettuce tradition — more complex and interesting than bland American loose-leaf types but not unpleasantly so — and pairs well with vinaigrette-dressed salads where the slight bitterness provides welcome contrast. Lollo Rosso is the standard accompaniment to Italian prosciutto and melon, appears in mixed salad bags throughout Europe as the red accent component, and is excellent alone dressed simply with olive oil and sea salt.

common_name: Long Black Spanish Radish (Winter Storage Radish with Black Skin)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer/early fall for fall and winter harvest; Long Black Spanish is a winter radish that requires a longer growing time than spring radishes (60–70 vs. 25–35 days). In zone 9, sow August–September for November–January harvest. Winter radishes should not be planted in spring — they bolt quickly in warming temperatures. Harvest when roots reach 6–8 inches; they keep in the ground for weeks and can be stored in damp sand in a cool location for months.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fall in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest when roots are 6–8 inches long; peel before eating as the black skin is tough and astringent. Long Black Spanish Radish is a winter storage radish with a very distinctive appearance: the long (6–10 inch), cylindrical root has deeply black skin — nearly jet black — contrasting with crisp, white flesh within. It is one of the oldest documented European radish varieties, with references dating to the 16th century; it was the standard large winter radish of European cuisine before the introduction of Asian types and remains common in Polish, German, and Ashkenazi Jewish food traditions where it appears in salads (grated with onion and oil) and as a medicinal digestive herb. The flavor is significantly sharper and more pungent than spring radishes — a biting, horseradish-adjacent pungency that mellows somewhat when the grated flesh is salted and rested. The winter storage capability distinguishes Long Black Spanish from spring radishes: properly harvested and stored in damp conditions near freezing, the roots keep for 3–4 months, providing a root vegetable throughout the winter.

plant_note: Direct sow in rich, well-drained soil 1–2 weeks after last frost; Long Island Cheese is a Cucurbita moschata type (related to butternut squash) with exceptional disease resistance and heat tolerance compared to jack-o-lantern types — excellent for zone 8–10 gardens. Vines are vigorous, reaching 10–15 feet.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds, thinning to 2; Long Island Cheese Pumpkin is a large, flat, deeply ribbed, tan-buff heirloom that looks remarkably like a wheel of French cheese — hence its popular name. Developed by Long Island market gardeners in the 19th century, it was once the dominant commercial pumpkin variety in the northeastern United States because of its excellent eating quality, dense orange-yellow flesh with a smooth, rich, sweet flavor particularly prized for pumpkin pies (significantly better than jack-o-lantern types). Being a Cucurbita moschata variety, it is substantially more resistant to squash vine borers, powdery mildew, and heat than C. pepo types, making it one of the most practical large pumpkins for zone 8–10 Gulf Coast gardens where summer disease and pest pressure is high. Fruits weigh 8–15 pounds and store well for months.

common_name: Long Island Cheese Squash (Heirloom Flat Wheel-Shaped Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; as a moschata-type squash it resists squash vine borer better than maxima or pepo types, a real advantage in Gulf South gardens.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room to run. Long Island Cheese is a 19th-century New York heirloom named for its flattened, ribbed, buff-tan fruit that closely resembles a wheel of cheese, with dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh well suited to pies, soups, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata type, it shares that species' strong resistance to squash vine borer, a serious pest of pepo- and maxima-type squash in warm, humid climates. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks to concentrate sweetness and improve storage life, which can extend several months in a cool, dry space.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera 'Long Island Improved'
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date, transplanting 12–16 weeks before first expected frost; in zones 3–7 start in late spring for fall harvest. Brussels sprouts require a very long cool growing season (90+ days) and develop best flavor only after exposure to hard frost — zones 3–7 are ideal, with zones 8–9 being very challenging due to insufficient sustained cool weather for quality sprout development. In zone 9 Brussels sprouts may produce a partial crop in the coolest winters but results are often disappointing compared to more appropriate cool-climate growing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — Brussels sprouts are heavy feeders requiring substantial nitrogen throughout their long growing season; Long Island Improved is the standard open-pollinated Brussels sprouts variety — the classic 'compact' type (as opposed to taller, older varieties) that has dominated American horticulture since the early 20th century. The small, round, tightly packed miniature cabbage heads (sprouts) that form along the stem are harvested from bottom to top as they mature, with each stem producing dozens of 1–2 inch sprouts over several weeks of harvest. Brussels sprouts' reputation for strong, unpleasant flavor is entirely a product of poor growing conditions — specifically, heat stress — rather than the plant's inherent flavor. Brussels sprouts grown to maturity in cool weather with frost exposure are mild, nutty, sweet, and completely different from heat-stressed sprouts with the intense sulfurous off-flavors that give the vegetable its negative reputation. The conversion of starches to sugars after frost exposure transforms Brussels sprouts from a challenging, strong-flavored vegetable into a genuinely delicious one — a transformation that zone 9 gardeners rarely witness but that northern gardeners who harvest after repeated freezes experience routinely.

plant_note: Time so the long crop matures into cool fall weather; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: This time-tested heirloom from the late 1800s is valued for compact plants, dependable yields, and excellent cold tolerance. Start seeds indoors and transplant so the long-season crop matures into cool fall weather, when the sprouts taste sweetest after light frosts. Keep plants well watered and side-dress with nitrogen for steady growth. Harvest the firm sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach about an inch across.

plant_note: Start indoors in early to mid summer and transplant for a fall harvest; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: Start this heirloom Brussels sprout indoors and transplant for a fall harvest, as the sprouts sweeten and firm up after light frosts. Give plants plenty of water, rich soil, and a long season, spacing them 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. Row covers help protect young plants from cabbage worms and other pests. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach about an inch in diameter, and top the plants a few weeks before harvest to encourage uniform sizing.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harvest fruit while still pale orange-yellow just before frost for the longest storage life, rather than waiting for vine-ripening.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, caging or staking the semi-sprawling vines. Long Keeper is grown specifically for its ability to ripen slowly off the vine when picked mature-green to pale blush before the first fall frost, gradually coloring to an orange-red over weeks or months in cool, dark storage so gardeners can enjoy fresh tomatoes well into winter. The flavor is milder than a summer-ripened tomato but remains a valued novelty among gardeners who want to extend the tomato season past the growing year.

plant_note: Direct sow into deeply worked beds and thin early for straight roots; a strong, old-fashioned keeper well suited to fall storage.
directions: A refined selection of the historic Dutch Long Orange carrot line that traces back to 17th-century Netherlands and was further developed by American seed houses in the 1800s, making it one of the direct ancestors of modern Danvers and Chantenay types. It produces long, tapered, deep-orange roots with a somewhat coarser core than modern Nantes hybrids but dependable yields in open garden soil. Direct sow into deeply worked beds and thin early for straight roots; it is a strong, old-fashioned keeper well suited to fall storage.

common_name: Long Pie Pumpkin (New England Long Pie Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost, giving vines ample room to run; the elongated fruit needs a long, dry curing period after harvest for maximum storage life.
directions: Plant seeds in hills of two or three after frost danger passes, and let the long vines sprawl since the fruit is too heavy and elongated to trellis practically. Long Pie is an old New England heirloom, cylindrical rather than round, growing two to three feet long and resembling an overgrown zucchini more than a typical jack-o'-lantern pumpkin. Its smooth orange rind and dense, mild-flavored flesh make it a traditional substitute for butternut or sugar pumpkin in pies and baking, and its thick shell allows it to store for many months longer than most winter squash. Harvest before hard frost when the rind resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before moving to cool winter storage.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth and transplant well after frost when soil and nights are warm.
directions: Start this heirloom eggplant indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, providing bottom heat and warm soil for good germination. Transplant only after nights are reliably warm, as eggplant is very cold sensitive, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. The long, slender purple fruits are flavorful in countless dishes and are best harvested young when the skin is glossy. Stake taller plants, keep them evenly watered, and pick fruits regularly to encourage continued production.

common_name: Long Red Cayenne Pepper (Classic American Cayenne)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Long Red Cayenne is the standard, classic cayenne pepper variety — a long-season heirloom producing pencil-thin, wrinkled, 6–8 inch red pods with 30,000–50,000 SHU heat, the benchmark from which all other cayenne peppers are measured and the source of commercial cayenne powder, hot sauce, and the classic Louisiana-style hot sauce heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained, fertile soil; Long Red Cayenne is a vigorous grower that benefits from staking when loaded with fruit; pick all red and drying fruits promptly to encourage continued production through the season. Long Red Cayenne is the classic cayenne pepper — an old heirloom open-pollinated variety that represents the original 'cayenne' type from which the broad category of cayenne peppers takes its name (likely from Cayenne, French Guiana, where related chiles were grown). The fruits are distinctive: pencil-thin (1/2 to 3/4 inch in diameter), 6–8 inches long, wrinkled and irregular in cross-section, tapering to a point, and ripening to a bright red — characteristics that make Long Red Cayenne immediately identifiable and distinct from the smooth-skinned, shorter 'Ring of Fire' type. The heat level of 30,000–50,000 SHU is moderate-hot — significantly hotter than jalapeños but substantially milder than habaneros — in the range that defines 'cayenne heat' in American cuisine. Long Red Cayenne is the source (via cultivated strains) of commercial cayenne powder, an essential spice in Cajun and Creole cooking, Indian cuisine, and most dry spice blends; of Louisiana-style hot sauce; of the dried cayenne pods used in Chinese and Sichuan cooking; and of the classic sriracha-style sauces. Prolific production on vigorous plants (24–36 inches) in warm climates; excellent for drying on the plant or on strings.

common_name: Long Red Slim Cayenne Pepper (Classic Slender Drying Cayenne)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Long Red Slim produces the classic thin, wrinkled, fiery red cayenne pods traditionally strung and dried for homemade cayenne pepper powder and pepper flakes.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Long Red Slim is a classic, widely grown cayenne cultivar producing narrow, tapering, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to bright red, packing substantial heat in a lightweight, easily dried pod. The thin walls make it ideal for stringing into traditional pepper ropes (ristras) or oven-drying and grinding into homemade cayenne powder or crushed red pepper flakes. Plants are productive over a long season and tolerate heat well, making cayenne one of the more reliable hot peppers for Gulf South summers; pick pods at full red color for maximum heat and flavor when drying.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January and transplant in March. Long Slim Cayenne is highly productive in zone 9's long warm season and often overwinters as a perennial — cut back in late winter and the woody plant regrows to produce even more heavily the next year. For dried cayenne, harvest fully red fruits and dry on strings or in a dehydrator. The thin-walled fruits dry quickly and completely.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Long Slim Cayenne is the standard form of cayenne pepper — the elongated, thin-walled, moderately wrinkled red pepper that is one of the most important culinary chile peppers in the world and the source of commercial cayenne pepper powder and red pepper flakes. The fruits are 4–6 inches long, pencil-thin, and bright red when fully ripe, with heat levels typically measuring 30,000–50,000 Scoville Heat Units — a penetrating, clean, sharp heat that has made cayenne the dominant hot pepper in Louisiana Cajun and Creole cuisine, Indian cooking, and dozens of other culinary traditions. Long Slim Cayenne dries easily and completely due to the thin walls, and the dried pepper grinds to the characteristic bright red powder of commercial cayenne spice. Fresh red cayenne peppers are also used in hot sauce production — Tabasco-style sauces use fermented cayenne-type peppers as their primary ingredient. In zone 9 the plants bear enormous crops of drying-quality peppers over the full warm season.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant March–April for spring and August for fall. Long of Naples produces very long vines (12–15 feet) requiring generous space or a large trellis. The moschata type is more heat-tolerant and powdery mildew-resistant than pepo squashes, making it a better choice for zone 9 summer production. Harvest immature fruits at 12–18 inches for summer squash use, or leave to mature fully for winter storage.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Long of Naples (Lunga di Napoli, Serpentina di Napoli) is a renowned Italian heirloom squash from the Campania region surrounding Naples, producing extraordinarily long cylindrical fruits of 24–36 inches or more — occasionally reaching 4–5 feet under optimal conditions. At maturity the tan-to-buff skin covers dense, deep-orange flesh with a sweet, rich flavor similar to butternut but with a creamier texture and less watery flesh. Immature fruits at 12–18 inches can be harvested and used as a superior summer squash — far more flavorful than standard zucchini, with firmer flesh and more concentrated sweetness. Fully mature fruits cure well and store for 6–12 months in a cool, dry location. As a Cucurbita moschata type, Long of Naples shows excellent heat and humidity tolerance, resistance to vine borers, and superior performance in zone 9 compared to pepo-type squashes. The vines are vigorous and spreading — allow 8–12 feet per plant.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost once soil has warmed; plants spread by rhizomes and will naturalize readily.
directions: Long-leaf Ground Cherry is a hardy native husk tomato found across central and eastern North America in prairies, disturbed areas, and open woodlands, producing small yellow fruits enclosed in papery husks similar to a miniature tomatillo that are edible fresh or cooked. Direct sow seeds after the last frost into well-drained soil in full sun, as this perennial spreads vigorously from spreading rhizomes and will naturalize in favorable conditions. Plants are extremely drought-tolerant once established and require little care beyond occasional thinning to prevent them from crowding out neighboring plants. Harvest fruits when the husk has turned tan and dried, and the berry inside has dropped naturally, as this indicates peak ripeness and sweetness.

plant_note: Root 4–6 inch stem cuttings in water or moist mix after last frost; they root in 1–2 weeks and are ready to transplant when roots reach 1 inch.
directions: Root cuttings easily in water and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; the plant sprawls attractively as a groundcover or can be trained onto a low trellis. Harvest leaves and shoot tips regularly; the raw leaves have a crunchy, mild, slightly succulent texture and are popular in Southeast Asian salads and as an anti-diabetic traditional food. Unlike the closely related Okinawa spinach, this species has smooth (not wavy-edged) leaves without the purple underside. Bring cuttings indoors before first frost for overwintering; in frost-free areas it grows year-round and can be lightly sheared to encourage fresh growth.

common_name: Longfellow Flint Corn (New England Yellow Flint Corn)
plant_note: Plant in blocks after the soil has warmed; its short, reliable season suits northern New England gardens.
directions: Plant in blocks after the soil has warmed; its short, reliable season makes it well suited to northern New England gardens where longer-season dent corns struggle to dry down before frost. Longfellow is an old New England eight-row yellow flint corn, kept in circulation by regional seed savers and small farms in Maine and neighboring states for its dependable yields and cold-season resilience. Ears dry hard and quickly on the stalk, and the kernels grind into a sweet, full-flavored yellow cornmeal typical of the flint corns that sustained early New England farm households through winter.

plant_note: Plant shallot sets 4-8 weeks before the last frost in spring, or in fall in zones 7-10 for a heavier early-summer crop.
directions: Longor is a traditional French shallot valued for producing unusually long, slender bulbs with coppery skin and pink-tinged flesh, distinguishing it from the rounder Dutch-type shallots grown for the fresh market. Plant sets shallow with the tip just showing above the soil surface and keep the bed weed-free, since each set divides into a cluster of several elongated bulbs by midsummer. Reduce watering once foliage begins to yellow and topple, then lift, dry, and cure the bulbs in a warm, airy spot before storing. Longor is prized in French cooking regions such as Brittany for its slightly sweet flavor and long storage life, and gardeners choose it over rounder shallot types specifically for its distinctive shape and keeping quality.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March after nights stay above 55°F. Lorz Italian is productive through the Gulf Coast summer and performs best when harvested green; if left to ripen red, pick before fruits become overripe and mushy in summer humidity.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Lorz Italian is a Washington State heirloom sweet frying pepper, a classic Italian-style variety with thin-walled, pendent fruits that are 8–10 inches long — among the longest sweet peppers available. The mild, sweet flesh is nearly seedless and ideal for the classic Italian-American preparation of frying in olive oil with garlic and salt (peperonata), as well as roasting, stuffing, and fresh eating. The thin walls roast and collapse beautifully without the wateriness of thicker-walled sweet peppers. Plants produce prolifically once established, with multiple fruits per branch; the long, elegant fruits are also ornamental hanging from the plant. Harvest green for crispest texture or allow to ripen red for sweetest flavor.

common_name: Lorz Italian Softneck Garlic (Pacific Northwest Italian Immigrant Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall around the time of first frost; Lorz Italian is a softneck Artichoke-type garlic brought to the Walla Walla area of Washington State by Italian immigrant Lorenzo 'Lorz' Lorenzi in the late 1800s, where it was grown and preserved through generations of Italian-American farming families in the Columbia River valley before entering heirloom seed networks.
directions: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall; softneck types like Lorz Italian can be planted over a wider window than hardnecks — from 4 weeks before first frost to a week or two after; mulch after planting; keep weed-free in spring; harvest when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure thoroughly. Lorz Italian is an Artichoke-type softneck garlic with a remarkable Italian-American immigrant story: it was brought to the Walla Walla Valley of eastern Washington State by an Italian immigrant named Lorenzo 'Lorz' Lorenzi in the late 19th century, where it became a staple of the Italian immigrant farming community in the Columbia River valley region, passed down through family seed-saving for generations before being preserved by heirloom garlic collectors and specialist growers. The large, roundish bulbs typically contain 12–20 cloves arranged in multiple overlapping layers (characteristic of Artichoke types), with white to pale ivory outer skin; the cloves are plump, meaty, and moderately spicy — a full-flavored softneck with more character than commercial supermarket garlic but without the intensity of the finest Rocambole hardnecks. The great practical advantage of Lorz Italian and other Artichoke softnecks is excellent storage — bulbs typically keep 9–12 months in good conditions, far outlasting any hardneck type; the flexible stems also make it excellent for braiding. Adapted to a wide range of climates from cool Pacific Northwest conditions to warm Southern winters.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sections in still or slow-moving water 1–2 feet deep after last frost when water temperature stays above 65°F.
directions: Plant intact rhizome sections (with at least one growing tip) horizontally in the mud bottom of a pond, tub, or container submerged under 12–18 inches of still water; never allow the growing tip to dry out. Full sun is essential — lotus will produce only foliage and few flowers in shade. Harvest rhizomes in fall once foliage dies back by reaching into the mud and carefully pulling out the chain of large, starchy sections; the distinctive lacy, hole-patterned cross-section is a signature feature. Rhizomes must be cooked before eating; they are eaten stir-fried, pickled, or braised throughout East and Southeast Asia and have a crunchy texture even after cooking.

common_name: Louisiana Green Velvet Okra (Long Smooth Dark Green Southern Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow 2–6 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; Louisiana Green Velvet is a smooth-podded, heavy-yielding heirloom okra variety that produces long (5–7 inch), straight, smooth dark green pods with minimal ribbing and particularly tender texture — one of the top-recommended varieties by LSU AgCenter for Gulf Coast okra production, prized for consistent tenderness and yield through humid Louisiana summers.
directions: Soak seeds overnight before planting; direct sow 1 inch deep 12–18 inches apart after soil warms; harvest pods at 4–5 inches for the finest texture; once production begins, harvest every 2 days during peak summer heat as pods elongate rapidly. Louisiana Green Velvet is an heirloom open-pollinated okra variety with a strong association with Louisiana and Gulf Coast traditional food culture — it is one of the most historically prominent varieties in the region and has been grown by Louisiana gardeners for generations as the standard for gumbo okra and fresh summer side dishes. The pods are smooth, deep green, and slightly ridged rather than heavily ribbed like Clemson Spineless, with a velvety (not bristly) surface texture that makes handling comfortable and gives the variety its name. 'Green Velvet' pods remain tender at 4–5 inches under high summer temperatures — a practical advantage in the Gulf South where summer heat causes many okra varieties to become tough and fibrous quickly if not harvested every day. The variety is adapted to the humid, hot climate of coastal Louisiana and the Gulf South and performs especially well in the clay soils and high humidity of the Louisiana bayou region where it originated as a preferred variety. Louisiana Green Velvet is the traditional okra of Cajun and Creole cooking — most commonly used in gumbo, where the natural mucilage (thickening quality) of properly cooked okra is considered essential to authentic texture and flavor.

common_name: Louisiana Long Green Eggplant (Old South Elongated Green Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Louisiana Long Green is particularly productive in the Gulf South's long, hot growing season — transplant in spring and again in August for maximum productivity.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Louisiana Long Green is a traditional old-South eggplant variety producing elongated, cylindrical fruits 8–12 inches long in an unusual pale green to light green-white color that stands in stark contrast to the standard purple-black American eggplant. The pale green color indicates ripe fruit — unlike purple-black types where color darkens as they ripen, Louisiana Long Green turns a light, creamy green to yellow-green when mature. The flesh is white, mild, and very low in bitterness — outstanding for frying, grilling, and the classic Louisiana preparation of eggplant dressing (a traditional Gulf South casserole combining eggplant with shrimp, crabmeat, bread crumbs, and Cajun seasonings). Louisiana Long Green is a regional heirloom that has been grown continuously in Louisiana and lower Mississippi kitchen gardens for generations — selected by Southern gardeners for its outstanding heat tolerance, prolific production in the Gulf South summer, and excellent culinary qualities in traditional regional recipes. Harvest when fruits are 8–10 inches long with pale, slightly shiny skin — over-mature fruits become yellowish and develop more seeds and bitterness. Plants are vigorous and can reach 4 feet tall in the long Gulf South growing season, requiring staking when heavily loaded with fruit.

common_name: Louisiana Purple Pod Bean (Heat-Tolerant Southern Heirloom Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; Louisiana Purple Pod is a vigorous heirloom pole bean bred for Gulf South heat and humidity, and its deep purple pods stand out sharply against the green foliage for fast harvest. In zone 9, plant March-May for a summer crop and again in August for a fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep at the base of a sturdy 6-8 foot trellis or pole support after the danger of frost has passed. Louisiana Purple Pod is a Deep South heirloom pole bean selected over generations for reliable production through the heat and humidity that stall many snap bean varieties, and it shows good resistance to common bean mosaic virus and rust compared to older commercial types. Pods emerge deep purple, which makes them easy to spot among the leaves at harvest time, and the color cooks away to ordinary green so the beans can be prepared exactly like any other snap bean. Pick pods at 5-6 inches long while still tender for the best snap texture, and pick regularly to keep vines producing; left longer, pods can also be shelled fresh or dried for winter storage. Vines climb vigorously and benefit from consistent moisture during flowering and pod set to prevent blossom drop during extreme heat.

plant_note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Louisiana Purple is a deep-purple-stalked heirloom cane traditionally grown for cane syrup and chewing cane.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Louisiana Purple is an heirloom sugarcane variety with deep purple-to-maroon stalks, long grown in Deep South dooryard patches both for chewing fresh (stripping and gnawing the sweet fibrous stalk) and for cooking down into dark cane syrup. Its rich color makes it a popular choice for ornamental use along fences and property lines in addition to its culinary role. Traditionally harvested in November and December after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, it is then stripped of leaves, crushed to extract the juice, and slow-cooked into syrup, a staple of Southern country cooking. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows vigorously from the root each spring, though a hard freeze can reduce syrup yield if it strikes before harvest.

common_name: Louisiana Ribbon Cane (Heirloom Striped Syrup Cane)
plant_note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Ribbon Cane is a traditional Gulf South heirloom variety grown chiefly for syrup rather than table sugar, prized for its distinctive green-and-purple striped stalks.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Louisiana Ribbon Cane is a historic heirloom sugarcane variety, distinguished from modern commercial hybrids by its slender, green-and-purple striped stalks, that has been maintained by Deep South farm families and seed savers for generations specifically for making cane syrup rather than refined sugar. It is traditionally harvested in November and December after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, then stripped, crushed, and the juice slow-cooked down into dark, richly flavored cane syrup, a staple of Louisiana and Georgia country cooking. The tall, clumping perennial grass also makes a striking, fast-growing screen or accent planting; in zone 9 it typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze and regrows vigorously each spring.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil; pick young for a flat snap bean or leave pods to fully dry on the bush for a mahogany-red dry shell bean.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in well-drained garden soil after frost danger has passed; the compact bush habit needs no staking, making it an easy dry bean for smaller gardens. Low's Champion is a New England bush bean introduced in 1884 by the Aaron Low Seed Company of Boston and believed to derive from an older Abenaki variety, producing broad, flat pods that can be picked young as tender snap beans or left to mature into glossy mahogany-red oval dry beans. Its dual usefulness as both a green bean and a soup bean made it a dependable staple in old New England kitchen gardens. Harvest pods regularly if using fresh to keep plants productive, or let the whole crop dry down at season's end for winter storage beans.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a large bicolor beefsteak with stunning golden-orange skin blushed red and equally beautiful red-and-gold marbled flesh — one of the most visually dramatic heirloom tomatoes available.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed and stake or cage firmly to support the large, heavy fruits. Lucky Cross is an exquisite heirloom bicolor tomato producing large, 1–2 pound beefsteak fruits with golden-yellow to orange skin blushed with a red blush at the blossom end and extraordinarily beautiful red-and-gold marbled flesh that is as ornamental sliced on a plate as it is delicious — the flavor is sweet, low-acid, and tropically fruity with exceptional richness. Its rarity and stunning appearance make it a prize at farmers' markets and seed saving circles. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive; harvest when fruit softens at the blossom end and the skin transitions fully from green.

common_name: Lucullus Chard (Heirloom White-Stemmed Large-Leaf Swiss Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; Lucullus produces very large plants and benefits from wider spacing (9–12 inches) than many chard varieties for full-sized leaves. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest, February–March for spring. Lucullus is one of the most productive and heat-tolerant chard varieties for warm climates, making it particularly well-suited to the Gulf South winter garden where it can be grown nearly year-round with mild management.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fertile, well-amended soil; thin to 9–12 inches for full-sized production. Harvest outer leaves regularly from 40 days onward; the plant continues producing new leaves from the center for months with consistent harvesting. Lucullus is one of the oldest and most established Swiss chard varieties in American cultivation — named after Lucullus, the Roman general and gourmet famous for his extravagant feasts, a name that captures both the impressive size of the plant and the generous quality of its harvest. Lucullus produces very large (18–28 inch tall), broadly spreading plants with thick, heavily crinkled, dark green leaves and thick, ivory-white to pale green stems and ribs — a classic white-stemmed chard in the traditional style before the development of colored-stem varieties. The large, deeply savoyed leaves have substantial texture and rich, minerally chard flavor that is excellent cooked — wilted with olive oil and garlic, added to soups and pasta, or incorporated into quiches and casseroles. The very large leaf size makes Lucullus impractical for baby salad mixes (too coarse when young) but exceptionally productive for cooked greens — a single plant at peak production can provide a large bundle of cooking greens per week. Lucullus is often noted for better heat tolerance than some other chard varieties, making it one of the more productive summer leaf vegetables in hot climates.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. Luffa requires a long, hot season.
directions: Nick or soak seeds for 24 hours before sowing 1/2 inch deep indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost to give this long-season crop a head start. Provide a very sturdy trellis, as vines can reach 15 feet and carry heavy fruit. For eating, harvest young fruits at 4–6 inches before the fibrous skeleton hardens. For sponges, allow fruits to fully mature and dry on the vine until the skin browns, then soak in water, peel, and rinse out the seeds.

plant_note: Needs a long, hot season; start indoors and transplant onto a strong trellis.
directions: This vigorous climbing gourd serves two purposes: harvest young fruits as a tender, okra-like vegetable, or let them mature and dry into natural loofah sponges. It needs a long, hot season, so start seeds indoors and transplant onto a sturdy trellis once soil is warm. The heavy vines produce long, hanging fruits that require strong support. For sponges, leave the gourds on the vine until the skin browns and the interior fibers dry, then peel, shake out the seeds, and rinse.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; luffa needs a long season (150+ days frost-free) and benefits from the head start in all but the Deep South. In zone 9 the long summer provides ample time for full maturation when started in March. Direct sow is possible in late March–April.
directions: Grow on a strong trellis, arbor, or fence — luffa vines are extremely vigorous and can cover a large structure in a single season. The large yellow flowers are showy and attract bees and pollinators. Young fruits at 4–6 inches long are eaten as a tender vegetable in Asian cuisines (similar to zucchini but with a silkier texture); for sponge production, allow fruits to mature fully on the vine until the skin turns brown and papery, then soak in water to loosen and remove the outer skin, revealing the fibrous interior skeleton. Dry the sponge in the sun and rinse several times until the fiber is clean and pale yellow. Each vine can produce dozens of sponges.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a white-skinned pumpkin that makes a striking alternative to orange jack-o'-lanterns for fall decoration and has sweet, edible flesh that works well in baking.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-amended soil, spacing hills 5–6 feet apart; Lumina is a vigorous vine type that needs plenty of room and full sun. Lumina is the most widely grown white pumpkin, producing round, 10–20 pound fruits with a smooth, creamy-white to ghostly-white exterior rind that makes it one of the most sought-after decorative pumpkins for Halloween and fall displays; the interior flesh is orange, sweet, and of good quality for cooking and pies — better than many orange carving pumpkins. The white skin provides an excellent canvas for painting, engraving, or decorative carving. Harvest when the rind is hard and the skin resists puncture with a thumbnail; cure for 1 week and store in a cool, dry location for 2–3 months.

common_name: Lunar White Carrot (Pale Ivory Sweet Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow into deeply worked, loose, stone-free soil in early spring or late summer; Lunar White is a pigment-free white carrot grown for its mild, sweet flavor and striking appearance in mixed rainbow carrot bunches.
directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in deeply worked, loose, sandy loam free of rocks and clumps, keeping the surface consistently moist until the slow-germinating seedlings emerge. Lunar White produces smooth, tapered, ivory-white roots with a crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor free of the slight bitterness some white carrots carry, making it a popular addition to mixed-color carrot bunches for market and home use. Because it lacks the orange and purple pigments of most carrots, it shows soil staining and surface blemishes more readily, so grow it in well-worked, debris-free soil for the cleanest roots. Thin seedlings early to prevent crowded, twisted roots, keep beds weeded while carrots are young and slow to establish, and harvest once roots reach full size, since white carrots left too long in the ground can develop a coarser texture.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Lunchbox is an AAS-winning series of compact plants producing abundant small, sweet, snack-sized peppers in red, orange, and yellow, perfect for eating whole straight from the garden.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Lunchbox is a popular sweet pepper series bred to produce large numbers of small, thin-walled, crunchy, sweet fruit about the size of a large grape or small egg, perfect for snacking whole, tossing into lunchboxes, or adding to salads without any need to slice. The compact, well-branched plants are productive over a long season and work well in both garden beds and containers. Harvest continuously as pods ripen to their full color (red, orange, or yellow depending on the specific variety) to keep the plant producing more fruit.

common_name: Lutz Green Leaf Beet (Winter Keeper Storage Beet)
plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; Lutz is a late-maturing beet bred specifically for long storage rather than early eating, so allow it a full season to size up.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist to prevent woody roots. Lutz Green Leaf, also called Winter Keeper, is a classic American heirloom beet bred to grow to a large size (often 3-5 inches or more) without becoming woody, fibrous, or losing its sweet flavor the way most beets do when oversized — a trait that makes it uniquely suited for fall harvest and long winter root-cellar storage.
