Mountaineer is a West Virginia Appalachian heirloom half-runner bean, a growth habit intermediate between bush and pole types that produces short climbing runners while still setting a concentrated, earlier harvest more like a bush bean. The tender, stringless, flavorful pods are a favorite for fresh eating and traditional Appalachian canning and pickling ('leather britches' style stringing and drying is also common with half-runner types), and the plants tend to keep producing over a longer window than most bush beans. Pick regularly once pods reach full size but before seeds bulge visibly inside, since frequent picking is the single most effective way to keep any snap bean, including half-runners, producing longer.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; slow to germinate so give it warmth.
directions: These grape-sized fruits look like miniature watermelons but taste like tart cucumber, perfect for pickling or garnishing drinks. Vines can reach 10 feet, so provide a trellis for tidy growth and easy picking. Harvest fruits when firm and about the size of a grape, before they soften and turn sour. Plants tolerate heat well and produce steadily until frost.

common_name: Mr. Big Pea (AAS-Winning Large-Podded Shelling Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter to early spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Mr. Big is an All-America Selections winner bred for unusually large, sweet pods on vigorous vines.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked, providing a trellis or netting for the vines to climb. Mr. Big is an All-America Selections winner prized for its unusually large, plump, sweet pods, often 4-5 inches long and packed with 9-10 large peas, produced heavily on vigorous vines over a fairly long harvest window for the cool season. Its exceptional pod size makes shelling faster and more rewarding than many standard shelling peas. Harvest pods when well-filled but still bright green and firm, picking every couple of days to encourage continued production before summer heat ends the crop.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Mr. Snow is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing pale ivory-white fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Mr. Snow bears medium fruit in a pale, creamy ivory-white with mild, low-acid, sweet flavor typical of white tomato varieties, on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant that brings this unusual color to a small-space garden. Its pale fruit stands out strikingly against green foliage and in a mixed harvest basket. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and develops a faint cream-yellow tone, since it never colors red.

common_name: Mr. Stripey Tomato (Large Bicolor Yellow-Red Striped Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Mr. Stripey is not the same as the British 'Tigerella' tomato — Tigerella is a smaller red-and-yellow striped variety; Mr. Stripey is a larger American heirloom bicolor with different size and flavor characteristics.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Mr. Stripey is a large bicolor heirloom beefsteak tomato producing very large (10–20 oz), somewhat flattened, irregularly shaped fruits with a yellow-to-golden exterior prominently striped and mottled with red or pink-red in an irregular, abstract pattern across the fruit surface. The bicolor exterior reveals a matching interior when sliced — yellow and red-tinted flesh arranged in an irregular pattern that makes each fruit slightly different in cross-section. The flavor is sweet and mild with low acidity — characteristic of yellow-dominant bicolor tomatoes — and with a melon-like, fruity quality that is outstanding in fresh eating. Mr. Stripey is an indeterminate heirloom with vigorous vines requiring sturdy support throughout the season. The very large size of the fruits makes them slow to mature — zone 9 gardeners should start seeds early (8 weeks before last frost) and plant out as early as safely possible to maximize the spring growing window before summer heat arrives. As with most large bicolor heirlooms, the thin skin requires careful handling. Not to be confused with the British variety 'Tigerella' which shares a similar name but is a much smaller (4–6 oz), earlier-maturing, red-with-yellow-striped variety of completely different character.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Mt. Washington was selected and released for its ability to set fruit in cold conditions similar to those at the summit area of Mt. Washington in New Hampshire — one of the coldest and windiest spots in the eastern United States — making it among the earliest-producing cherry tomato varieties available and suitable for the most challenging cold-summer and short-season climates.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Mt. Washington is a compact, determinate-type cherry tomato that does not require staking; the plants concentrate production in a relatively tight window (good for canning or preserving in quantity); harvest when fully red and slightly soft. Mt. Washington is an ultra-early cherry tomato selected specifically for cold-tolerance and short-season performance, named for Mt. Washington in New Hampshire — famous for its extreme weather (the site held the world record for the highest surface wind speed ever recorded at 231 mph in April 1934) and the notoriously harsh conditions of its summit area. The variety produces small, round, red cherry tomatoes (about 1 inch) with good, sweet-tart flavor in 52–60 days from transplant — one of the fastest-maturing cherry tomatoes available. The compact, determinate plants (24–36 inches) are appropriate for container growing and produce a compressed flush of fruit ideal for gardeners who want to can or preserve cherry tomatoes in quantity rather than harvest over an extended season. Cold tolerance allows fruit set at nighttime temperatures approaching 45°F, making this variety one of a handful suitable for truly short growing seasons with cold nights throughout the summer.

common_name: Mucho Nacho Jalapeño Pepper (Extra-Large AAS Jalapeño)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Mucho Nacho is an All-America Selections award-winning jalapeño variety producing exceptionally large fruits (4–5 inches long versus standard jalapeño's 2–3 inches) with thick, meaty walls and heat in the 10,000–12,000 SHU range — hotter than TAM Jalapeño but similar in shape, designed for nachos and poppers where large size matters.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Mucho Nacho is a vigorous, productive plant well-suited to Gulf Coast and Southern growing seasons. Mucho Nacho is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning jalapeño developed specifically to produce extra-large (4–5 inch long), thick-walled jalapeño fruits that are large enough for easy stuffing for jalapeño poppers and have enough surface area for maximum nacho topping use — the name directly references its intended use. The heat level (10,000–12,000 SHU) is somewhat hotter than many standard jalapeño varieties and significantly hotter than TAM Jalapeño, making it authentic jalapeño heat in a much larger package. The very thick walls (up to 1/4 inch) make Mucho Nacho excellent for grilling whole (the thick walls hold up without burning through) and for stuffing with cream cheese or other fillings. Ripens from dark green to red; can be harvested and used at the green stage (most common) or allowed to ripen red for a slightly different, sweeter flavor. High productivity and disease resistance make it one of the most reliable jalapeño varieties for home garden use.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring through late spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop; Muir is notably heat- and bolt-tolerant for a loose-leaf lettuce, extending the harvest window later into warm weather than most leaf types.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; thin to 6–10 inches and harvest as cut-and-come-again or as full heads. Muir is a French heirloom oakleaf-type loose-leaf lettuce developed as a heat-tolerant selection, producing a loose, upright rosette of thick, savoyed, chartreuse-green leaves with a distinctively crisp, succulent texture and mild, sweet flavor that holds up better than most leaf lettuces once temperatures start climbing. Its unusually thick, crinkled leaf texture also makes it more forgiving of the wilting summer sun than thinner-leafed varieties, and it is slower to turn bitter as it approaches bolting. A useful bridge variety for gardeners who want fresh salad greens into the early part of a Gulf South summer before switching to heat-adapted greens, in zone 3–10.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist soil or water, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; mukunuwenna roots readily from stem cuttings placed in moist soil or water and can be harvested repeatedly by tip-pruning, which also promotes bushy new growth for subsequent harvests.
directions: Root stem cuttings or direct-sow in moist, average to fertile soil in partial shade; mukunuwenna (sessile joyweed, dwarf copperleaf, alternanthera) is a pantropical low-growing perennial herb widely consumed as a leafy vegetable throughout South and Southeast Asia — the young shoots and leaves are a staple green vegetable in Sri Lanka (where it is a major ingredient in mallung, a coconut-based herb salad), and in Indian, Thai, and Vietnamese cooking. The mild, slightly crunchy leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked briefly in stir-fries, curries, and soups. The plant is exceptionally shade-tolerant for a warm-season leafy green, maintaining vigorous production in partial shade where spinach and lettuce would bolt in summer heat, making it a highly practical leafy green for Gulf Coast and tropical summer shade gardens. It grows along the margins of streams, ponds, and wet ditches in its natural habitat and tolerates wet, waterlogged soil conditions. Multiple harvests per season are obtained by tip-pruning. In zone 9–12 it persists as a perennial; elsewhere it is grown as a summer annual.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Mulato Isleno is a dried chile variety that requires the full summer season to develop and ripen; allow fruits to turn chocolate-brown on the plant before harvesting for drying. In zone 9 the long, warm growing season is ideal for this variety's development.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato Isleno is a poblano-type dried chile grown specifically for its distinctive chocolate-brown dried form rather than for fresh use — unlike the more common ancho (dried red poblano), the mulato is harvested at a later stage when fruits turn from green directly to dark brown, producing a darker, smokier, more complex dried chile with chocolate, coffee, and dried fruit undertones. It is one of the three chiles traditionally used in mole negro (with ancho and pasilla), contributing a smoky depth that neither ancho nor pasilla provides alone. Dry fully ripe, dark-brown fruits in a dehydrator or low oven for 2–4 hours until leathery and pliable. Plants are productive on fertile soil in zone 9 and tend to be tall with upright growth habit.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start January–February and transplant February–March. Mulato is a full-season pepper requiring 80–100 days to first mature fruit — start early for best zone 9 production before summer heat peaks.
directions: Start seeds at 75–80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato is a Mexican dried chile closely related to poblano but from a distinct gene pool (the seed color is tan, versus black for poblano/ancho) that produces heart-shaped, medium-large fruits, dark green turning dark brownish-black (rather than red) when fully ripe and dried. In dried form, mulato is one of the trio of chiles (together with ancho and pasilla) used in traditional Mexican mole negro sauce — its distinctive contribution is a dark, chocolate-tobacco, raisin-like complexity that makes mole negro deep and bittersweet. Heat level is mild to moderate (500–2,500 Scoville). Fresh mulato fruits are used in chiles rellenos and sauces; dried mulatos are rehydrated for mole and enchilada sauces. The plants are productive in zone 9's warm season and the fruits dry naturally on the plant in hot, dry conditions or can be dried in a dehydrator. An essential ingredient for serious Mexican cooking and home food preservers.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Multipik carries the 'precocious yellow' gene, which keeps fruit a clean, bright yellow even when the plant is infected with mosaic viruses that would otherwise mottle and discolor the skin of most yellow squash — a real practical advantage in aphid-prone Gulf South gardens where mosaic virus is common.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Multipik is a widely grown yellow straightneck summer squash hybrid valued for heavy, sustained production and for its 'precocious' gene, which masks the green mottling that mosaic viruses normally cause, so fruit keeps its attractive, uniform bright yellow color for market and table even under virus pressure. The compact, open bush habit produces slender, smooth-skinned fruit best picked young at 5-6 inches for the most tender texture. Because summer squash is highly attractive to aphids that spread mosaic viruses in humid Gulf Coast gardens, Multipik's cosmetic virus tolerance helps keep the harvest looking good even in a bad aphid year. Check plants daily during peak production and pick promptly, since squash left on the vine quickly grows oversized and seedy.

plant_note: Plant sets (small bulbs) in fall — September through November in zone 9 — for harvest the following spring. Multiplier onions form clusters of 4–12 small bulbs underground; the cluster is divided at harvest, with the largest bulbs eaten and the smallest saved for replanting. They can also be planted in late winter for a summer harvest.
directions: Plant small sets 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; multiplier onions are a perennial system that perpetuates itself through vegetative division rather than seed. One planted bulb will produce a cluster of 4–12 bulbs at harvest; sort the cluster at harvest, eating the largest and replanting the smallest to maintain the planting year after year. The flavor is milder and sweeter than common onions, and the green tops can be harvested as scallions throughout the growing season. In zone 9 they perform best planted in fall; in hot, dry summers the tops die down and the bulbs go dormant, much like garlic. This heirloom vegetable was once widely grown in kitchen gardens before commercial onions became cheap.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost, or start indoors 3 weeks early.
directions: Muncher is a burpless heirloom cucumber prized for mild, low-acid flavor and thin, tender skin that needs no peeling. Harvest fruits young at four to six inches for crisp snacking, or let them size up to eight or nine inches for slicing. Direct sow in warm soil in full sun after frost, or start early indoors, and grow on a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Pick regularly and keep the plants evenly watered to prevent bitterness.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil once frost has passed.
directions: This mini slicing cucumber produces tender, burpless, thin-skinned fruits with a crisp bite, best picked around 5 inches long. High yields come from steady moisture and full sun, so water consistently to avoid bitterness. Train vines on a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Harvest frequently to keep plants productive throughout the season.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills or rows after last frost; Munchkin pumpkin vines are shorter and more compact than full-sized pumpkin vines, making them suitable for smaller garden spaces. For fall decorative harvest, count back 100 days from desired harvest date. In zone 9, plant May–June for a September harvest. Each vine typically produces 8–15 miniature pumpkins; harvest when rind is hard and fully orange.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost in full sun; harvest when rind has hardened completely and is uniformly deep orange. Munchkin is a 1996 All-America Selections-winning miniature pumpkin that produces perfectly proportioned, small (4–5 inches in diameter, 3–5 oz) pumpkins with the classic Halloween pumpkin shape — deeply ridged, round, bright orange, with a proportionally large corky stem — in quantities of 8–15 per vine. The scale and perfect form of Munchkin pumpkins have made them the dominant decorative miniature pumpkin in the American market: they look like standard pumpkins shrunk to one-tenth their normal size, with all the visual appeal intact. Their most popular use is as tabletop decorations, door step arrangements, and centerpieces for autumn events; the small size and hard rind give them good postharvest longevity (4–8 weeks in cool conditions) for extended decorative use. Munchkin also has the distinction of being edible — the sweet, dense flesh makes excellent pumpkin puree, though the small size means significant work for a small yield — but most growers treat it purely as a decorative crop. Very productive and highly marketable at farm stands, farmers markets, and pumpkin patches where customers specifically seek miniature varieties. A top-selling item for autumn specialty crop producers.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil reaches 65°F in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mung bean grows rapidly in warm conditions and is ready for harvest in 55–80 days — multiple successions can be planted from spring through early fall in zone 9 for continuous production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; inoculate with Rhizobium legume inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Vigna radiata (mung bean or green gram) is among the most widely consumed legumes in the world — a staple of Indian, Chinese, Southeast Asian, and Korean cuisines in its many forms: whole cooked beans in dal and soups, split (moong dal) for creamy lentil dishes, sprouted (bean sprouts) as a fresh vegetable, ground into flour for cheela pancakes, and processed into bean thread (glass) noodles. The bean is particularly nutritious — high in protein, folate, magnesium, and iron — and easier to digest than many other legumes, producing less flatulence. Mung beans are also the most common source of fresh bean sprouts: seeds germinate and develop edible sprouts in just 3–5 days at room temperature, making them one of the few vegetables that can be produced entirely indoors year-round. In the garden, mung bean grows as a fast-maturing, upright, bushy annual producing small, cylindrical black or brown pods with 8–15 seeds each, harvested when pods turn black-brown and dry.

plant_note: Soak seed overnight; often grown as sprouts or in trays with frequent rinsing.
directions: Soak mung beans overnight so they swell and sprout rapidly, then spread them in an even layer on a tray or in a sprouting jar. They germinate within a day or two and thrive in warmth, so keep them covered and rinse or mist frequently to prevent souring. If growing as tray microgreens, give them light once shoots appear to green them up slightly. Harvest the crunchy, protein-rich shoots after roughly a week, or eat earlier as classic bean sprouts.

plant_note: Sprout indoors year-round in a jar; no field planting needed.
directions: Mung beans are prized for quick, protein-rich sprouts used in stir-fries, egg rolls, and salads. Soak seeds overnight, then rinse and drain two to three times daily in a sprouting jar kept out of direct sun. Sprouts are ready to eat in four to seven days once the shoots are an inch or two long. Keep them moist but well-drained to prevent souring.

common_name: Munich Bier Radish (German Beer Garden Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather; Munich Bier grows considerably larger than salad radishes and needs a bit more room and time to size up, so thin seedlings generously.
directions: Sow seed directly half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to a few inches apart, since this variety forms a substantially larger root than typical salad radishes. Munich Bier is an old German heirloom traditionally served whole, sliced, or spiraled and lightly salted as a salty, crunchy snack alongside beer in Bavarian beer gardens, a use quite different from the quick-growing salad radishes most American gardeners know. Its large white roots stay crisp and mild-flavored even at full size, resisting the pithiness and heat that ruins many radishes left in the ground too long. Harvest once roots reach 3-4 inches across, and keep soil evenly moist throughout growth for the best crisp, mild-flavored roots.

common_name: Murasaki Sweet Potato (Japanese Purple Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant slips 2–4 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Murasaki requires a full 95–110 days, so plant as early as possible in the South. It performs well in the Gulf Coast heat and produces excellent tubers with a slightly longer season than standard varieties.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose, sandy-loam soil in full sun; murasaki (purple in Japanese) sweet potato is a Japanese-origin variety producing long, slender tubers with striking dark purple skin and off-white to cream-colored flesh — a distinct and useful contrast to the Okinawan purple-flesh type, with a dry, chestnut-like sweetness and firm texture that holds up beautifully in roasting, frying, and sautéing where orange-flesh sweet potatoes would become too soft. The flavor is rich, mildly sweet, and nutty with a savory quality that makes it more versatile in non-sweet preparations than moist orange types. Widely grown in Japan and increasingly popular in the United States as interest in Asian sweet potato varieties grows; excellent for Japanese-style roasted sweet potatoes, tempura, and savory preparations that benefit from a firmer texture.

plant_note: Plant cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes; harvest the following summer.
directions: This porcelain hardneck cultivar produces very large bulbs with 4 to 6 big, easy-to-peel cloves and excellent cold tolerance. Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, mulch heavily, and let them overwinter. Snip the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into the bulbs. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy spot for storage.

common_name: Musica Romano Pole Bean (Wide Flat Italian-Style Pole Bean with Exceptional Tenderness)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; Musica is a Dutch-bred flat Romano-type pole bean with unusually wide, flat pods (up to 1 inch wide) reaching 8–10 inches long. It requires a trellis or pole support to 6–7 feet. Unlike round-podded pole beans that become stringy and coarse as they size up, Musica maintains remarkable tenderness and sweet flavor well past the size at which most beans become tough — pods can be harvested at full size (9–10 inches) without significant loss of texture. This characteristic makes Musica one of the most forgiving pole beans for busy gardeners who cannot harvest daily. In zone 9, direct sow March–April after last frost for spring production and again August–September for fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart; provide a sturdy trellis or poles to 7 feet and harvest pods when flat and full-length (8–10 inches) but before seeds develop prominently inside. Musica Romano Pole Bean is a Dutch commercial variety developed specifically to combine the flat Romano-style pod shape beloved in Italian cuisine with the productivity and extended harvest window of a modern pole bean. The flat pod shape — wide (nearly 1 inch across) with a slightly rectangular cross-section rather than round — is the defining characteristic of the Romano bean type, which originated in Italy and represents a fundamentally different pod morphology from the round, pencil-thin beans of French filet types or the oval cross-section of standard American snap beans. Romano types are prized for a distinctive beany, almost meaty flavor that is more pronounced than round-podded types; this flavor intensity comes partly from the thicker pod walls and slightly higher dry matter content of the flat pod structure. Musica improves on older Romano varieties in two key ways: pods remain tender and stringless at large sizes (a significant practical advantage, since older Romano types become stringy once pods exceed 6–7 inches), and the plant produces heavily over an extended harvest window rather than the concentrated burst typical of bush bean types. The vigorous climbing plant (to 7 feet) is highly productive in warm conditions and particularly well-suited to zone 9's long warm season, where it can continue producing through fall when given a midsummer break from heat. Steam or blanch briefly for the best texture; Musica also holds up well in longer-cooked dishes like minestrone where flat Romano beans contribute body without dissolving.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; in zone 9 plant March–June. Musquee de Provence requires a long, warm growing season — at least 110 days of warm weather. In zone 9 planting in April gives the fruit time to cure fully on the vine. As a Cucurbita moschata, it has better heat and humidity tolerance than Cucurbita maxima types. The large fruits (12–20+ lbs) benefit from being elevated on boards or straw to prevent rot where soil stays moist.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, rich, slightly acidic soil; Musquee de Provence (Musk of Provence) is a magnificent French heirloom pumpkin from the Provence region, producing large, deeply ridged, flat-round fruits with a muted tan to bronze-brown skin that develops rich russet-copper tones when fully mature. The deep orange-yellow flesh is exceptionally sweet, dense, and aromatic — the 'musquee' (musky) name refers to the intensely sweet, rich, slightly musky fragrance and flavor of the ripe flesh, considered among the finest-flavored of any large pumpkin. Fully matured fruits from this Cucurbita moschata variety develop complex flavor notes beyond ordinary pumpkin sweetness. The large, photogenic fruits (often 12–20 pounds) are classic French market pumpkins seen in Provençal farmers' markets in fall. In zone 9 the summer heat and humidity are well tolerated by this C. moschata type, which is more disease-resistant in warm climates than C. maxima varieties.

common_name: Musquée de Provence Pumpkin (Fairytale Pumpkin, Cheese Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Musquée de Provence is a large, sprawling Cucurbita moschata pumpkin requiring substantial space (15–20 feet vine length) and a long, warm growing season of 95–115 days, making it well-suited to the Gulf South's extended warm season.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills (3–4 seeds per hill, thinned to 2) after last frost in warm, rich soil; Musquée de Provence is a spectacular heirloom pumpkin from the Provence region of southern France that produces deeply ribbed, flat-lobed, heavily textured fruits that turn from dark green to a rich tan-bronze at maturity, resembling giant rounds of aged cheese (it is often sold under the marketing name 'Fairytale Pumpkin' in the US). The large fruits (10–20 pounds, sometimes to 30 pounds) are as stunning ornamentally as they are culinarily valuable — the deep orange, dense, sweet flesh is comparable to butternut squash in flavor (Musquée de Provence is Cucurbita moschata, the same species as butternut) with excellent sweetness, minimal stringiness, and superb flavor when roasted, pureed into soups, or made into pie. The thick skin and hard rind give outstanding storage life (6–12 months in a cool, dry location), and the impressive size and dramatic appearance make the fruits valuable for both Thanksgiving decorations and serious cooking. Well-adapted to the heat and humidity of Gulf South summer production and a rewarding long-season crop in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Very winter-hardy; can stand in the ground for winter harvest.
directions: This hardy Scottish heirloom leek withstands hard freezes and can be harvested through winter in many climates. Start seed indoors early, then transplant seedlings into deep dibble holes so the shanks blanch white. Hill soil around the stems or drop plants into holes to lengthen the tender white portion. Keep well watered and side-dress with nitrogen midseason for thick shanks. Dig leeks as needed all winter, lifting the last before spring regrowth begins.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil as early as 2–3 weeks before last frost; mustard greens are extremely fast-growing and can be harvested within 40 days of sowing. Fall crops are preferred in zone 7–10 where they continue producing through mild winters.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun as early as 2–3 weeks before last frost in spring, or 4–6 weeks before first fall frost for the preferred fall crop; mustard greens are a staple leafy vegetable of Asian and Southern US cuisines, prized for their pungent, peppery, mustardy flavor that ranges from mildly spicy to intensely sharp depending on variety. Young leaves are used raw in salads; mature leaves are braised, stir-fried, or cooked with salt pork and vinegar in Southern tradition. They bolt quickly in summer heat but tolerate light frosts, improving in flavor after cold exposure. In zone 7–10 fall-planted mustard greens can produce through winter; Southern flat-pod varieties like 'Florida Broadleaf' and Asian varieties like 'Mizuna' and 'Red Giant' are popular choices.

plant_note: Fast, spicy brassica microgreen; mucilaginous seed sown dry on moist trays.
directions: Sow mustard seed dry and dense on a moist tray, since it develops a gel coat when wet that makes presoaking messy. It sprouts fast, so keep the blackout period short and move it into bright light within a couple of days. Mist to keep the surface moist and provide airflow to keep the fast growth healthy. Harvest the zesty, peppery greens at the cotyledon stage in about a week for maximum heat and aroma.

plant_note: Sow direct from late summer through fall in any reasonably fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; mâche germinates best in cool soil and is one of the most cold-hardy salad greens, surviving hard freezes to 10°F.
directions: Sow direct from late summer through fall (or in early spring in cold climates) in any reasonably fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; thin to 4–6 inches apart and harvest the outer rosettes, or pull entire plants at 45–70 days. Valerianella locusta is the premier winter salad green for cold-hardy production; a small-rosette-forming annual with smooth, oval, soft, blue-green leaves and a distinctively mild, nutty, slightly sweet flavor quite unlike any other green — the taste that makes genuine French salade de mâche so sought-after in winter bistros. It is among the most cold-hardy of all salad crops, surviving temperatures to 10°F under light row cover or as low as 20°F with cold frames; in the Gulf South (zones 8–10) it can be harvested from October through April as a continuous cool-season salad. It self-seeds readily and often naturalizes in garden beds.

common_name: München Bier Radish (German Beer Garden White Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow in spring 2–6 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for fall harvest; München Bier (Munich Beer) is a large, round, white-skinned German radish cultivated specifically for the traditional Bavarian custom of serving thick radish slices with beer — large (tennis ball to baseball-sized) round roots with pure white skin and flesh, mild-to-moderate radish bite, and a dense, juicy texture ideal for the accordion-sliced 'Radi' presentation traditional in Bavarian beer gardens.
directions: Sow 1/2 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 4–6 inches apart (important for large root development); keep consistently moist to prevent cracking; harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter for best flavor — overripe roots become pithy and hot. München Bier is a traditional Bavarian radish variety with an intimate connection to German beer garden culture: in Munich's famous outdoor beer gardens and throughout Bavaria, a 'Radi' (the Bavarian German word for radish) served alongside a Masskrug (liter) of beer is as traditional and culturally fixed as pretzels and sausages. The Bavarian Radi is always München Bier or a similar large, white, round variety — never the small red radishes of American experience — and it is served in a specific traditional way: the entire large root is scored with a spiral cut from top to bottom using a special tool (a Radihobel), accordioned apart to fan out into a long, beautiful spiral, rubbed with salt to draw out the juices, and eaten slice by slice as an accompaniment to beer. The flavor is mildly peppery and refreshing, with good crunch and juiciness, and the large size allows the elaborate spiral cutting presentation impossible with small radishes. München Bier is one of the few radish varieties specifically sized and textured for this presentation; it is also excellent sliced thick for salads, grated for German-style radish salads with vinegar and oil dressing, or pickled.

common_name: Nadia Eggplant (Heat-Tolerant Glossy Italian Hybrid Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Nadia is a vigorous, heat-tolerant hybrid that sets fruit reliably even in the hottest part of a Gulf South summer, when many eggplant varieties slow production.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm. Nadia is a widely grown hybrid eggplant producing glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit with tender, non-bitter flesh and few seeds, on a vigorous, high-yielding plant especially valued for continuing to set fruit through peak summer heat when many other eggplant varieties slow down. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm; dull, soft skin signals overripe fruit with more seeds and tougher flesh. Regular harvesting every few days keeps the plant productive over a long season, and staking helps support the heavy fruit load on the branches.

common_name: Naga Morich Pepper (Snake Pepper, Bangladeshi Naga)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, then transplant once soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost, providing bottom heat to speed the naturally slow chinense germination, and pot up seedlings before setting them out in warm soil. Give plants a long, hot growing season and steady moisture for the heaviest pod set. Naga Morich is a traditional Bangladeshi and northeastern Indian pepper closely related to bhut jolokia, prized for its intense heat and slightly fruity aroma, and it is a parent of several later superhot hybrids. Pods ripen from green to a wrinkled orange-red and should be handled with gloves.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since this hybrid superhot germinates slowly.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with consistent bottom heat, then harden off and transplant once nights stay warm, since this hybrid resents cool, wet soil. Keep the compact plants evenly watered and staked once fruit sets heavily along the branches. Naga Viper was bred in England by crossing Bhut Jolokia, Naga Morich, and Trinidad Scorpion lines, and it briefly held recognition as the world's hottest pepper around 2011 before later superhots surpassed it. The knobby pods ripen from green to red and carry a sharp, lingering heat.

common_name: Nancy Hall Sweet Potato (Moist Southern Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant rooted slips 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm, in loose, well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; Nancy Hall is an old Deep South dooryard heirloom grown for its exceptionally moist, sweet flesh.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil formed into ridges in full sun; Nancy Hall is a Deep South heirloom variety grown since the early 20th century for pale copper-pink skinned tubers with soft, exceptionally moist, deep-orange flesh that cooks up custardy rather than dry or mealy, a texture many older Southern gardeners still prefer to modern commercial types like Beauregard. Vines are long and vigorous and tubers form somewhat irregularly shaped, so hill soil up generously and harvest carefully to avoid bruising the tender skin. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall, before the first frost, and cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to firm the skin, heal nicks, and sweeten the flesh before storing.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in loose, deep, stone-free soil; Nantes-type carrots are virtually coreless and have a nearly cylindrical shape that requires deep loose soil — break up any compaction to 12 inches before sowing.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, stone-free, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches when 2 inches tall; Nantes is the most widely grown home garden carrot type, originating in Nantes, France — producing 6–7 inch, blunt-tipped, cylindrical carrots with remarkably sweet, crisp, virtually coreless flesh and thin skin that doesn't require peeling. The standard against which other home garden carrots are judged for flavor and tenderness. Requires loose, deep, stone-free soil for best shape; rocky or compacted soils produce forked, stunted roots. Excellent raw, steamed, or roasted; also one of the best for juicing.

plant_note: For fall crop, direct sow 8–10 weeks before first frost; for spring, sow as soon as soil can be worked and harvest before summer heat triggers bolting.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to 12–18 in once seedlings are 3–4 in tall. Water regularly, as dry spells encourage premature bolting in warm weather. Fall planting generally produces better-quality heads with fewer pest problems. Harvest when heads feel firm and compact, cutting at the base before temperatures drop below 20°F.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest. Blues is particularly tolerant of warm fall temperatures at the start of the season, which is the most common reason napa cabbage fails in zone 9 — it sets heads even when early fall temperatures are still warm, then matures perfectly in December–February. Spring plantings in zone 9 (January–February transplant) are shorter-season and may bolt before heading fully.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Blues is a high-performing napa cabbage hybrid selected specifically for resistance to tipburn and premature bolting — the two primary failure modes for napa cabbage in warmer regions. The compact, upright heads weigh 4–6 pounds with tightly wrapped, pale yellow-green interior leaves and crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flavor that is ideal for fresh eating, kimchi, stir-fries, braises, and raw slaws. Blues develops solid heads without the loose, poorly-wrapped outer structure common in heat-stressed napa cabbage; the improved tip-burn resistance means more marketable heads per planting. In zone 9 fall is the primary season — transplant in September for harvest from November through January. Consistent soil moisture is critical for head development; water stress causes loose, poorly-filled heads and encourages premature bolting.

plant_note: Best sown in mid to late summer for a fall harvest to avoid bolting.
directions: This Michihili-type Napa cabbage forms tall, barrel-shaped heads of tightly wrapped, mild, tender leaves ideal for kimchi and stir-fry. It grows best as a fall crop; sow in mid to late summer so heads mature in cool weather, since spring heat and long days trigger bolting. Keep the soil consistently moist and rich in nitrogen for fast, uniform growth. Harvest when heads feel firm and dense, and cut before hard freezes.

common_name: Napoli Carrot (Early Spring Nantes-Type Hybrid Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow in well-tilled, loose soil; Napoli is a fast-maturing Nantes type that can be sown earlier than most carrots in spring as it germinates reliably in cool soils. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall/winter harvest. Napoli is particularly well-suited to early spring sowing in colder climates (USDA zones 5–7) where it can be direct-sown as soon as soil can be worked, producing an early crop before summer heat arrives. Harvest when roots reach 6–7 inches for best flavor.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly, 0.25 inch deep, in loose, well-amended soil; thin to 2–3 inch spacing when plants are 2 inches tall. Napoli is a Bejo Seeds Nantes-type hybrid that has earned a strong reputation among market gardeners and home growers as one of the most consistent early-season carrots available — reliably producing smooth, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots 6–7 inches long with rich orange color, good internal uniformity, and the clean, sweet Nantes flavor in just 58–68 days. The Nantes type is distinguished from other carrot forms by its nearly cylindrical shape (minimal taper from shoulder to tip), blunt end, almost coreless interior with minimal differentiation between phloem and xylem, and clean, crisp texture that makes it the most versatile shape for both fresh eating and cooking. Napoli's early maturity makes it especially valuable for areas where the growing season is short or where spring planting must be followed by summer crops. The roots have good storage quality and hold well in the ground after reaching maturity without significant quality loss. Napoli has been a consistent top performer in university carrot variety trials across the northeastern United States and Europe, where its combination of earliness, quality, and reliable stand establishment have made it a standard recommendation. A dependable all-purpose Nantes carrot well suited to both home garden and small-farm production.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in shallow water (0–12 inches depth) or permanently moist soil in full sun; narrowleaf cattail grows naturally in shallow marshes, pond margins, and ditches and spreads aggressively by rhizomes to form dense stands. Better suited to moderate-sized water features than broadleaf cattail.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in shallow water (0–12 inches depth) or saturated soil in full sun; narrowleaf cattail is a cosmopolitan aquatic native with narrower leaves than broadleaf cattail (T. latifolia) and a distinctive gap between the male and female portions of the brown, sausage-like seed head — a reliable identification feature. Like all cattails, it provides extraordinary wildlife value: the fluffy seed cotton is used for nest lining by ducks and wrens; the seed heads provide food for marsh wrens and red-winged blackbirds; the dense rhizome mats provide spawning habitat for fish and shelter for amphibians. All parts of cattail are edible — the young spring shoots taste like cucumber; the green male flower heads can be cooked like corn on the cob; the pollen is a protein-rich flour substitute; and the rhizomes yield a starchy flour. Spreads rapidly — contain in pots sunk in water or with barriers to prevent unwanted spread.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil once frost has passed.
directions: National Pickling is an open-pollinated heirloom bred for firm, blocky fruits about five to six inches long that are perfect for pickling and canning. The productive vines set fruit heavily and quickly, so pick often to keep new cucumbers coming. Direct sow into warm soil in full sun after frost and keep evenly watered for crisp, uniform fruit. Harvest at the size you want, from small gherkins to larger slicing cucumbers.

plant_note: Sow in warm soil after frost; drought tolerant once established.
directions: This drought-tolerant heirloom, originally grown by the Navajo people, produces 3 to 7 pound melons with sweet orange flesh and a yellow rind. It thrives in poorer soils and hot, dry conditions where other melons struggle. Give it full sun and room to sprawl, watering deeply but infrequently. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine and develops a fragrant aroma.

common_name: Navy Bean (Haricot Bean, Boston Bean, White Pea Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, warm, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after last frost; navy beans are compact bush types that set pods heavily in a concentrated period. In zone 9a they perform best with spring planting for early summer harvest before peak summer heat.
directions: Sow 1–2 inches deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; navy beans are the small, oval, ivory-white dried beans of New England baked beans, Senate bean soup, and countless European cassoulet and bean dishes. The compact bush plants are highly productive and concentrate their pod set for a single, efficient harvest period — more practical for dry bean production than many spreading pole types. Allow pods to turn yellow-brown and papery before harvest; pull the entire plant and dry in a warm, well-ventilated location for 1–2 weeks, then shell. Navy beans are rich in fiber (19g per cup) and folate. In zone 9a, spring plantings avoid the hottest summer weather; flowers drop in temperatures above 90°F, so early planting is key to a full harvest.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Nebraska Wedding grows on relatively compact plants that still benefit from a stake or cage as fruit loads increase.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed, providing support for the fruit-laden branches. This variety was carried by pioneer families from Minnesota to the Nebraska plains in the late 1800s, and tradition held that a pinch of its seed was given to Nebraska brides as a wedding gift so they could grow it in their own gardens. The plants yield deep orange, globe-shaped fruit with a rich, sweet flavor and few seeds, and the variety was later documented and preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; Nelson is a fast-maturing Nantes-type carrot bred to hold good sweetness even when sown or harvested in warm weather, a real advantage in the Gulf South where summer heat usually turns carrots bitter and woody.
directions: Sow seed thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in well-loosened, stone-free soil 2-4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2-3 inches between plants when seedlings are 2 inches tall. Nelson is a fast-maturing Nantes-type hybrid carrot specifically noted for retaining good, consistent sweetness even when grown through warmer weather than most carrots tolerate well, since heat typically pushes carrots toward a stronger, more bitter flavor and woody texture. The smooth, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots are uniformly deep orange with a small core and crisp, juicy texture. In zone 8-9, sow in late winter for an early spring harvest and again in late summer for a fall crop, and expect Nelson to hold its sweet flavor through a wider harvest window than standard carrot varieties.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Neon is compact and early-maturing, making it a good fit for containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Neon produces smooth, glossy, vividly hot-pink to magenta fruit that stands out sharply against the plant's foliage, with mild, tender, nearly seedless flesh similar to standard Italian eggplants. It matures notably early for an eggplant and sets fruit heavily on a relatively compact plant, making it a productive choice for smaller gardens and containers as well as open beds. Harvest at 4-6 inches long while the skin is still glossy and firm, since fruit left too long dulls in color and toughens. Its striking coloring also makes it a popular market and specialty-produce variety.

plant_note: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before transplanting out; in most regions transplant in late summer for a fall harvest. Neos is a uniform hybrid frisee bred for reliable self-blanching and faster maturity than heirloom curly endives.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun once seedlings have several true leaves. Neos is a hybrid frisee endive selected for a compact, upright habit and finely cut, curled leaves that shade the heart naturally, producing a pale, tender center with little need for tying. It matures faster and more uniformly than many open-pollinated curly endives, which makes it a favorite among market growers for consistent harvests. Use the mildly bitter, delicate leaves raw in composed salads such as salade lyonnaise, or briefly wilted with warm bacon dressing.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; transplant into warm soil after frost danger passes and stake the vigorous, potato-leaved vines.
directions: Collected from a Himalayan village garden, this heirloom is distinguished by soft, blue-green, potato-leaf foliage and heavy clusters of smooth, pink-red, medium-large globe fruits with few seeds and a rich sweet-tart flavor. The vigorous indeterminate vines are reliably productive through hot, humid conditions and have shown good foliage disease tolerance in Gulf South trial gardens compared to many other pink heirlooms. Stake or cage plants well, since the potato-leaf vines are dense and heavy once fruit sets, and pick at full color for the best flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting. Neptune was bred by the University of Florida specifically to keep setting fruit through the high-heat, high-humidity stretch of the Gulf South summer.
directions: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Neptune is a heat-set tomato developed by the University of Florida as part of a long-running Southeastern breeding effort to keep fruit set going once nighttime temperatures climb into the mid-70s, a point at which most standard hybrids stop setting fruit. The medium-to-large, round, red fruits have solid, well-balanced flavor and enough firmness to ship and hold well, making Neptune a dependable choice for a continuous summer harvest rather than a single early flush. Plants carry good resistance to common Southern tomato diseases, but a preventive fungicide or copper spray schedule still helps in the humid Gulf South. Stake or cage plants early, since they grow vigorously, and keep watering consistent to avoid blossom end rot in the region's heavy summer rains followed by dry spells.

plant_note: Sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since roots develop their best flavor and store best when they mature in cool weather.
directions: Nero Tondo, Italian for round black, is a refined selection of the old Black Spanish type bred for rounder, more uniform roots and notably better bolt tolerance than the traditional heirloom strain. The rough, matte-black skin conceals dense, snow-white flesh with a sharp, peppery bite that mellows into an earthy sweetness when roasted or braised. Because the roots hold in the ground and in storage far longer than spring radishes, gardeners grow it as a keeper crop, pulling roots through fall and into winter for slaws, pickles, and cooked preparations.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. palmifolia 'Nero di Toscana'
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a November–March harvest. Nero di Toscana is cold-hardy to about 10–15°F and is one of the kales with the longest productive season in zone 9, providing a continuous harvest of lower leaves from fall through late spring. The flavor improves dramatically after cold exposure — first frost converts starches to sugar and deepens the savory, mineral flavor of the dark leaves.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nero di Toscana (also known as Lacinato kale, Dinosaur kale, or Cavolo Nero) is the traditional Italian black kale of Tuscany, producing long, strap-like leaves with a deeply blistered (savoyed) surface and an almost blue-black dark green color — the darkest of all kale types. The texture is firmer and the flavor is more savory, mineral, and complex than curly kale, with less bitterness and a sweeter, earthier depth that develops most fully after frost. Nero di Toscana is the authentic ingredient in ribollita (Tuscan bread and vegetable soup), farinata di cavolo nero, and braised Tuscan kale side dishes where curly kale cannot substitute. The long, upright growth habit exposes the lower leaves for continuous harvest while the growing tip extends upward — a productive cut-and-come-again pattern that provides months of harvest from a single planting. Remove individual outer leaves for harvest to allow continuous new growth from the center growing point.

common_name: Netted Gem Melon (Ancestor of the Modern Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; Netted Gem, introduced around 1881, is the historic Michigan-area heirloom widely credited as the direct ancestor of the modern netted commercial cantaloupe.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced around 1881, Netted Gem produces small, round, densely netted fruit with sweet, salmon-orange flesh, and its heavy netting pattern and reliable sweetness made it enormously influential in American melon breeding — most of the netted cantaloupe types sold in grocery stores today trace back to selections made from this variety. The compact vines are productive and well suited to home gardens. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with gentle pressure and the netting has fully developed, indicating peak ripeness and sweetness.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; in zone 9 sow January–February for spring or September–October for fall. Nevada is particularly tolerant of heat and is one of the best choices for extending the spring lettuce season in zone 9 — it holds without bolting 1–2 weeks longer than most lettuce varieties under warm conditions. Successive sowings every 3 weeks extend the harvest window. Shade cloth in late spring reduces bolting pressure.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Nevada is a French batavian-type lettuce selected specifically for heat tolerance and slow bolting — it holds usable quality in warm spring conditions 1–2 weeks longer than standard butterhead or looseleaf varieties before flowering, providing a meaningfully extended harvest window in warm climates like zone 9. The large, crisp, slightly frilly green leaves form a dense, semi-heading rosette similar to a looseleaf but with better structure and more crunch than floppy butterhead types. The flavor is fresh, mild, and slightly crisp — closer to iceberg in texture but without the blandness, and closer to looseleaf in flavor but with more body. Nevada is widely used by commercial producers in California and the Southwest who need a heat-tolerant green-leaf lettuce for late spring production windows. In zone 9 it is one of the most reliable lettuces for bridging the February–May spring season before summer heat ends production.

common_name: Neves Azorean Red Tomato (Portuguese-American Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Neves Azorean Red is a Portuguese-American heirloom brought to the United States by Azorean immigrant families and preserved through home seed saving, valued for its huge, meaty, low-seed fruit.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date and provide sturdy staking, since the vigorous indeterminate vines carry a heavy load of large fruit. Neves Azorean Red traces to Azorean immigrant families who brought tomato seed with them to New England and California and kept it going in home gardens for generations before it entered the wider heirloom seed trade; the deep pinkish-red beefsteak fruit is prized for its dense, meaty flesh, relatively small seed cavities, and low acidity, which makes for a tomato with almost no watery waste when sliced. Individual fruits commonly reach a pound or more on well-grown plants, and the rich, well-balanced flavor holds up in sandwiches and fresh salads as well as in sauce. As an open-pollinated heirloom it saves true from seed with basic isolation, letting gardeners keep the family line going the same way it has been passed down for decades.

common_name: New Hampshire Midget Watermelon (Ultra-Compact Short-Season Icebox Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, or start indoors 3 weeks early in short-season areas.
directions: Bred at the University of New Hampshire and released in 1951, this is one of the earliest true short-vine watermelons ever developed, making it a workhorse for northern gardeners and anyone with a short frost-free window. Vines stay compact enough for a large container or a small raised bed, and the round 4-6 pound fruits with pale flesh mature fast rather than for exceptional sweetness. Keep soil evenly moist through fruit set, then ease off watering as the melons near ripeness to concentrate what sugar they do develop. Its main value is reliability where longer-season Southern varieties simply run out of summer.

common_name: New Mexico No. 6-4 Green Chile (Classic Hatch-Style Mild Roasting Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; New Mexico No. 6-4 is the foundational Hatch-type green chile developed at New Mexico State University in the 1950s from the original New Mexico No. 6. It produces long, pendant pods (6–8 inches) with mild-to-medium heat (1,000–4,000 SHU) that are the standard for roasting green chiles. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the Hatch valley grows these chiles from June through September in a desert climate, but the variety also performs in humid Gulf Coast conditions if given well-drained soil and good airflow to minimize fungal issues. Harvest green (before color break) for roasting; allow to ripen red for dried red chile powder.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake lightly. Harvest green pods at full size before any color break for roasting, or allow to ripen to deep red for drying. New Mexico No. 6-4 is the chile pepper variety that defined an entire regional food culture: the mild, thin-walled roasting pepper grown in the Hatch Valley of southern New Mexico and marketed under the 'Hatch Chile' designation that drives an enormous annual harvest festival and roasting tradition every August and September in New Mexico and throughout the American Southwest. The variety was developed by Dr. Roy Harper at New Mexico State University in Albuquerque in the 1950s through selection from the original New Mexico No. 6 variety, with the '6-4' designation referring to the parents used in the cross. The resulting variety became the commercial standard for New Mexico green chile production because it combined the mild-to-medium heat level preferred by most consumers with a pod shape and size (6–8 inches long, 1.5–2 inches wide) that roasts evenly on a flame or in a large drum roaster without burning before the flesh is fully cooked through. Thin walls and high moisture content allow steam to separate the charred skin from the flesh during roasting, enabling the characteristic step of peeling the blackened skin to reveal the moist, mildly pungent chile beneath. Home gardeners can replicate commercial roasting by placing whole pods under a broiler or directly on a gas burner flame, turning until charred on all sides, then placing in a sealed plastic bag for 10–15 minutes to steam before peeling. For red chile production, allow all pods to fully ripen to deep red on the plant or allow to ripen after harvest in a warm, dry location before drying whole or grinding to powder.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after the last frost, or transplant young seedlings for an earlier start in short-season areas.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed, or start transplants a few weeks early to get a jump on the season, and thin to strong single plants once vines begin to run. New Queen was named an All-America Selections winner in 1999 for its early, compact icebox-sized fruit and its unusual bright orange-yellow flesh, a departure from typical red-fleshed watermelons of its era. The globe-shaped fruits typically weigh 5 to 6 pounds and offer crisp, honey-sweet flavor well suited to small gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked; sow again in late summer for fall.
directions: This flame-tipped green leaf lettuce holds its flavor even in summer heat and resists downy mildew, bottom rot, and tipburn. Its slow-to-bolt habit lets you harvest over a long window. Sow shallowly in cool soil and keep evenly moist for tender leaves. Pick outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head, and provide light afternoon shade in hot weather to extend the season.

common_name: New Red Fire Lettuce (Improved Heat-Tolerant Red Leaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; New Red Fire is an improved loose-leaf red lettuce bred for better heat tolerance and slower bolting than older red leaf varieties, making it one of the more reliable red lettuces for a longer Gulf South spring and fall season.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. New Red Fire is a loose-leaf lettuce bearing large, ruffled, deep red-tinged leaves over a green base, an improved selection bred for better heat tolerance and slower bolting than older red leaf lettuce varieties, which makes it noticeably more forgiving for gardeners in warm climates trying to stretch the lettuce season into early summer or start it earlier in late winter. Because it is a loose-leaf type, it never forms a tight head, and outer leaves can be harvested continuously while the center keeps producing new growth, extending the useful harvest window from a single planting. Flavor is mild and pleasant even as leaves size up, without the pronounced bitterness that develops quickly in less heat-tolerant lettuce under stress. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings in zone 9 to further delay bolting as temperatures climb.

common_name: New York Improved Eggplant (New York Spineless)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and hold seedlings under warm, bright conditions until the soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm since eggplant germinates poorly below 70F, then transplant out only after nights stay reliably warm. Give plants full sun, even moisture, and a stake or cage to support the heavy fruit load once pods set. This is one of the oldest American commercial eggplant selections, dating to the late 1800s, prized for its large glossy purple-black fruit and mild, tender flesh, and it stands as a direct ancestor of many modern hybrids sold today. Because it lacks the disease tolerance bred into newer types, gardeners often see best results with crop rotation and floating row cover early in the season.

common_name: New York White Garlic (Heirloom Porcelain Hardneck)
scientific_name: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'New York White'
plant_note: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in mid-fall once soil has cooled, mulching after the first hard frost.
directions: New York White is a long-preserved heirloom Porcelain hardneck strain maintained in northeastern American seed-saver collections for generations, valued for dependable bulb formation in cold Northeast winters and clean, glossy white wrappers. Bulbs typically produce 4-6 large cloves with a hot, pungent raw bite that sweetens dramatically when roasted or slow-cooked. As a true Porcelain type it needs a sustained cold period to vernalize properly, so gardeners in mild-winter climates should choose a different type. Grow it for its regional heirloom story and its reliability as an old New York homestead strain that has outlasted many modern hybrids.

plant_note: Sow direct after all danger of frost in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; soak seeds overnight to improve germination — New Zealand spinach thrives in summer heat where true spinach bolts.
directions: Sow direct after all danger of frost has passed in warm, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; soak seeds 12–24 hours in warm water before sowing to soften the hard seed coat and improve germination — thin to 18–24 inches apart. New Zealand spinach is the premier heat-tolerant, summer-substitute for true spinach, producing a sprawling, succulent-leaved groundcover of succulent, triangular, bright-green leaves with a mild, slightly salty flavor that can be harvested continuously by tip-pruning throughout summer and fall without bolting; it is ideal for the Gulf Coast and similar hot, humid climates where true spinach is impossible in summer. Despite the common name it is not closely related to spinach; it is in the family Aizoaceae. Frost-tender but can naturalize in zone 9–10 from self-seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when the soil has warmed, providing poles or a strong trellis for this vigorous climbing heirloom.
directions: Direct sow after last frost when the soil has warmed, providing poles or a strong trellis for this vigorous climbing heirloom. Nickajack traces its name to a historic Cherokee community in the Tennessee River valley of the southern Appalachians, and it has been passed down among mountain gardeners as a reliable dual-purpose bean, with large, flat pods that can be picked young for snapping or left to mature into tan, speckled dry beans. Harvest at the snap stage for the tenderest eating, around 70 days, or let pods dry fully on the vine for a longer-season soup bean. The vines are productive and well adapted to the humid summers of the Southern Appalachians.

common_name: Night Shadow Eggplant (Reliable Classic Black-Skinned Hybrid)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Night Shadow is a Seminis-bred hybrid listed among Cornell's recommended disease-tolerant eggplant varieties, valued for its consistent yield and classic fruit quality.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Night Shadow is a hybrid eggplant bred for reliable, sustained production of classic glossy black-purple, oval fruit on a sturdy, vigorous plant that tolerates the heat of a Gulf South summer well. It is listed among Cornell University's recommended disease-tolerant eggplant selections, giving it an edge in the humid, disease-prone conditions common across the Southeast. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, since dull, hard fruit signals it has gone past peak quality and developed more seeds and bitterness. Keep soil consistently moist and pick regularly to encourage the plant to keep setting new fruit through the season.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to its permanent position as nine star broccoli is a long-lived perennial that does not want to be moved once established. It requires a permanent, deeply dug, fertile position.
directions: Transplant to deeply dug, richly amended soil in full sun; nine star is a remarkable perennial broccoli variety that sends up multiple small white or pale yellow broccoli-like heads in early spring, year after year, for up to 4–5 years from a single planting. The key to maintaining the perennial habit is to harvest all the heads before any can flower and set seed — once a plant is allowed to flower, it may cease to perennial and become biennial. The heads are smaller than commercial broccoli (tennis ball-sized) but very numerous on established plants, and the flavor is excellent. After harvesting the heads, the plant sends up side shoots producing cut-and-come-again broccoli for weeks. Feed heavily after harvest to support the following year's growth.

plant_note: Sow in early spring, 4-2 weeks before the last frost; nipplewort is cold-hardy and germinates readily in cool soil under dappled light.
directions: Scatter seeds shallowly on the soil surface or cover with no more than 1/8 inch of soil in a partially shaded spot in early spring; nipplewort is one of the few edible annuals that performs well in the shade of hedges or woodland edges. Thin or transplant seedlings to 6-12 inches apart and keep soil evenly moist through cool weather. Harvest the young, tender basal leaves and shoot tips before the plant bolts, cooking them briefly like spinach to reduce their mild bitterness. Allow a few plants to self-seed at the end of the season; nipplewort will reliably return each year with no further effort.

common_name: Noir des Carmes Cucumber (Heirloom Black-Spined French Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after soil has warmed; a fast-maturing, historic French variety well suited to succession planting for continuous harvest.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after the soil has warmed, and provide a trellis or ample vine room. Documented in French seed catalogs since the mid-1800s, Noir des Carmes produces short, chunky, dark-green fruit that ripens quickly and is covered in distinctive black spines when young, an old-world trait bred out of most modern cucumbers. It is one of the fastest-maturing open-pollinated cucumbers available, ready in under two months from sowing, making it a good choice for short-season succession planting through the summer. Pick fruit small and young for the sweetest, least bitter flavor, and harvest frequently to keep vines productive.

common_name: Noir des Carmes Melon (Black Rock Melon)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-amended soil; Noir des Carmes is a French heirloom melon dating to at least 1883, one of the earliest-maturing Charentais-type melons, with dark green to almost black skin that ripens to orange-yellow and contains brilliant, deep-orange, extraordinarily fragrant flesh — one of the finest European muskmelons.
directions: Sow in hills or rows after last frost in warm, enriched, well-drained soil; Noir des Carmes performs best with reduced watering as the fruits approach maturity — drying out slightly at the end concentrates the sugars and perfume. Noir des Carmes (Black of the Carmelites, named for the dark-robed Carmelite friars who reportedly cultivated it) is a French heirloom muskmelon first listed in catalogs in 1883 and described by Vilmorin-Andrieux in their famous 1885 The Vegetable Garden; the young fruits are dark green to nearly black (the 'noir'), ripening to orange-yellow at maturity with a pronounced perfume. Inside, the flesh is deep orange, very sweet, and extraordinarily fragrant in the way characteristic of the finest Charentais-type melons of Poitou-Charentes. One of the earliest European muskmelons (70–80 days from seed), making it suitable for shorter seasons. Somewhat rare but increasingly available from specialty seed companies.

plant_note: Plant cloves in fall before the ground freezes; harvest the following summer.
directions: This widely adapted softneck heirloom from the San Juan Islands stays productive from wet to arid and cool to hot climates, forming bulbs with 12 to 20 cloves. Plant cloves in fall, mulch, and let them overwinter for a summer harvest. Softneck types store especially well and can be braided. Harvest when the lower leaves yellow, then cure in a shaded, airy place before storing.

plant_note: Detach a mature pad, allow the cut end to callus for one week in dry shade, then plant 2–3 inches deep in sandy soil; water sparingly until roots form (about 4–6 weeks).
directions: Allow a pad cutting to callus (dry) for one week before planting in sandy or rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; overwatering is the most common cause of failure. Young pads (nopales) are harvested when 6–8 inches long and still tender, using tongs and a sharp knife to remove glochids (small barbed spines) by scraping before cooking. The pads are eaten grilled, in tacos, scrambled with eggs, or in soups, with a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture. The pear-shaped red or yellow fruits (tunas) that ripen in late summer are sweet and edible; wear thick gloves when harvesting as glochids penetrate skin on contact. Established plants are extremely drought and heat tolerant and require virtually no care.

common_name: North Georgia Candy Roaster (Southern Appalachian Cherokee Heritage Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; North Georgia Candy Roaster is a very large squash (15–30 lbs) requiring 100–120 days and substantial space (vines 12+ feet). In zone 9, plant March–April for October–November harvest. The variety is cold-sensitive as a young plant but very heat-tolerant once established, making zone 9's long warm season ideal for the extended maturation time this variety requires. Fruit is large, elongated to cylindrical with slight taper, with salmon-pink to apricot-tan skin with a distinctive bluish bloom at full maturity. The flesh is thick, bright orange-yellow, sweet, and very dry — the 'candy roaster' name references the traditional method of roasting the squash in front of a fireplace or in a slow oven until the flesh caramelizes, producing a very sweet, concentrated flavor.
directions: Direct sow in hills 5–6 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin turns salmon-pink and develops waxy bloom. North Georgia Candy Roaster is one of the most historically significant Appalachian heirloom vegetable varieties — a large winter squash that has been grown in the mountain regions of North Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and adjacent Appalachian areas for centuries, with the variety associated with Cherokee and Scots-Irish Appalachian agricultural traditions of the southern mountain region. The 'candy roaster' name is shared by several closely related Appalachian squash varieties that differ somewhat in size, color, and shape but all share the characteristic of extraordinary sweetness when roasted — the candy-like sweetness that develops when the dense, high-starch flesh is slowly baked or roasted until caramelized. The specific 'North Georgia' designation distinguishes this variety from the similar but distinct 'Tennessee Candy Roaster,' 'Big Orange Candy Roaster,' and other regionally-named selections, with the North Georgia type typically producing cylindrical to elongated fruits with characteristic salmon-pink to apricot skin. The squash can reach enormous sizes: typical fruits are 15–20 lbs, and exceptional specimens exceed 30 lbs, making this one of the largest winter squash varieties in heirloom cultivation. The flesh — thick, dense, bright orange-yellow — is exceptional in nutritional value (very high beta-carotene) and flavor, with a sweetness and complexity that rewards the long growing season required. The variety has been maintained by Appalachian farming families and seed-saving organizations including the Seed Savers Exchange as an important cultural heritage variety of the southeastern mountain region.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to fall for winter harvest under row cover or in a cold frame; also suitable for early spring sowing.
directions: Sow in late summer for a fall crop, or in early spring for a quick spring harvest; North Pole thrives in cold, short-day conditions and largely stops growing once winter cold sets in, then resumes as days lengthen. Small, unprotected plants can survive temperatures well below freezing, and with the light protection of a cold frame or row cover it reliably carries a crop of compact, buttery, lime-green heads through winter in cold climates. It resents summer heat and bolts quickly if grown in warm conditions, so it is best reserved for the coldest part of the lettuce calendar. Harvest whole heads once they feel dense, or pick individual leaves through the winter for a slower, extended harvest.

common_name: North and South Okra (Sand Mountain Alabama Heirloom Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost; North and South is an Alabama heirloom passed down on Sand Mountain, prized for tender pods produced over a long season.
directions: North and South is a Southern heirloom okra preserved by gardening families on Sand Mountain in northeast Alabama, grown for slim, ridged green pods that stay tender well past the size most okra turns woody. Direct sow after the soil is reliably warm, since okra seedlings are slow to establish in cool soil, and thin plants to give them room to branch. The tall, productive plants keep setting pods over a long summer season if picked every day or two at 3-4 inches. As an open-pollinated heirloom it is easy to save seed from, helping keep a piece of Alabama foodways history in circulation.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into a sunny, well-drained bed after frost danger passes. In cold-winter regions apply a thick winter mulch over the dormant crown to help the root system survive freezing temperatures and resprout the following spring.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into a sunny, well-drained bed after frost danger passes. In cold-winter regions apply a thick winter mulch over the dormant crown to help the root system survive freezing temperatures and resprout the following spring. Northern Star was selected specifically for the ability to survive winters far colder than traditional Mediterranean-bred artichoke varieties can tolerate, extending true perennial artichoke growing into regions that previously had to treat the crop strictly as an annual.
