It produces medium-sized green buds with good flavor, and growers in cold climates report it returning from the crown for multiple seasons when given adequate mulch protection.

common_name: Nothstine Dent Corn (Wisconsin Yellow Dent Heirloom Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Nothstine Dent is a Wisconsin farm-family heirloom yellow dent corn preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Nothstine Dent is a Wisconsin heirloom yellow dent corn passed down within a single farm family for generations before being preserved and distributed through the Seed Savers Exchange, valued for reliable yields of good-quality meal and feed corn adapted to short-season Upper Midwest growing conditions. Its relatively short season to maturity makes it a practical choice for regions with a shorter frost-free window than the Gulf South typically has. Harvest and dry ears fully before shelling and storing kernels for grinding or seed.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; the tangled, tendril-heavy growth is largely self-supporting and needs only minimal staking.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sowing a bit thicker than usual so plants can lean on and support one another. Novella is a semi-leafless ('afila') type pea in which most of the normal flat leaflets are replaced by curling tendrils, causing plants to knit themselves together into a dense, self-supporting tangle that stands mostly upright with little or no staking, a real convenience compared to conventional pea vines that flop without support. The reduced foliage also means better airflow and light penetration through the planting, which can reduce fungal disease pressure, while still producing a solid crop of sweet, tender shelling peas in well-filled pods. Pick regularly once pods fill out for the best flavor, and enjoy the relatively low-maintenance, self-supporting habit that sets this type apart from standard pea varieties.

common_name: Nozawana (Japanese Turnip Greens, Nozawana Pickled Leaf Turnip)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer/early fall for fall and winter production; in zone 9 direct sow September–October for harvest November through February. Nozawana is primarily grown as a fall/winter crop for pickling and fresh use, tolerating frost to about 20°F and improving in flavor after light frost.
directions: Direct sow in late summer or early fall in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; nozawana (also called 'nozawa-na' or 'nozawana turnip') is a cool-season Japanese brassica grown primarily for its large, textured, dark-green leaves rather than its turnip root (the root is small and incidental) — the leaves are the classic ingredient in nozawana-zuke, the Nagano Prefecture traditional pickle that is one of Japan's most beloved preserved vegetables. The large, crinkled, somewhat coarse-textured leaves (larger and more substantial than most Asian greens) are harvested whole and salt-pickled in large crocks over winter, developing a complex, slightly funky, fermented flavor that is eaten alongside rice and miso soup throughout Nagano winters. Fresh young leaves can also be blanched and stir-fried or used in miso soup. In zone 9, nozawana grows as a reliable fall-to-winter crop; it tolerates frost well and improves in sweetness after cold weather. A wonderful specialty brassica for gardeners interested in Japanese fermentation traditions and Asian vegetable diversity.

common_name: NuMex Big Jim Pepper (World's Longest Chile Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; NuMex Big Jim was released in 1975 by New Mexico State University (NMSU) plant breeder Dr. Roy Nakayama and holds the Guinness World Record for the longest chile pepper — individual fruits can reach 12–13 inches — it is the standard New Mexico/Hatch green chile for roasting, stuffing, and making authentic red and green New Mexico chile sauces.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture for maximum fruit size; NuMex Big Jim is most famous when roasted over open flame or under a broiler in the New Mexico tradition. NuMex Big Jim was developed at New Mexico State University's Chile Pepper Institute by Dr. Roy Nakayama and released in 1975 as a breakthrough in Hatch/New Mexico green chile breeding; it holds the Guinness World Record for the world's longest chile pepper, with individual fruits measured up to 13 inches in length and 2–2.5 inches in diameter — fruit of this size are capable of being stuffed whole (for chile rellenos) without cutting, which drove the commercial appeal. The heat level is moderate (500–2,500 SHU — from virtually nil to mild-moderate depending on growing conditions, with hotter summers producing hotter fruit), characteristic of New Mexico green chiles rather than the sharp heat of jalapeños or serranos. The flavor when roasted is rich, smoky, earthy, and complex with characteristic New Mexico chile character — the basis of authentic Hatch green chile sauce, the iconic topping of New Mexico cuisine from green chile cheeseburgers to burritos and sopapillas. One of the most important American regional chile varieties.

common_name: NuMex Heritage Big Jim Hatch Chile Pepper
plant_note: Start indoors under warmth; transplant after nights stay above 55 F.
directions: This improved Hatch-type chile offers thick flesh, large flavorful pods, and consistent mild-to-medium heat ideal for fire roasting. Start seeds early indoors since peppers need a long warm season, and transplant only after the soil is thoroughly warm. Feed lightly and water evenly to size up the pods. Harvest green for roasting or leave to redden for deeper, sweeter flavor.

common_name: NuMex Joe E. Parker Anaheim Chile Pepper
plant_note: Start indoors under warmth; transplant after frost when soil is warm.
directions: This productive Anaheim-type pepper bears thick-walled, uniform 6 to 8 inch fruits with few seeds, excellent for roasting, stuffing, or canning. Mild heat around 500 to 2,500 Scoville units makes it versatile in the kitchen. Start seeds indoors early and set out sturdy transplants once nights are warm. Peppers ripen from green to red, so pick at whichever stage suits your recipe.

common_name: NuMex Joe E. Parker Pepper (Standard New Mexico Green Chile)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; NuMex Joe E. Parker is the dominant commercial green chile variety for the New Mexico Hatch Valley and performs comparably well throughout the Gulf South where its heat tolerance and thick-walled flesh suit the long, warm growing season. Harvest at the mature green stage (full size, firm, bright green) for fresh roasted green chile use; leave remaining fruits to mature to red for dried red chile or ristras.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; transplant to full sun, deeply watered soil after last frost. NuMex Joe E. Parker is one of the most commercially important New Mexico chile varieties — a New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute release named in honor of Joe E. Parker, a former NMSU Board of Regents member. The variety occupies the essential middle ground of New Mexico chile heat: mild to medium-hot, approximately 500–2,500 Scoville Heat Units, hot enough to have authentic New Mexico chile character but mild enough for broad consumer acceptance. Joe E. Parker is the standard commercial variety for Hatch-brand green chile operations, grown across thousands of acres in the Rio Grande Valley and producing the long (7–9 inch), flat, meaty-walled green fruits used for fresh-roasted whole chiles, canned green chile, green chile stew, and freezing. The fruits roast exceptionally well: thick walls hold up under direct flame, the skin blisters and chars cleanly, and the interior steams to the silky texture essential for authentic New Mexico green chile preparations. When left to mature to red and dried, NuMex Joe E. Parker produces the bright, papery-red pods used in New Mexico ristras and traditional dried red chile. For gardeners who want to grow the authentic Hatch valley chile experience, NuMex Joe E. Parker is the single most representative variety — it defines the flavor and character that New Mexico green chile has meant to American Southwestern cuisine for generations.

common_name: NuMex Lemon Spice Jalapeno Chile Pepper
plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant after frost when soil warms.
directions: This colorful jalapeno from the Chile Pepper Institute ripens from green to bright yellow with full jalapeno heat and a citrus undertone. Pick pods at either the green or yellow stage for a varied jar of pickled peppers. Start seeds indoors well before your last frost, then transplant into warm, sunny beds. Steady watering and a light feeding keep the compact plants cranking out fruit.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, providing bottom heat for slow-to-germinate chinense seed, and transplant once nights stay warm.
directions: NuMex Suave Red was released by the Chile Pepper Institute at New Mexico State University as a nearly heatless habanero, measuring only a few hundred Scoville units yet retaining the same fruity, tropical aroma prized in hot habaneros. Plump, wrinkled fruit ripens from green to a deep red on productive plants that need a long, warm season to reach full size. Because the pepper carries little to no burn, it lets cooks use habanero flavor generously in salsas and sauces without overwhelming heat. Give it the same rich soil, consistent watering, and full sun that other chinense peppers require to perform well.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; NuMex Twilight was developed at New Mexico State University's Chile Pepper Institute as a compact ornamental-edible pepper producing upright, small fruits that ripen through an extraordinary sequence of colors — purple, yellow, orange, and red — all simultaneously visible on a single plant, resembling a fiesta of colors inspired by the Southwestern twilight sky.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; NuMex Twilight is compact enough for containers (8–12 inches) and makes an outstanding patio plant both for ornamental color and edible use. NuMex Twilight was developed at New Mexico State University's internationally renowned Chile Pepper Institute as part of their ornamental-edible pepper breeding program; the variety takes its name from the brilliant multicolor sky of a New Mexico twilight that it is said to evoke — each plant produces upright clusters of small (1–2 inch), conical fruits that transition through the colors purple (immature) → yellow → orange → red (fully ripe), with all four colors simultaneously visible on a mature, productive plant. The heat level is approximately 50,000–75,000 SHU — significant but not extreme, in the range of cayenne peppers — and the small fruits are fully edible at any color stage; purple fruits are mildest, red fruits are hottest. As an ornamental plant, NuMex Twilight is among the most stunning of all edible plants, combining constant visual interest through the growing season with genuine culinary utility for dried chile flakes, hot sauces, and fresh use. Outstanding in containers, as a border plant, or as an annual focal point in vegetable and ornamental beds.

common_name: O'Henry Sweet Potato (White-Skin White-Flesh Beauregard Sport)
plant_note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F; O'Henry is a white-skinned, white-fleshed sport of Beauregard with a milder, less sweet flavor than orange-fleshed types.
directions: O'Henry arose as a natural sport of Beauregard, sharing its parent's vigor and productivity but with cream-white skin and white flesh in place of Beauregard's copper skin and orange flesh, giving a milder, less sweet, drier-textured potato favored by cooks who want a sweet potato that behaves more like a baking potato. Vines are vigorous and trailing, producing heavy yields of smooth, uniform, blocky roots under the same growing conditions Beauregard thrives in. Cure freshly dug roots at warm temperature and high humidity for about a week before storage to heal skin cuts and convert starches to sugars, improving both flavor and keeping quality. Roots can develop pronounced lenticels if soil stays wet close to harvest, so time digging for a dry stretch.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; oak leaf lettuce is distinguished by its distinctive deeply lobed, oak leaf-shaped leaves that make it one of the most heat-tolerant looseleaf lettuces and among the slowest to bolt in warm conditions — an excellent choice for spring and fall production in zones 8–11.
directions: Scatter seed thinly on the soil surface and firm in; keep consistently moist until germination at 50–70°F. Oak Leaf lettuce is one of the most recognizable and popular looseleaf lettuces in American home gardens, with deeply lobed, ruffled leaves that resemble the silhouette of an oak leaf — a form distinct from the curled frill of Lollo Rosa types or the smooth curves of Butterhead. The bright green (or burgundy, in the 'Red Oak Leaf' variety) deeply cut leaves form loose, open rosettes that can be cut-and-come-again repeatedly; the leaf texture is tender and buttery, and the flavor is mild with excellent heat tolerance compared to most lettuces. It was one of Thomas Jefferson's preferred salad plants at Monticello and has been grown in American gardens continuously since the colonial era. Outstanding for cut-and-come-again salad production in spring and fall.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for fall.
directions: Oakleaf is a classic loose-leaf heirloom lettuce with tender, deeply lobed leaves that resemble oak foliage. It is a reliable cut-and-come-again type, letting you harvest outer leaves while the center keeps growing. Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer, giving it full sun in cool weather or partial shade to slow bolting in heat. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest young for the sweetest flavor.

common_name: Oaxacan Green Dent Corn (Traditional Mexican Blue-Green Flour Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of 4+ rows; isolate from other corn by 300 feet to preserve the distinctive green-blue kernel color — cross-pollination with yellow or white corn will dilute the color. In zone 9, plant March–May. Harvest as dried corn when ears are fully mature and husks are completely dry; the blue-green color may fade slightly in storage but remains distinctive. Oaxacan Green was traditionally grown in the short-day conditions of southern Mexico and may require some adaptation in longer-day northern locations.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of 4 rows; harvest when husks are completely dry and papery. Oaxacan Green Dent is a traditional flour and dent corn from the valley of Oaxaca, Mexico — a staple landrace corn of the indigenous Zapotec and Mixtec agricultural traditions maintained over centuries in the high-altitude valley environment of southern Mexico. The most visually striking characteristic is the kernel color: at maturity, the kernels are an unusual blue-green to aqua-blue, sometimes with silvery-white highlights — a color found in few other corn varieties and quite distinct from the blue-black of Hopi Blue or the rainbow of Glass Gem. The color comes from the same anthocyanin pigments that color other colored corns, but in a combination that expresses specifically in the blue-green range. In traditional Oaxacan cuisine, Oaxacan Green corn is used as masa for the deep green, smoky-flavored specialty tamales and tlayudas, where the colored masa produces a visually distinctive product unlike standard yellow or white corn preparations. The ears are medium to large, somewhat irregular in kernel arrangement as expected of a landrace variety, and the plants are tall. Oaxacan Green is maintained and distributed by Native Seeds/SEARCH and the Seed Savers Exchange as part of preserving Mesoamerican corn diversity.

common_name: Obsession Sweet Corn (Vigorous Bicolor Supersweet Hybrid)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees; keep isolated from standard or sugary-enhanced corn to protect kernel sweetness. Obsession is a vigorous supersweet (sh2) bicolor hybrid bred for strong stalk vigor and high-quality ears for Southern home gardens.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Obsession is a supersweet bicolor sweet corn hybrid bred for vigorous stalk growth and consistent ear quality under warm Southern growing conditions. It produces well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels that stay sweet in storage longer than standard sugary-type corn thanks to its supersweet genetics. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, since drought stress at this stage leads to poorly filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.

common_name: Oca (Andean Wood Sorrel, New Zealand Yam)
plant_note: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep after last frost in cool soil; oca is photoperiod-sensitive and only initiates tuber formation once days shorten below about 12 hours in late summer or fall — in long-summer climates, use season-extension techniques to hasten tuberization or choose early-bulking varieties such as 'New Zealand Red'.
directions: Plant seed tubers 3–4 inches deep in loose, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; oca is the second most important Andean root crop after potato, cultivated for thousands of years across the Andes from Colombia to Argentina at elevations of 7,000–13,000 feet, where its tangy, lemony tubers are boiled, roasted, freeze-dried into 'caya', or left in the sun for several days to mellow the oxalic acid and develop sweetness. Tubers come in striking colors — white, yellow, orange, pink, red, and near-black — and range from pleasantly tart to mild and starchy depending on cultivar and post-harvest sun exposure. Harvest after the first light frost kills the foliage, which signals peak tuber development; in frost-free zones, cut back the vines in November to trigger dormancy.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil as early as it can be worked; sow again for fall.
directions: This spinach yields deep green, easy-to-clean leaves that are ready as baby greens in about 25 days and full size in 40. Sow directly in cool spring or fall soil since heat triggers bolting. Keep the bed evenly moist and thin seedlings for good airflow. Harvest baby leaves with scissors or pull whole plants, and provide afternoon shade to stretch the harvest into warmer weather.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is consistently warm; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. October Bean is a climbing pole bean requiring a trellis, fence, or pole support 5–8 feet tall. The primary fresh-shelled eating stage (the classic Southern 'shellout') is when pods are plump and seeds are fully developed but still moist — at this stage they cook quickly and have a rich, creamy flavor. Pods allowed to dry fully can be stored and used as dry beans through winter.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy pole or trellis support; October Bean is an Appalachian mountain heirloom shellout bean (also called 'fall bean', 'shelly bean', or 'October shellout') that has been grown in Southern Appalachian kitchen gardens continuously for generations — the bean is named for its traditional harvest period in September and October when the seeds have filled the pods but before autumn frosts dry the plants down. The large, tan to cream-colored, maroon-streaked seeds inside swollen pods are shelled and cooked fresh like a combination between fresh lima beans and dry beans — with a rich, meaty, potato-like texture and earthy, slightly sweet flavor quite different from green snap beans or fully dried beans. The freshly shelled October bean is a cornerstone of traditional Appalachian cooking, served with cornbread, potatoes, and green onions. The climbing vines produce abundantly over a long season, and any mature pods that escape the fresh-shelled harvest can be allowed to dry for a dried soup bean with excellent winter storage.

common_name: October Bean (Peanut Butter Bean, Speckled Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost; October bean is a pole or half-runner type requiring 4–6 foot support; in zone 9 plant in May–June to mature in September–October when cooler temperatures improve the flavor of the shelled beans.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing 4–6 feet of vertical support; October bean is a traditional Appalachian heirloom pole or half-runner bean whose primary value is as a shelling bean — harvested when pods are fully filled but still green to slightly dried ('fall colored'), when the speckled tan-and-maroon seeds shell out easily and cook quickly with a rich, creamy, almost peanut-buttery flavor. Named for October when they traditionally matured in the mountain regions of the southern Appalachians, the plants produce best when planted in late spring to mature into cooler fall temperatures. In zone 9 a June planting produces a September–October shell bean harvest with ideal timing. The shelled beans cook in 45–60 minutes without soaking, absorbing seasoning beautifully, and are outstanding cooked with ham hocks and served over cornbread.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–October in zone 9) in well-drained to dry, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; okahijiki is a cool-season Japanese saltwort vegetable grown for its tender, bright-green, spiny young shoots — it is an unusual cool-weather specialty vegetable that tolerates salty, lean soils and grows in conditions where most vegetables fail.
directions: Direct sow seeds shallowly in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in fall or early spring; thin to 3–4 inches. Salsola komarovii (okahijiki or land seaweed) is a Japanese saltwort vegetable — an annual succulent herb related to the Russian thistle (tumbleweed), grown in Japan for its tender, crisp, spiny young shoots that are bright green, cylindrical, and highly reminiscent in texture and mild, slightly salty flavor of sea vegetables (seaweed). The 'okahijiki' name literally means 'land hijiki,' comparing the plant to hijiki (a Japanese seaweed); the 'land seaweed' comparison reflects both the plant's mild marine-like flavor and its coastal saltmarsh habitat. Young shoots are harvested at 3–6 inches when most tender and used in salads, blanched as a side vegetable, or incorporated into Japanese cuisine as a seasonal vegetable; the texture is pleasantly crisp and slightly mucilaginous. The plant is extremely drought-tolerant and grows in salty, lean, sandy soils where most vegetables fail. As it matures, it becomes increasingly spiny and fibrous; harvest young for best eating quality. An unusual and underutilized cool-season specialty vegetable for adventurous gardeners.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings after all frost danger has passed and nighttime temperatures stay above 50°F; in frost-free zones plant any time of year.
directions: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix; they strike quickly at warm temperatures and are ready to transplant in 10–14 days. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade — full afternoon shade is ideal in hot climates, where the ornamental two-toned leaves (dark green above, vivid purple beneath) are most striking. Harvest young leaves and stem tips continuously; the raw leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture and are eaten as salad greens or briefly stir-fried. In zones 9–11 the plant grows as a sprawling perennial; in cooler climates bring cuttings indoors over winter.

plant_note: Plant slips after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant April–June for a fall harvest. Okinawa sweet potato requires a long season (100–120 days) and does not produce quality roots if harvested early; the full summer growing period is needed for the characteristic purple flesh to fully develop. Grow in the ground rather than containers for best root development.
directions: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, slightly sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Okinawa sweet potato is a Japanese heirloom variety with cream-colored skin and brilliantly purple flesh — the vibrant purple color comes from exceptionally high anthocyanin content, among the highest of any food crop. The slightly sweet, nutty, dry-textured flesh holds its purple color through roasting, steaming, and baking (though water boiling may leach some pigment). Okinawa sweet potato is a staple of the Okinawan diet, studied extensively as part of the traditional diet associated with unusual longevity on the island. The flavor is subtly sweet and starchy with an earthy, slightly nutty aftertaste. Cure harvested roots at 85°F and 90% humidity for 10 days before eating or storing to develop sweetness and heal any cuts.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; Okinawan spinach produces new growth continuously and can be harvested by snipping stem tips every few weeks — the new growth is most tender and flavorful.
directions: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix and plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; Okinawan spinach (Cholesterol spinach, edible velvet plant, han tsai tai) is a tropical perennial leafy vegetable from Southeast Asia and Okinawa that is one of the most productive and effortless greens for subtropical gardens in zones 9–12 — the plant grows continuously year-round in frost-free climates, producing an inexhaustible supply of young, tender growing tips that are harvested by snipping and regrowing for months. The leaves are bicolored — dark green on the top and deep purple-red underneath, with a velvety, slightly hairy texture — creating an attractive ornamental plant that functions simultaneously as an edible garden specimen. Young leaves and tips are eaten raw in salads (pleasant, mild flavor) or briefly sautéed. The plant is rich in antioxidants and flavonoids associated with the traditional Okinawan diet. Tolerates partial shade better than most vegetables, making it valuable for shaded garden beds where conventional leafy greens would bolt. Distinct from the related Gynura procumbens (longevity spinach) in its ornamental bicolored foliage.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings — rooted cuttings establish rapidly in warm, moist soil. Plant in spring after frost risk passes in zone 9 and grow as a perennial; the fleshy stems root easily at nodes wherever they contact moist soil. No seed is typically available commercially.
directions: Grow in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Okinawan spinach thrives in the heat and humidity of zone 9 summers when cool-season greens have long since bolted. The dark green leaves with purple undersides are harvested young and eaten raw in salads, lightly stir-fried, or blended into smoothies; they have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture and are rich in antioxidants. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep plants bushy and productive; the sprawling stems root at nodes when they touch moist soil, making propagation effortless. This species is distinct from Okinawan sweet potato — it is a member of the daisy family and produces small yellow flowers.

common_name: Okinawan Sweet Potato (Purple Sweet Potato, Hawaiian Purple Yam)
plant_note: Plant slips in warm soil (above 65°F) after last frost; Okinawan purple sweet potato requires a longer growing season (100–130 days) than standard varieties — plant as early as possible in the season in the South.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, loose, warm soil in full sun after last frost; Okinawan sweet potato has creamy-white skin concealing spectacularly vivid purple-violet flesh — the deep purple color comes from extremely high anthocyanin content (among the highest of any sweet potato), making it a genuine superfood with powerful antioxidant properties. The flavor is mildly sweet, slightly nutty, and drier than orange-flesh types; it is prized in Hawaiian cuisine (where it's called 'Hawaiian purple sweet potato'), Japanese cuisine, and modern farm-to-table cooking for its dramatic color that holds remarkably well through most cooking methods. Excellent roasted, steamed, in ice cream, and in colorful desserts.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil temperature reaches at least 65°F; okra thrives in heat.
directions: Soak seeds in water for 12–24 hours before sowing 1 inch deep to soften the hard seed coat and speed germination. Plant in the hottest, sunniest spot available, as okra is a true heat-lover and grows slowly in cool conditions. Side-dress with a nitrogen-rich fertilizer when plants reach 12 inches tall to promote vigorous growth. Harvest pods every 2–3 days when they are 3–4 inches long and still tender; pods left to mature become tough and woody and reduce plant productivity.

common_name: Old German Tomato (Mennonite Bicolor Yellow-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Old German is believed to have originated with Mennonite German immigrant communities in Virginia and been preserved by Mennonite seed-saving traditions before entering the American heirloom seed trade.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Old German is an heirloom beefsteak tomato of Mennonite German ancestry — producing very large (1–2 lb), deeply flattened, lobed beefsteak fruits with a striking bicolor pattern of golden-yellow skin marked with deep-red and orange streaks, marbling, and patches distributed across the fruit surface in irregular patterns. The cut interior reveals the characteristic bicolor flesh of this German heirloom tradition: yellow and red sectors arranged in a beautiful mosaic pattern that is outstanding in sliced fresh presentations — the multicolored cross-section of Old German makes it one of the most visually beautiful tomatoes when displayed on a cutting board or serving plate. The flavor follows the pattern of the best bicolor heirlooms: very sweet, extremely low-acid, with a complex, fruity, mild quality that makes it exceptional for fresh eating. Old German is most clearly distinguished from similar bicolor heirlooms (Pineapple, Hillbilly, Big Rainbow) by the specific distribution and proportion of its red-and-yellow coloring — the exact pattern varies somewhat from fruit to fruit but consistently produces the beautiful bicolor marbled effect. An open-pollinated heirloom with saveable seed. In zone 9, grow as a spring crop for best results before summer heat.

common_name: Old Timey Blue Collard (Traditional Southern Heirloom Collard)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Old Timey Blue is an heirloom passed down within Southern families for generations and is prized for reliable cold hardiness and traditional flavor.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and thin or transplant to final spacing as seedlings develop true leaves. Old Timey Blue is a traditional Southern heirloom collard, one of many regional strains passed down and re-saved within families for generations before being preserved by seed-saving organizations, valued for its dependable vigor, good cold tolerance, and classic blue-green collard flavor that sweetens after a frost. Tall, productive plants yield heavily over a long harvest window when picked cut-and-come-again, taking outer leaves while the center keeps producing. Fertilize with a balanced or nitrogen-rich feed through the season for the best leaf growth, and watch for cabbage worms and aphids, managing with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide if needed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Oldham's bamboo is a clumping species that does not spread invasively by underground rhizomes — each new cane emerges adjacent to the parent and the colony expands slowly outward, unlike the aggressively spreading running bamboos.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Oldham's bamboo is one of the most important timber and edible bamboos for warm-climate gardens in zones 8b–12, producing straight, strong culms 3–4 inches in diameter and 30–50 feet tall that are used in construction, furniture, and crafts. Unlike the running (monopodial) bamboos that spread aggressively by underground rhizomes, this is a tight-clumping (sympodial) species that expands slowly and predictably without invasive spreading — making it safe to plant near structures and property boundaries. The large, young shoots in spring are edible — milder and less bitter than many bamboos. An excellent choice for tall tropical screening, erosion control on slopes, and sustainable bamboo production in the warm Southeast. Water generously in summer to support rapid growth of new culms.

common_name: Ole Timey Blue Collards (Traditional Southern Heirloom Collard)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Ole Timey Blue'
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Ole Timey Blue is a tall, vigorous, open-pollinated Southern heirloom maintained by generations of home seed savers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Ole Timey Blue is a tall, vigorous, open-pollinated Southern heirloom collard with broad, blue-green leaves, representing the traditional dooryard collard type grown throughout the Deep South long before modern compact hybrids became widely available. Plants grow quite tall over a long season, and the leaves carry the classic robust, full-bodied collard flavor that sweetens further after the first light fall frosts. Because it is a genuine open-pollinated landrace rather than a stabilized commercial variety, some plant-to-plant variation in leaf shape and color is normal and part of its heirloom character, and seed can be saved from the best plants to maintain the strain. Harvest outer and lower leaves as needed, leaving the central growing point intact so the plant continues producing fresh leaves from the top through a long cool-season harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil; best flavor develops in fall.
directions: Also called frisee, this endive forms lacy, finely cut leaves with a mild flavor that dresses up a salad or serves as an ornamental. Sow in cool weather and keep evenly watered to reduce bitterness. Blanch the center by tying up outer leaves a week or two before harvest for a pale, sweeter heart. Harvest before hard frost, cutting whole heads at the base.

common_name: Oliver Brussels Sprout (Very Early F1 Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost; Oliver is a very early-maturing F1 Brussels sprout that initiates sprout development earlier in the season than most varieties, making it one of the best choices for short-season northern gardens (zones 3–5) where the growing window is compressed, and for Gulf Coast gardeners who need sprout harvest to complete before heat arrives in spring.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into firm, rich, consistently moist soil; stake tall plants against wind; remove the growing tip when bottom sprouts reach marble size to encourage rapid maturing of the rest; harvest from the bottom upward when sprouts are 1–1.5 inches across. Oliver is an F1 hybrid Brussels sprout bred for early sprout initiation — one of the earliest-maturing Brussels sprout varieties commercially available — that produces uniform, round, high-quality sprouts beginning earlier in the fall season than standard types. The relatively compact plants (24–30 inches) with short internodes produce sprouts packed closely on the stem in tight, uniform clusters that are excellent for harvest. The early initiation of sprout development makes Oliver particularly valuable in two challenging situations: in zones 3–5 where the growing season is short and standard Brussels sprouts often don't finish before hard freeze, and in zones 7–9 where the goal is to get sprout harvest completed before the arrival of hot spring weather. Oliver's flavor is mild and sweet, comparable to other modern hybrid Brussels sprouts, with the characteristic improvement in flavor and sweetness after frost exposure. A practical, reliable choice for gardeners who want Brussels sprouts without the 100–120 day wait of heirloom types.

plant_note: In zone 8-9 gardens sow in fall for a winter and early spring harvest; elsewhere sow 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost.
directions: Direct sow a half inch deep into cool, moist soil and thin seedlings once true leaves appear, harvesting outer leaves or whole plants as needed. This hybrid produces smooth to lightly crinkled, dark green leaves on a slow-to-bolt plant, making it a reliable choice for stretching the spring harvest window a bit longer than older heirloom types. It performs well as both a baby-leaf and full-size crop and holds quality in cool, short-day conditions common to winter gardening in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Omar Arab is a Middle Eastern heirloom with elongated, pleated, deep red fruits that are outstanding for stuffing whole in the traditional Levantine style; well-adapted to hot, dry summer conditions and therefore an excellent choice for zone 8–11.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Omar Arab is a Syrian heirloom tomato with elongated, ribbed or lobed, deep red to crimson fruits 8–12 ounces in weight with a distinctive beaked tip and meaty, near-seedless flesh with very few gel pockets that makes it outstanding for traditional Levantine-style stuffed tomatoes (mahashi), where the tomato is cored, filled, and cooked whole; the balanced, savory-sweet flavor is excellent fresh as well. Adapted to hot, dry Mediterranean-type climates, it performs reliably in zone 8–11 high-summer conditions where other heirlooms drop flowers or crack. Seed was collected and introduced more widely through the work of heritage seed savers in the Arab world.

common_name: Omar's Lebanese Tomato (Middle Eastern Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun; the huge, heavy fruit clusters need sturdy caging or staking from an early age.
directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes, spacing plants generously to allow air movement around the sprawling vine. Omar's Lebanese is a Middle Eastern heirloom brought into wider American circulation through the Seed Savers Exchange network, grown for enormous, smooth, pale to deep pink beefsteak fruit that regularly reaches one to two pounds with a mild, low-acid, juicy sweetness. The indeterminate vines are notably productive for such a large-fruited variety, setting fruit steadily through summer heat where many other big pink slicers slow down. Provide even moisture and consistent feeding, since fruit of this size draws heavily on the plant, and support the heaviest clusters to prevent limb breakage.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep and thin generously, since this hybrid produces unusually large, heavy roots that need more room than typical spring radishes.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep and thin generously, since this Sakata-bred hybrid produces unusually large, heavy roots that need more room than typical spring radishes to size up properly. Omny is grown through spring and summer for a dependable harvest of smooth white daikon suited to grilling, baking, stir-frying, or simmering as well as fresh salads. Keep soil consistently moist as roots swell to prevent splitting, and harvest before roots become oversized and woody.

common_name: On Deck Sweet Corn (Compact Container Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65F; because plants stay short, block-plant even a small number of stalks in a large container or short row for reliable wind pollination.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows, even in a large container, once the soil has warmed to ensure adequate cross-pollination between the short stalks. On Deck is an All-America Selections winner bred specifically for small-space and container gardening, reaching only about 4-5 feet tall while still producing two 7-8 inch bicolor ears per stalk with classic sweet corn flavor. Its shrunken stature makes it one of the few sweet corn varieties genuinely practical for a patio or deck planter.

common_name: One Ball Squash (Round Yellow Hybrid Summer Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed; compact size suits succession planting through a long warm season.
directions: One Ball is the bright yellow counterpart to the dark green Eight Ball and pale Cue Ball round squash, bred by Hollar Seeds to round out a trio of billiard-themed globe-shaped summer squash. The vigorous, disease-resistant bush plant sets shiny yellow fruit best picked at 2-3 inches across for the crispest texture and nuttiest flavor, well before the rind toughens. Its resistance to watermelon mosaic virus and zucchini yellow mosaic virus is valuable in warm, humid Gulf Coast gardens where these aphid-vectored viruses are common late-season problems. The compact habit and small mature fruit size make it a good choice for succession planting in raised beds through a long Texas growing season.

common_name: One Kilo Slow Bolt Napa Cabbage
plant_note: Best sown in mid to late summer for a fall crop to avoid bolting.
directions: This napa cabbage forms tight, creamy-yellow heads with a delicate flavor and texture between lettuce and regular cabbage. Its slow-bolt habit lets it hold in the garden longer, and it grows most reliably as a fall crop. Keep the soil consistently moist and fertile for solid heads. Protect young spring plantings from cold snaps, which can trigger premature bolting.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or press stem cuttings into waterlogged soil or gravel at the edge of a cold, clear, slow-moving stream or pond; plants root readily from stem nodes in contact with wet substrate and quickly colonize suitable aquatic margins.
directions: Grow in cold, clean, slow-moving to still water or in consistently saturated soil at the water's edge — ideal conditions are a spring-fed stream with a gravel substrate and constant cool temperatures below 70°F; One-rowed Watercress is closely related to the common watercress (Nasturtium officinale) sold in grocery stores and is harvested and eaten in the same way, but its flavor is noticeably more peppery and pungent, making it preferred by those who want a stronger bite in salads, sandwiches, and garnishes. It can be distinguished from common watercress by its smaller, rounder leaflets and, botanically, by its seeds being arranged in a single row inside the seed pod rather than the double row of N. officinale. Like common watercress, it is best harvested in cool weather — spring and fall — as summer heat triggers bolting and intensifies bitterness. Only harvest from water sources confirmed to be free of agricultural runoff, animal grazing upstream, and waterborne pathogens such as Fasciola hepatica (liver fluke), which can colonize watercress in contaminated streams; thoroughly cook the greens if water quality is uncertain.

common_name: Ong Choy (Water Spinach, Morning Glory Greens, Kangkong)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant rooted stem cuttings after last frost when soil is warm; ong choy is a heat-loving, fast-growing tropical green that produces heavily in warm, moist conditions and is outstanding for the Gulf South summer season when most temperate greens have bolted. Note: Ipomoea aquatica is a federally regulated noxious weed in the US — it is legal to grow for food in contained garden beds or pots but may not be sold live or transported across state lines without a permit in some states.
directions: Direct sow or plant rooted cuttings after last frost in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; ong choy (also called water spinach, kangkong in Southeast Asia, or 'rau muống' in Vietnamese) is the principal summer green of tropical Asia — a remarkably productive, fast-growing vining plant that produces enormous quantities of tender, mild, spinach-like shoots and arrow-shaped leaves in hot, humid conditions where temperate greens fail. Ong choy is the go-to summer stir-fry green across all of East and Southeast Asia and is extraordinarily common in Chinese, Vietnamese, Thai, Filipino, and Malaysian cooking — most famously in the Thai preparation 'phad phak bung fai daeng' (morning glory cooked with garlic, oyster sauce, and roasted chilies over high flame) and in Vietnamese simple stir-fries with garlic. The flavor is mild, spinach-like, and slightly mucilaginous; stems are hollow (hence the name water spinach, as it grows in or near water in its native habitat), and tender enough to eat whole including stems. Harvest by snipping growing tips; plants regenerate vigorously and yield continuously through the hot season. IMPORTANT: Ipomoea aquatica is a federal noxious weed in the US — confirm local regulations before cultivating outside a contained area.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting out in early spring, or plant onion sets outdoors as soon as soil is workable; transplant seedlings when about pencil-thick, burying the green tops to 1 inch above the soil to encourage strong bulb development.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the outdoor transplant date in late winter, keeping them in bright light to prevent leggy growth; transplant pencil-thick seedlings outdoors as early as the ground can be worked and plant 4–6 inches apart in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil. Onion bulb size is determined by day length: long-day varieties (zone 3–6) bulb in summer when days exceed 14–16 hours; short-day varieties (zone 7–10) bulb in spring when days are 10–12 hours; intermediate-day varieties work in zone 5–7. Keep well-weeded as onions compete poorly with weeds, and water evenly throughout bulb development to prevent cracking. Stop watering when tops begin to fall over naturally; cure bulbs in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for 2–4 weeks before storage.

common_name: Onyx Red Ornamental Pepper (AAS-Winning Purple-Black Foliage Pepper Ripening Red)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant after all danger of frost into full sun; Onyx Red is grown chiefly as an ornamental bedding and container pepper, prized for foliage and fruit color over culinary use.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after all danger of frost; Onyx Red is an AAS-winning ornamental pepper bred for striking near-black, glossy purple foliage that provides season-long color contrast even before fruiting begins. Small, upright, conical fruits emerge dark purple-black and ripen through red-orange to bright red, often showing several colors on the plant at once against the dark leaves, creating a dramatic, jewel-toned display in beds, borders, and mixed containers. The compact, uniform mounded habit and heat tolerance make it a reliable performer through the full Gulf South growing season, needing only light, regular feeding to keep the color intense. Fruits are technically edible and quite hot, but the variety is bred and marketed primarily as an ornamental rather than a culinary pepper.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; Opal flowers readily in its first year without a demanding cold-treatment schedule, so a simple cool spell of a couple of weeks after transplanting is generally enough to bring on good bud set.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Opal is an F1 hybrid bred for fast, dependable first-year bud production and stands out for the striking violet-purple color of its rounded, tender buds, which hold their color well even after light cooking. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining strong ornamental appeal with genuine first-year productivity from seed, making it a popular dual-purpose choice for gardeners who want both a harvest and a bold accent plant among vegetables or in a mixed border. Plants are moderately compact for an artichoke and produce a good number of secondary buds after the central bud is harvested. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest buds while still tightly closed, since the purple color and tender texture are both best before scales begin to loosen.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Opalka is a Polish heirloom paste tomato renowned for producing extraordinarily long, pointed, banana-pepper-shaped fruits 4–8 inches in length with extremely thick, meaty walls, minimal seeds, concentrated flavor, and very low moisture content — considered by many tomato growers the finest heirloom paste variety for sauce and preserving.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide staking or caging as plants grow 5–7 feet tall. Opalka is a Polish heirloom paste tomato (named for the Opalka family who brought it to America) producing distinctively long, tapering, banana-pepper to Italian horn-shaped fruits of 4–8 inches with a pointed blossom end and the distinctive characteristic of exceedingly thick, dense walls surrounding very small seed cavities — the result is a paste tomato with more dry matter per pound than virtually any other variety, producing sauce with exceptional body and concentrated tomato flavor without hours of reduction time. The flavor fresh is rich and complex, with more sweetness and less tartness than most red paste types; the thick walls and dry flesh make Opalka exceptionally well-suited to drying (dried Opalka are comparable to sun-dried tomatoes in Italy). An indeterminate plant that bears a large late-season crop; very productive in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens in spring and fall seasons.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; seeds need cold stratification or cool soil to germinate well and the crop runs to seed in summer heat.
directions: Press seeds firmly into soil no deeper than 1/4 inch; germination is improved by pre-soaking seeds for a few hours before sowing. Orach grows quickly into an upright plant with red, gold, or green leaves that can substitute for spinach in any cooked preparation. Pinch the central growing tip when the plant is 12 inches tall to encourage bushy side growth and delay bolting. Harvest young leaves frequently; once flower stalks emerge, leaves become less palatable.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant after nights stay warm.
directions: This heirloom bell pepper ripens from green to a bright, juicy orange with a crisp, sweet flavor ideal for salads, stuffing, and fresh snacking. Start seed indoors well before the last frost and transplant into full sun once nights are reliably warm. Peppers need steady warmth, even moisture, and moderate feeding to size up well. Allow fruits to fully color on the plant for the sweetest taste, then harvest to encourage continued production.

common_name: Orange Blaze Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Orange Mini Bell Pepper with Early Production)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Orange Blaze is a compact, upright sweet bell pepper variety that produces medium-sized (3–4 inch) blocky orange fruits on a plant shorter and more manageable than standard bell pepper varieties. In zone 9, start seeds January–February and transplant March–April. Orange Blaze was an AAS winner recognized for its earlier production timeline compared to standard orange bell peppers — orange bells typically require very long maturity periods because they must reach full green bell size and then ripen fully to orange, a process that can take 75–90+ days from transplant. Orange Blaze achieves mature orange color faster without sacrificing fruit quality. The compact plant habit (18–24 inches vs. 30–36 inches for standard bells) makes Orange Blaze practical for containers and smaller garden spaces. Fruits are blocky, firm, and uniformly orange with sweet, crisp flesh.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at full orange for maximum sweetness; can harvest at green stage but flavor improves considerably at full ripeness. Orange Blaze Pepper won the All-America Selections award in 2010 for its compact plant habit, early production of fully mature (orange-colored) fruit, and excellent flavor quality in a category (orange sweet bell peppers) where most available varieties required exceptionally long growing seasons that limited their usefulness in many North American climates. Standard orange bell peppers are derived from bell pepper varieties with the genetic trait for orange ripening (rather than red or yellow), and this trait is typically associated with an extended maturation period: the fruits must first reach full green bell size before beginning the color transition, and the transition from green to full orange requires additional time beyond what red peppers need for their color change. The result is that many orange bells require 80–95 days from transplant to reach edible orange maturity — too long for gardens with short warm seasons, and even in zone 9 limiting the productive harvest period. Orange Blaze's AAS recognition reflected its ability to achieve full orange maturity 10–15 days earlier than other orange bell varieties while maintaining good fruit size and quality, expanding the practical use of orange bell peppers in home gardens. For zone 9 spring gardens where April–May transplanting targets a June–July harvest before extreme summer heat, Orange Blaze's earlier maturity maximizes the productive harvest window within zone 9's optimal pepper-growing period.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: This indeterminate cherry tomato bears heavy clusters of vibrant golden-orange fruits with a sweet, mild, almost tropical flavor. Start seed indoors several weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once soil is warm, setting plants deep. The tall vines need staking or a cage and keep bearing right up to frost. Pick the small fruits as they ripen fully for the best sweetness and to encourage more production.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date; sow again in mid to late summer for a fall and winter crop in mild climates.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to 8-10 inches apart. Orange Fantasia stands out among chards for its vivid, saturated carrot-orange stalks, midribs, and veining, a deeper and more solidly orange tone than the paler gold seen in yellow-stemmed chards, set against dark, glossy, savoyed green leaves. It is slow to bolt and holds its color well when cooked, making it a favorite for both the ornamental vegetable garden and the kitchen. Harvest baby leaves at about a month for salads, or let plants mature for six to eight weeks and harvest outer stalks continually, since the plant regrows from the center through a long season.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost in warm soil and transplant out after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; habanero needs consistent heat and a long growing season to fully ripen and develop maximum heat and fruitiness.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost in warm soil and transplant out after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; habanero needs consistent heat and a long growing season to fully ripen and develop maximum heat and fruitiness. This classic habanero selection produces small, lantern-shaped fruit that ripens from green through yellow to a vivid bright orange, carrying an intense, fruity, floral heat in the 100,000-350,000 Scoville range that has made habanero peppers a staple of Caribbean, Yucatecan, and hot sauce cuisine. The compact, bushy plants are heavy producers over a long season and thrive in the same hot, humid conditions favored by many tropical Capsicum species, continuing to set fruit through the hottest part of summer when some other peppers slow down. Harvest fruit at full orange color for maximum heat and flavor, wear gloves when handling, and avoid touching your face or eyes after working with the fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors early; germination is slow and needs steady warmth.
directions: The classic orange habanero delivers intense heat with a fruity, tropical sweetness that shines in salsas and hot sauces. Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, as germination is slow and demands consistent warmth. Transplant into full sun only after nights are reliably warm, and the productive plants do well in containers. Handle the ripe pods with gloves and harvest regularly once they turn deep orange.

common_name: Orange Smoothie Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Smooth-Rind Small Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Orange Smoothie is an AAS-winning small pumpkin bred for an unusually smooth, rib-free rind, unlike the deep ridges typical of most jack-o-lantern and pie pumpkins.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Orange Smoothie is an AAS-winning small-to-medium pumpkin distinguished by an unusually smooth, nearly rib-free rind — most pumpkins have pronounced vertical ridges, but Orange Smoothie's clean, rounded surface gives it a distinctive look for decoration and makes it especially easy to carve or paint without ridges interrupting the design. The fruit is a good size for both decorative use and cooking, with reasonably good flesh quality for pies and purees. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and color deepens to solid orange, cutting the stem with a few inches attached, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before use or fall display.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. The elongated, oxheart shape makes the large fruits (1–2 pounds) less likely to crack than large round beefsteak types. In zone 9 the fall planting in August produces particularly sweet, rich-flavored fruits as cooler October-November temperatures concentrate the sugars and reduce water content in the flesh.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with cage or stake support; Orange Strawberry (also known as Strawberry Oxheart Orange) is an oxheart-type heirloom tomato producing large, elongated, pointed fruits with a distinctive heart or strawberry silhouette in vivid, deep orange — the 'strawberry' in the name refers to the fruit shape, not the flavor. The thick, meaty, deep orange flesh is extraordinarily dense and nearly seedless, with a small hollow interior cavity common to oxheart types — the low water content and minimal seed-gel gives Orange Strawberry one of the meatiest, most substantial textures of any tomato type, with a concentrated, rich, fruity-sweet tomato flavor that becomes even more intense when the dense flesh is sliced for sandwiches or diced for salads. Orange tomatoes are distinguished by their lycopene profile — beta-carotene and tetra-cis-lycopene rather than the all-trans lycopene of red tomatoes — which is more bioavailable than the red form and contributes to the characteristic rich, fruity sweetness of orange-fleshed varieties.

common_name: Orange Sun Pepper (Fully Orange-Ripening Sweet Bell Pepper, Early and Productive)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Orange Sun is a fully orange-ripening bell pepper that reaches mature orange color rather than the halfway-ripened red-orange of some varieties that are harvested early. In zone 9, transplant March–April for spring production; a fall crop started from seed in July can extend production into October–November. The full orange color develops several weeks after the green harvest stage — allow peppers to reach full orange before picking for the sweetest, most nutritious fruit. Orange bell peppers are higher in certain carotenoids (beta-cryptoxanthin) than red or green bells, and the flavor at full orange ripeness is sweet and mild with none of the grassy notes of green-stage peppers. Plant in full sun with good drainage; consistent watering during fruit development prevents blossom end rot and promotes even development.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Allow to fully color orange before harvesting for best flavor. Orange Sun is an F1 hybrid bell pepper variety selected for fully orange fruit at maturity — the distinctive bright orange color of an orange-ripe bell pepper rather than the mixed red-orange of incompletely ripened red varieties harvested early. Orange bell peppers as a category occupy an intermediate position in the bell pepper maturity and flavor spectrum: green peppers are harvested immature, red peppers are harvested fully ripe (or harvested orange-yellow then gassed), yellow and orange peppers represent distinct genetic selections that color differently from red-maturing types. True orange varieties like Orange Sun have the genetics to produce stable, uniform orange coloring at maturity — different from red varieties picked early, which produce a mottled, inconsistent orange appearance and inferior flavor. The walls of Orange Sun are thick and firm, excellent for fresh eating, roasting, and stuffing. The flavor at full orange ripeness is notably sweeter and more complex than green bells from the same plant, as the conversion of chlorophyll to carotenoids during ripening is accompanied by conversion of starches to sugars and development of aromatic compounds. Orange Sun is early-maturing for a bell pepper, reaching the green harvest stage approximately 70 days from transplanting and full orange ripeness a few weeks later — making it practical for the Gulf South's spring production window before summer heat limits continued setting.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant after frost when soil is warm.
directions: This large bell pepper ripens from green to glowing orange with thick, sweet, juicy walls. Pick fruit at either stage to boost overall production and add color to meals. Start seeds indoors well ahead of your last frost, then set sturdy transplants into warm soil. Stake heavily laden plants and water evenly to prevent blossom-end rot.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil thoroughly warmed; in zone 9 plant March–May. OrangeGlo produces large (20–30 lbs) oblong fruits — space rows widely. The orange flesh can be difficult to judge for ripeness by internal color alone; use the standard external cues: yellow ground spot, dried tendril nearest the fruit, and hollow thump. In zone 9 the long, hot summer is ideal for this variety's full flavor development.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, fertile, slightly acidic soil; OrangeGlo is an heirloom watermelon producing large, oblong fruits with striped yellow-green skin and vivid deep orange flesh — the orange color results from high beta-carotene content rather than the lycopene responsible for red watermelon flesh, giving OrangeGlo significantly higher vitamin A precursor content than conventional red varieties. The flavor is sweet and mild with a distinctive tropical, honey-melon note that many tasters describe as sweeter and less watery than red watermelons — the orange flesh has a slightly different sugar profile and flavor that creates a tropical-fruity sweetness. OrangeGlo has been selected from an heirloom lineage for consistent large size (typically 20–30 pounds), high sugar content, and the distinctive orange flesh color that makes it immediately striking when cut open at the table. The unusual orange interior creates a dramatic visual contrast in fruit arrangements and makes OrangeGlo watermelon a reliable conversation piece at summer gatherings.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost, or start indoors 3 weeks early.
directions: Orangeglo is a beloved heirloom watermelon with brilliant orange flesh and a crisp, exceptionally sweet, tropical flavor. The large oblong fruits ripen on vigorous vines over a long, warm season. Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger, giving the vines ample room to run. Water consistently while fruit develops, then reduce watering as the melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars.

common_name: Orangetti Spaghetti Squash (Orange Spaghetti Squash, Golden Spaghetti Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Orangetti is a compact, early-maturing spaghetti squash that matures to a vivid deep orange exterior (rather than the cream-white of standard spaghetti squash) with higher beta-carotene content and the same characteristic stranded flesh texture — it is earlier, more flavorful, and more nutritious than standard spaghetti squash.
directions: Direct sow after last frost; Orangetti is semi-compact with shorter vines than standard spaghetti squash; harvest when the outer skin is a uniform deep orange and the rind is firm; bake halved at 375°F for 40–50 minutes and scrape the interior with a fork to produce the characteristic pasta-like strands that give spaghetti squash its name. Orangetti is a distinctive type of spaghetti squash developed in Israel through breeding work at the Negev branch of the Agricultural Research Organization, selected for its vivid orange skin color (versus the pale cream-yellow of standard spaghetti squash), higher beta-carotene content in both the skin and the stranded flesh, and slightly earlier maturity than most spaghetti squash varieties. The vegetable has the same characteristic feature that makes all spaghetti squash unique — the interior flesh separates into long, pasta-like strands when cooked — but the Orangetti variant produces strands that are slightly yellower-orange than the pale yellow of standard varieties, reflecting the higher pigment content. The flavor of Orangetti is considered by many cooks to be sweeter and more complex than standard white spaghetti squash, though still with the mild, somewhat neutral quality that makes spaghetti squash a versatile pasta substitute for low-carbohydrate diets. The compact, semi-bush vine habit is more manageable than standard spaghetti squash in small gardens. Orangetti typically yields 3–5 fruits per vine weighing 2–4 lbs each.

common_name: Orca Bean (Killer Whale Bean, Half-and-Half Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Orca is a bush dry bean type that matures in 75–90 days to full dry-shell stage; the beans are famous for their striking two-tone coloring — exactly half black, half white on each bean — that resembles the coloring of orca (killer) whales and makes them one of the most visually distinctive dry beans available.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; harvest for dry beans when pods are fully dry and papery on the vine; in humid climates pull whole plants before complete drying and hang in a sheltered, airy space to finish drying to prevent mold on pods. Orca beans are a relatively modern open-pollinated dry bean variety that quickly gained wide popularity among seed savers and heirloom gardeners for their extraordinary visual appearance: each bean is precisely two-toned, with exactly one half black and one half white in a pattern that closely resembles the distinctive black-and-white coloring of the orca whale — hence the common names 'Orca Bean' and 'Killer Whale Bean.' The coloring is remarkably consistent across all seeds from a plant, though the exact position of the color boundary and the ratio of black to white can vary slightly between individual seeds. The seeds are medium-sized, slightly plump, and oval. When cooked, the dramatic two-tone coloring fades and the beans become a more uniform dark brown to black, as with most vividly colored beans — the show is in the seed, not the cooked dish. The flavor is mild and creamy, similar to black beans, with a pleasantly earthy character. Orca beans are excellent in soups, stews, rice dishes, and any preparation where black beans are used. They are often added to seed displays and mixed bean soups specifically for visual interest, and the raw seeds make a striking addition to craft projects, seed collages, and botanical displays.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil as soon as it can be worked.
directions: This snow pea produces some of the largest, crispest, sweetest flat pods you will grow, on vines that stay under 30 inches and need little support. It carries strong resistance to powdery mildew, Fusarium wilt, and pea enation mosaic virus. Sow directly in cool spring soil and keep evenly moist. Harvest pods young and flat, before the seeds swell, to keep plants producing.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before transplanting; Oregon Spring can be set out slightly earlier than most tomatoes since it sets fruit at cooler temperatures than typical varieties.
directions: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into the garden with minimal staking needed, since the compact determinate plants stay under three feet. Oregon Spring was bred by Dr. James Baggett at Oregon State University from a cross involving the cold-adapted Russian variety Severianin, and it was released in 1984 specifically for short, cool growing seasons in the Pacific Northwest and similar climates. The nearly seedless, medium-sized fruit sets even when nights stay chilly, giving gardeners in short-season regions a dependable early, low-acid harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: Oregon Sugar Pod II is a productive snow pea bearing crisp, sweet, flat pods that are delicious raw or lightly cooked. The compact vines resist common pea diseases and crop heavily over the cool season. Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, and provide short netting or twiggy supports. Pick pods young and often, before the peas inside swell, to keep the plants producing.

common_name: Oregon Sugar Pod II Snow Pea
plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil as soon as it can be worked.
directions: This heavy-yielding snow pea bears large numbers of 4 inch flat pods on manageable 28 inch vines that resist mildew, pea enation virus, and leaf roll. Sow directly in cool spring soil and keep the bed moist. A short trellis or brush keeps vines upright and pods clean. Pick pods while flat and tender, before the peas inside develop, for the best flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before last frost; Oregon Sugar Pod is a 1971 All-America Selections winner snow pea with large, flat, edible pods and resistance to pea enation mosaic virus — one of the most popular and disease-resistant snow peas available, excellent for both Pacific Northwest and Southern gardens.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart; provide a 2–3 foot trellis or fence for support. Oregon Sugar Pod pea won the All-America Selections award in 1971 and remains one of the most widely grown and most reliable snow peas, selected for both outstanding pod quality and resistance to pea enation mosaic virus (PEMV), a significant disease problem in humid growing regions. The semi-dwarf plants produce large (4–4.5 inch), flat, very sweet pods harvested when the pod wall is still translucent and peas inside are just barely beginning to swell — the 'snow pea' harvest window when the entire flat, stringless pod is eaten. Used in stir-frying, sautéing, and raw in salads, where the flat pods retain their crisp texture and bright color well when cooked quickly over high heat.

common_name: Orient Express Eggplant (AAS Early Japanese-Type Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Orient Express is an All-America Selections award-winning Japanese-type eggplant producing long (8–10 inch), slender, dark purple fruits in 58–68 days from transplant — one of the earliest-maturing eggplants available — making it the top choice for northern gardeners with short seasons and for Gulf Coast gardeners who want eggplant harvest to begin before peak summer heat reduces fruit set.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 80°F; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Orient Express benefits from staking in windy locations; harvest fruits when 6–10 inches long and the skin is glossy dark purple — do not allow to over-ripen; continuous picking encourages continued fruit production. Orient Express is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning F1 hybrid Japanese-type eggplant that combines the long, slender fruit shape, thin skin, and tender flesh of Asian eggplant varieties with very early maturity (58–68 days from transplant) — a combination that makes it highly productive across a wide range of climates. The long (8–10 inch), slender (1.5–2 inch diameter) fruits have glossy, near-black purple skin and white, very tender flesh with minimal seeds and virtually no bitterness — the thin skin makes Orient Express excellent for eating with skin on in stir-fries, Japanese-style preparations (nasu dengaku — miso-glazed grilled eggplant), grilling, and dishes where the skin texture would be noticeable in a thick-skinned globe eggplant. The early maturity is particularly valuable for Gulf Coast and Southern gardeners who want to get the eggplant harvest in before peak summer heat reduces fruit set, and for northern gardeners who need production in 60–70 days rather than 80–90 days. Highly productive — a well-grown plant can produce 6–10 fruits at once — and the early season timing allows for multiple successive harvests.

common_name: Orient Wonder Pole Yard Long Bean
plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; loves heat and humidity.
directions: Also called Chinese long beans, this dark green pole variety produces smooth, slender pods that stay tender because the seeds develop slowly. It tolerates weather swings from cool and dry to hot and humid better than common beans. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis for the vigorous vines. Harvest pods young at 12 to 18 inches, picking often to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost, or start a fall crop in mid to late summer since Orion resists bolting better in longer days than older Florence types.
directions: Orion is a hybrid Florence fennel selected for improved bolt resistance and uniform, rounded bulb formation, making it more reliable than open-pollinated types for both spring and fall sowings. Bulbs develop a tight, flattened-round shape with tender, sweetly anise-flavored flesh and stay in good condition in the field longer than older cultivars before splitting or flowering. Give it consistent moisture and full sun to encourage smooth, well-formed bulbs, and harvest promptly once bulbs reach baseball to tennis-ball size. Gardeners who have struggled with fennel bolting in variable spring weather choose Orion for its dependability across a wider sowing window.

plant_note: Plant certified slips after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65F in well-drained, loamy soil in full sun; Orleans is an LSU AgCenter release bred as a higher-yielding, more disease-resistant alternative to Beauregard for Gulf South growers.
directions: Plant certified sweet potato slips after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Orleans is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release developed as a modernized alternative to the industry-standard Beauregard, bred for higher yields, improved resistance to soil-borne diseases, and a slightly longer storage life after curing. Skin and flesh are both a rich orange, with smooth, uniformly shaped roots that store and cure well. Like all sweet potatoes, newly dug roots are starchy rather than sweet; cure at 85-90F and 85-90% humidity for 5-7 days to heal skin wounds and convert starches into the sugars that give sweet potatoes their characteristic flavor. Plant certified, virus-indexed slips rather than home-grown slips from grocery-store roots to avoid introducing sweet potato virus disease, which reduces yield over successive seasons. Well suited to Louisiana's long, humid growing season and heavy summer rainfall.

common_name: Ormskirk Late Cabbage (Lancashire Winter Savoy Cabbage)
plant_note: Start seed in late summer for transplanting out for a winter harvest, or start in early spring for fall harvest; Ormskirk Late is a very cold-hardy Savoy-type winter cabbage from Lancashire, England.
directions: Start seed in a nursery bed or trays and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, timing planting so heads mature through the cool season. Ormskirk Late is a traditional Savoy-type winter cabbage bred in the town of Ormskirk in Lancashire, England, valued for its deeply crinkled, dark blue-green leaves and dense, sweet-flavored heads that improve in flavor after exposure to frost, and for standing in the garden through hard winter weather without splitting. It is well suited to a long, cool fall-to-winter growing season in mild climates like the Gulf South. Harvest heads once firm, cutting at the base and leaving the outer wrapper leaves in the garden.

plant_note: Start mid to late summer for fall and winter color; frost intensifies the hues.
directions: Ornamental kale, a flowering cabbage, forms compact rosettes of frilly leaves in pink, purple, cream, and white that light up cool-season beds and containers. Start seed in mid to late summer so plants color up as temperatures drop, since the vivid hues develop with cold. Give full sun and steady moisture for full, dense rosettes. Frost only deepens the color, making this a standout for fall and winter displays; the leaves are edible but grown mainly for looks.
