In the bird-feeding context, black oil sunflower seeds (Peredovik or similar black-seeded varieties) are universally recommended as the premier wild bird food: the thin, easy-to-crack shell is accessible to a wider range of small songbirds than the thick-shelled striped types, and the high oil content provides superior energy density for birds — particularly important for overwintering and migratory species. For wildlife food plots in the Gulf South, Peredovik-type black oil sunflower is one of the primary dove and songbird attractants planted specifically for the September-October dove season. The seeds are also excellent for human consumption (roasting, pressing for oil) though small in size.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out divisions after last frost in sandy, saline, or coastal soil; unlike annual Salicornia, perennial glasswort forms a persistent woody base and returns year after year, spreading slowly to form a low mat in salt marsh or brackish garden conditions.
directions: Sow seed or plant divisions in sandy, well-drained, saline to brackish soil in full sun; perennial glasswort is a close relative of annual Salicornia, sharing the same leafless, jointed, succulent green stems and briny, oceanic flavor prized as 'sea beans' or samphire in gourmet cooking, but distinguished by its perennial habit — the base of the plant becomes woody and persists through winter, resprouting fleshy new stems each spring rather than dying back to seed like annual glasswort. This makes it a useful low, spreading edible groundcover for a genuinely saline coastal garden bed, salt marsh restoration planting, or tide-edge landscape where few other edible plants survive, and once established it slowly forms a dense, low mat rather than requiring reseeding each year. Harvest the tender young stem tips through the growing season with scissors, leaving the tougher, woodier base intact to keep producing; flavor and texture are best on actively growing spring and early summer growth before stems begin to harden. Like its annual cousin, it tolerates direct seawater irrigation and thrives in salinity that would kill ordinary vegetables.

common_name: Perkins Long Pod Okra (Classic Tall Southern Heirloom Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); Perkins Long Pod is a classic tall Southern heirloom okra and the parent line behind later spineless Perkins selections.
directions: Soak seed overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F. Perkins Long Pod is a traditional Southern heirloom okra grown for generations before the spineless Perkins strains were selected from it, producing heavy yields of long, ribbed, dark green pods on tall, vigorous plants that can reach 6 feet or more by season's end. Harvest pods every two to three days at 2-4 inches long for the most tender eating, since larger pods quickly turn woody and fibrous; regular picking keeps the plant producing continuously through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer. Stake or support plants in windy sites, and remove any overgrown pods promptly to keep new flowers and pods coming.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Perkins Mammoth Long Pod is an 1890s heirloom okra that produces very long (up to 8–10 inch), slightly ridged, green pods with outstanding flavor and a notably long harvest window before pods become tough — a longtime favorite in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is warm; soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Perkins Mammoth Long Pod is an heirloom okra variety introduced in the 1890s that produces exceptionally long (6–10 inch) ribbed green pods with a more tender quality at larger sizes than most okra varieties — meaning the pods remain acceptable for eating somewhat longer than standard varieties, which quickly become fibrous and tough once they exceed 3–4 inches. The plants are vigorous (5–8 feet), highly productive, and heat-tolerant, performing well throughout the Gulf Coast and Deep South. Harvest pods at 4–6 inches for optimal tenderness; though the pods can be eaten somewhat larger, regular harvesting every 1–2 days in hot weather is essential to keep production high — missed pods left on the plant stop production quickly.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; the biennial keeps producing into fall.
directions: Perpetual spinach is actually a leaf chard grown for tender, mild leaves that eat like true spinach but far more heat- and bolt-resistant. As a cut-and-come-again crop it produces for months, and being biennial it can carry over for a second season in mild areas. Direct sow in spring in full sun to partial shade and keep evenly watered. Harvest outer leaves regularly and the plant will keep pushing out new growth well into fall.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall and winter crop in zone 9; unlike true spinach, this leaf beet resists bolting through summer heat while still tasting spinach-like.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Perpetual Spinach is an old English strain of leaf beet grown specifically as a heat- and bolt-resistant substitute for true spinach, with smaller, smoother, thinner-stalked leaves than standard Swiss chard and a milder, more spinach-like flavor when cooked. Unlike true spinach, which bolts quickly in warm weather, this leaf beet keeps producing tender new leaves through much of the growing season, giving gardeners a reliable spinach-flavored green across a far longer window. Harvest outer leaves continuously as needed, leaving the growing center intact, and expect the plant to keep cropping for months with regular cutting.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost; keeps producing through the season.
directions: Despite its name this thin-ribbed Italian heirloom is a Swiss chard grown for its tender, spinach-like leaves, and it is slow to bolt in hot weather. Sow directly and thin seedlings, then harvest outer leaves regularly so the plant keeps producing new growth for months. Keep the soil evenly moist and feed occasionally for lush leaves. It tolerates both spring and fall conditions and mild frost.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Persian melon is a large-fruited, heavily netted muskmelon type popular in California and the American West, producing large (8–15 lb), round, deeply netted, fragrant fruits with deep salmon-orange flesh of excellent sweetness — one of the standard commercial and home-garden melons for hot, dry Western climates.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Persian melon requires hot, dry conditions for best sweetness and is most successful in California, Arizona, Texas, and Gulf Coast gardens. Persian melon is a large-fruited, heavily netted muskmelon of Middle Eastern origin that became a California commercial standard in the early 20th century; the large (8–15 lb), round to slightly oval fruits have a thick layer of fine, closely woven gray-green netting over dark green skin that transitions to golden-green at maturity, with deeply aromatic, thick, deep salmon-orange flesh with a rich, spicy sweetness. Persian melon is rounder and larger than cantaloupes and has thicker, denser flesh with a more pronounced, spicy aromatic complexity than American cantaloupe types. It requires a longer season (90–100 days) and performs best in hot, dry conditions; California's Central and Imperial Valleys have historically produced most commercial Persian melons sold in Western markets. The thick rind and firm flesh give Persian melon better shipping quality than more delicate muskmelon types, and it stores 1–2 weeks refrigerated after harvest.

common_name: Persian Star Hardneck Garlic (Marbled Purple Stripe, Samarkand Heritage)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 4–6 weeks before first frost in fall; Persian Star is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic collected in Samarkand, Uzbekistan (the historic Silk Road city) by John Swenson for the Seed Savers Exchange in 1989 — it produces strikingly beautiful bulbs with vivid violet-purple inner clove skins and a rich, earthy, complex flavor characteristic of the Marbled Purple Stripe type.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch after planting; keep weed-free and consistently moist in spring; remove scapes when they curl; harvest in early to midsummer when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure in a warm, dry, airy location. Persian Star is a Marbled Purple Stripe-type hardneck garlic with a remarkable provenance: it was collected in Samarkand, Uzbekistan — the ancient Silk Road city at the crossroads of Central Asia — by John Swenson, a garlic enthusiast and Seed Savers Exchange member who traveled to the former Soviet Union in 1989 collecting traditional garlic varieties grown in the region for centuries. The provenance from Samarkand, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and a center of Central Asian agricultural tradition, gives Persian Star historical and botanical significance as a window into the genetic diversity of garlic in its center of diversity (Central Asia is believed to be the region where cultivated garlic first developed). The bulbs are 2–3 inches across with 8–12 cloves; the outer skin is white with subtle purple striping typical of the Marbled Purple Stripe group, while the inner clove skins are often vivid violet-purple — beautiful when peeled. The flavor is rich, earthy, moderately pungent, and complex — slightly different from Rocambole types with a distinctive minerality. Storage life is better than Rocambole (5–7 months) but less than softneck types.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; a large, golden-orange beefsteak heirloom with very low acid and sweet, fruity flavor — an excellent choice for gardeners who want an orange type that ripens reliably in hot summer conditions.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem deeply and staking or caging firmly. Persimmon is a Ukrainian heirloom beefsteak tomato with fruit that resembles the color of a ripe persimmon — vivid golden-orange — with very meaty flesh, a small seed cavity, extraordinarily sweet, low-acid, fruity flavor, and fruits weighing 10–16 ounces; it is among the finest-tasting orange or golden beefsteak heirlooms and has been prized by serious tomato growers since its introduction through Seed Savers Exchange. The vigorous indeterminate vines produce steadily through the season; stake firmly and maintain consistent moisture to prevent blossom-end rot. Harvest when fruits are fully colored and yield slightly to pressure at the blossom end.

common_name: Perth Pride Tomato (Australian-Bred Red Beefsteak Dwarf Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Perth Pride is an Australian-bred Dwarf Tomato Project release producing red beefsteak-type fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Perth Pride, developed through the Australian arm of the international Dwarf Tomato Project, bears deep red, beefsteak-style fruit with good, rich flavor on a compact plant, combining full-size tomato quality with a footprint suited to small gardens and containers. It reflects the collaborative, worldwide nature of the Dwarf Tomato Project breeding effort. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost, since this bush-type dry bean, like most common beans, resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination.
directions: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost, since this bush-type dry bean, like most common beans, resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination. Also sold as Mayocoba or canary bean, Peruano is a pale golden-yellow bean central to everyday Mexican and Mexican-American cooking, valued for a creamy texture and mild flavor that holds up well in refried preparations. The compact bush habit needs no staking and produces a concentrated harvest suited to home drying. Let pods mature fully and dry on the plant before shelling, then store the beans in a cool, dry, airtight container.

common_name: Peruvian Purple Pepper (Ornamental Edible Hot Pepper with Purple Foliage and Upright Fruits)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Peruvian Purple is a compact ornamental edible pepper (18–24 inches) with distinctive deep purple-black foliage, purple stems, and small upright fruits (1.5–2 inches) that mature from purple-black through a transitional stage to vivid red. The purple pigmentation in both foliage and immature fruits results from anthocyanin accumulation triggered by light exposure, making it one of the most visually striking ornamental peppers available. Heat level is high (estimated 50,000–80,000 SHU), reflecting the small fruit size typical of high-heat Capsicum annuum types. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the compact habit makes it excellent for containers and ornamental mixed plantings where edible and decorative plants are combined.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun and harvest fruits at any stage from purple-black (immature, high heat) to fully red (ripe). Peruvian Purple Pepper is a compact ornamental-edible hot pepper variety distinguished by its unusual anthocyanin-rich foliage — a deep purple-black that makes the plant visually dramatic from seedling stage through maturity. The purple coloration in the leaves and immature fruits results from anthocyanin pigments produced in response to high light intensity; the same plant grown in reduced light will show less purple coloration and more green foliage, making sun exposure a direct visible factor in the plant's ornamental effect. Fruits emerge deep purple-black and upright — pointing skyward rather than pendant — which is a characteristic of many small ornamental hot pepper types and adds visual interest as the small fruits are held prominently above the purple foliage. As fruits ripen to full maturity they transition through a mottled purple-and-red stage before reaching solid vivid red; many gardeners harvest throughout this color progression since the flavor and heat level remain high at all stages. The heat level is substantial for a Capsicum annuum variety — comparable to Thai or bird's eye types — and is proportional to the small fruit size, as capsaicin concentration tends to increase as fruit diameter decreases within the species. Culinary uses mirror those of other small hot peppers: used fresh in salads, salsas, and stir-fries; pickled; or dried whole for later use. As a compact container plant with dramatic foliage, Peruvian Purple also functions effectively as a purely ornamental annual in mixed containers where its purple leaves provide contrast against chartreuse, silver, or deep green companions.

common_name: Petai (Stink Bean, Bitter Bean, Twisted Cluster Bean)
plant_note: Plant container-grown seedlings in well-drained, deep, fertile, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; petai is a tall tropical legume tree that requires many years to fruit — it is rarely grown outside of its native Southeast Asian range except in southern Florida, the Caribbean, and similar frost-free climates.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free tropical conditions; petai requires a long growing season with warm temperatures year-round. Parkia speciosa (petai or stink bean) is a large, tropical legume tree of Southeast Asia producing distinctive, long (12–18 inch), flat, twisted seed pods containing 10–18 large, flat, bright-green seeds with an intensely pungent, sulfurous odor (similar to but stronger than garlic and fenugreek combined) that is a celebrated ingredient in Malaysian, Indonesian, and Thai cooking. The seeds are eaten raw, stir-fried with shrimp, added to curries and sambals, or mixed with garlic, chili, and shrimp paste — those accustomed to the flavor consider it a prized delicacy despite (or because of) its extreme pungency. Like asparagus with certain compounds, petai causes urine to smell strongly of its sulfurous compounds for several hours after eating — considered a normal, if somewhat inconvenient, effect. The tree is a nitrogen-fixer (fixing atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules) and has been used in agroforestry systems throughout Malaysia and Indonesia. Rarely available in the continental US except in specialty tropical fruit nurseries.

common_name: Peter Pan Pattypan Squash (AAS-Winning Green Scallop Summer Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Peter Pan is a bush-type pattypan suitable for smaller gardens than vining summer squash. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August for fall harvest. Harvest at 3–4 inches diameter for best flavor and texture — pattypan squash becomes seedy and watery if allowed to grow much beyond 4–5 inches. The scalloped edges that give pattypan its distinctive star or UFO shape become more pronounced and decorative as fruits approach full harvest size.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost; harvest fruits at 3–4 inches diameter for best eating quality. Peter Pan is a 1982 All-America Selections-winning pattypan (scallop) summer squash — an early-maturing, bush-habit variety producing pale green, disc-shaped fruits with the characteristic scalloped, fluted edges of the pattypan type. The distinctive flat, disc-like shape with scalloped margins distinguishes pattypan squash from all other summer squash types (zucchini, yellow crookneck, yellow straightneck) and has no equivalent in other vegetable categories — the shape makes individual fruits look like tiny flying saucers or UFOs and creates an unusually attractive presentation on the plate when halved or stuffed whole. Peter Pan's light green color is gentler and less common than the white pattypans that dominated before its introduction. The flavor is mild and slightly sweet — similar to other summer squash but with a distinctive nuttiness that develops in the scallop varieties at the ideal 3–4 inch harvest size. The bush habit (24–36 inch spread vs. the 6–8 foot spread of vining squash) makes Peter Pan practical for smaller raised beds and gardens.

common_name: Peter Pan Squash (AAS-Winning Pale Green Scallop Squash, Early and Compact)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Peter Pan is a scallop (pattypan) squash that produces pale sage-green to silvery-green flat, scallop-edged fruits on a compact bush plant. In zone 9, plant March–May and August–September for fall production. Harvest Peter Pan at 3–4 inches when the skin is still tender and the green color is uniform and pale — the skin toughens significantly if the squash is left to grow beyond 4–5 inches. The distinctive pale green-grey color (lighter than most green summer squash) and scalloped edge make Peter Pan one of the most immediately recognizable summer squash varieties at harvest. The flavor is mild and nutty, somewhat different from zucchini in a pleasant way — scallop types have a slightly different flesh texture and a subtly nuttier quality that distinguishes them from elongated zucchini types.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when pale sage-green and tender. Peter Pan Squash is an All-America Selections (AAS) winner in the summer squash category, honored for its early production, compact plant habit, and the distinctive pale sage-green to silvery-blue-green color of the scallop-shaped fruits. The AAS recognition confirmed Peter Pan's performance advantage over other scallop squash varieties of its time in trials across multiple growing regions and climates. The scallop squash form — a flat, disc-shaped fruit with distinctively scalloped or fluted edges — is one of the oldest American summer squash forms, with historical precedent in both Native American cultivation and early colonial American gardens. Peter Pan's F1 hybrid vigor contributes to both its compactness (more manageable plant than many bush zucchini) and productivity (abundant fruit set throughout the season). The color is a notable characteristic: the pale, muted sage-green to silvery green of Peter Pan is unlike the darker green of standard zucchini or the yellow of Sunburst, occupying its own distinctive color space that many gardeners find attractive for mixed variety plantings and market displays where color diversity is valued. The flat scallop form also makes Peter Pan an exceptionally attractive stuffed squash: the naturally hollow interior of the scallop form (relative to the solid flesh core of zucchini) allows more filling capacity per fruit when halved for stuffing, and the shallow depth of the squash makes even cooking possible at the small sizes most suitable for stuffing preparations.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat; transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the danger of frost has fully passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; stake taller plants if heavily loaded with fruit. Peter Pepper is a well-known Southern heirloom hot pepper, famous for its unmistakably novelty shape, which has made it a popular curiosity and conversation piece for generations of home gardeners across Texas and Louisiana. The medium-heat fruits (roughly 10,000–25,000 Scoville units, comparable to a strong jalapeño or mild cayenne) ripen from green to red and carry a fruity, tangy flavor good in salsas, pickling, and hot sauce once the novelty value has been enjoyed. Plants are productive and reasonably compact, performing well in containers as well as garden beds, and the fruit's thick walls hold up nicely to stuffing or pickling whole. A fun, genuinely productive heirloom for gardeners who want something distinctive alongside their standard pepper lineup, in zone 4–11.

common_name: Petit Gris de Rennes Melon (French Heirloom Gray-Green Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Petit Gris de Rennes is a French muskmelon type that requires warmer growing conditions than some European varieties — it performs well in the Gulf South's warm summer climate but needs protection from excessive humidity that can cause Alternaria blight. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest. The 'Petit Gris' (little gray) refers to the grayish-green skin when fully ripe.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; maintain consistent moisture during vine development and reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity. Harvest when the skin transitions from green to gray-green (the characteristic 'petit gris' color) and the stem cracks slightly at the base — this muskmelon type does not 'slip' from the vine like American cantaloupes but has a less decisive harvest cue. Petit Gris de Rennes (small gray of Rennes) is a traditional French muskmelon heirloom from Brittany, the coastal region of northwestern France, where it has been grown for centuries as the area's distinctive local melon. In France, Petit Gris de Rennes has Slow Food Ark of Taste recognition as a threatened traditional variety of significant cultural importance. The small to medium (1–2 lb) round fruits are distinguished by their unusual grayish-green to slate-green skin coloration with shallow ribs and fine, irregular netting — a very different appearance from the tan-netted American cantaloupe standard. The deeply orange, firm-textured, extremely sweet and aromatic flesh has a rich, complex character that many tasters consider superior to standard Western cantaloupe types — more complex in flavor, with floral and spicy notes beyond simple sweetness. Petit Gris de Rennes represents the French horticultural tradition of flavor breeding, where appearance is secondary to eating quality, and is a fascinating variety for gardeners interested in growing traditional European melon types beyond the standard muskmelon.

common_name: Petite Treat Watermelon (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Seedless Melon)
plant_note: Start seed indoors and transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; as a seedless triploid, Petite Treat needs a nearby seeded watermelon variety planted for pollen to set fruit properly.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply pollen for this seedless triploid to set fruit. Petite Treat is an All-America Selections winner bred for genuinely personal-sized fruit, producing round melons small enough for one or two people to finish in a single sitting, with sweet, crisp, deep red, seedless flesh and a thin rind. The compact vine takes up less garden space than standard large-fruited watermelon varieties, and the smaller fruit size means a shorter time from pollination to harvest-ready ripeness. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries and the ground spot beneath the fruit turns creamy yellow, the most reliable ripeness indicators for seedless types.

plant_note: Sow direct in late summer for a fall crop, since cool weather brings out its characteristically sweet, mild flavor.
directions: A Central/Eastern European heirloom turnip grown historically in Poland and Russia for its round, golden-skinned roots with pale yellow flesh, a distinct look and flavor compared to the purple-top white types common in American gardens. It was traditionally valued for dual use as both a table vegetable and livestock forage. Sow direct in late summer for a fall crop, since cool weather brings out its characteristically sweet, mild flavor and reduces the sharper bite common in summer-grown turnips.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, moist soil; in zone 9–11 sow year-round as a perennial, cutting plants back periodically to encourage fresh tender growth.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in warm, moist soil; talinum is an exceptionally heat-tolerant tropical leafy vegetable used across West Africa, the Caribbean, and Southeast Asia as a spinach substitute that thrives in hot weather that destroys most other greens. The thick, succulent leaves and stems cook quickly and have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to purslane. Harvest by cutting stem tips with young leaves regularly; plants regenerate vigorously from the base. In zones 9–11 it becomes a woody perennial subshrub 2–3 feet tall; cut back to 6 inches periodically to keep growth tender. Very drought-tolerant once established and requires little fertilizer. Also known as Lagos spinach and waterleaf.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Phoenix continues setting fruit through the high daytime and nighttime temperatures of a Gulf South summer that cause blossom drop in most other tomato varieties.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage for support; consistent watering reduces blossom end rot in humid conditions. Phoenix is a tomato variety developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife vegetable breeding program specifically to keep setting fruit through the extreme heat of a Texas and Gulf South summer, when night temperatures above 75°F cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in most standard varieties. The medium-sized, firm, deep red globe fruits also carry useful resistance to common soilborne diseases and cracking, and the vines continue producing through the hottest stretch of summer that typically causes a production gap in southern tomato gardens. It also carries a degree of protection against sunscald thanks to good foliage cover. A dependable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want tomatoes to keep coming through July and August rather than stalling out, in zone 4–11.

common_name: Pick a Bushel Cucumber (AAS-Winning Compact Bush Pickling Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Pick a Bushel is a compact, semi-bush pickling cucumber bred for container and small-space growing, needing far less room than vining pickling types.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container with a small trellis. Pick a Bushel is an AAS-winning pickling cucumber bred for a genuinely compact semi-bush habit, producing full-size yields of crisp, uniform, 3-5 inch pickling cukes on a plant small enough for patios, raised beds, and tight garden spaces where a standard vining pickler would sprawl out of bounds. It bears heavily and continuously over a relatively short, concentrated season, ideal for gardeners who want a big pickling harvest all at once for a canning batch. Pick fruit at the size wanted for the pickle style being made — small gherkins to full-size dills — and harvest every day or two once fruiting begins, since oversized cucumbers slow down further production. Keep soil evenly moist, especially as fruit is sizing, to avoid bitter or misshapen cucumbers.

common_name: Pickle Bush Cucumber (Compact Bush-Habit Pickling Cucumber for Small Spaces)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pickle Bush's compact, bush-habit vines (18–24 inch spread) make it excellent for raised beds and container growing — no trellis required and the plants are self-supporting.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pickle Bush is a bush-type pickling cucumber producing compact, self-supporting vines 18–24 inches across rather than the sprawling 4–6 foot vines of standard pickling cucumbers — making it the preferred choice for raised beds, containers, and small gardens where trellises are impractical and space is limited. The short (3–4 inch), blocky, warted, pickling-type cucumbers mature very early (48–55 days) in prolific clusters that concentrate harvest in a short window ideal for batch processing and canning. Pickling cucumbers are specifically bred for thin, tender skin that absorbs brine quickly, mild-to-bland flavor that allows pickle seasonings to dominate, and firm flesh that maintains crunchiness through the pickling process — qualities that distinguish them from slicing cucumbers in important culinary ways. In zone 9, the very early maturity (48–55 days) of Pickle Bush is a practical advantage — it completes its production cycle before summer heat drives cucumbers into bitter, poor-quality fruit stage. The bush habit allows high-density planting in raised beds (18 inches apart) compared to the 3–4 foot spacing required for trellised vining types. AAS Honorable Mention recognized Pickle Bush's outstanding performance in the small-space home garden category.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills or rows 1–2 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; pickling cucumbers are typically bush or short-vine types that produce prolifically over a short concentrated harvest period suited to batch pickling.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun 1–2 weeks after last frost, thinning to 12–18 inches apart; pickling varieties such as National Pickling, Calypso, and Boston Pickling bear shorter, blockier, thinner-skinned fruits than slicing types and set fruit more uniformly over a compressed harvest window — ideal for making dill pickles and bread-and-butter chips in a single session. Harvest at 2–4 inches for gherkins, 4–5 inches for standard dills; leaving even one overripe fruit on the vine significantly slows further production. Keep soil evenly moist — irregular watering causes bitter fruits. Succession-plant every 3 weeks for a season-long supply.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out transplants after the last frost in warm soil, providing a trellis to keep fruit straight; Picolino is a parthenocarpic mini cucumber bred to set seedless fruit without pollination.
directions: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed, training vines onto a trellis or cage for straighter, cleaner fruit. Picolino is a parthenocarpic mini cucumber, meaning it reliably sets thin-skinned, seedless, 3-4 inch fruit without needing pollinator activity, making it dependable even in low-bee conditions or under row cover. The skin is tender enough to eat without peeling and the flavor is mild and non-bitter, making it a popular choice for lunchbox snacking and pickling whole. Because fruit sizes up quickly, plants need picking every day or two at peak season to prevent cucumbers from overgrowing and to keep the vine setting new fruit.

common_name: Piel de Sapo Melon (Spanish Toad-Skin Winter Melon)
scientific_name: Cucumis melo var. inodorus 'Piel de Sapo'
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the soil is thoroughly warm; Piel de Sapo needs a long, hot growing season to fully sweeten, making it a strong fit for the extended Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room or a sturdy trellis with slings to support the heavy fruit. Piel de Sapo, meaning 'toad skin' in Spanish, is a classic Spanish winter melon named for its distinctive mottled dark and pale green rind, an oblong fruit that hides sweet, crisp, pale green-white flesh with a mild, delicate flavor. Unlike musky cantaloupe types, this inodorus-group melon develops little to no aroma at the stem even when fully ripe, so growers judge readiness by days from planting, a slight softening at the blossom end, and a duller rind color rather than by scent, and the fruit also stores notably longer after harvest than most melons. Water deeply but infrequently once fruit begins sizing up, and reduce watering in the final week or two before harvest to concentrate sugars.

common_name: Piennolo del Vesuvio Tomato (Vesuvius Hanging Cluster Storage Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Piennolo del Vesuvio is a traditional small red cherry-type tomato grown on the volcanic slopes of Mount Vesuvius near Naples, prized for its thick skin and long storage life.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Piennolo del Vesuvio is a traditional small, oval red tomato grown for centuries on the mineral-rich volcanic soils of the Mount Vesuvius region near Naples, its thick skin and low water content allowing whole trusses to be hung in bunches ('piennoli') and stored through winter without refrigeration, slowly concentrating in flavor as they cure. The tangy, intensely tomato flavor makes it prized in Neapolitan cooking, especially for a quick, bright sauce. Harvest whole clusters when fully colored and hang them in a cool, airy spot to store, checking periodically and using fruit as it continues to ripen.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65°F; in zone 9–12 pigeon pea grows as a short-lived perennial woody shrub and may produce pods for 2–5 years before needing replacement. In cooler zones grow as an annual and start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, low-fertility soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; pigeon pea is a deep-rooted, drought-tolerant shrubby legume that is one of the world's most important tropical food crops — the yellow, green, or red seeds (arhar dal, toor dal) are a dietary staple across the Caribbean, South Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa, used in dals, stews, rice dishes, and soups. The plants fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules and thrive in poor soils without supplemental fertilizer; overly rich or wet soils reduce pod production. Harvest green pods when plump for fresh use or allow to fully dry on the plant for dried dal; in zone 9–12 plants become woody perennial shrubs and will continue producing pods for several years if pruned back hard after the main harvest to stimulate new growth. In zone 8 and below, grow as a warm-season annual and expect a single late-season harvest.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall in partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist woodland or hedgerow soil in zone 5–9; Pignut (Earth Chestnut, Earthnut) is a slender, delicate, native British and European woodland herb — once eaten by children and common folk throughout Britain for its small, brown-skinned, sweet, nutty-flavored underground tubers — bearing finely divided, carrot-family foliage in hedgerows, meadows, and oak and beech woodland understories, and an important food plant for dormice, wild boar, and other woodland wildlife.
directions: Sow Conopodium majus seeds in fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; plants are slow to establish and the small underground tubers take 2–3 years to reach harvestable size; avoid disturbing the soil around plants once growing; harvest small tubers with a trowel in summer as foliage dies back. Pignut is one of the most charming native edibles of British and European woodlands — a slender, graceful plant of meadows, hedgerows, and open woodland that has been gathered for its sweet, nut-flavored tubers by country people for centuries. The small, round to irregularly shaped tubers (technically a corm-like swelling of the underground stem) are covered in brown skin and have cream-colored, very sweet, crunchy flesh with a flavor reminiscent of sweet chestnut or hazelnut — edible raw or cooked. Foragers prize them but they are difficult to dig without following the thin, brittle stem underground without breaking it (hence their reputation for elusiveness). Wild populations are protected in Britain, but cultivation from seed is permitted and encouraged for those wishing to grow them. The plant is an important food source for dormice, wild boar, and other wildlife in European woodland ecosystems. A genuinely rare and unusual woodland garden plant with culinary value and strong ecological connections.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and transplant to fertile, well-drained garden soil once the risk of frost has fully passed. The heart-shaped, thick-walled fruits ripen from green to deep red and are sweeter and more aromatic than most bell peppers, with a rich, almost spicy fragrance that is distinct to the type. Harvest at full red for fresh use, or roast and peel for preserving in oil — pimento is the classic stuffing for green olives. High yields from compact plants make this a productive choice for containers or small beds.

common_name: Pimiento Pepper (Classic Sweet Thick-Walled Pimento Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Pimiento is the traditional variety for making pimiento cheese — the classic Southern spread requiring the specific thick-walled, sweet, very mild flesh of the true pimiento variety.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Pimiento (also spelled pimento) is the traditional thick-walled sweet pepper of Spanish and Southern American tradition — producing heart-shaped to rounded, medium-sized (3–4 inches) fruits with exceptionally thick, sweet, juicy walls and very mild, sweet flavor with no heat. The thick walls and very sweet, low-acid flesh are the defining qualities that distinguish pimiento from other sweet peppers: the wall thickness (often twice that of standard bell peppers) makes pimiento ideal for roasting, stuffing, and jar-packing, while the sweetness and mildness make it the original pepper for stuffed olives and the authentic ingredient in Southern pimiento cheese. The fruits ripen from green to a deep, vivid red and are at their best flavor when fully red. Pimiento is less commonly found in grocery stores than bell peppers (most commercial pimiento production goes to food processing), making it a particularly worthwhile home garden variety for cooks who want the authentic ingredient. The plants are productive, compact, and well-adapted to Gulf South growing conditions. In zone 9, pimiento peppers have two productive seasons: spring planting (February–March transplant, harvest May–July) and fall planting (August transplant, harvest October–November). The rich red color and exceptional thick-walled quality make pimiento one of the finest peppers for roasting whole.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Pineapple ground cherry is a named selection of the cape gooseberry type with especially sweet, intensely tropical pineapple-vanilla flavor in small, papery-husked fruits that drop from the plant when ripe — an extraordinary, underused fruit for snacking, baking, and preserves.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Pineapple Ground Cherry is a named selection of the ground cherry (Physalis pruinosa) grown for its small (1/2–3/4 inch), golden-yellow fruits enclosed in dry, papery, tan husks (lantern-like husks much smaller than tomatillo husks) with an intensely sweet, tropical flavor reminiscent of pineapple, vanilla, and caramel — completely unlike tomatillos in flavor despite being related. The fruits drop from the plant when fully ripe and are gathered from the ground (hence the name); this drop-when-ripe characteristic is the easiest ripeness indicator. Extraordinarily productive in warm weather, with hundreds of fruits per plant. Delicious eaten fresh, in pies (often compared to cape gooseberry pies), in jams, and dried like raisins. A charming and unusual fruit for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens that is barely known to most gardeners.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost when soil is warm.
directions: This high-yielding beefsteak ripens to yellow-orange marbled with red streaks running through the meaty, low-acid flesh. Being indeterminate, the vines grow tall and need strong staking or caging. Start seeds indoors, transplant into warm soil, and water consistently to reduce cracking on the large fruit. Prune suckers lightly to boost airflow and support ripening of these big tomatoes.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring and July for fall. Tomatillos require at least two plants from different seed sources for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set; plant Pineapple Tomatillo alongside a green-fruiting type for maximum production. The papery husk turns tan and splits as fruits mature to gold-yellow.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pineapple Tomatillo is a named selection of Physalis ixocarpa that ripens to a distinctive golden-yellow rather than the standard tomatillo green, with a noticeably sweeter, more tropical flavor that includes a pineapple-like brightness absent from green-fruiting types. The medium-sized fruits, typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter, fill and split the papery husk as they ripen to gold, at which point they are at peak sweetness. The sweeter profile makes Pineapple Tomatillo less acidic than standard green tomatillos and more suitable for fresh eating out of hand, in fruit salsas, or in preparations where a less tart tomatillo flavor is desired. Standard green tomatillos provide better classic salsa verde acidity; Pineapple works best where a milder, sweeter, more unusual tomatillo experience is the goal. Like all tomatillos, plant at least two individuals for cross-pollination.

common_name: Pineapple Tomato (Giant Bicolor Yellow-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Pineapple produces very large fruits that take significant time to develop — start seeds early to maximize the harvest window before summer heat causes fruit quality to decline.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Pineapple is one of the most visually spectacular heirloom beefsteak tomatoes — producing enormous (1–2 lb), irregular, slightly ribbed fruits with a stunning bicolor pattern of golden-yellow base skin marked with bold red and orange streaking and marbling that creates a stained-glass appearance when sliced. The cut surface reveals a similarly bicolor red-and-yellow flesh pattern — an ornamental quality that makes Pineapple outstanding for fresh salads and sliced presentations where the visual effect can be appreciated. The flavor matches the visual quality: intensely sweet, fruity, and complex with a low-acid, tropical quality that justifies the variety's evocative name — the combination of golden-yellow color and sweet, fruity flavor genuinely suggests tropical fruit. Large, vigorous indeterminate plants require sturdy support (minimum 6-foot cage or stake). As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved from the most characteristic fruits for replanting. In zone 9, Pineapple produces best in the spring season (March–June) before summer heat arrives; the very large fruits require a relatively long, cool growing period for maximum development.

common_name: Ping Tung Long Eggplant (Taiwanese Heirloom Slender Purple Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Ping Tung Long is a Taiwan heirloom adapted to hot, humid conditions, making it an excellent choice for Gulf South gardens. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer and fall harvest. Harvest fruits when 10–15 inches long and still deep lavender-purple before any brown coloration develops at the calyx. Plants benefit from staking when fruit load is heavy — the long fruits can cause branches to lean.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil. Harvest fruits when 10–15 inches and still vivid lavender-purple. Ping Tung Long (named for Pingtung County in southern Taiwan where it originates) is a Taiwanese heirloom eggplant representing the classic Asian long eggplant type at its finest — producing exceptionally long (12–16 inch), slender, slightly curved, vivid lavender-purple to violet fruits with thin, tender skin. The variety is among the most widely grown and highly regarded long Asian eggplants in Taiwan and throughout the Chinese-American gardening community in the United States, where it has been maintained as an open-pollinated heirloom for multiple generations. The fruits are characterized by extremely thin, tender skin (no peeling needed), virtually no seeds, and very sweet, mild flesh with no bitterness — a flavor profile considered superior for raw preparations and quick stir-fries where the tender skin softens immediately without extended cooking. The vivid lavender-purple color is particularly attractive in the garden and at the table. Ping Tung Long's heat tolerance and prolific production in hot conditions make it especially well-suited to southern gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; eggplant needs sustained warmth and benefits from bottom heat during germination. Transplant in zone 9 February–March for a long growing season; eggplant thrives in the heat and often continues producing through October–November.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pingtung Long is a Taiwanese heirloom eggplant that produces slender, 12–18 inch fruits in a vibrant lavender-purple, among the longest eggplant fruits available. The skin is exceptionally thin and tender with minimal bitterness, making it prized for quick stir-fries and grilling without peeling. Plants are productive and heat-tolerant, continuing to set fruit through the hot zone 9 summers when other eggplant varieties may pause. Harvest fruits young when skin is glossy and before seeds develop; overripe fruits become seedy and bitter. A heavy producer that may need light staking to support the long, heavy fruits.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after all frost danger.
directions: Pink Banana is a large heirloom winter squash producing elongated, pink-skinned fruits with sweet, tender orange flesh on vigorous vines that can run fifteen feet. The big fruits store well for months in a cool, dry place. Direct sow into warm, rich soil in full sun after frost, giving the sprawling vines plenty of space. Harvest when the rind hardens and skin turns pink, then cure the squash before storing.

common_name: Pink Berkeley Tie Dye Tomato (Marbled Pink-Green Striped Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Pink Berkeley Tie Dye is a modern open-pollinated variety related to the original green Berkeley Tie Dye, bred by Wild Boar Farms and prized for its striking exterior of pink and green streaks and blushes, which give way when sliced to a marbled, jewel-toned interior of pink, red, and gold swirled together in a genuinely tie-dye pattern. Beyond the visual novelty, the flavor is rich, sweet, and complex, ranking among the better-tasting of the modern striped 'tie dye' tomato series that has become popular with heirloom and specialty tomato growers. The indeterminate vine is productive over a long season; water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and harvest once the distinctive coloring fully develops.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Pink Brandywine is the original pink-fleshed Brandywine heirloom and the one that gave the variety its legendary reputation for flavor — the Sudduth strain and Platfoot strain are the two main true-breeding lineages, both producing large, pink, irregular fruits of extraordinary depth of flavor.
directions: Start indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before last frost; plant deeply after frost, burying 2/3 of the stem, and stake or cage immediately — Pink Brandywine produces tall, sprawling, potato-leaved vines that are challenging to support and slow to set fruit. Pink Brandywine (distinct from the yellow Brandywine and red Brandywine strains) is widely considered by heirloom tomato enthusiasts to be the definitive Brandywine — a large (12–24 oz), oblate to irregular, deep pink-skinned, pink-fleshed tomato with extraordinary, complex, sweet-rich flavor that lacks the sharp acidity of red tomatoes; many growers consider it the best-tasting tomato they have ever grown. The Sudduth and Platfoot strains (the two main documented lineages preserved by Seed Savers Exchange) are both potato-leaved (a genetic marker associated with the true Brandywine) and behave similarly in the garden. A notoriously slow, difficult, but rewarding grow — plants are late to mature and require long, warm seasons, but the fruit quality when conditions are right is unmatched.

common_name: Pink Eye Purple Hull Pea (Classic Gulf South Dual-Color Summer Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pink Eye Purple Hull peas are highly heat-tolerant — they thrive and produce abundantly in Gulf South summer heat that limits production of most other vegetables.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pink Eye Purple Hull is one of the most widely grown and deeply traditional southern pea varieties of the Gulf South — a semi-bush to vining type producing distinctive purple-hulled pods that make harvest timing and identification visually clear (green hulls shade to purple as the peas approach maturity), with cream-white peas marked by a distinctive pink to rose-colored 'eye' or hilum that gives the variety its evocative name. The pink eye is the identifying mark: when a pot of fresh-shelled Pink Eye Purple Hull peas is spread on the counter, the cream peas with their small pink-rose eye marks are immediately recognizable as this specific variety. The flavor is excellent — classic southern pea quality with a rich, earthy, beany sweetness that is characteristic of the Gulf South summer pea tradition. Pink Eye Purple Hull is extremely productive in Gulf South conditions, continuing to produce through summer heat that limits most other garden vegetables. It is among the most important vegetable crops of the traditional Gulf South summer garden, providing fresh food through July, August, and September when garden production from other crops has ended. Nitrogen-fixing root system improves soil. The purple hulls are ornamentally attractive in the garden and make identifying ripe pods easy and unambiguous.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces after soil has warmed slightly; as a late maincrop fingerling it needs the longest season of any common salad potato.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil, and be patient, since this is a true late-season variety and tubers will not fully knobble and size up until the last weeks of the growing season. Pink Fir Apple is a Victorian-era heirloom fingerling named for its long, narrow, knobbly tubers with pink-blushed skin and waxy, nutty, pale-yellow flesh that holds its shape beautifully when boiled whole. It remains a favorite of chefs and home cooks for cold potato salads because the dense waxy texture does not turn mealy or fall apart. Choose it over a modern fingerling hybrid when a genuinely old salad-potato flavor and the classic irregular fingerling shape are the goal.

common_name: Pink Lipstick Chard (Vivid Magenta-Stemmed Savoy Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date; in warm winter regions like the Gulf Coast also sow in fall for a winter harvest.
directions: Sow seed clusters directly into fertile soil and thin to final spacing, watering consistently to keep leaves tender through summer heat. Bred for its intensely saturated hot-pink stalks and veins, this selection stands out even among rainbow chard mixes and holds its color well after cooking. Its heavily crumpled, deep green leaves are produced over a long season, and repeated cutting encourages continued new growth from the crown.

common_name: Pink Passion Chard (Vivid Hot Pink Stem Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall and winter crop in zone 9; Pink Passion holds its bright stem color well through the cool season.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Passion is a modern chard cultivar bred for exceptionally vivid, saturated hot-pink stalks and midribs that stand out strongly against dark, glossy, savoyed green leaves, making it a favorite for ornamental edible plantings as well as the kitchen. Both leaves and stalks are edible with classic chard flavor, the leaves cooking down like spinach and the crisp, colorful stalks holding their hue reasonably well when sautéed or roasted. Harvest outer leaves continuously as needed, leaving the growing center intact, and expect strong production through the cool season with regular cutting.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant in February–March for a spring crop. Stake or cage heavily — Pink Ponderosa vines are tall (5–7 feet) and produce very large, heavy fruits that require solid support. In zone 9 a fall planting in August for October–November harvest often produces better-quality fruit with fewer cracks.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy staking; Pink Ponderosa (also called 'Henderson's Pink Ponderosa') is a late 19th-century American heirloom tomato introduced by the Henderson seed company around 1891, noted for producing enormous, beefsteak-type fruits of a distinctive deep rose-pink color — the 'pink' refers to the red flesh showing through the colorless (no yellow pigment in skin) skin, creating the characteristic pink-red appearance of traditional beefsteak-type heirlooms. The very large fruits (often 1–2 pounds each) are meaty, low-acid, and juicy with a mild, sweet, rich tomato flavor that made Ponderosa-type tomatoes the standard fresh-eating tomato for most of the 20th century before uniform-color commercial hybrids replaced them. The indeterminate vine produces continuously until frost and can be especially productive in zone 9's long growing season. The mild, low-acid flavor makes Pink Ponderosa particularly appealing for sliced tomatoes where the full fruit flavor is experienced without cooking.

plant_note: Direct sow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade as soon as soil can be worked in spring; pink purslane self-sows prolifically in suitable shaded, moist conditions and will naturalize to provide a self-replenishing supply of edible greens in the woodland garden.
directions: Direct sow in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade as soon as soil can be worked; pink purslane (Siberian miner's lettuce) is a small, delicate annual or biennial native to Siberia and the Pacific Coast of North America that produces a rosette of fleshy, pale-green, succulent leaves and distinctive stems that pierce directly through their paired leaves (perfoliate, like its American relative Claytonia perfoliata), topped with clusters of small, pink, five-petaled flowers in spring. All parts are edible — the tender leaves, stems, and flowers are mild, slightly succulent, and pleasant in salads. Unlike most salad greens, pink purslane grows enthusiastically in full shade and can be naturalized as a self-sowing edible groundcover in shaded woodland gardens and under deciduous trees, where it self-sows to provide a recurring supply of early spring greens. Goes to seed quickly in heat but will resow for fall crops.

common_name: Pinkeye Purple Hull Cowpea (Southern Pea, Purple Hull Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep, 3–4 inches apart in rows 24–36 inches apart after soil thoroughly warms to 65°F and all frost danger passes; in zone 9, plant from late March through late July for successive harvests — Pinkeye Purple Hull is one of the most heat-tolerant crops and thrives in the peak Gulf South summer.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; Pinkeye Purple Hull is the most widely grown and most beloved Southern pea (cowpea) cultivar in Gulf South gardens — a semi-vining bush variety producing pods with a distinctive purple hull (pod exterior) that turns from green to vivid purple-magenta at the ideal harvest stage for fresh-shelling, making it easy to identify perfect harvest timing. The peas inside have the distinctive pink 'eye' (hilum marking) characteristic of this type, with a rich, full, starchy-creamy flavor that is the authentic taste of Southern cooking — distinctive, earthy, and satisfying in ways that fresh garden peas cannot replicate. Cowpeas are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables in cultivation and actually perform best during the hottest summer months when most other crops fail — the Gulf South summer that defeats beans, cucumbers, and squash is ideal cowpea growing weather. They fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule bacteria, enriching the soil for follow-on crops. For fresh eating, harvest when the majority of the pod has turned purple and feels firm and fully rounded but before the pod dries. For dried peas, allow the pods to turn tan and dry completely on the vine. The dried peas store indefinitely and are the foundation of traditional Southern New Year's black-eyed pea dishes.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; grow to full maturity for dry beans.
directions: Pinto is a heat- and drought-tolerant bush bean grown as a dry bean, producing pods of speckled beans on upright plants with short runners. Direct sow after frost into warm soil in full sun, and let the pods dry fully on the plant. Water moderately during flowering and pod set, then ease off as pods mature. Harvest when pods are brown and brittle, then shell and dry the beans further for storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for spring and July–August for fall. Pinto beans are primarily a dry bean — the plant must be allowed to fully mature and dry before harvest, which takes the full season. In zone 9 the spring crop typically produces dry beans by June–July; a fall planting dried in November–December. Bush habit requires no staking.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; pinto beans are the most widely grown dry bean in the United States, accounting for nearly half of all dry bean production, and the foundation of Southwestern and Mexican cooking — the primary bean in refried beans (frijoles refritos), bean soup, and chili. The tan seeds with reddish-brown speckles (the Spanish name 'pinto' means 'painted') turn uniformly tan-brown when cooked, at which point the flavor is rich, earthy, and starchy with a creamy texture that falls apart when mashed. Bush-habit pinto plants are compact and self-supporting, producing a single concentrated harvest suitable for home-scale production and storage. The dry beans store for 2–3 years in a cool, dry location. In zone 9 the plants are susceptible to bean rust in humid conditions; provide adequate spacing for air circulation.

common_name: Piquillo Pepper (Spanish Roasting Pepper, Lodosa Piquillo)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes; piquillo is a compact, highly productive sweet Spanish pepper turning vivid red at maturity with a characteristic pointed tip (piquillo = 'little beak') — the most important preserved pepper in Spanish cuisine, roasted and packed in jars, and a staple ingredient in tapas, pintxos, and modern Spanish cooking.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after frost danger passes; piquillo plants are compact and productive, setting numerous small, triangular fruits; harvest at full vivid red maturity; roast over open flame or under a broiler until charred, steam to loosen skin, peel and seed for the classic preparation. Piquillo is the defining preserved pepper of northern Spain, particularly the Navarra region around the town of Lodosa (in the Ebro River valley) where the Denomination of Origin 'Piquillo de Lodosa' protects the traditional pepper and its preparation. The pepper is small (2–3 inch), triangular to slightly flattened-conical with a characteristic pointed 'beak' tip (piquillo = 'little beak'), vivid scarlet-red at maturity, and sweet to very mildly pungent with no significant heat. The flesh is thin but intensely sweet and slightly fruity, with a subtle bitterness that is balanced by the roasting process — fire-roasting is inseparable from the piquillo's culinary identity. The traditional preparation involves hand-roasting individual peppers over wood fires, peeling and seeding each one by hand without any water washing (to preserve flavor and sugars), and packing them in their own juices in jars or tins without any additional preservation except salt. The result is one of the most refined and flavorful preserved vegetables in world cuisine. Jarred piquillo peppers are a staple of Spanish kitchens and are used stuffed with salt cod or cheese, arranged on pintxos, layered in pasta dishes, and pureed into smooth sauces. Growing piquillo at home and roasting them yourself produces a quality that commercially jarred peppers rarely match.

common_name: Piracicaba Broccoli (Heat-Tolerant Brazilian Sprouting Broccoli for Warm Climates)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting to garden; in zone 9, start seeds in August–September for fall transplanting in September–October, targeting harvest December–March. Piracicaba was developed in Brazil for production in subtropical warm-winter conditions where standard heading broccoli (such as Packman or Marathon) struggles with heat-induced bolting and premature heading. Rather than forming a single large central head, Piracicaba produces an abundance of small, tender loose florets on branching side shoots over an extended harvest period — a sprouting habit similar to De Cicco broccoli but with dramatically better heat tolerance. In zone 9, Piracicaba can be harvested continuously through the mild winter rather than requiring a single-harvest timing, and it continues producing side shoots well into spring when standard broccoli bolts.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant to garden in fall for zone 9 winter harvest. Harvest loose florets continuously. Piracicaba Broccoli originated at the Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) and agronomic research stations near Piracicaba, a city in São Paulo state, Brazil — a major center of Brazilian tropical agricultural research. The variety was developed specifically to address the fundamental incompatibility between standard broccoli breeding (which targets cool-climate heading formation) and the subtropical conditions of southern Brazil and other warm-climate growing regions. Standard broccoli varieties were bred primarily in Europe and California's cool coastal fog belt, where temperature ranges precisely suited to head development allow reliable production; in warm climates, standard broccoli heats prematurely, forms loose, open heads of poor quality, or bolts before any marketable crop develops. Piracicaba's breeding solution was to select for a sprouting growth habit that produces continuously rather than forming a single marketable head — an approach that converts the temperature sensitivity of head formation from a problem into an advantage. Since the plant never forms a central head to be ruined by heat, there is no precise temperature window to miss, and the plant produces usable florets across a much broader temperature range. The florets of Piracicaba are small and tender, with a delicate texture superior to the sometimes-coarse texture of oversized main-head broccoli, and the continuous harvest over weeks or months provides far greater total yield per plant than single-harvest heading types in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Capsicum frutescens peppers benefit from a longer indoor growing period than C. annuum. In zones 9–11 the plants grow as woody perennials and become increasingly productive in their second and third years.
directions: Start indoors early and transplant to warm, well-drained soil; piri piri is an African cultivar of Capsicum frutescens (the same species as tabasco pepper) producing small, erect, vivid red to orange fruits 1–2 inches long with an intense, bright heat (50,000–175,000 SHU). It is the essential ingredient in the famous Portuguese piri piri sauce, brought to Portugal from its colonies in Angola and Mozambique in the 1500s, and is now central to Portuguese, South African, and Mozambican cuisines. Nando's Peri-Peri sauce is based on this pepper. The fruits are blended with garlic, lemon, and oil to make a marinade-sauce for grilled chicken. Plants become perennial subshrubs in zones 9–11 and produce prolifically year-round.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed and frost danger has passed; Planters Jumbo is a 1930s commercial-standard cantaloupe that was widely grown across the South before modern hybrid melons became dominant.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills of two to three plants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has thoroughly warmed. Planters Jumbo is an heirloom cantaloupe dating to the 1930s, once a standard commercial variety grown widely across the South before modern hybrid melons largely replaced older open-pollinated types, prized for heavily netted rind and sweet, aromatic salmon-orange flesh. The vigorous, sprawling vines need plenty of room to run and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development, tapering off as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine at full slip, with a strong, sweet aroma at the blossom end signaling peak ripeness.

common_name: Plum Regal Tomato (Disease-Resistant Plum Paste Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Plum Regal is a determinate paste-type tomato that sets a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks. In zone 9, aim for spring harvest in May–June by transplanting in early March.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Plum Regal is a determinate plum-type paste tomato developed by Cornell University's tomato breeding program specifically to improve on the disease susceptibility of heirloom Roma and similar paste types while maintaining the thick walls, dense flesh, and low moisture content that make plum tomatoes superior for sauce-making and processing. Plum Regal carries resistance to late blight (Phytophthora infestans) — the disease that wiped out heirloom paste tomatoes across much of the Northeast during the late blight epidemic of 2009 — as well as Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt. The medium-large (3–5 oz), deep red, oval fruits have very thick walls, small seed cavities, and excellent sauce-making characteristics with rich, concentrated tomato flavor. An outstanding choice for humid-climate paste tomato production, for home canners who want reliable crops without the disease susceptibility of traditional paste heirlooms, and for any gardener growing tomatoes where late blight or Fusarium are recurring problems.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 2 weeks after frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and provide bottom heat around 80°F to speed germination. Transplant to fertile, well-drained soil once nights are consistently above 55°F. Water deeply but infrequently to encourage deep rooting and reduce disease pressure. Harvest dark green fruits at 4–5 inches long for fresh use, or allow to turn red and dry them for ancho chiles.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost date; transplant into warm, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date; in zone 9, transplant in mid-February for spring production and again in late July for fall production.
directions: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Poblano is the classic Mexican culinary pepper — a mildly hot (1,000–2,000 Scoville units), wide, heart-shaped to triangular pepper that is the foundational ingredient in chiles rellenos, mole negro, and dozens of traditional Mexican dishes. Harvested green (poblano) or dried red (ancho or mulato depending on variety), these peppers have a rich, complex, slightly smoky flavor with moderate heat that defines the deep, layered character of traditional Mexican cuisine. The large, thick-walled fruits reach 4–5 inches long and 2.5–3 inches wide, with deep green color maturing to red-brown. Poblano is one of the most heat-tolerant culinary peppers and performs exceptionally well in zone 9's summer temperatures — unlike many sweet bell peppers, poblano tolerates the high summer heat of the Gulf South and continues producing through the hottest months with consistent irrigation. In zone 9, the plant can become a perennial woody shrub if protected from hard freezes, producing for 2–3 years from a single planting. Dry ripe red-brown poblanos to make ancho chiles — a key ingredient in red mole — by hanging in bundles in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for 3–4 weeks.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Poinsett 76 is a Clemson University breeding program selection from the original Poinsett variety, released in 1976 and still widely grown in the Southeast for its outstanding combination of disease resistance, heat tolerance, and production in hot, humid conditions that challenges most cucumber varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; provide support or allow vines to sprawl with 3–4 feet between hills. Poinsett 76 was developed by the Clemson University vegetable breeding program in South Carolina and released in 1976 as an improved selection of the original Poinsett cucumber (released 1966) — both named for Joel R. Poinsett, the South Carolinian who brought the poinsettia plant from Mexico. Poinsett 76 is distinguished by its outstanding disease resistance package (angular leaf spot, anthracnose, downy mildew, mosaic, and powdery mildew resistance) and heat tolerance that makes it the cucumber of choice for hot, humid Southeastern gardens where most varieties decline quickly in summer; fruits are 7–8 inches long, dark green, cylindrical, and of good eating quality. An open-pollinated, seed-saveable classic that remains one of the best choices for Gulf Coast and Deep South summer cucumber production.

plant_note: Propagate from stem or root cuttings — both male and female plants are required for fruit production, so plant at least one of each; pointed gourd is dioecious and does not fruit from seeds alone without confirmed plant sex. Grows perennially in zones 10–12 and as an annual in zones 8–9.
directions: Propagate from rooted stem cuttings or root sections, planting male and female plants together (ratio of 1 male per 4–6 females); train on a strong trellis in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; pointed gourd is one of the most popular vegetables in Bengali, Odia, and North Indian cuisine, prized for its tender 2–6 inch elongated fruits with green-and-white striped skin that are stuffed, curried, fried, or used in sweets when fully mature. Distinct from snake gourd (Trichosanthes cucumerina) in being much smaller, more compact, and preferred for cooking fresh and stuffed. Plants in zone 9 may freeze to the ground in winter but resprout from the roots in spring; mulch heavily in the first winter. Harvest fruits when they reach 3–4 inches for best culinary quality.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is warm; erect a trellis or pole structure before sowing to avoid disturbing roots later.
directions: Plant seeds 1 in deep at the base of a sturdy trellis or teepee of poles set 6–8 ft tall, spacing 3 seeds per pole. Vines twine naturally but may need early guidance toward supports. Harvest pods before seeds bulge prominently for the tenderest texture. Pole beans produce over a longer season than bush types, so keep picking to prevent pod maturation from stopping new flower set.

common_name: Polish Linguisa Tomato (Sausage-Shaped Polish Heirloom Paste Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide staking or caging, since the indeterminate vine carries a heavy load of elongated fruit.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost, staking early to support the long fruit clusters. Polish Linguisa is a Polish heirloom paste tomato named for its distinctive elongated, curved, sausage-like fruit shape, which sets it apart from the blockier Roma and San Marzano types most gardeners know. The deep red fruit is dense and meaty with very little seed cavity or juice, cooking down quickly into a thick, richly flavored sauce or paste with minimal simmering. The vigorous indeterminate vines are heavy producers over a long season; pick fruit as it colors fully and process promptly, since the thin skin is more prone to splitting after heavy rain than dedicated modern paste hybrids.

common_name: Polish White Softneck Garlic (Eastern European Heirloom Artichoke Garlic)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall at or around first frost; Polish White is a traditional Eastern European softneck garlic (Artichoke type) with origins in Poland and surrounding countries, where garlic has been grown as a staple crop for centuries — it produces medium-large bulbs with 10–16 tightly packed cloves, clean white skins, and a reliable, full-flavored character suited to all cooking uses and excellent storage of 10–12 months.
directions: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall from 4 weeks before first frost to shortly after; Polish White performs well in both cold northern climates and mild southern winters; harvest in summer when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure thoroughly before storage; braid the flexible stems for attractive long-term storage. Polish White is an Artichoke-type softneck garlic originating in Poland and the broader Eastern European garlic-growing tradition, where garlic has been a staple culinary and medicinal crop since ancient times; it entered the North American heirloom garlic collection through the immigrant communities and seed-saver networks that preserved traditional European agricultural varieties throughout the 20th century. The bulbs are medium-large (2–3 inches across) with tightly packed multiple layers of cloves (10–16 per bulb) in the characteristic Artichoke arrangement, with clean white to ivory outer skins and a compact, rounded shape. The flavor is full, moderately pungent, and satisfying — not as complex as the finest Rocambole or Marbled Purple Stripe hardnecks, but very reliable and versatile for all cooking uses from fresh salsas and aioli to long-cooked soups, stews, and roasted garlic. The primary virtues of Polish White are reliability (excellent performance in a wide range of climates), productivity (high-yielding compared to hardneck types), and outstanding storage life of 10–12 months under proper conditions (cool, dry, dark) — making it the garlic of choice for those who want a year-round supply from a single fall planting.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 3–4 inches deep in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil after temperatures remain above 65°F; this understory plant prefers partial shade and consistent moisture year-round in its tropical range.
directions: Plant rhizome pieces in humid, tropical or subtropical gardens in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil; this Pacific island staple grows naturally in coastal and forest-edge habitats from East Africa to Polynesia. The deeply lobed leaves are attractive, and by 6–9 months the underground rhizomes are large enough to harvest; raw rhizomes are bitter and mildly toxic due to tannins and must be grated, washed repeatedly in water, and dried to yield a pure white starch.
