Its bright red skin and clean round shape make it visually appealing for slicing and garnishing as well as eating whole. Keep soil consistently moist for the best size and texture, and it was, at the time of its award, the first radish AAS winner in several decades — reflecting a genuinely useful improvement over standard varieties rather than just a color or shape novelty.

plant_note: Sow in early spring and again in late summer; bred for baby-size harvest.
directions: 'Robin' was bred for harvesting at baby size, delivering well-rounded, tender, sweet 1 to 1.5 inch roots with high bolt resistance. Direct sow the seed clusters 1/2 inch deep and thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart, since each cluster can produce several plants. Keep moisture even for crisp, crack-free roots, and harvest young for the best texture. The tender baby greens are also excellent raw or cooked.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks after frost for good pollination; isolate from other corn.
directions: 'Robust Pop R400MR' produces large, round popped kernels sturdy enough to hold coatings, unlike the more common butterfly popcorn. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil in blocks of at least four short rows to ensure good wind pollination. Give plants full sun, steady moisture, and rich soil through the long season. Let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvesting, then cure the kernels further before popping. Isolate from sweet corn to keep quality true.

plant_note: Plant cloves 2–3 inches deep in October–November; Rocambole requires 6–8 weeks of vernalization below 40°F for proper bulb formation, making it best suited to zone 4–7. In zone 9, pre-chill cloves in the refrigerator for 6–8 weeks before planting to compensate for mild winters — or choose Creole garlic instead, which requires no pre-chilling.
directions: Plant pre-chilled cloves 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Rocambole is considered by most garlic connoisseurs to be the finest-flavored garlic group — rich, complex, deeply savory, and mellow with a characteristic lingering warmth and almost chocolate-like earthiness that no other garlic group fully matches. Named varieties include 'Spanish Roja,' 'German Red,' 'Killarney Red,' and 'Music.' The medium-sized, brownish-purple skinned bulbs contain 8–12 cloves per head arranged in a single layer. The paper wrapping is loose, almost shaggy, and the inner skins of individual cloves are characteristically streaked with purple-brown. Rocambole is a hardneck garlic producing a central flower stalk (scape) that should be removed in June to direct energy into bulb formation; scapes are edible and delicious in stir-fries and pestos. In zone 9, Rocambole requires refrigerator pre-chilling of cloves for 6–8 weeks before October planting, or better yet, substitute Creole garlic, which is naturally adapted to mild winters without chilling. Rocambole stores only 3–5 months.

plant_note: Sow in spring or fall; perennial in mild zones 6-10.
directions: 'Rocky' is a fast-growing wild-type arugula forming a compact rosette with a stronger, more complex, nutty-peppery flavor than salad arugula. Direct sow shallowly and thin to 4-6 inches, harvesting leaves young and often for the mildest taste. It tolerates cold well and behaves as a short-lived perennial in USDA zones 6-10, resprouting after cutting. Grow in cool weather and shear back before flowering to prolong tender leaf production.

common_name: Rocky Ford Cantaloupe (Colorado Classic Heirloom Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Rocky Ford reaches peak flavor in dry, hot summer conditions and performs best in climates with hot days, warm nights, and low humidity — it is excellent in the arid Southwest and Mountain West but somewhat prone to fungal diseases in humid Gulf Coast conditions.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; harvest when stem slips easily from the vine ('slip' stage) and the blossom end is slightly soft. Rocky Ford is the historic heirloom cantaloupe variety that made the Arkansas River Valley around Rocky Ford, Colorado famous for melon production in the late 19th century — producing medium-sized, netted, round to slightly oval fruits with bright green skin under tan netting and pale green to orange flesh with exceptional sweetness and classic old-fashioned cantaloupe flavor. The variety was so famous that 'Rocky Ford' became synonymous with high-quality cantaloupe across America in the early 20th century, and special rail cars shipped Rocky Ford melons to Chicago, New York, and other major cities during the peak season. Rocky Ford performs best in dry climates with hot days and cool nights (like the high-altitude semi-arid conditions of Colorado) where low humidity reduces fungal disease and water-stressed plants concentrate sugars at maturity. In humid Gulf Coast conditions it requires careful disease management, but dedicated heirloom melon enthusiasts appreciate its distinctive flavor, which has a more complex, old-fashioned character than modern hybrids.

plant_note: Start on a heat mat 6–8 weeks before last frost; Rocotillo is a traditional Caribbean seasoning pepper related to the habanero but with minimal heat (1,500–2,500 SHU), prized entirely for its intensely tropical, fruity habanero aroma and flavor with none of the fire — a favorite seasoning pepper in Cuban, Puerto Rican, and Dominican cooking.
directions: Germinate on a heat mat at 80°F; transplant outdoors after frost when soil is warm and nights are above 60°F. Rocotillo is a Capsicum chinense seasoning pepper of Caribbean origin that looks remarkably like a miniature, squashed habanero with its distinctive ribbed, round, flattened form — but carries minimal heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) while retaining the intensely fruity, tropical, citrusy habanero aroma that makes this species unique; it is used in Cuban, Puerto Rican, Dominican, and Venezuelan cooking wherever the habanero flavor without the fire is desired. The small, round, ribbed fruits ripen from green through yellow to orange or red and are used fresh in sofrito, salsas, sauces, and seasoning blends. Related to and sometimes confused with the aji dulce (sweet habanero) and cachucha peppers of the Caribbean. Highly productive in hot weather; perennial in zone 9b–12.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, as this pubescens type is notoriously slow to germinate and needs a long season to mature.
directions: Start seed indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, as this pubescens type is notoriously slow to germinate and needs a long season to mature its blocky, irregularly shaped fruit. Pods hold black seeds and thick, juicy flesh typical of rocoto, ripening to a bright yellow with heat ranging from moderate to fiercely hot (roughly 10,000-60,000 Scoville units). Plants form a more compact bush than typical rocoto and, like other pubescens types, set fruit best where summer nights stay relatively cool.

plant_note: Sow indoors 12-14 weeks ahead of the last frost; performs best with some afternoon relief from peak summer heat, since pubescens sets fruit poorly above roughly 90°F.
directions: Sow indoors 12-14 weeks ahead of the last frost, giving this rare rocoto selection the long, patient start every pubescens variety demands. Medium-sized fruits mature to a distinctive chocolate-brown, with the thick, crunchy walls and fruity, apple-like heat characteristic of the species. Because pubescens sets fruit poorly above roughly 90°F, plants perform best with some afternoon relief from peak summer heat in hot-summer regions.

plant_note: Start indoors 12–14 weeks before last frost; unlike most peppers, rocoto prefers cool nights and actually performs poorly in intense summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep at a cooler 65–70°F — unlike other peppers, Capsicum pubescens actually germinates better in cooler soil and is damaged by excessive heat. This Andean species is unique among cultivated peppers for its purple flowers and distinctive black seeds; it tolerates light frost better than any other pepper species. Transplant to a position with afternoon shade in hot climates, as rocoto stops setting fruit when temperatures exceed 90°F — coastal or mountain gardens suit it best. Fruits resemble small apples (hence 'manzano') and ripen to yellow, orange, or red with thick, sweet flesh and intense, burning heat.

plant_note: Start indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, well ahead of standard peppers, since pubescens seed is slow and erratic to germinate.
directions: Start indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, well ahead of standard peppers, since pubescens seed is slow and erratic to germinate. Unlike the round, apple-shaped manzano rocoto, the Perón type produces elongated, pear-shaped pods with thick, juicy walls that hold up especially well to stuffing and roasting. Deep purple flowers and fuzzy, hairy foliage distinguish the plant from every other cultivated pepper species, and it tolerates cooler nights better than typical warm-season chiles.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger once soil is warm.
directions: 'Roma II' is a bush-type Italian flat snap bean with a rich, nutty flavor rarely found in stores, borne on compact plants that need no support. Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, spacing them 3-4 inches apart in full sun. The 4-5 inch pods stay tender and slow to develop fiber, so harvest regularly to keep plants producing. Excellent fresh, frozen, or canned; good in containers.

plant_note: Start indoors about six weeks before the last frost, then transplant once nights are warm.
directions: Sow indoors six weeks ahead of transplanting and set plants deep to build strong roots. Roma is a compact, determinate paste tomato producing firm, meaty three-inch fruits with few seeds, ideal for sauces and canning. A single stake or small cage supports the tidy vines, which set most of their fruit in a concentrated window. Water evenly and mulch to prevent blossom-end rot, and expect a heavy flush of fruit that ripens over a few weeks.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost; for fall, sow 8–10 weeks before first frost.
directions: Sow seed at 1/8 in depth in cool soil and thin to 8–12 in; romaine forms an upright, elongated head that needs slightly more space than loose-leaf types. Keep soil evenly moist to prevent tip burn, which appears as brown leaf edges due to calcium deficiency from moisture stress. Harvest by cutting the whole head at soil level when it is 8–10 in tall and the inner leaves feel firm. Outer leaves can be removed individually as the head develops to extend the harvest period.

common_name: Romance Nantes Carrot (Very Sweet Crack-Resistant Bejo Hybrid Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow thinly; carrot seed is tiny and needs consistent moisture for the 10–21 day germination period. In zone 9, sow August–November for fall and winter harvest when carrots are at their best; spring planting (February–March) is possible but quality diminishes as temperatures rise. Romance is a Nantes-type hybrid: 7–8 inch, blunt-tipped, cylindrical, uniform roots. Thin to 2–3 inches after seedlings establish (3 weeks after germination); crowded roots become forked and deformed. Romance is noted for excellent crack resistance — roots hold in the ground without splitting even when mature, which extends the harvest window.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in loose, deep, well-worked soil free of rocks and clods; thin to 2–3 inches. Keep soil consistently moist until germination. Romance is a Nantes-type hybrid carrot from Bejo Seeds, a Dutch vegetable breeding company with a long history of Nantes-type carrot refinement. The Nantes type — originating in the Nantes region of western France — defines a carrot form that differs fundamentally from the long Imperator types common in grocery stores: Nantes carrots are shorter (6–8 inches vs. 9–11 inches), blunt-tipped rather than tapering to a point, rounder in cross-section, and notably sweeter with more tender, less fibrous flesh. Romance carries Nantes-type characteristics to a high standard: the roots are uniformly 7–8 inches long with a clean, blunt Nantes tip, bright orange interior color throughout (no pale core), very high sugar content, and notably fine-textured, tender flesh that makes Romance excellent for eating raw as well as cooked. The crack resistance that gives Romance particular value means that unlike some other sweet, high-sugar varieties that develop radial cracks if left in ground too long, Romance holds well after reaching maturity — a practical advantage for home gardeners harvesting over weeks rather than in a single commercial harvest. Fall-grown carrots in zone 9 achieve maximum sweetness as cold nights concentrate sugars in the roots.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant so heads mature in cool fall weather; aim to transplant about 16 weeks before first frost.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant date; romanesco demands consistent temperatures between 60–65°F during head formation or it fails to produce proper fractal spirals. Transplant into deeply amended soil and water evenly throughout the season, as any moisture stress affects head quality. Harvest the single central head when the spiral turrets are sharp and well-defined but before any yellowing begins. Unlike broccoli, romanesco rarely produces usable side shoots after the main head is cut.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–14 weeks before desired transplant date (July–August in zone 9 for a fall transplant); plant out in September–October in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Romanesco produces its characteristic spiraling, lime-green fractal heads (a naturally occurring example of a logarithmic spiral and Fibonacci sequence) and has a milder, nuttier flavor than either standard broccoli or cauliflower.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–14 weeks before transplanting; plant in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; cover heads as they develop to maintain lime-green color if desired. Brassica oleracea var. botrytis 'Romanesco' (Romanesco or Roman broccoli) is a variety of Italian origin — known since the 16th century in Rome — that produces one of the most visually spectacular vegetables in existence: a tightly packed head of lime-green, spiraling conical florets arranged in a precise logarithmic spiral following the Fibonacci sequence, creating a fractal pattern of remarkable mathematical beauty. Each floret replicates the overall head shape at a smaller scale, in a perfect example of self-similar fractal geometry visible to the naked eye. The flavor is equally noteworthy: milder, sweeter, and nuttier than both standard broccoli and cauliflower, with a crisp-firm texture that holds up well when roasted or steamed. Romanesco requires similar growing conditions to cauliflower — it is the most temperature-sensitive of the three major brassica heading types, requiring consistent temperatures during head formation for proper development; heat causes premature bolting or loose, irregular heads. In zone 9, grow as a fall crop, planted September–October for December–February harvest. The stunning heads make excellent centerpiece dishes and are highly popular at farmers markets.

plant_note: Best grown for fall harvest so the heads mature in cool weather; also a spring crop in mild areas.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant into rich, consistently moist soil, giving each plant ample room to develop. This Italian heirloom forms mesmerizing lime-green heads of spiraling Fibonacci cones with a mild, nutty flavor. It grows slowly and prefers cool conditions, so time plantings so heads mature before summer heat or in the cool of fall. Harvest the whole head while the fractal spirals are tight and firm, cutting with several inches of stem.

plant_note: Start indoors; often best as a fall crop maturing in cool weather.
directions: 'Romanesco' produces mesmerizing chartreuse, fractal-spiraled 5-6 inch heads with a delicate, nutty flavor between broccoli and cauliflower. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before transplanting and set plants 18-24 inches apart in rich, full-sun soil. Steady moisture and cool weather are essential for well-formed heads, so it often performs best as a fall crop. Harvest while the spirals are tight and firm.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or late summer; long days and heat can trigger bolting.
directions: 'Romanesco', a Florence (bulbing) fennel, forms a crisp, anise-flavored bulb prized raw, sauteed, or in soups and pasta, with feathery edible foliage. Direct sow shallowly and thin to 6-12 inches, keeping the plants evenly watered to encourage plump bulbs and discourage bolting. Mounding soil around the base as bulbs swell keeps them tender and pale. Grow in the cool ends of the season and harvest bulbs once they reach the size of a fist.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes for a midsummer harvest.
directions: Romanian Red is a porcelain hardneck garlic that yields large, dense bulbs of usually 4-5 easy-to-peel cloves with a hot, robust flavor and excellent storage. Separate bulbs into cloves just before planting and set each clove pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in fall. Mulch heavily after the ground cools to protect against heaving over winter. Snap off the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into bulb sizing. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy spot for two to three weeks.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil near a support structure; Romano is the Italian flat-podded snap bean standard in Italian and Mediterranean cooking, prized for its wider, flatter pods, tender texture when cooked, and rich, nutty flavor that is distinctly superior to standard round snap beans for braising and sautéing.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil after last frost; provide a 5–6 foot trellis or teepee for the vines and begin harvesting when pods are flat and 4–5 inches long, before they string. Romano is the classic Italian flat-podded or 'Italian flat bean,' a pole type with wide, flat, 5–7 inch pods that have a different texture and flavor profile from standard round snap beans when cooked — more tender, less fibrous, with a rich, earthy, slightly nutty flavor that makes them the preferred snap bean for Italian sautés (fagioli in padella), long-braised dishes with olive oil and garlic, and agrodolce preparations. The flat pods become stringy if left to mature too long; harvest when pods are still flat and not yet showing bean bulges. A bush Romano type is also available. Highly productive in warm climates; excellent for Gulf Coast spring and fall bean production.

common_name: Ronde de Nice Zucchini (Round French Zucchini)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-amended soil; Ronde de Nice is a classic French Provençal heirloom round zucchini, the traditional squash for stuffing in the Niçoise manner — the small, round fruits are hollowed out, filled with herbed meat or rice, and baked or braised in tomato sauce in what is arguably the definitive French stuffed squash preparation.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in well-amended, well-drained soil after last frost in full sun; Ronde de Nice is a bush-type that needs 2–3 feet of space and no support. Ronde de Nice is a French heirloom round summer squash of Provençal origin, the classic stuffing squash of Niçoise cuisine (courgettes rondes farcies à la niçoise) and one of the oldest and most culinarily significant French kitchen garden varieties still in regular cultivation. The fruits are perfectly spherical, 2–4 inches in diameter, with smooth, thin, pale to medium green skin and tender, mild, cream-colored flesh that has a somewhat denser texture than elongated zucchini — well-suited to stuffing as it holds its shape better during cooking. Harvest at 2–3 inches for fresh eating and 3–4 inches for stuffing; slightly larger fruits (4–5 inches) can still be stuffed but become seedy. Highly productive and heat-tolerant; excellent for Gulf Coast spring and fall production.

common_name: Rongai Lablab (Late-Flowering Vining Warm-Season Legume Cover Crop)
plant_note: Direct sow 1-1.5 inches deep after soil has warmed above 65°F and frost danger has passed; Rongai is a late-flowering, photoperiod-sensitive lablab selection bred to stay vegetative and keep producing heavy biomass well into fall rather than setting seed early.
directions: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed, inoculating seed with a cowpea-type Rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation in fields with no prior lablab history. Rongai is a vigorous, twining lablab selection valued as a summer cover crop for its late, photoperiod-triggered flowering, which keeps the plant putting energy into leafy vine growth and root nodulation for months rather than shifting early to seed production, producing an unusually heavy mat of biomass that smothers weeds and builds organic matter. It climbs readily on trellis, fence, or companion crop and can also be grown as forage or green manure, mowed or rolled and left as mulch, or turned under ahead of a fall planting. As a legume, it fixes substantial atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis and tolerates heat and drought once established, making it a reliable warm-season soil builder for the Gulf South growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring for roots to harvest in fall; this drought-tolerant perennial establishes easily.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in loose, deep soil so the taproots can grow long and straight. This hardy, drought-resistant perennial produces nutrient-dense greens and thick roots traditionally roasted as a coffee substitute. Thin seedlings to give each plant room, and keep beds weeded while young plants establish. Dig roots in fall of the first year for coffee-style use, and enjoy the bitter young leaves in salads throughout the season.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 sow October–March for fall through spring harvest. Roquette bolts quickly in warm weather — sow in succession every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest through the cool season. In zone 9 the fall sowing in October–November produces the best quality, most flavorful crop before the plant bolts in warm spring weather. The small white flowers that appear when the plant bolts are edible with the same peppery flavor as the leaves.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Roquette is the Italian heirloom arugula variety — the specific selection used for millennia in Italian cuisine that gave arugula its character and reputation as the quintessential Italian salad green. The deeply lobed, dark green leaves have the intense peppery, nutty, slightly bitter flavor that defines the arugula experience — more pronounced than milder modern selections. The flavor becomes sharper and more assertive as the weather warms (approaching bolting), while young winter-grown leaves are milder and more delicate. Roquette's use in Italian cooking spans from the simple classic of arugula, shaved Parmesan, and lemon in a pizza topping, to fresh salads with olive oil, to pasta dishes and antipasto plates across Italy. The small, lobed leaf shape and strong flavor make Roquette the most authentic form for Italian culinary preparations. The partial shade tolerance allows it to be grown under taller plants in a kitchen garden, extending the season slightly.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm. In zone 9 start in January and transplant in March–April. Rosa Bianca eggplants reach eating quality when the skin shows the characteristic white-lavender blush and the fruits feel firm — overripe fruits turn yellow and develop bitterness. In zone 9 eggplant thrives in the heat and can be grown as a perennial, overwintering with light frost protection and returning to produce in spring.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in the warmest available position; Rosa Bianca is an Italian heirloom eggplant producing large, round to slightly oval fruits with a beautiful rosy-lavender and creamy-white skin that lightens to nearly white at eating maturity — the name means 'pink and white' in Italian and accurately describes the distinctive pastel bicolor appearance that makes Rosa Bianca the most visually elegant of heirloom eggplant varieties. The white to very pale cream flesh has the mildest, least bitter flavor of any eggplant variety — traditional eggplant bitterness is largely absent in Rosa Bianca, which has a delicate, sweet, slightly creamy taste that has made it the preferred eggplant of Italian chefs for generations. The flesh does not need salting before cooking as most other eggplant varieties require. The large, bulbous fruits (6–8 inches across) have a spongy, moist texture that absorbs olive oil and seasonings beautifully in roasted, grilled, and baked preparations — particularly in traditional Italian dishes like caponata, parmigiana, and grilled vegetable preparations.

plant_note: Start indoors early with warmth; transplant only when nights stay warm.
directions: 'Rosa Bianca' is an Italian heirloom eggplant bearing plump, scalloped 4-6 inch fruits in pinkish-purple with white streaks, with mild, creamy, seedy-free flesh and no bitterness. Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, transplanting only after nights warm up. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and warmth, staking the plants as fruit sets. Harvest while the skin is glossy for the best texture.

common_name: Rose Finn Apple Potato (Rose-Skinned Heirloom Fingerling)
plant_note: Plant seed potato pieces with 2-3 eyes per piece in cool soil; Rose Finn Apple is a late-season Scandinavian heirloom fingerling. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling as vines grow; harvest when vines begin to die back. Rose Finn Apple is a Scandinavian heirloom fingerling potato with rose-pink to tan skin and creamy yellow flesh, valued for its smooth, dense, waxy texture and sweet, rich flavor that holds up especially well in roasting and potato salads. The elongated, knobby tubers form in loose clusters and the plant is a dependable, moderately productive grower. Being a later-maturing variety, it benefits from a full growing season; dig for tender new potatoes once flowering finishes, or let the vines die back naturally for mature tubers with better storage qualities. Like other fingerlings, its low-starch flesh keeps its shape well through cooking rather than turning mealy.

common_name: Rose de Berne Tomato (Swiss Heirloom Pink Slicer)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; a vigorous 6-8 foot indeterminate vine that needs firm staking and shows good resistance to cracking.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost risk passes. Rose de Berne is a classic heirloom from the Bern region of Switzerland, often described as the European counterpart to Brandywine for its reputation as one of the best-tasting pink tomatoes grown in France, Germany, and Switzerland. The smooth, deep-rose fruit has thin but durable skin and creamy, richly sweet-tart flesh. The vigorous 6-8 foot vines need firm staking and reward a long warm season with heavy, reliable yields.

common_name: Rosella Purple Tomato (Compact Dusky Purple-Pink Dwarf Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Rosella Purple is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bred to bring rich, dusky purple-pink 'black' tomato flavor to a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Rosella Purple bears medium fruit in a rich, dusky purple-pink, the deep, complex flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomato varieties, on a compact plant from the Dwarf Tomato Project bred to bring heirloom-quality flavor to gardens without room for a full-size indeterminate vine. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil warms to 70°F; in zones 9–11, direct sow outdoors after last frost. Roselle is a short-day plant that flowers in fall as days shorten, so planting earlier means more leaf and stem production before flowering.
directions: Start seeds indoors or sow directly after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; roselle is a tropical hibiscus grown primarily for its deep-red, fleshy calyces that envelop the seed capsules after the flowers fade in fall — these calyces are harvested fresh or dried to make hibiscus tea (agua de Jamaica), syrups, jams, and wines with a bright cranberry-like tartness. Plants grow rapidly to 4–8 feet tall and are ornamental throughout the season with attractive burgundy-tinged stems and lobed leaves. Harvest calyces when they are plump and fully colored but before they dry on the plant; check plants every few days as the harvest window is short. A single plant can yield 1–3 pounds of fresh calyces.

common_name: Rosette Pak Choi (Tai Sai, Flat Cabbage, Taisai)
plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring crop; sow again in late summer (8–10 weeks before first fall frost) for fall crop; an excellent shade-tolerant spring and fall green.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 10–12 inches when seedlings are 2 inches tall; rosette pak choi (tai sai) forms a distinctive flat, spreading rosette of dark green spoon-shaped leaves with broad white midribs — entirely different in shape from upright pak choi but equally tender and excellent in stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. The flat growth habit makes it wind-tolerant and very space-efficient as a cut-and-come-again crop or whole heads spaced wider for full size. Extremely fast to harvest at baby stage (25–30 days); cold-hardy to about 22°F and less bolt-prone than standard pak choi. Grows well in light shade, making it suitable for interplanting under taller crops in spring.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer; excellent fall green.
directions: Tatsoi forms a flat, decorative rosette of spoon-shaped, dark green leaves with a mild, slightly mustardy flavor and high calcium and vitamin content. Direct sow shallowly and thin to 6-10 inches apart, or harvest crowded plants young as baby greens. It thrives in the cool weather of spring and fall and tolerates light frost, which sweetens the leaves. Cut the whole rosette or pick outer leaves for salads, stir-fries, and soups.

common_name: Rosita Eggplant (Rutgers-Bred Puerto Rican-Type Lavender Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay warm. Rosita was bred at Rutgers specifically for growers serving Puerto Rican and Caribbean markets.
directions: Rosita produces blocky, egg-shaped fruit with pale lavender-pink skin and creamy white flesh that stays mild and tender even as fruit sizes up, a trait bred in by Rutgers to suit fresh-market growers serving Caribbean and Latino communities. The vigorous, heat-loving plants set fruit reliably through hot, humid summers and hold up well without staking in most home gardens. Pick fruit while still glossy at 4-6 inches long for the best texture, since the thin skin means it bruises more easily than thicker-skinned purple types. Its milder flavor and lower seed count make it a good choice for cooks who find standard purple-black eggplant too bitter or seedy.

plant_note: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop, since plants grown in warm weather stay green and only redden as temperatures drop.
directions: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop, since plants grown in warm weather stay green and only redden and firm up as temperatures drop, with a light frost sweetening the flavor. Named for the lagoon town of Chioggia near Venice, this classic Italian radicchio forms tight, round, cabbage-like heads of deep wine-red leaves once cool autumn nights trigger the pigment. It is one of the most widely grown radicchio types in Italy and forms the template most people picture when they hear the word radicchio.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for harvest November–February. Rouge Grenobloise is exceptionally cold-hardy for a butterhead type, surviving temperatures to 15–20°F, which makes it the standard butterhead for fall-through-winter production in zone 9. A spring planting in January–February provides a second harvest before heat causes bolting. The deep red color intensifies in cold weather — fall and winter heads are the most deeply colored.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Rouge Grenobloise is a French heirloom butterhead lettuce from the Grenoble region of southeastern France, selected for exceptional cold-hardiness in the alpine climate of the French Alps — its ability to withstand temperatures to 15–20°F makes it one of the most cold-tolerant butterhead lettuces available. The large, loose heads have deeply red-bronzed outer leaves with green-to-yellow-green interior leaves, creating a bicolor head that is visually striking at harvest. The flavor is the classic buttery, tender, mild butterhead type with a slight sweetness that intensifies with cold exposure — the deep burgundy-red outer leaves have a richer, slightly more complex flavor than the green interior. In zone 9 Rouge Grenobloise provides the most reliable fall-to-winter butterhead harvest of any lettuce variety, forming substantial heads from October plantings that are ready from November through February. Harvest whole heads or strip outer leaves for a continuing harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in deeply amended soil; the 'Cinderella pumpkin' of legend — deeply ribbed, brilliant red-orange, and flat like a coach wheel — sold at Parisian markets since the 1880s and still considered one of the finest pumpkins for French cuisine.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in enriched, well-drained soil, hills spaced 6–8 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill once true leaves appear. Rouge Vif d'Etampes — 'vivid red of Etampes,' the French market town where it was sold — is a century-old French heirloom pumpkin famous for its dramatically flattened, deeply ribbed, vivid red-orange form that resembles the coach from the Cinderella fairy tale; fruits weigh 15–35 pounds and have brilliant orange, fine-grained, dry, sweet flesh of outstanding quality for soups, gratins, and tarts in the French culinary tradition. Cure for 2 weeks at warm temperatures after harvest and store in a cool, dry place for up to 4 months; the unusual shape makes it a dramatic autumn centerpiece as well as an excellent culinary pumpkin.

plant_note: Sow in late summer 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for a fall-into-winter harvest; Rouge d'Hiver is a French heirloom romaine lettuce bred specifically for cold weather production, surviving temperatures well below freezing and producing elongated, bronzy-red to burgundy heads through winter and early spring in zones 6–10.
directions: Sow in late summer in rich, moist, well-drained soil and thin to 9–12 inches; Rouge d'Hiver tolerates hard frost and is best grown as a fall-to-winter crop in mild climates, or with cold frame protection in colder zones. Rouge d'Hiver (Red Winter) is a French heirloom romaine-type lettuce bred for extreme cold tolerance — a critical trait in French kitchen garden tradition where gardeners have long maintained winter salad production under cloches and frames. The upright, elongated, semi-cos heads develop deep bronzy-red to burgundy coloring that intensifies in cold weather, with firm, crunchy texture and rich, slightly nutty flavor that is superior to most warm-season lettuces. In zones 8–10 it can be grown outdoors through winter without protection; in zones 6–7 it thrives in cold frames or low tunnels. One of the most valuable and underused lettuces for Gulf Coast and Southeastern winter salad gardens where it will produce from October through March.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer; notably cold tolerant for overwintering in mild areas.
directions: This 1800s French heirloom romaine forms a compact, 12-inch head with a tender green heart wrapped in bronze-red leaves and a rich, buttery flavor. Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them, and thin to 8-12 inches apart in full sun to partial shade. True to its name meaning 'Red Winter', it is quite cold tolerant and good for fall and mild-climate overwinter crops. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest heads before hot weather brings bitterness.

plant_note: As a winter radish, sow in mid to late summer for fall harvest and storage.
directions: 'Round Black Spanish' is a large winter radish with rough black skin and pungent, crisp white flesh grown in the U.S. since the 1800s. Sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since winter radishes need a longer season and cooler weather than spring types. Thin to 4-6 inches apart and keep soil evenly moist for smooth, non-woody roots. The spiciness mellows when cooked, and roots store exceptionally well through winter.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy soil in full sun; round melon (tinda) is an Indian subcontinental cucurbit popular in Indian, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi cooking — it grows rapidly in hot weather and produces abundantly but must be picked young at 3–4 inches for best texture and flavor.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; harvest fruits at 3–4 inches across before skin hardens. Praecitrullus fistulosus (round melon or tinda) is an Indian subcontinent cucurbit — closely related to but distinct from watermelon — that is an important summer vegetable throughout India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. The small, round, pale-green, slightly fuzzy fruits (2–4 inches across when harvested young) have a mild, delicate flavor and a slightly spongy, moist texture when cooked; they absorb spices and sauces well, making them excellent for Indian curries (tinda masala), stuffed preparations, and stir-fries. The plant is compact and less vigorous than many cucurbits — it can be grown on a small trellis or allowed to sprawl as a groundcover. The fruits must be picked when young and tender; overripe fruits become pithy and seedy. It grows best in the hot summer conditions of zone 8–12 and is rarely available in North American grocery stores, making home growing especially rewarding for Indian cooking enthusiasts. An essentially unknown vegetable in Western horticulture that deserves wider recognition.

plant_note: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before the last frost and transplant into hot, fertile soil once nights stay above 60°F, giving vines a large trellis or ample ground space.
directions: A round-fruited strain of winter melon that develops large, globe-shaped fruit up to 14-22 pounds, in contrast to the more common oblong wax gourd types. As fruit matures it develops the characteristic waxy white bloom on pale green skin that gives the vegetable its storage-friendly reputation; whole melons can keep for months in a cool, dry spot after harvest. Its round shape and generous size make it the traditional choice for the banquet presentation known as dong gua zhong, where the entire hollowed melon is steamed and served as a soup tureen. Give the sprawling vines plenty of room or a very sturdy trellis with fruit slings, since ripe melons are heavy.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; germinates fast in warmth.
directions: Sow seeds one inch deep in warm, fertile soil, planting a couple of seeds per spot and thinning to the strongest. This heirloom summer squash produces charming globe-shaped fruits about three to four inches across that are ideal for stuffing. Keep the plants well watered and harvest fruits young, when they are tender and the skin is still glossy. Picking frequently keeps the productive plants setting new fruit throughout the warm season.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil is warm.
directions: This round zucchini bears tender, ball-shaped fruits especially suited for stuffing or serving as individual soup bowls. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil and give the bushy plants full sun and room to spread. Harvest fruits young at 3-4 inches wide for the best flavor, picking often to keep the plant productive. The edible blossoms are delicious fried, and consistent watering supports steady fruit set.

common_name: Roxanne Radish (AAS-Winning Uniform Red Globe Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; Roxanne is an AAS-winning early radish bred for strong resistance to pithiness and heat stress, holding good quality longer than most globe radishes.
directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; Roxanne is an AAS-winning globe radish producing uniform, bright-red, smooth roots with crisp, mild white flesh, bred for unusually strong resistance to the pithiness and hollow centers that often develop in radishes that sit in the ground a few extra days past ideal harvest size or face a warm spell. This forgiveness makes it a good choice for gardeners who cannot harvest on the exact first day of readiness. It matures quickly, in as little as 24 days, allowing several successive plantings through a spring or fall cool season. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, fast-sizing roots, and harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across for the crispest texture.

common_name: Roy's Calais Flint Corn (Vermont Abenaki Flint Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as danger of frost passes; among the most cold-adapted flint corns available.
directions: Direct sow as soon as danger of frost passes; this is among the most cold-adapted flint corns available and reliably dries down even in short, cool Vermont-style growing seasons. Roy's Calais Flint traces to Abenaki agriculture in the Calais, Vermont area and was preserved through the twentieth century by farmer Roy Fair before seed steward Sylvia Davatz continued growing and distributing it, making it one of the best-documented survival stories among Northeastern landrace corns. Ears show a striking mix of yellow, red, and burgundy kernels on the same cob, and the corn is prized both for cornmeal and for polenta with a distinctively rich, sweet flint-corn flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into warm soil; sow again every few weeks for a continuous harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds one inch deep once frost danger has passed and soil is warm, with no trellis needed for these compact plants. The 15-20 inch bushes are well suited to containers and small gardens, producing deep-purple, stringless pods that stand out against the foliage. The pods turn green when cooked, making harvest easy since the purple is simple to spot. Pick regularly while pods are young and tender to keep the plants producing.

common_name: Royal Burgundy Bush Bean (Purple Pod Snap Bean That Turns Green When Cooked)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 60°F in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; the purple pod color disappears when Royal Burgundy is blanched or cooked — pods turn standard green, which some gardeners find surprising.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, thinning to 4–6 inches apart; Royal Burgundy is a bush snap bean producing vivid deep-purple pods that are immediately striking in the garden and make harvesting easy — the bright-purple color stands out against green foliage so ripe pods are much easier to spot than the green pods of standard snap beans. The purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that disappear completely when the beans are cooked — pods turn a standard snap-bean green when blanched or boiled, which is useful to know so the color loss is not mistaken for poor quality. The flavor is excellent: full, classic snap bean flavor with slightly more robust character than some modern hybrids. Royal Burgundy is notably cold-soil tolerant for a snap bean — germinating reliably in soil temperatures down to 60°F (versus the 65°F+ preferred by most snap beans), making it a good choice for early spring and fall plantings in zone 9 where soil temperatures can be borderline for bean germination. The bush habit (18–24 inches, no staking required) and reliable early productivity (50–60 days) make Royal Burgundy one of the more practical ornamental-vegetables for Gulf South kitchen gardens, combining harvest efficiency with decorative garden impact.

common_name: Royalty Purple Pod Bean (AAS-Winning Purple Bush Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Royalty Purple Pod germinates well in cooler soil than most snap beans (down to 55°F) — an advantage for early planting in zones 5–7 where it is often planted 2 weeks before the safe date for other beans. In zone 9, plant March–May or August–September. The purple pod color allows easy pod detection during harvest — the purple pods stand out visually against the dark green foliage, making picking faster and more complete than with green-podded varieties.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost; harvest pods when 5–6 inches long, while still tender and before the purple color begins to fade. Royalty Purple Pod is a 1976 All-America Selections-winning bush bean known for its striking deep purple pods — an unusual color in the snap bean world and a practical advantage because the vivid pods are easy to see against green foliage during harvest. The purple color results from anthocyanin pigments that disappear completely when cooked, leaving behind the standard green of cooked snap beans — a fact that surprises first-time growers who expect to retain the purple color. The flavor of Royalty is notably good — richer and slightly more complex than many modern bush bean hybrids — and the plants show slightly better cool-soil germination tolerance than green-podded snap beans. Royalty Purple Pod has maintained its status as a respected open-pollinated variety for nearly 50 years since its AAS award, used both as a practical garden bean and as a visual accent in edible landscapes where the purple-podded plants contrast attractively with green foliage.

plant_note: Start seed indoors and transplant 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost for the classic autumn crop; Rubicon's bolt tolerance also allows a riskier late-summer direct sowing in cooler climates.
directions: Transplant into rich, consistently moist soil, keeping plants well watered to prevent tipburn and premature bolting. Rubicon forms dense, barrel-shaped heads with good resistance to fusarium yellows, making it a reliable choice where soilborne disease has hurt other napa types. Harvest when heads feel firm and heavy; the tight wrap holds well in the field and in cold storage. Its balanced sweet-mild flavor suits both fresh kimchi and quick stir-fries.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–March. Ruby chard is more ornamental than standard white-stalked chard — the deep crimson stems and dark green leaves are striking in kitchen and ornamental gardens. Harvest outer leaves continuously to extend production. In zone 9 Ruby Chard is productive from fall through early spring; it tolerates light frost and continues growing through mild zone 9 winters, providing fresh greens when little else is producing.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ruby Chard is the classic red-stemmed Swiss chard variety with deep crimson-red midribs and stems against dark, slightly crinkled green leaves — one of the most ornamental of all vegetables and a perennial favorite in both kitchen gardens and edible ornamental designs. The striking color contrast of red stem against dark green makes Ruby Chard effective as a garden border plant, in containers, and in ornamental beds where most vegetables would look out of place. The same mild, slightly earthy, spinach-like flavor of all Swiss chard makes Ruby excellent for sautéing with garlic, adding to soups, and wilting into pasta dishes where the vibrant red stems retain some color even after cooking. As a dual-use ornamental and culinary vegetable, Ruby Chard demonstrates that the most productive kitchen garden plants need not sacrifice ornamental appeal. The partial shade tolerance makes it one of the better vegetables for partially shaded kitchen garden spaces.

common_name: Ruby Crush Tomato (Texas Superstar Compact Disease-Resistant Grape Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Ruby Crush is a Texas Superstar determinate grape tomato bred with a broad disease resistance package, previously honored as a San Antonio Stock Show and Rodeo tomato before its Superstar designation.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Ruby Crush is a Texas Superstar-designated determinate grape tomato, compact enough for smaller garden beds and large containers, bred with a broad package of disease resistance that helps it hold up through the humid, disease-prone conditions of a Texas and Gulf South growing season. It produces heavy clusters of sweet, crack-resistant red grape tomatoes over a concentrated harvest window typical of determinate varieties, making it a good choice for gardeners who want a big, manageable crop for fresh eating or canning without the sprawling growth of an indeterminate vine. A light stake or cage helps keep the fruit-laden branches off the ground. Harvest regularly as fruit ripens to keep the plant productive through its season.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant outdoors once nights stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Ruby King is an American heirloom sweet bell pepper documented since at least 1902 and preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network after a 1977 donation. It sets heavy clusters of blocky, thick-walled fruit that ripen from green to a deep glossy red, with a mild, sweet flavor that holds up well fresh or cooked. Give plants full sun and consistent moisture, and stake or cage heavily loaded branches since the large fruit can weigh down stems. Its earlier maturity than many modern giant bells makes it a reliable choice for gardeners in shorter-season regions.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out for a spring crop, or start in mid to late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Ruby Perfection is an All-America Selections winner bred for uniform, dense red heads and reliable performance.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in late summer for a fall crop. Ruby Perfection, an All-America Selections winner, forms dense, round, deep reddish-purple heads that hold their color and quality well, both in the garden and in storage, on a compact plant bred for uniform heading and dependable performance across varying growing conditions. Its rich color makes it a striking addition to salads, slaws, and pickled preparations in addition to standard cooked use. Keep soil evenly moist through head formation to prevent splitting, and harvest when heads feel firm and dense to the touch.

plant_note: Sow in early spring and again in late summer; beets grow best in cool weather.
directions: Sow the seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings so each root has a few inches to swell. This 1957 All-America Selections winner produces round, dark-red roots with mild, sweet flavor and tender texture. Keep soil evenly moist for smooth, non-woody roots, and do not skip thinning, since each cluster yields several plants. Harvest roots when they reach two to three inches, and enjoy the nutritious greens as an added bonus.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks after danger of frost has passed; plant alongside another sugary-enhanced variety to improve pollination and kernel fill.
directions: Ruby Queen is a sugary-enhanced hybrid grown as much for its deep ruby-red kernels as for its old-fashioned corn flavor, with 8 inch ears carrying 16 to 18 rows on 7-foot stalks. Harvest at the blush stage for the sweetest eating, or let ears ripen further to full red for a richer, more traditional corn taste; steam, grill, or microwave rather than boil to keep the color from fading into the cooking water. The red tassels and husks make the standing plants attractive in the garden and useful for fall decorating even before the ears are picked. Choose it when a gardener wants a novelty-colored sweet corn that still delivers genuinely good fresh eating rather than an ornamental-only variety.

plant_note: Sow in spring for a long harvest through fall; year-round in mild climates.
directions: 'Ruby Red' is an 1850s heirloom chard with vivid red stems and veins that beautifies the garden and provides greens from early summer into fall. Direct sow the seed clusters 1/2 inch deep and thin to 6-12 inches apart for full-size plants. This vigorous, long-season grower keeps producing when outer leaves are harvested regularly. Use young leaves raw in salads and mature leaves and stems cooked; it tolerates light frost.

common_name: Ruby Red Chard (Rhubarb Chard, Red-stalked Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow fall through early winter (September–November in zone 9) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Ruby Red chard is one of the most ornamental edibles for the vegetable garden — the brilliant crimson stems and red-veined, glossy dark-green leaves are as decorative as they are nutritious.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 6–9 inches; harvest outer leaves continuously. Beta vulgaris 'Ruby Red' (Ruby Red chard or Rhubarb chard) is a variety of Swiss chard selected for its dramatic, brilliant red stems (petioles) and red-veined dark-green to red-flushed leaves — making it simultaneously one of the most ornamental and one of the most nutritious crops in the vegetable garden. The vivid crimson stems get their color from betalain pigments (the same pigment group responsible for red beet color) which have antioxidant properties. The flavor is mild and slightly earthy, similar to spinach with a slightly stronger taste; the stems are firmer and need slightly longer cooking than the leaves. In zone 9, Ruby Red chard is a superb fall-through-spring crop, sown from September through November for harvest from November through May — it tolerates light frost and performs through the cool season until summer heat bolts it. The ornamental value is substantial: planted in rows or mixed borders, the glowing red stems create strong visual impact, making this one of the few vegetables that earns a place in ornamental beds. As with all chard, cut-and-come-again harvest extends production for months.

plant_note: Long-day type for northern gardeners; start early and transplant while weather is cool.
directions: Start seeds indoors about two months before transplanting, since onions require a long growing season. This long-day variety forms bulbs as summer days lengthen, making it well suited to northern gardens. Set transplants into loose, fertile soil and keep them weeded and evenly watered as the bulbs size up. The medium to large globes have firm white flesh and burgundy skins that store well after proper curing.

plant_note: Sow in early spring for a long harvest; a second sowing extends production into fall.
directions: Soak seed clusters overnight and sow half an inch deep, then thin the seedlings since each cluster produces several plants. This heirloom chard shows off deep ruby stems against glossy green leaves, adding bold color to the garden. Harvest tender baby leaves for salads or let leaves mature for cooking, always taking the outer ones first. With steady moisture and regular picking, the plants keep producing through the season on a cut-and-come-again basis.

common_name: Ruby Red Swiss Chard (Classic Deep-Red Stem Rhubarb Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest, or February–March for spring. Ruby Red is one of the most cold-tolerant chard varieties, surviving light freezes and tolerating temperatures into the mid-20s°F in established plantings. The intense red stem color develops most vividly in cool fall and winter growing conditions — heat reduces the pigmentation intensity. Begin harvesting outer leaves once plants are 6–8 inches tall; regular harvest encourages continued production from the growing center.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; thin to 9–12 inches. Harvest outer leaves regularly, leaving the growing center intact. Ruby Red Swiss Chard (also called Rhubarb Chard for the resemblance of the brilliant crimson stems to culinary rhubarb stalks) is the original and defining red-stemmed chard — the variety from which all colored-stem selections and rainbow chard blends derive. Ruby Red produces large, dark green, heavily crinkled and savoyed leaves on vivid crimson to ruby-red stems and midribs — a color combination that makes the plant one of the most ornamentally striking vegetables in the cool-season garden, visually dramatic against the dark green leaf tissue. The crimson pigment in Ruby Red's stems is betacyanin — the same class of pigment found in red beets (Beta vulgaris, the same genus) — a natural antioxidant with deep red to violet-red coloration. Ruby Red has longer American cultivation history than most colored chard types, appearing in American seed catalogs under 'Rhubarb Chard' nomenclature for well over a century. The flavor is classic chard — mild and slightly earthy-sweet when young, more substantial and beet-adjacent in mature leaves. The red stem color is retained reasonably well through steaming but bleeds in boiling water; roasting or sautéing in fat preserves the best color.

common_name: Ruby Streaks Mustard (Red Frills Mustard, Deeply Cut Red Mustard)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall (zones 7–11) or early spring (zones 3–7); Ruby Streaks is a deeply serrated, feathery, ruby-red to dark burgundy mustard green whose finely cut leaves resemble flat-leaf parsley in form but are dramatically larger, more colorful, and with the characteristic sharp mustard bite — it is the standard 'red frills' mustard in mesclun and salad mix production and one of the most visually striking cool-season greens available.
directions: Broadcast seed thinly or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep; for baby leaf harvest sow thickly and cut at 3–4 inches (2–3 weeks); for mature plants thin to 6–8 inches; harvest outer leaves or cut the whole plant at 4–6 inches above the crown for cut-and-come-again; the pungent flavor mellows with cooking. Ruby Streaks is a deeply serrated, feathery-leaved mustard green with deeply incised, almost pinnately cut leaves that create a lacey, frilly appearance dramatically different from the broad flat or ruffled leaves of traditional Southern mustard varieties — the leaf form is sometimes compared to flat-leaf parsley or baby arugula but scaled up and colored an intense burgundy-red to dark purple-red throughout. The name describes the appearance perfectly: the stems and veins are ruby-red while the deeply cut leaf tissue is a rich burgundy-maroon that becomes most intense in cold weather, making Ruby Streaks one of the most visually dramatic cool-season greens available for garden beds and mesclun mixes. The flavor is strongly mustardy with a sharp, spicy edge that makes it an excellent salad mix component providing flavor contrast to milder greens (lettuce, spinach, mild arugula) and visual color interest; young leaves (3–4 weeks) are mild enough for raw eating while mature leaves (5–6 weeks) have significant heat that benefits from brief cooking or a vinegar-dressed wilted salad. Ruby Streaks is one of the standard components of the premium mesclun salad mix sold under names like 'Braising Mix' and 'Asian Salad Mix' in American specialty markets.

common_name: Rudolf Radish (Extra-Early Bright Red Spring Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; Rudolf is one of the fastest-maturing spring radishes available, producing smooth, bright red, round roots in as little as three weeks.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Rudolf is bred for extremely fast maturity, often ready to harvest in as little as three weeks from sowing, among the quickest radishes available, making it an excellent choice for gardeners wanting the fastest possible turnaround or squeezing in an extra succession planting before summer heat arrives. Roots are smooth, round, and bright cherry-red with crisp white flesh and a clean, mild flavor typical of quick-maturing spring radishes. Because it matures so fast, timing the harvest promptly is especially important, since even quick radishes turn pithy and hollow if left in the ground too long after reaching full size. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows.

plant_note: Sow around or just after last frost; runner beans prefer cooler summers than common beans and will drop flowers in intense heat.
directions: Sow seeds 2 in deep at the base of a robust trellis or obelisk at least 6 ft tall; runner beans are vigorous climbers and will overwhelm light supports. The scarlet flowers attract hummingbirds and are themselves edible. Pick pods frequently at 6–8 in before they become stringy; pods left to mature inhibit further flowering. In frost-free climates, tuberous roots can be overwintered and will regrow the following spring.

plant_note: Direct sow every 2-3 weeks from early spring through fall; Runway was bred for a slower bolt response, extending the harvest window in warm weather compared to older arugula strains.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly into cool, moisture-retentive soil for fast, even germination. Runway produces smooth, rounded, dark green leaves with a clean, moderately spicy flavor and was selected by seed breeders for a notably slower bolt response, letting growers hold plantings longer into warm weather before they turn bitter and go to seed. It performs well both as a quick baby-leaf crop for salad mixes and, with wider spacing, as a full-size bunching arugula. Succession sow every couple of weeks for continuous cutting through the cool season.

common_name: Russet Burbank Potato (Classic Idaho Baking Potato, Most Widely Grown US Potato)
plant_note: Plant seed potato pieces (each with 2–3 eyes) in cool soil; Russet Burbank is a late-season variety requiring 80–100 days and a long cool season to develop its characteristic large, well-formed tubers. In zone 9, plant January–February for a spring harvest (April–June), before summer heat forces the plant into dormancy. Russet Burbank performs better in cool climates (zones 3–7) than in zone 9, where the brief cool window and tendency for early spring heat can limit tuber size and number; varieties such as Red Norland or Kennebec may perform more consistently in zone 9. However, the Russet Burbank can produce good crops in zone 9 with January planting in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Harvest when vine tops die back and skins have set. Cure in a cool, dark location for 10–14 days before storage.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces in trenches 4 inches deep; hill soil around plants as they grow. Harvest when tops die back. Russet Burbank is the most economically important potato variety in the United States — the potato that defined American french fry culture and continues to be the dominant variety grown commercially in Idaho, Washington, and Oregon. The variety's history traces to Luther Burbank, the famous plant breeder of Lunenburg, Massachusetts, who developed the 'Burbank' potato in 1875 — a white-skinned, prolific variety. A natural bud sport of the Burbank with netted russet skin emerged in the late 19th century and was selected for its superior baking qualities: the russet skin variety produced the floury, high-starch, dry flesh that makes for the ideal baked potato — a fluffy interior with a crisp, well-cured skin that holds its shape. The high starch content of Russet Burbank also makes it the preferred variety for making french fries: when fried, the high starch content produces the crispy exterior and fluffy interior texture that defines the classic fast-food french fry. McDonald's adopted Russet Burbank (specifically the 'Russet Burbank' and later selected clones) as the basis for their standardized french fry program, and this relationship made the variety synonymous with American potato processing. The tubers are very large (often 8–16 oz), oblong, with rough russet-brown skin and bright white flesh — the visual standard for 'Idaho potato' that most Americans associate with baked potatoes.

plant_note: Plant whole small tubers or cut large ones with 1–2 eyes in January–February in zone 9; Russian Banana fingerlings are typically planted whole (they are small enough) rather than cut. They mature in 70–90 days and should be harvested before summer heat in zone 9 — target April–May harvest.
directions: Plant whole small tubers or cut pieces 3–4 inches deep in loose, rich soil; Russian Banana is the most widely grown fingerling potato in the United States, an heirloom variety brought from Eastern Europe (likely Latvia or Russia) by immigrants in the early 20th century. The distinctive, curved, 3–4 inch tubers with smooth, pale yellow skin and deep golden-yellow flesh look remarkably like small bananas when harvested and rinsed — hence the name. Flavor is exceptional: buttery, nutty, and intensely potato-tasting with the creamy texture of a waxy potato that holds its shape beautifully when roasted, boiled, or pan-fried with herbs. Russian Banana fingerlings have become the premium specialty potato at farmers' markets and upscale restaurants because of their appearance, flavor, and versatility. Harvest when plants begin to die back; fingerlings store well in a cool, dark location after curing. In zone 9, plant January–February for April–May harvest. The small size makes them quick to cook — roasted whole with olive oil and rosemary, they are outstanding.

plant_note: Sow 12–14 weeks before the expected first autumn frost so roots mature in cool weather.
directions: Sow seeds 1/2 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil; rutabagas need more time and space than turnips to produce their large storage roots. Thin to 6–8 in once seedlings are established and keep soil evenly moist to prevent splitting. Flavor is significantly improved by frost, so aim to leave roots in the ground until after the first hard freeze. Harvest before the ground freezes solid and store in a cool, humid root cellar for several months.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Rutgers is an indeterminate variety that performs well with staking or caging and produces reliably in a wide range of climates from spring through early fall.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Rutgers tomato is a historically significant American heirloom, developed in 1934 as a joint project between Rutgers University and the Campbell Soup Company, that became the dominant processing and fresh-market tomato in America from the 1940s through the 1970s — the reference standard for what a traditional American garden tomato should taste like. The medium-large (6–8 oz), slightly flattened, deep red, globe-shaped fruits have a firm but yielding texture with balanced sweet-acid traditional tomato flavor that is widely praised as a benchmark for real tomato taste in contrast to modern flavorless commercial varieties. Rutgers is neither the most disease-resistant nor the highest yielding tomato today, but it remains a beloved open-pollinated heirloom for gardeners who want authentic vintage tomato flavor, the ability to save seeds, and a piece of American agricultural history. The indeterminate plants reach 4–5 feet and benefit from staking; Rutgers is well-suited to the Northeast and mid-Atlantic where it was developed but grows well in most climates including the Gulf South in spring and fall seasons.

common_name: Sacha Inchi (Inca Peanut, Mountain Peanut, Star Nut)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of frost passes; provide a sturdy trellis or support structure (12–15 feet or more) for the vigorous climbing vines. In zone 9, sacha inchi can be grown as a perennial in the warmest sites, dying back in frost but resprouting from roots.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant into well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun with a strong trellis for support; Sacha inchi (also called Inca peanut, star nut, or sacha mani) is a high-altitude Amazonian climbing vine (Plukenetia volubilis, family Euphorbiaceae) native to the cloud forests and montane tropics of Peru, Colombia, and Bolivia, grown for its remarkable star-shaped seed capsules (typically 4-lobed, looking like geometric 4-pointed stars) containing large, oil-rich seeds with an extraordinary nutritional profile — the roasted seeds contain 48–54% oil (the highest of any cultivated edible nut, higher than macadamia) with exceptionally high omega-3 fatty acid content (49% of the oil by weight), making it among the richest plant sources of alpha-linolenic acid. The oil is marketed internationally as a premium cooking and supplement oil with a pleasant, nutty flavor. The seeds are eaten roasted (raw seeds contain alkaloids that are destroyed by roasting) and have a mild, pleasant flavor similar to peanuts. Sacha inchi grows vigorously in humid tropical to subtropical conditions (zones 9b–12) and produces the decorative star-shaped green to brown capsules approximately 6–9 months after planting; the fruits are attractive in the landscape as well as productive.

plant_note: Nick or file the hard seed coat until the white inner surface is visible, then soak in warm water (changed daily) until the seed swells and a sprout emerges; transplant to a wide, shallow container of heavy clay garden soil without drainage holes, submerged 2–6 inches below the water surface in full sun.
directions: Nick the hard seed coat and soak in warm water until sprouting; transplant to a wide, shallow tub of heavy clay soil submerged 2–6 inches below the water surface in full sun — sacred lotus is one of the most magnificent aquatic plants on Earth and one of the most culturally significant plants in human history, sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, and ancient Egyptian tradition. The enormous, water-repelling leaves (2 feet across) on tall stems and fragrant, luminous pink or white flowers up to 12 inches wide rising 4–6 feet above the water are incomparably beautiful. Every part is edible: the crunchy, lace-patterned rhizomes (lotus root) are a prized vegetable in Asian cuisine, the seeds are eaten raw when young or dried and roasted, the large leaves are used to wrap food for steaming. The lotus is winter-hardy in zone 5–10 if the rhizomes are protected from freeze. It grows best in a large (15+ gallon) container sunk in a pond or placed in full sun.

common_name: Sadandy Southern Pea (Early Purple Hull Cream Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has passed; Sadandy is a fast, heat-tolerant Louisiana heirloom that can be succession sown every few weeks through midsummer for a continuous Gulf South harvest.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing seeds a few inches apart in rows and thinning if needed. Sadandy is a Louisiana heirloom purple hull-type southern pea prized for its unusually early maturity and heavy, concentrated fruit set on compact, bushy plants, letting gardeners get a full picking in one or two passes rather than the extended trickle typical of many purple hulls. Pods mature to a deep purple that shows clearly against the green foliage, signaling when the cream-colored peas inside are ready to shell, and the pods hold well without shattering even in Gulf Coast heat and humidity. Like other cowpeas its roots fix nitrogen, so it also serves well as a quick-turnaround soil-building crop between spring and fall vegetables. Harvest at the purple-pod stage for fresh shelling or let dry fully on the vine for storage peas.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, spring-sow February–March and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Safari is a modern hybrid zucchini bred for a strong disease-resistance package, including tolerance to several common squash viruses and powdery mildew, which helps the compact, open bush stay productive and healthy later into the season than many older open-pollinated varieties manage in humid climates. The smooth, dark green, cylindrical fruit has tender, mild flesh typical of good zucchini, and the plant's heavy, sustained yield makes it a solid choice for gardeners who have struggled with squash bugs, vine borers, or mildew shortening the productive life of past plantings. Pick at six to eight inches long for the best texture, and harvest every day or two once fruit begins setting to keep the vigorous plant in steady production.

plant_note: Sow early in spring; safflower has a deep taproot that scavenges subsoil moisture, making it the most drought-resistant oilseed for dryland gardens.
directions: Plant seed 1 in deep at 6–10 in apart in rows 18–24 in wide; safflower needs a long growing season so early planting in cool soil is critical. The plant grows a large rosette in the vegetative phase, then bolts to form spiny, branching heads with brilliant orange or yellow florets. Harvest when the heads are dry and papery — cut and place in cloth bags to finish drying, then thresh by rubbing to release the seed. Safflower oil is prized for its high linoleic acid content and heat stability; the petals can also be used as a saffron substitute.

common_name: Saint Valery Carrot (Heritage French Long Orange Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (August–September in zone 9) in deep, loose, sandy loam or well-prepared raised beds; Saint Valery produces long roots (8–10 inches) requiring very deep, stone-free, loosened soil — amend heavy clay with raised beds or deep double-digging for good root development.
directions: Direct sow in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Saint Valery is one of the oldest and most prestigious heritage carrot varieties — a 19th-century French heirloom from the Normandy coast town of Saint-Valery-en-Caux, producing long (8–10 inches), tapered, vivid deep-orange roots with a smooth skin, blunt tip, and sweet, richly flavored orange flesh that is considered among the finest-flavored of all heirloom carrot varieties. The deep, saturated orange color (more vivid than many modern varieties) comes from very high beta-carotene content, giving Saint Valery both excellent flavor and outstanding nutritional quality. The long, tapering root form requires deep, loose, stone-free soil for straight, well-formed roots — in shallow or compacted soil, the roots fork and twist around obstacles. Raised beds filled with deep, friable, sandy loam produce the best specimens. In zone 9, Saint Valery is a fall and winter crop: sow in August or September for harvest from November through February when the cool temperatures bring out the characteristic sweetness that makes heritage carrots like Saint Valery memorable. Carrots actually improve in flavor after light frost exposure — the cold converts starches to sugars, intensifying sweetness. Leave in the ground and harvest as needed through winter rather than pulling the entire crop at once.

plant_note: Direct sow in deeply worked, stone-free soil 12-16 weeks before the first fall frost; this landrace needs a long, cool finishing period to bulk up its enormous root.
directions: Sow directly since the massive taproot resents transplanting, and thin aggressively to give each plant a full 2-3 foot circle of loose, deeply tilled soil. Named for the volcanic island near Kagoshima where it originated, this cultivar can swell to 40-100 pounds while staying surprisingly dense and low-fiber compared to other giant radishes. Harvest before hard freezes and store in a cool root cellar; despite its size the flesh stays sweet and is prized locally for simmered dishes and pickling.

plant_note: Succession sow from early spring; heat tolerance extends the harvest window.
directions: This blend combines award-winning 'Green Salad Bowl' and 'Red Salad Bowl' loose-leaf lettuces for a colorful, flavorful, heat-tolerant mix. Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them since light aids germination, and thin to 8-12 inches or grow densely for baby greens. Harvest young leaves in a few weeks or pick outer leaves for a continuous cut-and-come-again supply. Its heat tolerance and slow bolting extend the picking season into warm weather.

common_name: Salad Bush Cucumber (AAS-Winning Compact Container Slicer)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Salad Bush is a compact bush-type cucumber with vines spreading only 24–30 inches — approximately half the spread of standard vining types — making it well suited to raised beds, container gardens, and small gardens where standard cucumbers would take too much space. No trellis is required, though light support improves air circulation. Plant 2 per 15-gallon container for patio production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; no trellis required for bush types, though light support improves air circulation and fruit quality. Salad Bush is a 1988 All-America Selections-winning slicing cucumber selected specifically for compact, bush-type growth that makes cucumber growing accessible in small gardens, raised beds, and large containers. Standard cucumber vines sprawl 5–8 feet in diameter and require significant trellis support; Salad Bush was bred to produce a compact plant (vines spreading only 24–30 inches) that fits in a large container or small raised bed section without consuming excessive space.
