The compact habit comes without sacrificing fruit quality: the 8-inch, dark green fruits have the same smooth, mild, sweet flavor and tender skin of the best standard slicing cucumbers, with good disease resistance including cucumber mosaic virus, scab, angular leaf spot, and powdery mildew. Fruit production is concentrated over a shorter window than vining types but can be extended with succession sowings 2–3 weeks apart. Salad Bush remains one of the most practical cucumber choices for balcony, patio, and small-space gardeners who want fresh cucumbers without a large garden footprint.

common_name: Saladmore Bush Cucumber (AAS-Winning Compact Slicing Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Saladmore Bush is a compact, semi-bush slicing cucumber (about 24 inches of spread) bred for strong disease resistance and small-space growing.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Saladmore Bush is an AAS-winning slicing cucumber bred for a genuinely compact semi-bush habit that still delivers a full-size harvest of straight, dark-green, 8-inch slicing cucumbers with crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor, on a plant that fits easily into small beds and large pots where a standard vining slicer would sprawl. It also carries strong resistance to several common cucumber diseases, giving it good vigor through a long summer season in humid climates. Keep soil evenly moist, especially as fruit is sizing, to avoid bitterness and misshapen cucumbers, and harvest regularly once fruiting begins to keep the plant productive.

common_name: Salanova Lettuce (Compact Cut-and-Come-Again Salad Lettuce Series)
plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Salanova is a breeding breakthrough lettuce series designed so that a single head, cut once at the base, falls apart into dozens of perfectly bite-sized, ready-to-eat baby leaves, dramatically speeding harvest compared to picking individual leaves by hand.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Salanova is a lettuce series bred specifically to solve the labor problem of harvesting baby salad greens leaf by leaf: each Salanova head grows as a tight rosette of dozens of small, uniform, bite-sized leaves attached at a single central core, so cutting the plant once at the base instantly yields a full bowl of ready-to-eat, pre-washed-looking salad leaves rather than a single lettuce head that needs chopping. It comes in multiple types — butterhead, oakleaf, and incised (frilly) forms in both green and red — allowing gardeners to plant a mix for varied color and texture in a single cutting. Because the leaves are already small, individual heads can be spaced fairly closely for high-density production, and successive sowings every two to three weeks keep a steady supply coming through the cool season. It bolts readily in summer heat, so plant in early spring and again in fall for the best results in zone 9, and provide afternoon shade for any late-spring or early-fall plantings that overlap with warm weather.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in sandy, saline, or coastal soil; salicornia is a remarkable halophyte (salt-tolerant plant) that thrives in conditions where almost no other vegetable grows — salt marshes, coastal flats, saline soils, and tide-edge gardens — and produces crunchy, bright green, segmented stems with a naturally salty, oceanic flavor used in gourmet cuisine as 'sea beans' or 'sea asparagus.'
directions: Sow seeds after last frost in sandy, well-drained soil; salicornia is one of the few vegetables that can be watered with dilute seawater or grown in genuinely saline soil where other vegetables die; harvest bright green stems by snipping with scissors when 3–6 inches long for the most tender eating quality. Salicornia (also called sea beans, glasswort, sea asparagus, samphire — not to be confused with rock samphire, Crithmum maritimum) is an annual succulent halophyte — a plant not merely tolerant of salt but actually thriving in salty, coastal environments — native to salt marshes, coastal mudflats, and tidal edges around the world. The plant is entirely leafless: instead of conventional leaves, it consists of jointed, fleshy, cylindrical green stems that branch repeatedly, creating a plant that looks like bright green coral or a miniature cactus. These stems are the edible part — crunchy, bright green, and naturally seasoned with sea salt stored in the plant tissues, with a distinctive briny, fresh, oceanic flavor and a crisp texture that makes raw eating possible without additional seasoning. Salicornia is prized in gourmet cooking as 'sea beans' — sautéed briefly in butter (excellent with fish and shellfish), pickled, used raw in salads for their crunch and natural seasoning, or served alongside seafood dishes where the marine flavor echo is an elegant touch. The plant was historically used in glass-making in coastal areas (hence 'glasswort' — the burned ash was used as an alkali source for soda-lime glass production). For Gulf Coast gardeners in zones 8b–10, salicornia can be grown in garden soil without salt amendment, or cultivated in genuinely saline coastal conditions where nothing else will grow.

plant_note: Direct sow as early as 2–4 weeks before last frost; the long season requires early sowing and deep, loose soil.
directions: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in deeply dug, stone-free soil; salsify develops long taproots that fork and deform in rocky or compacted ground. Thin to 3–4 inches after germination and keep weed-free, as salsify's grass-like tops are easily overwhelmed early on. Roots are ready in autumn when they reach pencil thickness and finger length; flavor improves markedly after hard frost. Roots can overwinter in the ground and be harvested as needed through winter in mild climates, or dig all roots in late fall and store in damp sand.

common_name: Salt and Pepper Cucumber (AAS-Winning White Speckled Seedless Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Salt and Pepper is a parthenocarpic (sets fruit without pollination) compact vining cucumber that can be grown in tunnels or outdoors. In zone 9, plant March–May for spring production and August for fall. The parthenocarpic character means the plant produces fruit without bees visiting — an advantage in early spring or in protected tunnel growing environments where pollinator access is limited. Harvest at 3–4 inches before the characteristic speckled pattern begins to fade to solid cream — once the speckles disappear the cucumber has become slightly overripe and may develop a slightly bitter note. The compact vine (4–5 feet) does not require extensive trellising but benefits from support for cleaner, straighter fruit.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when speckles are visible. Salt and Pepper is an F1 hybrid cucumber that received All-America Selections recognition for its distinctive appearance and exceptional eating quality. The fruit skin is white to pale cream with characteristic dark green to near-black speckles distributed across the surface — the 'salt and pepper' pattern that gives the variety its name and makes it immediately visually recognizable. Unlike heirloom types with similar light-colored skin (such as Boothby's Blonde), Salt and Pepper is an F1 hybrid bred for the parthenocarpic (seedless) character that allows fruit set without pollination — the interior is nearly seed-free and extremely tender, with no tough seed cavity. The resulting texture is among the finest of any outdoor cucumber: exceptionally crisp, with virtually no bitterness, tender skin that requires no peeling, and very high water content producing a refreshing fresh-eating quality. Salt and Pepper produces abundantly and early — with the first ripe fruit typically appearing 57 days from direct sowing, making it one of the earliest-producing cucumbers available. For zone 9 gardeners, the early maturity and heat-set ability allow the variety to produce heavily in spring before summer heat becomes limiting, and the fall planting typically produces prolifically through October or November. The seedless character and very thin skin make Salt and Pepper one of the few cucumbers that market gardeners can sell without refrigeration for brief periods, as the intact skin and low seed cavity reduce the moisture loss that causes conventional cucumbers to shrivel.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings directly in consistently wet, saline to brackish sandy or muddy soil in full sun; saltwort is a true salt marsh specialist and will not thrive in ordinary garden soil or fresh water alone — it needs tidal, brackish, or salted conditions to perform.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings directly into consistently wet, saline to brackish sand or mud in full sun along tidal flats, salt marsh edges, or artificially salted raised beds; saltwort is one of the few true halophytes grown for food, an edible succulent similar in use to samphire or sea beans. Jointed, cylindrical, fleshy stems form a low, spreading, olive-green mat, and the crisp, salty-tangy young stem tips are harvested and eaten fresh in salads, pickled, or lightly sautéed. It naturally colonizes the upper edges of salt marshes and mangrove fringe, tolerating regular tidal inundation and salinity that would kill nearly any other vegetable crop, but it needs that salinity to compete against weeds and grow vigorously. Harvest tips regularly to encourage bushy branching, and expect the planting to spread steadily by rooting stems across suitable wet, saline ground.

plant_note: Fast-growing; sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Direct sow seeds shallowly in cool soil and thin lightly, as this fast crop is grown for its leaves, stalks, and buds rather than large heads. Also called rapini or rabe, it develops a bold, pleasantly bitter flavor prized in Italian cooking. Harvest when the flower buds appear but before they open, cutting the whole plant near the base. Because it grows quickly and prefers cool weather, succession sowing keeps a steady supply of tender greens.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: 'San Marzano' is the legendary Italian paste tomato, an indeterminate pole type bearing meaty, low-seed plum fruits ideal for sauce and canning. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, full-sun soil. Support the tall vines with sturdy stakes or cages and prune suckers to focus energy on fruit. Consistent watering helps prevent blossom-end rot; harvest when fully red for peak flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights stay above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a spring crop and again in August–September for a fall crop, as the extreme summer heat causes blossom drop. San Marzano is an indeterminate vine requiring sturdy caging or staking.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake as San Marzano is a vigorous indeterminate vine reaching 5–6 feet or more. The elongated, plum-shaped fruits with pointed blossom ends are the gold standard for pasta sauce and canned tomatoes — they are low in moisture, dense in flesh, mildly acidic, and have few seeds, making them ideal for reduction into rich sauces. Prune to 2–3 main stems for the largest individual fruits; unpruned plants produce more fruits but smaller. This Italian heirloom from the Campania region near Naples has DOP status in Italy, though the variety sold in the U.S. performs very differently from its Italian counterpart under different soil and climate conditions.

common_name: Sandia Pepper (New Mexico Green Chile, Medium-Hot Roasting Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Sandia is a medium-hot New Mexico-style green chile excellent for roasting at both the immature green stage and the fully ripe red stage. Harvest green peppers when they are full-sized (6–8 inches) for fresh roasted green chile use; allow remaining fruits to mature to red for dried red chile production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; Sandia is a New Mexico State University-developed chile variety named after the Sandia Mountains near Albuquerque, bred to fill a flavor and heat niche between the mild Anaheim-type peppers and the hotter NuMex Big Jim — producing long (6–8 inch), meaty, thick-walled green chiles with a medium heat level (approximately 1,000–2,500 Scoville units) that provides a pleasant warmth without overwhelming heat and excellent roasted green chile flavor. The thick walls and dense flesh roast beautifully — the skin blisters and chars evenly while the interior steams to a silky, rich texture — making Sandia an excellent choice for all traditional New Mexico green chile preparations including green chile stew, chile rellenos, and roasted chiles packed in the freezer for winter use. As the fruits mature to red and dry, Sandia provides good red chile powder with medium heat and authentic New Mexico chile flavor. Sandia performs well in a wide range of climates including the humid Gulf South, where its thick-walled flesh resists decay better than thinner-walled varieties. One of the most important green chile varieties in the New Mexico tradition alongside NuMex Big Jim, Hatch, and Numex Joe E. Parker.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, and again in late summer for fall harvest; Sandy is a compact oakleaf lettuce, the first AAS lettuce winner since 1985, bred for slow bolting and strong powdery mildew resistance.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer, thinning to about 8-10 inches apart since Sandy forms a compact, uniformly mounded loose head rather than a large sprawling plant. Named an All-America Selections winner as the first lettuce to earn the award since 1985, Sandy is an oakleaf type with a multitude of sweet, frilly, dark green lobed leaves, notable disease resistance (especially to powdery mildew), and a strong tolerance for heat and heat-stress bitterness that lets it hold quality well past when older lettuces would bolt. Its compact 10-12 inch mounded habit fits neatly into a flowerpot, raised bed, or tight garden row. Harvest by cutting whole loose heads at maturity, or pick outer leaves cut-and-come-again style for baby leaf salads in as little as 30 days.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this early-to-mid season red potato sizes up quickly for a June or early-summer harvest.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Sangre is a Colorado-bred round red potato developed for the western US fresh-market trade, prized for its smooth, bright red skin and shallow eyes that make for clean, attractive market tubers. The white flesh is moderately moist and holds its shape well when boiled, making it a solid choice for potato salads, roasting, and general table use. It bulks up earlier than many maincrop reds, making it a good option where an early harvest of good-looking red new potatoes is wanted. Grow it alongside a russet or yellow variety for a mixed-color early harvest.

plant_note: Start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; Sangria carries resistance to anthracnose and Fusarium wilt and produces the classic large, oblong shipping-type melon long grown across Southern watermelon country.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Sangria is a widely grown seeded watermelon hybrid bred with resistance to anthracnose and Fusarium wilt, giving it reliable performance in the hot, humid disease pressure typical of a Gulf South summer. It produces large, oblong, dark green-striped fruit in the classic 20-24 pound shipping-melon range, with firm, deep red, sweet flesh that holds up well to handling and short-term storage. The vigorous vines set fruit dependably over a long harvest window. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.

common_name: Santa Claus Melon (Christmas Melon, Piel de Sapo)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Santa Claus melon (Piel de Sapo = 'Toad's Skin' in Spanish) is a late-season Spanish heirloom with extraordinary keeping quality — mature fruits store for 3–6 months at room temperature, traditionally used to provide fresh melon for the Christmas holiday season, which gives it both its nicknames.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Santa Claus melon requires 90–110 days to maturity, so start early or choose a long-season location; it is well-suited to Gulf Coast and California gardens. Piel de Sapo (literally 'Toad's Skin') is a Spanish winter melon variety widely grown throughout the Iberian Peninsula and used as the Christmas melon (melon de invierno) because its extraordinary keeping quality — 3–6 months at room temperature without refrigeration — allows harvest in October to be enjoyed fresh through December and January. The large (8–15 lb), elongated-oval fruits have mottled green and yellow skin with irregular markings resembling a toad's skin (the Spanish common name); the flesh is pale green to white-cream with a sweet, mild, refreshing flavor different from the aromatic intensity of muskmelon types. Sold in American markets as 'Santa Claus melon' and widely available in Hispanic grocery stores year-round due to its storage ability. Requires full sun and a long, warm season; sets fruit reliably in Gulf Coast and Western gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Santa Fe Grande is an outstanding heat-tolerant pepper that produces prolifically through the Gulf Coast summer and is highly resistant to tobacco mosaic virus.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Santa Fe Grande is a versatile wax-type pepper that ripens through yellow, orange, and finally red, with heat levels ranging from very mild at the yellow stage to moderately hot at full red maturity (500–1,000 SHU). This variety is particularly valued by Southern gardeners for its exceptional summer productivity — the plants set fruit even in high heat and humidity and continue producing well past the point where most pepper varieties slow down. The thick, waxy, cone-shaped fruits are 3–4 inches long with a crisp texture excellent for pickled peppers, fresh eating, and stuffing. Excellent disease resistance including tobacco mosaic virus.

plant_note: Start indoors early with warmth; transplant well after frost.
directions: 'Santaka' is a hot Japanese chile, just 2 inches long but delivering 40,000-50,000 Scoville units of spicy heat. Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before the last frost with warm soil for reliable germination, then transplant once nights stay warm. Grow in full sun with even moisture and light feeding; the compact plants do well in containers. Harvest peppers red for full heat, and dry them for use in stir-fries and soups.

plant_note: Direct sow 1-2 weeks after last frost once soil reaches 65F, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early; Sarah's Choice was bred by Dr. Brent Loy at the University of New Hampshire for unusually high sugar content and resistance to powdery mildew and Fusarium wilt.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile hills after all frost danger has passed, planting 4-5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2. Sarah's Choice is a widely respected muskmelon bred by Dr. Brent Loy's public breeding program at the University of New Hampshire, selected for unusually high sugar content — commonly 14-15% Brix, well above many commercial cantaloupe varieties — along with resistance to powdery mildew and Fusarium wilt, two of the most common disease problems that shorten the productive life of melon vines. The medium-sized, heavily netted fruit has firm, deep-orange, aromatic flesh with excellent flavor. Reduce watering as fruits near maturity to concentrate sugars further. Ripe melons develop a sweet fragrance at the blossom end and slip easily from the vine with gentle pressure — the classic 'full slip' sign of peak ripeness. Avoid overwatering late in the season, which dilutes flavor and can cause fruit to split.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Saticoy is a California commercial cantaloupe variety bred with good resistance to powdery mildew and fusarium wilt, two diseases that shorten productive vine life in warm growing regions, helping the vine stay healthy and productive through a full summer season. The uniform, well-netted, orange-fleshed fruit has good sweet flavor and consistent size, traits that made it a reliable choice for commercial growers and equally useful for home gardeners wanting dependable production. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the rind's netting has turned from green to tan, and hold off on extra watering in the final week before harvest for the sweetest flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer; Savanna tolerates more heat than most mustard without bolting, extending the harvest window on both ends of the season.
directions: Savanna is a fast-growing F1 hybrid mustard bred for exceptionally tender, smooth leaves and stems that stay mild and non-fibrous even as plants size up, letting the whole leaf and stem be harvested without trimming. It grows quickly enough to cut for baby salad greens within three weeks or left longer for a traditional cooked green, and its slow-bolting habit keeps it productive across a wider temperature range than older open-pollinated Southern mustards. Home gardeners and market growers choose it for cut-and-come-again harvesting, since new leaves regrow readily after cutting through the cool season.

common_name: Savoy Ace Cabbage (AAS-Winning Crinkled-Leaf Savoy Cabbage)
plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out for a spring crop, or start in mid to late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Savoy Ace is an All-America Selections winner bred for reliable heading and the tender, crinkled leaves characteristic of savoy-type cabbage.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in late summer for a fall crop, spacing plants to allow full head development. Savoy Ace, an All-America Selections winner, forms attractive, deeply crinkled, blue-green leaves wrapped into a dense, tender head, with the savoy type's characteristically milder flavor and more tender texture compared with smooth-leaf cabbage, making it excellent for salads as well as cooked dishes. It heads reliably even in less-than-ideal conditions that can cause other savoy cabbages to form loose or split heads. Keep soil evenly moist through head formation to prevent splitting, and harvest when heads feel firm when squeezed.

plant_note: Start transplants 6–8 weeks before setting out; set out 10–14 weeks before first fall frost for the classic autumn crop, or set out 4–6 weeks before last spring frost for a spring crop. Savoy cabbage is significantly more cold-tolerant than regular cabbage — hard frosts markedly improve sweetness and texture.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, deeply prepared soil; savoy cabbage is distinguished from standard green or red cabbages by its deeply wrinkled, crinkled, blistered leaves that form a less tightly packed, more loosely structured head — the deeply textured leaves are more tender, delicate, and sweet than smooth-leaved cabbages and are prized for raw salads, braising, stuffed cabbage rolls, and colcannon. The plant is markedly more cold-hardy than standard cabbages, tolerating hard frosts below 20°F when mature, and improves considerably in sweetness after exposure to frost. The spring crop tends to be less satisfying than fall-harvested heads; time fall planting so heads mature in cool autumn temperatures. Excellent varieties include 'Savoy Express' (early, compact), 'Savoy King' (large, late), and 'Deadon' (very cold-hardy). Rotate brassica family crops on a 3-year cycle to prevent clubroot buildup.

common_name: Savoy King Cabbage (AAS-Winning Savoyed Crinkled-Leaf Hybrid Cabbage)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, start in July and transplant late August–September for November–January harvest. Savoy King's crinkled leaves make it the most cold-hardy of common cabbage types — the loose, blistered structure allows the cells to flex during freezing rather than rupturing. Use savoy cabbage raw in salads (the tender leaves are softer than standard cabbage), cooked in soups where the crinkled leaves add texture, or wrapped around meat for stuffed cabbage rolls.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun, fertile soil. Savoy King is a 1965 All-America Selections-winning savoy (crinkle-leaved) cabbage — a type that differs fundamentally from standard smooth-headed cabbages in leaf texture, flavor, and culinary applications. Savoy cabbage produces the characteristic deeply blistered, puckered, crinkled leaves that make the head appear almost frilly compared to the smooth-skinned heads of standard green or red types. The crinkled texture comes from the faster growth rate of the leaf blade relative to the midrib — the excess blade tissue buckles and folds into the distinctive savoy pattern. Flavor-wise, savoy cabbage is notably sweeter, more tender, and less sulfurous than standard round cabbages — the crinkled leaves have a more delicate character that makes savoy preferred for raw salads (the soft, tender leaves wilt pleasantly rather than staying tough) and for elegant stuffed cabbage preparations where the flexible leaves wrap easily around fillings. Savoy King produces large (4–6 lb), well-domed, attractive heads with deep blue-green coloring and the decorative crinkled surface that makes it one of the most ornamental cabbages in the winter garden.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil is warm.
directions: This colorful patty pan blend combines the heirlooms 'Early White Bush', 'Bennings Green Tint', and 'Yellow Bush' for a bowl-worthy mix of scalloped summer squash. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil and space the bushy plants 24-36 inches apart in full sun. Harvest fruits young at 2-4 inches across when tender and flavorful, picking frequently to keep the plants producing. Steady moisture and rich soil support a heavy summer crop.

common_name: Scallopini Squash (AAS-Winning Hybrid Bush Scallop Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give each compact bush adequate airflow to reduce powdery mildew risk.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give each compact bush adequate airflow to reduce powdery mildew risk. Introduced in the mid-1970s as an All-America Selections winner, this cross between zucchini and pattypan types yields small, dark-green scalloped fruit with a mild, nutty flavor and tender skin that needs no peeling. Harvest young at 3-4 inches across for the best texture, picking every day or two once plants begin producing heavily. Its compact, non-vining habit made it a popular choice for small-space and container vegetable gardens when it was introduced.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost once the soil has warmed.
directions: Scarlet Emperor is a vigorous pole runner bean prized for its brilliant clusters of edible red flowers as well as its rich-flavored pods. Sow seeds 1 inch deep and 4-6 inches apart at the base of a tall trellis, fence, or pole after the soil warms in spring. Pick young pods for tender snap beans, or leave them to mature and shell for green or dried beans. Keep vines watered during flowering and harvest regularly to keep new pods forming. This variety doubles as an ornamental screen thanks to its showy blooms that attract hummingbirds.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; runner beans tolerate slightly cooler soil than common beans.
directions: Erect a tall trellis or teepee before sowing, since these vigorous vines climb up to ten feet. Direct sow seeds one to two inches deep after frost, and enjoy the showy scarlet blossoms that draw hummingbirds and pollinators. This ornamental heirloom is both beautiful and productive, yielding plenty of edible pods over the season. Pick pods young for tender eating, or let them mature to harvest the large seeds for cooking.

common_name: Scarlet Frills Mustard (Deep Maroon Frilled Mustard)
plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer; cooler temperatures deepen the maroon color and mellow the mustard's heat.
directions: This ornamental-edible mustard produces deeply fringed, almost lacy leaves in a rich burgundy-maroon that intensifies in cool weather and full sun. Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin to final spacing, using thinnings as spicy microgreens. Leaves can be harvested young for salad mix, where the color and frilled texture stand out, or left to mature for a peppery cooked green. Plants are attractive enough for mixed ornamental beds as well as the vegetable garden, but bolt quickly once summer heat arrives.

plant_note: Sow in spring or late summer; color and sweetness intensify with cold fall weather.
directions: Sow seeds half an inch deep and thin plants to give the upright rosettes room to grow. This edible and ornamental heirloom produces curly leaves in brilliant scarlet, magenta, and deep purple that stand two to three feet tall. Cool weather deepens both the color and the sweetness, making it a standout in the fall and winter garden. Harvest outer leaves as needed, and the plants will keep pushing new growth for months.

plant_note: Direct sow in loose, stone-free soil; keep the surface moist until seedlings emerge.
directions: Sow seed shallowly directly in the garden and thin seedlings to about 2 inches apart once they reach a couple inches tall. This sweet, nearly coreless heirloom develops best in deep, loose, well-drained soil free of rocks that can fork the roots. Keep the seedbed evenly moist during the slow germination period, which can take up to three weeks. Harvest when roots reach about six to seven inches and full color for the tenderest, sweetest flavor. Successive sowings from spring through midsummer extend the harvest.

common_name: Scarlet Ohno Revival Turnip (Red-Leafed Dual-Purpose Japanese Turnip)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall for fall harvest; Scarlet Ohno Revival is a visually stunning Japanese turnip with dramatic red-scarlet to magenta skin and flesh — one of the most beautiful root vegetables available — with mild, sweet turnip flavor at the small 2–3 inch stage; both the root and the brilliant red-tinged leaves are edible, making it a dual-purpose vegetable.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 4–6 inches apart for best root development; harvest at 2–3 inches diameter for the sweetest, mildest eating quality; the red coloration intensifies in cool weather; the leaves can be harvested as greens throughout the season. Scarlet Ohno Revival (sometimes marketed as 'Scarlet Queen Turnip') is a Japanese turnip variety with striking visual characteristics: the round roots have vivid scarlet to magenta-red skin with pink-red flesh throughout — much more deeply and uniformly colored than the more common 'Tokyo' types — and the broad basal leaves have dramatic red-tinged stems and midribs that make the plant ornamental in the garden as well as functional. The turnip was selected from an older Japanese variety ('Ohno Scarlet') by seed savers and represents a revival of an older type that had become rare. At harvest size (2–3 inches), the roots have a mild, slightly sweet turnip flavor quite different from the sharp, peppery bite of older turnip types — the Japanese breeding tradition favors mild, salad-turnip types that can be eaten raw, and Scarlet Ohno follows this tradition. The roots are excellent sliced thin into salads (the red color is dramatic against green lettuce), quick-pickled in the Japanese style (the red pigment turns the pickling brine a beautiful deep pink), roasted with the skin on (which deepens the color), or used in any turnip recipe where visual impact is valued.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after danger of hard frost in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; scarlet runner bean prefers cooler temperatures than most beans and slows or stops flowering in summer heat above 80°F — in zone 9a it is best grown in spring and fall. A sturdy trellis 5–6 feet tall is required.
directions: Direct sow after frost danger in fertile, moist soil on a tall trellis in full sun; scarlet runner bean is a dual-purpose ornamental and edible vine native to the mountains of Central America, producing brilliant scarlet (occasionally white or bicolor) flowers beloved by hummingbirds throughout the growing season, followed by long flat pods with striking maroon-speckled white seeds. Pods are harvested young as snap beans (very similar to pole beans in texture and flavor) or allowed to mature for the attractive dried beans used in soups and stews. The plant is a perennial in zones 7–11, where established tuberous roots resprout each season; in cooler zones treat as an annual. In zone 9a spring plantings often stop producing in summer heat — plant a second succession in late August for fall harvest.

common_name: Schoon's Hard Shell Melon (Heirloom Shipping Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Schoon's Hard Shell is a heirloom muskmelon long prized for its exceptionally tough, durable rind that let it stand up to shipping and field handling far better than most old melon varieties, while still ripening to richly flavored salmon flesh.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after soil has warmed well past last frost, allowing ample room for the vigorous vines to sprawl. Schoon's Hard Shell is a long-season heirloom muskmelon producing large, oval, heavily netted fruits, 7-8 inches long and 5-8 lbs, encased in an unusually thick, tough rind that made it an outstanding shipper and field-stander in an era before refrigerated transport, while the thick red-salmon flesh ripens to an intensely sweet, richly aromatic flavor. Because it is slow to mature relative to modern hybrids, gardeners in shorter-season regions may want to start it a bit earlier or choose a warm, sheltered planting site. Keep soil consistently moist through vine growth and fruit development, then reduce watering as melons approach maturity, and harvest at full slip when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit.

plant_note: Sow direct as soon as soil is workable in spring in deep, stone-free, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scorzonera requires deeply cultivated soil for long, straight roots — raised beds work well.
directions: Sow direct as soon as soil can be worked in spring in deep, stone-free, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; double-dig or use raised beds as scorzonera needs at least 12–18 inches of loose, unobstructed soil for long, straight roots — rocky or compacted soil produces forked, misshapen roots. Scorzonera hispanica is an underappreciated European root vegetable with long, black-skinned, white-fleshed taproots with a delicately sweet, oyster-like flavor that can be harvested in the first year but improves dramatically if left to mature for 18–24 months; the white sap that oozes from cut surfaces (a latex) can be rinsed away with cold water. Unlike most root vegetables, scorzonera is a true perennial that can be harvested selectively over multiple years; the young spring leaves and flower buds are also edible in salads. A gourmet vegetable widely popular in Belgium and the Netherlands.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant 2 weeks after frost danger has passed once soil is thoroughly warm.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in moist starting mix, maintaining soil at 85°F for best germination results; this Capsicum chinense type is among the slower starters. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil only after the garden is fully warm, and consider black plastic mulch to boost soil temperatures in cooler climates. The bonnet-shaped fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, or red depending on the strain and carry a distinctive fruity aroma alongside intense heat. Use gloves when handling ripe fruits; they are essential in Caribbean jerk seasoning and hot sauces.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant only after nights stay reliably warm.
directions: Start seed indoors eight or more weeks before the last frost, as this Caribbean chile needs warm soil and a long season to ripen. Transplant into the warmest part of the garden after the soil and nights have settled into the 60s. The fiery, fruity fruits mature from green to bright yellow-orange or red, so wait for full color for maximum heat and flavor. Consistent watering and a steady feed produce the heaviest yields. Wear gloves when handling the exceptionally hot pods.

plant_note: Start indoors 10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum chinense is slow to germinate and requires warm soil (80°F+) and a long growing season. In zone 9 start in January for a March transplant date. The plants thrive in the Gulf Coast's summer heat and produce prolifically through the fall; they may overwinter in protected zone 9b–10 locations.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil and nights have thoroughly warmed; the Scotch bonnet is the defining pepper of Caribbean cuisine, particularly Jamaican jerk and Trinidadian cooking, with a distinctive fruity-floral heat (100,000–350,000 SHU) and a unique, tropical, almost fruity aroma that separates it from habanero despite the close botanical relationship. The small, flattened, wrinkled fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, and red, and can be used at any ripe stage — the green stage has the most vegetal flavor while red fruits are sweetest and hottest. Unlike habaneros, genuine scotch bonnets have a more complex, sweeter aroma profile with notes of cherry and apple. The plants are tall and bushy, very productive in warm conditions, and benefit from staking as fruit clusters become heavy.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall in sandy, saline, or well-drained soil; sea beet establishes easily from seed and can be treated as a perennial in zones 8-11 or as a cool-season annual elsewhere.
directions: Sow seeds in coastal, sandy, or well-drained soil in full sun; sea beet is the wild ancestor of all cultivated beet varieties including table beet, chard, sugar beet, and mangelwurzel — the original plant from which millennia of selection produced all these crops. It grows naturally along European and North African coastlines in dry, sandy, often saline soils and is remarkably tolerant of salt, drought, and poor soil. The glossy, dark green leaves are edible exactly like chard, with an excellent fresh flavor that is actually more tender and less strongly flavored than cultivated chard. The fleshy root is small and woody compared to cultivated beets but edible. A fascinating plant for edible garden history and for coastal gardens where most vegetables struggle.

plant_note: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sea Island cotton needs an especially long, warm, humid growing season to produce its signature extra-long fiber.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm; Sea Island cotton is the extra-long-staple cotton species historically grown along the coastal Sea Islands of Georgia and South Carolina and now the source of premium Pima and Egyptian cotton fiber, distinct from the shorter-staple upland cotton grown across most of the Cotton Belt. Pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers fade to pink before dropping, revealing bolls that mature more slowly than upland cotton and split open to reveal exceptionally long, silky, fine fibers prized by hand-spinners for their smooth, lustrous quality. It requires a longer, warmer, more humid growing season than upland cotton to fully mature its bolls, making it best suited to the Gulf Coast and Deep South rather than shorter-season northern climates. Watch for the same boll weevil and aphid pressures common to cotton generally, and rotate planting location yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring harvest and July–August for fall. Sea Island Red Pea is a deeply historic Gullah/Geechee heirloom preserved for generations on the sea islands of Georgia and South Carolina, recently revived as part of Southern food heritage preservation.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; the Sea Island Red Pea is a semi-vining, dark-red-to-brown speckled cowpea that was the foundation of Gullah/Geechee cuisine on the sea islands of Georgia and South Carolina from the colonial period through the early 20th century. The variety served as the original ingredient in hoppin' john and purloo dishes before black-eyed peas replaced it in most recipes. It is an exceptional-flavored cowpea with earthy, rich, deeply savory notes and a dense, creamy texture when fresh-shelled that surpasses commercial black-eyed peas in the estimation of many who have tasted both. The vine habit is moderate — plants sprawl 2–3 feet and may benefit from short supports. Revived through efforts by the Anson Mills and Slow Food USA Ark of Taste programs.

plant_note: Sow seeds direct in early spring in deep, sandy to gravelly, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sea kale requires 2–3 years of establishment before harvesting — patience is rewarded with long-lived, extremely productive plants.
directions: Sow seeds direct in early spring in deep, sandy to gravelly, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; sea kale has a very long taproot and deeply resents transplanting — choose its permanent location carefully. Crambe maritima is a spectacular, ornamental-as-well-as-edible native of European coastal shingle beaches, producing large, blue-gray, crinkled, cabbage-like leaves and billowing clouds of tiny, honey-scented white flowers on 24–36-inch stems in early summer that are outstanding in the border; the young, blanched shoots are the edible crop, harvested in early spring by covering the dormant crown with a forcing pot or dark bucket 4–6 weeks before harvest, producing pale, sweetly nutty, asparagus-like shoots. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and long-lived, thriving in poor, well-drained soils in coastal and hot, dry inland gardens.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist sand or soil after last frost; the plant establishes quickly and can be planted directly into saline or sandy coastal soils.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this remarkable halophyte naturally colonizes tidal flats, beach margins, and coastal dunes where few other edibles survive, tolerating periodic saltwater flooding and saline spray. The succulent, bright-green to purplish leaves and stems have a pleasantly salty, crisp flavor — rinse before eating to reduce saltiness — and are excellent raw in salads, briefly stir-fried, or used as a sea-vegetable garnish. The plant forms a dense, prostrate mat that suppresses weeds and helps stabilize sandy soils against erosion. In zone 9–11 it is a reliable perennial that can be harvested throughout the year.

plant_note: Sow in early spring directly into sandy, free-draining soil; tolerates saline conditions and coastal exposure where most vegetables struggle.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, about 1/4 inch deep, directly into sandy or well-drained soil in a sunny position in early spring. Sea rocket is exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, coastal winds, and drought once established, requiring very little supplemental water. Harvest young, succulent leaves and stems regularly for use raw in salads where they contribute a pleasant peppery bite; young seed pods are also edible and can be added to salads or pickled. Allow some plants to set seed for reliable self-seeding in subsequent years.

common_name: Sea of Red Lettuce (Deep Red Frilly Oakleaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Sea of Red is a deeply colored, frilly-leaved oakleaf lettuce that holds its intense burgundy-red color and resists bolting and bitterness longer than many other red lettuce varieties, making it a reliable performer through a wider harvest window.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Sea of Red is an oakleaf-type lettuce prized for deeply lobed, ruffled, deep burgundy-red leaves that stay glossy and appetizing-looking even as outer leaves are repeatedly harvested, making it a favorite for cut-and-come-again baby leaf production as well as full-head harvest. It holds its rich color and resists premature bolting and the bitterness that develops in many red lettuces once temperatures climb, giving it a somewhat longer productive window than more heat-sensitive varieties, though it still performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons in zone 9. Harvest outer leaves as needed for continuous production, or cut the whole loose head at once for a single larger harvest. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings to further delay bolting as the weather warms.

plant_note: Sow in early fall while soil is still warm for a long fall-through-winter harvest window in mild-winter climates.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained beds and thin to stand a few inches apart, keeping soil consistently moist to support quick establishment in warm soil. This hybrid was bred with above-average heat tolerance and downy mildew resistance, allowing it to be sown earlier in fall or later into spring than many spinach types without bolting prematurely. Its dark green, savoyed leaves hold good texture and flavor even as temperatures rise, making it a strong pick for extending the cool-season window along the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Start seed indoors for a spring crop, or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; Self Blanche is a classic cauliflower whose leaves naturally curl inward over the developing head, largely eliminating the need to manually tie leaves for blanching.
directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Self Blanche is a classic cauliflower variety whose outer leaves naturally curl inward to cover the developing head as it forms, largely eliminating the tedious task of hand-tying leaves over the curd to keep it white, a labor-saving trait especially appreciated by home gardeners growing more than a plant or two. It produces solid, well-formed white heads of good size and quality with this convenient self-blanching habit doing most of the work automatically. Check occasionally to make sure leaves are covering the head adequately, tying loosely if needed, and harvest promptly once heads reach full size before curds begin to separate or yellow.

plant_note: Plant divisions after last frost into wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; Semanggi spreads by rhizome and is best confined to a container or contained bog bed.
directions: Plant divisions after last frost into wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; Semanggi spreads by rhizome and is best confined to a container or contained bog bed. Small, four-lobed leaves resembling a four-leaf clover float or stand just above the mud of rice paddies and shallow wetlands across Indonesia, where the tender young leaves and stems are harvested and traditionally steamed as the key ingredient in the East Javanese dish pecel semanggi, tossed with a spicy peanut sauce. This true fern (not a clover, despite the resemblance) spreads readily by creeping rhizomes across wet mud, forming a low, dense mat useful for the shallow-water margin of a bog garden or paddy-style planting. Harvest young leaves and stems regularly for the best eating quality, and keep the planting confined to prevent it from spreading beyond the intended wet area.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained soil; in zone 9–10 an excellent late summer/fall planting (August–September) allows the long vines to run through fall when powdery mildew pressure is lower. The Seminole pumpkin is the most heat-tolerant, disease-resistant winter squash for Gulf Coast and Florida gardens and should be a standard in zone 8–10 gardens where other pumpkins and squash struggle in summer humidity.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in any well-drained soil in full sun; Seminole pumpkin is a historic Native American heirloom cultivated by the Seminole people of Florida for generations and is exceptionally well-adapted to the hot, humid Gulf Coast climate where most pumpkins and butternut squash struggle with vine borers, powdery mildew, and heat collapse. It produces tan-buff, round to pear-shaped fruits weighing 5–10 pounds on very vigorous vines that can reach 15–20 feet — the vines are traditionally trained up trees or fences in Florida to keep the fruits off the moist ground. The buff-orange flesh has excellent butternut-like flavor, keeping quality of months, and outstanding resistance to diseases and insects that devastate other squash. Once established, vines are genuinely drought-tolerant. One of the most important heirloom vegetables for sustainable subtropical gardening.

common_name: Seneca White Corn (Haudenosaunee White Flour Corn)
plant_note: Sow in blocks of several short rows in fertile soil, hilling stalks slightly as they grow; let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest and shelling.
directions: Sow in blocks of several short rows in fertile soil, hilling stalks slightly as they grow for stability, and let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest and shelling. Seneca White is a traditional white flour/flint corn central to Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) agriculture in what is now upstate New York, grown for generations alongside beans and squash in the Three Sisters planting system. The soft, starchy white kernels are traditionally parched, ground, or simmered into corn soup, and community-led seed-saving efforts such as the Iroquois White Corn Project have kept this culturally vital variety in cultivation after it nearly disappeared from wider circulation in the twentieth century.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer to early fall for fall/winter/spring production in zones 7–11; Senposai is a Japanese hybrid leafy green that is significantly more heat-tolerant than standard cabbages and brassicas, making it one of the better cool-season leafy greens for the Gulf South where the heat ends conventional brassica production early — it continues producing into warmer temperatures than kale, collards, or Chinese cabbage.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 8–14 inches apart; harvest outer leaves continuously as cut-and-come-again from about 30 days; Senposai is mild enough to eat raw as well as cooked; spring plantings should go in very early since it bolts in sustained heat. Senposai is a hybrid leafy green developed in Japan by crossing common cabbage (Brassica oleracea) with komatsuna or Japanese mustard spinach (Brassica rapa var. perviridis), producing a vigorous, fast-growing green that combines characteristics of both parents — the large, smooth, broadly oval leaves of cabbage with the faster maturity, milder flavor, and somewhat greater heat tolerance of komatsuna. The resulting hybrid fills a useful niche in both Japanese home gardens and warm-climate gardens worldwide: it is ready for harvest significantly faster than heading cabbages (40–60 days versus 80–120), produces continuously as a cut-and-come-again crop rather than requiring a single heading harvest, and tolerates heat better than most brassicas while retaining the mild, slightly sweet, cabbage-family flavor without the sharpness of mustard greens. Senposai is versatile in the kitchen — the large, smooth leaves are excellent raw in salads, quickly stir-fried or sautéed, braised in Japanese-style dashimono or miso soup, or used like savoy cabbage leaves for wrapping. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Senposai is most valuable as a fall-through-spring cool-season green, sown from September through February for harvest from October through April. Available from Kitazawa Seed Company and other Asian vegetable seed specialists.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees; Serendipity was the original TripleSweet-type bicolor hybrid, blending sugary-enhanced tenderness with supersweet-level sugar content for excellent flavor and good holding quality.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Serendipity is a widely grown bicolor sweet corn hybrid combining sugary-enhanced tenderness with the high sugar content and slower sugar-to-starch conversion typical of supersweet types, giving it both excellent eating quality and good holding time after picking. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on tall, vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for the best-filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.

plant_note: Start indoors and set out after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: Start seed indoors about six to eight weeks ahead of transplanting and provide bright light and warmth for sturdy seedlings. Move plants outdoors once the soil warms and frost danger has passed, spacing them about a foot and a half apart. These prolific plants set many slender, spicy peppers used green for salsas and pico de gallo. Pick fruits green for the classic sharp heat, or leave them to ripen red for a slightly sweeter kick. Steady moisture and full sun keep production high through the season.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth and transplant only after the soil has warmed.
directions: Start seeds indoors with warm soil about eight weeks before transplanting, since peppers need heat to germinate. Move seedlings outdoors only after nights are reliably warm, spacing plants for good airflow. This heirloom produces slender 3-4 inch peppers with medium heat around 10,000 to 25,000 Scoville units and a bright, crisp flavor. Harvest green for classic salsa heat, or let the pods ripen to red for a slightly sweeter, hotter bite.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; sesame demands heat for germination and will rot in cool, wet soil.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in rows 18–24 in apart after soil reaches at least 70°F; sesame seed is very small, so mixing with dry sand aids even distribution and prevents clumping. Thin to 6–12 in once plants are 3 in tall and keep well-weeded until the canopy closes. The upright plants produce attractive tubular flowers along the stem that develop into rectangular seed capsules; the key challenge is timing harvest before 'shattering' — when ripe capsules split and scatter seed spontaneously. Cut entire stalks when the bottom capsules begin to yellow, invert plants into large paper bags, and allow to dry for a week indoors; the capsules then split easily and seed falls into the bag when shaken.

common_name: Seven Top Turnip (Leafy Greens Turnip for Gulf South)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (August–October in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Seven Top can be sown thickly and harvested by cutting young, regrowing from the base for multiple cuttings over the cool season.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Seven Top is a turnip variety grown exclusively for its prolific, tender, flavorful greens (tops) rather than its roots — the roots of Seven Top are small, tough, and not typically eaten, but the plant produces an extremely vigorous canopy of large, lush, tender, deeply flavored greens that are among the most productive and flavorful of all Southern cooking greens. The variety's name describes its characteristic of producing an exceptionally dense canopy of seven or more vigorous shoots per plant — creating a tall, productive leafy mass that yields far more greens per plant than Purple Top or other root-type turnips when grown for tops. Seven Top is a staple of traditional Gulf South fall and winter gardening — it's the turnip greens variety most commonly grown for pot greens in Mississippi, Louisiana, Alabama, and Georgia gardens where a large quantity of flavorful cooking greens from a small space is the primary objective. The greens are best harvested young and tender (6–10 inches tall) and become progressively more robust in flavor as they mature — a quality that appeals to those who prefer the traditional strong, minerally flavor of Southern cooking greens. Seven Top tolerates temperatures well into the teens once established. Cut-and-come-again harvesting (cutting to 4 inches, allowing regrowth) produces multiple flushes through the cool season.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm; provide a tall trellis.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost once the soil is warm, planting alongside a sturdy trellis or pole seven to nine feet tall. This All-America Selections winner bears clusters of tender four-to-six-inch pods well ahead of many standard pole beans. Pick pods young and often to keep the vines producing over a long season. Even, moderate watering during flowering and pod set gives the best yields. Avoid handling the plants when wet to reduce the spread of disease.

plant_note: Plant cloves 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring; in mild climates, an autumn planting produces larger bulbs.
directions: Separate shallot clusters into individual cloves and plant each with the tip just at or slightly above the soil surface, 1 in deep, in fertile, well-drained soil. Each clove multiplies into a cluster of 6–12 new bulbs by season's end, so generous spacing pays off. Harvest when most of the green tops have toppled and turned papery. Dry clusters on screens in good airflow for 2–3 weeks and store in a cool, airy spot; well-cured shallots keep for 6 months or more.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks well after last frost and isolate from other corn by distance or staggered timing to protect popping quality and kernel color.
directions: Shaman's Blue was the first widely offered dark-blue hybrid popcorn, bred for large, tender kernels that pop bright white despite their deep bluish-purple hull color, unlike the small, chewy kernels typical of older open-pollinated blue popcorns. Leave 8 inch ears on the stalk until husks are fully dry and kernels are hard, then cure indoors before shelling and storing in a sealed container to preserve popping moisture. The anthocyanin-rich hull gives raw kernels a deeper color than yellow popcorns, which growers selling at farmers markets often use as a selling point alongside its reliably fluffy pop. Choose this variety when a gardener wants the visual novelty of blue corn without sacrificing tender, large-kernel popping performance.

plant_note: Plant cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes.
directions: Break bulbs into individual cloves and plant them pointed end up about two inches deep in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes. This early-maturing Turban-type hardneck yields white bulbs with six to eight cloves and matures noticeably faster than most hardnecks. Mulch after planting to protect the cloves through winter and conserve moisture. Cut the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into bulb sizing. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer/early fall for a fall crop; Shanghai pak choi bolts quickly in long, hot days, so in zone 8–9 it performs best as a fast fall-through-winter and very early spring green rather than a summer crop.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade; keep evenly watered, since any dry stress speeds bolting. Shanghai pak choi is a compact, fast-maturing bok choy type with pale jade-green, spoon-shaped petioles and glossy dark green leaves that form a tidy, vase-shaped rosette — smaller and quicker to mature than standard white-stemmed bok choy varieties, and prized for its exceptionally tender, mild, sweet stems that need no peeling or trimming before cooking. Its speed and compact size make it ideal for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season, providing a steady supply of baby greens for stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. In warm-winter climates like the Gulf South it can be grown nearly through the whole cool season, from fall through early spring, before rising temperatures push it to bolt. Zone 2–10.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills or rows; Sharlyn is a hybrid type combining honeydew and cantaloupe parentage and needs a long, warm growing season to fully sweeten.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart or in rows 6 feet apart, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sharlyn is a hybrid melon combining traits of honeydew and cantaloupe, with smooth, pale ribbed skin like a honeydew but sweet, aromatic, pale orange flesh with the rich flavor of a cantaloupe, giving it an unusual combination of exterior and interior appearance that often surprises gardeners who haven't grown it before. Unlike true cantaloupe, ripe fruit does not slip easily from the vine, so judge ripeness by a color shift toward pale cream-yellow and a sweet fragrance at the blossom end rather than by fruit separation. It stores somewhat better after harvest than standard cantaloupe, making it a good choice for gardeners wanting a melon that holds a bit longer at peak quality.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall in lean, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; sheep sorrel self-sows freely and may spread aggressively in garden beds. In many gardens it is managed as a foraged weed rather than intentionally sown.
directions: Direct sow in lean, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; sheep sorrel is a diminutive native of Eurasia, now naturalized as a common weed across North America in sandy, acidic, infertile soils. The small, arrowhead-shaped leaves with backward-pointing lobes are more strongly acidic and citrusy than common sorrel (R. acetosa), with a bright lemon-sour flavor from oxalic acid. Young leaves are excellent in salads, soups, and sauces — the same culinary uses as garden sorrel — and the plant has a long history of use in traditional medicine as a spring tonic herb. Consume in moderation as with all oxalic-acid-containing plants. The plant spreads by both seed and underground rhizomes and becomes a persistent presence once established in appropriate acidic, lean soil; treat it as a semi-wild foraged herb rather than a crop requiring intensive management.

common_name: Sheepnose Pimento Pepper (Ohio Amish Heirloom Sweet Pimento)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of frost has passed; an Ohio Amish heirloom pimento pepper grown for its thick, sweet flesh.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into the garden after soil has warmed and space plants 18-24 inches apart. Sheepnose Pimento is a cherished Ohio Amish heirloom named for its squat, heart-shaped fruit, which ripens from green to a glossy deep red and is prized for exceptionally thick, meaty walls and an intensely sweet, almost sugary flavor. Sturdy, bushy plants are highly productive over a long season, yielding abundant fruit well suited to roasting, stuffing, canning, and fresh eating. Keep soil evenly moist and fertile through fruit set, and harvest at full red ripeness for the best flavor and thickest flesh.

plant_note: Sow as early as the ground is workable, typically 4–6 weeks before the last frost date.
directions: Sow seeds 1 in deep in rows 18 in apart and provide support for tall types. Consistent moisture from flowering through pod fill is critical; drought during this window sharply reduces yield. Harvest when pods are well rounded and the peas inside feel firm through the pod wall; sugar converts rapidly to starch after picking, so chill or eat immediately. Shell and freeze any surplus the same day for best sweetness.

plant_note: Heat-tolerant, so it can be sown into late spring and summer.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in loose, deep soil and keep the surface moist during the slow germination. Unlike many carrots, this heat-tolerant Kuroda type can be sown well into late spring and summer for fall harvests. Thin seedlings to about two inches so the tapered five-inch roots with broad shoulders can size up. Steady moisture prevents cracking and keeps the roots sweet and tender. Harvest before roots become oversized for the best texture.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this open-pollinated Japanese heirloom edamame needs consistent summer warmth to fill its pods.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this open-pollinated Japanese heirloom edamame needs consistent summer warmth to fill its pods. Plants set heavy clusters of two- to three-bean pods on compact, well-branched bushes and are valued in trials for their reliably smooth, sweet, nutty-flavored beans. Harvest whole pods when plump but still green, then steam or boil briefly in salted water for a classic edamame snack; being non-hybrid, seed can be saved from healthy plants for replanting.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out after the soil warms. This popular Japanese frying pepper produces heavy sets of slender two-to-four-inch fruits with a mild, citrusy, slightly smoky flavor. Harvest peppers green and small for the best flavor when blistered in a hot pan or on the grill. Roughly one in ten pods surprises with mild heat, adding to the fun. Pick frequently to keep the highly productive plants setting new fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights stay consistently above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant in February–March and expect harvests from May through October. The plants tolerate heat well and remain productive through the Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; shishito peppers are a slender, thin-walled Japanese variety harvested green at 3–4 inches long, when they are mild and sweet with an occasional — roughly 1 in 10 — surprisingly hot fruit that keeps diners guessing. Plants produce prolifically once they begin fruiting and require consistent moisture and monthly fertilization with a balanced vegetable fertilizer to maintain production. Harvest frequently to keep plants productive; once fruits redden they become hotter and the plant redirects energy away from new fruit. The standard preparation is to blister whole fruits in a dry or lightly oiled cast-iron skillet over high heat until charred and softened, then finish with sea salt and a squeeze of lemon.

plant_note: Sow direct around last frost date or lightly earlier indoors; seeds require light to germinate — press them onto the soil surface rather than burying them — and the seedlings tolerate mild frost but are killed by a hard freeze.
directions: Surface-sow seeds (they need light to germinate) directly in the garden around last frost or start indoors 3–4 weeks earlier in trays, transplanting after frost danger has passed into moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Perilla frutescens (green shiso) is an annual herb used as a vegetable throughout East Asian cooking — the large, ruffled, vivid green, anise-and-clove-scented leaves are used to wrap sashimi, roll rice and pickles in, scatter over noodles and salads, and deep-fry as tempura; it is a fundamental ingredient in Japanese cuisine. Shiso self-seeds prolifically and often becomes a welcome recurring presence in the garden without any replanting effort; deadhead promptly if you do not want it to naturalize. Harvest individual leaves as needed from the outside of the plant, or snip whole stem tips to encourage bushier growth.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (August–October in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Shogoin is an excellent dual-purpose turnip — the mild, sweet roots are outstanding for fresh eating and the tender tops are milder-flavored than most American turnip greens.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Shogoin is a Japanese heirloom turnip cultivar that is outstanding in two distinct ways: it produces unusually mild, sweet, tender-fleshed white roots appropriate for fresh eating and light cooking, and simultaneously produces exceptionally mild, tender, palatable greens that are significantly less pungent than the traditional American turnip greens grown for Southern cooking. This dual mildness — both roots and tops — makes Shogoin the turnip of choice for those who find standard American turnips too strongly flavored but want to grow a dual-purpose root vegetable for fall and winter. The pure-white, globe-shaped roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter at ideal harvest size — smaller and more tender than Purple Top White Globe when harvested young. The roots are outstanding raw in salads and slaws, steamed or roasted with light seasoning, and pickled (Shogoin is commonly used for Japanese-style pickled turnips). The tender greens can be used raw in salads when young, stir-fried, or lightly sautéed. In zone 9, Shogoin is a fall and winter crop — sow from August through October for harvest from October through February. The mild flavor makes Shogoin an outstanding variety for introducing turnips to gardeners and cooks unfamiliar with or averse to the pungency of traditional varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; make a second sowing 6–8 weeks before first fall frost. In zones 8–11 sow in fall for a winter crop. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks.
directions: Broadcast seed or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches; shungiku is a cool-season Asian vegetable in the chrysanthemum family grown for its highly aromatic, slightly bitter leaves that are fundamental to Japanese hot pot (nabe), sukiyaki, and Korean soups. The flavor is herbal, slightly medicinal, and distinctly chrysanthemum-like — beloved in East Asian cooking, particularly in winter one-pot dishes where the leaves add fragrance as well as nutrition. Harvest outer leaves when plants reach 6–8 inches; or cut whole plants at soil level for a cut-and-come-again crop. It bolts quickly in heat, producing bright yellow daisy-like flowers — these are also edible as a garnish. Sow in succession for continuous harvest through cool seasons.

common_name: Shunkyo Semi-Long Radish (Japanese Rose-Pink Heirloom Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in early fall or late winter, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up without crowding.
directions: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in early fall or late winter, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up without crowding. This Japanese heirloom produces rose-pink, tapered roots four to five inches long with crisp, notably sweet and mild flesh that holds its quality and stays crisp longer than typical round spring radishes as temperatures fluctuate. Its extended harvest window and resistance to turning pithy or overly hot in warm soil make it a reliable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners working with a short, mild winter rather than a true hard freeze. Both the roots and the peppery young leaves are edible.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, several weeks before the ground freezes, so roots develop ahead of winter.
directions: Set cloves 2 inches deep in loose, fertile soil and mulch well for the winter, uncovering gradually as spring shoots appear. Cut the curling scape in early summer to focus growth into the bulb, then cure harvested heads in a dry, shaded, airy location for a few weeks. Shvelisi is a Republic of Georgia heirloom porcelain hardneck brought to the United States by garlic researcher Ron Engeland, known for its tall stature, large white bulbs, and rich, warm flavor that reflects its Caucasus mountain origins.

common_name: Siberian Hardneck Garlic (Marbled Purple Stripe, Cold-Climate Heritage)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 4–6 weeks before first frost; Siberian is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic of Russian origin, known for exceptional cold hardiness that makes it one of the most reliable varieties in zones 3–4 — it produces large, 5–9 clove bulbs with a rich, full-bodied flavor and an attractive purple-striped outer wrapper typical of its garlic group.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch heavily after the ground cools (especially important in zones 3–4); keep consistently moist in spring; remove scapes when they curl and straighten; harvest in early to midsummer when lower leaves yellow. Siberian is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic originating in Russia and introduced to North American garlic culture through seed-saver networks and specialist garlic growers in the 20th century; it is particularly valued for its exceptional cold hardiness, with reliable performance in zones 3–4 where many garlic varieties struggle with winterkill or produce reduced bulb size. The bulbs are medium-large (2–3 inches across) and typically contain just 5–9 large, easy-to-peel cloves — fewer than most garlic types but each clove is substantial in size, making them easy to use in cooking. The outer skins are cream-colored with distinctive purple-violet streaking and spotting characteristic of the Marbled Purple Stripe group; the flavor is rich, moderately pungent, and earthy with good complexity — similar in character to Persian Star and other Marbled Purple Stripe types. Siberian is an excellent choice for northern gardeners in zones 3–5 who struggle with hardneck variety performance, and for seed-saving gardens that want geographic diversity in their garlic collection. Storage life of 5–7 months under good conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (or early spring in cooler climates) in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; unlike its relative miner's lettuce, Siberian miner's lettuce spreads by shallow rhizomes as well as self-seeding, forming a persistent shade groundcover rather than an annual colony.
directions: Direct sow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siberian miner's lettuce is a Pacific Northwest and northern Asian native cool-season green, closely related to the round-leaved miner's lettuce but with pointed, spade-shaped leaves and dainty pink-veined white flowers held in loose sprays above the foliage from late winter into summer in cool, shaded gardens. The tender leaves and flowers have a mild, slightly tart, spinach-like flavor and are eaten raw in salads or lightly cooked, and the plant tolerates deeper shade than nearly any other salad green. Unlike annual miner's lettuce, it spreads by shallow rhizomes as well as self-seeding, gradually forming a low, semi-evergreen groundcover in a consistently moist, shaded woodland garden or the north side of a building. Thin or divide congested patches in fall to keep it in bounds, and expect it to die back in extended summer heat, returning with cooler fall weather.

common_name: Sibley Squash (Pike's Peak Heirloom Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Sibley, also known as Pike's Peak squash, is an 1880s heirloom prized for its distinctive teardrop shape, thin blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-grained orange flesh that many heirloom growers consider among the best-flavored of all winter squash.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the long, vigorous vines. Sibley squash, introduced in the 1880s and also sold as Pike's Peak squash, is an American heirloom valued by generations of gardeners for its unusual teardrop or pear shape, thin, smooth, blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-textured deep orange flesh with almost no fiber, a texture and flavor that many long-time growers rank above modern hybrid winter squash. Fruits typically run 6-10 pounds, large enough to serve a crowd, and the thin rind, while making the squash slightly more vulnerable to handling damage than thick-shelled types, also makes it easier to peel and cook than harder-shelled Hubbard-type squash. Vines are long and productive given full sun and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry, then cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry location before storing in a cool, dry spot, where well-cured fruit keeps for several months while its sweetness continues to improve.

plant_note: Fall-plant cloves; softnecks also do well in milder winter regions.
directions: Separate bulbs into cloves and plant them pointed end up about two inches deep in fall. This Artichoke-type softneck forms twelve to twenty cloves per bulb with classic pearl-white papery skin sometimes streaked purple. Softnecks store especially well and are ideal for braiding, and they perform reliably in milder-winter regions. Mulch for winter protection and keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist through spring. Harvest when the lower leaves yellow, then cure in a dry, ventilated spot before storing.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; Sierra Blanca is an intermediate/short-day white hybrid onion widely recommended across Texas, New Mexico, and the Gulf South as one of the most reliable large sweet onions for home gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter regions, since this intermediate/short-day hybrid needs a southern winter's shorter daylight to bulb well.
