plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+), at the base of a sturdy 6–8 foot pole or trellis, since Speckled Cutshort is a vigorous heirloom climber.
directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest pods young and tender for snap use, or let mature for a flavorful dry soup bean. Speckled Cutshort is a member of the Appalachian 'cutshort' family of heirloom pole beans, so named for the short, blunt, somewhat flattened pod tip characteristic of the type, and passed down for generations among mountain families in Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia, and the Carolinas, with many named strains maintained within individual families and communities. The pods are speckled with purple-brown markings while developing, turning fully green as they mature, and the tender, meaty texture makes them excellent as a snap bean; left to dry, the attractively speckled seeds cook into a rich, traditional Appalachian soup bean. Vigorous and productive on a sturdy support, it is a genuine piece of living Appalachian food heritage for gardeners who want an authentic regional heirloom, zone 4–10.

common_name: Speckled Hound Pumpkin (Green-Speckled Orange Heirloom Baking Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Speckled Hound is a moschata-type heirloom pumpkin with distinctive dark green speckling over an orange rind and dense, sweet, moist flesh good for pies and roasting.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills of warm, fertile soil and give the vigorous vines room to sprawl, since Speckled Hound belongs to Cucurbita moschata, the same heat- and pest-tolerant species as butternut squash and generally outperforms Cucurbita pepo pumpkins in hot, humid Southern gardens. The medium-sized, slightly flattened fruit has a striking dark green speckled pattern over deep orange skin, and the moist, dense, sweet flesh is well suited to pies, soups, and roasting, holding its flavor and texture through long storage better than most jack-o'-lantern types. Moschata squash also tends to shrug off vine borers better than pepo types, a real advantage in the Gulf South where borers are a persistent problem. Harvest once the rind resists a fingernail scratch and the stem has begun to dry, and cure fruit in a warm, airy spot for a week or two before moving to cool winter storage.

common_name: Speckled Purple Hull Pea (Old Timer Semi-Crowder Southern Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65F and all frost danger has passed; Speckled Purple Hull, sometimes called Old Timer, is a semi-crowder pea with curved purple pods and cream peas mottled with tan-brown speckles.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Speckled Purple Hull, an old Southern heirloom also known as Old Timer, bears curved, rich purple pods about seven inches long, shelling out to reveal cream-colored peas mottled with distinctive tan-brown speckles, a semi-crowder texture prized for the classic flavor it brings to a pot of Hoppin' John. Its purple pods turn a deeper shade as they mature, making picking time easy to judge, and like other cowpeas it thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South summer when many other vegetables falter. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Speckled Roman is a distinctive paste-type heirloom with dramatically striped red-and-orange fruits and equally striped leaves, producing meaty, flavorful paste tomatoes with more complex flavor and better fresh-eating quality than standard smooth-skinned paste varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide substantial staking or caging as plants grow 5–7 feet tall. Speckled Roman tomato was discovered by Doreen Howard in Illinois and is distinguished from virtually all other paste tomatoes by its dramatically striped appearance — the fruits have alternating red and orange stripes (or speckles when young) that persist to full ripeness, making them visually striking among the usually uniformly red paste types. The foliage is similarly striped, with green and yellow banding on the leaves. Beyond the ornamental appeal, Speckled Roman produces exceptionally flavorful paste tomatoes with more complexity and better texture for fresh eating than standard San Marzano or Roma types while retaining the meaty, low-moisture flesh needed for sauce and paste production. Medium-large (4–8 oz), cylindrical to elongated-oval fruits. Outstanding for both fresh use and preserving, and a beautiful conversation piece in the garden.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; needs a long, warm season and a sturdy trellis.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, or start indoors to gain time in short seasons. These vigorous vines need a long, warm season and benefit from a strong trellis that lets the swan-necked fruits hang and shape naturally. The emerald green shells speckled with light green make striking autumn displays. For crafts, let gourds mature fully on the vine, then cure them in a dry, airy place for weeks to months until the shells harden. Cured hard-shelled gourds last indefinitely and take paint and carving well.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall-winter harvest or January–February for spring. Speckles is an Austrian heirloom butterhead type with excellent cold hardiness and some heat tolerance. In zone 9 it is most productive from October through March; the red-speckled pattern on the leaves intensifies in cool weather. Successive sowings every 3 weeks extend the harvest season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Speckles is an Austrian heirloom butterhead lettuce distinguished by large, soft, pale-green leaves heavily spotted and speckled with red-maroon freckles — a distinctive appearance unlike any other lettuce. The speckle pattern varies from plant to plant, and no two heads are identically spotted, making it one of the most visually interesting lettuces for mixed salads and fresh presentations. The flavor is classic butterhead — tender, buttery, mild, and slightly sweet — without the bitterness of some red-pigmented lettuces. Speckles is a slow-to-bolt Austrian type that holds quality in the garden longer than many butterhead varieties before heat causes it to flower. The unique spotted appearance makes it highly marketable at farmers' markets and popular in mesclun mixes where the speckled leaves stand out visually. In zone 9 it produces excellent fall-through-winter heads with the speckle pattern intensifying in cool temperatures.

plant_note: Sow 2–6 weeks before the first fall frost; spelt establishes before winter dormancy and resumes vigorous growth in early spring.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed at 80–100 lb per acre (approximately 2–3 oz per 100 sq ft) in fall to 1 in depth; spelt is taller than modern wheat and slightly more susceptible to lodging in rich soils, so avoid high-nitrogen amendments. It tolerates clay and compacted soils better than most small grains and has reasonable resistance to rust diseases. Harvest at hard dough stage in early summer by cutting, sheaving, and drying for a week before threshing; spelt retains a tough hull (spikelet) that requires a dedicated pearler or dehuller before milling. The resulting flour has a mild, nutty flavor and is widely used by those who tolerate ancient wheats better than modern varieties, though it does contain gluten.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; spinach germinates best in cool soil (45–65°F) and bolts rapidly in hot weather. A fall sowing 4–6 weeks before first frost often produces the best crop, as cool autumn temperatures improve flavor and delay bolting.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil as early as 4 weeks before last frost in spring or 4–6 weeks before first fall frost; spinach is a cool-season crop that thrives in soil temperatures below 65°F and bolts rapidly when days lengthen and temperatures exceed 75°F in late spring. Choose slow-bolting varieties for spring planting; fall-planted spinach often overwinters in zone 6–9 and produces an abundant early spring harvest before heat sets in. Harvest outer leaves frequently once plants have 5–6 leaves; baby spinach can be cut-and-come-again at 3 inches tall for the highest yield per square foot. Rich in iron, folate, vitamin K, and lutein; oxalic acid in the leaves binds some minerals and is reduced by light cooking.

plant_note: Sow densely in cool weather; can also be grown indoors year-round.
directions: Sow seed densely in shallow rows or broad bands and keep the surface moist for even germination. Fast-growing baby spinach leaves add flavor and nutrients to salads, sandwiches, smoothies, and pesto. This crop can be grown indoors at any time of year, so move containers as needed for the best light and cool temperatures. Harvest leaves young, when just a few inches tall, by cutting above the growing point so plants regrow. Successive sowings keep tender baby leaves coming through the cool seasons.

common_name: Spineless Beauty Hybrid Zucchini (Commercial-Grade Itch-Free Zucchini)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early; use drip irrigation to help manage mildew in humid climates.
directions: Spineless Beauty is a widely grown commercial-grade hybrid zucchini bred with smooth, nearly spine-free petioles, sparing gardeners the itchy rash that comes from brushing bristly zucchini foliage during harvest. The open, mounding plant sets glossy, speckled medium-green fruit that hold quality even when picked slightly larger than typical zucchini, at 6-8 inches. Because powdery and downy mildew can move fast through humid Gulf Coast gardens, growers should keep foliage dry with drip irrigation and watch closely during rainy spells since this variety carries no built-in mildew resistance. Regular harvest every two to three days keeps the vigorous, heavy-yielding plant productive through the season.

plant_note: Plant pad cuttings in spring; allow cut surfaces to callus for 1–2 weeks before planting in dry, well-drained soil. In zone 8–11 this cactus grows year-round as a perennial shrub. Harvest new pads (nopales) when they are 4–6 inches long and bright green — typically spring through summer — before they harden and develop glochids.
directions: Plant paddles upright with the cut end 2–3 inches deep in gritty, extremely well-drained soil — wet soil in any season will cause rot. Opuntia ellisiana is the premier spineless edible nopal cactus for home gardens, prized because even young pads lack the large spines of most prickly pears, though fine glochids still develop on mature pads. Harvest only young, tender spring pads (nopales) at 4–6 inches before glochid development; use gloves and scrub pads under running water to remove any remaining tiny spines before cooking. Nopales taste mildly tangy and have a mucilaginous texture when cooked — excellent grilled, scrambled with eggs, in tacos, or pickled in escabeche. The plant survives full drought periods once established and requires no irrigation or fertilization in zone 8–9 soils.

plant_note: Plant tubers or rooted cuttings in spring after soil warms to 70°F or above in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; spiny gourd is a dioecious perennial (separate male and female plants needed for fruit) that stores tubers underground through dry season and grows as a tender perennial in zone 9.
directions: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide strong trellis or fence support; plant both male and female plants (approximately one male per 3–5 females) for fruit set. Momordica dioica (spiny gourd, kantola, or teasle gourd) is an important seasonal vegetable in India, Bangladesh, and Southeast Asia — a perennial climbing vine in the cucurbit family that stores energy in underground tubers through dry or cool seasons and produces vigorous new growth annually. The small, 2-to-3-inch, oval fruits are densely covered in soft spines (the 'spiny gourd' name) and harvested young and green for cooking — their flavor is distinctively bitter-sweet, similar to bitter melon but milder and less intensely bitter, making them more versatile for sautéing, stuffing, curries, and stir-fries. In Indian cuisine, kantola is considered a delicacy and commands premium prices in markets. The plant is dioecious (separate male and female individuals) — an unusual trait in cucurbits — requiring both sexes for fruit production. The tubers can be left in the ground through zone 9 winters if mulched. Spiny gourd is a nutritious vegetable rich in protein, iron, and phytonutrients.

subcategory: AAS-winning semi-bush jack-o-lantern and baking pumpkin
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost; the semi-bush habit takes noticeably less garden space than sprawling heirloom pumpkins, a real benefit in smaller Gulf Coast vegetable beds.
directions: Sow seeds directly in hills once the soil has warmed, thinning to two or three plants per hill; the compact, semi-bush vine allows closer spacing than traditional long-vined field pumpkins. Spirit was named an All-America Selections winner in 1977 for producing bright orange, deeply oval fruit averaging 10-15 pounds on a plant that stays far more contained than open-pollinated heirlooms. The thick, meaty flesh makes it genuinely dual-purpose, equally suited to a classic jack-o'-lantern face and to being baked down for pumpkin puree. Harvest once the rind has hardened and colored fully, cure briefly in a warm spot, and store in a cool, dry location out of direct sun.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist loamy soil in full sun; sponge gourd is a vigorous tropical vine requiring a sturdy trellis or fence, at least 10 feet of vertical space, and a long, hot growing season — at least 150 frost-free days for the fruit to develop and the fiber to mature. Start indoors 3-4 weeks before transplanting in short-season areas.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist loamy soil in full sun; sponge gourd is best known as the source of the loofah sponge — the fibrous interior skeleton of the mature fruit that becomes the natural bath and scrubbing sponge found in health food stores worldwide. The fruits are edible when young and immature (before the fibrous network fully develops) — harvested at 4–6 inches long and cooked like zucchini or opo squash, with a mild, slightly mucilagenous texture popular in East Asian and South Asian cuisine (called 'ghi tow' in Chinese, 'louki' or 'turai' in Hindi). To harvest loofahs, allow the fruit to mature and dry completely on the vine until the outer skin turns brown and papery and rattles when shaken — then peel the dry skin, shake out the seeds (save some for replanting), and rinse the fibrous sponge. A highly productive vine requiring a long, hot summer; grow in a greenhouse or polytunnel in short-season climates. The ornamental yellow flowers attract pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; needs room to vine.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm, rich soil, planting in hills with plenty of room for the vines to run. This small pie pumpkin, a 1966 heirloom crossing Sugar Pie and Jack O'Lantern, averages six to seven inches tall with sweet, fine-textured yellow-orange flesh. Give plants steady water and consistent feeding for good fruit set and size. Harvest when the rind hardens and turns fully colored, leaving a length of stem attached. Cure the fruit in a warm spot to improve flavor and storage life.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; spring cress grows naturally in wet woodland springs, seeps, and stream banks and requires consistently moist to wet, cool soil. It self-sows to naturalize in appropriate wet, shaded conditions.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; spring cress is a native American Cardamine (mustard family) of woodland springs, seeps, and shaded stream banks — one of the earliest edible wild plants of the year, producing rosettes of smooth, edible leaves in late winter with a pleasant, mild watercress-like flavor, followed by masses of small white 4-petaled flowers in early spring. Both leaves and flowers are edible fresh in salads or as a potherb. It grows naturally in the same wet, shaded, cool conditions as watercress and is an excellent native alternative in the shaded water garden or boggy woodland edge. The small bulb-like stem base gives it the common name 'bulbous cress.' A beloved early spring edible in Appalachian foraging tradition. Naturalizes to form showy colonies in appropriate conditions.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant to the garden 8–10 weeks before first frost so plants establish before cold weather arrives.
directions: Start seeds at 65–75°F in small pots and grow under bright light to prevent leggy transplants; harden off over 7–10 days before setting in the garden. Unlike heading broccoli, sprouting types produce many small floret clusters on branched side shoots rather than a single large central head — harvest shoots when tight and before flowers open, cutting with 4–6 inches of stem to encourage continued production. Regular harvesting extends the season for weeks; uncut shoots quickly flower and the plant stops producing. Mulch heavily for overwintering in zones 6–8 to harvest the earliest spring shoots, often before any other fresh vegetable is available.

plant_note: Plant tuber sections with one or more eyes 4 inches deep in early spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Stampede is the earliest-maturing Jerusalem artichoke variety — tubers are ready approximately 90–110 days from planting vs. 130+ days for unnamed varieties. In zone 9 this makes a spring planting viable for summer-fall harvest before the worst heat. Jerusalem artichokes spread aggressively — plant where containment is possible or in isolated beds. Harvesting all visible tubers at the end of the season prevents uncontrolled spread.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, loose, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Jerusalem artichoke is forgiving of poor soil and minimal care; Stampede is an early-maturing selection of Jerusalem artichoke (Helianthus tuberosus) that was developed for northern short-season gardens where standard varieties may not mature tubers before killing frost. The smooth, relatively uniform, white-to-tan tubers are significantly easier to clean and prepare than the knobby irregular tubers of wild-type plants, and the early maturity reduces the waiting period before harvest. Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke) tubers have a crunchy, slightly sweet, nutty flavor reminiscent of water chestnuts when eaten raw, and a creamy, buttery quality when roasted or pureed — they are used in soups, stir-fries, gratins, and roasted as a potato substitute. The tubers store inulin (a prebiotic fiber) rather than starch, making them lower-glycemic than potatoes but causing digestive discomfort in some people — the nickname 'fartichoke' reflects this effect, which diminishes with acclimation.

plant_note: Plant tuber sections 3-5 inches deep around the last frost date in any well-drained soil in full sun; Stampede matures noticeably earlier than most sunchokes, forming large tubers before other varieties have finished bulking up, which suits areas with a shorter frost-free window.
directions: Plant tuber pieces in well-drained soil in a dedicated bed, since sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground and are difficult to fully remove once established. Stampede is prized among Jerusalem artichoke growers for maturing its large, smooth-skinned tubers earlier than most other varieties, allowing an earlier fall harvest and giving northern growers a reliable crop even where the growing season is on the short side. Foliage grows tall and topped with small yellow sunflowers in late summer before dying back after frost, at which point the tubers are ready to dig; a light frost is said to improve their sweet, nutty flavor by converting stored inulin into simple sugars. Harvest tubers from fall through early spring as needed, leaving a few in the ground to resprout the following year, and rotate or contain the bed to keep the planting from spreading into unwanted areas.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Star of David is an Israeli heirloom okra producing fat, round, six-ridged pods that look like a Star of David in cross-section, with a distinctive flavor and substantially larger pod diameter than standard American okra varieties — excellent for stuffing whole.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; soak seeds 12–24 hours for faster, more uniform germination. Star of David okra (also called Israeli okra or Giant Israeli okra) is a Middle Eastern heirloom producing fat, broadly triangular, six-ridged pods that create a hexagonal or Star-of-David shape in cross-section; the pods are substantially wider in diameter (1.5–2 inches) than the slender American varieties, making them excellent for stuffing whole (halved lengthwise and filled with seasoned meat and rice in the Middle Eastern manner, or stuffed and baked with tomato sauce). The flavor is mild and tender at 3–4 inch harvest size; the large pod diameter keeps them from becoming stringy at slightly larger sizes than standard okra. Plants are very tall (6–9 feet), vigorous, and ornamental with large yellow hibiscus flowers.

common_name: Starbor Kale (Compact Dwarf Curly Hybrid Kale)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 4-6 weeks before the last frost; also sow in mid to late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed a half inch deep and thin or transplant to final spacing, side-dressing with compost as plants size up. This compact, uniform hybrid produces tightly curled, dark blue-green leaves on short stems, making it well suited to close spacing and mechanical or hand bunch harvesting. Its short, dense habit and slow bolting have made it a standard choice for market growers wanting a tidy, consistent curly kale.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Starbrite is a widely grown hybrid watermelon producing large, oblong fruit with the classic dark and light green striped rind most gardeners picture when they think of watermelon, and sweet, crisp, deep red flesh with a small, manageable seed cavity. The vigorous vine carries good resistance to fusarium wilt and anthracnose, two diseases that shorten productive vine life in warm, humid growing regions, helping the plant stay healthy and productive through a long summer season. As a dependable, well-proven hybrid with a long track record, it remains a solid standard choice for gardeners wanting a classic, reliable watermelon without the added complexity of seedless triploid pollination requirements. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit browns and the ground spot turns creamy yellow.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, spring-sow February–March and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Starship is a distinctive pale, cream-white zucchini that stands out visually from the far more common dark green types, with smooth, cylindrical fruit and tender, mild flesh good for all standard zucchini preparations, from grilling to sautéing to baking into bread. Beyond its novelty color, the compact, productive bush is a reliable, disease-tolerant performer well suited to home gardens wanting to diversify a summer squash planting beyond the usual green varieties. Pick fruit at six to eight inches for the best eating quality, and harvest frequently once production ramps up, since oversized fruit turns seedy and tough quickly, a trait shared by all zucchini types regardless of skin color.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+); soak seed overnight to speed germination. Stewart's Zeebest is a tall, vigorous Louisiana heirloom that continues producing tender pods over a long, hot Gulf South summer.
directions: Sow directly into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest pods every 1–2 days at 3–4 inches, since this tall, heavy-yielding variety puts on pods quickly in summer heat and older pods turn woody fast. Stewart's Zeebest is a Louisiana heirloom okra, grown for generations by home gardeners in the Gulf South for its tall, vigorous plants and heavy, extended production of smooth, tender, dark green pods with excellent flavor and relatively low fiber even at a slightly larger picking size than typical spineless varieties. The tall habit (commonly 6–8 feet by late summer) makes it useful as a seasonal privacy screen or windbreak in the vegetable garden in addition to its culinary value, and the plants shrug off the heat and humidity that stress many garden crops in July and August. A reliable, long-producing regional heirloom for Gulf South okra lovers, zone 5–11.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in autumn or early spring in a sunny, well-drained bed enriched with aged manure or compost.
directions: Stockbridge Arrow is a modern British-bred maincrop rhubarb selected for long, straight, uniformly deep-red stalks and strong disease resistance, and it has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It holds its color and firm texture well into midsummer rather than fading to green like many older varieties, which makes it popular with market growers as well as home gardeners. Vigorous, disease-resistant crowns establish quickly and produce heavy yields once mature. Divide congested clumps every four to six years in dormancy to keep stalk quality high.

common_name: Stockton Red Onion (California Heirloom Red Storage Onion)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil is workable; Stockton Red is an intermediate-day type adaptable to a fairly broad range of latitudes, including much of the mid-South.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and water evenly through the growing season. Stockton Red is an old California heirloom onion, named for the San Joaquin Valley growing district around Stockton, producing flattened, deep-red-skinned bulbs with pink-tinged white flesh and a flavor milder than many storage reds, making it good for both fresh eating and cooking. It is an intermediate-day type with somewhat more latitude flexibility than strict long-day heirlooms, and it stores respectably for a red onion when properly cured. Taper off watering once the tops begin to yellow and topple, then pull the bulbs, cure in a warm, dry, airy location for two to three weeks, and store in a cool, dry spot out of direct light to preserve color and firmness.

common_name: Stokes Purple Sweet Potato (Deep Purple Ultra-High Anthocyanin)
plant_note: Plant slips after last frost when soil warms above 65°F; Stokes Purple needs a full 110–125 days and benefits from the long season of Gulf Coast and warm Southern gardens; developed by Stokes Tropicals nursery in Lafayette, Louisiana, selected for extraordinarily high anthocyanin content — higher per serving than blueberries — making it one of the most antioxidant-rich foods commercially available.
directions: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil after soil warms above 65°F; Stokes Purple needs its full 110–125 days to develop; harvest after first frost threat in cooler climates. Stokes Purple was developed by Stokes Tropicals nursery in Lafayette, Louisiana from crosses involving Asian purple-flesh sweet potato types and selected specifically for American growing conditions and maximum anthocyanin content; the resulting variety has skin ranging from deep purple to nearly black and flesh that is uniformly rich purple-violet throughout — the highest level of anthocyanin pigments of any readily available sweet potato cultivar, higher per serving than blueberries or Concord grapes. The flavor is less sweet and more starchy than orange-flesh types, with an earthy, wine-like complexity and dense texture suited to roasting, savory preparations, smoothies, and applications where the dramatic color matters most. The vivid purple holds reasonably well through cooking, making dishes visually spectacular. Now grown commercially in California and Hawaii; available in health food stores and some major grocery chains.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 8–10 feet of room to sprawl.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Stone Mountain is a classic early 20th-century Southern heirloom watermelon, grown for generations across the South for its large, oblong, dark green fruit and exceptionally sweet, deep red, fine-grained flesh with relatively small seed count for an old-time variety. The vigorous vines are productive and well adapted to the long, hot growing season of the Gulf South, and the tough rind travels and stores reasonably well for a heritage variety, a trait that made it a popular market melon in the era before modern shipping cultivars took over. Its rich, old-fashioned flavor and reliable performance in southern heat and humidity have kept it a favorite among heirloom gardeners who want the taste of a bygone-era watermelon, zone 4–11.

common_name: Stonehead Cabbage (AAS-Winning Compact Early Green Cabbage)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, transplant late August through September for November–January harvest. Stonehead is also excellent for spring production: start indoors January–February and transplant when temperatures allow. The compact size makes Stonehead ideal for small gardens where a full-sized cabbage would take too much space; plant at 12–15 inch spacing for full-sized heads or 10 inch spacing for smaller, tennis-ball-size heads.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil. Stonehead is a 1969 All-America Selections-winning hybrid cabbage that earned recognition for combining early maturity with compact plant size — producing well-formed, 3–5 lb solid round heads on plants that occupy roughly half the space of standard cabbage types. The 'stone' in the name refers to the rock-solid firmness of the tightly packed, dense heads — when thumped, a properly matured Stonehead sounds and feels like a stone ball. The compact habit (spread of 12–15 inches vs. the 18–24 inches of standard types) at 12-inch spacing allows 25–30% more plants per row, making Stonehead one of the most space-efficient cabbage varieties for home gardens. The heads are round, attractively formed, medium blue-green with smooth skin (not savoy-type), and crack-resistant — holding in the garden for an extended period after reaching maturity without splitting. The mild, tender cabbage flavor is excellent raw in coleslaw, fermented as sauerkraut, or cooked; the dense texture holds up well in both applications. Stonehead remains one of the most widely recommended cabbage varieties in the United States more than 55 years after its AAS recognition.

common_name: Stowell's Evergreen Corn (Classic White Heirloom Late Sweet Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; Stowell's Evergreen is a large, late-maturing corn (90–100 days) suited to long-season climates. In zone 9, plant February–March for a May–June harvest, or plant mid-August for a fall crop. The 'Evergreen' name refers to the variety's long window for harvesting in the roasting ear stage — the kernels remain tender and at peak quality for a longer period than most corn before starch sets in, a trait that made this variety especially valued in the 19th and early 20th centuries before home refrigeration.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks at least 4 rows wide for adequate wind pollination; fertilize well at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Stowell's Evergreen is one of the oldest and most important heirloom sweet corn varieties in American gardening tradition — a white su (standard sugary) corn introduced before 1848 by Nathan N. Stowell of Burlington, New Jersey, who reportedly sold the variety for $4 (a substantial sum) before it was propagated and spread widely by seed companies. The variety dominated American sweet corn production and home gardens throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries, remaining one of the most popular sweet corn varieties in America for over 100 years before hybrid varieties began displacing open-pollinated types in the mid-20th century. The 'Evergreen' in the name refers to the variety's characteristic long harvest window in the milk stage — the kernels remain tender and edible for longer than most corn before converting sugar to starch, a property especially valuable before refrigeration when fresh corn had to be consumed quickly. Stowell's Evergreen produces large (8–9 inch) ears with 14–20 rows of pure white kernels that are tender, sweet (for an su type), and deeply flavored with the rich, starchy-sweet character of traditional open-pollinated corn that many old-timers consider superior to modern hybrids for preserving, canning, and creamed corn preparations. An irreplaceable heirloom variety with a direct connection to the entire American sweet corn tradition.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–April for a late spring/summer crop. Stowell's Evergreen has a long harvest window (the 'Evergreen' name refers to the fact that the milky stage stays edible for an extended period, unlike earlier varieties that must be harvested within hours).
directions: Sow 1–2 inches deep in blocks of at least 3–4 rows in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stowell's Evergreen was introduced in 1848 by Nathan Newman Stowell, originally a hybrid between a white field corn and an early sweet type. It was the dominant home garden sweet corn throughout the latter half of the 19th century and remained popular well into the 20th. The tall (7–8 feet) plants produce 8–9 inch ears with white kernels in 16–20 rows, each kernel deep and richly flavored with classic sweet corn taste. The name refers to an actual characteristic: unlike many older sweet corns where the milky eating stage lasts only a few days, Stowell's Evergreen holds at milk stage for 1–2 weeks — a valuable trait before refrigeration and the dominant reason for its century-long popularity. The tall stalks require some wind protection in exposed sites. An important heirloom for corn breeding and a satisfying producer for gardeners who prioritize old-fashioned flavor and the ability to harvest over an extended window.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Straight Eight is the All-America Selections-winning classic American slicing cucumber of the mid-twentieth century, the standard by which all slicers were measured from its 1935 AAS Gold Medal through the 1980s — still an excellent garden variety with reliable production and the classic cucumber form.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; train vines up a trellis for cleaner fruits or let sprawl in ample space. Straight Eight won the All-America Selections Gold Medal in 1935 and for decades became the definitive American garden cucumber — named for its uniform, straight, exactly 8-inch, dark green fruits with rounded tips, blunt blossom ends, thin skin, crisp flesh, and reliable productivity. It remained the standard garden slicing cucumber through the mid-twentieth century and was the one cucumber every American seed company carried. While modern hybrids have surpassed it in disease resistance and uniformity, Straight Eight remains a beloved heirloom for gardeners who want a reliable, seed-saveable, classic slicer. Produces well in warm conditions; good for Gulf Coast spring and fall production.

plant_note: Sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow Straight Eight seeds about 1 inch deep once soil temperatures reach at least 70F, spacing plants 12 to 18 inches apart or in hills of three to four seeds. This heirloom slicer yields uniform, smooth 6 to 8 inch dark green fruits with crisp, tender flesh. Provide a trellis to keep vines tidy and fruit straight, and water consistently to avoid bitterness. Harvest cucumbers young and often to keep the vines producing through summer.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil is warm.
directions: Plant seeds 1 inch deep in warm, loose, well-drained soil enriched with aged compost. Thin to one plant per hill and keep the bed consistently moist throughout the growing season. Monitor frequently for squash vine borers and squash bugs, which are the most serious pests. Harvest fruits at 6–8 inches long while the skin is still soft and pale yellow for the best flavor and texture.

plant_note: Direct sow once the soil is warm and frost has passed.
directions: Plant Straightneck seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, thinning to one strong plant every 24 to 36 inches on a bushy, space-saving habit. This early yellow summer squash produces smooth, tapered fruits with tender skin and mild sweetness. Harvest fruits at 6 to 8 inches long while young for the best texture, picking frequently to keep new squash forming. Keep soil evenly moist and watch for squash bugs and vine borers during warm spells.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (60°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Strawberry Popcorn is harvested for dry kernels rather than fresh eating — leave ears on the stalks until the husks are fully dried and brown, then harvest and continue drying in a warm, well-ventilated location for 3–4 weeks. When the kernels are completely dry, rub ears together to shell the kernels off the cob. The dried ears are ornamental for months before shelling and can be used as fall decorations. Plant in blocks of at least 4 rows (not single long rows) for good wind pollination.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — corn is a heavy feeder requiring nitrogen-rich soil and consistent moisture during ear development; Strawberry Popcorn is an heirloom ornamental and edible popcorn variety producing tiny, round, deep burgundy-crimson ears that are remarkably realistic miniature strawberry look-alikes — the round, plump shape and rich dark red color create an almost uncanny resemblance to a strawberry when the ear is viewed with fresh eyes. The small ears (2–3 inches long) are produced one to two per stalk on compact (4–5 foot) plants, making Strawberry Popcorn both a space-efficient popcorn crop and one of the most attractive ornamental corn varieties for fall decoration. The dark red kernels pop into white popcorn — the kernel color disappears in the heat of popping — producing popcorn with the same light, airy, slightly sweet flavor as standard popcorn. The ornamental appeal (dried ears make excellent fall table decorations, wreaths, and displays) combined with the culinary value (genuinely edible popcorn) makes Strawberry Popcorn one of the best dual-purpose plants for the home garden, particularly appealing to children who delight in both the process of growing them and the surprise of popping the dramatic red kernels into white popcorn.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost when soil is reliably warm.
directions: Sow Strawberry Popcorn seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows to ensure good wind pollination. This dwarf heirloom grows compact 3 to 4 foot stalks bearing small, cone-shaped ears packed with jewel-toned deep red kernels. Let the ears dry fully on the stalk, then cure them further indoors before shelling for popping or ornamental use. Keep it isolated from other corn types to preserve its distinctive color and popping quality.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in blocks for good pollination.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows to ensure good pollination. Each compact four-foot stalk produces two or more ruby-red, strawberry-shaped ears two to three inches long. The ornamental foliage and ears look striking at the back of a border as well as in the vegetable patch. Let the ears dry fully on the stalk, then harvest and cure the kernels before popping. Keep this popcorn separated from other corn types to avoid cross-pollination.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in early spring or in late summer for fall; in zone 9 sow October–February. Strawberry Spinach self-seeds prolifically — allow one or two plants to go to seed and a permanent self-seeding colony will establish. In zone 9 the cool-season planting from fall through early spring produces the best foliage harvest before summer heat causes bolting. The colorful berries ripen progressively up the stem from bottom to top through spring and early summer.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Strawberry Spinach (also called strawberry goosefoot or blite) is a unique dual-purpose edible plant that provides both tender, spinach-like young leaves and bright red, strawberry-resembling berries on the same plant — the plant is grown first for its spring leaf harvest (mild, slightly earthy flavor used raw in salads or cooked like spinach) and then for the clusters of small, fleshy, bright red fruits that develop up the stem in a pattern that closely resembles a miniature strawberry. The berries are edible, mild, and slightly sweet but lack the intense flavor of true strawberries — they are used as a colorful garnish, in fruit salads, and as an ornamental edible curiosity. The plant is a cool-season annual from North America and Europe that tolerates partial shade better than most garden vegetables, making it useful for growing in dappled light under trees or in partly shaded beds. Strawberry Spinach is a reliable self-seeder that naturalizes easily in suitable conditions, providing a low-maintenance perennial food source once established.

common_name: Strike Bush Bean (Early Disease-Resistant Heat-Tolerant Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Strike is an early-maturing bush bean noted for disease resistance and a long harvest window, with good heat tolerance suited to a long, warm Gulf South growing season.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Strike is an early, disease-resistant bush snap bean prized for a long, sustained harvest window rather than a short, concentrated flush of pods like many bush varieties. It holds up well to summer heat, continuing to set new pods over an extended period when many other bush beans slow down. Pods are straight, tender, and best picked young before seeds bulge visibly through the pod wall. Harvest every couple of days to encourage continued flowering, and succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the warm season for an even longer supply of fresh beans.

common_name: Striped German Tomato (Bicolor Yellow-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Striped German produces very large fruits on vigorous indeterminate vines — provide sturdy support to 6+ feet and prune to one or two main stems for largest fruit development.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Striped German is a classic bicolor beefsteak heirloom — a large (10–16 oz), irregularly shaped, old-fashioned beefsteak type with golden-yellow skin striped and mottled with red, creating a vibrant, contrasting bicolor appearance on the exterior. The cut interior reveals the characteristic bicolor flesh of this variety: red and yellow sectors arranged in alternating patterns that create an artistic cross-section pattern — a visually striking effect that makes Striped German outstanding for fresh sliced presentations. The flavor is exceptional — sweet, rich, low-acid, and complex in the tradition of old German beefsteak heirlooms. Striped German is believed to have originated in Appalachia from German immigrant seed stock and has been maintained by Appalachian seed savers for generations before entering the commercial heirloom seed trade. As with most large bicolor heirlooms, Striped German produces best in the spring season in zone 9 (March–June) and can be challenging to grow in the high summer heat that damages large fruit quality. The combination of visual beauty, excellent flavor, and historical significance makes Striped German one of the most rewarding heirlooms for zone 9 spring production.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed shallowly as early as the soil can be worked, and leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts to sweeten.
directions: Bred in England in the mid-1800s through deliberate selection from wild parsnip stock, Student was one of the first named parsnip cultivars developed with a scientific breeding approach rather than simple farm selection. It produces smooth-skinned, creamy white roots with strong vigor and reliable germination for a crop notorious for erratic sprouting. Sow fresh seed shallowly as early as the soil can be worked, and leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts, which convert stored starches to sugar and sweeten the harvest considerably.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 start January–February and transplant March. Stump of the World is an indeterminate variety that continues producing through the season; in zone 9 the heavy spring flush continues until peak summer heat slows setting, then resumes in fall. Prolific production means fruit load can be heavy — provide sturdy caging or staking.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stump of the World is a Russian heirloom tomato preserved by Seed Savers Exchange, producing abundant clusters of small to medium (2–3 ounce) round to slightly oval red fruits with a rich, sweet-tart old-fashioned tomato flavor. The prolific, indeterminate vines are particularly valued for their consistent production even during hot, humid periods when many larger-fruited heirlooms stop setting — a significant advantage in zone 9 where the growing season is compressed and productivity through heat stress is paramount. The firm-skinned fruits hold well on the vine and in storage longer than thin-skinned heirlooms, and their medium size makes them versatile for fresh eating, salads, and saucing where small cherry tomatoes are too small and large beefsteaks are too large for single-use. The Russian origin suggests cold-climate breeding priorities — early maturity and prolific production — that translate to better zone 9 heat performance than many European heirloom varieties.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Stupice is a Czech heirloom from Stupice in the former Czechoslovakia, one of the earliest-ripening tomatoes available for cool-climate and short-season gardens — producing ripe fruit in 52–65 days from transplant with exceptional cold tolerance that allows fruit set at temperatures too low for most varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after danger of frost passes; Stupice is unusually tolerant of cold nighttime temperatures and can be transplanted somewhat earlier than standard heat-loving varieties. Stupice (pronounced 'STOO-peet-seh') originates from the village of Stupice in what is now the Czech Republic and was brought to the Seed Savers Exchange network by gardener Dr. Carolyn Male in the early 1990s, where it rapidly became one of the most popular heirloom tomatoes in cold-climate gardens of the Pacific Northwest, Canada, and Northern states. It is a potato-leaved, indeterminate variety producing clusters of small to medium (2–4 oz), round, uniformly deep red fruits — not large by beefsteak standards, but remarkable for their combination of earliness (ripening weeks before most other varieties) and rich, full-flavored, sweet-tart tomato character that is often absent in other very-early varieties. The ability to set fruit in cool temperatures makes Stupice the first choice for short-season gardeners in coastal climates and high altitudes; it also makes an excellent spring variety for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens planted early in the season.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or plant onion sets directly 4–6 weeks before last frost; Stuttgarter Riesen ('Stuttgart Giant') is a traditional German heirloom short-to-medium-day onion prized throughout Europe for its distinctive flat-globe shape, pale yellow-brown skin, mild-sweet flavor, and exceptional keeping quality — the standard European storage onion for much of the 20th century.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or plant sets directly in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost at 2–4 inches apart; for seed-grown bulbs, thin to 4–6 inches in rows 12–18 inches apart. Stuttgarter Riesen (literally 'Stuttgart Giant') is a traditional German heirloom onion named for Stuttgart in Baden-Württemberg and widely grown throughout Central Europe as the standard yellow storage onion; it is recognized by its distinctive flattened or slightly disc-shaped globe form (wider than tall), straw-yellow to golden-brown thin papery skin, and crisp white flesh with a mild-sweet flavor that is less pungent than many other yellow storage types. The relatively flat shape and thin skin were historically valued because the flatter bulbs cured and dried quickly without molding, and the thin skin peeled easily — practical advantages that made Stuttgarter both the preferred home-garden and commercial variety. Now widely grown from sets (small bulblets sold by the bag) as well as from seed; set-planted Stuttgarter is often the earliest onion to mature in northern gardens. Exceptional storage quality — properly cured bulbs keep 6–9 months in cool, dry conditions.

common_name: Success PM Squash (Powdery Mildew-Resistant Yellow Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Success PM was bred specifically for resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that typically ends a Gulf South summer squash planting by midsummer once the white, dusty coating spreads across the foliage.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Success PM is a yellow summer squash bred to carry meaningful resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that coats squash leaves in a white, dusty film and typically shuts down production in a Gulf South garden by midsummer, well before the season would otherwise end. Because the foliage stays healthier and photosynthesizing longer, plants tend to keep setting good-quality fruit later into the summer than mildew-susceptible varieties. Harvest fruit young, at 5-6 inches, for the most tender texture and mildest flavor, checking plants daily during peak production since summer squash quickly grows oversized if missed for even a couple of days.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November or January–February. Sucrine is a small-heading type that produces compact, single-serving heads of 4–5 inches — plant more densely at 6–8 inch spacing. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for a continuous harvest. The sweet, crisp flavor and compact size make Sucrine a favorite for container growing and raised beds.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Sucrine is a French mini-romaine lettuce producing compact, upright, 4–5 inch heads with thick, crunchy, deeply green leaves and an exceptional sweetness that is apparent even in the name — 'sucrine' derives from the French 'sucre' (sugar). It is considered by many French market gardeners to have the best flavor of any small lettuce, combining the crunch and structure of romaine with a delicate sweetness entirely absent from full-sized romaine varieties. The small, compact heads are the right size for a single salad portion, and the thick leaves hold up to dressings without wilting — ideal for individual Caesar salads and composed appetizer plates. Sucrine is the standard small romaine type in French markets and has become highly popular in North American specialty food markets and upscale restaurants. The tight, compact head formation and small size allow close spacing (6–8 inches) that maximizes production from small garden spaces.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm, spacing hills generously since vines spread widely, and reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate sugars.
directions: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm, spacing hills generously since vines spread widely, and reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate sugars. Originating in the Berry region of central France, this squash produces flattened, deep-orange, lightly ribbed fruit with notably dense, dry, sweet flesh reminiscent of chestnuts, making it a favorite for soups and roasting. It shares ancestry with Musquée de Provence but stays smaller and matures faster, fitting gardens with shorter seasons. Cure fruit in the sun for a week or two after harvest to harden the rind and intensify flavor before storing.

plant_note: Sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring.
directions: Direct sow Sugar Ann seeds 1 inch deep and 2 to 3 inches apart as soon as the soil is workable in spring. This early, compact snap pea forms short 24 to 30 inch vines that need little or no support, making it ideal for containers and small beds. Harvest the plump, sweet pods when they fill out but are still crisp, picking regularly to prolong production. Provide steady moisture and enjoy the harvest before summer heat shuts the plants down.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 sow November–February for a winter-spring harvest. Sugar Ann is a compact, bush-type snap pea requiring no staking — plants reach only 18–24 inches and are self-supporting. In zone 9 the fall-through-spring season is ideal; pods are ready to harvest in 52 days (faster than most snap peas) before spring heat causes the plants to decline. Pick pods when the peas have just begun to swell in the pod.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil; Sugar Ann is the first snap pea cultivar to achieve a compact, self-supporting, bush habit — it was awarded the All-America Selections award in 1984 for this breakthrough characteristic, which made snap pea growing practical for small gardens and container growing where the typical 4–6 foot Sugar Snap vines require substantial trellis infrastructure. The pods are genuine snap peas (edible pod, no strings in the eating-ripe stage) with sweet, crunchy, crisp pod walls and rounded, sweet peas inside — the classic snap pea flavor that has made snap peas one of the most popular garden vegetables since their introduction in the late 1970s. At only 52–56 days to maturity, Sugar Ann is also the fastest-maturing of the main snap pea varieties, providing an early crop before hot weather ends the pea season. In zone 9 the bush habit and fast maturity make Sugar Ann particularly valuable for the short cool-season window available.

plant_note: Compact icebox type suited to shorter seasons and small gardens.
directions: This compact icebox watermelon produces round 8 to 10 pound fruit with sweet red flesh on shorter vines. Start seed indoors or direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm, and use black mulch in cool regions. Water steadily during vine growth and fruit set, then ease off as melons ripen to intensify sweetness. Signs of ripeness include a yellowing ground spot and a dried tendril nearest the fruit. Because it matures relatively quickly, it succeeds even where summers are short.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Sugar Baby produces 7–10 lb icebox-sized fruits — small enough to fit in a refrigerator whole. Judge ripeness by the tendril nearest the fruit turning brown and dry, the ground spot (where it rests on soil) turning yellow, and a dull hollow sound when thumped. In zone 9 watermelons perform excellently in summer heat; provide consistent moisture during fruit development but reduce watering as fruits approach maturity to concentrate sweetness. Allow 6–8 feet between hills for the sprawling vines.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral sandy or loamy soil — watermelons require deep, loose, well-drained soil and abundant heat to develop properly; Sugar Baby is the classic icebox watermelon variety — the small, round, dark-green fruits (7–10 pounds) that fit neatly into a home refrigerator, in contrast to the large oblong types (20–30+ pounds) traditional in Southern watermelon culture. The small fruit size makes Sugar Baby the most practical watermelon for small family gardens where a single large watermelon represents more than could be consumed before spoiling. The bright red, crisp, very sweet flesh with few seeds has made Sugar Baby one of the most popular home garden watermelons for decades — reliable, productive, and delivering the classic watermelon experience in a manageable size. As a true tropical fruit, watermelon is perfectly suited to zone 9's long, hot summers — in fact, the consistent 90°F+ temperatures of June through August produce the sweetest, most flavorful watermelons possible, as the combination of intense sun and heat maximizes sugar development in the fruit.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring once the soil can be worked.
directions: Sow sugar beet seeds about half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 4 to 8 inches apart to give the large roots room to swell. This heirloom biennial forms sucrose-rich white roots up to 12 inches long with leafy tops nearly two feet tall. Keep the soil loose, evenly moist, and free of competition so the roots grow smooth and full. Harvest in late fall before hard freezes for home sugar extraction, livestock feed, or soil improvement.

common_name: Sugar Bon Pea (AAS-Winning Dwarf Snap Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Sugar Bon is an All-America Selections winner bred as a dwarf snap pea that needs little to no staking while still producing sweet, crisp pods.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked. Sugar Bon, an All-America Selections winner, combines the sweet, crisp, whole-pod-edible quality of snap peas with an unusually compact, dwarf vine that needs little to no staking, making it a convenient choice for small gardens, containers, or gardeners who want to skip trellising. It sets pods heavily and matures quickly, an advantage in the Gulf South's relatively short cool-season pea window before summer heat arrives. Harvest pods once they fill out but are still tender and glossy, picking every couple of days to encourage the vine to keep producing through its productive window.

common_name: Sugar Buns Sweet Corn (Early Cool-Soil Sugary-Enhanced Hybrid)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches at least 60 degrees; Sugar Buns germinates more reliably in cooler soil than many sugary-enhanced corn varieties, allowing an earlier first planting in the Gulf South's spring corn window.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Sugar Buns is an early, sugary-enhanced (se) yellow sweet corn valued for reliable germination in cooler soil than many other sweet corn types tolerate well, letting Gulf Coast gardeners get a jump on the spring planting window. It produces 7-inch ears with tender, sweet, deep yellow kernels that hold their eating quality well for several days after picking. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, since drought stress at this stage causes poorly filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.

plant_note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2–3 nodes in spring after last frost; in zone 9 plant February–April. Lay sections horizontally 4 inches deep in a furrow or plant vertically with the top node just below soil surface. In zone 9, sugar cane is perennial — freeze back to the ground in cold winters but regrow from the rhizomes.
directions: Plant stalk cuttings (billets) with 2–3 nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sugar cane (Saccharum officinarum) is the world's largest crop by tonnage and one of the most important agricultural plants in human history, providing approximately 70% of the world's sugar supply. In Louisiana, the Gulf Coast's sugar cane belt, it is a significant commercial crop harvested each fall. For home gardeners in zone 9, sugar cane serves multiple purposes: as a dramatic ornamental grass growing 8–12 feet tall with thick purple, green, or striped stalks; as a source of fresh-pressed cane juice (simply feed stalks through a sugar cane press or juicer); and as chewing cane, where stalks are peeled and chewed to extract the sweet juice — a traditional treat throughout the Gulf South and tropics. Commercial varieties include 'LCP 85-384,' 'HoCP 96-540,' and ornamental types like 'Pele's Smoke' (dark purple) and 'California Striped.' Louisiana cooperative extension services offer specific variety recommendations for the Gulf South. In zone 9, the cane may freeze to the ground in severe winters but returns from rhizomes in spring.

common_name: Sugar Cube Melon (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Sweet Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Sugar Cube can be trellised on a sturdy fence or arbor, with individual fruits supported in cloth slings — the small fruit size (2 lbs) makes vertical growing practical. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest. The personal-sized fruits are ideal for harvesting 2–3 at a time as they ripen sequentially, providing a more extended harvest than single large-fruited types.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity to maximize sugar concentration. Harvest at full slip or when the stem end yields to gentle pressure and the typical musky cantaloupe aroma is detectable. Sugar Cube is a 2000 All-America Selections-winning personal-size cantaloupe from Burpee that produces small (1.5–2.5 lb), round, heavily netted fruits — perfectly sized for a single serving, an individual lunch, or a couple's dinner without leftover melon. The personal melon size (compared to the 4–8 lb fruits of standard cantaloupe varieties) addresses the practical issue of melon waste in smaller households: a 6-lb cantaloupe purchased for one or two people must be stored cut for multiple days, losing quality rapidly, while a 2-lb Sugar Cube is consumed in one sitting at peak freshness. Beyond the practical size advantage, Sugar Cube produces exceptional flavor — dense, aromatic, intensely sweet orange flesh with the classic cantaloupe character that earned it AAS recognition. Each plant typically produces 4–6 fruits per vine, ripening over 2–3 weeks rather than all at once, providing a longer harvest window than some single-headed varieties. Sugar Cube also has the advantage of being growable on a trellis (the small fruits can be supported in fabric slings), making it one of the few viable trellis-grown melons for gardens where horizontal space is limited.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring.
directions: Direct sow seed as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, since peas thrive in cool weather. Bred by the developer of the original snap pea, this improved variety offers stringless three-inch pods, shorter vines, and better disease resistance. The compact plants need only light support and produce sweet, crunchy edible pods. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod fill for the best flavor and yield. Pick pods often while young and plump to keep the plants producing.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil once all frost danger has passed; Sugar Drip is a tall, long-season sweet sorghum that benefits from the Gulf Coast's long, hot growing season to fully load the stalks with sugar before harvest.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in rows in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed, thinning seedlings to their final spacing. Sugar Drip is a classic Southern heirloom sweet sorghum, grown not for grain but for its tall, juicy canes, which are cut, crushed, and boiled down into sorghum syrup — a traditional sweetener across the rural South before cane sugar became widely available and still prized today for its distinctive, robust, molasses-like flavor. Plants grow into tall, cane-like stalks resembling corn, topped with a grain head that can be left for birds or harvested for feed once the syrup-bearing stalks are cut. Harvest when seed heads reach the hard-dough stage and stalks are packed with sweet juice, typically signaled by the lower leaves beginning to dry; press stalks promptly after cutting, since sugar content declines quickly once cut canes sit.

common_name: Sugar Dumpling Squash (Small Sweet Winter Squash with Cream-and-Green Stripes)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Sugar Dumpling is a miniature winter squash producing 1–2 pound individual fruits about 4 inches in diameter — the personal serving size of the squash is one of its primary practical advantages, as each fruit is exactly right for halving and stuffing or baking as a single portion without the waste of cutting a large squash. The striped cream-and-green skin pattern closely resembles the Delicata/Sweet Dumpling type but Sugar Dumpling produces distinctly smaller, rounder, slightly more compact fruits. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer production and again in late July–August for fall harvest. The flesh is deep orange-yellow, very sweet (high in natural sugars), and dry-textured with excellent baking quality. Sugar Dumpling's compact vining habit (4–5 foot vines) is more manageable than large winter squash varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 36–48 inches. Harvest when skin shows orange or cream color without green and stem begins to dry. Sugar Dumpling Squash is a miniature winter squash variety in the Cucurbita pepo species that combines the sweet, dry, chestnut-flavored flesh of the best small winter squash types with an individual serving size (1–2 lbs, 4 inches diameter) that makes it supremely practical for home cooking. Unlike large winter squash varieties that require days of eating to finish once cut, Sugar Dumpling's small fruits provide a single meal's worth of squash for 2–4 people when halved and baked — eliminating the challenge of storing cut large squash and the quality loss that comes with refrigerating cut raw winter squash. The skin is a distinctive cream-white with thin green stripes that transition as the squash matures, eventually showing more orange-cream at full maturity (a ripeness indicator). The flesh is deep orange-yellow, very sweet, with the dense, dry texture that characterizes the best winter squash for baking and stuffing rather than the watery texture of summer squash types. Sugar Dumpling's vines are shorter (4–5 feet) than large pumpkin or Hubbard varieties, making the variety more practical for smaller garden spaces. For zone 9 fall production, plants started in late July can produce ripe squash by October–November, well-timed for the fall harvest and holiday table.

common_name: Sugar Lace II Snap Pea (Semi-Leafless AAS Winner)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked, 4-6 weeks before the last frost; the compact, mostly self-supporting vines need little or no trellising compared to standard snap peas.
directions: Sugar Lace II is a semi-leafless snap pea, meaning many of its leaflets are replaced by extra curling tendrils that let neighboring plants hook together into a self-supporting mass, reducing or eliminating the need for a trellis. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining good disease tolerance, including resistance to powdery mildew, with heavy sets of sweet, crisp, stringless pods that are eaten whole. Direct sow early in cool soil and keep evenly moist through flowering and pod fill for the best flavor and texture. Harvest when pods are plump and glossy but before they lose their bright green color.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a November–February harvest. Sugar Loaf chicory is considerably milder and less bitter than radicchio or Belgian endive — the name 'Pain de Sucre' (bread of sugar) reflects its unusual sweetness for a chicory. In zone 9 it produces consistently through winter without protection and is harvested before spring warmth causes the plant to bolt.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sugar Loaf Chicory (Pain de Sucre) is a French chicory producing tall, upright, cylindrical heads similar in shape to a Belgian endive or small romaine — but green throughout rather than blanched white. The name reflects the characteristic sweetness of this chicory type: the tightly-wrapped leaves are significantly milder and less bitter than radicchio or loose-leaf chicories, making Sugar Loaf accessible to people who find standard chicory too bitter for raw salad use. The crisp, substantial leaves with a mild, slightly bitter, refreshing flavor are excellent raw in salads, braised, or used as a sturdy wrap for composed appetizers. Sugar Loaf tolerates storage better than most lettuces — wrapped heads keep 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator, providing fresh salad greens long after harvest. In zone 9 the fall-through-winter growing season produces excellent Sugar Loaf chicory from October plantings harvested through February, when mild winters allow unprotected outdoor overwintering.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; tall vines need a sturdy trellis.
directions: Direct sow seed in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked and set up a tall, sturdy trellis. This striking variety bears tender, fine-flavored purple edible pods and lovely purple flowers on six-to-seven-foot vines. Long hypertendrils act as extra supports, helping the vigorous plants cling to their trellis. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and pod set for the best flavor. Harvest pods young and often while the vines climb, picking before they toughen.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed well into the 70s.
directions: Sugar Nut is a personal-size muskmelon bred for small households and small gardens, producing heavily netted, orange-fleshed fruit that average just under 2 pounds so a single melon serves one or two people without waste. Its compact vines and shorter internodes let it perform well in raised beds and large containers compared with sprawling standard cantaloupe types. High sugar content and a small seed cavity give a favorable flesh-to-seed ratio for its size, and its early maturity suits gardeners in shorter-season regions who struggle to ripen full-size cantaloupe. Vine to a trellis or let it sprawl, keeping fruit off wet soil to prevent rot.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; give vines room to run.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm, rich soil, planting in hills with ample space for the vines. This heirloom, a standard since the 1800s, produces small six-to-seven-inch fruits with sweet flesh ideal for pies, soups, muffins, and casseroles. The compact fruits also work for small carving jack-o'-lanterns. Provide steady water and feeding for good fruit set, and harvest when the rind is hard and fully colored. Cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry place.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; stake or cage the tall, rangy plants and provide consistent moisture through fruit set.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this modern baccatum selection, first found as a natural mutation of a South American aji type, needs the long, warm season typical of the species to size up. The glossy, peach-colored pods bring a habanero-adjacent heat wrapped in intense sweetness, with tropical and citrus notes that make them popular fresh in salads and ceviche or fermented into hot sauce. Plants grow tall and rangy, so stake or cage them and provide consistent moisture through fruit set.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; provide staking for the tall, productive plants and harvest regularly to prolong the season.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost. This variety arose as an off-type selection within Sugar Rush Stripey plantings and ripens to a solid, glossy red rather than the parent's stripe pattern, with a milder heat range of about 5,000-45,000 Scoville units. It shares the same sweet, tropical-fruit flavor profile as its siblings and works well fresh, fermented, or dried. Provide staking for the tall, productive plants and harvest regularly to prolong the season.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, and give this vigorous baccatum plenty of vertical support since it can top 5 feet in a single season.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, and give this vigorous baccatum plenty of vertical support — it can top 5 feet in a single season. Fruits begin lime green and ripen through a striking peach-and-red striped pattern that stays fairly stable from seed, with a Scoville range of roughly 25,000-100,000 that leans hotter than most other aji types. The flavor combines sweet, fruity, citrus, and stone-fruit notes, making it a favorite for colorful hot sauces and fresh garnishes.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 sow January–February. Sugar Snap pea requires a trellis at 4–6 feet tall for the original tall strain; dwarf bush strains are available but the original tall type produces more heavily over a longer period. In zone 9 the pea season closes in April–May when heat arrives; maximizing yield requires early planting and heavy harvesting every 2–3 days. Powdery mildew can be a problem in humid zone 9 springs; plant early to harvest before disease pressure peaks.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a trellis or fence for the tall vines; Sugar Snap Pea was bred by Calvin Lamborn and introduced in 1979, winning the All-America Selections award and transforming the edible-pod pea category — it combined the thick, succulent, fleshy pod of snow peas with the full, plump, sweet peas inside, creating a pod that is outstanding eaten raw, pod-and-all, with no tough strings to remove at the right harvest stage. The crisp snap when a mature pod is broken — and the burst of sweetness from the swollen peas inside — made Sugar Snap immediately distinctive from flat snow peas. Harvest when pods are round and full but still bright green before the pod skin begins to wrinkle; at this stage the natural sugars are at their peak. Overmature pods develop a tough string along the suture and the peas inside become starchy. In zone 9 Sugar Snap pea is primarily a January–April crop that provides the most rewarding fresh vegetable of the cool season.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; tall vines benefit from a trellis.
directions: Direct sow seed as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring and provide a trellis for the tall vines. This All-America Selections winner produces an extended harvest of thick, crunchy three-inch edible pods bursting with sweet flavor. The vigorous plants have some heat tolerance but still perform best in cool weather. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and pod fill for tender, sweet pods. Pick regularly while young to encourage continued production and enjoy them fresh off the vine.

common_name: Sugar Sprint Pea (Sugar Sprint Snap Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, since this pea thrives in cool weather and finishes before summer heat arrives.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in double rows along a low trellis or netting, since the compact vines benefit from light support even though they stay shorter than many climbing snap peas. This variety was bred for extra earliness and a concentrated harvest window, producing thick, crisp, stringless pods that are sweet enough to eat whole straight off the vine. Its shorter, sturdier vines make it a good choice for windy sites or gardeners who want snap peas without tall trellising, and it shows good tolerance to powdery mildew compared to older snap pea varieties. Pick pods promptly once they fill out to keep plants productive and pods tender.

plant_note: Plant 12–18 inch cane sections ('seed cane') with 2–3 nodes horizontally in a furrow 3–4 inches deep; joints sprout in 2–3 weeks in warm soil. In zone 9a, plant by early May to allow maximum growth before the first frost.
directions: Plant cane cuttings ('seed cane') horizontally 3–4 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; sugarcane is an enormous, bamboo-like tropical grass that has been cultivated for thousands of years for its sugar-rich stems. In the Gulf Coast home garden it is harvested in fall (October–November) when the stems are at peak sweetness, cut at ground level, and either pressed for fresh juice or chewed directly. The 'ratoon' growth from established root clumps often produces for several years before replanting. Most home gardeners in zone 9a treat it as an annual or protect the root clumps over winter with heavy mulch. Heirloom varieties popular in the Gulf South include 'Louisiana Purple,' 'Green German,' and 'Home Green,' all available from local growers and Southern specialty nurseries. Excellent as a tall seasonal privacy screen in the vegetable garden.
