common_name: Sugaretti Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Sweet Spaghetti Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Sugaretti is a compact, bush-habit spaghetti squash bred for sweeter flavor than standard spaghetti squash on a vine that takes much less space to grow.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Sugaretti is an AAS-winning spaghetti squash bred for a genuinely compact, bush-type habit that fits into much smaller garden spaces than traditional sprawling spaghetti squash vines, while also improving on the flavor of standard spaghetti squash with noticeably sweeter, less bland flesh once the strands are separated after cooking. The fruit is a good single-family size, with pale-yellow, oval, ridged rind. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens fully and turns a deep golden-yellow; cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two after harvest before storing or cooking. Roast, bake, or boil the whole squash, then scrape the cooked flesh with a fork to separate it into spaghetti-like strands.

plant_note: Sow in midsummer (July to early August) in most climates for fall harvest; in zone 9, sow in August–September for harvest from November through January. Sugarloaf is harvested in fall after cool nights sweeten the heads.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows 18 inches apart, thinning to 12 inches when seedlings are established; Sugarloaf or Pan di Zucchero is a distinctive Italian chicory that forms an upright, elongated pale green head resembling a light-green romaine lettuce — quite different in form from the compact red Chioggia or the torpedo-shaped Treviso radicchios. The flavor is characteristically chicory-bitter when young, but sweetens considerably after several frosts or cold nights, becoming almost endive-like in the inner white heart. The heads can be stored after harvest for several weeks in a cool, humid location; the outer leaves are removed and the inner pale heart is eaten fresh in salads or braised. Self-blanching as the tight leaves exclude light from the interior; no additional blanching is required.

plant_note: Direct sow in deep, very loose, stone-free soil — Sugarsnax develops long roots (8–9 inches) and requires at least 10–12 inches of deep, unobstructed, well-amended soil for straight root development. Thin to 2–3 inches apart when seedlings reach 2 inches tall. In zone 9, sow September through November for harvest December through February. The cooler temperatures of fall and winter enhance sweetness significantly over summer-grown crops.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in very deeply tilled, loose, stone-free soil enriched with compost; water consistently through germination (10–14 days) and thin to 2–3 inches when plants are 2 inches tall. Sugarsnax 54 (developed by Harris Moran Seed Company) is an Imperator-type hybrid carrot bred specifically for maximum sweetness at minimum days-to-maturity — its name reflects the two core attributes, 'sugar' for sweetness and '54' for the early maturity date that brings exceptionally sweet carrots to harvest in just 54–60 days. The roots are long and slender (8–9 inches) with a tapered Imperator shape, smooth bright-orange skin, and orange flesh that is noticeably sweeter than most other carrot varieties when grown under ideal cool conditions — the elevated sugar content is a breeding trait rather than solely a growing-condition effect, though cool weather amplifies it further. Sugarsnax is one of the most popular carrots for direct fresh-eating, CSA bunching, and farmers market premium carrot sales because customers can taste the difference: the sugar content is high enough to be perceptibly sweeter than standard storage carrots when eaten raw. The slender shape and smooth skin make Sugarsnax particularly attractive in bunched presentation with the green tops attached. Requires loose, deep soil to develop full-length roots without forking; heavier soils produce shorter, sometimes misshaped roots.

scientific_name: Raphanus sativus var. longipinnatus 'Summer Cross No. 3'
plant_note: Sow from late spring into midsummer; this hybrid was specifically bred to resist bolting and disease under the heat and humidity that cause most daikon to fail in summer plantings.
directions: Bred by Takii as a Minowase-type hybrid for the summer sowing window, Summer Cross No. 3 combines a distinctive white-shouldered, cylindrical root with strong tolerance to heat, virus, and Fusarium wilt that ordinarily plague daikon planted before cool fall weather sets in. Direct sow into deeply worked soil and thin to a wide final spacing so roots can size up straight and unforked. Growers who want daikon in mid-to-late summer, rather than waiting for a fall-only crop, choose this hybrid specifically for its ability to hold quality and resist bolting through hot conditions that would ruin open-pollinated types.

plant_note: Direct-sow 2–3 seeds per hill, 1 inch deep, after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F; thin to one plant per hill. Can be started indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost in individual pots but resents root disturbance at transplanting.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in groups of 2–3 after last frost when soil is warm — squash seeds rot in cool, wet soil; thin to the strongest plant. Summer squash (zucchini, yellow crookneck, patty pan) is the most productive vegetable in the summer garden and is one of the easiest to grow, producing an abundant harvest within 50–65 days. Harvest frequently when fruits are small and tender (6–8 inches for zucchini) to encourage continuous production — fruits overlooked for even a few days become enormous and tough, and the plant stops producing. Water consistently at the base and avoid wetting the leaves to reduce powdery mildew. Squash vine borer is a major pest in the eastern US; row cover early in the season provides protection.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil; repeat-sow every two to three weeks through summer and into fall for a steady supply.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil and thin young plants for baby-leaf harvest or wider spacing for bunching-size heads; Summerfest is an upright hybrid komatsuna bred specifically for heat and disease tolerance, so it can be sown through the warmer months when standard mustard spinach types would bolt. The smooth, spinach-like dark-green leaves and pale stems have a mild flavor that holds up well in stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. Successive small sowings every two to three weeks keep a steady supply of tender greens.

common_name: Summertime Green Tomato (Sweet Green-Fleshed Dwarf Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Summertime Green is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing sweet, green-fleshed-when-ripe fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Summertime Green bears medium fruit that ripens to a translucent amber-green, the flesh staying green even at full ripeness, with a sweet, mild flavor typical of green-when-ripe tomato types, on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant bred to bring specialty tomato flavor to small-space gardens. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers where indeterminate vines would be impractical. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and develops a faint amber blush, since color alone won't signal ripeness.

plant_note: Direct sow from early spring through early summer; bred specifically to resist bolting in warm weather better than most crisphead lettuce, extending the harvest window into the early Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to ten to twelve inches apart. Summertime is a crisphead lettuce bred specifically to resist bolting under the lengthening days and rising heat of late spring and early summer, holding its tight, crisp head and mild flavor for a longer harvest window than most iceberg-type lettuces manage before turning bitter and sending up a seed stalk. The dependable heat tolerance makes it a useful choice for stretching the fresh lettuce season further into warm weather on the Gulf Coast than most crisphead varieties allow. Harvest once heads feel firm and solid, and monitor closely as temperatures climb, since even heat-tolerant lettuce will eventually bolt once conditions become too warm.

common_name: Sumor Sweet Potato (Dry White-Fleshed Baking Type)
plant_note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost in warm soil; Sumor needs a full, long warm season to size up its roots properly.
directions: Sumor stands apart from most named sweet potato cultivars by being dry and mild rather than sweet and moist, with tan-to-yellow skin and firm white to pale yellow flesh that holds its shape when cooked. It behaves in the kitchen more like a russet potato than a typical Southern sweet potato, making it a useful choice for cooks who want a starchy, low-sugar substitute for regular potatoes in a Gulf Coast garden too hot for real potatoes in summer. The vines are vigorous and the roots show good field resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode, both common headaches in Southern sweet potato beds. Because it is slower to mature than orange types, get slips in the ground as early as the last frost date allows.

common_name: Sun Gold Cherry Tomato (Orange Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Sun Gold is an indeterminate cherry tomato that produces continuously from June through frost in zone 9 when kept well-staked and fertilized.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sun Gold is widely considered the finest-tasting cherry tomato ever developed and consistently ranks as the top-rated cherry tomato in taste trials — a Japanese hybrid producing small (3/4-inch), round to slightly elongated, deep orange fruits with exceptional sweetness, complex fruity-tropical flavor notes, and almost no acidity. The fruity, candy-sweet flavor of Sun Gold is distinctly different from other cherry tomatoes — a tropical, almost perfumed sweetness that makes it irresistible eaten directly from the vine. In zone 9, Sun Gold can be expected to produce continuously from transplanting in February through June and again from September through frost in the fall — the summer heat above 95°F temporarily stops fruit set but the plant remains and produces heavily once temperatures moderate. The vigorous, indeterminate vine requires a sturdy cage or staking to 5–8 feet and sets fruit in prolific clusters (trusses) of 10–20 tomatoes simultaneously. Sun Gold is a patented F1 hybrid — seed cannot be saved true-to-type. The attractive orange fruit color and extraordinary flavor make it one of the most popular and most widely recommended garden tomatoes.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out after frost danger passes. This indeterminate favorite produces long clusters of plump, tangerine-colored cherry tomatoes that are exceptionally sweet and juicy. Provide a tall stake or cage, since the vigorous vines easily reach six feet or more. Keep watering even to reduce cracking and pick fruit at peak color, or a bit early to finish ripening indoors. These low-acid tomatoes are rarely found in stores and are a special garden treat.

common_name: Sun Gold Tomato (Sungold Cherry Tomato, Orange Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile seed mix; transplant after all frost danger passes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sun Gold is consistently rated among the sweetest, most intensely flavored cherry tomatoes in existence — an F1 hybrid producing small, tangerine-orange, bite-sized fruits with extraordinarily high sugar content and a complex, tropical-sweet, apricot-citrus flavor.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with strong support; harvest clusters of cherry tomatoes when bright tangerine-orange. Solanum lycopersicum 'Sun Gold' (Sun Gold cherry tomato) is arguably the most beloved cherry tomato in home gardening — a Japanese F1 hybrid that consistently receives top ratings for flavor in nearly every comparative tasting. The fruits are small (3/4 to 1 inch), round to slightly oblong, brilliant tangerine-orange when ripe, and remarkably sweet — consistently the highest sugar content among widely grown cherry tomato varieties — with a complex, aromatic flavor combining intense sweetness with tropical-fruit and apricot notes and just enough acid to balance. The flavor is so intense that eating a ripe Sun Gold warm from the vine is often cited by gardeners as a transformative experience — the difference from a grocery store tomato is dramatic. 'Sun Gold' is an indeterminate vine that grows vigorously (staking required), produces prolifically throughout the season, and sets fruit reliably in a wide range of conditions. The thin skin causes occasional cracking near harvest in wet conditions — harvest promptly when ripe. In Gulf Coast zone 9, grow in spring (March–June harvest) and again in fall (September–November harvest), skipping the hottest summer months when fruiting stalls. A must-grow for anyone who wants to understand what a truly great tomato tastes like.

common_name: Sun Leaper Tomato (NC State Heat-Set Hybrid)
plant_note: Transplant after all frost danger has passed and nights stay reliably above 60°F; Sun Leaper keeps setting fruit through warm summer nights that stall most other slicing tomatoes.
directions: Sun Leaper was bred at North Carolina State University from the heat-tolerant breeding line NC HS-1 specifically to keep setting fruit when nighttime temperatures stay warm — a common failure point for standard slicing tomatoes across the Deep South. The determinate vines carry thin foliage that sheds heat well, so give plants a stake or cage and moderate afternoon shade in the hottest zone 9 gardens to reduce sunscald on the shoulders. Fruit are large, firm, deep red with a small blossom scar, and hold up better against cracking and rough-scar disorders than comparable heat-set hybrids like Solar Set. Because it is determinate, plan a second late-summer transplanting for a fall crop rather than relying on a single planting to carry through the whole season.

common_name: Sun Sugar Cherry Tomato (Extremely Sweet Orange F1 Cherry Tomato, Japan Tokita Seed)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Sun Sugar is an indeterminate cherry tomato that benefits from caging or staking and grows throughout the season. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production. Sun Sugar's exceptional crack resistance — unusual in cherry tomatoes, which commonly split at the stem end when they absorb excess water rapidly after dry periods — makes it more practical in zone 9's irregular summer rainfall than crack-prone cherry types. The fruits are orange to golden-orange (slightly deeper than the orange of Sungold under some growing conditions — though Sun Sugar and Sungold are sometimes confused in the US market, they are distinct varieties), and the sweetness consistently registers among the highest of any commercial cherry tomato variety. The flavor profile combines intense sweetness with mild acidity and a complex, fruity tomato character. Harvest clusters when uniformly orange.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake or cage. Harvest clusters when uniformly orange. Sun Sugar is an F1 hybrid cherry tomato developed by Tokita Seeds of Japan — one of the premier vegetable seed breeding companies in the world — and became widely popular in North America through distribution by companies including Park Seed and Renee's Garden Seeds, where it is sometimes sold under the Park Seed exclusive name 'Sun Sugar.' Sun Sugar consistently ranks among the highest-rated cherry tomato varieties for sweetness and flavor in home garden and market garden trials — its Brix (sugar content) measurements frequently exceed 10 (compared to 6–8 for standard slicing tomatoes), and the flavor combines this exceptional sweetness with mild acidity and what tasters frequently describe as a complex, almost citrus-tropical fruitiness distinct from standard red cherry types. The color — orange to golden-orange, slightly more orange than Sungold (which is from Takii Seeds, a different Japanese company) — is part of the flavor differentiation: orange cherry tomatoes in this category contain different proportions of carotenoids than red types, often with higher beta-carotene content and lower lycopene, contributing to their distinctively fruity, mild-acid flavor. Sun Sugar's crack resistance in the field is a practical advantage that Sungold (its main competitor) has been criticized for lacking — the characteristic of splitting when water uptake increases rapidly after drought periods plagues many cherry tomato varieties, and Sun Sugar's better resistance reduces the frustration of finding split fruit after rain events.

common_name: SunGold Cherry Tomato (Takii Seed Golden-Orange F1 Cherry)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; SunGold is an F1 hybrid cherry tomato from Takii Seed (Japan) widely considered the sweetest and most popular cherry tomato in American home gardens — the small, golden-orange fruits ripen early and continuously, offering exceptional sweetness with tropical-fruity overtones unlike any other cherry tomato.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after last frost; SunGold is an indeterminate vine that benefits from strong staking or a tomato cage at least 5–6 feet tall; remove suckers for concentrated fruiting or allow to develop for maximum production; harvest when golden-orange and slightly soft. SunGold is an F1 hybrid cherry tomato developed by Takii Seed of Japan and first introduced to American gardeners in the early 1990s; it has since become the most widely grown and most frequently praised cherry tomato in American home gardens, consistently ranked first or near-first in taste comparisons by extension services, seed companies, and tomato enthusiasts for its exceptional sweetness and complex flavor. The small (3/4 to 1 inch), round to slightly oval fruits ripen from green through yellow to a distinctive rich golden-orange color; the flavor at peak ripeness is extraordinary — intensely sweet, with brix values of 9–10 or higher (far above standard tomato sweetness), and distinct tropical-fruity notes (mango, passion fruit, tangerine) that are unique among tomatoes and make SunGold recognizable in a blind taste test. The indeterminate vines are extremely productive, bearing prolific clusters of 15–30 fruits from early summer until frost; the fruits are crack-resistant for a cherry type. Not an open-pollinated heirloom (seed saved from SunGold will not come true), but the exceptional flavor makes it a standard in virtually every serious home garden.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; an All-America Selections winner with brilliant yellow, scallop-edged pattypan fruits and bushy, compact habit that produces prolifically over a long season in hot climates — well-suited to Gulf Coast spring and fall gardening.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil; Sunburst is a bush-type pattypan that requires no support and takes up significantly less space than vining squash. Sunburst is an All-America Selections award-winning summer squash producing vivid golden-yellow, flying-saucer-shaped pattypan fruits with slightly scalloped edges and tender, mild, buttery white flesh that is best harvested at 3–4 inches when the skin is still soft and the seeds are immature; left to grow larger the skin toughens and flavor diminishes. The compact bush plants are highly productive in hot weather and are excellent for Gulf Coast gardens where the fast harvest window allows planting in both spring and early fall. Sunburst is virtually identical to Bennings Green Tint but with consistent bright yellow rather than pale green coloring.

common_name: Sunburst Scallop Squash (Bright Yellow AAS-Winning Patty Pan Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Sunburst is an AAS-winning hybrid patty pan squash producing bright golden-yellow, scalloped, saucer-shaped fruit best picked small and tender.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sunburst is a widely grown hybrid patty pan (scallop) squash producing cheerful, bright golden-yellow, saucer-shaped fruit with the classic scalloped edge, best harvested small, at two to three inches across, when the skin is tender and the flavor is sweetest. Picking regularly, every day or two during peak season, keeps the compact, bushy plants productive over a long summer harvest and prevents fruit from becoming tough and seedy. Like other summer squash it is a heavy producer and benefits from consistent moisture and monitoring for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common pests in Gulf South gardens.

common_name: Sunburst Squash (AAS-Winning Golden Yellow Pattypan, Compact and Prolific Summer Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Sunburst is a bush-type pattypan/scallop squash with a compact growth habit that is significantly more manageable in small gardens than the sprawling zucchini types. In zone 9, plant March–May and August–September for fall production. The distinctive golden-yellow color at harvest maturity is an important cue: harvest Sunburst when the fruits are 2–3 inches across and uniformly golden-yellow. At this small size the skin is tender and edible, the flesh is firm and slightly sweet, and the distinctive scalloped edge with pale yellow skin is at its most attractive for presentation. Larger fruits (5+ inches) become tough-skinned and starchy. Sunburst's compact plant habit and prolific production make it one of the best summer squash varieties for containers and raised beds in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 2–3 inches when golden-yellow and edges still tender. Sunburst Squash is an All-America Selections (AAS) winning summer squash recognized for its distinctive golden-yellow color, compact plant habit, and excellent productivity in home garden conditions. The pattypan or scallop squash form (a flattened disc with scalloped edges, sometimes called 'flying saucer' for its distinctive shape) represents an older squash form that predates the elongated zucchini in American kitchen garden history; pattypan varieties were among the first summer squash grown widely in early American gardens, and the distinctive scalloped shape remains one of the most visually attractive squash forms. Sunburst's breakthrough was producing the pattypan form in a vivid, uniform golden-yellow rather than the pale yellow, white, or green of earlier pattypan varieties — the bright color made it immediately eye-catching at farmers markets and in garden displays, and its AAS recognition reflected consistent performance across trial locations. The flavor of small Sunburst squash is mild and slightly sweet, with a firmer texture than zucchini at comparable sizes — the denser flesh of scallop types holds up better in sauté, roasting, and stuffed preparations than the waterier flesh of standard zucchini. For zone 9 gardeners, the compact plant size and abundant production of Sunburst make it one of the more practical summer squash choices for space-limited raised beds and containers, where a standard zucchini plant's 3–4 foot spread would be excessive.

plant_note: Direct-sow at or after last frost; oilseed sunflower varieties have smaller, black-hulled seeds with a higher oil percentage than confection types.
directions: Plant seed 1 in deep and 8–12 in apart in rows spaced 24–30 in; oilseed varieties like 'Peredovik' or 'Rostov' are grown more densely than confection types to reduce branching and produce a single large head per plant. Harvest when the back of the head turns yellow to brown and the seeds are hard — cut heads and hang upside-down in a covered, airy space to cure. Rub seeds out over a screen, then cold-press for oil or roast and use as a whole food. Birds are the main pest; protect ripening heads with netting or paper bags.

plant_note: Grow indoors in trays year-round; not dependent on outdoor season.
directions: Soak the black oil sunflower seed for several hours, then sow densely across a shallow tray of moist growing medium. Keep the tray covered and dark until the seedlings push up, then move to bright light to green up. These nutrient-dense greens are high in iron, calcium, protein, and healthy fats and can be grown indoors year-round. Harvest by snipping the stems just above the soil once the first true leaves begin to show, usually within about ten days. Keep the medium evenly moist and provide good airflow to prevent mold.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring production. Sunmaster is specifically bred to set fruit at temperatures above 90°F when most varieties drop blossoms, making it one of the best heat-set tomatoes for the Gulf Coast.
directions: Transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake; Sunmaster is an indeterminate heat-set tomato developed by the University of Florida specifically for production in hot, humid climates where daytime temperatures regularly exceed 90°F. Unlike many tomato varieties that drop blossoms at high temperatures, Sunmaster sets fruit reliably even when nights stay above 75°F, giving zone 9 gardeners a productive window from early May through June and again in September–November from fall plantings. The large, smooth, red globe fruits average 8–10 ounces with good flavor and crack resistance. Consistent watering is essential — irregular moisture leads to blossom-end rot and fruit cracking in the summer heat.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings into a permanent, well-drained bed once soil is workable in spring. Because Sunrise is a seed strain rather than a division-propagated clone, expect some natural variation in stalk color and vigor among seedlings.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings into a permanent, well-drained bed once soil is workable in spring. Because Sunrise is a seed strain rather than a division-propagated clone, expect some natural variation in stalk color and vigor among seedlings, though most produce attractive red-tinged stalks in their first full season. Sunrise was selected to reach usable harvest size faster than older seed-grown rhubarb strains, giving gardeners who cannot source crown divisions a practical way to start a rhubarb patch from seed. Its flavor is bright and tart, typical of the species, and plants continue to improve in yield for several years after establishment.

common_name: Sunset Torch Tomato (AAS-Winning Striped Flame Grape Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Sunset Torch is a vigorous indeterminate grape tomato that needs a full-length warm season and sturdy staking or caging to support the long fruiting vine.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, then stake or cage the vine well since it is a tall, vigorous indeterminate grower. Sunset Torch is an AAS National Winner prized for fruit that ripens through a striking flame-like progression — green fruit color up in streaks of gold, orange, and finally red as they mature, so a single cluster shows several colors at once and individual fruits look hand-painted. The oblong grape-type fruits are sweet and crack-resistant, produced in long, heavy clusters over a long harvest window. Pick fruit as it fully colors for the sweetest flavor; because color develops gradually, clusters can be harvested a few fruits at a time as each one finishes ripening. Prune suckers lightly to keep air moving through the dense foliage in humid climates.

common_name: Sunshine Kabocha Squash (AAS-Winning Orange Kabocha-Type Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Sunshine is an All-America Selections award-winning (2004) kabocha-type winter squash producing compact 3–4 lb fruits with brilliant orange skin and intensely sweet, rich, dry orange flesh — the classic kabocha-style eating quality in a smaller, more manageable fruit size than traditional green Japanese kabocha varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in a warm, well-prepared bed; Sunshine squash vines are moderately vigorous and less sprawling than giant winter squash types; harvest when the stem corks and the skin is uniformly bright orange and resists fingernail denting; flavor improves significantly with 2–4 weeks of curing after harvest. Sunshine is a kabocha-type F1 hybrid winter squash that won the All-America Selections award in 2004 for outstanding garden performance — its combination of attractive appearance, reliable productivity, and outstanding eating quality made it an immediate success with home gardeners across the country. The squash belongs to the kabocha type (Cucurbita maxima), an East Asian tradition of winter squash with dry, dense, intensely sweet flesh that is considered the finest eating quality among all winter squash types. While traditional Japanese kabocha cultivars have dark green or grey skin with pale stripes, Sunshine was selected for brilliant orange skin that is instantly attractive and visually distinctive in the garden and at market. The flesh is the characteristic kabocha type: intensely deep orange, very dry, sweet, and starchy — so dense and sweet that it bakes without becoming watery, purées into thick soups without thickening, and can be used in dessert preparations. The compact 3–4 pound fruit size is practical for household use (one squash makes 2–4 servings without left-over waste) and the moderate vine size makes it manageable in home gardens with less space than butternut or hubbard types. Excellent storage for 3–4 months under cool conditions.

common_name: Sunshine Squash (AAS-Winning Bright Orange Kabocha with Rich Sweet Flesh)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Sunshine is a kabocha-type Cucurbita maxima producing small to medium fruits (3–5 lbs) with a distinctive bright orange skin — virtually identical in form to red kuri / Uchiki Kuri except with orange skin rather than red-orange. In zone 9, plant March–April for a fall harvest (October–November) as the squash approaches maturity in cooler fall weather that improves sweetness. The skin of fully ripe Sunshine changes from mottled orange-tan at immature stages to a uniform, vivid orange at harvest. The small size (3–5 lbs) makes Sunshine practical for single-household use without the waste of cutting into a very large squash. Sunshine received All-America Selections (AAS) recognition for consistent performance across North American trial locations, including warm climates where some kabocha types underperform.
directions: Direct sow in hills 3–4 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when fully vivid orange and stem begins to dry. Sunshine Squash is an F1 hybrid kabocha-type winter squash that received All-America Selections recognition for its exceptional productivity, vibrant visual appearance, and excellent eating quality in the kabocha class — a category of Cucurbita maxima squash that includes some of the highest-rated winter squash varieties for flavor intensity, flesh texture, and sweetness. Kabocha squash (from the Japanese name for pumpkin, itself derived from 'Cambodia' in Portuguese, reflecting the trade route by which the squash reached Japan) have been developed in Japan into a distinctive style — typically flattened globe form, dense, dry, sweet orange to yellow-orange flesh, and rich, complex chestnut-like flavor — that differs substantially from the North American traditions of summer squash (Cucurbita pepo) and large pumpkin (C. maxima). Sunshine's orange skin sets it visually apart from the dark green and grey-green Japanese kabocha types that inspired it — the vivid orange exterior makes it immediately recognizable at harvest and provides a decorative harvest-season display function alongside its culinary utility. The flesh is dense, dry (low water content), very sweet at full maturity, and with the characteristic kabocha texture that some cooks describe as between sweet potato and chestnut — a distinctive dry, starchy sweetness that makes kabocha the preferred squash for soups, tempura, and Japanese-inspired preparations where excess moisture would dilute the flavors.

common_name: Super Fantastic Tomato (Burpee F1 Hybrid Large Vigorous Disease-Resistant Slicer)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Super Fantastic is indeterminate and requires staking or caging — the plant produces heavy crops of large fruits over a long season that weigh down unsupported canes. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring production. Super Fantastic is noted for producing fruits later into the warm Gulf Coast spring than some other beefsteak varieties — its heat tolerance gives it slightly extended production in zone 9 before summer heat stops fruit set. The disease resistance (VF — Verticillium and Fusarium wilt resistance) is particularly valuable in the Gulf South's humid soil conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage immediately. Super Fantastic is a Burpee F1 hybrid tomato released in 1978 — one of the most successful and widely sold hybrid tomatoes of the latter 20th century, bred at the W. Atlee Burpee Company by Dr. Elwyn Meader's breeding program. Super Fantastic hit the market at a time when home gardeners were increasingly adopting the first generation of disease-resistant hybrid tomatoes, and the combination of large fruit size (fruits commonly 12–16 oz), vigorous plant growth, early maturity (70–80 days), and dual disease resistance (VF designation) made it extremely popular in the American home garden market through the 1980s and 1990s. The fruits are classic large red beefsteak form — round to slightly oblate, firm, meaty, with relatively few seeds and good thick walls — the standard large slicing tomato character for sandwiches, burgers, and fresh eating. Super Fantastic remains in production and widely sold despite the explosion of alternative hybrid and heirloom beefsteak types since its introduction, maintained in home garden seed racks and catalogs by its reputation for reliable, heavy production and disease resistance across a wide range of conditions. For zone 9 gardeners, the VF disease resistance tag is particularly relevant in humid soils where Fusarium and Verticillium wilt are common causes of premature plant death.

common_name: Super Sugar Snap Pea (Improved High-Yield Snap Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked and set a sturdy 5-6 foot trellis at planting time, since vines are tall and vigorous and set pods quickly once warm days arrive.
directions: Super Sugar Snap is an improved selection bred from the original Sugar Snap pea to offer stronger vigor, better tolerance of powdery mildew, and a few days' earlier, heavier first flush of pods. The tall vines still need a sturdy trellis or fence but reward the extra support with thick-walled, sweet, fully edible pods over a longer harvest window than the older strain. Pick every two to three days once pods are round and glossy to keep plants producing and to catch pods before the pod wall starts to toughen. Because it holds up well to warm spring weather, it is a good choice for gardeners in regions where the cool pea season is short.

common_name: Super Sweet 100 Cherry Tomato (Red Cherry Cluster Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Super Sweet 100 is a vigorous indeterminate that needs very sturdy staking or caging to at least 6 feet.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Super Sweet 100 is one of the most prolific and most frequently recommended cherry tomato varieties in American home gardening — a hybrid producing massive, long clusters (trusses) of 20–30 small (1-inch), round, brilliant red cherry tomatoes with exceptional sweetness and high sugar content that makes each fruit taste like concentrated tomato candy. The 'Sweet 100' line was introduced in the 1970s and immediately became one of the best-selling tomato varieties; 'Super Sweet 100' is an improved hybrid with better disease resistance. In zone 9, Super Sweet 100 produces from February or March transplanting through June, and again from September through November transplanting for a fall crop — two productive growing windows that can yield hundreds of fruits per plant. The enormous, arching clusters of brilliant red tomatoes draping from a well-established vine are a spectacular sight. The high Brix (sugar content) makes Super Sweet 100 outstanding for snacking, caprese salads, and any use where raw tomato sweetness is the primary quality desired. Vigorous growth requires staking or caging — an established Super Sweet 100 vine can reach 8 feet or more and must be supported to prevent collapsing under the weight of developing fruit clusters.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors and transplant carefully; give this giant type much more room than standard kohlrabi so the stem can bulk up over a long season.
directions: Sow into fertile, well-drained soil with wide spacing, since Superschmelz — German for super melter — is bred to swell to eight or ten pounds while staying crisp and tender rather than turning woody like most oversized kohlrabi. Keep watering consistent through the growing season to avoid splitting the enlarging stem, and side-dress with compost as the bulb sizes up. Harvest young for a milder, thinner-skinned bite, or let it grow to full giant size for slicing, roasting, or long winter storage.

common_name: Supersonic Tomato (Large Crack-Resistant Red Beefsteak Hybrid Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Supersonic's outstanding crack resistance is particularly valuable in Gulf South gardens subject to alternating wet and dry periods — irregular watering that causes cracking in thin-skinned varieties has less impact on Supersonic.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Supersonic is a classic large-fruited beefsteak-type hybrid tomato developed for outstanding crack resistance — one of the most crack-resistant large-fruited tomato varieties available, a quality of significant practical importance in Gulf South gardens where irregular rainfall and alternating wet-dry conditions cause cracking in thin-skinned large varieties. The large (8–12 oz), round to slightly flattened, deep-red, firm-fleshed fruits have classic fresh-eating and slicing quality — Supersonic produces the large-scale, meaty beefsteak tomato slices valued for sandwiches and fresh presentations. Supersonic is an indeterminate variety reaching 5–7 feet that requires sturdy staking or caging throughout the season. The crack resistance advantage comes from a thicker skin and firmer flesh than many large-fruited varieties — the practical benefit is significantly less fruit loss during wet periods that would crack softer-skinned types. Supersonic carries V and F disease resistance. In zone 9, Supersonic is best grown as a spring crop (February–May) to maximize the early harvest before summer heat affects fruit set on large-fruited types. The variety has been in continuous production since its introduction in the 1970s — maintained by home gardeners who value the reliable production of large, crack-resistant, good-quality red slicing tomatoes.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Supersteak is a Burpee hybrid bred for exceptionally large beefsteak fruit, some of the biggest slicing tomatoes available, on a vigorous indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, providing sturdy staking or caging since this vigorous vine bears exceptionally heavy fruit. Supersteak is a Burpee hybrid beefsteak tomato bred for some of the largest fruit of any tomato variety, often exceeding a pound per tomato, with meaty, flavorful flesh well suited to thick slices for sandwiches. Its designation as VFN indicates built-in resistance to verticillium wilt, fusarium wilt, and nematodes, helping it stay productive through a long, humid Gulf South growing season. Water deeply and consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking on the large fruit, and feed generously to support the heavy crop load.

common_name: Supersweet 100 Cherry Tomato (Classic Sweet Indeterminate Cherry)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Supersweet 100 is an indeterminate vine that produces prolifically throughout the season when grown with strong support (cage or stake 6+ feet tall). In zone 9, transplant late February through early March for harvest May through July, with a second planting in August–September for fall production. The long clusters (20–30+ tomatoes) must be harvested regularly; overripe fruits split easily.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with strong support and consistent, even watering to prevent blossom end rot. Supersweet 100 is one of the most important cherry tomato varieties ever developed — a Petoseed hybrid released in the 1980s that set the standard for sweet cherry tomatoes and has remained one of the top-selling cherry tomatoes in America for over 40 years based solely on its exceptional eating quality. The name states the performance promise: 'super sweet' flavor from fruits with approximately twice the sugar content of beefsteak types, and '100' (now sold as 'Supersweet 100 F1') referencing a very early working name for the variety's productivity. The red, round, 1-inch fruits are produced in long, abundant clusters of 20–50+ tomatoes per cluster on indeterminate vines that require staking or caging and continue producing until frost. The flavor is memorably sweet, bright, and richly tomato-forward — thin-skinned enough to burst slightly on the palate, sweet enough to eat like candy, and balanced with just enough acidity to be complex rather than cloying. Supersweet 100 has also demonstrated excellent virus resistance for a variety of its era, which contributes to its continued commercial success. Every tomato gardener who grows cherry tomatoes should try Supersweet 100 as the benchmark against which other cherry varieties are compared.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out once frost danger passes. This determinate Roma sets a dependable mid-season crop of large, uniform paste tomatoes even in heat. The concentrated harvest is ideal for making sauce or paste, and the meaty fruits also chop well for salads and salsas. As a bush type it needs only light support and produces most of its fruit over a short window. In long-season areas a successive planting extends the harvest.

plant_note: Plant corm divisions or cormels in well-drained, humus-rich, fertile soil in late spring once soil is thoroughly warm; suran produces one enormous leaf (a deeply divided umbrella-like structure on a single mottled petiole) per season and then dies back to the corm in autumn. In zone 9 leave corms in the ground with mulch protection, or dig and store above freezing. Partial shade is tolerated well and preferred in zone 9+ summers.
directions: Plant corm sections with at least one bud 4–6 inches deep in loose, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil; suran is a major root crop of South and Southeast Asia — a different species from konjac (Amorphophallus konjac) and much more important as a direct food source, producing starchy corms that can weigh 2–5 kg and are used extensively in Indian cooking as suran or oal, in Indonesian cooking as iles-iles, and across tropical Asia in curries, stews, and chips. The corm must be cooked before eating to neutralize calcium oxalate crystals that cause irritation when raw — boiling, roasting, or frying renders the corm safe and gives a texture similar to taro or potato with a mildly earthy flavor that absorbs spices beautifully. The plant emerges in spring as a single dramatic mottled petiole supporting an enormous, deeply divided leaf canopy 3–5 feet wide — extraordinary as a tropical foliage accent in the garden. Corms multiply readily and can be divided each year, building a productive patch.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Surefire is a determinate tomato bred by Texas A&M AgriLife specifically to keep setting fruit through the high nighttime temperatures that shut down bloom-to-fruit set in most tomato varieties across the Gulf South and Deep South summer.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Surefire is a Texas A&M AgriLife release and Texas Superstar-designated tomato bred specifically to hold fruit set through the punishing high nighttime heat of a Central and South Texas summer, when most tomato varieties stop setting fruit almost entirely — a trait directly useful across the wider Gulf South wherever midsummer heat causes the familiar tomato slump between the spring and fall crops. The compact, determinate plant produces a concentrated, heavy crop of medium-size, firm, flavorful red fruit over a shorter, more manageable staking and pruning window than a sprawling indeterminate vine. Because it is bred to keep fruiting through heat rather than avoid it, it is a good choice to extend the harvest into the hottest stretch of a zone 9 summer where other varieties stall.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in partial shade in moist, well-drained soil; in zone 9–11 it acts as a perennial or self-sowing annual, persisting year-round in frost-free areas.
directions: Direct sow in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade after temperatures warm; surinam spinach (also called Philippine spinach or waterleaf) is a heat-loving tropical leafy vegetable used throughout West Africa, the Caribbean, and Southeast Asia, where the succulent leaves and stems are harvested young and cooked in soups, stews, and stir-fries. In zone 9–11 it is remarkably productive in the hot, partially shaded spots where most greens fail completely, filling a critical gap for summer leafy vegetable production under trees or on north-facing beds. It is tender to frost but self-sows prolifically in warm climates to return each year. Harvest the tender growing tips regularly to encourage continuous bushy production. The small magenta flowers are ornamental and attract bees.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall; Susanville is a California-origin artichoke-type softneck bred from California Early stock and noted for reliable low-chill performance, adapting well to both warm and cold-winter climates alike.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil in fall; Susanville is an artichoke-type softneck improved from California Early stock, valued for a wide climate range and dependable bulbing even where winters are too mild to satisfy hardneck garlic's chilling needs. Bulbs form in a layered, artichoke-like pattern with a good number of easy-to-peel cloves in white to lightly purple-streaked wrappers, carrying a robust flavor that mellows nicely when roasted or cooked. As a softneck it braids easily and cures into long-storing bulbs. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store for use through much of the year.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Suyo Long is a traditional Chinese burpless cucumber with exceptionally long (12–18 inch), ribbed, slightly curved fruits, tender thin skin, seedless-to-few-seed interior, and mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor — one of the finest cucumbers for fresh eating and extraordinarily productive in hot weather.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines up a trellis to keep the long fruits straight and prevent rot — trellising is particularly important for Suyo Long to develop straight fruits. Suyo Long is a traditional Chinese slicing cucumber producing very long (12–18 inch), slightly ribbed, tapered fruits with a distinctive light green, slightly warted skin and an interior that is almost entirely flesh with very few seeds; the flavor is exceptionally mild, sweet, and refreshing with none of the bitterness common in cucumbers grown in heat stress. It is the burpless cucumber par excellence — the thin skin and low cucurbitacin content make it highly digestible and virtually non-gassy even when eaten in large quantities. Extremely productive in hot weather and much more heat-tolerant than European greenhouse cucumbers; outstanding for Gulf Coast and Southern summer production. Best trellised vertically for straight fruits and improved air circulation.

common_name: Swedish Brown Bean (Öland Heirloom Soup Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; a Scandinavian heirloom bush bean documented since the 1890s and traditionally grown on the island of Öland.
directions: Sow seeds directly 1 inch deep after the last frost date, spacing compact bush plants 4-6 inches apart; the low, sturdy habit needs no support. Swedish Brown, also sold as Öland Swedish Brown, is a Scandinavian heirloom dating to at least the 1890s that produces short pods holding five to seven glossy tan-brown seeds marked with a small white eye. Leave pods on the plant until they dry and rattle, then shell and store the beans, which cook to a nutty, dense texture well suited to baked bean dishes and hearty soups. The short, stocky plants tolerate cooler summers better than many bean varieties, reflecting their northern European origin.

common_name: Sweet 100 Cherry Tomato (Classic Ultra-Productive Sweet Red Indeterminate Cherry)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Sweet 100 is a vigorous indeterminate plant that grows very tall (6–8+ feet) and produces enormous clusters of cherry tomatoes throughout the season — staking is essential, with minimum 6-foot stakes or a sturdy cage recommended. In zone 9, transplant March–April for early summer production that continues until fall or first frost. The '100' in the name references the extremely large number of tomatoes per cluster — a single cluster can hold 50–100 or more cherry tomatoes, and a well-established plant in zone 9's long season produces continuously from June through November with minimal stopping. Sweet 100 is somewhat susceptible to cracking in irregular watering conditions (a common complaint), but the sheer productivity and classic sweet-acid cherry tomato flavor have maintained its popularity for decades.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and provide minimum 6-foot stake. Harvest clusters when uniformly red. Sweet 100 is one of the most famous and historically significant cherry tomato varieties in American home gardening — an F1 hybrid first introduced in the early 1980s that set a new standard for cherry tomato productivity and established the category of 'sweet cherry tomato' as distinct from larger slicing tomato types. Before Sweet 100, cherry tomatoes were typically valued for novelty and ease of snacking rather than for the combination of extremely high productivity and genuinely sweet, complex flavor that Sweet 100 provided. The variety produces long, branching clusters with an extraordinary number of fruits per cluster — sometimes 50–100 per cluster, as the name implies — with uniformly round, 1-inch red fruits and a flavor that combines sweetness with the right amount of acidity to create what many gardeners consider the definitive cherry tomato flavor. The flavor balance of Sweet 100 — sweet but not cloying, with genuine tomato acid and complexity — made it the reference standard against which subsequent cherry varieties were judged for a generation. Sweet 100's high vitamin C content (documented to be substantially higher than larger slicing tomatoes) and prolific production made it popular both as a garden plant and as a crop for farmers markets where volume production of cherry tomatoes was economically important. Several improved varieties building on Sweet 100's genetics followed, including Sweet Million (improved crack resistance), Supersweet 100 (same name but improved disease package), and others — but the original Sweet 100 remains widely grown and available.

common_name: Sweet 100 Tomato (Classic Prolific Hybrid Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Sweet 100 is an exceptionally vigorous indeterminate hybrid and needs a tall, sturdy cage or trellis to support its long, heavily fruiting vines.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, providing a tall, sturdy cage or trellis for the vigorous, sprawling vines. Sweet 100 is a classic F1 hybrid cherry tomato introduced in the 1980s, prized for producing extraordinarily long clusters of small, intensely sweet, bright red fruit in such abundance that a single healthy plant can yield hundreds of tomatoes over the season, giving the variety its name. Its exceptional sweetness, disease tolerance, and reliable heavy production made it one of the most widely grown cherry tomatoes for home gardens and remains a benchmark variety against which many newer cherry tomato hybrids are compared. Harvest continuously as fruit ripens to encourage ongoing production, since the plant sets new clusters rapidly throughout a long summer season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors and transplant after all frost danger passes.
directions: Start Sweet Banana seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost, keeping the soil warm for even germination. Transplant seedlings 12 to 18 inches apart once nights stay warm. This heirloom produces long, slender fruits that ripen from pale yellow to orange and red with a mild, sweet flavor. Harvest at any stage for fresh eating, pickling, or stuffing, and keep plants evenly watered to support steady fruit set.

common_name: Sweet Banana Pepper (Classic Long Yellow Sweet Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Sweet Banana peppers are excellent for pickling — harvest at the pale yellow to light orange stage for maximum crispness in pickled applications.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sweet Banana is one of the most popular sweet pepper varieties in American home gardens — a long (6–8 inch), tapering, banana-shaped pepper with thin to medium walls and very mild, sweet flavor with absolutely no heat at any stage of maturity. The fruits ripen from pale creamy-yellow through orange to red, with the best flavor for fresh eating at the orange to red stage and the best texture for pickling at the pale yellow stage. Sweet banana peppers are the standard pepper for the famous deli-style pickled banana peppers — the crunchy, mildly tangy, bright-yellow pickled pepper slices ubiquitous on Italian subs, pizza, and in Greek salads. Home-pickled banana peppers from fresh-harvested yellow fruits are far superior in flavor and crunch to commercially processed versions. For fresh use, allow to ripen fully red — the red stage develops sweeter, richer flavor approaching the sweetness of roasted red pepper. The productive, upright, sturdy plants are easily distinguished by the numerous hanging yellow peppers at varying stages, creating a colorful harvest display. In zone 9, sweet banana peppers are among the most productive warm-season vegetables — the long growing season allows multiple picks per plant from spring through late fall.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after frost danger passes. This 1941 Hungarian heirloom is the traditional pickling type, bearing long, bright yellow, thick-walled sweet peppers. Enjoy the fruits fresh as a snack, in salads, grilled, or in any recipe calling for sweet pepper. Left on the plant, the peppers ripen through orange to red and grow even sweeter. Keep plants evenly watered and pick regularly to encourage a heavy set.

common_name: Sweet Beauty Watermelon (AAS-Winning High-Brix Icebox Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 3 weeks ahead for an earlier harvest; this variety was recognized by All-America Selections judges specifically for its eating quality.
directions: Sweet Beauty is a small-space, single-serving icebox watermelon that won an All-America Selections award for consistently outscoring other compact varieties in sugar content during trials, with recorded Brix readings above 11. Fruits are oblong, 5-7 pounds, with dark green rind and medium green stripes and dense, sweet red flesh, and the vines stay manageable at roughly 8-10 feet, making the variety a good fit for smaller vegetable gardens. Grow it with full sun and even moisture through fruit development, then cut back watering as fruits ripen to keep the sugar concentration high. Its combination of compact vine habit and top-tier flavor makes it an easy choice for gardeners who don't have room for sprawling full-size Southern types but still want genuinely sweet, crisp melon.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed; cherry peppers are very heat-tolerant and productive in warm climates, making them well-suited to zone 8–11 summer conditions.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost in warm starting mix; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed and soil temperature reaches 60°F. Sweet cherry peppers produce round, apple-sized fruits 1.5–2 inches in diameter that ripen from green to deep red and have thick, sweet, crisp walls with mild to no heat, making them among the best peppers for stuffing, pickling, and eating fresh off the plant. The compact, bushy plants are ornamental and prolific, producing dozens of round fruits per plant over a long season. Stuff raw fruits with cream cheese or pickled vegetables for appetizers, or pack them whole into brine for a classic Italian condiment.

plant_note: Start indoors and set out after frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow Sweet Chocolate seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks ahead of the last frost and transplant when the soil has warmed. This heirloom bell ripens from green to a striking deep mahogany-brown with crisp, mild, sweet flesh. Space plants 12 to 18 inches apart in full sun and stake if fruit load gets heavy. Harvest peppers once they turn fully brown for the richest flavor, and keep watering consistent to prevent blossom-end rot.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 60°F; sow in blocks of at least 4 rows (not single rows) for adequate wind pollination and good ear fill. Plant successive blocks every 2–3 weeks for extended harvest.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F, planting in blocks of at least 4 rows rather than single rows to ensure adequate wind pollination of the silks — poor pollination produces ears with scattered missing kernels. Provide consistent, deep watering especially during tasseling and silking, as moisture stress during pollination is the leading cause of poor ear development. Harvest when silks have turned brown and dry, ears feel filled to the tip, and a kernel punctured with a fingernail releases a milky juice (clear juice = immature; no juice = overripe). Sweet corn sugars convert to starch rapidly after harvest; cook or refrigerate immediately. Plant well away from popcorn or field corn to prevent cross-pollination, which reduces sweetness.

common_name: Sweet Daisy Tomato (High-Yielding Compact Grape Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the compact, well-branched plant benefits from a cage or stake for support.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, providing a cage or stake for support. Sweet Daisy is a modern grape tomato bred for exceptionally heavy, early, and sustained production of small, sweet, crack-resistant fruit on a compact, well-branched plant that fits well into smaller garden beds and large containers. The reliable disease tolerance and continuous fruit set through summer heat have made it a popular choice for gardeners wanting a low-maintenance, high-yield snacking tomato without the sprawling size of full-scale indeterminate vines. Harvest fruit as clusters fully color, picking regularly to keep the productive plant setting new fruit throughout a long summer season.

plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Start seed indoors in peat pots a few weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once the soil is warm, giving vines plenty of room. This honeydew ripens to an unbelievably sweet, almost wine-like flavor far superior to store-bought melons. Each seven-by-eight-inch fruit weighs about seven to eight pounds with light green flesh and skin. Water consistently while vines grow and fruit sets, then ease off as melons ripen to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the blossom end softens and the rind lightens to creamy color.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm above 65°F; Sweet Dumpling is a moderately vining variety that fits well in smaller gardens compared to full-size winter squash types — it can be grown on a sturdy trellis with the developing fruits supported in mesh slings.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in compost-enriched hills 2–3 weeks after last frost, thinning to 2 plants per hill; Sweet Dumpling is one of the most popular small winter squash varieties, producing cream-colored, deeply ribbed, round to slightly flattened fruits weighing 1–2 pounds with distinctive dark green stripes and flecks that turn orange at full maturity. The single-serving-size fruits are among the sweetest of all winter squash — the pale yellow-orange flesh is dry, fine-textured, and sweet enough to eat simply baked with butter and a touch of salt, making it an outstanding small family vegetable garden variety for households that do not need the large quantity of a full butternut or Hubbard. Harvest when the rind is fully hard and the green striping has faded to cream or begun turning orange; cure for 1–2 weeks at room temperature before storing.

common_name: Sweet Favorite Watermelon (AAS-Winning Classic Striped Picnic Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Sweet Favorite is a long-standing AAS-winning watermelon prized for exceptional sweetness on a large, classic oblong striped fruit good for feeding a crowd.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms. Sweet Favorite is a long-established AAS-winning watermelon, producing large, oblong, classically striped fruit in the traditional picnic-watermelon style, prized above all for exceptional sweetness that has kept it a favorite for decades since its introduction. Fruit commonly reaches 15-25 pounds with crisp, bright-red flesh and a good, thin-but-sturdy rind for handling and short-term storage. Its large size makes it well suited to feeding a crowd at a summer gathering, in keeping with its classic picnic-watermelon role. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil, ample space, and consistent irrigation through fruit development, since drought stress during fruit fill causes smaller fruit and hollow heart. Judge ripeness by the ground spot yellowing, the tendril nearest the fruit drying and curling, and a dull, hollow thump when tapped.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 start November–December and transplant February–March. Sweet Hungarian is a prolific, dependable frying pepper well-suited to zone 9 heat; the compact plants continue setting fruit through the summer heat when bell peppers often pause. A second planting in July provides fall production. Plants benefit from light afternoon shade in peak summer to prevent blossom drop.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Hungarian is a classic frying and pickling pepper producing long, tapered, light yellow-green to red fruits of 5–8 inches with thin, tender walls, very mild heat (500–1,000 SHU), and a sweet, slightly tangy flavor that makes them the preferred pepper for Hungarian paprika production, pickled peppers, stuffed peppers, and traditional frying preparations. The thin-walled, tapered fruits cook quickly without the wateriness of thick-walled bell peppers, making them excellent for sautéing whole in olive oil, frying until blistered, stuffing with rice and ground meat, or pickling in brine. The fruit color progression from yellow-green through orange to brilliant red allows harvest at multiple stages — yellow-green for crisp, mild frying, red for maximum sweetness and paprika production. In zone 9 the compact, productive plants withstand summer heat far better than bell peppers and continue producing through the warmest months.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March after nights stay above 55°F. Sweet Hungarian Wax is productive through Gulf Coast summers and handles high humidity well, producing heavily from June through October with regular fertilization.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sweet Hungarian Wax is the mild counterpart to the hot banana pepper — a waxy, thick-walled, banana-shaped variety that ripens from pale yellow through orange to red and carries virtually no heat (0–500 SHU). The sweet, crisp, 5–7 inch fruits are outstanding for pickling, fresh eating, roasting, and stuffing, and their attractive color progression makes them ornamental on the plant. Harvest at yellow to orange stage for the sweetest, mildest flavor; the fully red fruits are slightly sweeter but softer. This variety is particularly valued for pickling operations as the thick walls hold their crunch through the canning process. Plants are compact and tidy, ideal for raised beds and container growing.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for a May–June harvest and August for fall. Kabocha-type squashes including Sweet Mama are more heat-tolerant than most maxima types, making them better suited to zone 9 than Blue Hubbard or Buttercup. The compact vine is more manageable than sprawling maxima types, but still needs 5–8 feet of space per plant.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Mama is an All-America Selections-winning kabocha-type squash selected for exceptional sweetness and a compact vine habit. The small, flattened, dark green fruits (3–4 pounds) have brilliant deep-orange flesh with an almost impossibly sweet, nutty, dry flavor — more concentrated and dessert-like than butternut or acorn squash. When cut open the flesh is so dense and dry that it steams and bakes with a chestnut-like texture, and the sugar content is high enough to caramelize beautifully on cut surfaces. The thin edible skin softens when cooked, eliminating the need for peeling. Sweet Mama's superior flavor comes from its Japanese kabocha parentage, which Japanese breeders developed over decades specifically for sugar content and dry, flavorful flesh. In zone 9 harvest when the stem has dried and corked over and the skin has hardened — squeezing should produce no give in the flesh. Cure 2–4 weeks at room temperature before eating for best flavor development.

common_name: Sweet Meat Squash (Oregon Homestead Sweet Meat, Gray Hubbard-Type)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Sweet Meat is a large (8–15 lb) slate-blue to gray-green winter squash of the Cucurbita maxima species, historically important in the Pacific Northwest as a premier eating and storing squash; it is the variety that defined the 'gray Hubbard' category of dry, sweet, long-storing winter squash in American home gardens.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; Sweet Meat requires a long vine (8–12 feet) and ample space; harvest when the skin is fully gray-blue and rock-hard; it stores exceptionally well (6–8 months in cool, dry conditions) and the flavor improves with several months of storage as starches convert to sugars. Sweet Meat squash is a prized heirloom of the Pacific Northwest, where it has been grown in Oregon and Washington for generations as the gold standard of winter keeping squash — valued above all other varieties for the combination of very long storage life, exceptional flavor, and high-quality flesh. The fruits are large (8–15 lbs), somewhat flattened round to oval, with a smooth, dry, slate-blue to gray-green skin that turns distinctly grayish-blue at full maturity — a color that is characteristic of the very best long-storing Cucurbita maxima varieties. The flesh is uniformly deep orange, very dry, dense, and extremely sweet — with a characteristic thick, starchy quality that makes it ideal for baking, puréeing, and any preparation where flavor concentration and dry texture are paramount. The famous Oregon home economist and food writer Carol Deppe championed Sweet Meat squash extensively in her book 'The Resilient Gardener' as the ideal squash for serious food gardeners seeking long storage life and superior flavor; her advocacy brought Sweet Meat to wider national attention. Unlike most winter squash that peak at harvest and slowly decline in storage, Sweet Meat actually improves for the first 2–3 months in storage as the chemistry continues to develop, making it the ideal squash for a Thanksgiving centerpiece planted in late spring.

common_name: Sweet Million Cherry Tomato (F1 Red Cluster Cherry)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant after last frost into full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Sweet Million is a widely grown F1 red cherry tomato bearing prolific clusters of crack-resistant, uniformly sized 1-inch red fruits with excellent sweet flavor — an improvement on the classic Sweet 100 type with better crack resistance, disease resistance, and fruit quality for both home gardens and market growers.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; stake or cage early as Sweet Million produces vigorous indeterminate vines; the fruits ripen in large clusters of 15–30 and can be harvested cluster by cluster. Sweet Million is an F1 hybrid red cherry tomato developed as an improved successor to the classic Sweet 100 cherry tomato — retaining Sweet 100's exceptional productivity and sweet flavor while adding meaningfully better crack resistance, improved disease resistance (including resistance to fusarium and verticillium wilts), and more uniform fruit sizing than the original Sweet 100. The fruits are small, round, and uniformly 3/4 to 1 inch, ripening a brilliant red; the flavor is classic cherry tomato — sweet, high in sugar relative to acids, bright and fruity with good tomato character. The vines are indeterminate and extremely productive, bearing what appears to be a literally endless succession of clusters from midsummer through frost — the name 'Sweet Million' suggests the volume of fruit a well-grown plant produces. Sweet Million is an outstanding choice for home gardeners who want maximum production of reliable, sweet red cherry tomatoes for fresh eating, salads, and snacking; it is particularly recommended for humid climates (including the Gulf Coast) where crack-prone cherry varieties fail in summer rains. Disease-resistant foliage is an advantage in humid zone 8–10 conditions.

common_name: Sweet Olive Tomato (Very Sweet Small Oval Grape-Type Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sweet Olive's thick skin and oval shape give it significantly better shelf life and handling durability than round cherry tomatoes — the firmer skin resists cracking and damage during harvest.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sweet Olive is a grape-type cherry tomato — small (1–1.5 inch), oval to elongated, bright-red fruits with thick skin and meaty, low-moisture flesh that gives this type better handling durability, shelf life, and crack resistance than round cherry tomatoes. The grape-type classification refers to the oval, elongated shape resembling table grapes rather than the classic round cherry tomato form. The flavor is very sweet and concentrated — the firm, meaty flesh with lower water content intensifies the sweetness-per-bite relative to juicier round types. Sweet Olive produces large trusses of fruit on vigorous indeterminate vines. The thick skin and oval shape make grape-type tomatoes like Sweet Olive particularly practical for container growing, patio harvesting, and fresh snacking — the fruits don't burst when squeezed gently and hold their quality well at room temperature for several days after harvest. In zone 9, grape-type cherry tomatoes are among the most reliable summer producers because the thick skin provides some protection against cracking from uneven moisture that affects large-fruited and thin-skinned types. An excellent choice for continuous production through the warm season in zone 9 gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; sweet paprika pepper is a Hungarian/Central European cultivar group bred specifically for drying and grinding into paprika powder, with extraordinarily high carotenoid content giving both the brilliant red color and the sweet, distinctive paprika flavor — grown domestically to produce fresh, vivid paprika far superior in flavor to commercial dried paprika.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; sweet paprika peppers are harvested when fully red and then dried whole (traditionally strung on twine and air-dried) or split and dehydrated before grinding. Sweet (édes) paprika peppers are a cultivar group of Capsicum annuum developed in Hungary for the production of paprika spice, the defining seasoning of Hungarian cuisine and a cornerstone of Central and Eastern European cooking; the peppers themselves are characterized by exceptionally high carotenoid content (primarily capsanthin and capsorubin) that produces both the brilliant deep red color of dried paprika and its characteristic sweet, slightly fruity, mildly smoky flavor with zero heat. Fresh sweet paprika peppers can be eaten like any sweet bell pepper — they have a somewhat thicker, crunchier texture and a distinctive paprika aroma even when raw. For making paprika powder, dry the fully ripe red fruits at 140–160°F until brittle, then grind; freshly ground home paprika is dramatically more vivid in color and flavor than commercial imported paprika.

plant_note: Plant rooted slips (not seeds) 2-3 inches deep and 12-18 inches apart after soil warms to at least 65°F in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic, low-nitrogen soil in full sun; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers which promote vine growth at the expense of root tubers.
directions: Ipomoea batatas is a tropical American vine domesticated in Central or South America before 2500 BCE and now grown worldwide as one of the most nutritious staple vegetables — the orange-fleshed varieties are among the richest plant sources of beta-carotene, vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber. Grow from slips (rooted stem cuttings) purchased in spring or sprouted from a store-bought tuber in a jar of water; harvest after 90-120 frost-free days when vines begin to yellow, digging carefully to avoid cutting the roots. In zone 9-10, slips left in the ground may overwinter and produce a perennial planting; cure harvested tubers at 85-90°F for 1-2 weeks before storage to convert starch to sugar and heal surface cuts.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; the compact bush habit suits smaller gardens and tighter row spacing than vining acorn types.
directions: Sweet REBA (Resistant Early Bush Acorn) is a Cornell University release bred for a truly compact, non-vining bush habit combined with earliness and improved powdery mildew tolerance, making it well suited to short-season and small-space gardens. Despite its small footprint, plants set heavy yields of dark green, ribbed, one-to-one-and-a-half-pound fruit with notably sweet, dry, deep-orange flesh. Its bush form allows closer in-row spacing than sprawling acorn varieties, so it fits well in raised beds or intensive plantings. Choose Sweet REBA when garden space is limited but you still want reliably sweet, early-maturing acorn squash for fall roasting.

common_name: Sweet Sandwich Onion (F1 Long-Storage Sweet Onion)
subcategory: storage onion, hybrid long-day sweet type
plant_note: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings outside about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil once frost risk has passed, spacing them to allow bulbs room to size up. Maintain even moisture through the growing season and let foliage fall over naturally before curing bulbs in a dry, ventilated space.
