Sweet Sandwich is a long-day hybrid bred for a rare combination of mild, sweet flavor and genuinely good storage life, addressing the usual tradeoff where sweeter onions typically spoil faster than pungent storage types.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Sweet Siberian is one of the shortest-season watermelons available, maturing in 65–75 days, with more cold-tolerant germination than most varieties — making it the top choice for zone 3–5 gardens with short summers where most watermelons cannot ripen, while still producing sweet, flavorful fruit.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Sweet Siberian can germinate in soils as cool as 60°F (compared to 70°F+ needed by most watermelons), making early establishment easier in northern gardens. Sweet Siberian is a Russian heirloom watermelon developed for the short, cool growing seasons of Siberia and Central Russia, where conventional watermelon varieties fail to ripen before fall frost; it is one of the most cold-tolerant watermelons for germination and early growth while maturing in 65–75 days from seed — roughly 15–25 days earlier than most mainstream varieties. The small to medium fruits (8–15 lbs) have pale green, lightly striped skin and unusual salmon-orange to pale yellow flesh that is surprisingly sweet and fragrant with a distinctive aroma different from standard red-fleshed varieties. Compact vines suit smaller gardens. An outstanding variety for northern zone 3–5 gardeners who have given up on watermelons, and produces a fast summer crop in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens as well.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed to 65°F; in the Gulf South, May is traditionally the preferred planting month for sweet sorghum to ensure the plant matures before the hot summer peak while still achieving the high sugar accumulation in the stalks that requires a long season.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; sweet sorghum is grown for its tall, juicy, sugar-rich stalks rather than for grain — the canes are milled to extract sweet sap that is then boiled into sorghum molasses (sorghum syrup), a traditional Southern sweetener with a distinctive robust, complex flavor quite different from sugar cane molasses. The tall canes reach 6–15 feet with loose seed heads at the top; they are harvested at soft dough stage before the seeds fully harden. Children can chew raw pieces of stalk as a field snack with mildly sweet, refreshing juice. Growing your own sweet sorghum for syrup is a true farm-to-table tradition in the Appalachian South and Gulf States, requiring a simple press or roller mill to extract the juice and an outdoor evaporating pan to boil it into syrup.

common_name: Sweet Success Cucumber (AAS-Winning Burpee Seedless Slicer)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Sweet Success is parthenocarpic (self-fruitful without pollination), making it valuable in greenhouses, low-pollinator areas, and early in the season when bee activity is low. Train vines vertically for best fruit quality — fruits grown suspended tend to be longer and straighter than those touching the ground. Harvest fruits at 9–12 inches for best quality; overripe fruits develop seeds.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a vertical support for best fruit quality and air circulation. Sweet Success is a 1983 All-America Selections-winning burpless cucumber from Burpee that was among the first parthenocarpic (sets fruit without pollination) cucumbers released for home garden use — a trait that allows fruit production in greenhouses, screen porches, or early in the season when pollinators are scarce, without any compromise in fruit quality. The long (10–14 inch), thin, dark green fruits have tender, smooth skin that doesn't require peeling, virtually no seeds when harvested at the right size, and the characteristically mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor of 'burpless' cucumber types — the term referring to reduced cucurbitacin content that causes the bitterness and digestive upset some people experience with older cucumber types. Sweet Success carries resistance to cucumber scab, cucumber mosaic virus, and angular leaf spot. The thin, tender skin and virtually seedless flesh make Sweet Success excellent for fresh eating and sandwich slicing, with a crisp, sweet quality that compares favorably to expensive English greenhouse cucumbers. A landmark variety in the development of the American burpless-seedless cucumber category and still a strong performer nearly 40 years after its introduction.

common_name: Sweetie Cherry Tomato (Classic Open-Pollinated Small Sweet Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Sweetie is an indeterminate vine that produces prolifically on a long, cascading vine — provide a 5–6 foot cage or strong staking. In zone 9, transplant March–April for May–October production. Like most cherry tomatoes, Sweetie can crack if irrigation is inconsistent (wet-dry-wet cycles cause rapid fruit expansion); consistent moisture management reduces cracking.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; cage or stake before growth gets away from support. Sweetie is an open-pollinated small cherry tomato that has been grown in American gardens since at least the 1970s — one of the classic heirloom small cherry tomatoes alongside Sweet 100 and Gardener's Delight. The round, 0.75–1 inch fruits are produced in large clusters of 15–25 or more on long, indeterminate vines, and have a flavor profile that lives up to the name: very sweet, with high sugar content relative to acid, and the concentrated pure tomato essence that has made small cherry tomatoes universally popular. Sweetie is open-pollinated, meaning seed can be saved from year to year to maintain a self-sustaining garden supply — an advantage over Sweet 100, which is a hybrid. The plants produce heavily from midsummer through frost, providing abundant cherry tomatoes for snacking, salads, roasting, and pasta for the entire season. Sweetie is particularly well-suited to gardeners who want to maintain their own seed from a reliable, high-quality cherry tomato variety.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; install a 30-mil rhizome barrier 24–36 inches deep before planting. Sweetshoot bamboo produces the most palatable raw-edible shoots of any temperate bamboo.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, contained with a rhizome barrier; sweetshoot bamboo earns its name from its exceptional culinary qualities — the spring shoots are notably less bitter than most bamboos and sweet enough to be eaten raw in thin slices, without the blanching required for most species. The shoots are harvested in spring as they emerge from the soil, before the sheaths open, when they are at peak sweetness and tenderness. Mature culms reach 15–25 feet and 1–2 inches in diameter, providing attractive screening material and lightweight bamboo poles. Like all Phyllostachys species, it spreads by underground rhizomes and requires containment. The coppery-bronze color of new culm sheaths in spring is ornamental. Plant in groves of 3 or more for heavier shoot production.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/2 inch deep as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or for the main crop in zone 6–10, plant in late summer 6–8 weeks before first fall frost. Each chard 'seed' is actually a cluster containing multiple seeds; thin to one seedling per spot.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade as early as spring soil can be worked; Swiss chard is the most heat-tolerant and adaptable of the cool-season leafy greens, bridging the gap between the cool spring lettuce season and the fall crops by continuing to produce through summer heat that would bolt most other leafy greens. Each chard seed cluster contains 2–4 seeds; thin to one seedling per 9–12 inches. Harvest outer leaves continuously, leaving the growing center to continue producing — a well-tended planting can produce for 6 months or more. Rainbow chard types with red, orange, yellow, and pink stems are highly ornamental as well as edible. Mildly earthy flavor that is more versatile than spinach.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide a sturdy trellis or fence — sword bean vines grow vigorously to 10–15 feet. Do not eat raw seeds or undercooked beans; thorough cooking is required to destroy the toxic amino acid canavanine.
directions: Direct sow after last frost, providing a sturdy trellis, in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun — sword bean is a vigorous tropical climbing annual from Asia and Africa, producing enormous, curved, sword-shaped pods up to 18 inches long that are among the most dramatic in the legume family. When harvested young (3–4 inches long), the whole immature pods can be cooked and eaten like snap beans; the mature seeds can be eaten when thoroughly cooked through multiple water changes (raw seeds and undercooked beans contain canavanine, a toxic amino acid, and must be thoroughly boiled). In traditional Southeast Asian and African cuisines, the young pods are stir-fried, pickled, and used in curries. The plant is a prolific nitrogen-fixer used as a cover crop and soil improver in tropical agriculture. An ornamental conversation-piece in the summer garden where its enormous pods hanging from a trellis never fail to impress visitors.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; Sylvesta is a French Batavian-type lettuce prized for holding its crisp texture and mild flavor and resisting bolting longer than many lettuce varieties as the weather warms.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Sylvesta is a French Batavian-type lettuce forming loose, semi-crisp heads with a texture between soft butterhead and crunchy iceberg, valued for holding good quality and resisting premature bolting longer than many lettuce varieties as spring temperatures rise, extending the harvest window into warmer weather. The pale green leaves have a mild, sweet flavor and good crispness that holds up well in salads. Harvest as a loose head or pick outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again approach, and provide light afternoon shade in the warmest part of the season to further extend its quality.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer; Sylvetta is a refined, more compact selection of wild arugula bred specifically for salad-mix growers and tolerates heat better than standard arugula.
directions: Scatter seed thinly over cool, fertile soil and cover lightly, since Sylvetta germinates best when kept consistently moist. This named selection of wild arugula produces smaller, more deeply lobed leaves than the species and a denser, more compact rosette that regrows readily after cutting. Its flavor is intensely nutty and peppery, sharper than salad arugula, and it holds up in heat and resists bolting far longer than Eruca types, making it a mainstay of Italian-style mesclun mixes. In mild-winter regions it behaves as a short-lived perennial and can be harvested for several seasons from the same planting.

common_name: TAM Jalapeño Pepper (Texas A&M Mild Jalapeño)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; TAM Jalapeño was developed by Texas A&M University in 1992 in partnership with USDA to produce a jalapeño pepper with dramatically reduced heat (400–1,500 SHU versus the standard jalapeño's 2,500–8,000 SHU) while retaining the characteristic jalapeño flavor, size, and appearance — important for the food industry and gardeners who want jalapeño flavor without significant heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. TAM Jalapeño-1 was developed by Texas A&M University's pepper breeding program in cooperation with the USDA and released in 1992 specifically for the commercial food processing industry, which required a jalapeño with the characteristic jalapeño flavor, uniform size (3–4 inches), and appearance for use in products like jalapeño poppers, nachos, and salsas — but without enough heat to cause consumer complaints when consumed in quantity. The resulting variety has the same thick, meaty walls, dark green color, and characteristic jalapeño aroma as standard jalapeños but only 400–1,500 SHU (compared to 2,500–8,000 SHU in standard varieties), making it easily tolerable for most heat-sensitive individuals. TAM Jalapeño is an outstanding choice for Gulf Coast home gardeners who want to grow their own jalapeños for cooking without excessive heat, and for making fresh salsa, pico de gallo, and pickled jalapeños accessible to children and heat-sensitive family members.

common_name: TAM Jalapeño Pepper (Texas A&M Mild Jalapeño, Low-Heat Jalapeño)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; TAM Jalapeño performs best in full sun with consistent moisture and modest fertilization. In zone 9, transplant March–April for a June–August harvest. The plants are productive and compact, well-suited to container growing, and perform reliably in the Gulf South warm season.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; TAM Jalapeño is compact, productive, and easy to grow as a warm-season annual in any vegetable garden. TAM Mild Jalapeño I is a Texas A&M University release (developed in 1992 by the university's vegetable breeding program) that addressed a specific and widely held preference: many cooks and eaters want the distinctive fresh, grassy jalapeño flavor that defines Tex-Mex and Southwestern cooking without the significant heat of a standard jalapeño. Standard jalapeños test at 2,500–8,000 Scoville Heat Units — enough to be noticeably and persistently hot for heat-sensitive eaters; TAM Jalapeño measures approximately 1,000–3,500 SHU, a 70–80% reduction in heat while retaining the characteristic jalapeño aroma and flavor profile. The fruits are indistinguishable from standard jalapeños in size and appearance — medium-large (3–4 inches), dark green to red, thick-walled, and blocky — making them ideal for all jalapeño applications where the full flavor is wanted without the burning heat: nachos, salsa, pickled jalapeños (called escabeche), jalapeño poppers, and fresh eating. TAM Jalapeño is widely grown in Texas for processing and fresh market and has developed a devoted following among home gardeners who cook frequently with jalapeños and want to moderate the heat for family members of different heat tolerances. Very productive plants with a long harvest window from green through red ripeness.

common_name: TAM Mild Jalapeno Pepper (Low-Heat Texas A&M Jalapeno)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; TAM Mild was bred at Texas A&M to keep the classic jalapeno shape and flavor while cutting the heat to a fraction of a standard jalapeno's, making it a good choice for gardeners who want jalapeno flavor without much bite.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, and harvest fruit at any stage from glossy dark green through fully ripe red. TAM Mild Jalapeno was developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife breeding program specifically to lower the capsaicin content of a standard jalapeno to a mild 500-2,500 Scoville units, roughly a tenth the heat of a typical jalapeno, while keeping the same thick-walled, classic jalapeno shape, size, and flavor that makes it useful for salsas, poppers, and pickling. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season and tolerate Southern heat well, though heat and moisture stress can occasionally nudge individual peppers hotter than the variety's baseline. It's a good choice for gardeners, and especially families with children, who want the jalapeno's flavor and crunch without much of its punch.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed. Bred at Auburn University in the 1970s to replace tobacco-mosaic-susceptible stock, this cultivar produces the same slender, upward-facing, fiery fruit as classic tabasco but on virus-resistant plants, making it a more dependable choice for home growers and small producers. Pods ripen from pale yellow through orange to red, and are traditionally mashed and aged into vinegar-based hot sauce, though they work equally well fresh or dried.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 65°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and provide consistent heat of 80°F until seedlings emerge. Transplant to well-drained soil in the sunniest garden position, as Capsicum frutescens types thrive with maximum heat accumulation throughout the season. Distinctive erect fruits ripen from yellow-green through yellow and orange to red; harvest at the red stage for the highest capsaicin concentration. Plants are short-lived perennials in frost-free climates and can be overwintered in pots to produce a second heavy crop.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost; in zone 9 direct sow February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Table Ace's semi-bush habit is more compact than most acorn squash, making it suitable for smaller garden plots where standard spreading vines would overwhelm the space.
directions: Direct sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil and thin to the strongest plant; Table Ace is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid acorn squash with a compact, semi-bush habit that takes up considerably less garden space than standard vine-type acorn squash. The dark green, 1–2 pound fruits have the classic acorn shape with ridged skin and deep orange, dry, sweet flesh that pairs well with butter and brown sugar. Harvest when the skin resists fingernail pressure and the underside rind in contact with the soil turns orange; fruits left on the vine too long become fibrous. Store cured fruits in a cool, dry location for up to 3 months. The semi-bush habit makes Table Ace the preferred choice for gardeners who want acorn squash flavor in a space-efficient plant.

common_name: Table Gold Acorn Squash (Golden Acorn Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, allowing room for the bushy, semi-compact vines.
directions: Sow directly in warm soil after frost danger has passed, and keep plants evenly watered through fruit set for the best flavor. Table Gold was bred by horticulturist Dr. Oved Shifriss, known for his work developing compact bush-type squash, and produces bright golden-yellow acorn-shaped fruit on space-saving vines. The tender flesh has a notably nutty, sweet flavor that distinguishes it from the more common dark-green acorn types.

plant_note: Direct sow once the soil is warm and frost has passed.
directions: Sow Table King seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, thinning to the strongest plant every 24 to 36 inches. This All-America Selections winner grows as a compact dwarf bush rather than a sprawling vine, so it fits smaller gardens. It yields dark green, sweet, nutty-flavored acorn squash on tidy plants. Harvest when the rind is hard and dull, cure briefly, and store the fruits for winter meals.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; compact vines suit small gardens.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, or start indoors in peat pots for an early crop. This bush-type acorn squash matures early on compact four-foot vines, making it great for small gardens, large containers, and short seasons. The fruits offer the rich, sweet flavor of baked winter squash prized on cool autumn days. Water steadily during vine growth and fruit set, then let the rinds harden fully before harvest. Cure and store the squash in a cool, dry place for use through fall and winter.

common_name: Table Queen Acorn Squash (Classic Dark-Green Heirloom Acorn Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer (July–August in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for a fall harvest; acorn squash can also be direct sown in March–April for a spring crop in zone 9, harvested before summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Table Queen is the classic American acorn squash — an heirloom variety that has defined the acorn squash category since its introduction in the 1890s and remains one of the most widely recognized winter squash forms in American cooking. The deeply ribbed, dark-green to nearly black fruits (1.5–2 lb, 4–6 inches long) have dense, golden-yellow, sweet flesh with a nutty, slightly dry texture that is outstanding for baking: cut in half, brush with butter, season with brown sugar and cinnamon, and bake until caramelized — the classic American acorn squash preparation. The deep ribs and dark color are distinctive enough that 'acorn squash' has become synonymous with Table Queen's specific shape. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved from season to season. Table Queen stores well for 1–2 months at cool room temperature after proper curing (10 days at 80°F). In zone 9, acorn squash is most reliable as a fall crop (August planting, October–November harvest) — the spring planting often struggles in early summer heat. The fall crop benefits from the cooling temperatures of fall that improve the sweetness and flavor of the flesh. Space plants generously as the vines spread 6–8 feet in all directions.

common_name: Tadorna Leek (Cold-Hardy Fall and Winter Leek)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or start in summer for a fall/winter main crop; Tadorna is a reliable open-pollinated leek noted for strong cold tolerance and good disease resistance, making it well suited to the Gulf South's cool-season leek window.
directions: Start Tadorna leeks indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting, or start seed in summer for a main fall and winter crop, then set pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Tadorna is a dependable open-pollinated leek that produces long, thick, blue-green stalks with excellent cold tolerance, standing well in the garden through cool weather without becoming tough or bitter, and shows good resistance to common leek diseases. Hill or trench soil around the stems as they grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion. In the Gulf South's mild winters, Tadorna can often be left in the ground and harvested as needed through the cool season rather than lifted all at once, giving a long, flexible harvest window.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for harvest November–February. Tah Tsai is exceptionally cold-hardy for an Asian brassica, tolerating temperatures below 20°F, and is the best choice for overwintering green harvests in zone 9 without protection. Successive sowings every 3 weeks extend the harvest window. Plants hugging the ground create a natural cold-air barrier that further protects against frost damage.
directions: Direct sow in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Tah Tsai (also spelled Tatsoi or Ta Tsai, Brassica narinosa or B. rapa var. rosularis) is an Asian brassica that forms a distinctive flat, ground-hugging rosette of dark green, spoon-shaped leaves radiating outward from the center — an almost architectural form entirely unlike the upright habit of bok choy or komatsuna. The very dark, glossy leaves have a mild flavor similar to spinach with a gentle mustardy note, making Tah Tsai one of the most versatile winter greens for raw use in salads, baby green mixes, braising, and stir-fries. The flat rosette form protects the growing center from frost and allows Tah Tsai to survive temperatures that would kill most other leafy greens — down to 10–15°F. In zone 9 it is one of the most reliably productive cool-season greens, thriving through the entire fall-winter-spring season from September sowing through April before bolting in summer heat. The flat habit allows it to grow in partial shade beneath other plants in the fall garden.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed, giving the long rampant vines plenty of room or a sturdy trellis to climb.
directions: Tahitian Melon Squash grows a huge, pale blue-green, club-shaped fruit that can reach 2 feet long and 20-plus pounds, with dense, deep orange flesh notably lower in fiber and sweeter than most butternut types, closer in eating quality to a sweet potato. The extremely long, vigorous vines need generous space or a strong trellis to support the developing fruit off the ground. Despite its huge size, a single fruit stores well for months and yields a lot of smooth, easily pureed flesh for soups and baking. A conversation-piece squash for gardeners with room to let vines ramble and a taste for very sweet, low-fiber winter squash.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes or offsets in spring, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; Tahitian spinach is one of the most productive and shade-tolerant edible aroids and will produce continuous leaf harvests in the partial-shade conditions of a tropical garden where most edible greens would fail in summer heat.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; Tahitian spinach (arrowleaf elephant ear, belembe) is a South American tropical aroid grown throughout the Pacific Islands, Caribbean, and tropical Africa as an important leafy vegetable — the large, glossy, arrow-shaped, deep-green leaves are regularly harvested and prepared like spinach or taro leaves: briefly cooked (the raw leaves contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals that disappear with cooking) in soups, stews, coconut milk curries, and as a wilted side vegetable. A mature plant can produce a steady supply of large, nutritious leaves throughout the warm season. It is one of the most productive leafy green vegetables for hot, humid, partially shaded growing conditions, thriving in the summer heat and partial shade that would cause spinach, chard, and most temperate leafy greens to bolt and fail. The plants spread by underground rhizomes and produce offsets that extend the colony. In zone 9–10 it is often frozen back in winter but regrows from the rhizomes in spring. An underused and highly productive tropical leafy vegetable for zone 9–12 edible gardens.

common_name: Taiwanese Flat Cabbage (A Choy, Chinese Flat Cabbage)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant as young seedlings; in zone 9, the primary growing season is October–March for spring harvest, as summer heat causes bolting and poor head formation.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost or direct sow in fall for cool-season production; Taiwanese flat cabbage is a classic East Asian cabbage variety producing distinctly flat, wide, loosely-structured heads (12–16 inches in diameter but only 4–6 inches tall) with extremely tender, delicate leaves — a completely different texture and flavor experience from the dense, hard European round-head cabbages. The tender leaves are less pungent and more delicate than round cabbage, with a slightly sweet, mild flavor that holds up beautifully in quick-cooked preparations like stir-fries, hot pots, and braised dishes, while also working well in fresh preparations like slaws and salads. The flat shape and loose construction mean the heads do not store as long as round types but they are extraordinarily tender and pleasant to eat. Very popular in Taiwanese and Chinese fresh markets, restaurant kitchens, and among Asian-American home gardeners; the quick maturation (60–80 days from transplant) and cool-season preference make it an excellent fall-to-spring crop in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring production. Talladega is a heat-set determinate hybrid with excellent blemish resistance in humid conditions — it is among the most reliable heavy-cropping varieties for the hot, humid Gulf Coast and Deep South.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil with a cage or stake; Talladega is a determinate, heat-tolerant hybrid tomato that produces large harvests of smooth, firm, 8–10 ounce red globe tomatoes with excellent shelf life and crack resistance. It was bred specifically for commercial and home production in the hot, humid South, where disease pressure from early blight, grey leaf spot, and bacterial spot is severe — Talladega carries broad disease resistance that keeps foliage healthy through the summer months when other varieties defoliate. The concentrated fruiting habit of this determinate variety makes it easy to time a large harvest for canning or preserving. Fall plantings in late July–early August often produce the heaviest yields as the fruits ripen into the cooler October–November weather.

common_name: Tampiqueno Serrano Pepper (Classic Mexican Hot Serrano)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Tampiqueno is a classic serrano cultivar producing small, thin-walled, very hot pods used fresh in salsas and Mexican cooking.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Tampiqueno is a widely grown, classic serrano pepper cultivar producing small, slender, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to red, packing more heat than jalapeno in a smaller package, and used extensively fresh in salsas, pico de gallo, and other Mexican dishes where a bright, grassy heat is wanted. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season and tolerate heat well, making serrano peppers one of the more reliable hot pepper choices for Gulf South gardens. Harvest pods at any stage of ripeness, though full red pods have somewhat more sweetness alongside the heat.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since celery seed is slow to germinate and seedlings grow slowly at first; transplant out after danger of hard frost has passed, keeping soil consistently moist through the season.
directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of transplanting, since celery germinates slowly and seedlings need a long head start before warm weather arrives. Tango is a modern celery cultivar bred for compact size, crisp, stringless stalks, and good resistance to common celery diseases that plague older cultivars in humid climates, producing dark green, flavorful stalks over a somewhat shorter growing season than heirloom types. Consistent, even soil moisture is essential throughout the growing season, since celery stalks turn stringy and bitter under moisture stress. In hot-summer regions it does best as a fall or early spring crop rather than attempting to carry it through peak summer heat, since celery bolts and becomes bitter in prolonged high temperatures.

common_name: Tango Lettuce (Frilly Deeply-Cut Green Leaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; in zone 9 sow January-February for spring or September-October for fall. Tango produces deeply frilled, ruffled, bright green leaves and is a popular cut-and-come-again variety for baby leaf and mesclun mix production.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Tango produces densely frilled, deeply cut, curly bright green leaves that hold up well as a cut-and-come-again crop, regrowing quickly after repeated light harvests for baby leaf salads and mesclun mixes. Its crisp, mild flavor and attractive ruffled texture make it a popular addition to mixed salad greens, and it tolerates cool weather well, making it a strong choice for both an early spring and a fall crop in zone 8-9 gardens. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head an inch above the crown to allow regrowth for a second and sometimes third harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost near a trellis or tall support in full sun; Tarbais is a semi-vining pole-type bean traditionally grown up corn stalks in southwestern France and is best harvested dry for the classic cassoulet preparation, though it can be eaten as a fresh shell bean earlier in the season.
directions: Sow after last frost near a trellis, fence, or tall pole in full sun; Tarbais is the classic French heirloom bean of Gascon cuisine, historically grown climbing up corn stalks in the countryside around Tarbes in southwestern France, and it is the traditional bean specified in authentic cassoulet, the slow-cooked white bean and meat casserole of the region. The dry beans are creamy white, thin-skinned, and known for cooking up exceptionally tender and creamy while holding their shape, absorbing the rich flavors of the pork, duck, and sausage traditionally simmered with them in cassoulet. While best known dried, pods can also be picked earlier at the plump green shell-bean stage for a more delicate fresh bean dish. Let pods mature and dry fully on the vine for the classic dry-bean harvest, picking before fall rains can cause mold, and finish drying indoors in a well-ventilated spot before shelling and storing.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a December–February harvest. Tardivo requires a forcing technique: in late fall, cut the tops of the plants to 1 inch, dig the roots, pack them tightly in boxes of moist sand or sawdust, and force in darkness at 50–60°F for 3–5 weeks. This forcing step is essential — without it, Tardivo produces standard chicory leaves rather than the distinctive elongated, curled Tardivo form. In zone 9 the mild winter allows some growers to force plants in place with dark covers.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Tardivo is the most prized and most expensive radicchio in Italy — a Treviso-type radicchio that requires a traditional forcing process in which the plants are dug after fall frosts, packed in darkness, and allowed to produce elongated, curved white-and-red leaf chicons resembling a firework spray or an open hand. The resulting forced Tardivo heads have long, narrow, spoon-shaped, curling red-and-white leaves with a dramatic, sculptural appearance that makes them a luxury vegetable in Italian restaurants and specialty markets — they are served raw in salads, grilled whole, braised, or used as striking garnishes. The bittersweet flavor is the most refined of all radicchio types, with the forcing process reducing bitterness while concentrating sweetness. Tardivo commands the highest price of any radicchio in Italian markets; in home gardens the complex forcing requirement is rewarded with a genuinely special vegetable unlike any other readily available.

plant_note: Plant cormels or corm divisions 2–4 inches deep in warm, consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil 2–4 weeks after last frost; taro can be grown in boggy conditions, at pond margins, or in containers kept standing in water — it requires heat and abundant moisture throughout its long growing season.
directions: Plant small cormels or divided corm sections 2–4 inches deep in deep, organic-rich, consistently wet to moist soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost risk has passed and soil temperatures exceed 70°F; taro tolerates and even thrives in standing water, making it suitable for rain gardens, swales, and pond edges. Colocasia esculenta is one of the world's oldest cultivated crops, grown throughout tropical Asia, the Pacific Islands, Africa, and the Caribbean for its starchy, edible corms — all parts of the raw plant contain calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense oral irritation, so corms and leaves must always be thoroughly cooked (boiling, steaming, or roasting for at least 30–45 minutes) before eating. The corms are the source of Hawaiian poi, taro chips, and cocoyam fufu, and have a distinctive, pleasantly earthy, slightly sweet, starchy flavor; the large, dramatic, heart-shaped leaves are used in Pacific Island cooking as wrappers (lau lau) and are edible after extended cooking. In zones 8b–9, plants may survive a mild winter with heavy mulching over the crown but should be treated as annuals in cooler climates, with corms lifted and stored above 50°F after the first frost.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost in cool, well-drained soil; inoculate seed with the correct Bradyrhizobium lupini strain before sowing, since standard pea or clover inoculant will not work. Tarwi is a highland Andean crop adapted to cool nights and long, mild growing seasons — it performs best where summer heat is moderate rather than in prolonged intense heat.
directions: Sow in well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; tarwi is a highland Andean lupin domesticated in Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador thousands of years ago and grown as a protein- and oil-rich grain legume, with seed protein content rivaling soybean. The plant produces attractive blue-to-purple pea-family flower spikes followed by pods containing pale, disc-shaped seeds that are intensely bitter and contain alkaloids in their raw state, requiring a traditional debittering process before eating — seeds are boiled, then soaked in several changes of running or repeatedly refreshed water for several days until the bitterness is leached out, after which they are eaten much like a lupini bean, added to soups and stews, or ground into flour. Like other lupins, the deep taproot fixes atmospheric nitrogen and improves soil fertility, and the plant tolerates poor, thin mountain soils and considerable drought once established. Harvest pods once they dry and rattle, then thresh and process the seed before use; never eat the raw, unprocessed seed, as the alkaloid content can be harmful undiluted.

common_name: Tasti-Lee Tomato (University of Florida High-Lycopene Red Slicing Tomato with Superior Flavor)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Tasti-Lee is an indeterminate tomato released by the University of Florida IFAS program with both disease resistance appropriate for Gulf South conditions and substantially higher lycopene content than standard red tomato varieties. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The elevated lycopene content produces a slightly more orange-red skin color than typical red tomatoes — the skin appears almost orange-red rather than crimson red. Tasti-Lee's disease resistance package (Fusarium, Verticillium, root-knot nematodes) addresses the primary limitations of home tomato production in zone 9. The variety was released with the specific goal of delivering both health value (high lycopene) and genuine flavor — a combination not typical of the commercial tomato market, which has historically prioritized yield, appearance, and shelf life over flavor and nutrition.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly red-orange and gives to slight pressure. Tasti-Lee Tomato was released by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) around 2010, developed through a breeding program that specifically targeted the combination of high lycopene content, improved flavor, and Gulf South disease resistance in a single red slicing tomato variety. The UF/IFAS vegetable breeding program, one of the most active in the southeastern United States, has produced multiple important commercial tomato varieties for Florida's significant commercial tomato industry; Tasti-Lee represents a branch of that program targeting quality attributes (flavor, nutrition) rather than the shipping durability and uniformity that commercial Florida tomato breeding has primarily emphasized. The variety's elevated lycopene content — documented by UF/IFAS researchers as substantially higher than industry-standard slicing tomatoes — combined with higher-than-typical sugar content and genuine tomato flavor creates a profile closer to the flavor of a well-grown heirloom tomato than most disease-resistant hybrid varieties provide. The variety has been noted by home gardeners and researchers for producing genuinely good-flavored tomatoes in zone 9's challenging summer heat, a combination difficult to achieve with either heirloom varieties (which lack disease resistance) or standard commercial varieties (which sacrifice flavor for durability). Tasti-Lee is sold through specialty seed companies and has been grown for research comparisons confirming its superior flavor and nutritional profile relative to commercial standards.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; grow on a trellis for straight fruit.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, or start indoors in peat pots to gain a head start. This Japanese-type cucumber bears slender, long, burpless fruits with thin, sweet, non-bitter skin and very few tiny seeds. Grow the highly productive plants on a trellis to save space and encourage straight, clean fruit. Keep watering even to prevent bitterness and misshapen cucumbers. Harvest frequently while fruits are still young and tender to keep the vines producing.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for main crop and again in August–September for fall production. Tasty Jade is a long, thin burpless-type cucumber that produces abundantly on vigorous vines; provide a trellis or cage. In zone 9 the fall crop often produces higher-quality fruits as temperatures moderate after September.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Tasty Jade is an AAS Award-winning Asian burpless cucumber hybrid producing very long (10–12 inch), slender, uniformly dark green fruits with thin, tender, virtually seedless flesh and an exceptionally mild, non-bitter flavor. Unlike slicing cucumbers that can be bitter and require peeling, the thin skin and low cucurbitacin content of Tasty Jade makes it excellent for eating without peeling — just wash and slice. The crisp, sweet, mild-flavored fruits are ideal for fresh eating, salads, sushi accompaniments, and quick pickling. Tasty Jade's All-America Selections award recognized its superior flavor, production, and disease resistance compared to competing Asian cucumber types. In zone 9 the vigorous vines produce abundantly in spring and again in fall; summer production may slow during the hottest weeks of July–August but resumes as temperatures moderate in September.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; excels as a fall crop sown 6–8 weeks before first frost, as light freezes sweeten the leaves.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and thin to 6–12 inches for full rosettes; closer spacing produces baby greens for salad mix. Tatsoi forms a flat, ground-hugging rosette of dark spoon-shaped leaves and is remarkably cold-hardy, surviving temperatures into the low 20s°F under row cover. Harvest whole plants when 4–6 inches across or pick outer leaves progressively. Avoid planting in summer as heat causes immediate bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; tatume is one of the most heat-tolerant summer squash for Gulf Coast and Texas gardens, producing well through summer heat where zucchini collapses. In zone 9 it can be grown as a first planting in spring and a second planting in late August for fall harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; tatume is a traditional Mexican summer squash producing round to slightly oval, smooth, dark green fruits 3–5 inches in diameter that are harvested young (before the rind hardens) for use as a summer squash, or left to mature fully into a yellow-tan winter squash. Young fruits have mild, tender flesh similar to zucchini but firmer and slightly sweeter; mature fruits have dry, pale orange flesh similar to a butternut squash. This dual-use quality, combined with exceptional heat tolerance that keeps plants productive through Texas and Gulf Coast summers when standard zucchini quits, makes tatume one of the most practically useful squash for hot-climate gardeners. Extremely popular in Mexican American communities in Texas, where it is used in caldos, guisados, and stuffed as chiles rellenos de calabaza. The vining plants produce abundantly over a long season.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; no staking needed.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost once the soil is warm, planting in rows or blocks for easy picking. This French filet bean, or haricot vert, is at its best when harvested young and slender and picked frequently. The disease-resistant bush plants need no staking and grow well in containers. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod set for tender, straight pods. Pick every couple of days at petite size to keep the plants producing over a long window.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and give seedlings 10–14 days near 50°F once they have several true leaves to encourage earlier, heavier bud set; in zone 9, an August–September sowing for a fall transplant also performs well and often yields the largest buds.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Tavor is a vigorous Israeli-bred F1 hybrid selected for heavy, reliable production of medium, tightly closed green buds on a large, upright, spineless plant, and it is widely favored by growers in hot, dry-summer climates for its strong heat tolerance and steady yield of multiple side buds after the central bud is cut. Like other seed-grown annual types it flowers and produces a usable first-year harvest without needing the extended cold vernalization that older perennial varieties require, though a short cool spell after transplanting still improves bud set and uniformity. Keep soil consistently moist and fertile through the growing season, and cut buds while still tight and firm, well before the scales begin to loosen and spread.

common_name: Taxi Tomato (Bright Yellow Early Determinate Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Taxi is a determinate tomato that sets its crop over a concentrated 3–4 week window before slowing. In zone 9, transplant late February through early March for a May harvest; the early to mid-season maturity makes Taxi practical for both spring and fall Gulf Coast production windows.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Taxi is a determinate yellow tomato that produces a concentrated crop of uniformly bright taxi-yellow, medium (6–8 oz), round to slightly flattened fruits with a smooth, attractive appearance and mild, sweet, low-acid tomato flavor — the distinctive mellow sweetness typical of most yellow tomatoes, which have lower levels of the malic and citric acids that give red tomatoes their sharpness. The low-acid character makes Taxi an excellent choice for gardeners and eaters who find standard red tomatoes too acidic, for children who prefer milder flavors, and for fresh applications where the visual contrast of bright yellow adds interest to a salad or platter. The meaty flesh has a good firm texture that holds up in sliced presentations without becoming watery. Taxi is practical, productive, and early enough to complete its crop before the worst Gulf South summer heat; its concentrated set makes it useful for batch processing or sharing. A reliable, attractive yellow option for home gardens where some visual and flavor variety beyond standard red tomatoes is desired.

common_name: Taylor Dwarf Horticultural Bean (Cranberry Bush, Shell Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Taylor Dwarf Horticultural is grown primarily as a shell bean — harvested when pods have begun to turn from green-streaked to fully tan/buff and the beans inside are plump and fully developed but not yet dry. This 'shelling' window lasts about 2 weeks per planting; successive sowings extend the season.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; harvest as shell beans when pods have mottled tan-and-red coloring and beans are plump. Taylor Dwarf Horticultural is a classic New England and Mid-Atlantic heirloom horticultural (shell) bean — one of the oldest and most storied varieties in American seed saving tradition, producing beautiful red-streaked, cream-and-crimson pods and plump, cranberry-red-speckled beans that are used primarily at the fresh-shelled stage, when they have a rich, creamy, potato-like flavor and a velvety texture that is quite different from the firmer, drier character of the same beans when fully dried. Fresh-shelled horticultural beans are a seasonal delicacy that was once far more common in American cooking — they require no soaking, cook in 20–30 minutes, and have a rich, substantial flavor and a dense, satisfying texture that is superior to the canned or dried equivalents. Taylor Dwarf is compact (14–20 inches), making it well-suited to small gardens, and produces abundantly over a 2–3 week harvest window. As a dry bean it is also excellent (the same as a cranberry or borlotti bean), providing versatility across the whole season. A foundational heirloom with genuine culinary value and beautiful pod markings.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is warm; teff tolerates both waterlogged and drought conditions better than most grain crops.
directions: Surface-broadcast seed — it is extremely small (poppy-seed sized) and must not be buried; mix seed with sand to achieve even distribution at roughly 2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, then press lightly with a roller or board for good soil contact. Teff tillers prolifically and forms a graceful, open canopy with hundreds of fine panicles per plant; harvest the entire plant at the base when the majority of seeds have turned brown but before they shatter in a breeze. Thresh by beating bundles over a smooth tarp and winnow carefully in a gentle airflow — the seed is light and easily blown away. Teff grain is naturally gluten-free and is the basis for Ethiopian injera flatbread.

common_name: Telegraph Cucumber (Victorian English Long Greenhouse Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors for an earlier crop; provide a sturdy trellis so the long fruit hangs straight, since fruit that rests on the ground tends to curl.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil, then train vines up a trellis for the straightest fruit and easiest picking. Telegraph is a Victorian-era English heirloom, originally bred for greenhouse culture, that produces long, slender, dark green fruit twelve to eighteen inches at full size, with thin, tender, nearly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor prized for slicing. It performs well outdoors in warm climates given a trellis and consistent moisture, though fruit is best picked at eight to twelve inches for the crispest texture, since fully mature fruit can turn coarse. Keep watering even throughout fruit development, since irregular moisture is the most common cause of bitterness and misshapen fruit in this and most cucumber varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; grow on a trellis for long, straight fruit.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost in warm soil, or start indoors in peat pots for an early crop. This English-type heirloom from the 1800s bears long, thin-skinned, burpless fruits up to eighteen inches with very small, soft seeds. Originally bred for greenhouses, it now thrives outdoors and produces best when trained up a trellis. Keep watering even to keep fruit straight and free of bitterness. Harvest the long cucumbers while young and tender for the sweetest flavor.

plant_note: Sow 4–6 weeks before last frost date; Telephone is a tall climber reaching 5–6 feet and requires sturdy support — grow on strong netting or trellis strung between tall posts.
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep and 2–3 inches apart in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, 4–6 weeks before last frost; Telephone pea (sold in Britain as Alderman) is the classic tall heirloom main-crop shell pea, a vigorous climber to 5–6 feet that produces large, curved dark-green pods with 8–10 sweet, tender peas per pod — significantly more productive per plant than bush varieties and the pod size that made it famous in Victorian kitchen gardens. Requires strong netting or pea sticks for support. Harvest when pods are well-filled and peas are young and sweet; productivity drops rapidly if pods are left to mature fully on the vine.

common_name: Tender and True Parsnip (English Heirloom Smooth-Skinned Parsnip)
plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as soil can be worked in spring; parsnip seed loses viability fast, so buy new seed each year.
directions: Sow seed shallowly into deeply worked, stone-free soil, since forked or stunted roots result from compacted ground; keep the seedbed evenly moist through slow germination and thin seedlings to a few inches apart. This long-standing English heirloom is prized for roots that are smooth-skinned, nearly coreless, and unusually tender for a full-season parsnip, with good field tolerance to canker. Leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts, which convert starch to sugar and give the roots their signature sweet, nutty flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost, sowing in succession for continuous pods through summer.
directions: Plant seeds an inch deep directly in warm garden soil, thinning to a few inches apart so bushy plants have room to fill out without crowding. This long-popular bush bean produces slender, rounded, curved pods that are notably tender and stay stringless even at a fairly large size, giving gardeners a wider harvest window than many snap beans. Plants are heat tolerant and continue setting pods reliably through summer warmth, making this a dependable choice for extending the fresh bean harvest. Pick regularly to encourage continued flowering and pod set throughout the season.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; tolerant of cool soil conditions.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost, though this variety tolerates cooler soil better than most cucumbers. The thin-skinned, sweet, burpless, acid-free fruits are a delight harvested at eight inches or shorter. Pick early for pickling or let fruit grow to full size as a slicer, since it works well for both. Tendergreen resists powdery mildew, adding to its reliability in the garden. Keep watering even and harvest frequently to keep the vigorous vines productive.

plant_note: Direct sow spring through fall; tolerates both heat and cold well.
directions: Direct sow seed shallowly and keep the bed moist for quick germination. This versatile Japanese green, also called komatsuna, is milder than most mustards and very easy to grow. It quickly produces flat, smooth, dark, glossy green leaves and tolerates both heat and cold better than spinach. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut whole plants young for tender greens. Successive sowings from spring through fall keep a steady supply for stir-fries and salads.

plant_note: Direct sow in loose, stone-free soil once the ground can be worked; make succession sowings.
directions: Sow seed shallowly, about a quarter inch deep, directly in deeply worked, loose soil so the long imperator-type roots can grow straight. Keep the seedbed consistently moist during the slow germination period and thin plants to a couple inches apart once seedlings are established. Harvest these long, slender, nearly coreless roots at around 8 to 9 inches for the sweetest flavor; the deep orange-red color holds up well to steaming, baking, and freezing.

plant_note: Sow in warm soil after frost, or start indoors in short-season areas.
directions: Sow Tendersweet Orange seeds 1 inch deep in warm hills, thinning to the two strongest vines per hill. This heirloom produces large 30 to 35 pound melons with vivid orange flesh, exceptional sweetness, and a thick, durable rind that stores and ships well. Give the vigorous vines plenty of room and water deeply while fruit sizes up. Harvest when the ground spot turns yellow and the nearby tendril withers.

common_name: Tennessee Red Cob Corn (Appalachian Heirloom White Dent Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile soil; Tennessee Red Cob is an Appalachian heirloom dent corn grown for cornmeal and grits, easily identified in the field by its distinctive dark red cob under white kernels.
directions: Sow directly in well-drained soil in blocks for reliable pollination, and let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest since this is a grinding corn rather than a fresh-eating sweet corn. Tennessee Red Cob is a long-grown Appalachian and upland Southern heirloom prized by home millers for producing a notably white, fine-textured meal, with the vivid red cob making it easy to sort visually from other corn at harvest. Plants tolerate the hot, humid conditions and periodic dry spells typical of Southern summers reasonably well once established, and the variety has a long history of on-farm seed saving. Store dried ears in a mouse-proof container with good airflow, and shell only what you need for milling at a time to keep meal fresh.

common_name: Tennessee Sweet Potato Squash (Southern Cushaw-Type Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil, giving vines ample room to run; this Southern heirloom is well adapted to hot, humid summers and performs reliably across the Gulf South.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills in full sun, allowing generous room for the sprawling vines. Tennessee Sweet Potato is an old Southern heirloom squash bearing pear- to bell-shaped, buff-tan fruit with a smooth rind and dense, sweet, fine-textured orange flesh reminiscent of sweet potato, a resemblance that gives the variety its name. As a moschata-type squash it shows good resistance to squash vine borer and performs reliably through hot, humid Southern summers, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South gardens where other winter squash struggle. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure for a couple of weeks in a warm, airy spot to concentrate sweetness before moving to cool, dry storage.

common_name: Tennis Ball Lettuce (Thomas Jefferson's Monticello Heirloom Butterhead)
plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; sow shallowly, since lettuce needs light to germinate.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. Tennis Ball is a small, dense, dark-green butterhead lettuce documented in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden records from the early 1800s, forming tight, tennis-ball-sized heads with a sweet, buttery, mild flavor and crisp inner leaves. Its small, quick-maturing heads make it well suited to close spacing, containers, and succession planting for a steady supply of tender lettuce through the cool season. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade as temperatures rise in late spring to delay bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil reaches 65°F; tepary bean requires warmth and actually performs poorly in cool, wet conditions. In the desert Southwest, traditional plantings coincide with the summer monsoon season.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in very well-drained, low-fertility, sandy or rocky soil in full sun well after soil has warmed; tepary bean is the most drought-tolerant domesticated bean in the world, an ancient crop of the Sonoran Desert developed over thousands of years by the O'odham and other indigenous peoples of the American Southwest and northern Mexico. Plants complete their entire life cycle — from germination through harvest — on as little as 8 inches of rainfall and perform poorly in heavily irrigated or rich, wet soils where they become disease-prone. Both bush and semi-vining types exist; small seeds come in white, brown, tan, buff, and speckled patterns and are high in protein, soluble fiber, and resistant starch. Harvest entire plants when most pods have dried and turned tan, thresh to release seeds, and cure in a dry, well-ventilated location before storage. An outstanding crop for hot, dry garden conditions where common beans fail.

common_name: Terenzo Tomato (AAS-Winning Trailing Tumbler Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Terenzo is a compact, self-branching trailing cherry tomato bred specifically for hanging baskets and containers, needing no staking or pruning.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into a hanging basket, window box, or large container filled with fertile, well-drained potting mix in full sun. Terenzo is an AAS-winning cherry tomato bred as a true tumbler type — a compact, mounding, self-branching plant that spills gracefully over the edge of a container rather than climbing, producing a heavy, non-stop crop of small, sweet red cherry tomatoes without any staking, caging, or pruning. Its small scale and container-ready habit make it one of the easiest tomatoes for a patio, balcony, or small-space garden with no in-ground bed at all. Water container plantings regularly, since pots dry out faster than garden soil, and feed every couple of weeks through the season to sustain the heavy, continuous fruit set.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; this interspecific kabocha-butternut cross needs a long, vigorous vine run and rewards gardeners with unusually heavy yields even in stressed conditions.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after all danger of frost has passed, spacing hills 6-8 feet apart to accommodate the exceptionally vigorous vines. Tetsukabuto is a hybrid cross between a kabocha-type Cucurbita maxima and a moschata parent, prized by growers for hybrid vigor that shrugs off vine borers and powdery mildew far better than either parent species alone. Fruits are near-round, 4-6 pounds, with dark, mottled black-green skin and deep orange-yellow flesh that is dry, dense, and nutty-sweet, closer in eating quality to a fine kabocha than a butternut. Cure in a warm spot for a week after harvest before moving to cool storage, where the fruit keeps remarkably well, often into the following spring.

plant_note: In zone 8–10, set transplants in October through December for spring harvest; Texas 1015 is a short-day onion requiring less than 12 hours of daylight to bulb up — it is specifically adapted to the Gulf Coast climate and should be planted in fall for harvest in April–May. Named '1015' for its ideal planting date of October 15 in South Texas.
directions: Set transplants 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in October–December for Gulf Coast and South Texas; Texas 1015 (Texas Super Sweet) is the premier commercial and home garden short-day sweet onion of Texas and the Gulf Coast, developed by Texas A&M AgriLife Research and named for its recommended planting date of October 15 in the Rio Grande Valley. The large, globe-shaped, golden-yellow onions have exceptionally mild, sweet, low-pyruvate flesh with virtually no sharpness — one of the mildest onions grown anywhere in the world, comparable to Vidalia and Walla Walla in sweetness and suitable for eating raw in salads, sandwiches, and fresh salsas without the bite of storage onions. It has the distinctive pale yellow, thin skin and high moisture content of sweet onions. Harvest when tops fall over naturally; cure in a warm, airy location for 2 weeks before storing in a cool, dry spot (sweet onions have shorter storage life than sharp onions due to high moisture and sugar content).

common_name: Texas 1015Y Supersweet Onion (Texas A&M Short-Day Gulf Coast Sweet Onion)
plant_note: Start transplants indoors in September–October; the traditional planting date is October 15 in South Texas (the '1015' in the name), and transplants should go into the ground mid-October through November in zone 9. 1015Y is a short-day onion that requires day lengths under 12 hours to initiate bulbing — it cannot be grown in northern zones where short-day conditions don't align with warm enough temperatures for bulb development. Harvest in late March–May when tops begin to fall over naturally. Cure bulbs in a warm, airy location before storage.
directions: Start transplants indoors in September–October at 60–70°F; set out in the garden mid-October in zone 9. Apply nitrogen fertilizer every 2–3 weeks through winter and spring. Texas 1015Y Supersweet (the name means: Texas, October 15 planting date, Yellow skinned) is the signature short-day sweet onion of the Gulf Coast and South Texas — a variety developed at Texas A&M University by Dr. Leonard Pike and released in 1983 that became the defining onion of Gulf Coast commercial and home production. The '1015' refers to the optimal planting date of October 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, where the variety's potential is most fully realized — planted on that date, the onions experience the precise seasonal day-length and temperature progression that produces the largest, sweetest bulbs. Texas 1015Y is the Vidalia of the Gulf Coast: producing enormous (3–5 inch diameter), slightly flattened, sweet, mild bulbs with very low pungency and high water content — a mild enough onion to eat like an apple. The sweetness comes from low pyruvic acid content (the compound responsible for onion bite and tear-inducing character); 1015Y has some of the lowest pyruvic acid levels measured in onion varieties. It stores only moderately (2–3 months) due to the high moisture content that gives the sweet flavor, distinguishing it from pungent storage types.

common_name: Texas Cream 40 Cowpea (Compact Early Cream Southern Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; the compact, bush habit and short 55–65 day maturity make Texas Cream 40 well suited to successive plantings for an extended harvest through summer.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods when they lighten from green to a pale cream color. Texas Cream 40 is a compact, bush-type cowpea bred for a short, roughly 55–65 day maturity and a concentrated pod set well suited to gardeners who want an early, efficient harvest without the sprawling vines of older heirloom cowpea types. The smooth, cream-colored peas have a mild, sweet flavor and tender texture prized for fresh shelling, and the plant's compact size makes it a good fit for smaller garden beds or closer spacing than rangier Southern pea varieties. Its short season also allows two or more successive plantings through the Gulf South summer for an extended harvest window. As with other cowpeas, the roots fix nitrogen, leaving the soil enriched for the next crop.

common_name: Texas Cream 40 Pea (Extended-Harvest Cream Southern Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 40 is a semi-vining selection from the Texas A&M cream pea breeding series, bred to hold a longer, later harvest window than the more compact Texas Cream 8.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 40 is part of the Texas A&M cream-type southern pea breeding series, selected for a longer, more extended pod set than the earlier-released Texas Cream 8, giving home gardeners a steadier trickle of pods for fresh picking rather than one concentrated flush. Seeds are creamy-white with the mild, delicate, slightly sweet flavor typical of cream peas, prized for fresh shelling and quick cooking. Plants are semi-vining and slightly more sprawling than Texas Cream 8, so allow a bit more row width or provide light support for easier picking. Pick pods while still slightly immature and the seeds are plump but not hardened for the best fresh-shell texture; pods left to fully dry make good storage peas as well. Consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill improves yield in the Gulf Coast heat of midsummer.

common_name: Texas Cream 8 Pea (Compact High-Yield Cream Pea for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 8 is a semi-determinate, compact bush type that can be grown without staking — the self-supporting, upright plants concentrate pod set for a defined harvest window.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 8 is a compact, high-yielding cream southern pea selected through the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station breeding program — producing uniform, cream-colored seeds in short, upright plants that are self-supporting and well-suited to intensive raised-bed production. The 'Cream 8' number designation indicates its classification in the cream-type southern pea category, where seeds are creamy-white to tan without the eye coloring of black-eyed peas or the mottled colors of crowder types. Cream peas have a mild, sweet, delicate flavor considered more refined than the earthier crowder types — they are prized for their tender texture when fresh-shelled and their clean, creamy appearance in finished dishes. Texas Cream 8 has performed consistently well in Gulf Coast trials for productivity, uniformity, and disease resistance. The compact, semi-determinate bush habit allows closer spacing (3–4 inches in rows) than standard sprawling cream peas, increasing productivity per garden square foot. The concentrated pod set makes Texas Cream 8 practical for batch shelling and freezing — the defined harvest window means a larger quantity of pods reaches maturity simultaneously, enabling more efficient processing than the trickle harvest of indeterminate types.

plant_note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant out as soon as the soil is workable; a short-day type best for southern gardens.
directions: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings out once the ground can be worked, spacing them four to five inches apart for large bulbs. This is a short-day variety, so grow it in southern regions where it forms bulbs as days lengthen only slightly; the sweet, mild bulbs can reach up to a pound. Keep the soil evenly moist and weed-free, then cure the harvested bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination, in fertile soil in full sun, after all frost danger has passed; allow ears to fully dry down on the stalk before harvest for grinding into meal.
directions: Sow in blocks at least 4 rows wide in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and well adapted to the heat of a long Texas or Gulf South growing season. Texas Gourdseed is an old Southern dent corn named for the distinctive deep, thin, wedge-shaped indentation at the crown of each dried kernel, resembling the shape of a small gourd seed — a hallmark trait of the historic 'Gourdseed' corn family that was among the most widely grown field corns across the antebellum and postbellum South before hybrid corn displaced open-pollinated varieties in the 20th century. The tall, vigorous stalks are well adapted to hot, humid Southern summers and produce a reliable grain crop even under the drought stress that limits many other corns, grinding into a flavorful, traditional cornmeal and grits. A genuine piece of Southern agricultural history for gardeners interested in growing and preserving heritage field corn, zone 6–10.

common_name: Texas Grano Onion (Classic Gulf South Short-Day Sweet Onion)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; Texas Grano is a short-day onion requiring only 10-12 hours of daylight to bulb, making it well suited to fall planting and spring harvest in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens rather than a spring-planted crop as in the North.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in the fall in mild-winter areas, since Texas Grano is a short-day type that needs the shorter daylight of southern winters to trigger bulbing rather than the long summer days farther north. Developed in Texas in the early 20th century, it became one of the foundational sweet onion cultivars of the Gulf South and is a direct ancestor of many modern short-day sweet onions, including some of the parent lines behind Vidalia-type onions. The large, globe-shaped bulbs have straw-yellow skin and mild, sweet flesh with low pungency, best used fresh rather than stored long term since sweet onions generally keep less well than pungent storage onions. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb formation and reduce water as tops begin to fall over before harvest.

common_name: Thai Bird Chili (Bird's Eye Chile, Tiny Ultra-Hot SE Asian Cooking Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; Thai bird chili requires high soil temperature (80–95°F) for germination — use a heat mat and be patient, as germination can be slow (14–21 days). In zone 9, transplant March–April; Capsicum frutescens is actually a short-lived tropical perennial that may overwinter in zone 9b–10 in protected locations, potentially producing for 2–3 seasons. Plants become highly productive in Gulf Coast summers, setting hundreds of small peppers per plant. Harvest green for a fresher, slightly less hot flavor or allow to ripen red for maximum heat and a fruitier note. One plant produces more peppers than most households can use.
directions: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. A single plant produces abundantly — dry excess peppers for storage. Thai Bird Chili (Bird's Eye Chile, Phrik Khi Nu in Thai) is the foundational hot pepper of Thai, Vietnamese, and Southeast Asian cuisines — small (0.5–1 inch), thin, pointed, upright peppers that measure 50,000–100,000 Scoville heat units, making them significantly hotter than jalapeños (8,000 SHU) and approaching the lower range of habaneros. The name 'Bird's Eye' or 'Bird Chile' refers to the upright-pointing, small fruit that resembles a bird's eye, and also to the belief that birds (which lack capsaicin receptors) eat the peppers and spread seeds — a genuine ecological relationship that explains why the plant produces small, highly visible peppers. Thai Bird Chili is not a single variety but a group of similar Capsicum frutescens and Capsicum annuum types grown across Southeast Asia under various local names. The peppers are used in Thai cooking in virtually every form of heat addition — fresh sliced in curries and soups, dried and ground in chili pastes, pickled, or dried whole for fish sauce preparations. For Gulf South gardeners, Thai Bird Chili is one of the most productive and low-maintenance hot peppers in the summer garden: the plant thrives in heat and humidity that challenges most other pepper types, setting fruit prolifically even in July-August conditions that cause many pepper varieties to drop flowers.

common_name: Thai Bird's Eye Pepper (Phrik Khi Nu, Bird's Eye Chile)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; in zone 9 Thai bird peppers are effectively perennial — established plants survive mild winters, producing prolifically for 2–3 years before eventually declining. To overwinter, mulch heavily at the base; plants resprout from roots in spring if temperatures don't drop below about 28°F.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–90°F; Thai bird's eye pepper (called 'phrik khi nu' — literally 'mouse dropping pepper' — in Thai, or simply 'bird's eye chile' across Southeast Asia) is the small, intensely hot pepper that provides the backbone of heat in Thai, Vietnamese, Lao, and Cambodian cuisines. The tiny fruits (1/2 to 3/4 inch long, narrow, conical) start green and ripen to vivid red, with heat levels measuring 50,000–100,000 Scoville units — substantially hotter than jalapeños but less scorching than habaneros — and a clean, bright, fruity heat without the floral overtones of chinense-type peppers. The small size means many peppers are sliced directly into dishes or pounded whole in mortars; Thai bird's eye peppers carry their heat through both flesh and seeds with essentially no mild portion, making them one of the most reliably fiery culinary peppers. Capsicum frutescens produces smaller, more compact plants than C. annuum with multiple upright-pointing fruits on each branch — the characteristic upright fruit habit distinguishes it from most common peppers. In zone 9+, plants become woody perennial shrubs (2–3 feet tall and wide) producing enormous numbers of peppers continuously from summer through fall and into winter during warm years. Production per plant is staggering once established — a mature zone 9 plant produces thousands of peppers per season, far more than most families can use fresh.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and nights stay above 55°F.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix at 82–85°F; Thai chili needs more heat for germination than most C. annuum types. Plants are compact and extremely productive, bearing dozens of small (1–2 inch) upright fruits that ripen from green to bright red and carry intense heat of 50,000–100,000 Scoville units. Harvest red-ripe fruits for maximum heat and full flavor; the plants can be brought indoors as houseplants before frost and often survive multiple seasons. Excellent for drying — the small fruits air-dry on the plant or can be strung and hung in a warm spot.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil warms to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix at 80–85°F and maintain consistent heat throughout the seedling stage; Thai eggplant germinates and grows faster than larger-fruited types. Transplant to a warm, sheltered bed after last frost and mulch heavily to retain soil warmth. The round, golf ball-sized fruits ripen from white-striped green to fully white or yellow depending on the cultivar, and are harvested while still firm and slightly underripe for use in Thai green curry. Overripe fruits become bitter; check plants every 2–3 days and harvest promptly to keep plants productive.

common_name: Thai Green Eggplant (Small Striped Round Eggplant for Curry)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55F. Thai Green thrives in Gulf South heat and humidity, continuing to produce through the hottest part of summer.
