directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young at golf-ball to small-egg size for the crisp, mild, low-seed texture prized in Thai cooking. Thai Green is a small, round eggplant with pale to medium green skin lightly streaked with cream, borne in heavy clusters on compact, productive plants that thrive in hot, humid conditions. The firm, dense flesh holds its shape well when simmered whole or halved directly into Thai green curry, a traditional use where the small green fruit is added along with pea eggplants and other aromatics. Its heat tolerance and continuous production over a long summer season make it an excellent, prolific choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors with bottom heat; transplant only after nights stay reliably warm.
directions: Start seed indoors with warm bottom heat several weeks before the last frost, since these peppers need heat to germinate well. Transplant the compact, mounding 8-inch plants outdoors only after all danger of frost has passed and nights are warm. Each plant carries dozens of upright, slender 1.5 to 3 inch fruits that ripen from green to red at the same time for a very ornamental, very spicy display; they do well in containers.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant in March–April. Thai Hot plants become large and very productive in zone 9's long warm season and often overwinter as woody perennials, returning to bear even heavier crops in subsequent seasons. Plants are ornamentally attractive when laden with clusters of upright red and green fruits in different stages of ripeness.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Thai Hot (also called Thai Bird Pepper or 'prik kee noo' in Thai, meaning 'mouse droppings pepper') is the standard small, intensely hot pepper used in authentic Thai, Vietnamese, Lao, and broader Southeast Asian cuisines. The thin, pointed, upright fruits (1–2 inches long, pencil-thin) ripen from bright green through red, with clusters of fruits in different ripening stages creating an ornamental display. The heat level of 50,000–100,000 Scoville Heat Units produces the sharp, penetrating, instant heat characteristic of Thai cuisine — different in character from the deeper, slower-building heat of dried Mexican chiles. Both green (unripe) and red (ripe) fruits are used in Thai cooking — green fruits appear in green curry paste, papaya salad, and stir-fries; red fruits are used in red curry paste and dried for chile flakes. The highly prolific plants bear continuously through warm weather, producing far more peppers than most home cooks can use fresh.

common_name: Thai Long Green Eggplant (Slender Pale-Green Asian Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. This slender Southeast Asian type sets fruit reliably through Gulf South summer heat and humidity.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm. Thai Long Green produces slender, curved, pale jade-green fruit up to a foot long with a mild flavor and few seeds, a traditional Southeast Asian type widely used in stir-fries, curries, and grilling, where the thin skin and tender flesh cook quickly without needing to be peeled. The productive, heat-loving plants continue setting fruit through the hottest, most humid stretch of summer, when many Western eggplant varieties slow down. Harvest fruit young and glossy for the best texture — overripe fruit turns dull and develops tougher flesh and larger seeds — and pick every few days to keep plants producing.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 plant March–May. Thai Red is a short-day plant that begins flowering as days shorten in August–September; calyces are harvested through October until frost. Plant early enough to establish before the heat of summer.
directions: Sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Thai Red is a deeply pigmented roselle cultivar from Southeast Asia, selected for extraordinarily high anthocyanin content that produces calyces (the fleshy red structures around the seed pod) of an intense ruby-red that yields a dramatic magenta-crimson juice when steeped. Harvest calyces when they are plump, firm, and fully red — typically 5–7 days after the flower petals drop — by snapping them off the branch. Thai Red calyces produce a more intensely flavored, darker red hibiscus tea (agua de Jamaica) than standard roselle varieties, and are prized for naturally colored beverages, syrups, jellies, and dried flower teas. The tall, bushy plants are as ornamental as they are productive, with attractive red-veined leaves and showy flowers.

common_name: Thelma Sanders Sweet Potato Squash (Missouri Heirloom Acorn-Type with Sweet Nutty Flesh)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Thelma Sanders Sweet Potato Squash produces medium-sized fruits (2–3 lbs) with a form similar to acorn squash but with cream to tan skin rather than acorn squash's dark green, and the characteristic lightly ridged, oval to oblong shape. In zone 9, plant March–April for summer production or July–August for a fall crop that matures in October–November when cooler weather improves flavor and texture. The cream skin color deepens to tan as the squash fully cures, providing a visual harvest maturity cue. Thelma Sanders is an open-pollinated heirloom available through Seed Savers Exchange — it originated with Thelma Sanders of Missouri who maintained the seed before the Seed Savers Exchange helped distribute it more broadly, a typical pattern for regional heirloom vegetable varieties preserved by individual gardeners.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin is tan-cream and stem has dried. Thelma Sanders Sweet Potato Squash is a Missouri heirloom winter squash with an unusually devoted following among winter squash enthusiasts — one of the open-pollinated acorn-type squashes most frequently cited for superior eating quality among the many heirloom varieties preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network. The variety produces oval to oblong fruits, 6–8 inches long, with smooth to lightly ridged cream to tan skin that turns uniformly tan at full maturity. The name 'sweet potato squash' references the flesh character: the texture is drier and denser than standard acorn squash, with a sweet, slightly dry, nutty quality reminiscent in some ways of baked sweet potato — particularly the way the flesh separates into fibrous, sweet sections when baked. This dry, dense texture is highly valued by cooks who find standard acorn squash flesh too watery: Thelma Sanders bakes to a fluffy, dry interior that absorbs butter and seasonings distinctly better than wet-fleshed varieties, and the sweetness at full maturity is exceptional. The flavor is genuinely complex — sweet, nutty, slightly starchy — in a way that distinguishes it from hybrid acorn types selected for uniformity and yield rather than flavor depth. Thelma Sanders' origin traces to an individual Missouri gardener of the same name who maintained the seed through her personal gardening before sharing it through the Seed Savers Exchange community.

common_name: Thomas Laxton Pea (Heirloom English Main-Crop Shelling Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; the medium-height vines benefit from light staking or pea netting to keep pods off the ground and easy to pick.
directions: Thomas Laxton was introduced in England in 1898 by the Laxton Brothers breeding firm as an improved early-to-main-season shelling pea and has remained popular with seed savers ever since for its reliable yields and classic sweet English pea flavor. Vines are shorter and easier to manage than tall telephone-type peas but still produce well-filled pods over a solid harvest window. Sow early for the sweetest peas, and pick pods promptly once they fill out, since flavor declines quickly as peas mature and starch content rises. Its heirloom status and open-pollinated seed make it a good choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed year to year.

common_name: Thorogreen Lima Bean (Green-Seeded Bush Baby Lima)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; a compact bush type needing no trellis.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F. Thorogreen is a bush-type baby lima bean prized for seeds that stay a pale green color even after cooking, rather than the more common cream or white of most lima beans, giving finished dishes an appealingly fresh, vibrant appearance. The compact plant sets pods over a relatively short, concentrated window typical of bush lima types, making it convenient for a single main harvest for canning or freezing, and the small, tender seeds cook quickly with a mild, sweet flavor. Harvest pods at the green shell stage once well filled, and pick promptly once pods mature, since lima pods left too long on the plant can toughen.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in partial to full shade; three-cornered garlic is one of the few alliums that thrives in shade and tolerates competition from tree roots. NOTE: this species has naturalized invasively in parts of California and Pacific coastal regions; check local invasive plant lists before planting.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; three-cornered garlic is named for its distinctively triangular stem cross-section, visible when the stem is cut. This Mediterranean allium is one of the most useful for shade gardens because it genuinely thrives under trees where garlic and chives fail. The small white bell flowers in spring are pendulous and nodding, borne in a one-sided umbel, and all parts — leaves, stems, flowers, and bulbs — have a mild garlic flavor and are fully edible. Leaves can be harvested like chives throughout fall and winter in mild climates; use them raw in salads, cooked in omelets, or as a mild garlic substitute wherever a delicate garlic presence is wanted.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost, or start indoors a couple weeks early.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after the danger of frost has passed, or start indoors a couple weeks early and transplant carefully. This compact vine saves garden space while producing uniform 1 to 1.25 pound fruits with creamy-white rinds boldly striped in green and orange. Let fruits fully mature and cure the hard rinds before storing; the smooth, sweet flesh is as good for eating as the striking rinds are for autumn displays.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for fall harvest; Thumbelina, an All-America Selections winner, forms small, round, golf-ball-sized roots that mature quickly and grow well even in shallow or heavy, rocky soil unsuited to long-rooted carrot varieties.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up. Thumbelina, an All-America Selections winner, produces small, round, sweet roots about the size of a golf ball rather than the long tapered shape of standard carrots, making it uniquely well suited to shallow, rocky, or heavy clay soils where long-rooted carrots often grow forked or stunted, as well as to container growing. Its quick maturity and compact size also make it a fun, kid-friendly carrot for small gardens. Harvest as soon as roots reach full size, since round carrots can become woody if left in the ground too long, and keep soil consistently moist for the sweetest, most tender roots.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop; Tiara is a fast-maturing, small-headed cabbage bred for close spacing and high-density planting, giving a much larger yield per bed than standard full-size cabbage.
directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants closely since Tiara is bred specifically for high-density planting. It forms small, dense, round green heads of about 1-2 pounds in a notably short season, one of the fastest-maturing cabbages commonly grown, which lets gardeners fit in an extra planting or squeeze a crop into a narrow spring or fall window between other vegetables. The compact head size also suits smaller households better than a large storage cabbage does. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm and solid, since fast-maturing types can split if left in the ground too long after reaching full size. Watch for cabbage worms and aphids, common pests on all brassicas in the Gulf South.

common_name: Tifleaf Pearl Millet (High-Yield Summer Cover Crop and Wildlife Food Plot Grass)
plant_note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep after the last frost when soil is consistently warm (65°F+); Tifleaf 3 can be broadcast-seeded or drilled at 15–25 lbs/acre for cover crop use; for garden plots, 1 oz per 100 square feet provides dense stand coverage; plant after spring crops are removed for a summer-to-fall cover crop terminated before fall vegetable plantings.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained to moderately moist, average to fertile soil in full sun; Tifleaf Pearl Millet is the premier summer cover crop and wildlife food plot annual grass for Gulf South gardens and farms — a rapidly growing warm-season grass developed by the University of Georgia that establishes extremely quickly in warm conditions, producing dense, tall (5–8 foot) stands within 6–8 weeks of planting. The rapid establishment makes pearl millet exceptionally effective as a summer cover crop in Gulf South gardens that experience the challenging June–August gap between spring vegetable harvest and fall planting — a period when bare soil erodes, weeds proliferate, and soil organic matter degrades under summer sun. Tifleaf 3 is one of the most productive of all cover crop grasses for total biomass per acre in summer conditions, providing substantial green manure when terminated by mowing or incorporation before fall planting. The tall, dense stand also creates an effective summer screen, privacy hedge, or windbreak for garden areas. For wildlife gardeners, pearl millet provides outstanding deer forage and dove attractant — the seed heads produced in late summer are among the most palatable of all wildlife food plot plantings for mourning doves. Drought-tolerant once established. Terminated easily by mowing at the soil surface — the shallow root system decomposes quickly, improving soil organic matter. Grows as a warm-season annual, killed by first frost.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills 1-2 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed, or transplant 3-week-old seedlings to avoid disturbing the taproot.
directions: Tiger Baby gets its name from the dark gray-green rind striped with bold tiger-like markings, wrapped around a compact 7-8 pound icebox-size fruit with sweet, crisp red flesh. Its shorter maturity window compared to full-size Southern heirlooms makes it a good pick for gardeners north of the traditional watermelon belt who still want a full-flavored melon. Fertilize modestly since excess nitrogen favors vine growth over fruiting, and thump or check the ground spot for creamy yellowing to judge ripeness. The single-serving size makes it easy to chill whole and slice fresh without leftovers going to waste.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; a bush bean needing no support; pick pods frequently if harvesting as a snap bean.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Tiger Eye is a stunning heirloom bush bean with large seeds in a rich golden-yellow to tan background covered with auburn to deep brown streaking and marbling — the pattern resembles a tiger's eye gemstone and retains some color on cooking. The flavor is particularly rich and buttery for a dry bean, often described as creamy with a hint of chestnut, making it excellent in soups and stews or as a simple side dish. A productive and reliable bush bean that dries beautifully on the plant and stores well.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; an indeterminate variety that needs staking or caging despite its compact clusters of small-medium fruit.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before last frost in a warm, moist seed-starting mix kept at 70–85°F; transplant deeply after frost danger has passed, burying the stem up to the lowest leaves to encourage a strong root system. Tigerella is a British heirloom also sold under the name Mr. Stripey in the UK, producing heavy clusters of 2–3 ounce fruits with vivid red skin and irregular gold-yellow stripes and a tangy, balanced flavor that is excellent fresh or in sauces. Stake or cage plants early and begin harvesting when the fruit is firm but fully colored at the blossom end; unlike many striped types it ripens evenly and does not crack easily. Regular irrigation helps maintain even soil moisture and reduces blossom-end rot.

plant_note: Plant tubers (chufa nuts) 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; tigernut produces its best yields in loose, sandy soil that allows the tubers to develop freely and be harvested easily.
directions: Plant tubers 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, loose, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; tigernut (chufa, earth almond) is a cultivated sedge grown for its small, starchy, walnut-flavored underground tubers — the basis of the traditional Spanish drink horchata de chufa — that are rich in fiber, healthy fats, and natural sugars and may be eaten raw, roasted, or processed into milk, flour, or oil. Plants produce a dense clump of grass-like, bright-green leaves with triangular stems (a sedge, not a grass). The tubers multiply prolifically underground and are harvested after the foliage dies back in fall. Excellent as a forage crop for wildlife food plots (ducks and deer are attracted to tigernuts) or as a human snack crop. Distinct from the wild weed form (C. esculentus var. esculentus) which is an invasive nuisance; always plant only the cultivated var. sativus.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-amended soil; Tigger melon is a striking ornamental-edible Middle Eastern/Central Asian heirloom with bright yellow skin dramatically striped and splashed with crimson and orange, producing small to medium fruits with cream to pale orange flesh and a sweet, spicy, slightly fruity flavor.
directions: Sow in hills after last frost in warm, well-amended, well-drained soil; thin to 2 plants per hill and allow vines to sprawl or train on a sturdy trellis with sling support for fruits. Tigger is a Central Asian or Middle Eastern heirloom melon with one of the most striking exteriors in the melon world — the smooth, round to oval, medium-sized (1–2 lb) fruits are a brilliant golden-yellow with dramatic crimson-to-orange zigzag stripes, spots, and splashes that make them resemble the fictional tiger character they are named for. The flesh is cream-colored to pale orange with a sweet, spicy, slightly fruity aroma that is pleasant rather than intensely musky; more of an ornamental conversation-piece melon than a flavor standout, but still delicious and perfectly edible. Extremely heat-tolerant and productive in hot climates; outstanding as a farmers market novelty and ornamental edible.

plant_note: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while dormant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Timperley Early is the classic English cultivar bred specifically for forcing an extra-early harvest, and like other rhubarb it needs a period of winter chilling for vigorous spring growth.
directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Timperley Early is a long-established English rhubarb cultivar bred and selected specifically for forcing — covering the crown in late winter with an upturned pot or forcing jar to exclude light produces exceptionally early, pale pink, sweet, tender stalks weeks ahead of an uncovered planting, a traditional practice in British kitchen gardens. Left unforced, it is simply an early-cropping, reliable garden rhubarb with slender, bright red-pink stalks and good flavor. As with all rhubarb, it performs best where winters provide real cold to satisfy its chilling requirement, so it is more reliable in temperate and upper Southern gardens than in the mild winters of the Deep South. Harvest by pulling individual stalks from the outside of the crown rather than cutting, always leaving several stalks per plant to sustain it, and never eat the leaves, which contain toxic levels of oxalic acid.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after the last frost.
directions: Sow Tiny Tim seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then move seedlings to their final container or bed once frost danger passes. This dwarf determinate reaches only about 12 inches tall, making it perfect for patios, windowsills, and indoor pots. It sets an early, generous crop of bright cherry tomatoes on compact plants that need little or no staking. Give it plenty of light and steady moisture, and harvest the fruit as it ripens fully red.

common_name: Tivoli Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Bush Spaghetti Squash for Small Gardens)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Tivoli is a compact bush-habit spaghetti squash that produces the familiar cream-colored oval fruits (4–5 lbs) on a plant only 3–4 feet wide — dramatically smaller than standard spaghetti squash vines that can trail 6–10 feet. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer harvest and again August for fall production. Tivoli won an All-America Selections award for this characteristic compact bush habit combined with full-sized, excellent-quality spaghetti squash fruits; standard spaghetti squash requires far too much space for most home gardens, where a single plant's sprawling vines can take over a 6×8 foot area. Tivoli's bush habit limits spread to approximately 3×3–4 feet, making it practical for raised beds and small gardens. The flesh, when cooked, separates into the characteristic spaghetti-like strands that give the squash type its name — mild, slightly sweet, and excellent as a low-carbohydrate pasta substitute.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest when skin is cream-yellow and thumps with a hollow sound. Tivoli Squash was developed by W. Atlee Burpee and received All-America Selections recognition in 1991 specifically for solving one of the primary practical limitations of spaghetti squash production in home gardens: the sprawling, space-consuming vine habit of standard spaghetti squash varieties makes them impractical for most garden spaces. While standard vining spaghetti squash can trail 6–10 feet in multiple directions from a single plant, requiring 40–80 square feet per plant for uncrowded production, Tivoli's compact bush habit limits the footprint to approximately 3–4 feet in diameter — manageable within a raised bed or small garden plot. The fruits produced by Tivoli are standard-sized spaghetti squash (4–5 lbs, 8–10 inches long, cream-colored skin), with the same characteristic flesh that separates into noodle-like strands when cooked — a texture that makes spaghetti squash one of the most popular vegetable substitutes for pasta. For zone 9 gardeners, spaghetti squash performs well in spring (transplanted or direct sown in March–May for a June–August harvest) and in fall (planted in late August for October–November harvest), with the compact bush habit of Tivoli making both planting windows practical in average-sized raised bed gardens.

common_name: Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn (Desert-Adapted Sonoran Flour Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn was bred by the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert to mature quickly, ahead of the end of the summer monsoon season.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn is a remarkably fast-maturing flour corn developed by the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, bred to reach maturity in about two months so a crop could be planted and harvested within the brief window of the summer monsoon rains. Its speed and drought adaptation make it valuable for short-season gardens or a fast succession planting anywhere. Harvest and dry ears fully before grinding the kernels into flour for traditional dishes like pinole and tortillas.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into loose, deeply cultivated soil free of stones so the long, tapering roots can grow straight; also sown in late summer for fall harvest.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into loose, deeply cultivated soil free of stones so the long, tapering white roots can grow straight and unforked. Tokinashi is a traditional Japanese heirloom valued for its unusual all-season adaptability and its resistance to becoming pithy, allowing roots to be left in the ground to reach 15-18 inches without losing quality. The firm, crisp, assertively pungent flesh is a staple for grating, pickling, and simmering, and the variety is a reliable open-pollinated choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed.

plant_note: Bolts in heat; best as a spring and fall crop.
directions: This tender Asian green forms loose, frilly, pale chartreuse leaves used raw in salads or lightly cooked. Direct sow shallowly and thin to about 8 inches, or harvest thinnings as baby greens. It grows very fast and prefers cool weather, bolting quickly once temperatures climb. Keep soil evenly moist to maintain the crisp, mild leaves and prevent bitterness. Sow in early spring and again in late summer for tender harvests bracketing the heat of summer.

common_name: Tokyo Cross Turnip (AAS-Winning Hybrid Salad Turnip)
plant_note: Sow directly as soon as soil can be worked, and again in late summer for fall roots; thin early since this hybrid grows fast and can crowd itself.
directions: Tokyo Cross is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid turnip, an All-America Selections winner bred from the open-pollinated Tokyo Market type, valued for producing smooth, pure-white globes that stay tender, mild, and crack-free even if left in the ground past ideal size. Direct sow shallowly into loose soil and thin to a few inches apart, keeping the bed consistently moist for the fastest, sweetest roots. Both the crisp roots and the tender young tops are edible, making it a dual-purpose crop for salads, quick pickles, or braising greens. Its speed and heat tolerance for a turnip make it well suited to succession planting through much of the season.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; can be resown for continuous harvest.
directions: Sow Tokyo Long White seeds a quarter inch deep and thin plants to about an inch apart for tall, tender green stalks. This non-bulbing Asian heirloom forms long white shanks topped with mild green tops rather than a round bulb. It tolerates cold well and can be grown in containers or resown every few weeks for a continuous supply. Harvest whole plants when they reach usable size, or trim tops as needed for a cut-and-come-again crop.

common_name: Tokyo Market Turnip (Japanese Fast-Growing Salad Turnip)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer for fall harvest or in early spring; Tokyo Market is a very fast-maturing Japanese salad turnip (30–40 days) producing small, round, smooth, pure white roots with very mild, sweet flavor — harvested at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the finest eating quality; similar in type to Hakurei but a slightly larger, more market-focused variety.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 3–4 inches apart; harvest at 2–3 inch diameter for finest quality (overripe roots become pithy and strongly flavored); both roots and tender greens are edible. Tokyo Market is a Japanese-type salad turnip closely related to (but distinct from) Hakurei — both belong to the mild, sweet, fast-maturing Japanese turnip tradition that is quite different from the traditional European turnip types grown for cooking. Tokyo Market matures in just 30–40 days from direct seeding, producing smooth, round, pure white roots with a mild, slightly sweet, and almost fruity flavor that is excellent raw — sliced thin into salads, served with dipping sauces, or eaten out of hand like an apple in the garden. Unlike European cooking turnips (which are generally too sharp and starchy to eat raw), Japanese salad turnip types like Tokyo Market and Hakurei have been bred for low pungency and high sugar content, making them the most accessible and enjoyable turnips for most modern palates. The tender, mild young greens are equally edible — excellent in salads, stir-fries, and anywhere turnip greens are used with a preference for milder flavor. Tokyo Market is preferred in farmers market growing for its consistent, uniform appearance and rapid turnover; for home gardeners it provides the fastest-maturing turnip option for succession planting every 3–4 weeks.

common_name: Tom Thumb Lettuce (Miniature Heirloom Butterhead Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow thinly with barely 0.125 inch of soil coverage; Tom Thumb forms very small heads (3–4 inches in diameter) that can be planted at much closer spacing than standard lettuce — 6 inches apart rather than the 10–12 inches standard butterheads require. The small head size allows one head per person per serving, making it practical for restaurant-style presentation. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile soil with barely 0.125 inch coverage; keep consistently moist through germination. Tom Thumb is an English heirloom butterhead lettuce that produces perfectly proportioned miniature heads — fully formed, well-blanched butterhead-type lettuce compressed into a head 3–4 inches in diameter and 4–6 inches tall at maturity, roughly one-quarter the size of a standard butterhead like Buttercrunch or Boston. The miniature scale is not a compromised or immature form of standard lettuce; Tom Thumb is a true miniature variety that completes its growth cycle and forms a proper, compact head with the characteristic blanched, cream-colored inner leaves and tender, buttery texture of butterhead types. The small head size makes Tom Thumb exceptionally practical in multiple ways: it can be spaced 6 inches apart rather than 10–12 inches, fitting significantly more plants in a given area; it produces one serving per head, eliminating the common problem of leftover half-heads wilting in the refrigerator; and it is particularly suited to container growing, window boxes, and very small raised beds where a full-sized lettuce would be overwhelming. Tom Thumb has been grown in English kitchen gardens since at least the 19th century and represents the miniaturization approach to vegetable breeding that has recently become popular again in urban and space-limited gardening.

plant_note: Direct sow thickly in cool early spring soil; this dwarf Victorian-era heirloom needs no staking and matures quickly.
directions: Direct sow thickly in cool early spring soil; this dwarf Victorian-era heirloom needs no staking and matures quickly, making it one of the earliest garden peas to harvest. Bred in England in the mid-1800s as a compact alternative to the era's towering pea vines, Tom Thumb tops out under a foot tall, which has made it a longtime favorite for small beds, cold frames, and containers. Because the plants are so short, keep them weed-free, as taller neighbors will shade them out quickly. Harvest pods as soon as they plump for the sweetest flavor, since this small-statured variety produces a modest but concentrated crop over a short window.

common_name: Tom Thumb Popcorn (Dwarf Heirloom Strawberry-Type Popcorn)
plant_note: Sow in blocks in average garden soil or containers; its dwarf habit lets it thrive in small spaces.
directions: Sow in blocks in average garden soil or containers; its dwarf habit lets it thrive in small spaces where a full-size popcorn would be impractical. Tom Thumb is a diminutive heirloom popcorn reaching only three to four feet tall, producing small, deep-red ears reminiscent of miniature Strawberry Popcorn but on an even more compact plant. Left to dry fully on the stalk, the small hard kernels pop up light and tender, and the short ears and petite plants also make this variety popular for autumn ornamental displays as well as a genuinely productive novelty popcorn for the home popper.

common_name: Tom Watson Watermelon (Classic Georgia Heirloom, Very Large Southern Picnic Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F minimum); Tom Watson is a very large variety requiring substantial space — vines spread 10–15 feet and individual fruits can weigh 30–50 pounds, requiring ample room and warm nights for full sugar development. In zone 9, plant April–May. The oblong, mottled-green striped fruits (12–18 inches long) develop over 85–95 days of warm weather. Tom Watson needs a long, hot summer to reach full size and sweetness — the Gulf South's reliable summer heat is ideal. Harvested before full ripeness, Tom Watson can be bland and watery; the full flavor requires the heat accumulation that makes zone 9 an excellent watermelon climate. Detect ripeness by dried tendril adjacent to fruit, creamy yellow ground spot, and hollow thud when thumped firmly.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; space hills 6–8 feet apart. Harvest when tendril dries and ground spot turns creamy yellow. Tom Watson is one of the most historically important American watermelon varieties — a large, oblong, Southern heirloom that was the dominant commercial watermelon in the southeastern United States from approximately 1906 through the mid-20th century, and that is named (with slight uncertainty as to whether intentionally or as a coincidence of personal name similarity) after one of Georgia's most prominent politicians of the era. Tom Watson melons are large to very large (typically 25–50 lbs), oblong with mottled medium-dark green skin and faint lighter stripes, with red to deep red flesh and moderate seed content. The flavor at full maturity is excellent — sweet, richly flavored, and typifying the character of old-style Southern watermelons grown in sandy, hot-summer soil. Tom Watson was particularly prized for its performance in the sandy, well-drained soils of the Georgia and Carolina coastal plain, where the warm nights, deep sandy loam, and long growing season produced melons with exceptional sweetness and the size that made watermelons the centerpiece of summer picnics, church suppers, and community celebrations throughout the South. The variety's historical significance extends beyond flavor: Tom Watson represents a type of community and agricultural identity in the South where the production of very large, high-quality melons was a point of regional pride and a staple of summer social life in farming communities.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger has passed.
directions: Start Toma Verde seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings 24 to 36 inches apart in warm soil. This early-maturing variety produces bright green fruit in papery husks with the classic tart flavor prized for salsa verde. Plant at least two tomatillos, since they need cross-pollination to set fruit well. Harvest when the fruit fills and splits its husk, and stake the sprawling plants to keep fruit off the ground.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger; tomatillos are self-infertile — plant at least two for cross-pollination and fruit set; in zone 9, start seeds in January–February for March–April transplanting, or direct sow in March for summer harvest.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; set transplants in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; plant at least two for pollination. Physalis philadelphica (tomatillo) is the green or purple, husked fruit essential to Mexican salsas, mole verde, and enchilada sauce — a fruity, tart, citrusy tomato relative encased in a papery, lantern-like calyx that expands as the fruit develops and splits open to signal ripeness; harvest when the husk fills tightly and the fruit turns from green toward yellow, or use green for maximum tartness in salsa verde. Tomatillos are extremely productive warm-season annuals that bear heavily in zone 9 through summer and fall; they are more heat-tolerant than tomatoes and continue producing when summer temperatures exceed 90°F. The plants sprawl considerably and benefit from caging or staking; prune to 2–3 main stems for higher yields. 'Verde Puebla' and 'Gigante' are large-fruited green types; 'Purple de Milpa' has purple-tinged fruits. Unlike tomatoes, tomatillos must be planted in pairs or groups because they are self-incompatible — single plants produce no fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant 1–2 weeks after last frost.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and keep at 70–85°F until sprouts emerge. Transplant after nights reliably stay above 50°F, burying the stem up to the lowest leaves to encourage a strong root system. Provide a cage or stake for support, and water consistently at the base to reduce the risk of blossom-end rot. Harvest when fruit is fully colored and gives slightly to gentle pressure.

common_name: Tommy Toe Tomato (Australian Heirloom Salad Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; stake or cage firmly, since Tommy Toe is a vigorous, heavy-yielding indeterminate variety.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, staking or caging plants firmly to support the vigorous vines. Tommy Toe is a beloved Australian heirloom producing an abundance of round, golf-ball-sized fruit larger than a typical cherry tomato but smaller than a standard slicer, with rich, well-balanced, classic tomato flavor that many gardeners rate above modern cherry hybrids for taste. Its heavy, sustained production over a long season and good disease tolerance have made it a favorite for fresh eating, salads, and snacking straight off the vine, occupying a useful middle ground in size between cherry and full-sized tomatoes. Harvest regularly as fruit ripens to keep the prolific vines setting new fruit throughout the summer.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil is workable; ideal for shallow beds and containers.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in loose soil as soon as the ground can be worked, keeping the bed evenly moist through the slow germination. This Italian heirloom, whose name means Round of Paris, forms deep-orange, golf-ball-shaped roots that are sweet and tender. Its short, round shape means shallow roots, so it thrives in shallow beds and containers where longer carrots would struggle; harvest young for the best texture.

common_name: Tongue of Fire Bean (Borlotto Lingua di Fuoco)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after all frost danger passes in warm soil; Tongue of Fire is a bush bean that also has a pole-type strain — check the seed packet. In zone 9, plant for a spring crop (February–March) and a fall crop (September–October) to avoid peak summer heat, which causes pod set failure above 90°F.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Tongue of Fire is an Italian heirloom bean with extraordinary visual appeal — the pods are cream-colored with vivid red-orange streaks and splashes, as if painted with fire. The seeds inside are cranberry-colored with dark red stripes. The beans are harvested green as a snap or shell bean, or left to dry for storage as a dry bean. As a fresh shell bean the flavor is rich, creamy, and nutty — superior to most commercial beans. The striped coloring unfortunately fades when cooked, but the flavor more than compensates. An excellent choice for Italian and Mediterranean-style cooking, particularly in minestrone, pasta e fagioli, and bean salads.

common_name: Tongues of Fire Bean (Lingua di Fuoco, Italian Shell Bean Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Tongues of Fire (Lingua di Fuoco in Italian) is a traditional Italian borlotto bean variety famous for its spectacular appearance — the pods are cream-colored with dramatic scarlet-red flame streaks (the 'tongues of fire') and the shelled beans within are cream-white with vivid red speckles that fade to a uniform brown when cooked; harvested as a shell bean or allowed to dry completely for a dry borlotto bean.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; Tongues of Fire is a bush bean that can also be harvested as a snap bean at 5–6 inches (though the pods are somewhat coarse) — harvest as a shell bean when pods are plump and fully developed (60–70 days) or allow to dry completely for a dry borlotto bean (75–85 days). Tongues of Fire (Lingua di Fuoco) is a traditional Italian borlotto bean with some of the most dramatically beautiful pods in the vegetable garden — the medium-length pods are a creamy or pale yellow background completely covered with irregular streaks, splashes, and flames of scarlet-red that give the variety its evocative Italian name. The raw pods are so visually striking that harvesting them from the plant is genuinely exciting; unfortunately (from a visual standpoint), both the red pod markings and the speckled cream-and-red seed coloring fade completely when the beans are cooked, resulting in uniform tan to brownish seeds. The flavor of shell-stage Tongues of Fire beans is excellent — rich, earthy, and starchy in the characteristic Italian borlotto style that makes them the preferred bean for ribollita soup, pasta e fagioli, and other classic bean dishes of central and northern Italian cooking. Borlotti are used across Italy as the fresh shell bean equivalent of cranberry beans in New England cooking — they are always shelled before cooking, never eaten as whole pods. Tongues of Fire is reliable and productive in summer gardens throughout the US.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring or late summer; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: Sow seed directly or start transplants for spring and late-summer crops, spacing plants 12 to 18 inches apart. This vigorous hybrid produces tall, upright plants with slightly savoyed leaves and regrows quickly for repeated cut-and-come-again harvests. Collards are cold hardy and grow well far beyond the South; a light frost actually sweetens the nutritious, vitamin-rich leaves, so leave plants standing into cold weather.

common_name: Top Crop Bush Bean (AAS-Winning Classic Heirloom Bush Snap Bean, Early and Dependable)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is at least 60°F; beans rot in cold, wet soil. Top Crop is a classic early bush snap bean that can also tolerate warm conditions — it was originally selected and trialed specifically for heat resistance and productivity under the warm, humid conditions of the southeastern United States and received an All-America Selections award in 1951 for its superior performance over existing bush bean varieties. In zone 9, direct sow March–May for spring production and August–September for fall production; bean plants decline quickly when summer temperatures consistently exceed 95°F but spring and fall crops can be very productive. The plants are compact and upright (18–24 inches), producing straight, round, stringless or nearly stringless pods 5–6 inches long in abundance at 49–54 days.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; space 4–6 inches in rows 18 inches apart. Harvest at 5–6 inches before seeds bulge. Top Crop is one of the historically significant All-America Selections winners in the vegetable category, recognized in 1951 for performance and quality that exceeded the bush bean standard of the era. At the time of its AAS recognition, Top Crop represented a meaningful improvement over other widely grown bush bean varieties in terms of pod quality (straight, stringless, and uniform), plant habit (upright and compact, making harvest easier), and importantly for southeastern gardens — its tolerance for warm, humid growing conditions that cause many bean varieties to set pods poorly or produce stringy, misshapen pods. The variety became one of the most widely grown bush snap bean varieties in American home and market gardens through the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s, establishing itself as a regional standard especially in the South where the heat tolerance advantage mattered most. Top Crop produces round, stringless pods (the 'Top Crop' designation reflects the goal of beans that crop densely at the top of the plant, making harvest efficient) that are firm, tender at optimal harvest size (5–6 inches), and of classic, straightforward snap bean flavor. The variety is open-pollinated and remains available through seed companies as a historical heirloom standard. For zone 9 spring and fall gardens, Top Crop's heat tolerance and early maturity (49–54 days) make it practical for getting a bean crop harvested before summer heat peaks or after it subsides in fall.

common_name: Top Mark Cantaloupe (Classic Western Shipping Melon)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Top Mark was bred by the Dessert Seed Company of El Centro, California as a firm-fleshed Western shipping cantaloupe and remains popular with home gardeners for its reliable disease tolerance and classic flavor.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of two to three plants in full sun once soil has warmed well past last frost, thinning to the strongest seedling per hill. Top Mark produces slightly oblong, well-netted, 3-4 lb fruits with thick, firm, sweet salmon-colored flesh, and was long grown as a standard commercial shipping melon in California's Imperial Valley thanks to good tolerance of powdery and downy mildew. Keep soil evenly moist through vine growth and fruit set, then reduce watering as melons approach maturity to concentrate sweetness. Harvest at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit with light pressure and the blossom end yields slightly to thumb pressure.

common_name: Top Pick Pinkeye Southern Pea (Easy-Harvest Purple Hull Type)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil is thoroughly warm; Top Pick Pinkeye is an improved open-pollinated pinkeye purple hull type bred to concentrate its pods at the top of the plant for faster, cleaner picking — a real time-saver during the peak of a Gulf South summer harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; Top Pick Pinkeye is an improved pinkeye purple hull southern pea bred so that pods set concentrated near the top of the plant rather than scattered throughout, letting a picker harvest a full basket quickly without hunting through foliage — a meaningful advantage during the heavy summer flush when Southern peas are at their most productive. The cream-colored peas with a distinctive pink eye have the classic mild, slightly sweet flavor prized in Southern cooking. Harvest pods when they've turned the characteristic purple-pink color and the peas inside have filled out but are still tender for fresh shelling, or let pods dry fully for storage. Like other Southern peas, the plant fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility as it grows, and thrives in the long, hot Gulf South summer.

common_name: Torvum Vigor Rootstock Eggplant (Turkey Berry Rootstock)
plant_note: Start indoors well ahead of the scion variety, since seed germinates slowly and unevenly, then graft a favorite eggplant scion onto it once stems are pencil-thick, heal in a humid shaded chamber, and transplant after frost into full sun.
directions: This wild, thorny relative of eggplant is grown as a grafting rootstock rather than for its own small, bitter fruit, valued for an exceptionally vigorous, deep root system that confers strong resistance to bacterial wilt, fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and root-knot nematodes, all serious soil-borne problems that shorten the productive life of own-root eggplant in warm, humid climates. Grafting a favorite eggplant scion onto this rootstock is a traditional practice in parts of Asia and is gaining adoption among home and market growers in the humid Gulf South seeking longer-lived, more disease-resistant eggplant plants without resorting to soil fumigation or long rotations. Start rootstock seed well ahead of the scion, since germination is slower and less even than standard eggplant, graft when stems are pencil-thick, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy support.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil is workable; sow successions for a steady supply.
directions: Direct sow the corky seed clusters as soon as the soil can be worked, thinning seedlings to three or four inches apart since each cluster yields several plants. This golden beet holds its bright color when cooked and is notably sweet and mild, with less of the earthy flavor of red types. Harvest roots when they reach two to three inches across, and enjoy the nutritious tops as cooked greens.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring and again in late summer; more bolt tolerant than most.
directions: Direct sow seed in cool weather for spring and fall crops, thinning to about four to six inches apart. This miniature variety grows just 5 inches tall and is ready to harvest in as few as 30 days, with thick white stems and glossy dark green leaves. It tolerates warm weather better than most bok choy, but grow it quickly and keep it evenly watered to discourage bolting; its compact size suits containers well.

common_name: Trafalgar Brussels Sprout (Late Mid-Season F1 Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 14-18 weeks before first fall frost; Trafalgar is a late mid-season hybrid that fills the harvest window from mid-November into January, sweetening further with each hard frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors 14-18 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into firm, fertile, well-drained soil and stake the medium-tall stems against wind; top the plants once lower sprouts reach marble size to even out ripening, and harvest from the bottom up as sprouts firm up. Trafalgar is a British-bred F1 hybrid valued for producing abundant, uniformly round, tightly wrapped sprouts with a sweet, low-bitterness flavor that holds up well through a long late-season harvest window running from mid-autumn into the new year. Its intermediate resistance to powdery mildew and reliable, heavy-yielding habit have made it a standard late mid-season choice in UK trial and market gardens, and the sprouts stand well on the stalk without splitting, giving flexibility about exactly when to pick. Choose Trafalgar when the goal is a long stretch of classic, mild-flavored sprouts spanning Thanksgiving through the winter holidays rather than a single early flush.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Traviata is an early, disease-resilient Italian-type eggplant bred by Vitalis Organic Seeds and listed among Cornell's recommended disease-tolerant eggplant varieties, a useful trait for humid Gulf South gardens.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Traviata is an early-maturing, high-yielding Italian-type eggplant hybrid bred for vigor and improved disease resilience, producing a heavy, sustained crop of glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit with few seeds and tender, mild flesh. Its early maturity lets Gulf Coast gardeners get a jump on the harvest before summer disease pressure builds, and the sturdy, well-branched plant continues setting fruit steadily through the season. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, since dull skin signals overripe fruit with more seeds and a bitter edge. Keep soil consistently moist, since eggplant grown under drought stress develops tougher skin and a more bitter flavor.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings 6–8 inches long in moist soil or water; tree collard roots easily from cuttings and is not commonly grown from seed. In zones 9–11 it grows as an evergreen perennial shrub and can be planted and harvested year-round.
directions: Root 6–8 inch stem cuttings from an existing plant in moist compost; tree collard is a long-lived perennial brassica that grows as a woody shrub 4–8 feet tall, producing continuously harvestable blue-green to purple leaves with the same flavor as regular collard greens. Unlike annual collards that must be replanted each season, a single tree collard plant can produce edible leaves for a decade or more. They are propagated only by stem cuttings, never true to seed. In hot climates, tree collards perform best with some afternoon shade. Two main types exist: green-leaved (more vigorous) and purple-leaved (more ornamental). An outstanding plant for permaculture and food forest systems where perennial productivity is valued over annual yields.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings (not seed) taken from established plants. Root cuttings in moist potting mix and transplant in fall for establishment over winter. In zone 9 tree collards grow year-round as a woody perennial shrub, reaching 6–8 feet tall, and produce harvestable leaves every month if watered consistently.
directions: Root stem cuttings 6–8 inches long in moist potting mix or directly in garden soil; tree collards are essentially perennial collards that develop a woody trunk over time and can produce harvestable leaves year-round in mild-winter climates. The purple-leaf variety is the most common and most ornamental, with deep blue-green to purple foliage that intensifies in color after cool weather. Harvest the large lower leaves from the bottom of the plant up, leaving the growing tip intact; consistent harvest keeps plants productive and prevents them from becoming leggy. Unlike annual collards, tree collards do not bolt and can remain productive for 5–10 years with occasional hard pruning to rejuvenate the growth.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; tree spinach self-seeds prolifically and, once introduced to a garden, typically maintains itself as a self-renewing annual — thin seedlings to the desired spacing and harvest thinnings as baby greens.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; tree spinach (magenta spreen, giant goosefoot) is a Himalayan annual of the goosefoot family grown as an ornamental and edible plant — it grows remarkably tall (4–10 feet) for an annual leafy vegetable, producing large, deep-green, arrowhead-shaped leaves that are eaten raw or cooked in exactly the same way as spinach or lamb's quarters, with a mild, pleasant, slightly mineral flavor. The ornamental distinction of the species is the vivid, magenta-pink meal (a waxy powder similar to that on lamb's quarters) that coats the youngest emerging leaves, shoot tips, and stems, creating a strikingly colorful display at the growing tips that fades on older leaves to plain green. The plant self-seeds freely, ensuring persistent garden colonies once established. It grows rapidly, is tolerant of partial shade, is highly nutritious (rich in protein, calcium, and iron, like other Chenopodium species), and provides both an ornamental feature and a productive edible leafy green from a single plant. An underused dual-purpose annual for the edible landscape.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October. Tres Fine is the most finely cut of the frisee endive types, with leaf cutting so delicate it resembles ornamental moss — making it the premium choice for restaurant-quality frisee presentations. In zone 9 fall planting from September transplants produces full heads by November.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Tres Fine (Very Fine) is the most elegantly cut of all frisee endive varieties, producing an open, flat rosette of very finely divided, thread-like, deeply lacinated leaves with a delicate, airy, almost moss-like texture — more finely cut than standard frisee types and considered the premium grade for restaurant use. The characteristic pale yellow to cream heart forms naturally as the outer leaves shade the center; for maximum blanching, loosely tie the outer leaves 10 days before harvest. The very fine leaf cutting makes Tres Fine endive the lightest, most delicate-textured of the endive family in the salad bowl, where it provides a feathery contrast to dense leaves and holds vinaigrette dressings in the finest leaf surfaces. The flavor is gently bitter with a clean, slightly nutty edge. Tres Fine is widely used in French and Italian fine dining as the benchmark frisee for composed salads and the traditional salade lyonnaise.

plant_note: Sow in mid-summer for a fall harvest; in warm climates like zone 9, sow in August–September for harvest from October through December. The variety requires exposure to cool temperatures (below 50°F at night) to trigger the formation of tight, red-veined heads.
directions: Sow seeds in summer for fall harvest, thinning to 10–12 in apart when seedlings are established; Treviso radicchio forms elongated, torpedo-shaped heads with deep red leaves and contrasting white veins, quite different in form from the round Chioggia-type radicchio. Flavor is intensely bitter before cold exposure, then sweetens significantly after several frosts. Some gardeners cut the plant back to 1 inch above the crown after initial growth, then allow it to resprout for tighter, sweeter heads — a technique called 'forcing.' In zone 9, the best crops are grown from September sowing, harvested November through January. The grilled heads, split lengthwise and drizzled with olive oil, are a classic Italian preparation.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; a rare 19th-century Australian heirloom valued for its unmistakable three-lobed shape and exceptionally long storage life.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in enriched, well-drained soil, giving the sprawling vines 6-8 feet of room. Triamble is an Australian heirloom dating to at least the 1820s, named for its distinctive tri-lobed, clover-like shape formed by three fused lobes curving back toward the stem; the tough, slate-blue-grey rind gave rise to its nickname 'Ironbark pumpkin.' Fruits average around 8 pounds and hold sweet, dry, deep-orange flesh similar in quality to Queensland Blue. The hard rind makes Triamble notably difficult to cut but also gives it outstanding keeping quality, with properly cured fruit reported to store for a year or more in a cool, dry space.

plant_note: Start on a heat mat 10–12 weeks before last frost; Trinidad Moruga Scorpion is one of the hottest naturally occurring chiles in the world, measured at 1.2–2.0 million Scoville units — handle with gloves and avoid touching eyes or face; it was certified by the Chile Pepper Institute as the world's hottest pepper in 2012.
directions: Germinate at 85–90°F on a heat mat — germination can take 3–4 weeks for superhot varieties; grow under bright lights and transplant only when nighttime temperatures are consistently above 60°F. Trinidad Moruga Scorpion originated in the Moruga district of Trinidad and was certified by the Chile Pepper Institute at New Mexico State University as the world's hottest pepper in 2012, with an average heat of 1.2 million SHU and individual samples reaching 2 million SHU — making it one of the hottest naturally occurring chile varieties ever measured. The fruits are round to elongated with a characteristic tail or 'stinger,' ripening to red (sometimes yellow or chocolate depending on the phenotype), with intense fruity tropical flavor beneath the extraordinary heat. Widely grown by superhot enthusiasts for hot sauce and extreme culinary use; handle seeds and fruits with nitrile gloves and eye protection.

common_name: Trinidad Perfume Pepper (Heatless Aromatic Habanero-Type Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Trinidad Perfume is a heatless habanero-type pepper prized for the intense fruity, floral, apricot-like aroma and flavor typical of Capsicum chinense peppers, without any of the heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Trinidad Perfume is a heatless selection within the Capsicum chinense species, the same species as habaneros and Scotch bonnets, bred to capture the intensely fruity, floral, almost apricot-and-citrus aroma and flavor characteristic of that species without any of the fiery heat, making it usable in far larger quantities than a true habanero for salsas, sauces, and dishes where habanero flavor is wanted but the heat is not. The wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits look nearly identical to a habanero, ripening from green to orange or red, and can be used fresh, dried, or blended into sauces for a burst of tropical fruit flavor. Plants are productive and grow similarly to other Capsicum chinense peppers, benefiting from a long, warm growing season. Harvest regularly to encourage continued fruit set through the season.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost using bottom heat, as chinense superhots germinate slowly and need a long season.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since germination can be slow and irregular, then transplant into warm, well-drained soil after all frost danger passes. Stake plants and prune early flowers to build a stronger frame before letting the heavy fruit set develop. This is the original Trinidad Scorpion strain from which the later 'Butch T' selection was bred, named for the narrow curled tail at the pod's tip and known for ferocious, lingering heat. Wear gloves when harvesting and processing the ripe red pods.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since Capsicum chinense germinates slowly; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the plants are productive and reasonably compact, doing well in raised beds or large containers. Trinidad Seasoning Pepper is a habanero-relative (Capsicum chinense) grown not for heat but for its intense, distinctively fruity, floral habanero-type aroma without the accompanying pungency — a genetic quirk that produces essentially all of the characteristic C. chinense flavor with almost none of the capsaicin heat. It is a foundational ingredient in Trinidadian and broader Caribbean cooking, where it is blended into 'green seasoning' marinades, curries, and sauces to deliver deep habanero-family flavor that can be used generously without overwhelming heat. The wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, or red depending on the specific strain. An essential, distinctive pepper for gardeners interested in Caribbean cuisine who want the flavor of a habanero without the fire, zone 8–11.

common_name: Triomphe de Farcy Bean (French Haricot Vert Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Triomphe de Farcy is one of the most important French heirloom haricot vert varieties — a fine-podded bush bean with elegant, slender pods featuring distinctive red-violet streaks and speckles on a green background (the markings fade when cooked), harvested at pencil-thin stage for the finest haricot vert quality.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18 inches apart; harvest when pods are 4–5 inches long and pencil-thin for the finest haricot vert quality; pick every 2–3 days to maintain production; the red-violet streaking on raw pods fades to a uniform green when cooked. Triomphe de Farcy is a French heirloom bush bean dating to the 1880s, when it was listed in Vilmorin's famous seed catalog as one of the finest haricots verts — the slender, pencil-thin snap beans of French cuisine that differ fundamentally from the round, plump beans favored in American cooking. The variety is named for its triumphal quality (triomphe = triumph in French) and the Farcy region of Brittany where a similar bean type was cultivated. The pods are distinctive: slender (3/8 inch diameter at most), long (5–7 inches), and marked with beautiful irregular red-violet streaks and flecks on a pale green background — the coloration is reminiscent of a speckled trout and makes raw pods strikingly beautiful in the kitchen; the markings fade completely to solid green when cooked. The flavor is characteristically French haricot vert — tender, fine-grained, buttery, and subtly sweet — quite different from the starchier, coarser texture of standard American snap beans harvested at the same age. Triomphe de Farcy is the bean for gardeners who want authentic French-style haricots verts; harvest young and often, steam or blanch briefly, and serve with good butter.

plant_note: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and set a trellis or poles at planting time, since this vigorous Italian climbing bean quickly reaches six to eight feet.
directions: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and set a trellis or poles at planting time, since this vigorous Italian climbing bean quickly reaches six to eight feet. Long grown in Italian kitchen gardens, Trionfo Violetto is prized for its double ornamental value — deep violet flowers followed by glossy purple pods — as much as for the table, and the pods turn a deep green when cooked, losing their color but keeping excellent flavor and tenderness. Pick pods young and often, around five to six inches, to encourage continued production and to catch them before they toughen. The striking purple pods also make the plants easy to spot for harvest against their green foliage.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; harvest fruit young and often.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, spacing plants for good airflow. This zucchini has an open growing habit on compact bush-type plants with reduced spines, making harvest much easier on the hands. It offers intermediate resistance to zucchini yellow mosaic virus and watermelon mosaic virus; pick the tender fruits young and frequently to keep plants producing.

plant_note: Sow directly in early spring and again in late summer, since it resists bolting better than most soft-leaf lettuces.
directions: Sow directly in early spring and again in late summer, since it resists bolting better than most soft-leaf lettuces and holds quality through warm spells. A French Batavian heirloom dating to the 1880s, Trocadero forms loose, crunchy pale-green heads with a crisp, sweet, faintly nutty flavor reminiscent of iceberg but grown far more easily. It was long grown in French market gardens as a reliable source of crisp texture without the fuss of true crisphead types.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost and provide a trellis or sturdy fence immediately; tromboncino climbs vigorously and produces better-formed, straighter fruits when grown vertically than when sprawling on the ground.
directions: Sow seeds and train the vine up a strong trellis or chain-link fence; tromboncino is an Italian heirloom climbing zucchini with long, curved fruits shaped like a trombone — reaching 20–30 inches when mature — harvested young at 10–15 inches as a summer squash substitute with a nutty, buttery flavor. Being Cucurbita moschata rather than C. pepo, tromboncino has excellent resistance to squash vine borer — the borer does not prefer this species, making it the best choice for gardeners who have lost zucchini crops to this destructive pest. It also tolerates heat and humidity better than most summer squash. Fruits left to mature fully develop into golden winter squash with superb flavor; the seeds are also edible roasted.

plant_note: Eat young as summer squash or mature as winter squash.
directions: This Italian moschata squash produces long curved fruit eaten green like zucchini or ripened tan for winter storage. Direct sow in warm soil and trellis the vigorous climbing vines to save space and keep fruit straight. Harvested young at 8 to 12 inches, the dense flesh has few seeds and resists getting mushy when cooked. Its moschata parentage gives it strong resistance to squash vine borers. Left to ripen fully, the mature fruit stores for months like butternut.

common_name: Tronchuda Cabbage (Portuguese Cabbage, Sea Kale Cabbage)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or start in midsummer for fall harvest 60–75 days before first fall frost; Tronchuda is a traditional Portuguese cabbage/kale that represents an intermediate type between heading cabbage and kale — it produces a loose, open rosette of large, heavily veined, gray-green leaves with prominent white midribs and a mild, sweet, buttery flavor that is considered among the finest brassica vegetables in Iberian cuisine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant 18–24 inches apart in rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil; harvest outer leaves progressively to extend the harvest season; the large white midribs can be cooked separately and have a flavor somewhat resembling chard. Tronchuda (Brassica oleracea var. costata) is a traditional Portuguese vegetable with centuries of cultivation in Portugal, particularly in the Azores and coastal regions of Portugal where it is a staple of Caldo Verde (the famous Portuguese green soup) alongside the more familiar Galician version using curly kale. Tronchuda is classified as a distinct variety of Brassica oleracea that sits between cabbage, kale, and kohlrabi — it produces a large, loose rosette of heavily crinkled, gray-green leaves (not forming a tight head like cabbage) with exceptionally prominent white midribs that can be quite thick and juicy. The flavor is notably sweet and mild compared to other brassica vegetables, with the characteristic savoy/collard family character but more delicate and buttery — considered superior to standard kale for soups and slow-cooked brassica dishes by Portuguese cooks. Tronchuda is cold-hardy, producing some of its finest quality after light frosts, and it can be harvested over an extended season by removing outer leaves while the center continues to produce. Also called 'sea kale cabbage' in some English references (not to be confused with true sea kale, Crambe maritima).

plant_note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant in early spring.
directions: Start Tropea Rossa Tonda seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost and transplant the seedlings 4 to 6 inches apart. This long-day Italian heirloom forms deep rose-red, globe-shaped bulbs with sweet, mild flesh and high sugar content. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and keep the bed weed-free while bulbs size up. Harvest when the tops fall over and cure the bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9–11 this is an outstanding tomato for both spring and fall production — developed specifically for tropical and subtropical climates where standard varieties fail to set fruit in summer heat. In South Florida and the Gulf Coast, Tropic outlasts other varieties well into summer.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Tropic tomato was developed at the University of Florida IFAS and released in 1963 specifically for tropical and subtropical climates — the most durable, disease-resistant open-pollinated tomato for zone 8b–12. It continues setting fruit at temperatures where most tomatoes stop, has resistance to fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and gray leaf spot (the diseases that devastate most tomatoes in South Florida's humid heat), and produces good-sized (6–8 oz), red, globe-shaped fruits with solid, meaty flesh and good flavor from spring well into summer. For Gulf Coast and Florida gardeners who struggle with tomato diseases and summer heat, Tropic remains the benchmark open-pollinated variety after 60 years because no other variety has combined its disease resistance and tropical performance as consistently.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant out after frost and provide sturdy support.
directions: Start seed indoors about six weeks before your last frost and transplant seedlings out once nights stay warm. This indeterminate cherry vine keeps growing all season, so give it a tall stake or trellis and prune as needed. Each ripe 1.5 inch fruit is nearly translucent and golden with orange-to-pink stripes, bright, fruity, and very sweet with a long shelf life; harvest continuously to encourage new fruit set.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in cool weather; sow successions for a steady supply.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in cool weather, since lettuce needs light and cool soil to germinate; make successive sowings for a continuous harvest. This deep-red mini-romaine is compact and easy to grow in small spaces, with uniform, upright leaves that stay clean and are perfect for Caesar salads. It carries disease resistance to downy mildew and lettuce dieback, and part shade helps it hold quality in warmer weather.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Plant in blocks of at least 4 rows for good wind pollination — long single rows pollinate poorly, resulting in incomplete ear fill. In zone 9 plant in spring and again in August for a fall crop. Trucker's Favorite has a broader window between roasting-ear and field-corn stages than modern sweet corn — if roasting-ear harvest is missed, the larger, dough-stage ears can be used for grits and dried cornmeal.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with good air circulation; Trucker's Favorite is an open-pollinated Southern heirloom corn variety that was the standard large-eared roasting corn sold at Southern roadside stands, farmers markets, and farm stands for much of the 20th century — the 'trucker' in the name refers to produce truck farmers who grew it as their preferred selling variety because the large ears (8–10 inches, white to yellow-white kernels) made an impressive and reliably satisfying roasting ear crop. At the roasting-ear stage (about 20 days after silk), the white to cream-colored ears are tender, starchy-sweet, and deeply flavored with the old-fashioned, rich, full corn character that modern hybrid sweet corns bred for extreme sugar content often lack — a more complex, substantial corn flavor similar to mid-century American corn. As a dual-purpose variety, Trucker's Favorite dried to an excellent yellow cornmeal with full corn flavor prized for Southern cornbread, grits, and polenta.

common_name: Truckers Favorite White Corn (Market Garden White Dent Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; Truckers Favorite White is one of the most historically significant Southern market garden corns — grown for over 150 years by market farmers (the 'truckers' who hauled produce to market) for its excellent fresh-eating quality at the roasting ear stage, large white kernels, tall productive plants, and reliable performance in the hot, humid summer conditions of the South.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows for good pollination; thin to 8–12 inches; Truckers Favorite is tall and produces 1–2 ears per stalk; harvest at the milk stage (when kernels exude a milky liquid when punctured) for best fresh-eating quality; allow to dry on the stalk for grinding into grits or cornmeal. Truckers Favorite White Corn is a classic Southern open-pollinated white dent corn that has been grown in the American South since before the Civil War and takes its name from the small-scale produce farmers ('truckers') who grew and hauled vegetables to regional markets throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries — the same context that gave rise to terms like 'truck farming' and 'market gardening.' The variety was selected over generations specifically for the combination of early-maturing roasting ear quality (harvested at the milk stage for fresh eating) and excellent flour/grits quality when allowed to dry fully. The white kernels are large and doughy at the roasting ear stage, sweet enough for fresh eating but not as sugary as modern sweet corn varieties — the characteristic semi-sweet, starchy quality that old-fashioned cornbread and grits recipes were designed around. In the Gulf South, Truckers Favorite White is particularly valued as a heritage Southern cornbread corn — ground into coarse grits or fine meal, it produces the authentic white stone-ground cornmeal preferred in traditional Southern cooking. Plants are tall (7–9 feet), productive, and heat tolerant, maturing in the relatively modest time of 85–95 days that suits the Gulf Coast growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; plant in blocks for good pollination.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after frost, planting in blocks of at least four short rows rather than one long row to ensure good wind pollination. This old-fashioned sugary (su) corn produces large 9 inch ears that are very sweet and tender. The plants resist stalk-lodging and are less likely to bend or kink in windy areas; keep them well watered and harvest at the milk stage for peak sweetness.

common_name: True Red Cranberry Bean (Heirloom Speckled Shell Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed; pole plants need a sturdy trellis. Pick at the shell stage around 65 days or let pods dry fully for storage beans around 90–100 days.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis, since this is a vigorous climbing variety. True Red Cranberry is a New England heirloom dating to the 1700s, producing plump, cream-colored pods streaked in deep red-maroon that shell out to reveal beans mottled in burgundy and cream, cooking up to a rich, nutty flavor and creamy texture prized for baked beans and soups. Pick pods at the shell-bean stage for the best flavor and texture, or leave them to dry fully on the vine for long-term storage as a dry bean.
