It is more heat-tolerant than most Asian brassicas and can extend into early summer in zone 9 before bolting. Successive sowings every 2 weeks provide a continuous harvest of tender young greens.
directions: Direct sow thinly in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Vitamin Green is a non-heading Asian brassica green selected for extremely rapid growth, mild flavor, and excellent nutritional value — the name reflects its high vitamin content (particularly vitamins A, C, and K) relative to other leafy greens. The smooth, round to slightly oval, bright medium-green leaves are strikingly mild in flavor — among the mildest of all Asian brassica types, with a clean, grassy-vegetable taste more like spinach or mild bok choy than the mustardy pungency of standard Asian mustard greens. This mildness makes Vitamin Green accessible to people who find other Asian greens too strongly flavored. In the kitchen it is interchangeable with bok choy or baby spinach in virtually any preparation — stir-fries, soups, braising, steaming, and raw use in salads and baby green mixes. The combination of very rapid growth (30–45 days to full size, 20–25 days to baby green stage), mild flavor, and excellent nutritional content makes it one of the most practical cool-season greens for zone 9.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after last frost; also does well as a late-summer planting timed to mature in cool fall weather.
directions: Vitaverde produces a pale apple-green curd with the domed, tightly beaded texture of a classic cauliflower rather than the looser florets of broccoli, giving it a hybrid appearance often marketed as broccoflower. The lime-green color comes from chlorophyll in the curd tissue and carries a milder, slightly sweeter flavor than white cauliflower with no need for blanching or leaf-tying. It holds its curd quality in the field longer than many white types before the curd begins to open or discolor, giving a wider harvest window. Grow Vitaverde for a striking, easy-care alternative to white cauliflower that performs reliably without extra fussing.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces after soil has warmed slightly; Vitelotte Noire is a French heirloom fingerling with deep purple skin and flesh, also called 'Truffe de Chine.'
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil; as a late-maturing fingerling it needs a full season to size up its knobby tubers. Vitelotte Noire is a classic French heirloom potato with deep purple skin and equally deep purple flesh throughout, nicknamed 'Truffe de Chine' (Chinese truffle) for its dark, irregular tuber shape, and prized by chefs for the striking color it brings to gratins, chips, and purées without losing much pigment when cooked. Its dense, nutty flavor and firm texture hold up well in roasted and sautéed preparations. Harvest once foliage yellows and dies back, and cure tubers in a cool, dark spot before storage.

common_name: Viva Italia Tomato (Hybrid Roma Paste Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Viva Italia is a determinate paste tomato that ripens a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for sauce-making; in zone 9 aim for spring harvest in May–June before summer heat.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Viva Italia is an improved hybrid roma-type paste tomato that addresses the main weakness of heirloom Roma — its susceptibility to disease. An AAS (All-America Selections) winner, Viva Italia combines the thick-walled, low-moisture flesh and rich, concentrated paste-tomato flavor of traditional Roma with VFFNTA disease resistance (Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and Alternaria), making it far more reliable in humid climates and typical garden soils than open-pollinated Roma varieties. The determinate, compact (3–3.5 foot) plants produce large, concentrated sets of uniform, thick-skinned, 2–4 oz, elongated-oval, bright red fruits with very low moisture content and dense, meaty flesh — exactly what's needed for sauce, paste, sun-dried tomatoes, and canning. Because of the dense flesh and concentrated flavor, Viva Italia produces much higher yields of usable sauce per pound of fruit than wet, beefsteak-type tomatoes. An outstanding choice for serious sauce-makers who want disease resistance and reliability.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; IMPORTANT: Install a high-density polyethylene rhizome barrier (30 mil or thicker) at least 24–36 inches deep around all running bamboos before planting to prevent invasive spreading.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, contained within a rhizome barrier; vivax bamboo is one of the tallest, fastest-growing temperate bamboos, with culms reaching 25–45 feet and diameters of 2–3.5 inches — making it among the most productive timber bamboos available in zones 5–10. The spring shoots are edible and moderately sweet; the culms are strong and used for construction, fencing, and crafts. Its extreme cold hardiness (to about –10°F / USDA zone 5) makes it one of the few large-statured bamboos reliable in cold climates. CAUTION: Like all Phyllostachys species, vivax is a spreading 'running' bamboo with invasive potential — rhizome barriers are mandatory in all garden settings. The cultivar 'Aureocaulis' has yellow culms with green stripes.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in cool weather; bolt resistant for later sowing.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in cool weather, keeping the soil moist and cool for good germination, and make succession sowings for continuous salads. This emerald-green romaine forms tight heads that reach a striking 12 to 16 inches tall and 4 to 6 inches across, giving large, sturdy leaves ideal for salads and lettuce wraps. Its bolt resistance and vigorous growth let it hold longer into warm weather than many romaines.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. The deep purple-blue exterior color of Vorlon develops most intensely with sun exposure on the skin — fruits shaded by foliage will be less colorful. In zone 9 fall planting in August for October–November harvest often produces the best fruit quality. Support with cages or stakes as the large, indeterminate vines require substantial support.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy cage or stake support; Vorlon is a large beefsteak tomato bred by Tom Wagner, the Washington State plant breeder also responsible for Green Zebra, known for developing novel tomato colors and flavors. Vorlon produces large (often 12–20 ounce) fruits with a distinctive deep purple-to-near-black exterior that develops from sun exposure on the skin — the dark color comes from anthocyanin pigments (the same blue-purple compounds in blueberries and purple cabbage) that accumulate in the skin when exposed to sunlight. When sliced, Vorlon reveals a complex interior with dark-streaked red flesh and a rich, full-bodied, complex tomato flavor with earthy, wine-like undertones that distinguish dark tomato varieties from standard red types. The anthocyanin content in dark tomatoes like Vorlon represents significantly higher antioxidant levels than red-only tomatoes — a characteristic that has made dark-skinned tomatoes of interest in nutritional research. The dramatic appearance of the purple-black exterior with rich red interior when sliced makes Vorlon outstanding in salads and fresh presentations.

common_name: Vulcan Swiss Chard (Brilliant Red-Stemmed French Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date and thin seedlings once established; plants tolerate light frost in fall.
directions: Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin seedlings to their final spacing, watering consistently to keep stalks tender and prevent bitterness. This French heirloom is grown chiefly for its glossy, deep crimson stalks and veins that hold their vivid color even after cooking, contrasting with dark green, slightly savoyed leaves. It is a dependable cut-and-come-again green that keeps producing new leaves from the crown for months.

plant_note: Give plants more room than standard mizuna since Waido forms noticeably larger, more upright rosettes; also suited to a late-summer sowing for fall harvest.
directions: Waido, meaning wide leaf in Japanese, is a larger-statured mizuna selection bred for bunching markets, with broader, less deeply cut leaves than standard mizuna and thicker, crisp petioles. Direct sow into fertile soil and keep evenly moist to encourage tender, mild-flavored growth. Whole heads can be cut for bunching or leaves picked individually for stir-fries and hot pot greens. Cold-hardy and slow to bolt compared to smaller mizuna types, making it a good choice for extended fall harvest.

plant_note: Plant divided bulb clusters in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wakegi onion is a sterile hybrid grown only from bulb divisions, never from seed, and multiplies quickly into a clump that can be split every year.
directions: Plant divided bulb clusters in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wakegi onion is a sterile hybrid grown only from bulb divisions, never from seed, and multiplies quickly into a clump that can be split every year. A traditional Japanese hybrid between bulb onion and bunching onion, it produces slender, mild-flavored, scallion-like stalks from a clustering base of small bulbs, combining the easy perennial habit of a bunching onion with a slightly stronger, more onion-like flavor. Harvest by pulling whole young stalks as needed through fall, winter, and spring in mild climates, leaving several bulbs in place to keep the clump multiplying, or dig and divide the whole clump every one to two years to maintain vigor and share starts. It is far less prone to bolting than seed-grown bunching onions and provides a reliable, low-effort source of fresh green onions for most of the year.

common_name: Walking Stick Cabbage (Jersey Cabbage, Jersey Kale)
plant_note: Direct sow or start transplants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Walking Stick Cabbage is grown over a long season to develop its tall, thick stalk, so give it a permanent, undisturbed spot for the better part of a year.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking young plants in windy sites and stripping lower leaves as they yellow to encourage the tall, straight stalk this heirloom is famous for. Walking Stick Cabbage, also called Jersey cabbage or Jersey kale, is a historic giant kale from the Channel Islands traditionally grown for two purposes at once: the young leaves are edible and used as livestock fodder or cooked greens, while the plant is left to grow over a full season into a remarkably tall, woody stalk that was traditionally dried, straightened, and varnished into walking sticks and canes, a cottage tradition dating back centuries on Jersey. In the vegetable garden it makes an unusual, dramatic vertical accent as well as a productive source of greens over many months, tolerating poor soil and coastal conditions well. Harvest lower leaves continuously through the growing season for eating, and let a stalk mature untouched at season's end if canes are wanted.

common_name: Walking Stick Collard (Tall Perennial Heirloom Collard from the Carolina and Gulf South Tradition)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, start seeds in August for September transplanting ahead of fall. Walking Stick Collard is a truly perennial (or at minimum biennial) collard that develops an upright, thick stem over multiple years of growth — eventually reaching 4–8 feet in height with a distinctive woody stem that in the South was historically harvested for use as a walking stick, giving the variety its name. Unlike annual collard varieties grown as single-season crops, Walking Stick Collard can remain productive for 2–5 years in zone 9's mild winters, producing new growth from the upper portion of the plant as it elongates. Individual leaves are harvested from the lower portion of the stem as new growth continues from the top. In zone 9, the plants perform well through winter (tolerating multiple frosts and brief freezes) and may slow in summer heat but rarely die entirely, giving them a distinctly perennial character that sets them apart from annual collard varieties. Space widely (24–36 inches) to allow each plant to develop its multi-year structure.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant to permanent location and allow to develop over multiple seasons. Harvest outer lower leaves as needed year-round. Walking Stick Collard is one of the most historically distinctive vegetables of the American South — a tall, perennial collard type that was maintained for generations in family gardens across the Carolinas, Georgia, and the Gulf South as a semi-permanent garden plant rather than an annual crop. The 'walking stick' in the name refers to the thick, woody stems that develop as the plant grows upward over multiple years: historical accounts describe Southern farmers and homesteaders harvesting old Walking Stick Collard stems, drying them, and using them as walking sticks, canes, and tool handles — a practical byproduct of a plant grown primarily for its edible leaves. The leaves are classic collard — large, blue-green, thick, and of the rich, mild-bitter flavor that defines Southern greens cuisine — harvested continuously from the lower stem as the plant elongates upward. A well-established Walking Stick Collard plant can produce leaves continuously for 3–5 years in zone 9's mild climate, making it a true perennial food plant for gardens where winter rarely kills brassicas completely. The variety is maintained by seed savers and small heirloom seed companies as a Southern heritage vegetable; it is not available in commercial mass-market seed catalogs but has been preserved through the living tradition of Southern kitchen gardens and organizations like Seed Savers Exchange and Southern Exposure Seed Exchange. Walking Stick Collard's extraordinary height (sometimes reaching 6–8 feet) and its multi-year productive life make it one of the most distinctive and visually arresting vegetables possible in zone 9 gardens, forming a structural element with year-round productivity that no annual collard variety can match.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; walking stick kale is biennial, producing a thick, very tall central stem in its second year that can reach 6–10 feet — the dried stems were traditionally harvested in the Channel Islands and Cornwall for use as walking sticks and umbrella handles.
directions: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost, transplant after last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; walking stick kale (Jersey kale) is a traditional biennial brassica of the Channel Islands and Cornwall, where it was grown for the extraordinary height its main stem achieves in the second year — up to 6–10 feet tall — with stems so strong and straight that they were traditionally dried, lacquered, and sold as walking sticks, canes, and umbrella handles, a traditional cottage industry on the Isle of Jersey. The large, dark green, curled leaves produced at the top of the tall stem are edible (though tough) throughout the growing season, and the plant is also fed to livestock. Primarily a curiosity and heritage vegetable today, prized by collectors of unusual brassicas. Requires staking as it grows taller. Harvest leaves from the base upward as needed, leaving the growing tip intact for continued height.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; wall rocket tolerates light freezes without damage and is best as a spring or autumn crop. It self-seeds so freely that once established in a garden it rarely needs replanting.
directions: Broadcast seeds lightly over prepared soil and press in gently without covering, as the tiny seeds need light to germinate well; thin to 4-6 inches apart once seedlings are established and harvest the outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production. Wall rocket is a wilder, more pungent relative of common arugula, with deeply lobed, almost dandelion-like leaves that carry a sharper, more sulfurous edge and pair especially well with cured meats, strong cheeses, and dressed lentils. It thrives in poor, dry, even gravelly soils where most salad greens would fail, making it useful for difficult spots in the garden. Allow a few plants to flower and set seed each season and they will self-sow prolifically, often producing volunteers in cracks in paving, at wall bases, and in disturbed soil across the garden.

plant_note: Start indoors or overwinter in mild areas; a long-day type that matures early.
directions: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant out once the soil is workable, or sow in fall to overwinter in mild-winter regions. This famous long-day onion traveled from Italy to Walla Walla, Washington, and produces enormous, juicy, sweet bulbs that are one of the best for eating fresh. It matures early enough to grow as an intermediate-day type; these sweet onions do not store long, so enjoy them soon after harvest.

plant_note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant in early spring.
directions: Start Walla Walla seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost and transplant seedlings 4 to 6 inches apart. This long-day heirloom produces exceptionally sweet, crisp, juicy yellow bulbs and performs best in northern gardens. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and keep the bed weeded while the large bulbs form. These onions are sweet but do not store long, so use them fresh soon after the tops fall and dry.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Walter is an outstanding spring and fall tomato with excellent disease resistance for humid Gulf Coast conditions. Determinate habit means a concentrated, predictable harvest good for canning large batches.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set determinate plants 2–3 feet apart in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Walter tomato was released by the University of Florida in 1963, the same year as Tropic, and quickly became a commercial and home garden staple in the Southeast for its reliable production, disease resistance, and compact determinate growth habit. It produces medium-large (6–8 oz), red, round fruits with smooth skin, firm flesh, and good canning and fresh-eating quality, with resistance to fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot. Walter's determinate habit (which concentrates flowering and ripening into a defined period rather than producing continuously like indeterminate types) makes it efficient for gardeners who want a single large harvest for preserving and canning. Once the standard commercial processing tomato in Florida, it remains an important heirloom for Gulf Coast gardeners who need a reliably productive, disease-resistant, compact-season tomato.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or sow in midsummer for a fall crop; Waltham 29 is a classic American open-pollinated broccoli developed by the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1954 — long the standard garden broccoli before modern hybrids and still prized for heat tolerance, blue-green color, and reliable production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after hardening off when temperatures are consistently below 80°F during the day. Waltham 29 broccoli was developed by the Waltham Field Station of the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1954 as an improvement over earlier open-pollinated varieties; for decades before hybrid broccoli varieties became dominant in the 1970s and 80s, Waltham 29 was the standard home garden and market broccoli. It produces a large, domed, blue-green to grey-green central head of excellent flavor and tight bead formation, followed by adequate sideshot production; it is notably more tolerant of fall frost than many varieties and holds well in the field without yellowing. Still widely grown for its reliable open-pollinated nature (seed-saveable), cold tolerance, and classic blue-green broccoli flavor. Excellent for fall production in zones 5–11.

plant_note: Start for a fall crop, or in early spring for a spring harvest.
directions: Start Waltham 29 seeds indoors 5 to 6 weeks before transplanting, setting plants 18 to 24 inches apart in rich soil. This cold-tolerant heirloom is bred for fall harvests, producing large blue-green central heads followed by side shoots. Keep the plants well watered and feed with nitrogen to encourage big, tight heads. Cut the central head while the buds are still firm and closed, then keep harvesting the smaller side shoots for weeks.

plant_note: Start indoors for spring, or sow in summer for a fall crop; adapted to fall.
directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. This heirloom is specially adapted to fall growing and produces 4 to 6 inch blue-green central heads followed by a prolific flush of side shoots. Cut the central head while the buds are still tight, then keep harvesting the smaller side shoots for weeks; the plants tolerate frost well.

common_name: Waltham Butternut Squash (Classic Long-Storing Winter Squash Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer (July in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for a fall harvest; Waltham Butternut is a Cucurbita moschata variety with better heat and humidity tolerance than pepo-type winter squash — an important practical advantage for Gulf South production.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Waltham Butternut is the standard commercial and home garden butternut squash — developed by Robert Young at the Waltham Experiment Station in Massachusetts and recognized with an All-America Selections award for its exceptional production, uniformity, and storage quality. The classic cylindrical fruits with tan skin, small seed cavity, and large neck of deep-orange flesh represent the butternut ideal: consistent shape, excellent flavor, and long storage life (3–6 months at cool room temperature). The Cucurbita moschata species provides better heat and humidity tolerance than C. pepo winter squash types — allowing Waltham Butternut to succeed in Gulf South conditions where pepo types (acorn, Delicata) often struggle with disease and heat in late-season production. In zone 9, the most reliable production method is a late-summer planting (July–August direct sow) for a fall harvest (October–November) — the fall planting avoids peak summer heat during vulnerable early growth and produces during the cooler fall weather that improves storage quality. Cure harvested fruits for 10 days at 80–85°F to harden the skin and develop the characteristic butterscotch sweetness that distinguishes fully cured butternut from freshly harvested green fruit. Waltham Butternut vines spread extensively (6–10 feet) and require substantial garden space.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; give vines plenty of space to run.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the long vines room to spread. This classic butternut yields four to five tan, richly sweet fruits per plant, and its solid stems help resist squash vine borers. Let the squash mature fully to a hard rind and cure it in a warm, dry spot; properly cured butternut stores for months and is excellent roasted, baked, or pureed into soup.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–6 weeks before last frost in spring or in fall 8–10 weeks before first frost; Wando is the most heat-tolerant commonly available shelling pea, developed by USDA for Southern gardens — it sets pods in warmer conditions that cause bloom drop in all other pea varieties, making it the recommended choice for Gulf Coast and Southern spring pea planting.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep 2–6 weeks before last frost; Wando tolerates both cool and moderately warm conditions and is particularly valuable for later-season spring planting in Southern zones. Wando pea was developed by USDA and named for the Wando River in the Charleston, South Carolina area, reflecting its adaptation to warm Southern conditions. Unlike most shelling peas that drop flowers and fail to set pods when temperatures rise above 75°F, Wando continues producing pods at temperatures 5–10°F warmer than other varieties, extending the harvest window in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens. The 24–30 inch plants produce smooth-seeded peas (less sweet than wrinkled but better adapted to warm-soil planting) in pods with 6–8 peas; the flavor is good. Exceptionally valuable for fall pea production in zones 7–10 when planted in late August–September.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked; more heat tolerant than most peas.
directions: Direct sow seed as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, since peas germinate and grow best in cool soil. Introduced in 1943 as a cross between Laxton's Progress and Perfection, this heirloom is both cold tolerant for early sowing and more heat tolerant than most peas, extending the season on both ends. The sturdy 24 to 30 inch plants carry seven to nine medium peas per pod; provide light support and pick regularly to keep them producing.

common_name: Wapsie Valley Corn (Iowa Heirloom Dent-Flint Corn)
plant_note: Sow in blocks of at least four rows in average garden soil; forgiving for gardeners outside the traditional Corn Belt.
directions: Sow in blocks of at least four rows in average garden soil; its relatively short season and dent-flint hybrid vigor make it forgiving for gardeners outside the traditional Corn Belt. Wapsie Valley is an Iowa heirloom named for the Wapsipinicon River valley and preserved by Sand Hill Preservation Farm, combining dent and flint characteristics in the same ears along with striking orange, red, and multicolor kernels. It is valued both for its ornamental appeal on the stalk and for producing flavorful cornmeal, and it has become a favorite among small-scale growers seeking a productive, easy-to-grow open-pollinated corn with real regional history.

common_name: Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato (Iowa Heirloom Peach-Yellow Sweet Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Wapsipinicon Peach is an indeterminate open-pollinated cherry tomato producing 1–1.5-inch round fruits with a distinctive pale peach-yellow color and a slightly fuzzy-looking surface texture that inspired the 'peach' descriptor. Named for the Wapsipinicon River in northeastern Iowa where it originated, this variety has been maintained by seed-savers as an example of mid-American heirloom tomato diversity. In zone 9, transplant March–April and stake or cage to 6 feet; indeterminate growth continues until frost. The pale coloration indicates low lycopene (the pigment responsible for red color) and high carotenoid content of a different type, contributing to the notably sweet, low-acid flavor profile that has made this variety a favorite among cherry tomato enthusiasts seeking flavor over color.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake or cage to 6 feet. Harvest when fruits yield gently to pressure and separate easily from the calyx. Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato is an Iowa heritage cherry tomato distinguished by its pale peach-yellow coloration and the exceptionally sweet, low-acid flavor that develops as fruits ripen fully. The name refers to both the peach-like appearance of the ripe fruit (the pale skin with a subtle blushed tinge on the sunny side closely resembles a small yellow peach) and the Wapsipinicon River region of northeastern Iowa where the variety was grown and saved by farm families through the twentieth century. The variety reached national seed-saver networks through the Seed Savers Exchange network and has been grown in trial gardens across the country where it consistently earns high marks for flavor complexity — a balance of sweetness with sufficient acid to provide depth, rather than the flat sweetness of some low-acid cherry types. As an indeterminate variety, Wapsipinicon Peach continues to grow and produce throughout a long warm season, which is particularly advantageous in zone 9 where the long frost-free period extends production well into fall. Fruits cluster in modest-sized trusses and are best harvested when fully colored and just soft; they have a thinner skin than many modern cherry types, which is prized for fresh eating but means they are more susceptible to cracking after rain or irrigation following dry periods. Cage or stake firmly and prune suckers selectively to manage plant size and improve air circulation in humid conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; cold hardy and can overwinter in many areas.
directions: Direct sow seed in spring for summer harvests, thinning to about an inch apart, or leave clumps to overwinter. This 2016 All-America Selections winner is a cold-hardy bunching onion with crisp texture and a strong, pungent flavor, and it resists pink root rot. Harvest by pulling whole clusters of upright green stalks, or cut individual stems and let the plants regrow for repeated cut-and-come-again picking.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, deeply amended soil; needs a long season of 100–115 days; this is the classic 'True Hubbard' type with heavily warted, dark blue-green skin and exceptional 6-month storage life.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, in hills enriched with compost, spacing 5–7 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill and provide consistent moisture through the long growing season. True Hubbard is the heavily warted, dark blue-green Hubbard squash that was a staple of 19th-century New England kitchens; fruits weigh 10–20 pounds and have extremely hard, deeply ribbed and warted blue-green skin and dense, dry, bright orange flesh with outstanding sweet, nutty flavor. The exceptional storage quality — fruits in good condition can last 6 months or more at cool temperatures — made it the premier cellar squash before canning became widespread. Harvest only after the vine has fully died back and the rind cannot be dented with a thumbnail; cure for 2 weeks in a warm, airy spot before moving to cold storage.

common_name: Warty Goblin Pumpkin (F1 Warted Novelty Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; a novelty hybrid grown for its heavily warted rind rather than eating quality, popular for spooky fall displays.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, giving vines 6 feet of room to sprawl. Warty Goblin is a novelty hybrid pumpkin bred purely for eerie ornamental appeal, producing 8-20 pound fruit with a hard orange rind studded in dense, gnarled green warts that persist for weeks after harvest before slowly fading. The plants show useful intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, helping the vines stay productive later into the season than many older open-pollinated types. Because the flesh is stringy and thin compared to culinary pumpkins, Warty Goblin is grown strictly for Halloween decorating rather than cooking; harvest once the rind has fully hardened and cure briefly before display.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in cool, constantly moist, highly oxygenated, slightly acidic to neutral, rich soil in partial to full shade; wasabi requires temperatures between 46–70°F and is extremely temperature-sensitive — it will not survive zone 9 summers without deep shade, cooling irrigation, and careful microclimate management.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, cool, well-oxygenated, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial to full shade; wasabi is one of the most challenging and rewarding edible plants a gardener can grow, requiring very cool temperatures (46–70°F) and near-constant moisture. In Japan it grows along cold mountain streams in deep shade where water temperature remains near 55°F year-round. The thick rhizome (the 'root') takes 12–18 months to reach harvest size, grated fresh at the table in a circular motion on a sharkskin grater to produce the intensely pungent, clean-heat paste. The authentic flavor is entirely different from the horseradish-and-dye paste sold as 'wasabi' in most restaurants. In zone 7–8, wasabi can be grown in a deeply shaded, cool, constantly moist garden bed or container with refrigerated-water irrigation; in zone 9 it requires careful site selection, mulching to keep roots cool, and may struggle in summer heat. The large, heart-shaped leaves are also edible and pungent.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wasabi arugula bolts and turns fiery hot quickly in summer heat, so plan for cool-season harvest and succession sow every two to three weeks.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wasabi arugula bolts and turns fiery hot quickly in summer heat, so plan for cool-season harvest and succession sow every two to three weeks. This selection of salad arugula is bred for an intense, sinus-clearing heat reminiscent of true wasabi, with deeply lobed, dark green leaves that pack noticeably more pungency than standard arugula, especially as plants mature or experience heat or drought stress. Harvest young leaves for a milder bite in mixed salads, or let plants grow larger for a bold, spicy addition to sandwiches and cooked greens where its heat mellows somewhat with cooking. Partial shade in warm climates helps delay bolting and keeps the intense flavor from becoming overwhelming; keep soil consistently moist to slow premature flowering.

plant_note: Best harvested young as a baby-leaf salad green; the horseradish-like bite intensifies as leaves mature and in warmer weather.
directions: Wasabina is a mizuna-type mustard green selected for a sharp, wasabi-like bite that adds punch to salad mixes without needing actual wasabi root. Direct sow shallowly into rich soil and grow as a cut-and-come-again crop, snipping the glossy, deeply serrated leaves at baby size for the mildest, most versatile flavor. It thrives in cool spring and fall conditions and tends to bolt in summer heat, so succession sow every few weeks for continuous harvest. Use sparingly as a spicy accent in mesclun mixes, sandwiches, or sushi-style garnishes.

common_name: Water Caltrop (Bat Nut, Water Chestnut of Europe)
plant_note: Drop nuts into still, shallow water (1–6 feet deep) after last frost; water caltrop is invasive in many US states and banned in several — check local regulations before planting; grow only in contained garden ponds where escape into natural waterways is prevented.
directions: Place fresh nuts in shallow, still water in full sun after last frost; water caltrop is a floating aquatic annual with attractive diamond-shaped floating leaves and distinctive 4-horned nut fruits (resembling a bat or medieval caltrop weapon) that have been consumed in Asia and Europe since the Neolithic period. The large starchy nuts are boiled, roasted, or eaten raw and have a pleasant chestnut-like flavor; they are still commonly sold in Chinese, Japanese, and South Asian markets. Listed as invasive in many US states due to rapid spread and choking of natural waterways — only cultivate in well-contained, sealed garden ponds from which fruits are thoroughly collected to prevent seed escape. Historically important in China, where it is among the most ancient cultivated aquatic crops.

plant_note: Plant sprouted corms 2–4 weeks after last frost once water temperatures exceed 60°F in a container or shallow pond.
directions: Sprout small corms in a tray of moist soil indoors a few weeks before transplanting; plant sprouted corms 1–2 inches deep in the mud bottom of containers, tubs, or shallow water features kept filled to 2–4 inches above the soil surface. Water chestnuts are tropical grass-like sedges grown for their crunchy, sweet corms that form in the mud at the base of the rush-like stems. Drain the growing container in early fall before frost and allow the foliage to die back completely, then harvest corms by sifting through the mud; the crisp, mild corms can be eaten raw or cooked and retain their crunch even after stir-frying. In frost-prone climates store harvested corms in moist sand in a cool (40°F) location and re-plant the following spring.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings floated in water or planted in wet soil; water mimosa requires warm, shallow, still or slow-moving water or consistently wet mud in full sun. Zone 9-12 only; potentially invasive in Florida and Hawaii where it escapes waterways.
directions: Root stem cuttings in shallow water or wet mud in full sun; water mimosa (Neptunia oleracea) is an aquatic legume of tropical Asia, Africa, and the Americas, floating on the surface of ponds, ditches, and slow-moving water with spongy, air-filled white stems that provide buoyancy. The young shoots, leaves, and flower buds are widely eaten as a vegetable in Thai, Vietnamese, and Southeast Asian cuisine — blanched or stir-fried with a mild, crisp texture and slightly mucilaginous character similar to water spinach. The leaves also fold up when touched, like the related sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica). Caution: it is listed as invasive in Florida and should be grown only in contained water features in that state; elsewhere it is an interesting aquatic edible for warm-climate water gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow seed or plant stem cuttings after the last frost in rich, moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; water spinach grows extremely rapidly in heat and humidity and prefers consistently moist to wet conditions — it can be grown in shallow water up to 6 inches deep. Note: cultivation is federally restricted in the US due to invasive potential — check local regulations before growing.
directions: Direct sow or root stem cuttings after frost in rich, moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; water spinach (kangkong in Filipino/Malaysian, rau muống in Vietnamese, ong choy in Cantonese) is one of the most important leafy green vegetables in Southeast, South, and East Asian cuisines, prized for its mild flavor, tender texture, and extremely rapid growth in warm, humid weather — it can be harvested in as little as 30 days from planting and can produce multiple harvests per season. The hollow stems and young leaf tips are stir-fried in garlic and oyster sauce in countless Southeast Asian dishes. It grows prolifically in the heat and humidity of zone 9–12 and is one of the most productive warm-season greens available. Important regulatory note: Ipomoea aquatica is classified as a federal noxious weed in the US and cultivation may require a state permit in some states — verify local regulations before growing. In Florida and other Gulf states it should be grown in contained beds well away from natural waterways.

plant_note: Sow in cool, wet conditions 2–4 weeks before last frost; can also be started from cuttings rooted in water.
directions: Sow seed on the surface of consistently moist, fertile soil near a stream, pond edge, or other reliably wet site; watercress requires more water than almost any other salad green. In garden beds without standing water, water deeply every day and mulch heavily to retain moisture. Harvest stem tips of 4–6 in regularly to encourage bushy growth; the plant becomes bitter and coarse after flowering. Succession plantings from rooted stem cuttings placed in shallow water provide a continuous supply through the cool season.

common_name: Waterleaf (Gbure, West African Talinum Leaf Vegetable)
plant_note: Direct sow or set out rooted cuttings once soil is warm and all frost danger has passed; waterleaf thrives in hot, humid conditions and grows fastest during the peak of Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Sow seed shallowly or root stem cuttings directly in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade, keeping the bed consistently damp since this succulent-leaved green wilts quickly in dry conditions. Waterleaf, known as gbure in Yoruba and grown widely across West Africa, is a fast-growing, heat-loving leafy green with thick, glossy, mildly mucilaginous leaves used much like spinach in soups and stews, most famously in Nigerian edikang ikong soup. The plant grows as a spreading, succulent-stemmed perennial in frost-free climates but is easily grown as a warm-season annual elsewhere, tolerating both the intense heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer that stresses many temperate greens. Harvest by pinching young stem tips and leaves regularly, which encourages new branching and keeps a steady supply of tender growth; plants regrow quickly after cutting.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring after soil warms in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; waterleaf is a fast-growing tropical leafy vegetable that thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers and can be harvested as a cut-and-come-again crop from 30 days.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in warm soil in full sun to part shade in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production. Talinum fruticosum (waterleaf, Philippine spinach, or Lagos spinach) is a widespread tropical leafy vegetable native to South America but naturalized and cultivated throughout the tropics of Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean — it is one of the most important leafy green vegetables in West African cuisines (especially Nigerian cooking, where it is called 'waterleaf' or 'gbure') and is increasingly grown in Southeast Asian communities across the United States. The thick, succulent, slightly mucilaginous leaves are highly nutritious (rich in protein, iron, calcium, and vitamins) and are cooked in soups, stews, and stir-fries much like spinach — they have a mild, pleasant flavor that intensifies slightly when cooked. The plant produces cheerful, tiny, bright-pink, five-petaled flowers continuously through the growing season. It is extremely heat-tolerant and productive during Gulf Coast summers when cool-season greens have long expired, filling the important summer greens gap in zone 9 gardens. Self-seeds readily in warm climates.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–3 weeks after last frost once soil temperature reaches at least 70°F; or start indoors 2–3 weeks early.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, sandy loam hills with generous compost worked in; watermelons thrive with long, hot summers. Avoid overhead irrigation once fruits are sizing up, as uneven moisture causes cracking. Ripeness indicators include a dull surface sheen replacing the glossy skin, a cream or yellow ground spot on the underside, and a dry tendril nearest the fruit. Thump the fruit and listen for a deep, hollow resonance to confirm ripeness.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Watermelon radish performs best in cool fall weather — the pink interior color is more vivid and the flavor milder in fall-grown roots than spring plantings. In zone 9 the fall planting (September–November) produces the finest quality. The large roots (2–4 inches diameter) require 60–70 days — significantly longer than small spring radishes — and develop best in cool soil with consistent moisture. Thin to 4–5 inches apart.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of rocks and compaction; Watermelon Radish is a Chinese heirloom daikon-type radish producing large (golf ball to small apple sized), round roots with an unremarkable white-green exterior that opens to reveal a dramatically vivid magenta-pink interior — when sliced crosswise the cross-section closely resembles a miniature watermelon, with the pale green rind and pink-red interior creating the watermelon pattern that gives this radish its common name. The visual reveal of slicing a Watermelon Radish is one of the most surprising in the vegetable garden — the dramatic interior color makes it the most visually striking vegetable for salads, garnishes, and decorative vegetable presentations. The flavor is milder, sweeter, and less pungent than small red radishes, with only moderate spiciness and a crisp, juicy texture. The large size provides substantial raw radish slices for salads, vegetable platters, and pickled preparations. Fall-grown roots develop the most vivid pink color.

plant_note: Sow 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for the sweetest, most vibrant roots; spring plantings are possible but fall is strongly preferred.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in loose, deeply prepared, stone-free soil in late summer or early fall; thin seedlings to 4–6 inches for proper root development. Watermelon radish is a Chinese heirloom daikon type with a pale green exterior that conceals a vivid magenta-to-pink interior resembling watermelon flesh. Fall planting is strongly preferred over spring — cool nights concentrate sugars and deepen the interior color while reducing pungency. Harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter; slice thinly for salads, pickle in rice vinegar, or roast where the color intensifies to brilliant crimson.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wax rose pereskia is shade-tolerant for a cactus and grows naturally in humid tropical forests. In zone 9, grow as a container plant moved indoors in winter or in frost-protected positions.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in zones 10–12; wax rose pereskia is a leaf-bearing cactus from Central America and the Caribbean — one of the few cacti that retains broad, true leaves and tolerates partial shade, making it appear almost non-cactus-like in growth form. The large, waxy, orange-pink flowers are strikingly beautiful and ornamental. Throughout Southeast Asia and tropical America, the tender young leaves are consumed as a nutritious leafy vegetable — boiled briefly and eaten as a pot herb or raw in salads. The leaves are high in antioxidants and have been studied for anti-inflammatory properties in traditional Malay medicine. Unlike most cacti, it grows in humid tropical conditions with partial shade, making it a unique edible cactus suitable for shaded, moist positions in tropical gardens. The leaves have a slightly mucilaginous texture when cooked, similar to okra.

plant_note: Sow directly and thin to full spacing so heads can size up over a long, cool growing season.
directions: Sow directly and thin to full spacing so heads can size up over a long, cool growing season, since it matures more slowly than modern hybrid icebergs. Introduced by the Webbs seed company of Stourbridge, England, in the early twentieth century, this crisphead forms large, dense, frilly-edged pale green heads with a satisfying crunch and is long considered one of England's finest garden icebergs. It remains a staple of British allotments, valued for standing in the garden without premature bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a 1999 All-America Selections winner with true bush habit and short vines, making it one of the most space-efficient pumpkins for containers or small beds.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil; Wee-B-Little's compact bush habit and short 6-8 foot vines mean it needs far less garden space than standard pumpkins and grows well in large containers. This 1999 All-America Selections winner produces three to four miniature, deep-orange pumpkins per plant, each weighing only 8 ounces to a pound, with smooth skin that takes paint and carving detail beautifully. The uniform bush habit and heavy fruit set make it a favorite for classroom gardens and children's plots where kids can grow and claim their own small pumpkin. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, leaving 3-4 inches of stem attached to extend shelf life.

plant_note: Sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in spring; fall sowing in mild climates produces overwintered clumps ready for early spring harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows and thin to 4–6 inches, or start in trays and transplant in clusters of 3–5 seedlings. Welsh onion does not form a bulb but produces clumps of hollow, cylindrical green stalks that are harvested like scallions; the entire green top and white base are edible. Harvest outer stalks from established clumps as needed, leaving the center to continue growing; clumps also divide easily and can be split every 2–3 years. Extremely cold-hardy and virtually maintenance-free once established, it serves as a permanent perennial scallion in most temperate gardens.

common_name: Westland Winter Kale (Classic Hardy British Curly Kale)
plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow; kale is also an excellent fall crop, since cool weather and light frost sweeten the leaves' flavor.
directions: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Westland Winter is a classic, cold-hardy curly kale long grown in Britain for reliable winter harvests, producing dense, tightly ruffled, blue-green leaves on sturdy, productive plants that stand up well to cold, wind, and less-than-ideal soil. Its exceptional cold hardiness makes it a strong choice for extending the harvest deep into winter in colder climates, and like other kale it becomes noticeably sweeter and more tender after exposure to frost. Harvest outer leaves regularly from the bottom of the plant upward, leaving the central rosette to continue producing new growth over the season.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to early fall for continued production into the warm shoulder season; can also be sown in early spring before heat sets in.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil and thin to final spacing, watering deeply to sustain the plant's large leaf size through warm weather. Named for its oversized, smooth blue-green leaves, this hybrid was selected specifically to resist bolting under longer days and warmer temperatures than most spinach can tolerate. It gives Gulf Coast growers a wider sowing window on either end of the cool season, holding productive quality later into spring and earlier into fall.

plant_note: Soak seed, then sow densely in trays indoors year-round for juicing.
directions: Soak the hard red winter wheat seed overnight, then spread it densely over a tray of moist growing mix and keep it evenly moist and bright. The seed sprouts rapidly into lush green blades that are ready to cut in about eight to twelve days, when they reach 6 to 9 inches tall. Snip the grass at the base for juicing, which yields a drink rich in vitamins, minerals, and chlorophyll; sow fresh trays in succession for a continuous supply.

common_name: Whippoorwill Cowpea (Historic Speckled Southern Heirloom Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; Whippoorwill is a rangier, semi-vining heirloom that benefits from a bit more spacing than compact modern cowpea cultivars.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean soil in full sun, and avoid rich, heavily fertilized ground, which pushes vine growth at the expense of pod production in this vigorous heirloom. Whippoorwill is one of the oldest documented Southern cowpea varieties, grown since before the Civil War and named for its speckled brown-and-tan seed coat, which resembles the mottled plumage of the whippoorwill bird. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant, it was historically valued as a dual-purpose crop, grown both for its rich, earthy-flavored dried and fresh peas and as a soil-building, nitrogen-fixing cover crop plowed under to enrich depleted fields, a role it still serves well in a home garden rotation. Its tough constitution and long history make it a genuine piece of Southern agricultural heritage as well as a reliable, low-input summer crop. Harvest pods green for fresh shelling or let them dry fully on the vine for long-term storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring harvest and August–September for fall. Whippoorwill is a sprawling, vigorous heirloom that does best with room to spread; allow 36–48 inches between rows.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in well-drained soil and allow vines to sprawl freely; Whippoorwill is a pre-Civil War Southern heirloom with a sprawling, semi-vining habit that naturalizes well in field conditions. The speckled brown-and-cream seeds are distinctive and historically used both as a fresh shell pea and a dry bean, with a rich, slightly nutty flavor preferred by many Southern gardeners over modern varieties. It is particularly favored for field cultivation as a dual-purpose food and cover crop in the South, where it fixes substantial nitrogen and suppresses summer weeds. Seeds are saved easily — allow selected pods to dry fully on the vine.

common_name: White Acre Pea (Sweet Small-Seeded Gulf South Cream Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; White Acre pea is heat-tolerant and thrives in Gulf South summer heat — plant succession crops through summer for continuous fresh production from May through September in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Acre pea is one of the most distinctive and prized southern pea varieties of the Texas and Gulf Coast tradition — a small-seeded cream pea producing petite, white to cream-white seeds with exceptionally sweet, buttery, delicate flavor that differs meaningfully from the larger-seeded, more robust flavor of standard cream peas and blackeye peas. The small seed size of White Acre is characteristic — the peas are notably smaller than regular cream peas, more compact in the shelled bowl, and cook to a sweeter, creamier texture with a refined flavor profile that has made White Acre the preference of many Gulf South cooks for fresh summer pea dishes. In zone 9, White Acre produces abundantly from its first harvest through summer and into fall — planting succession crops every 3–4 weeks from April through August provides continuous fresh pea production throughout the longest part of the growing season. White Acre is a semi-bush to vining type reaching 18–24 inches and performs well without staking in most garden conditions. The vines fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility for subsequent crops. Harvest when hulls are well-filled but still green for fresh-shelled use; allow to dry completely for storage. White Acre is particularly important in Gulf Coast cuisine and is a foundational variety of the traditional summer pea dishes of Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi.

common_name: White Bermuda Onion (Classic Mild Flat Short-Day Onion)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; White Bermuda is a short-day type well suited to fall planting in the Gulf South, producing flattened bulbs with thin, papery white skin and very mild flesh.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter regions, since this classic short-day onion needs the shorter daylight of a southern winter to bulb properly. Long grown in Texas, Louisiana, and other Gulf Coast states before more modern hybrid sweet onions became common, White Bermuda produces flattened, disc-shaped bulbs with thin, pure white skin and mild, tender flesh with relatively low pungency. Because the papery skin is thin, cured bulbs do not store as long as pungent storage onions and are best used within a few months of harvest. Keep soil evenly moist through bulb development and reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over ahead of harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with a trellis for support in zone 9–12; White Bitter Melon is a pale-cream to white-skinned variety of the bitter melon vine (Momordica charantia var. alba) — widely grown in South and Southeast Asia and increasingly popular in Asian-American gardens — with longer, smoother, pale-white fruits that are notably less bitter than the standard green bitter melon, making them more accessible to those new to this important Asian vegetable.
directions: Direct sow White Bitter Melon seeds in warm soil in full sun after last frost; provide a sturdy trellis or fence and train vines upward for maximum production; water consistently at the base and fertilize every 3–4 weeks with a balanced vegetable fertilizer; harvest fruits when they are pale cream to white and firm, before they begin to yellow. White Bitter Melon is the pale-fruited form of the familiar bitter melon vine (Momordica charantia), grown throughout Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, and diaspora communities worldwide for its distinctive culinary role in curries, stir-fries, and stuffed preparations. The white-skinned variety differs from the standard warty green variety in bearing longer, smoother, paler-green to creamy-white fruits that are generally considered less intensely bitter — making it a better entry point for cooks unfamiliar with the characteristic bitterness, while retaining the distinctive gourd flavor that defines dishes like Kerala's Bitter Melon Thoran and Chinese stir-fried bitter melon with eggs. In zone 9–12, the vine grows vigorously and produces heavily from midsummer through fall; in zone 9, it may return from the root if the crown is protected from frost. Like the standard green bitter melon, the unripe fruits are the primary culinary use; ripe, yellow fruits split to reveal bright-red seed arils that are sweet and edible but the pulp becomes very bitter.

plant_note: Plant a whole, lightly germinated fruit of White Chayote on its side, pointed end down at a 45-degree angle with half the fruit above soil, in full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in zone 9–12; White Chayote is a traditional Mexican and Central American white-skinned variety of chayote (Sechium edule var. virens alba) — smoother-skinned and more delicate in flavor than the common green-spined chayote — popular in traditional Mexican cuisine and preferred in some markets for its attractive pale-cream to white skin and mildly sweet flavor.
directions: Plant a whole, slightly sprouted White Chayote fruit on its side with the sprouting end just above the soil level in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; provide a very sturdy trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vine; water deeply once or twice weekly during active growth; harvest fruits when they are 3–5 inches long for the most tender, mild-flavored results. White Chayote is a traditional variety of the widely grown Mesoamerican perennial vine vegetable, distinguished by its smooth to very lightly furrowed, cream-white to pale-green skin compared to the spiny, dark-green skin of the more common commercial variety. Like all chayote, it is planted by burying the entire fruit — the seed is inside and too large to separate without harm — and the vine emerges from the fruit and climbs vigorously. In zone 10–12, the vine grows as a long-lived perennial with a massive tuberous root system; a well-established vine can produce hundreds of fruits per season. White Chayote fruits are notably smoother and many cooks consider the flavor slightly milder and sweeter than spiny green varieties; they are used in all the same ways — raw in salads, steamed, boiled, stuffed, or pickled. The young leaves and shoot tips, tuberous roots, and seeds are all edible as with all chayote. An excellent year-round producer in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens, dying back to the ground in mild frost and re-emerging in spring.

plant_note: Sow after last frost; chia is a short-day plant that flowers in fall, so it is best suited to climates with a long frost-free autumn. White Chia produces pale cream-to-white seed rather than the typical dark brown-black.
directions: Surface-sow seed on a firm, moist seedbed and barely press in, as chia seed is mucilaginous and will stick to the surface when wet; thin plants to 18-24 inches once seedlings emerge. White Chia produces pale cream-to-white seed rather than the typical dark brown-to-black coloring of standard chia, an attractive variant for gardeners wanting visual variety in a home-grown chia harvest, with the same nutritional profile and whorled purple flower spikes appearing in autumn as day length shortens. Chia does not respond well to transplanting and should be direct-sown where it will grow. Harvest stalks when the calyces begin to dry and before birds consume the seed, placing harvested stalks head-first into paper bags to finish drying, then shake out seed and screen away debris.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (late August–October in zone 9) or very early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; White Egg is one of the fastest-maturing turnips and quickly turns pithy if left in the ground past size, so sow in succession and pull promptly.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and thin young seedlings to a few inches apart; White Egg is a classic 19th-century American heirloom prized for its smooth, pure-white, egg-shaped roots that sit mostly above the soil line, making them easy to spot and pull. Flesh is exceptionally fine-grained, crisp, and mild for a turnip, holding its quality raw in slaws as well as cooked, and the roots reach usable size faster than almost any other turnip variety. Because it matures so quickly it is an excellent choice for a fast catch crop between other plantings or for gardeners who want an early fall harvest well before frost; roots left in the ground too long lose their fine texture and become woody, so check size regularly and harvest promptly once roots reach 2–3 inches across.

plant_note: Start indoors in winter; a short-day type best for southern gardens.
directions: Start White Grano seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before transplanting, setting seedlings 4 to 6 inches apart. This short-day heirloom forms smooth white bulbs about 3 inches across with mild, low-pungency flavor and does best in southern regions. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and keep the bed free of weeds while bulbs develop. Harvest when the tops fall over, then cure in a dry, airy place before short-term storage.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; slow to germinate, so keep soil moist.
directions: Sow White Half Long seeds half an inch deep in deep, loose soil and keep the surface consistently moist, since parsnips germinate slowly and unevenly. Use fresh seed each year and thin seedlings to 3 to 6 inches apart. This heirloom develops smooth, creamy-white roots with a sweet, nutty flavor that deepens after frost. Leave the roots in the ground through cold weather and harvest as needed, since freezing converts starches to sugars.

common_name: White Half Runner Bean (Mountaineer Half Runner)
plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in any fertile, well-drained soil; white half runner needs only 2–3 feet of support — short stakes or a low fence is sufficient for the semi-vining habit. Successive plantings every 2–3 weeks extend the harvest through the season.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing 2–3 feet of support for the semi-vining plants; white half runner is the most popular snap bean in the home gardens and farmers markets of the Appalachian mountains and Southern uplands, occupying the productive middle ground between bush beans (no support needed, shorter production) and full pole beans (requires tall trellis, longer season). The semi-vining plants produce abundantly over a concentrated 2–3 week period, making them excellent for canning and freezing in large batches as well as fresh table use. The pods are round, stringless when young, and have excellent fresh-eating flavor. White seeds make it useful as a dry bean after pods mature fully. The Mountaineer White Half Runner was bred at the West Virginia Extension station specifically for the cool-summer Appalachian region but is equally productive in the Gulf South when planted in spring or fall.

common_name: White Icicle Radish (Long White Radish, Lady Finger Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall 4–6 weeks before first frost; White Icicle is an elongated, all-white heirloom radish producing 4–6 inch cylindrical roots that remain crisp, mild, and tender at larger sizes than typical round red varieties — making it a preferred choice for fresh eating and cooking when the texture and flavor of a larger, milder radish are desired.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep and thin to 2–3 inches apart; White Icicle is faster-maturing than daikon (25–35 days vs. 60+ days) and milder than Chinese black radish, fitting into the cool-season rotation between spring planting and summer heat; harvest before roots reach maximum size for finest quality. White Icicle is a classic heirloom radish that has been grown in American gardens since the 19th century and appears in Victorian-era seed catalogs as one of the standard garden radish varieties. Unlike the small, round, red radishes (Cherry Belle, Champion, Sparkler) that dominate modern radish offerings, White Icicle produces elongated, cylindrical, all-white roots 4–6 inches long with a gentle taper — resembling a large, smooth, pale daikon in miniature. The flavor is milder and less pungent than round red varieties at the same stage of maturity, and the texture is firm and crisp without the slight woodiness that can develop in large round varieties. White Icicle is excellent for fresh eating in salads (the white color is elegant against greens), for cutting into sticks for crudités platters, for Japanese-style pickles, for cooking in stir-fries (where it holds its shape better than rounder types), and for the traditional French preparation of radishes served with butter and salt. The elongated shape also makes White Icicle more practical for slicing in certain applications where round radishes are inconvenient.

common_name: White Jersey Sweet Potato (Dry-Type White Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant slips after last frost when soil warms above 65°F; White Jersey is an old American heirloom sweet potato grown in New Jersey since at least the mid-1800s, producing tan to buff-white-skinned, cream-to-white-fleshed roots of the 'dry' (starchy) type preferred in traditional American cooking before moist orange-fleshed types became dominant in the late 19th century.
directions: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in well-prepared, loose, well-drained, sandy loam soil after soil warms above 65°F; White Jersey produces best in sandy or light soils. White Jersey is an American heirloom sweet potato representing the 'dry' type that was dominant in American cooking before the mid-20th century when moist orange-fleshed varieties became the standard; grown in New Jersey's sweet potato tradition since at least the 1850s, it produces pale buff to tan-skinned roots with cream-white flesh that cooks to a dry, fluffy, mealy texture resembling an Irish potato more than a modern sweet potato. The flavor is mild, subtle, and lightly sweet without the intense caramel sweetness of orange varieties. This dry, starchy texture was highly prized in traditional American cooking for sweet potato pie (which sets firmer), sweet potato biscuits, and baked goods where a drier texture improved the final product. Now maintained by seed savers as a historical artifact of early American sweet potato culture; an excellent educational variety for understanding the dramatic change in American sweet potato preferences over 150 years.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill seed thickly 1/4 inch deep into warm, moisture-retentive soil after last frost; white jute is a close relative of molokhia (Corchorus olitorius) grown both as a fiber crop and, when picked young, as a mild potherb in Bangladeshi and West African kitchens.
directions: Broadcast seed thickly into warm, fertile, consistently moist soil, since dense stands both suppress weeds and are the standard method for fiber production; thin or transplant survivors to a few inches apart for leaf harvest instead. Pinch or cut young shoots and the topmost tender leaves regularly starting around 5–6 weeks to keep plants leafy and to delay the tough, fibrous stem growth that signals the shift toward fiber-stage maturity; cooked leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to okra. If left unharvested for fiber, stalks are cut at the base once the lower leaves yellow, then retted in water to separate the bast fiber. White jute tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic flooding far better than most leaf greens, making it a reliable warm-season crop through the Gulf Coast summer.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring and again in late summer for fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow seed in cool weather for spring and fall crops, thinning seedlings to two to four inches apart. This premium Japanese salad turnip forms pure white, smooth-textured roots that are mild and sweet, delicious raw in salads and crudite trays as well as pickled or cooked. Grow it quickly with steady moisture and harvest young as a baby turnip for the best crisp, tender quality.

plant_note: Direct sow in succession spring through summer; heat and cold tolerant.
directions: Direct sow seed in succession from spring through summer, thinning to about an inch apart for a steady supply of scallions. Popular since the 1700s, this dependable heirloom green onion thrives in a wide range of soils and tolerates both heat and cold. Blanch the stems by hilling soil around the bases for longer white shanks, and harvest young for mild flavor before any bulb forms.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant March–May. Soak seeds 24 hours in warm water before sowing to speed germination. White Malabar Spinach grows best in the hottest part of summer when all other spinach has bolted — it thrives from June through September in zone 9 and is one of the most productive summer leafy greens available. Provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous vines, which can reach 10 feet or more.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; White Malabar Spinach (Basella alba 'Alba') is the green-stemmed, white-flowered form of Malabar spinach — distinct from the red-stemmed Basella rubra (Ceylon Spinach) in having entirely green stems, greener foliage, and smaller white berries. The large, thick, glossy, heart-shaped to oval leaves have the same mild, slightly mucilaginous spinach substitute quality as the red form, used raw in salads when young and tender or cooked in the same manner as spinach — sautéed, in soups, curries, and braised dishes throughout Southeast Asian, Indian, and West African cooking. The white form is favored in some cuisines where the red pigment of the red form is undesirable in finished dishes; the green stems and white berries also make it slightly more attractive as an ornamental vine for trellises and fences. In zone 9 White Malabar Spinach is the premier summer leafy green — a vigorous, heat-loving vining plant that fills the summer gap when all cool-season greens have finished and heat prevents new sowings.

common_name: White Portugal Onion (Mild White Heirloom Spring Onion)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in late winter for fall harvest, or set out transplants 4–6 weeks before last frost; White Portugal is intermediate-day type performing well in zone 6–8 spring plantings where day length increases properly for bulb initiation. In zone 9, fall planting (October–November) as a short-day-adapted spring harvested variety is also possible. White Portugal is excellent harvested young as a scallion (bunching onion) before bulbs develop, making it dual-purpose.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in early spring; pull at any size from scallion stage through full bulb maturity. White Portugal (also called White Silver Queen, Italian White, or White Silverskin in some seed catalogs) is a traditional open-pollinated white-skinned onion with a long history in American and European kitchen gardens — one of the primary heirloom white onions before the development of modern F1 hybrid white types. The bulbs are medium-large, somewhat flattened to globe-shaped, with silvery-white papery skin and white flesh. The flavor is notably milder than yellow storage onions — White Portugal has lower pungency than standard yellow types, making it well-suited for fresh eating, pickling, and preparations where mild onion character is preferred. White Portugal is the traditional pickling onion for pearl onion preparations and for cocktail onions; the white color remains clean through pickling without the discoloration that sometimes occurs with yellow-skinned types. The variety is also excellent harvested young as a green/bunching onion (scallion), where the white sheath and mild flavor make it among the most attractive bunching onions. Being open-pollinated, seed can be saved year to year from the best-formed bulbs.

plant_note: Tolerates cooler soil than common beans but still frost tender.
directions: White-flowered runner bean prized for its large white seeds and vigorous ornamental vines. Sow seeds 1.5 inches deep at the base of a tall trellis or teepee once soil warms to 60 F. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering to ensure good pod set, as heat above 90 F can cause blossom drop. Harvest young pods for snap use or allow to dry on the vine for shell beans. In mild climates the fleshy roots may overwinter and resprout the following spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or late summer; flavor sweetens with cold weather.
directions: Direct sow or transplant this kale in spring or late summer, spacing plants 12 to 18 inches apart. Introduced in 1994, White Russian is a white-ribbed cross between Red Russian and Siberian kale that grows especially sweet in cool weather and stands up well to frost. Harvest young leaves for tender baby greens or let plants mature for full-sized leaves; a hard frost only improves the sweet flavor.

plant_note: Deep sandy loam gives the straightest, smoothest roots.
directions: A creamy white carrot with crisp, sweet, mild flesh and no pigment, popular in mixed rainbow bunches. Sow shallowly in deeply worked sandy loam and maintain constant surface moisture until emergence. Thin carefully to prevent crowding, which causes twisted or stunted roots. Keep beds weeded early since carrot seedlings are easily overtaken. Harvest at full size, wash gently, and store in cold, humid conditions to retain crispness.

plant_note: Direct sow once the soil is warm and frost has passed.
directions: Sow White Scallop seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, thinning to one strong plant every 24 to 36 inches. This heirloom patty pan squash produces flat, scalloped-edge fruits with tender white flesh on productive bush plants. Harvest the fruits young at 2 to 4 inches across for the best flavor and texture, picking often to keep new ones forming. Keep the soil evenly moist and watch for squash bugs during warm weather.

common_name: White Sprouting Broccoli (Hardy English Heirloom Overwintering Broccoli)
plant_note: Start seed in mid- to late summer and transplant in early fall so plants are well established but not yet flowering before winter; the plants overwinter as compact rosettes and send up their edible flowering shoots in late winter to early spring, well ahead of purple sprouting types.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer or early fall, spacing plants wide to accommodate a full season of growth before the harvest of edible flower shoots the following late winter. White Sprouting is a classic English heirloom broccoli grown as a hardy biennial: plants spend fall and winter building a large rosette of foliage, then in late winter to early spring send up a profusion of small, tender, cream-white flowering shoots that are harvested continually over several weeks, much like purple sprouting broccoli but ivory-headed and typically a touch earlier. Regular picking of the central and side shoots before flowers open encourages continued production, and the long harvest window makes it valuable for filling the late-winter garden gap when little else is producing. It needs a long, cool growing season to perform well and is best suited to mild-winter climates like the Gulf South where it can overwinter in the open ground without protection.

common_name: White Sweet Spanish Onion (Classic Long-Day Mild White Onion)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of hard frost has passed; White Sweet Spanish is a long-day type needing 14+ hours of summer daylight to bulb, making it best suited to northern and mid-latitude gardens rather than the short-day Gulf South.
directions: Start seeds indoors in late winter and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last hard frost. This long-established long-day onion produces large, globe-shaped bulbs with clean white skin and mild, juicy, sweet flesh with a milder bite than most storage onions, making it a popular choice for fresh eating, salads, and onion rings. Because long-day onions need the extended summer daylight of higher latitudes to bulb properly, it performs best north of about zone 7 and tends to produce poorly or bolt in the short-day Deep South. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb development and cure bulbs in a warm, airy spot after the tops fall over, though sweet types like this one store for a shorter time than pungent storage onions.

common_name: White Velvet Okra (Smooth Round-Pod Heirloom Okra with Velvety Texture)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm (70°F minimum); White Velvet okra produces round, pale green to cream-white pods rather than the elongated, ridged form of standard okra. In zone 9, plant April through July for summer production. Soak seeds overnight before planting to improve germination. The pods are smooth and rounded in cross-section (unlike the distinctly ribbed, angular pods of most standard okra) — the 'round' pod character reduces toughness at larger sizes, allowing harvest at 3–4 inches without the fibrous, over-mature texture that makes standard okra unpalatable when left too long. White Velvet has an old, well-documented history in American seed saving and is available through heirloom seed companies.
