The slightly different pod form and smooth surface give the cooked pods a different texture than standard okra — less 'slimy' than some types, which some cooks prefer.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms to 70°F; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest pods at 2–3 inches for most tender pods. White Velvet Okra is an heirloom okra variety distinguished from the standard elongated ridged types by its round, smooth pods — the 'velvet' texture of the surface, which lacks the prominent longitudinal ridges of varieties like Clemson Spineless, and the pale green to cream-white color at harvest maturity (before fully ripening to cream-white and drying). The round-pod okra group, of which White Velvet is one of the best-known American heirloom examples, represents a different selection from the standard commercial okra breeding that prioritized uniformly ridged, elongated pods for mechanical harvesting and packing. Round-pod types have thinner, more tender pod walls and a slightly different texture and mucilage content than ridged types — attributes that some cooks prefer, particularly for preparations where the 'sliminess' of okra is considered a negative quality. White Velvet's pods harvested at 2–3 inches have a tender, delicate texture and mild flavor appropriate for sautéing, grilling, pickling, and use in gumbo where the mucilaginous properties of okra serve as a natural thickener. The plant is vigorous and heat-tolerant — essential qualities for zone 9 summer production — and produces prolifically throughout the summer if harvested regularly. The cream-white color at harvest maturity (before pods fully dry and tan) makes White Velvet visually distinctive from the dark green and burgundy okra varieties and attractive for fresh-market presentation.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow White Vienna seeds half an inch deep and thin to 4 to 6 inches apart for well-formed bulbs. This heirloom cole crop develops smooth, pale green globes with crisp, mild, slightly sweet flesh where the stem swells above the soil. Keep growth fast and steady with even moisture, and harvest the bulbs while they are 2 to 3 inches across before they turn woody. Both the swollen stem and the young leaves are edible raw or cooked.

common_name: White Wing Onion (F1 Early Sweet White Onion)
subcategory: fresh-eating onion, hybrid white sweet type
plant_note: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings outside about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights and transplant hardened seedlings into rich, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants to let bulbs expand freely. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb development, since this fast-maturing type sizes up quickly and does not tolerate drought well during that stage. White Wing is a widely grown hybrid valued for its early maturity, glossy white globe-shaped bulbs, and mild sweet flavor best used fresh, as short-season sweet onions like this one are not bred for long winter storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August for fall. White Wonder matures ivory-white and should be harvested when fully colored but before any yellowing begins — at this stage the flesh is at its most crisp, cool, and mild. Remove overripe fruits promptly to keep the vine producing. Provide a trellis for more vertical growth and cleaner fruit.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; White Wonder is an heirloom slicing cucumber producing large, 7–8 inch fruits with ivory-to-cream-white skin, crisp white flesh, and an exceptionally mild, cool, lightly sweet flavor with virtually no bitterness — the mildest of all cucumber types. The white color results from the absence of chlorophyll in the skin rather than from immaturity; properly ripe White Wonder fruits are uniformly ivory-white and are never green. The skin is thin and does not require peeling, and the flesh is juicier and more tender than standard green cucumbers with the same thin-skinned type. White Wonder cucumbers are a curiosity and conversation piece in the garden and at farmers' markets, attracting attention precisely because the white color is unexpected. The heat tolerance is comparable to standard cucumber types, and the vigorous vines produce well through zone 9 spring and fall seasons. Pick every 2–3 days to maintain production.

plant_note: Plant sett tubers (sections of yam with at least one eye) 4–6 inches deep after last frost when soil has warmed to 75°F; provide a trellis or sturdy support for the twining vines.
directions: Plant sett pieces 4–6 inches deep in loose, deeply dug, well-drained soil — white yam tubers grow straight down and require at least 18 inches of loose, stone-free soil. Provide a sturdy trellis or fence for the twining vines, which can reach 15–20 feet. The large, starchy white or cream-fleshed tubers (distinctly different from sweet potatoes, which are Ipomoea) are the most important traditional food crop in West Africa, where yam is eaten pounded into fufu, roasted, boiled, or fried as chips. Unlike the common yam varieties in Western grocery stores (which are often actually sweet potatoes), true white yam has a dry, starchy texture and neutral flavor that complements bold sauces and stews. Harvest when vines yellow in fall, dig carefully to avoid breaking tubers.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun in fertile, well-drained, deep loamy soil in zone 9–12; White-seed Melon (Aro Egusi, Round Egusi, Mann's Cucumeropsis) is a West African cucurbit grown primarily for its large, flat, white-seeded fruits — the seeds dried, ground, or pressed for oil to make the foundational West African Egusi Soup, which is served throughout Nigeria, Ghana, Cameroon, and Côte d'Ivoire — distinct from the better-known egusi watermelon (Citrullus lanatus var. citroides).
directions: Direct sow Cucumeropsis mannii seeds in hills in full sun in rich, deep, well-drained soil after temperatures are consistently warm; train vines on a trellis or allow to sprawl on the ground; harvest mature fruits when the skin yellows and stems cork; dry seeds thoroughly before storage or use. White-seed Melon is one of two major 'egusi' cucurbits of West Africa (the other being the egusi watermelon, Citrullus lanatus var. citroides), distinguished by its round, smooth, cream-green fruits and large, flat, distinctly white seeds. The plant is a trailing or climbing annual vine with lobed, cucumber-like leaves and small yellow flowers — grown entirely for its seeds, which are the primary ingredient in Egusi Soup, the beloved national dish of Nigeria and a staple across much of West and Central Africa. The seeds are dried, then ground into a paste or coarse meal and fried in palm oil with onions and tomatoes before adding stock and leafy greens (typically bitter leaf or pumpkin leaf) to create the rich, deeply savory egusi soup. Seeds can also be pressed to produce egusi oil, a golden cooking oil with a mild, nutty flavor. The flesh of the fruits is not eaten (bitter and unpalatable) — the crop is exclusively a seed crop. An important protein and fat source in West African diets where meat is expensive.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Whopper Improved is a Park Seed hybrid beefsteak bred for large fruit size and broad disease resistance on a vigorous indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the vigorous vine to support the heavy fruit. Whopper Improved is a Park Seed hybrid beefsteak tomato bred for large, meaty, flavorful fruit and broad resistance to common tomato diseases, making it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting big slicing tomatoes without the disease susceptibility of many open-pollinated beefsteak heirlooms. It produces well over a long season in the Gulf South's extended warm months. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and fruit cracking, and feed regularly to sustain the large fruit size through the harvest season.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; wild achocha grows and fruits quickly through a single warm season.
directions: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; wild achocha grows and fruits quickly through a single warm season. A fast-growing Andean relative of the more widely grown achocha (Cyclanthera pedata), it produces smaller, spiny, hollow, cucumber-flavored fruit on vigorous tendril-climbing vines, harvested young and cooked or pickled much like its better-known relative, with a similarly mild, crunchy texture. Extremely productive and easy from seed, it thrives in ordinary garden soil with a support to climb and can produce a heavy crop of small fruit within two to three months of sowing in warm weather. Harvest fruit young, while still tender and before seeds mature and harden, for the best eating quality, and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive through the season.

common_name: Wild African Cucumber / African Horned Cucumber (wild)
plant_note: Sow seeds directly in a sunny, well-drained bed after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 65°F. Grows rapidly in hot, dry conditions and tolerates drought once established.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun after soil temperatures reach at least 65°F. This drought-tolerant scrambling vine needs little supplemental water once established but appreciates a deep soak at planting. Harvest the very young, pale-green fruits before they develop their characteristic spines and bitterness, as mature fruits require prolonged cooking or are best reserved for medicinal use. In cooler climates, start seeds indoors 3–4 weeks before the last frost and transplant after the weather settles.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2 inches deep in fall beneath deciduous trees; the plant grows actively in late winter and spring before the tree canopy leafs out, then goes dormant in summer.
directions: Plant bulbs in autumn in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade beneath deciduous trees; wild garlic is a spring ephemeral of European and Asian deciduous forests that completes its entire growing cycle from late winter through late spring before going fully dormant. The broad, lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive garlic aroma can be harvested as soon as they emerge in late winter for salads, pesto, and compound butters; they are milder and more versatile than cultivated garlic leaves. White star-shaped flowers in spring are also edible and edible. The plant naturalizes freely by self-seeding to form large carpets — plant densely from the start for a showy spring display under trees.

plant_note: Sow fresh seeds immediately after harvest in fall directly into waterlogged mud or still-shallow water (6–24 inches deep) at pond margins, slow rivers, or lake edges; seeds must never be allowed to dry out — store in water if not planting at once.
directions: Sow fresh, never-dried seeds in fall directly into waterlogged mud or 6–24 inches of still water at the margins of ponds, lakes, or slow-moving rivers; wild rice is one of the most ecologically and culturally important native grains of North America, forming dense stands in the Great Lakes region that have sustained Ojibwe and other Indigenous peoples for millennia and providing critical food for migrating waterfowl. The tall, feathery annual grass germinates in spring when water warms, forms a floating seedling stage, then rockets upward to 4–10 feet by midsummer, bearing separate male and female florets on a large open panicle. Grain shatters and falls into the water when ripe in late summer — harvest by canoe, bending stalks over the gunwale and knocking seeds loose. Because viability is lost within days of drying, only purchase or plant seeds stored in water.

plant_note: Sow fresh, water-stored seeds in early spring in shallow water 1–3 feet deep; wild rice seeds lose viability quickly when dried and must be stored wet in cold water throughout winter. Stratify seeds in wet storage at 35–45°F for 60–90 days before spring planting. This is a lake plant requiring persistent shallow water, not a garden vegetable in the traditional sense.
directions: Sow wet-stored seeds in 6–24 inches of clean, still or slow-moving fresh water in full sun over a muddy bottom — wild rice requires specific aquatic conditions and will not grow in conventional garden beds. It is an annual grass of northern North American lakes that produces one of the most prized indigenous food grains in its season, with a distinctively nutty, earthy, chewy character that is incomparably superior to the paddy-cultivated product sold commercially. The tall plants emerge from submerged seeds in spring, grow through summer, and produce loose, open grain heads above the water in late summer — traditionally harvested by canoe, knocking the ripe seeds into the hull. Because the seeds ripen unevenly and shatter easily when ripe, harvesting requires repeat passes or netting under the heads. An outstanding wildlife food for ducks, geese, and marsh birds. Best grown in a controlled pond, large rain garden, or constructed wetland.

common_name: Wild Rocket (Sand Rocket, Annual Wall Rocket)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–October in zone 9) in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; wild rocket is distinct from common arugula (Eruca sativa) with smaller, more deeply cut leaves, a sharper, more intensely peppery-bitter flavor, and faster reseeding — it is the traditional Italian 'selvatica' rocket used in authentic Italian mixed salads and Neapolitan pizza.
directions: Direct sow thinly in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 4–6 inches; harvest outer leaves continuously. Diplotaxis muralis (wild rocket or sand rocket) is a European native annual brassica closely related to but distinct from common cultivated arugula (Eruca sativa) — it is the species known in Italy as 'rucola selvatica' (wild rocket) and is considered by Italian chefs to produce a more authentic, intensely peppery-bitter arugula flavor than the cultivated form. Wild rocket has smaller, more deeply pinnately-lobed leaves, a more intensely pungent, sharp, mustardy-bitter flavor, and tiny, four-petaled yellow flowers (compared to arugula's cream-white flowers) — the flowers are also edible, mildly peppery and attractive as a salad garnish. This species tends to self-seed prolifically once established, naturalizing in disturbed, lean, dry soils where it forms self-perpetuating patches. In Italian cuisine, rucola selvatica is the traditional garnish for authentic Neapolitan pizza (layered fresh on the hot pizza immediately before serving), served with bresaola, aged cheeses, and in traditional Campanian and Pugliese salads. More bitter and pungent than cultivated arugula — use in smaller quantities or mix with milder greens.

common_name: Wild Sweet Potato (Man of the Earth, Manroot)
plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds after last frost in well-drained soil in a sunny to partially sunny location; the vine dies back to the ground each winter but re-emerges reliably from its enormous perennial taproot, which can weigh 20 pounds or more in mature specimens.
directions: Ipomoea pandurata is a native perennial vine of eastern North America that grows from a massive, starchy taproot — sometimes exceeding 20 pounds — which stores energy through winter cold and summer drought alike. The vine climbs or sprawls vigorously from late spring through fall, bearing large white morning-glory flowers with deep magenta-purple centers that open each morning from June through September. Scarify seeds by nicking the seed coat with a file or sandpaper and soak overnight before direct sowing after last frost in well-drained soil; established plants from the taproot need little supplemental water once settled. The root is edible and was used historically by Indigenous peoples across eastern North America, though it is starchy and bitter raw, requiring long cooking to be palatable.

plant_note: Direct sow in mid- to late summer, roughly three months before the first fall frost, for a sweet, storable fall and winter crop.
directions: Sow seed directly and thin to a final spacing of six to eight inches, since this Central European heirloom needs room for its globe-shaped root to bulk up. Wilhelmsburger produces a purple-topped, pale yellow-fleshed root known for dense texture and a mild, almost nutty sweetness that intensifies after a light frost. Leave roots in the ground into cool fall weather before harvesting for the best flavor and longest storage life, and use the tender young tops as cooked greens if thinning early plantings.

common_name: Willow Leaf Lima Bean (Heat-Tolerant Heirloom Pole Lima)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past frost danger, since lima beans are especially sensitive to cold, wet soil; Willow Leaf is an old heirloom pole lima named for its narrow, willow-shaped leaves and valued for continuing to set pods through summer heat that stalls many other beans.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has thoroughly warmed, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous climbing vines. Willow Leaf lima bean is a Southern heirloom named for its distinctively narrow, willow-shaped leaflets, quite different from the broader foliage of most lima beans, and is prized for continuing to flower and set pods through the intense heat of a Gulf South summer that causes many other lima varieties to drop blossoms and stall production. Harvest pods once well-filled but still bright green for fresh shelling, or let them dry fully on the vine for storage beans. Regular picking of mature pods encourages the vine to keep flowering and setting new pods through the long growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow shortly before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop; Win-Win Choi's improved heat tolerance allows a somewhat longer planting window than many pac choi types.
directions: Direct sow in early spring after danger of hard frost has passed, or in late summer for a fall harvest, spacing seedlings close together for the miniature form Win-Win Choi is bred to produce. Win-Win Choi is a compact, white-stemmed hybrid pac choi that forms a bulky, uniform, vase-shaped head only about a foot tall at full size, making it well suited to close spacing, containers, and gardeners who prefer a smaller-format bok choy to the larger green-stemmed types. Its improved heat tolerance compared to many pac choi varieties allows for a longer planting window into warmer weather before bolting becomes a concern. Harvest whole plants at the baby stage for tender salad use or let them fill out for a heartier stir-fry green.

common_name: Window Box Roma Tomato (Compact Paste Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a window box, patio pot, or small bed after frost danger has passed.
directions: Transplant into a sunny window box or small container after the last frost; the plant stays extremely compact, so it needs no staking or cage even when loaded with fruit. Window Box Roma is an All-America Selections winner bred to bring true plum-shaped paste tomatoes to the smallest growing spaces, producing 1.5-2 ounce oblong red fruit with meaty, low-moisture flesh well suited to sauces despite the plant's diminutive 12-18 inch stature. It offers one of the few genuinely dwarf paste-tomato options for balconies and windowsills.

plant_note: Direct sow very early in spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions.
directions: Direct sow seed very early in spring as soon as the soil can be worked, or in fall where winters are mild, since fava beans need cool weather to set pods. The sturdy, upright plants bear ornamental white-and-black flowers and reach several feet tall. Eat the young pods like snap beans, pinch the tender growing tips as a spring green, or shell the beans and cook them while still green for a sweet, buttery treat.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil reaches 70°F; a truly tropical legume requiring a long, warm, humid season.
directions: Scarify or soak seeds 12–24 hours before sowing 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained, low-fertility soil; inoculate with cowpea rhizobium to promote nitrogen fixation. Provide a sturdy trellis or fence at least 6 feet tall as soon as plants emerge, as vines climb rapidly and are very productive when vertical. Virtually every part of the winged bean is edible — harvest young pods at 3–4 inches with frilly wings still tender, leaves and shoot tips as greens, flowers as a colorful salad garnish, and mature dried seeds as high-protein pulses. In the tropics, tuberous roots also form and can be harvested and eaten like yam.

plant_note: Plant whole small tubers or tuber sections 3–4 inches deep after soil warms to 65°F; provide a sturdy trellis or fence for the rapidly growing twining stems.
directions: Plant tuber sections with at least one dormant eye in fertile, loose, deeply dug soil (tubers can reach 18 inches long) in full sun to partial shade; provide a strong trellis as vines grow vigorously to 15–20 feet. The large, starchy tubers are harvested after the vines die back in fall; a single tuber can weigh 20–50 pounds in good conditions. The most widely cultivated true yam in the world, Dioscorea alata is eaten boiled, baked, fried, or pounded into fufu and is a dietary staple across the tropics. In zone 8 the tubers may survive mild winters if mulched deeply; in zones 9–11 the plant can become invasive — check local regulations and avoid planting near natural areas.

common_name: Winter Bloomsdale Spinach (Cold-Hardy Overwintering Savoy Spinach)
plant_note: Sow 4-6 weeks before the first hard fall frost so plants are established but not overly mature going into winter.
directions: Sow directly in late summer or early fall so seedlings size up before short days and cold arrive, then protect with a low tunnel or thick mulch through the coldest months for an early spring harvest. This vigorous savoy-leaf hybrid was bred specifically for exceptional cold tolerance and holds its dark, crinkled foliage through hard freezes better than standard Bloomsdale types. Many growers value it as one of the most reliable spinach selections for season extension in cold climates.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall for overwinter harvest, or in early spring in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; winter cress overwinters as a rosette and produces tender leaves through fall, winter, and early spring — edible young and raw, becoming more pungent as it matures. Avoid summer planting.
directions: Direct sow in late summer or fall for winter harvest, or very early spring in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; winter cress is a naturalized European biennial widely established along roadsides, stream banks, and disturbed areas throughout North America, producing dark green, deeply lobed, pungent leaves throughout cold weather — an important wild food and forage vegetable in lean months. The young rosette leaves harvested in fall through early spring are pungent and slightly bitter, excellent as cooked greens (boiling twice mellows the bitterness) or raw in small amounts as a peppery salad green. The early spring flower buds (harvested before they open) are excellent steamed or sautéed like broccoli raab and milder than the leaves. Traditionally gathered as a spring tonic green throughout Europe and Appalachia. Self-sows prolifically to establish permanent patches in moist, disturbed, sunny to partially shaded sites.

common_name: Winter Density Lettuce (British Cold-Hardy Romaine-Butterhead Cross)
plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in spring or in late summer for fall harvest; Winter Density is the quintessential British cold-season lettuce — a Romaine/Butterhead cross with tight, upright heads, exceptionally cold-hardy (tolerating temperatures to 22°F), and slow-bolting even in warming spring conditions; outstanding for year-round production in mild climates and cold frames in zones 5–9.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; Winter Density tolerates more cold than most lettuces and can be direct-sown in early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) or late summer for fall harvest; thin to 8–10 inches apart; harvest as baby lettuce at 3–4 weeks or allow heads to mature fully; the heads hold in the garden well without bolting even in warm spring weather. Winter Density is a British heirloom lettuce representing a distinct type: a cross between the upright, crisp Romaine (Cos) type and the loose, buttery Butterhead type, producing compact, upright heads with the outer leaf structure and dark green color of Romaine but the soft, buttery, pale interior leaves and gentle flavor of Butterhead. The flavor is excellent — sweet, slightly nutty, and mild — while the cold tolerance (to around 22°F without protection) and slow-bolting behavior make it one of the most productive lettuces for extended spring seasons and for winter harvests in mild climates (zones 7–10). It is notably more shade-tolerant than most lettuces, performing well under tall vegetables in summer where direct-sun types would bolt. Winter Density was widely grown in English kitchen gardens throughout the 19th and 20th centuries as a reliable, all-conditions lettuce, and has been preserved through seed-saving networks and specialty seed companies.

common_name: Winter Luxury Pie Pumpkin (Heirloom Netted-Skin Pie Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost; Winter Luxury requires 95–105 days to reach harvest maturity. For fall baking pumpkins, count back 105 days from first frost date; in zone 9, plant May–June for a September–October harvest. Harvest when the skin has turned orange and the distinctive netted surface is clearly visible; the unusual lacy skin is the signature characteristic of this variety.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost in full sun in well-drained, rich, well-amended soil; harvest when rind is fully orange and the characteristic netting pattern covers the surface. Winter Luxury is a heirloom pie pumpkin dating to before 1893 that is distinguished from all other pumpkins by its striking surface appearance: the orange rind is covered with a delicate pattern of raised, interlacing cream-colored corky netting that gives each fruit a lacy, elaborately textured surface unlike any other pumpkin variety. Beyond the striking visual character, Winter Luxury is widely regarded as one of the finest pie pumpkins ever developed — the smooth-grained, dense, deep-orange flesh is finely textured, very sweet, and has a silky quality when cooked that produces exceptionally smooth pumpkin puree without the stringiness or wateriness of field-type pumpkins. The 5–9 lb fruits are the ideal size for fresh pie production, yielding enough puree for two large pies per fruit while remaining manageable to handle. Seed Savers Exchange and heirloom seed preservationists have long championed Winter Luxury as an example of what specialty breeding for cooking quality can achieve, and it consistently wins pie pumpkin taste tests among gardeners who grow multiple varieties side by side. A beautiful and genuinely outstanding baking pumpkin with over 130 years of cultivation history.

common_name: Winter Melon (Wax Gourd, Ash Gourd, White Gourd)
plant_note: Direct sow or start transplants 3–4 weeks before setting out; in zone 9, sow in March–April for summer-fall harvest; winter melon is one of the most important and widely grown gourds in Chinese and Southeast Asian cuisine and thrives in Gulf Coast heat and humidity.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, deeply cultivated, fertile, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a very sturdy trellis or along the ground; keep evenly moist. Benincasa hispida (winter melon or wax gourd) produces the largest cultivated gourd after pumpkins and bottle gourds — round to oblong fruits 8–32 inches long weighing 10–50 pounds, with a white, waxy powder coating the mature skin (which gives it the 'wax gourd' name) and very mild, white, watery flesh that absorbs surrounding flavors in cooking. Winter melon is a cornerstone ingredient in Chinese cuisine — the thick rind is scooped out and the hollowed gourd is used as a serving vessel for delicate winter melon soup garnished with carved decorations; the flesh is added to stir-fries, soups, and dim sum. It is called 'winter melon' despite being a summer crop because the mature fruits store exceptionally well at room temperature for months through winter (up to a year if undamaged), providing a critical source of fresh vegetable during historically difficult winters in Asia. In zone 9, it produces very well in summer heat; the large fruits are harvested in fall when the waxy bloom has fully developed.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Winterbor is an F1 hybrid with exceptional cold hardiness — repeated hard freezes convert the leaf starches to sugars, making late-winter harvested Winterbor noticeably sweeter than fall-harvested leaves. In zone 9 fall planting in September–October produces excellent quality through spring; the plants are one of the most productive over-wintering vegetables for zone 9 kitchen gardens. Harvest outer leaves from the bottom up to keep plants producing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Winterbor is an F1 hybrid curly kale developed for exceptional vigor, uniformity, and extraordinary cold hardiness — the 'Winter' in the name reflects its ability to withstand severe freezes that damage most other kale varieties, making it the standard commercial and home garden curly kale in northern climates. The very densely curled, heavily blistered, blue-green leaves are the archetypal kale-chip and sautéed-kale leaf — the extreme surface area created by tight curling traps oil and seasonings, making Winterbor the variety most frequently used in kale chip recipes where maximum crispiness requires maximum surface contact with the baking sheet. Unlike flat-leaf or lacinato kale varieties, the heavy curl structure of Winterbor makes the raw leaves quite firm and fibrous — they benefit from massage with oil and salt to soften before use in salads, making it primarily a cooking kale rather than a fresh salad variety. Repeated hard freezes dramatically improve the flavor of all kale, but particularly Winterbor: cold temperatures convert accumulated starches to sugars, making late-winter harvested Winterbor among the sweetest and most palatable versions of this species.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before first fall frost and transplant in late summer/early fall; in zone 9 direct sow or transplant September–October for fall and winter harvest. Winterbor kale tolerates temperatures to 15°F and improves significantly in flavor after frost.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before fall transplanting or direct sow in late summer for fall production; Winterbor is a Dutch hybrid kale developed by Royal Sluis that became one of the most popular commercial and home garden kale varieties worldwide, valued for its combination of highly productive, tight, attractive blue-green curly leaves, exceptional cold hardiness, and distinctively superior flavor after frost. The tightly ruffled, heavily curled leaves are more tender and less tough than some older kale varieties, making Winterbor more pleasant to eat both raw in salads and cooked. The blue-green color is attractive and the upright habit (plants grow upward rather than sprawling) makes garden management easy. Winterbor is exceptionally cold-hardy — tolerating temperatures to 15°F without damage — and the cold-sweetening effect that makes kale improve after frost is particularly pronounced in Winterbor, making late-season harvested plants dramatically sweeter and more tender than those harvested before cold weather. In zone 9, Winterbor is primarily grown as a fall-through-winter crop (September–February) when temperatures allow proper kale production; it tolerates Gulf Coast mild winters better than more tender greens.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this slow-germinating Guyanese landrace rewards patience and steady bottom heat.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since germination is slower and less even than most peppers; transplant only after nights stay warm. This heirloom from Guyana produces marble-sized, perfectly round fruit that dangle upright like tiny berries, ripening from pale green through orange to bright red on a compact, heavily branched bush. Heat runs fierce and fruity, typically well into habanero territory, and the little pods are the signature ingredient in Guyanese pepper sauce as well as a favorite for pickling whole. In frost-free gardens the plant persists as a short-lived shrubby perennial; elsewhere grow it as a warm-season annual and pick continuously to keep new flowers setting.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Wisconsin 55 is an indeterminate variety that benefits from staking to keep the disease-resistant foliage well aired.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, staking or caging the vines for support. Wisconsin 55 was developed by plant pathologist J.C. Walker at the University of Wisconsin in the 1940s to resist early blight and leaf spot, and it went on to become one of the most popular home garden tomatoes in the upper Midwest through the mid-20th century. The round, deep red, six- to eight-ounce fruit is notably resistant to cracking and holds firm texture for slicing, canning, and cooking.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Wisconsin SMR 58 was bred at the University of Wisconsin for scab and mosaic resistance and remains a widely grown standard open-pollinated pickling cucumber.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep after the soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil with room for vines to spread or climb a trellis. Wisconsin SMR 58, standing for Smooth or Spot Mosaic Resistant, descends from a University of Wisconsin breeding program that improved disease resistance in the older Wisconsin SMR line, becoming a standard pickling cucumber for home gardeners and small-scale growers because of its reliable yields, disease tolerance, and dependable performance across varied soils. Fruit is straight, blocky, and medium green with light spines, best picked young at 2-4 inches for pickles or left a bit larger for fresh slicing. Because it remains true from seed, it can be maintained by home seed savers who isolate it from other cucumber varieties.

plant_note: Sow in summer (August–September in zone 9) to grow roots by fall; the roots are then lifted and forced in darkness to produce the pale, blanched chicons called Belgian endive. In mild-winter zones 8–9 the roots can also be left in the ground to sprout blanched chicons naturally in winter if covered with soil.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in deep, loose, fertile soil; witloof chicory develops a long taproot like a parsnip that must be carefully dug in fall. To produce authentic Belgian endive chicons, lift the roots after tops die back, trim leaves to 1 inch, and force the roots upright in moist sand or potting mix in a dark, cool location (50–60°F) for 3–4 weeks until compact, pale yellow-white chicons 4–6 inches long emerge. The chicons have a pleasantly bitter flavor that mellows when cooked — they are traditionally braised, grilled, or wrapped in ham and baked with béchamel. In zone 9 the summer heat makes root development challenging; the fall-sow schedule is critical to success.

plant_note: Sow in early spring in moist shaded conditions; wood nettle spreads aggressively by both seed and rhizome in suitable conditions — plant where naturalization is acceptable or confine in raised beds.
directions: Sow seed in early spring in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in dappled shade to full shade — the natural habitat is rich woodland floodplains and stream banks; wood nettle bears stinging hairs on both stems and leaves that are completely deactivated by cooking, making the young leaves and stem tips harvested before flowering excellent when boiled, steamed, or sautéed, with a flavor comparable to stinging nettle but perhaps more delicate. Rich in iron, calcium, and vitamins. An important larval host plant for the red admiral butterfly (Vanessa atalanta). Always handle with gloves to avoid stinging; once wilted by heat or drying, all sting is gone.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and set transplants out once the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: World Beater, also sold as Ruby Giant, is a pre-1912 heirloom sweet pepper bred from a cross of Chinese Giant and Ruby King, combining the size of one parent with the productivity of the other. Fruits are exceptionally large and blocky with thick, sweet flesh that ripens from green to red, making it a favorite for stuffing or roasting whole. The sturdy, three-foot plants carry a heavy fruit load, so working in compost at planting and providing steady, even moisture helps size the peppers properly. Choose this variety when garden space allows for a true old-fashioned giant bell rather than a modern hybrid.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of sturdy support 6–8 feet tall; Wren's Egg is one of the oldest documented American bean varieties, known since the early 19th century, producing speckled cream and red or buff and maroon pods and seeds that strongly resemble a wren's speckled egg — grown as both a snap bean and a dry bean for its excellent flavor and historical significance.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; provide trellis or poles 5–7 feet tall for support; vines twine naturally. Wren's Egg (also called 'Bird Egg', 'Speckled Bird Egg', or 'Speckled Cranberry Pole') is one of the oldest heirloom pole beans in continuous American cultivation, documented in seed catalogs and garden records since at least the early 1800s and traditionally maintained in New England and mid-Atlantic home gardens; it is named for the distinctive speckled coloring of both the pods and the dried seeds, which closely resemble the delicate speckled pattern of a wren's egg — a mix of cream or buff background with irregular red-brown, maroon, or rose speckles. The flat pods can be harvested young (45–60 days) as a snap bean or left to mature fully (75–90 days) for dry bean use. As a dry bean, Wren's Egg produces plump, oval seeds with excellent, rich flavor for baked beans and soups. The pods become increasingly stringy as they mature; harvest snap pods at 4–6 inches for best eating quality.

common_name: Xtra-Tender 277A Sweet Corn (Warm-Soil Bicolor Supersweet Hybrid)
plant_note: Direct sow only after soil has warmed thoroughly, since supersweet (sh2) types germinate poorly in cool soil; Xtra-Tender 277A is a popular commercial and home-garden bicolor supersweet hybrid widely grown across the South for its tender, high-sugar kernels.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep only once soil has warmed thoroughly, since supersweet corn germinates poorly in cool, wet soil; plant in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination, and keep isolated from standard or sugary-enhanced corn to protect kernel sweetness. Xtra-Tender 277A is a popular bicolor supersweet hybrid known for exceptionally tender, high-sugar kernels that hold their sweetness well after picking, and it is widely grown by both market farmers and home gardeners across warm Southern regions. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, and harvest when silks have browned and kernels release a milky juice when pressed.

common_name: Y-Star Squash (Golden Yellow Star-Shaped Heirloom Pattypan)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; harvest small for the sweetest flavor, or let a few fruit mature fully for seed saving.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in full sun, spacing plants about 3 feet apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Y-Star is an heirloom pattypan type distinguished by its pointed, star-like scalloped edges and rich golden-yellow color, giving it a more angular silhouette than the rounded scallop shape of other pattypan squash. Harvest small, at about 2-3 inches across, for the sweetest flavor and most tender skin; larger fruit can be left to mature for seed saving or ornamental use.

plant_note: Plant rhizome offsets (propagating crowns) around the time of last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; yacon dies to the ground at first frost but the storage roots and rhizomes survive in the ground in zones 7–9 with light mulching — in colder zones, lift and store like dahlias.
directions: Plant rhizome crown divisions (not the large storage roots) in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun around the time of last frost; yacon grows into a large, sunflower-relative plant 4–8 feet tall and requires a long warm season of 5–7 months for best root development. Smallanthus sonchifolius is an Andean perennial grown for its large, sweet, crisp, apple-pear-textured storage tubers, which are uniquely high in fructooligosaccharides (FOS) — prebiotics that the human body cannot fully metabolize — making yacon one of the very few vegetables with a negligible glycemic impact despite its sweet flavor. Roots are harvested after the first frost kills the tops, then cured in sunlight for 1–2 weeks (which converts some FOS to fructose and sweetens the flavor considerably); they are eaten raw like jicama in salads, pickled, juiced, or roasted. Propagate exclusively from the knobby, reddish-purple rhizome crowns attached to the base of the stalks, not from the large tan storage roots, which will not sprout.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger passes and soil is warm (at least 65°F) near a trellis, fence, or other climbing support at least 5 feet tall; plants produce best in hot weather and are an excellent summer crop in zones 8-11.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the soil reaches 65°F and all frost danger has passed, spacing 6–12 inches apart along a sturdy trellis or fence at least 5 feet tall; yard-long beans (also called asparagus beans or Chinese long beans) are vigorous tropical vines that thrive in hot, humid summers and outperform standard snap beans in zones 8–11, producing slender pods that can reach 18–24 inches long and should be harvested when they reach pencil thickness, typically at 12–18 inches, before seeds bulge. Harvest every 2–3 days to keep vines productive through the season. Unlike common beans, these plants are drought-tolerant once established but perform best with consistent moisture and do not require staking if pods are kept picked.

plant_note: Sow 2–6 weeks after last frost once soil is warm; yardlong beans love Gulf Coast heat and humidity and outperform regular beans all summer.
directions: Sow seeds 1 in deep once soil is reliably warm; yardlong beans are vigorous climbers that need a sturdy trellis or fence at least 6 feet tall. Unlike common beans, they thrive in high heat and set pods prolifically during summer weather that causes snap beans to drop their blossoms. Harvest when pods are pencil-thin and roughly 12–18 in long, well before they reach their potential 36 in — longer pods become fibrous and bitter. Check daily once pods begin forming, as they move from prime to over-mature in just 2–3 days.

common_name: Yaya Carrot (Early Nantes-Type Hybrid Bunching Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow in deep, loose, well-amended soil; Yaya is an early maturing Nantes type that reaches harvest size in as few as 56 days — ideal for successive sowing every 2–3 weeks for continuous bunching-carrot harvest. Thin to 2 inches for bunching-size roots; allow 3 inches for larger storage roots. Harvest when roots are finger-thick and 6–7 inches long for best quality and sweetness.
directions: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in loose, deeply tilled, stone-free soil; keep consistently moist through germination (7–14 days) and thin to 2–3 inches apart. Yaya is a Bejo Seeds hybrid Nantes-type carrot that has become one of the most popular fresh-market and home garden bunching carrots in North America — selected specifically for its early maturity, exceptional sweetness, and consistent cylindrical uniformity that makes bunches visually attractive and professionally presentable. The roots are the classic Nantes shape: blunt-tipped, 6–7 inches long, uniform diameter, with smooth, bright orange skin and minimal core differentiation from the phloem to the xylem — the internal uniformity of color contributing to the sweet, mild, candy-sweet flavor that Yaya is known for. Yaya matures 10–14 days earlier than most mid-season Nantes types, allowing early-season bunching carrot production or an additional succession planting late in the season. It holds well in the ground after reaching maturity without rapid overgrowth or cracking, giving a flexible harvest window. Market gardeners consistently rate Yaya among the highest for customer satisfaction — the exceptional sweetness and uniformity of color and shape are immediately apparent to buyers. One of the best-performing bunching carrots for both farm market sales and home garden fresh eating.

common_name: Yellow Baby Watermelon (AAS-Winning Yellow-Fleshed Icebox Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost once soil is reliably warm; this fast-maturing hybrid rewards an early start under black plastic mulch in cooler regions.
directions: An All-America Selections winner from the 1970s, Yellow Baby was one of the first widely available yellow-fleshed watermelons bred for home gardens, packing bright lemon-yellow flesh and thin, tender rind into a round 7-pound icebox-size fruit. The novel flesh color and honeyed flavor make it a conversation piece at the table, and its fast maturity suits shorter growing seasons better than full-size Southern types. Grow it exactly as you would any bush-type icebox watermelon: full sun, consistent moisture until fruit begins to ripen, then reduced watering to concentrate sugars. Because the pale flesh makes the usual red-ripeness cues useless, rely on the drying tendril and yellowing ground spot to judge harvest timing.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all frost danger passes.
directions: Start Yellow Bell seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost in warm soil, then transplant 12 to 18 inches apart once nights stay warm. This heirloom ripens from green to a bright golden yellow with sweet, crisp, thick-walled flesh. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and stake plants carrying a heavy fruit load. Harvest peppers green for firmness or leave them to color up fully for maximum sweetness.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Yellow Brandywine is a yellow-fruited strain of the famous Brandywine heirloom with the same potato-leaf foliage and large, meaty fruit but ripening to golden-yellow with exceptionally sweet, mild, low-acid flavor that many prefer to the standard pink or red strains.
directions: Start indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before last frost; plant deeply after frost in rich soil, staking or caging immediately. Yellow Brandywine is a yellow-fruited version of the legendary Brandywine heirloom (or a closely related strain), producing the same large, potato-leaved plants and big, meaty, irregular fruits but ripening to a beautiful golden-yellow with a noticeably sweeter, milder, lower-acid flavor than either the pink or red Brandywine strains — many tomato connoisseurs actually prefer it for its tropical sweetness and lack of sharpness. Fruits reach 12–24 oz and are outstanding for slicing, caprese preparations, and tomato salads where the golden color provides visual contrast; the low acid level means less canning stability so use for fresh eating. Shares the Brandywine family's potato-leaved foliage (a dominant genetic marker that distinguishes true Brandywines from impostors) and late, slow maturity that rewards patient gardeners with exceptional fruit.

common_name: Yellow Cabbage Collard (Virginia Heading Heirloom Collard)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring; unlike open, loose-leaf collards, Yellow Cabbage Collard forms a loose head, so give it slightly more room and a longer season to fully develop.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving plants ample room to form their characteristic loose head. Yellow Cabbage Collard is a distinctive Virginia heirloom, unusual among collards for forming a semi-blanched, cabbage-like heart of pale yellow-green leaves at the plant's center rather than staying fully open-leaved, giving it a milder, sweeter flavor and more tender texture than typical collards, especially in the blanched inner leaves. Outer leaves can still be harvested cut-and-come-again style through the season, while the forming head is left to mature for a more tender harvest later. Cold exposure sweetens the flavor further, and the plant tolerates hard freezes well. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season for the best head development.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Yellow Cabbage Collards form an unusually loose, pale yellow-green head rather than the open rosette typical of most collards.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Cabbage Collards are a distinctive Southern heirloom type that blurs the line between collards and cabbage, forming a loose, blanched, pale yellow-green head at the center of the plant rather than the fully open rosette of leaves typical of most collard varieties. The blanched inner leaves are notably tender and mild, sweeter and less assertively cabbage-flavored than standard collards, making this variety popular for gardeners who find ordinary collards too strong. Like other collards it tolerates considerable cold and its flavor improves after light fall frosts. Because the plant's value lies partly in the self-blanched head, avoid stripping too many outer leaves early in the season and let the center fill in before beginning regular harvest, then continue picking outer leaves as the plant keeps producing from the growing point.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; the quintessential Southern summer squash, ubiquitous at roadside stands and farmers' markets across the Gulf Coast; highly heat-tolerant and productive even in zone 9–11 summer conditions.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, rich, well-drained soil; Yellow Crookneck is one of the fastest-producing and most heat-tolerant summer squashes, making it particularly well-suited to warm and humid Gulf Coast gardens where it produces heavily in spring and again in fall. Yellow Crookneck squash has been grown in American gardens since at least the 1700s — it was listed in American seed catalogs before the Civil War — producing curved, club-shaped yellow fruits with bumpy skin and mild, buttery, slightly nutty flesh that is the quintessential taste of Southern summer gardens; harvest at 4–6 inches when the skin is still tender and seeds are small. In hot climates, a fall planting (direct sow in late summer) often outperforms spring; the plants are relatively short-lived under heat stress but can be succession-planted.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; yellow crookneck is a traditional Southern summer squash and a warm-season staple in Gulf Coast vegetable gardens. Make a second planting in late July or August for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, warm soil after last frost; yellow crookneck is one of the oldest continuously grown summer squash types in North American gardens, with its distinctive curved neck and bumpy, golden-yellow skin being immediately recognizable. Harvest when 6–8 inches long for the best texture; fully mature fruits become tough-skinned and seedy. The sweet, mild flavor is excellent sautéed in butter with onions, grilled, or added to casseroles. Bush types have largely replaced the older spreading vine types; they produce heavily over a long season if harvested regularly. In humid climates, powdery mildew is common in midsummer — select modern disease-resistant cultivars like 'Supersett' or 'Gentry' for best results.

common_name: Yellow Doll Watermelon (Early Icebox Yellow-Fleshed Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds after last frost when soil is above 70°F; thin to 2 plants per hill. Yellow Doll's early maturity (65–75 days) makes it one of the fastest watermelons to ripen, suitable for shorter growing seasons where standard large varieties may not mature. The small fruit size (5–8 lbs) makes individual fruits manageable for families and the compact vine habit allows closer planting than large-fruited types. In zone 9, plant March–April for June harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; fertilize at planting and again when vines begin to run. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit turns brown and dry and the underside spot (where the melon touches the ground) turns from white to cream-yellow. Yellow Doll is an early-maturing, icebox-sized watermelon notable for its yellow flesh — a less common flesh color that surprises many people used to only red-fleshed watermelons. The small (5–8 lb), round to oval fruits have light green skin with subtle darker green stripes and the distinctive bright yellow to golden-yellow interior flesh that gives the variety its name. The yellow flesh is very sweet and mild, with a slightly different flavor character than red-fleshed types — some tasters describe it as cleaner, less assertive, and honey-sweet rather than the more complex sweetness of red watermelon flesh. This mild quality makes Yellow Doll particularly popular with children and those who find standard watermelon's flavor too strong. Yellow Doll's early maturity (65–75 days vs. the 80–95 days of standard large varieties) is a practical advantage for short-season gardeners, as is the small fruit size — a single 6-lb fruit is the right amount for 2–4 people without waste, compared to the 25+ lb fruits of standard varieties that require multiple meals to consume.

common_name: Yellow Eye Bean (Maine Yellow Eye, Steuben Yellow Eye, New England Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Yellow Eye is a dry bush bean — allow pods to fully mature and begin to dry on the vine before harvesting. In zone 9, sow in March–April for a May–June dry bean harvest before summer heat peaks.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; allow pods to dry fully on the vine before harvesting, then shell and continue drying beans before storage. Yellow Eye bean (also called Maine Yellow Eye, Steuben Yellow Eye, or Molasses Face bean) is one of the defining heirloom dry beans of New England — a white bean with a distinctive yellow-to-orange eye mark on one end (the hilum area) that resembles a yellow eye, giving the variety its evocative name. The bean has an extraordinarily long history in New England agriculture, where it has been the traditional baked bean variety for generations in Maine — the characteristic bean in the famous Maine Saturday Night bean suppers and baked bean tradition that stretches back centuries to Native American cooking and early colonial adaptation. The large, creamy-white beans cook to a silky, tender texture without becoming mushy, holding their shape while absorbing surrounding flavors; they have a mild, rich, nutty flavor that makes them outstanding for slow-baked preparations, bean soups, and any dish where bean quality is the focus. Yellow Eye is considered by many New England cooks to be the finest baked bean, superior in flavor and texture to navy beans or pinto beans for this application. An outstanding heirloom that connects culinary tradition, regional identity, and genuine eating quality.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before the last frost; this mid-season heirloom performs well in cooler northern climates as well as short winter-growing regions.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Finn is a Finnish heirloom predating the modern yellow-flesh varieties it helped inspire, producing round to oval tubers with tan skin and dense, buttery-yellow flesh. The flavor is rich and naturally buttery even without added fat, and the moderately waxy texture holds together well for potato salad while still mashing smoothly. It stores well for a fingerling-adjacent heirloom and tends to be more drought-tolerant than many modern hybrids once established. Choose it over Yukon Gold when a true heirloom lineage and slightly denser, more old-fashioned texture are preferred.

plant_note: Start indoors in winter; a short-day type for southern gardens.
directions: Start seed indoors in winter and transplant to the garden while still cool, since this is a short-day onion that bulbs best in southern regions. For really sweet, mild bulbs, grow it in soil that is low in sulfur; this pink-root-resistant type is among the few approved to be sold as a Vidalia onion. Keep plants weed-free and evenly watered, and cure the harvested bulbs before use, as sweet onions do not store long.

plant_note: Start indoors early; germination is slow and needs warmth.
directions: Start Yellow Habanero seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil around 85F since this species germinates slowly. Transplant the plants 18 to 24 inches apart into a warm, sunny bed. The lantern-shaped fruits ripen golden-yellow with intense heat around 100,000 to 350,000 Scoville units and a sweet, tropical, fruity flavor. Handle the ripe pods with gloves, and harvest steadily to keep the productive plants setting fruit through the warm season.

common_name: Yellow Indian Woman Bean (Buckskin Montana Heirloom Soup Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; a fast-maturing Montana heirloom bush bean well suited to short growing seasons.
directions: Sow seeds directly 1 inch deep after danger of frost has passed, spacing bush plants 4-6 inches apart in rows. Also known as Buckskin or Buckskin Girl, Yellow Indian Woman is a Montana heirloom that reached Native American communities through European settlers and is prized for producing heavy yields of small, milky-yellow seeds in under 75 days, among the fastest-maturing dry beans available. The mild, creamy flavor resembles a pinto bean and the seeds hold their shape well in slow-cooked soups and stews, while also cooking noticeably faster than most other dry beans. Water regularly through bloom and pod fill, then let pods dry completely on the plant before shelling and storing.

common_name: Yellow Jersey Sweet Potato (Dry-Fleshed Southern Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm, in loose, well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; Yellow Jersey is an old Southern heirloom grown for its pale yellow skin and dry, mealy flesh, a different texture than modern moist orange types like Beauregard.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun. Yellow Jersey is an old-fashioned Southern heirloom with pale yellow-tan skin and light yellow, dry, mealy flesh, a texture closer to a baking potato than the moist, syrupy sweetness of modern orange-fleshed varieties, and it was once among the most widely grown sweet potatoes in the South before moister types like Beauregard became dominant. Vines are moderately vigorous and productive, and the drier flesh makes the roots well suited to baking and frying rather than the candied dishes moist types are typically used for. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall and before the first frost, and cure the roots at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to heal cuts, firm the skin, and develop full sweetness before storing.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since Moruga Scorpion strains germinate erratically without warmth.
directions: This is a yellow-fruited selection of the Trinidad Moruga Scorpion, sharing the same bumpy, tailed pod shape and ferocious heat as the original red strain but ripening to a bright golden-yellow instead. Growers often note the yellow form carries a slightly more citrusy, less smoky flavor than red Moruga types, making it popular for hot sauces where color as well as heat matters. Give plants the same long, warm growing season and rich soil that other Trinidad superhots require, and expect a later, more compact fruit set than milder chinense varieties. Because pod color can be the only visible way to distinguish it from other Moruga strains, keep seed-saved plants isolated from red-fruited relatives to preserve the true-to-type yellow trait.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before outdoor transplant date in late winter, or plant onion sets (small bulbs) outdoors as soon as soil is workable in spring; choose long-day varieties for zone 3–6 and short-day varieties for zone 7–10 for best bulb development.
directions: Start seeds or transplant pencil-thick seedlings in full sun in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil early in spring; yellow onions are the most versatile and widely grown culinary onion, with their characteristic balance of sulfurous pungency and underlying sweetness that mellows to a rich sweetness when cooked, making them essential in virtually every cuisine worldwide. Long-day varieties (required for zone 3–6 where summer days exceed 14 hours) include 'Copra' and 'Patterson'; short-day varieties (zone 7–10) include 'Texas 1015', 'Candy', and 'Georgia Sweet'. Harvest when most tops have fallen over naturally; cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for 2–4 weeks. Well-cured yellow onions store for 3–6 months.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 to 4 weeks before the last frost and transplant after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: This indeterminate heirloom produces heavy clusters of small, bright yellow pear-shaped fruits with a mild, tangy flavor. Provide sturdy caging or staking, since vines sprawl vigorously all season. Pinch suckers if you want a more manageable plant and pick fruit regularly to keep production going. Water consistently at the base to avoid cracking and blossom-end rot.

common_name: Yellow Pear Tomato (Heirloom Yellow Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Yellow Pear is an heirloom cultivar with true-to-type seed that can be saved from year to year.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Yellow Pear is an heirloom cherry tomato with a history extending back to at least the 1800s — producing clusters of small, bright-yellow, pear-shaped fruits with a distinctive teardrop shape and mild, low-acid, sweet flavor. The fruit shape and bright yellow color make Yellow Pear one of the most visually distinctive tomatoes in the garden, and it is a consistent favorite at farmers markets and in mixed salads where its cheerful yellow color and unusual shape create visual interest. The low-acid flavor profile makes it approachable for children and adults who find standard tomatoes too acidic. The indeterminate vine grows vigorously to 5–8 feet and sets fruit prolifically throughout the growing season — an established Yellow Pear plant produces hundreds of fruits over the course of the season. Seed can be saved from non-hybrid heirloom Yellow Pear true-to-type for future seasons — select fruit from the most vigorous and productive plants. In zone 9, Yellow Pear performs well in the spring window (February–June) and fall window (September–frost) but stalls during the peak summer heat above 95°F. The low-acid taste makes it excellent for children's snacking, fresh salads, and pasta dishes where a mild tomato flavor is preferred.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 to 2 weeks after the last frost once soil is thoroughly warm.
directions: This compact, early-maturing heirloom yields round 5 to 7 pound melons with sweet yellow flesh, ideal for small gardens and containers. Sow in warm soil and give vines room to run along the ground or a low trellis with fruit support. Water deeply but reduce moisture as fruits ripen to concentrate sweetness. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit browns and the ground spot turns creamy.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall in mild-winter climates, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; yellow sarson is grown as a quick-maturing cool-season crop for both its greens and oilseed.
directions: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall in mild-winter climates, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; yellow sarson is grown as a quick-maturing cool-season crop for both its greens and oilseed. This South Asian mustard type produces bright yellow flowers on branching stems, and its distinctive yellow, rather than brown or black, seed is the traditional source of high-quality mustard oil used across northern India and pressed for cooking, along with young leaves harvested for the classic dish sarson ka saag. Fast-growing and adapted to cool weather, it bolts and sets seed quickly once days lengthen and warm, so plant it early enough to establish good leaf growth before it flowers if greens are the primary goal. Harvest leaves young and often for eating, or allow plants to flower and set seed pods for a home-scale oilseed or seed-saving crop, threshing dried pods once they turn brown and brittle.

plant_note: Start indoors 10 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant while weather is still cool.
directions: This heirloom long-day variety forms large, golden globe bulbs with a mild, sweet flavor, best suited to northern gardens with long summer days. Start seed early indoors and transplant seedlings while cool weather encourages leafy growth before bulbing. Keep beds weed-free and evenly moist, then taper off water as tops fall over. Cure the harvested bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storage.

common_name: Yellow Sweet Spanish Utah Bulb Onion
plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out; a long-day type for northern gardens.
directions: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant out as soon as the soil can be worked, spacing plants four to six inches apart. This long-day heirloom, grown in the U.S. since at least 1916, forms large 3 to 6 inch globe-shaped bulbs with mild, sweet flavor and grows best in states north of the 37th parallel. Keep the soil evenly moist during bulbing, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place before storing.

common_name: Yellow Tomatillo (Sweet Yellow-Ripening Tomatillo, Fruitier and Milder Alternative to Green)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; yellow tomatillo is grown identically to green tomatillo (Physalis ixocarpa) but ripens to yellow or golden rather than green, with a notably sweeter and less acidic flavor profile. In zone 9, transplant March–April; like all tomatillos, two plants are required for good fruit set (cross-pollination). Harvest when the papery husk is fully filled and just beginning to split — at this stage the fruit inside is plump, fully yellow, and at peak flavor. Overripe yellow tomatillo (husk fully split, fruit exposed) becomes starchy and flavor declines. Zone 9's long warm season allows multiple plantings from March through July; a July planting produces fall tomatillos in October–November when cooler temperatures improve flavor development.
directions: Start indoors; plant two or more for cross-pollination. Harvest when husk just fills completely and turns yellow-gold. Yellow Tomatillo (sometimes called 'miltomate amarillo' in its native Mexican context) is a color variant of the tomatillo (Physalis ixocarpa) that ripens to golden-yellow rather than the standard green, with a fundamentally different flavor profile: sweeter, less acidic, more fruity, and less pungent than the standard green tomatillo. The standard green tomatillo has an assertive, somewhat tart flavor with herbaceous, citrus-like notes that characterize the classic salsa verde (green sauce) of Mexican cuisine; the tartness and acidity are fundamental to the sauce's role of cutting through rich meats and cheeses. Yellow tomatillo has less of this characteristic tartness and more fruit-forward sweetness — a flavor profile that lends itself to milder, sweeter sauces and preparations where the aggressive acid of green tomatillo would be too dominant. Yellow tomatillo salsas tend to be used in different culinary contexts than green tomatillo salsas: they pair well with fish, light meats, and as a condiment where a sweeter, less assertive sauce is preferred. The plants grow identically to standard green tomatillo varieties — vigorous, spreading, 3–5 feet tall, requiring two plants for pollination — and have the same growing requirements. The papery husk that encloses the developing fruit is similar in color to green tomatillo husks (tan-brown with green veining) and turns slightly yellow-tan as the fruit inside ripens; the fully ripe fruit inside is a clear lemon-yellow to golden color.

plant_note: Plant divisions after last frost into rich, wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water in full sun; yellow velvetleaf spreads readily by seed and runners in warm, wet conditions and is best grown in a contained bog bed or submerged container.
directions: Plant divisions after last frost into rich, wet, mucky soil in shallow standing water in full sun; yellow velvetleaf spreads readily by seed and runners in warm, wet conditions and is best grown in a contained bog bed or submerged container. Broad, glossy, velvety-textured leaves rise on long stalks from the shallow water of rice paddies and wetlands across Southeast Asia, where the young leaves and flower stalks are harvested as a popular cooked vegetable, and cheerful three-petaled yellow flowers add ornamental value above the foliage. It grows and spreads quickly in warm, wet, nutrient-rich conditions, making it a fast-establishing addition to a pond margin or paddy-style bed, but its vigorous self-seeding habit means it can become weedy in the very rice paddies it is sometimes intentionally grown alongside. Harvest young leaves and flower stalks regularly for the best eating quality, and confine plantings to a contained wet bed to prevent unwanted spread.

common_name: Yellow Yam (Twelve-Month Yam, Yellow Guinea Yam)
plant_note: Plant tuber sections (2–3 oz minimum) 4–6 inches deep after last frost when soil is warm; this tropical vine needs 6–8 feet of strong trellis support; do not confuse with sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) which is unrelated.
directions: Plant tuber pieces with at least one eye 4–6 inches deep in loose, deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; the yellow guinea yam is a major food staple in West and Central Africa, producing large (up to 10 lb) elongated tubers with yellow-orange flesh and a pleasant earthy flavor quite different from sweet potato — the starchy tubers are boiled, roasted, fried, or pounded into fufu and other traditional preparations. Grows as a perennial tropical vine requiring sturdy staking; in frost-free zones it can remain in the ground year-round, multiplying year after year. Requires a long frost-free growing season of 8–9 months for full tuber development. Harvest when vine begins to die back.

common_name: Yellow Yam (Yellow Guinea Yam, Cayenne Yam, Yellow Cocoyam)
plant_note: Plant cut tuber sections ('setts') or small tubers in full sun after last frost in well-drained, deep, fertile, loamy to sandy soil; provide a sturdy vertical support (trellis, fence, or pole) as the vine will climb vigorously to 10–20 feet. Harvest when the vine dies back in late fall or early winter (240–300 days from planting). The distinctive yellow to deep-orange flesh (the 'yellow yam' characteristic) distinguishes D. cayennensis from white-fleshed yam species. Tubers must be cooked before eating (raw tubers contain toxic alkaloids). Cured tubers store for months. Zone 9-12 outdoor culture.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, loamy to sandy soil with a tall climbing support — Yellow Yam vines climb vigorously (10–20 feet) and require sturdy support throughout the growing season; deep, loose, well-worked soil allows the tubers to expand to their full size without impediment. Dioscorea cayennensis is a tuberous, annual to perennial twining vine native to West Africa and naturalized throughout the tropical world in the Dioscoreaceae family, one of the most important yam species in West African cuisine — the principal yam of the 'yam belt' that stretches across Ghana, Nigeria, Côte d'Ivoire, Benin, and Togo where yams are a dietary staple, ceremonially important, and economically critical. The distinctive feature of D. cayennensis is the yellow to deep orange-yellow flesh of the tubers — in contrast to the white-fleshed D. rotundata (white guinea yam), D. cayennensis tubers have the appearance of cooked sweet potato inside after cooking. The large (5–15 pound per tuber), cylindrical to irregularly shaped tubers are smooth-skinned and store well after curing. In zone 9-12 gardens, the vine grows vigorously through the warm months before dying back as days shorten, signaling tuber maturity. Raw tubers contain dioscorine and other toxic alkaloids — always cook before eating. One of the finest true yam species for Gulf Coast tropical food gardens.

common_name: Yellow of Parma Onion (Italian Heirloom Storage Onion)
plant_note: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant young onion sets outdoors about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost.
directions: Sow seed indoors under lights in late winter, then transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil once the danger of hard frost has passed, spacing plants a few inches apart to allow bulbs to swell. Keep soil evenly moist through bulbing, then stop watering and let tops fall over naturally before harvest to cure for storage. Yellow of Parma is a classic Italian heirloom valued for its large, globe-shaped, straw-colored bulbs, mild sweet flavor, and notably good keeping quality compared to other sweet onion types, making it a long-standing favorite in northern Italian kitchen gardens.

common_name: Yellowfin Zucchini (Bright Yellow Straight-Fruited Hybrid Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes, in warm, fertile soil in full sun; harvest young for the mildest flavor and most tender skin.
directions: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants about 30 inches apart. Yellowfin produces glossy, bright golden-yellow, straight cylindrical fruit on a compact, open bush plant, offering a color and shape alternative to more common golden zucchini types. Pick regularly at 6-7 inches long, since yellow-skinned summer squash can develop a tougher skin if left to oversize. The bright color makes Yellowfin easy to spot at harvest time and an attractive addition to mixed squash displays.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in loose, well-prepared soil; Yellowstone is one of the best yellow carrots, with a bright, true yellow exterior and interior and a distinctly sweet, mild, fruity flavor that stands out from standard orange carrots.
directions: Sow seed thinly 1/4 inch deep in deeply loosened, friable, stone-free soil 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2–3 inches when seedlings reach 2 inches tall. Yellowstone is one of the top-performing yellow carrots for home gardens, producing uniform, 7–9 inch, Nantes-type cylindrical roots with vivid yellow skin and flesh throughout and a notably mild, sweet, slightly fruity flavor that some tasters prefer to standard orange carrots; it lacks the beta-carotene of orange types but is rich in lutein, a carotenoid beneficial to eye health. Excellent for fresh eating, roasting (where it holds its color beautifully), and for adding visual variety to rainbow carrot mixes. The flavor improves after mild frost. Direct sow works best as the taproot does not transplant well.

plant_note: Grown mainly as a dry bean; needs full season to mature seed.
directions: Also called orca or calypso bean, this dry bush bean bears striking black-and-white seeds resembling the yin-yang symbol. Direct sow 1 inch deep after frost danger passes, spacing 4 inches apart in rows. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant until they rattle before harvesting. Pull whole plants and cure them in a dry, airy spot if wet weather threatens the maturing crop. Reduce watering as pods fill to encourage even drying and prevent mold.

plant_note: Direct sow after the soil warms and let the vigorous vine ramble across a wide bed or up a strong trellis, since a single plant can cover a large area over the long Gulf Coast growing season.
directions: Direct sow after the soil warms and let the vigorous vine ramble across a wide bed or up a strong trellis, since a single plant can cover a large area over the long Gulf Coast growing season. This dark-green, deeply ribbed Japanese heirloom shares Cucurbita moschata's excellent resistance to vine borers and squash bugs with better-known Gulf-adapted moschata types, making it a strong performer where humidity and pests knock out C. maxima and C. pepo squash. The dense, sweet orange flesh stores for months after curing in a warm, dry spot. Its heat tolerance and disease resistance make it a good companion or alternative to Seminole pumpkin for zone 8-10 gardeners wanting variety in their moschata winter squash.

common_name: Yolo Wonder Bell Pepper (Virus-Resistant Open-Pollinated Sweet Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Yolo Wonder's virus resistance is a practical advantage in zone 9 where tobacco mosaic virus and pepper mosaic virus persist in soil and infect peppers through insect vectors.
